News.title: Energy bill help, minimum wage rise and bank taxes - what could be in the Budget?
News.content:
Chancellor John Healey will set out Labour's tax and spending plans when he delivers his first Budget at around 12:30 on Wednesday.

The speech, which usually lasts about an hour, will be broadcast live on BBC iPlayer and on the BBC News website.

He and Prime Minister Andy Burnham are hoping to give households "breathing space" amid the ongoing high cost of living and they have already announced measures to change gas bills.

But Healey has also refused to rule out some tax increases to potentially pay for support he could distribute elsewhere.

The government has run an unusually tight ship, preventing policies leaking out ahead of time, but here are the key measures expected.

LIVE: Follow all the Budget coverage

News.title: Watch: What happens now after close vote in Israeli election?
News.content:
Polls have closed in the Israeli election and votes are being counted.

Exit polls suggest there is no clear winner, with neither veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor former military chief Gadi Eisenkot on track to secure a majority.

The BBC's Hugo Bachega looks at what might happen next.

Read more on this story.

News.title: Defeated presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro arrives in US after Brazil cancels his passports, sources say
News.content:
Defeated presidential candidate FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro has arrived in the US, hours after Brazil cancelled his passports, sources have told the BBC.

The right-wing candidate left the country after its Supreme Court ordered that he surrender his passports amid an investigation into alleged money laundering. Bolsonaro has not been charged and has denied the allegations.

His passports were cancelled on Tuesday after he missed a deadline to hand them over to authorities, prompting widespread speculation that he may have left Brazil.

Sources told BBC Brasil and BBC Mundo that Bolsonaro met with his younger brother, Eduardo, in Florida - though his exact travel route from Brazil to the US is unclear.

Neither brother could be directly reached for comment.

His reported arrival in the US came hours after a senior US official confirmed the US State Department would issue visas to Bolsonaro and his family and allow them entry into the country.

The BBC has contacted the White House, State Department and embassies in both the US and Brazil.

On Monday, Brazil's Supreme Court ordered Bolsonaro to hand his passports over to police within 24 hours as part of its alleged money laundering probe.

At the time, Bolsonaro said he had no plans to leave the country, and insisted that he would stay in Brazil to lead the opposition to his left-wing rival, President Luiz InÃ¡cio Lula da Silva, who on Sunday won the election.

After he missed the deadline, Bolsonaro's lawyers told BBC Brasil that they were "completely in the dark" about his whereabouts.

"We knew nothing about this, and we still have no information about what happened," one lawyer said.

Bolsonaro has not made any public statements since Monday afternoon local time, when he posted a video on social media.

Federal officers checked border crossings to establish if Bolsonaro may have travelled to neighbouring Argentina, a police source told BBC News Brasil.

However, Argentine authorities told the BBC there was no record of the senator entering their country through any border crossing.

Bolsonaro was already under investigation for alleged corruption over the financing of a film about his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, who was convicted of plotting a coup and is under house arrest.

A separate inquiry involves alleged links to a Brazilian lawyer, who is accused of laundering more than $1bn through a fraud scheme.

Police said earlier this month they had discovered Mr Bolsonaro had access to the bank accounts of a company owned by the lawyer.

Bolsonaro denied doing business with the lawyer, and described the passport confiscation as an attempt to intimidate him.

In addition to that investigation, Brazil's Supreme Court ordered police on Tuesday to examine FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro's electoral campaign over alleged foreign funding.

The 45-year-old senator suffered a stinging defeat on Sunday when he was beaten by Lula in a presidential run-off, which Bolsonaro had been widely expected to win.

His younger brother Eduardo Bolsonaro lives in the Texas, in the US, but was in Miami on Sunday, where he cast his vote at a polling station and attended an election viewing event which was streamed to his followers.

Sources have confirmed to the BBC that FlÃ¡vio has already met with his brother, Eduardo, in Florida, though details of his exact travel route from Brazil are unclear.

It's also unclear who travelled with him or whether FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro intends to stay and live in the US.

News.title: King acknowledges 'suffering of the past' as Caribbean tour begins
News.content:
King Charles III has begun his tour of the Caribbean by acknowledging the "great suffering of the past" as he faced calls for slavery reparations.

Speaking an event in the Bahamas celebrating local youth, the King said the country's culture was "born out of darkness", and it was "only right" to acknowledge historic injustices.

His nine-day tour will culminate in the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM), where the King has confirmed leaders will discuss the region's legacy of slavery.

The visit, his first as monarch, comes in the wake of renewed calls from Caribbean nations for Britain to apologise for its role in selling enslaved people for profit.

Prior to the trip, Buckingham Palace said the King would not shy away from "colonial legacy" and the impact of the slave trade during his visit but, in line with the UK government position, he will not apologise for Britain's role in the slave trade or offer reparations.

Upon his arrival on Tuesday, the King met Governor General Dame Cynthia A. Pratt and its Prime Minister Philip Edward Davis, before speaking with members of the Royal Bahamas Defence Force as he inspected a guard of honour.

King Charles, wearing sunglasses and a grey suit, was then met with cheers as he arrived for his first engagement at a youth rally at Clifford Park - where he attended independence celebrations for the Bahamas as Prince of Wales in 1973.

The young people in the crowd had been given time off school for the event. "It's my first time seeing him in person out of TikTok so he's out there, it's cool," one student told the BBC.

A small group of protestors gathered close to the rally shouting "pay us what you owe us" and "return artefacts you've stolen."

The group of around a dozen protestors was kept outside the main venue as they called on the King to help change the UK government's position on apologising and offering reparations.

"He's a man of influence. The Crown still has influence. And if they do not do it then we will become a republic and we will turn our backs on England if you do not show respect to the former colonies," said one protestor, Sharon Purcer-Cooper.

News.title: Trump says US voter fraud is 'rampant' - evidence suggests it is extremely rare
News.content:
For years, Trump has made repeated unsubstantiated claims that postal voting leads to widespread fraud.

He has also encouraged Republicans to vote by mail in the midterms and has said he has cast his ballot by post in the past.

The president has been unsuccessful in his push for Congress to pass an act which would only allow people to vote by mail if they are disabled, ill, serving in the military, or travelling.

The majority of states allow, external people to vote by mail without having to provide a reason, and in the 2024 presidential election about 48 million people cast postal ballots.

Trump signed an executive order last year which directed the US Postal Service to only deliver ballots to voters on lists of citizens compiled by government agencies. It also sought to require states to use the same envelope style for postal votes.

However, the order was rejected by the US Supreme Court which called such changes so close to the midterm elections "arbitrary and capricious" - but said it could revisit the issue afterwards.

US states have different rules for verifying postal ballots, but every state matches certain voter information on the ballots against what they have on file to check they are eligible and most also conduct signature checks, external.

News.title: Landline switchover could cut people off in emergency, minister warned
News.content:
Plans to switch off the UK's traditional landline phone network could leave people in remote areas unable to contact help in an emergency, MPs have warned.

Landline operators aim to complete the switch to an internet-based network instead of copper-wire cables by the end of January next year.

The government and operators say the move to digital landlines will offer a more reliable service.

But MPs representing remote areas of the UK urged security minister Dan Jarvis to ensure that scrapping the copper-wire network did not make their communities more vulnerable in a storm or other emergency.

Unlike digital services, the traditional landline network does not rely on mains electricity and continues to work in a power cut.

Labour MP Torcuil Crichton, who represents the Western Isles constituency of Na h-Eileanan an Iar, said: "Resilience is inbuilt in the islands but we have major problems with connectivity because of this move from analogue to digital phone lines."

He said that "when the power goes out people don't have the phone, they don't have the internet and often they don't have a mobile signal either".

Retail service providers have been giving back-up battery packs to vulnerable customers, which can keep landline phones operating for an hour or more.

But Crichton said this was "simply not adequate" and that mobile phone providers "simply don't have the means to maintain or keep their signal going during storms".

He urged the minister to get telecoms firms to "up their digital game" to protect places "on the edge where people are vulnerable, isolated from their neighbours, where the ambulance is an hour away and the storm is 70 miles an hour".

Similar concerns were raised by MPs from the West Country and the Lake District.

Markus Campbell-Savours, Labour MP for Penrith and Solway, said: "I ask the minister to imagine an elderly constituent living alone in an isolated Lake District valley where copper phone lines have been replaced by fibre.

"A storm takes out the power to their router in the night and by the time they wake, the modest battery back up has failed, as has the mobile mast, does the minister share my concerns that they would have no way to raise an alarm in an emergency and agree that we need a new technological solution to protect the elderly?"

News.title: Multiple sclerosis patient living in 'horrific pain' due to UK-wide drugs shortage
News.content:
A woman with multiple sclerosis (MS) has said she is living with "horrific pain" after being unable to get a drug she uses to manage her condition.

Jill Kenning has used Nabilone for 17 of the 18 years since she was diagnosed with MS and said the drug had been vital for managing her pain and helping her live a normal life.

She said she had spent most of her time in bed since running out of the drug last Tuesday.

Northern Ireland's devolved health department said there was disruption to supplies of the drug across the UK, meaning Nabilone was out of stock with wholesalers and not expected to be available again until December.

A spokesperson said they would not say why there was disruption as the information was "commercially sensitive".

According to a tracker published by the industry reference guide MIMS, the average number of drugs in short supply in the UK has trended upward this year, external.

The number of drugs in short supply reached 157 this week, up from a low of 107 in January.

News.title: 'Biggest night in club's history' as fearless Fleetwood stun Arsenal in EFL Cup
News.content:
Given their league positions, form and pedigree, there could surely only have been one winner.

Fleetwood played Arsenal on Tuesday with an 84-place gulf between the teams and most home fans arriving in hope rather than expectation. But remarkably, it was the hosts who booked their place in the Carabao Cup quarter-final thanks to their penalty shootout win over the Gunners.

For the side known as the Cod Army, who won six promotions in 12 years in an impressive journey from non-league, this result will surely be remembered longest of all. Against the reigning Premier League champions, the club from a small seaside town in Lancashire created history in claiming one of the biggest cup upsets ever.

Aaron Loupalo-Bi gave the hosts the lead after 21 minutes but, after the break, Viktor Gyokeres pulled the visitors level.

And from there, they might have been expected to take charge, but Fleetwood remained resolute, prospering from a wasteful performance from Arsenal that included Max Dowman being sent off for kicking out after a robust challenge from Harrison Neal.

Fleetwood, who sit 18th in League Two having won just once in their past eight league games, dared to dream and took the game to penalties, with fans spilling on to the pitch in the after Conor Haughey's decisive spot-kick.

"The biggest night in the club's history in terms of opposition coming to town and we've managed to beat the champions," boss Matt Lawlor told Sky Sports in the aftermath of his side's stunning victory.

"I'm a big football fan and I watch National League all the way through to the Premier League, Championship. So for me it was a tough game to prepare for, but I'm just so glad that the lads have the feeling the way they are and took that performance in to make that town, the club, everyone proud."

News.title: Minimum wage set to rise but 18-20 year-olds will not get bigger increase
News.content:
The rise in the minimum wage is expected to be announced in the Budget, but 18-to-20 year-olds are set to see lower increases than in previous years, the BBC understands.

Pay for younger workers will rise in line with the increase in minimum pay for employees aged 21 years and over.

However, the increase for younger workers is lower than that seen in the previous two years, when Labour raised the rate to meet a manifesto promise that it would remove "discriminatory age bands" with all adults entitled to the same minimum wage.

Chancellor John Healey is also announcing measures to give families what he is calling "breathing space" with the cost of living.

"The manifesto pledge on equalisation still applies but we were always clear it could happen over time," Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds told the BBC:

"Of course, you want not just good wages but good work, " he added. "It is a balance of making sure the pressures on the labour market are taken into account."

The Times reported that the National Minimum Wage for 18-to-20 year-olds is likely to rise by 3.9% from Â£10.85 an hour to around Â£11.27.

That is a smaller rise than the 26% increase the Labour government has put in place for younger workers since returning to power in 2024.

Even after the reported rise, the rate remains below the National Living Wage for older workers, which is currently Â£12.71 an hour. It is set to rise by 3.9% to Â£13.20, the Times said.

Andrea Egan, general secretary of the union Unison, said it was "deeply unfair" to keep paying different rates for the same job.

"Twenty year-old care workers, teaching assistants and security guards do the same work as their older colleagues," she said. "They don't pay less in the supermarket or at the petrol pump. They must be paid equally."

News.title: Thick fog to create dangerous driving conditions for UK commuters
News.content:
Thick fog is forecast for parts of the UK this week, creating dangerous conditions for motorists, particularly around the morning commute.

Wednesday will be a day of some sunny spells and showers but as winds turn lighter into Thursday, extensive fog is expected to form.

The fog will lead to difficult driving conditions through the Thursday morning rush hour.

While rain is also in the forecast for the end of this week, as high pressure builds into November, more mist and fog will form next week.

News.title: Two in court over alleged Iran-linked plot at RAF Fairford
News.content:
Two British nationals have appeared in court in connection with an alleged Iran-linked plot at RAF Fairford last month.

Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, from Westminster, London, has been charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service, which police earlier said they believed to be Iran.

Nouman Essghir, also 24 and from Westminster, has been charged with entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK on 22 August - weeks before he was arrested near the airbase in Gloucestershire alongside four other men.

The pair appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Tuesday.

A major incident was declared after three suspicious vans were seen near the US-operated airbase on 27 September.

Dozens of residents were evacuated and a large cordon was put up in the area around the base. No explosive materials were found in the vans by police but a quantity of petrol was seized.

The court heard vans bearing the logo "Fuel2You" were spotted close to the base.

In the early hours, the vans came across a Ministry of Defence Police cordon and re-routed to another location.

Police arrived and arrested five men. They later revealed that one had called 999 and reported what was going on.

During the hearing at Westminster Magistrates' Court, Essghir stood in the dock wearing a grey sweatshirt and confirmed his name and address.

His charge relates to an alleged "reconnaissance mission" on 22 August, around a month before the Fairford incident.

Abdulkarim is charged with helping with the plot.

He appeared in court in a wheelchair wearing a checked shirt, jeans and a baseball cap. He confirmed his name and address.

Both men are charged under the 2023 National Security Act.

Essghir has been remanded in custody, while Abdulkarim has been granted bail with conditions including the surrender of his passport.

The case will be next heard at the Old Bailey on 20 November.

News.title: Men abused woman after her husband drugged and advertised her online, court told
News.content:
Four men sexually assaulted a woman after her then-husband drugged her and advertised her on Craigslist, Grindr and swinging websites, a court has been told.

Norman Macksoni, 48, Richard Wilkins, 62, Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, and Mohammed Hassan, 38, are on trial at Winchester Crown Court after pleading not guilty to sexual offences against Joanne Young.

They are charged jointly with her ex-husband Philip Young, 50, a former Conservative councillor, who has admitted to drugging and raping her over 13 years.

As the trial began, prosecutor Sarah Jones KC told the jury: "This case is about whether it is ever reasonable to have sex with an unknown woman without checking with her first."

Warning: This story contains distressing details

Joanne Young, who has waived her right to anonymity, told police that to her knowledge she had a "fairly normal" and "always monogamous" sex life with her husband.

But on one occasion in 2023, she said she had woken up with restraints and a blindfold on while a man was carrying out a sexual act on her.

Jones told the jury Joanne had believed her husband was performing the sexual act on her when in reality he was "stage managing another unknown person" who was "taking his place without her knowledge".

Jones told the jury Young had advertised Joanne online, seeking "strangers to come and sleep with his wife".

"He presented it as a kink for both of them, but there was no information from Joanne herself to support this and the photos he posted of her to advertise his offer showed her inanimate and tied to the bed blindfolded," Jones told the court.

"The nightcap they shared, it appeared, would be used to plunge her into a state where anything could be done to her by whoever answered and she would be unaware or unable to remember."

News.title: Chancellor to promise £15m to tackle misogyny in Budget
News.content:
The "misogyny prevention fund" is expected to be confirmed in the Budget and is intended to support the work of a national taskforce established last month, external and chaired by Women and Equalities Minister Bridget Phillipson.

Healey said the money will support "practical action to tackle misogyny head-on" and he hopes it will attract additional funding from businesses and philanthropists to increase its reach.

Phillipson said daily incidents of misogyny, including sexist slurs and workplace discrimination, have "no place in modern Britain".

She said: "This funding is a critical step as we work to confine misogyny to the history books, where it belongs."

Phillipson added that "everyone, from big business to members of the public, can do their bit to stamp out misogyny and improve the lives of women and girls everywhere".

When launching the taskforce chaired by Phillipson, the government said last month that it would aim to ensure government policy is "shaped by those most affected by misogyny".

It added its first meeting would focus on young people and later look at "workplaces, digital spaces and social cohesion".

Statistics published by the Office for National Statistics this month showed an estimated 12.8% of females aged 16 and over in England and Wales - around 3.2m - experienced at least one of domestic abuse, sexual victimisation or stalking in the year to March 2026.

The figure was an estimated 8.9% for males - around 2.1m.

For the Conservatives, Morrissey cited the estimates for women and girls as she criticised the announcement.

She said: "Labour simply aren't serious about tackling the crisis of violence against women and girls.

"This week it seems they will get the hard-pressed British taxpayer to fork out Â£15m to fund projects to tackle the 'manosphere'."

News.title: Suspicious package sent to hotel contained explosive device
News.content:
A suspicious package delivered to a hotel in Londonderry contained a "viable" explosive device, police have said.

Army bomb experts were sent to the hotel at Ebrington Square in the city's Waterside after the package was discovered at about 15:20 GMT on Tuesday.

They carried out a controlled explosion on the device, which was later taken away for a forensic examination.

Det Supt Kearney of the Police Service of Northern Ireland said: "I condemn this reckless and targeted attack."

The detective said that "a number of people" were evacuated from the hotel, along with staff from neighbouring premises.

A Halloween funfair had been taking place a short distance away from the hotel.

It remained open during the security alert.

News.title: Unnamed celebrity accused of 'inappropriate sexual activities', court hears
News.content:
A celebrity has asked the High Court to prevent two news organisations from publishing his identity and allegations that he abused his status for many years to engage, or attempt to engage, in "inappropriate sexual activities with a large number of girls and young women".

The unnamed celebrity is seeking an injunction, and his legal team told the first day of a trial on Tuesday that any publication would be "highly likely" to lead him to kill himself.

They told the court that his drastic reaction was not because of any wrongdoing, but because of the fear of "trial by media".

The man denies abusing "his power and position as a celebrity to contact and forge relationships with young women and teenagers to try to have sex with them", the court heard.

The legal team for ITN and Guardian News and Media (GNM) told the court that the celebrity's "suicide risk" could be mitigated and there was no proper basis "to restrain the publication of public interest journalism".

A medical report carried out for the court said inpatient treatment could provide "significant, but not complete mitigation of the risk", but that treatment, perhaps for months, had "a realistic potential to reduce the risk".

The judge, Mr Justice Nicklin, said there was "significant public interest" in the proceedings and that "this is a difficult and important case".

He added: "The court must determine it fairly, on the evidence and legal submissions."

News.title: UK and EU officials to discuss freedom of movement
News.content:
Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Reynolds said current discussions ahead of the summit are around food and drink, electricity and emissions trading.

He said: "What the prime minister has also said, quite rightly, is we face a series of policy changes on the European side that will affect us.

"We need to get as little uncertainty as possible, we need to have a way to resolve what our long-term relationship will be and he is going to set that out after the summit.

"He is going to be frank with the British people about what the trade-offs are but no assumptions have been made on that."

Pressed on whether UK officials are talking to the EU about freedom of movement Reynolds said: "They will be talking to them about what the future options for our relationship might be.

"But here and now, the focus should be on the summit and the tangible difference improvements we're going to make."

A government spokesperson stressed there were no current discussions on freedom of movement.

"We are working with the EU on the areas set out and agreed ahead of the UK-EU Summit and within the manifesto red lines," the spokesperson added.

Burnham is far more willing to have a public conversation around Brexit than his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer, whose government was nervous about reopening a debate that proved so contentious in the past.

Some people within the Labour Party had been urging Sir Keir to go further and there is a widely held view that Burnham's comments are likely to go down well with voters tempted by the Liberal Democrats and Greens.

But there is nervousness among Labour MPs with small majorities in Brexit-supporting, Reform-facing constituencies.

Labour MP Melanie Onn, whose constituency Great Grimsby and Cleethorpes backed leaving the EU, told the Today programme Burnham risked losing trust by talking about going beyond the 2024 manifesto at a future election.

"I don't think that the scars have healed for many people around the country so I do think this is an unnecessary conversation to be having at this time," she said.

Onn, who lost her seat in 2019 to the Conservatives but won it back in 2024, warned against re-opening the conversation, saying: "Trust is incredibly important, it's hard-earned and easily lost, and on this matter I think that we should tread incredibly carefully."

Speaking to BBC Wales, Labour MP Ruth Jones said: "We need to be very careful here. We must respect the Brexit referendum result."

Asked if a referendum on freedom of movement was something she would support, the MP for Newport West and Islwyn said: "We're a long way from that. Andy Burnham is floating the idea, and it's great to float ideas, but let's talk it through and see what does it mean, because another referendum at this particular time would be divisive."

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage told BBC Breakfast that "Andy Burnham has no mandate to be in Brussels, to be negotiating any of this" and called for the prime minister to put his ideas to the public in a general election.

On Monday, Burnham left the door open to a potential referendum on freedom of movement with the EU.

The prime minister caused some confusion when he told broadcasters that he would not reintroduce free movement without a referendum, but Downing Street later said no decisions had been made on whether a public vote would be needed.

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner told the BBC on Sunday that no options for the UK's future relationship could be taken off the table.

But Burnham did appear to draw some red lines of his own when he told the Sunday Times, external that he would not be in favour of the UK joining the euro or the border-free Schengen zone.

The fact the prime minister has not been willing to say the same thing about free movement is being seen in Westminster as evidence that he believes it is a genuine option.

News.title: Great British Bake Off: Sixth contestant leaves tent after pastry week elimination
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Clara has become the sixth baker to leave The Great British Bake Off after pastry week proved her undoing.

The 24-year-old, a marketing graduate from Portugal, was sent home in Tuesday night's episode of the Channel 4 show. Tom, a 25-year-old hairdresser, was named star baker for the third time in the same episode.

Judges Paul Hollywood and Nigella Lawson set the remaining contestants three challenges across the week. The first asked the bakers to make handheld savoury pies.

A technical round followed, in which they had to whip up choux pastry for a dramatic Polish dessert. An eye-catching decorative pie was the showstopper that gave them one final opportunity to impress.

Clara said she had expected her exit from the tent, explaining that she “really struggled” during pastry week.

Clara was eliminated on Tuesday ( Channel 4/Love Productions/Patch Dolan )

Reacting to the news, she said: "I had a blast. This experience – it's not only that you are learning about baking, but you are learning a lot about you.

“I never thought I could do this with my disorder, and I am really proud that I did that and hopefully I can be an inspiration for other people.”

Despite her departure, Clara said she was proud of herself. She also encouraged anyone with a love of baking to “absolutely go for it” and apply for the next series.

She added: "I actually learned a big lesson: having a bad bake does not mean I am a bad baker, it means there's room for improvement, which is amazing because it motivates me to get the technique even better.

Clara, who took the star baker title in the third week of the competition, also spoke warmly of her fellow contestants. She said everyone was “so supportive” from the very beginning and they remained close.

She said: "I think we were all just truly blessed with this group as we got on really well. Everyone is so different and brings so much to the table so that was beautiful to see.”

Clara is the sixth contestant to be eliminated this year after Danni, Shannon, Molly, Nikki and Yannis.

The Great British Bake Off returns to Channel 4 next Tuesday at 8pm.

News.title: Mikel Arteta reveals Arsenal’s missing trio are injury doubts for Liverpool clash
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Mikel Arteta has revealed a triple injury blow for Arsenal in light of their shock Carabao Cup exit to League Two side Fleetwood Town.

The Gunners were beaten on penalties at Fleetwood on Tuesday night after being held to a 1-1 draw in 90 minutes, with Arteta’s decision to rotate heavily backfiring.

Injuries forced his hand on some selection decisions, however, with the Spaniard revealing after the match that Declan Rice, Riccardo Calafiori and Noni Madueke all missed out due to fitness problems.

“Riccardo was out, Noni was out with an ankle and Declan Rice was finished with a problem the other day. That's why I had to substitute him [against Everton],” Arteta said.

Declan Rice is among the trio now in doubt to face Liverpool on Sunday ( Getty )

The trio could now be doubts for the trip to Liverpool on Sunday, where Arsenal will need to bounce back from cup humiliation.

Their absence compounds Arsenal’s growing injury woes this season, with a crisis beginning to develop going forward.

Talismanic winger Bukayo Saka could be out until Christmas after being forced off against Bayern Munich with a thigh injury, joining summer recruit Christos Tzolis on the treatment table.

Madueke’s return to form, scoring a late winner at Nottingham Forest earlier this month, was welcomed as Arteta began to operate him on both flanks as a result of injuries, but his own setback will now give the Gunners boss an almighty selection headache.

This will be exacerbated by the suspension of teenager Max Dowman, who will miss the next three games after being sent off for kicking out at a Fleetwood player on a miserable night in the north west.

“I'm sad, I think we are all sad,” Arteta said after the match. “We have a massive responsibility to carry this badge in the best possible way.

“It had nothing to do with effort or application or determination to win it, but we lack other things to, to create a much bigger margin than today, with what we produce, they really should have been shown in the scoreline."

News.title: How long you brew tea can have a big health impact, study shows
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The strength and temperature of tea can have a significant impact on the heart-protective benefits of the hot beverage, a new study suggests.

Studies have shown that regularly drinking tea can lower one’s risk of diseases affecting the heart and blood vessels.

But how different types and brews vary in their effects has remained unclear.

A large study conducted in China has now found that the type, strength, and temperature of the tea can have a significant impact on the health of blood vessels in the body, with “burning hot” tea associated with elevated risk.

“Habitual tea consumption was associated with lower vascular disease risk, with associations varying by drinking characteristics and intake level,” researchers concluded in the study published in the Journal of Internal Medicine.

open image in gallery A worker prepares herbal tea in a cafeteria ( AFP via Getty Images )

In the research, scientists followed 485,934 adults for an average of about nine years.

Researchers recorded 14,863 cases of heart, lung, and brain diseases, as well as conditions affecting arteries.

These conditions included those affecting blood circulation in the heart and brain, as well as reduced blood flow through arteries supplying the limbs.

The analysis suggested regular tea consumption is linked to a 11 per cent lower risk of these outcomes compared with not drinking tea.

The favourable combination of “habitual tea consumption, non-current smoking and high physical activity” is associated with the “lowest risk”, according to the study.

Scientists observed the lowest risk among those consuming up to eight cups per day.

“The lowest estimated risk at approximately 6–8 cups a day among weekly drinkers,” they wrote.

open image in gallery Residents of Basrah distribute food to participants of an Imam Hussein religious procession in Basrah, Iraq ( Middle East Images/AFP via Getty )

Black tea seemed to have a more consistent link with a lower risk of vascular disease than green tea.

“Black tea showed more consistent inverse associations than green tea, moderate-strength tea was associated with lower risk,” scientists wrote.

Scalding hot tea also seemed to have a contrasting effect compared to the lower risk linked to regular tea consumption.

But the reported results do not explain why very hot tea is associated with higher risk or establish that heat itself caused the increase.

Researchers caution that the findings are associations, rather than establishing that a particular amount or preparation of tea prevents disease.

Yet they argue that the research supports calls for considering “multidimensional tea-drinking and lifestyle patterns in vascular health research”.

The latest findings are in line with previous research on the benefits of tea drinking.

“The findings point to the wider role of healthy lifestyle habits. The lowest risk was seen among people who drank tea, did not smoke and were physically active,” said Dell Stanford, senior dietitian at the British Heart Foundation, who was not involved in the study.

“There’s no single food or drink that will transform our heart health; our overall diet and lifestyle matter much more,” he said.

News.title: What the Budget will mean for pensions and income tax
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The first Budget under new prime minister Andy Burnham is just around the corner, with households across the country waiting to find out what the planned fiscal changes could mean for them.

Several policy plans have been rumoured in the build up to the event, as the cost of living remains a major concern for many households. Inflation rose to 3.5 per cent in September to mark the highest level in nearly a year, as rising energy costs continue to drive up prices.

It is thought that changes to benefits and pension policy could play a central role as the government looks to shore up its shrinking fiscal headroom and lower welfare spending.

The prime minister has already said his government will fight the next election on a contentious pledge to revise the triple lock. After taking effect in 2030, the changes could save £15bn per year by 2040 according to official estimates.

There are also plans to reform welfare spending, with the government expected to lay out its plans following the publication of a review into Personal Independence Payment (PIP), and another into youth unemployment, later this year.

open image in gallery The Budget will shed light on chancellor John Healey’s economic plan for the future ( PA )

But the upcoming fiscal event will shed more light on chancellor John Healey’s economic plan for the future, especially as he lays out the spending and saving commitments that will shape the year ahead and beyond.

Here’s what the 2026 Autumn Budget could mean for pensions and benefits:

Pensions

Mr Burnham’s pledge to revise the triple lock would not take effect until 2030 at the earliest. However, there are several changes the government could make to pension policy before this.

Ahead of the Budget, reports have indicated that chancellor John Healey is set to confirm how nearly a million pensioners will be shielded from paying income tax in the next financial year.

Invest at least £100 in Stocks or ETFs of your choice. Get fractional shares worth £50! Terms and conditions apply. Go to website 

The state pension is set to rise 3.9 per cent from April in line with wage growth, bringing the yearly total to £13,036. This will take the full new state pension amount above the income tax personal allowance threshold £12,570 for the first time.

Former chancellor Rachel Reeves had already committed to ensuring no pensioner with the state pension as their sole income would pay income tax on the payment. However, she did not lay out the precise mechanism that would ensure this before her tenure ended.

open image in gallery The first Budget under new prime minister Andy Burnham is less than a week away ( Getty )

It is understood that Mr Healey will deliver on this pledge by raising the tax-free income allowance to £13,036 – the exact value of the state pension – for low-income pensioners only.

Other rumoured plans are more likely to focus on private pensions rather than the state pension.

A recurring rumour every year is that the government may bite the bullet on a change to pension tax relief, which effectively boosts savers’ contributions with a top-up from HMRC.

Savers who pay basic rate tax get a 20 per cent boost to their pension contributions, while higher rate taxpayers get 40 per cent, and additional rate earners get 45.

The scheme is designed to ensure that no tax is paid on pension contributions. It aims to encourage people to save more for retirement, as income that would be taxed as wages can instead go virtually untaxed as pension deposits.

One proposal would see this relief cut back for high earners, meaning everyone gets pension tax relief at a flat rate of 20 per cent, regardless of their income tax bracket. This could save around £15bn a year, according to some estimates.

There are also calls from some analysts for the chancellor to reverse his predecessor Rachel Reeve’s move to subject salary-sacrificed pension contributions above £2,000 to national insurance from 2029. Neither he or the Treasury have commented on the possibility.

Benefits

Changes to the benefit system are likely to be announced after the Budget this year, rather than at the event. However, the amount of savings Mr Healey secures through his policies could shape how much pressure he remains under to reduce the welfare bill.

Major changes reportedly under consideration by ministers include cuts to disability benefits for younger claimants, alongside limiting eligibility for the Personal Independence Payment (Pip) on mental health grounds.

Another reform could see the health element of universal credit removed for claimants under 25, government sources told The Guardian earlier this month. This group contains over 250,000 claimants.

Changes could also involve Pip being replaced for under-25s, overhauled entirely for all claimants, or possibly those under a cut-off at around 50 or 60.

Mr Burnham has said that his government will not pursue “crude cuts” in attempting to bring down Britain’s benefits bill. However, the prime minister may face a showdown with his MPs if he attempts to cut spending too sharply, as his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer did in 2025.

The new government’s welfare plans sit alongside ambition to boost the rising amount of young people out of work or education, with any spending welfare spending cuts reportedly earmarked to fund employment support.

The Treasury maintains its longstanding policy of refusing to comment on Budget speculation ahead of the event.

News.title: Mapped: Where in the UK will see snow this week as first flurries of winter predicted
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The first flurries of snow were predicted to hit the UK this week, just days after two violent storms lashed the country.

With temperatures plummeting in the wake of Storms Austen and Boelo, parts of Scotland were forecast to see a little snow falling on high grounds in the early hours of Wednesday morning.

The snow was expected to fall in parts across the Central Highlands, near Loch Rannoch and Pitlochry, for a short time between 2am and 3.30am.

A Met Office weather map detailed the location of the scattered snowfall, with small patches of white and grey representing snow amid a band of blue rain.

It comes after the Met Office put in place a yellow weather warning for almost the entirety of Scotland lasting until Tuesday evening, as gusts of gale-force winds buffered the north of the UK.

A Met Office weather map shows snow hitting high grounds in parts of Scotland this week ( Met Office )

Meanwhile, freezing temperatures could sweep as early as November as El Niño continues to wreak havoc on global weather.

Forecasters warned the weather phenomenon, which has already smashed global benchmarks to become the strongest weather event in history, could disrupt a large, high-altitude ring of swirling cold winds spinning above the Arctic known as the stratospheric polar vortex.

While a strong polar vortex helps to contain very cold winds and conditions within the North Pole, disruptions can weaken the jet stream, sending severe, freezing Arctic air plunging southward into North America and Europe.

Experts are now predicting the polar vortex will become weaker as early as November rather than in January 2027 as originally thought.

The prediction comes after Scotland has been hit hard by severe weather in the last few days, with one man killed by a falling tree in Dumfries and Galloway on Sunday.

Thousands of homes were left without power after falling trees and debris brought down power lines, and several schools were forced to close on Monday because of the lack of power.

Last year, the first snows of 2025 fell early on October 25 in the Cairngorm Mountain Resort in Scotland following an Arctic air mass.

And in November, Scotland experienced a Met Office amber weather warning when heavy snow and icy hit the north and north-east of the country, closing more than 100 schools and causing chaos on the roads.

At the time of the cold snap, the temperature plummeted to a chilly -12.6C in Tomintoul.

With unsettled weather on the way for the rest of autumn, it will not be long before the UK braces itself for the next storm, which this season, by convention, is set to be named Storm Chloe.

It will be followed alphabetically with Storms Dano, Evelyn, Finn, Gwendolyn and Heather.

News.title: Which taxes will rise in Budget 2026? Here’s what the experts predict
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Chancellor John Healey’s first Budget on Wednesday is fast approaching and could change the amount of money you have each month.

Tax changes are near certain, the only question is where they will land.

Labour is under pressure to better balance the country’s books, as government borrowing continues to rise, which means either cutting spending or raising the amount of tax it brings in.

Mr Healey has been careful not to make any firm commitments before he delivers his speech in the House of Commons, but there are some clues on what to expect.

Income tax for NEETs and 100k cliff edge

Labour committed not to raise the income tax rate in its manifesto so increases to the headline rates are unlikely.

Leaving the bands unchanged would however effectively result a tax hike, due to wage rises, pushing more people into a higher band each year.

There may be some tweaks around the costs of hiring young people, or the so-called £100,000 cliff-edge which sees couples lose the personal allowance and right to free childcare.

Elsa Littlewood, private client services tax partner at accountancy firm BDO, said: “Although the prime minister has previously floated the idea of increasing the income tax personal allowance, the costs of doing so are likely to mean the chancellor looks to other measures to ease the cost of living.

John Healey is set to announce his first Budget ( Getty )

“We would expect to see specific measures targeting young taxpayers, like cutting income tax or employee NIC for three years for those entering work for the first time.

“This would give a clear incentive to NEETS [people aged 16-24 who are not in education, employment or training] to enter the workforce and could incentivise employers to increase employment.”

Ms Littlewood added that the 100k cliff-edge creates a “perverse distortion” whereby people entering or progressing into higher-salaried roles are penalised and can face an effective marginal tax rate of around 60 per cent.

Stamp Duty

The property market is front of mind for any chancellor, given its central role in people’s finances and the economy.

Chancellors are always keen to be seen as helping people ‘get on the property ladder’ so it would not be a surprise to see some tweaks to tax here.

Data from tax filing platform Taxd in a report on what British taxpayers would change in the tax system, found that among respondents who chose stamp duty as the tax they would tackle first, 67 per cent said they would scrap it completely, while 20 per cent wanted reform and 13 per cent would cut it.

Inheritance tax

This is always a political football that gets kicked around near the Budget, but there have not been any clear signals of change in the short term.

“With the political pain of the IHT changes for farmers and business owners fresh in the memory and with more controversy surrounding IHT on pensions coming into force from April 2027, you might think that the government would want to steer clear of further reforms,” said Ms Littlewood.

“Yet, the prime minister has said he is prepared to expend political capital to get a national care service up and running.

“As Baroness Casey’s independent commission on adult social care is not due to report until 2027, and the prime minister’s recent conference speech indicating that funding for a national care service will come in part from changes to the triple lock after the next election, any further tax moves are likely to be delayed until a future Budget.”

Reversing Reeves' pensions cap

The state pension triple lock has been put firmly on the table for a change by Prime Minister Andy Burham, but not right now. 2030 was the date mentioned.

Tweaks to the rules on private sector pensions are possible though, if not likely.

“In the lead-up to the Budget, we are likely to see continued speculation around individuals’ pension tax-free cash entitlements,” Ms Littlewood said.

“However, given the uproar caused by (former chancellor) Rachel Reeves announcing a capping of pension salary sacrifice arrangements from 2029, we believe that any major changes to pensions at Budget 2026 are an outside chance.”

“In our view, a reversal of the announced changes to salary sacrifice arrangement would be very welcome as it would help restore confidence in pensions saving at a time when we know that people aren’t putting enough away for their retirement.”

Capital gains tax and IHT

Ms Reeves raised capital gains tax from 10 per cent to 18 per cent for the basic rate and 20 per cent to 24 per cent at the higher rate.

It is possible Mr Healey will try to squeeze more out of this area, although experts see that as likely to backfire. When capital gains rates reach a certain level that people are not willing to bear, they reduce or eliminate sales of assets and the amount raised falls.

Instead of raising the rate, Chris Etherington, private client tax partner, RSM UK said the chancellor could look at how assets are taxed at death.

“An alternative approach of removing the forgiveness of CGT at death, meaning that capital gains would not be effectively wiped out on death, is more certain to raise funds in the short-term and could generate more in tax receipts in the future,” he said.

News.title: William Shatner 'deeply saddened' as Star Trek legend pays tribute to Walter Koenig
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

William Shatner has paid tribute to his former Star Trek co-star Walter Koenig saying that he was “deeply saddened” to learn of the actor’s death aged 90.

Walter Koenig, who played Ensign Pavel Chekov in the original 1960s series of Star Trek, died at his home in North Hollywood on Sunday night, according to his talent agency, Galactic Productions.

A Facebook post announcing his death remembered Koenig's legacy and career as being full of “talent, warmth, and unforgettable performances” which left a “lasting mark on generations of fans around the world”.

William Shatner, 95, who played Captain James T Kirk in the franchise, remembered Koenig in a heartfelt Instagram post. Shatner wrote: "I am deeply saddened to learn of Walter Koenig's passing.

"Although we did not know each other well away from the set, we shared the later seasons of the original Star Trek series and the six films that followed. "What I observed, and what so many fans have expressed over the years, was a man who genuinely loved the Star Trek community.

"At conventions, Walter was rarely content to remain behind a signing table. He preferred to be among the people who had kept Star Trek alive for so many decades. "That kind of genuine connection is rare, and it will be remembered by everyone who came into contact with him.

“My condolences to his family, his friends, and the countless fans whose lives he touched.”

Elsewhere, tributes have poured in for Koenig, including from Sex And The City star Kim Cattrall, who appeared in the 1991 film Star Trek VI: The Undiscovered Country as Lieutenant Valeris. She wrote on Instagram: "Rest well dear Walter. It was a pleasure sharing the bridge with you.”

Meanwhile, George Takei, 89, who played USS Enterprise helmsman Hikaru Sulu in the hit sci-fi series, said his “heart is heavy” and remembered the star as being a “thoughtful man” and a “loyal friend” Walter and I met on the bridge of the Enterprise in the 1960s, and we stayed friends for nearly six decades.

"When Brad and I married in 2008, Walter stood beside us as our best man. "Just last month, on September 14, he turned 90, on the same day Brad and I celebrated our 18th wedding anniversary. I will always treasure that he and I shared that date. Rest well, my dear friend. Keep navigating a steady course.”

TV director Adam Nimoy, the son of the late Leonard Nimoy – who played the half-Vulcan science officer Mr Spock in Star Trek, posted a snap of Koenig from one of his “favourite” episodes of the sci-fi series.

He wrote: "So sad to hear about the loss of Walter Koenig. Such a nice guy and when we were on the convention circuit together a pleasure to hang out with. Here he is with Celeste Yarnall in ‘The Apple’, one of my favourites of the oddball episodes. Farewell.”

Koenig joined Star Trek for its second series in 1967, starring alongside Takei, Nimoy and Shatner. He went on to reprise his role as the young Russian navigator in seven Star Trek films.

He also wrote a book about the series, titled Chekov's Enterprise, which was published in 1980.

Sci-fi fans continued to see him on their screens in the 1990s, when he starred as villainous psychic Alfred Bester in hit series Babylon 5.

His film appearances included Moontrap and Drawing Down the Moon.

In the later years of his career, he turned his hand to directing, writing and teaching. He continued to honour his Star Trek legacy with regular appearances at fan conventions.

He also voiced the son of his original character in the final season of Star Trek: Picard in 2023.

Koenig was married to actress Judy Levitt, who died in 2022. Their son, Andrew, died in 2010. He is survived by their daughter, Danielle.

News.title: Fleetwood knock out Arsenal in one of the biggest shocks in League Cup history
News.content:
An unfamiliar opponent at a very familiar sounding venue, Arsenal play Fleetwood Town for the first time this evening at the Lancashire club’s Highbury Stadium.

Fleetwood, 18th in League Two, are the lowest-ranked team remaining in this season’s League Cup, having booked their place in the fourth round thanks to a victory at Sheffield United.

They were playing in English football’s sixth tier in 2009, and so while their stadium may share its name with Arsenal’s former home, the two clubs are worlds apart.

The League Cup is fourth of four competitions on Arsenal’s list of priorities, but Mikel Arteta should be able to rotate extensively while progressing to the quarter-finals. With a trip to Anfield on Sunday, that is a welcome luxury.

Kepa Arrizabalaga, Piero Hincapie, Cristhian Mosquera, Martin Zubimendi, Mikel Merino and Viktor Gyokeres are seasoned internationals in need of minutes and in line to start.

Max Dowman lit up Arsenal’s third-round victory at Ipswich Town, and 17-year-old centre-back Marli Salmon was not far behind him. Young striker and Northern Ireland international Ceadach O’Neill is also expected to be involved, and he may be joined by other academy players.

While attention is fixed on Premier League and Champions League success, Arsenal’s stinging defeat by Manchester City in last season’s final of this competition will not have been forgotten by Arteta or his players.

Matt Lawlor, Fleetwood’s manager, was full of praise for Arsenal in his pre-match press conference: “The champions are coming to town and they’re coming to our patch. The players need to be excited by it, not overawed by it. The respect is through the roof, but the fear can’t be through the roof.

“We’ve earned a game like this. We’ve had to go through round upon round of tough games, and none of them were easy. To get to where we are, we deserve that.”

Arteta has told his players that they must keep their standards high, with a lack of concentration or professionalism potentially their worst enemy against fourth-tier opposition.

Arteta said: “Our reputation, our pride, everything is in play. So every time you play a football match, and especially against a team in a different division, respect the game, respect every opponent because they deserve that, and then try to win and try to play a bit better than them.



“We know the risk, and in football, things can get very equal the moment you are able to match certain things, and that’s why our basics and habits have to be through the roof to be able to win the game.”



Full team news on the way shortly.

News.title: High temperatures linked to more than 700,000 deaths in 2023, study estimates
News.content:
Record-breaking temperatures killed an estimated 710,00 people globally in 2023, an increase of more than 36 per cent since 2015, according to new research.

A report on climate change and health by the Lancet medical journal shows that since the Paris climate agreement was introduced in 2016 the number of deaths linked to heat has rocketed.

Between 2006 and 2015 the average annual number of deaths attributed to heat stood at around 398,400 but between 2016 and 2023 the number increased to an annual average of 540,800, hitting a high of 710,000 in 2023.

The authors of the Lancet study say that extreme heat, which is linked to cardiovascular problems and is particularly dangerous for older people, pregnant women and those with other health conditions, must be considered a global health emergency. And they warn that the risks from high temperatures have accelerated in recent years.

News.title: Nigeria’s women and girls impacted the most by British and US funding cuts, committee is told
News.content:
UK and US aid funding cuts in Nigeria have impacted the country’s women and girls more than other groups, MPs were told on Tuesday.

Nigeria has been among the hardest-hit countries as many Western governments have slashed overseas development budgets to increase defence spending.

At the International Development Committee’s first hearing on the impact of aid cuts on global health in Africa, MPs were told that UK government cuts had impacted water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) programmes in Nigeria significantly, putting women and girls at risk.

“WASH is one of the lowest-funded areas in UK government support to Nigeria. WASH enables girls to stay in school, enables them to manage their menstruation effectively, enables women to give birth safely, and protects the lives of children under 5,” Evelyn Mere country director of Water Aid Nigeria said.

“The UK government says one of its priorities is that it will educate girls, empower women and make sure their voices are heard. It means that the UK says one thing, but with the aid cuts does another,” she added.

The British Foreign, Commonwealth, and Development Office (FCDO) announced earlier this year it would reduce its aid spending in Nigeria by 50.2 per cent over the next three years, from £136 million in 2025 to £68 million by 2029.

Nigeria has also faced substantial funding reductions from the US after the Trump administration shuttered USAID, the government’s foreign assistance arm. This included more than $600 million (£450 million) in health funding.

An FCDO internal impact assessment, published in July 2025, acknowledged that the biggest casualties of African funding cuts would be frontline WASH and women’s health programmes.

“Overall, any reductions to health spending risk an increase in disease burden and ultimately in deaths, impacting in particular those living in poverty, women, children and people with disabilities,” the assessment concluded.

News.title: Taliban forbids ‘un-Islamic’ sight-saving operations
News.content:
Hundreds of people each year will be denied sight-saving operations in Afghanistan after the Taliban forbade corneal transplants, doctors have told the Telegraph.

Officials have ruled that the transplant procedure is not permitted under Islamic teachings and have ordered surgeons to halt operations.

It is the latest in a stream of edicts limiting access to health care issued by the regime since it swept to power in 2021.

The edict came just months after a medical charity had helped train up local doctors to conduct operations in the Afghan capital, Kabul, and the eastern city of Jalalabad.

Doctors say there is a severe need for corneal transplants in Afghanistan to restore sight in patients injured in explosions and accidents.

Dr Noor Zaman Hashim of Noor Eye Hospital in Kabul said his staff had conducted 90 transplants in recent months, before the programme had been halted by the Taliban order.

He said the hospital had a growing waiting list, comprising mostly young people who had lost their eyesight because of trauma, injuries, explosions and welding-related accidents.

“Decades of violence have devastated Afghanistan’s healthcare infrastructure. We neither have sufficient ophthalmologists nor locally available corneas to meet the demand for transplants,” he said.

“The Taliban have verbally instructed us to stop the transplants. Nobody has the courage to defy their orders because of the risk of severe punishment,” he said.

News.title: The silent war: As Israel chooses a new leader Gazans wait for life to begin again
News.content:
One year after the ceasefire, Gaza’s health system is still on its knees. Of Gaza’s 228 primary care facilities, only just over half are functioning, according to the WHO.

Medicines are getting in, with almost 87 per cent of requests granted, says the WHO.

It means that someone with a fever or a minor injury can be treated but if it’s anything more complicated there are few options.

None of Gaza’s 36 hospitals are fully functioning, with just 19 partially working, according to the WHO.

There is no MRI scanner anywhere in the Strip, only about 30 per cent of facilities have basic X-rays, and only 12 to 17 per cent have dialysis capability, according to Physicians for Human Rights-Israel (PHRI), a medical NGO founded by Israeli doctors

Chronic illnesses are getting worse. Sally Saleh, head of health and emergency response at Medical Aid for Palestinians (MAP), says there is no capacity to monitor patients or guarantee consistent medical access, so preventable complications from cancer, kidney disease and diabetes will accumulate.

“We need to move beyond simply keeping services alive from one week to the next,” she told The Telegraph.

Power is the biggest hurdle, doctors say. Gaza’s electricity grid has been dead since Israel turned off the supply in October 2023, so hospitals rely on expensive and unreliable generators.

Dr Ahmed Muhanna of Al-Awda Hospital in central Gaza said that when his generators broke down, the hospital rented one for $1,200 a day, but it may only run for 10 hours.

Fuel and spare generator parts are in short supply – but Cogat blames Hamas for stealing fuel and it says that because “Hamas operates inside hospitals” it has to monitor where spare parts end up.

One major problem for those trying to get supplies into the Strip is Israel’s ban on “dual use” items, material it deems serves both a civilian and military purpose. Items that have been blacklisted include generators and metal tent poles.

Cogat says generators, X-ray machines and oxygen concentrators are allowed in under monitoring arrangement with aid groups. But aid agencies told The Telegraph that the rules on what is permitted change from day to day.

Israel allows 15 trucks of dual-use items to enter every week. But the WHO says repeated delays in bringing medical equipment, prosthetics and diagnostic tools into Gaza are delaying patients’ recovery.

In the last six months alone, a single shipment of prosthetics and assistive devices for amputees was rejected four times, the WHO added. It is particularly concerning as Gaza is now home to “the largest cohort of child amputees in modern history”, according to the UN.

“Every rejection means another delay for someone who has already lost a limb and is simply waiting for the chance to walk again,” said Dr Reinhilde Van De Weerdt, WHO Representative in the Occupied Palestinian Territory (OPT).

In July Cogat said over 10,300 pallets of health products had been approved since the start of the year, but only 3,238 had reached the crossing. It blamed “a delivery bottleneck” among the organisations that requested them rather than a “Cogat controlled supply bottleneck”.

Crumbling hospitals mean that around 20,000 patients, including 4,000 patients, need urgent medical evacuation. The WHO says about 5,700 patients have been evacuated since the ceasefire. Save the Children estimates that at the current rate the backlog would take four and a half years to clear.

Cogat disputes WHO and UN figures, and says that it has approved the majority of evacuation requests.

News.title: Harry Kane ends England’s 25-year wait for Ballon d’Or winner
News.content:
The 70th Ballon d’Or ceremony takes place at the London Palladium as England and Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane aims to become the first Englishman in more than 20 years to win the award. Michael Owen was the last Englishman to win the award back in 2001.

The choice of London as the host city pays tribute to the award’s inaugural winner, England’s Stanley Matthews, who won it in 1956. This also marks the first time the ceremony will be organised outside France. Kane, who scored over 70 goals for club and country in the relevant year, is among the favourites for this year’s award alongside the likes of Barcelona and Spain’s Lamine Yamal and Real Madrid and France’s Kylian Mbappe.

Kane won the Bundesliga with Bayern Munich whereas Yamal won both La Liga and the World Cup. Yamal won the Kopa Trophy at last year’s ceremony as the best men’s young player.

Last year’s winners were Spain and Barcelona midfielder Aitana Bonmati and France and Barcelona forward Ousmane Dembele. Dembele is aiming to become just the 11th man to win the top prize at least twice, although it would appear to be very unlikely that the Frenchman will be winning the award this evening.

Selected international journalists cast their votes based on the performances of players throughout the season. The panel consists of one representative per country from the top 100 nations in the Fifa men’s world ranking and the top 50 in the women’s world ranking. Each voter ranks their top 10 candidates, with points distributed on a descending scale. They vote based on three factors: individual performance, team achievements, and class combined with fair play.

In total, 13 trophies will be presented across the men’s and women’s game, including the two man Ballon d’Or awards, the best young players and best teams. The awards take into account achievements from August 3, 2025, to July 19, 2026 (August 16 for the women).

The official ceremony begins at 8pm GMT.

Sports.title: ‘They don’t have Gyokeres and Havertz’ – Arsenal U21s beat HIGHER team than Fleetwood on same night as Carabao Cup exit
Sports.content:
Next

ARSENAL’S shock Carabao Cup exit was made even more embarrassing thanks to their Under-21s beating League One side AFC Wimbledon.

The Gunners suffered a stunning penalty shootout defeat to EFL minnows Fleetwood to miss out on a spot in the quarter-finals.



But Arsenal saw their young guns notch a 2-1 win over Wimbledon in the Jersey Mike’s Trophy.

The U21s fell behind thanks to Callum Maycock breaking the deadlock just three minutes after the break.



And the showdown was turned on its head through Evan Mooney and Emerson Nwaneri, who netted in the Uefa Youth League and donned the goalkeeping gloves earlier this month.

It resulted in the up-and-coming youngsters sealing a sensational comeback victory while the senior squad failed to beat League Two strugglers.

Viktor Gyokeres and Kai Havertz, who started the Carabao Cup humiliation at Fleetwood, found themselves in the firing line as furious Arsenal fans raced onto social media.

One said: “Luckily the U21s didn’t have Havertz and Gyokeres.”

Another added: “This is gonna be peak banter material for rival fans.”

ARSENAL’S Carabao Cup misery has been added to after Mikel Arteta revealed Declan Rice, Noni Madueke and Riccardo Calafiori are all injured.

The trio were left out of the squad for the Gunners’ trip to Fleetwood in the fourth round of the Carabao Cup, which they lost on penalties.



Calafiori had been a doubt for the game after struggling towards the end of Saturday’s 2-0 win over Everton.

Arteta, 44, said: “Calafiori was out, Noni was out with an ankle [issue].

Arteta added: “First of all, congratulations to Fleetwood for going through in the next round, in the manner they’ve done it, the atmosphere they have created, and, yeah, a really sad day for us.

MIKEL ARTETA has been slammed for his reaction to Max Dowman’s first professional red card.

The 16-year-old was given his marching orders in the 85th minute of Arsenal’s stunning Carabao Cup fourth-round exit at the hands of Fleetwood Town on Tuesday.



Dowman reacted angrily to a firm challenge from Harrison Neal on the touchline, KICKING OUT at the midfielder.

After the ensuing fracas had calmed down, referee Michael Salisbury didn’t hesitate to send the winger for an early shower.



Arteta was far from happy with Dowman, whom he gave a death stare after briefly muttering something to the teen before he trudged down the Highbury tunnel.

The Spaniard’s reaction to Dowman’s dismissal, which went viral, wasn’t well received by some of Sky Sports’ punditry team for the match.

Ex-Premier League star Jobi McAnuff said of the incident: “I didn’t like this at all.

Gunners cult hero Paul Merson said: “You’ve got to remember he’s 16, he’s a kid.

FLEETWOOD TOWN fans took part in a mass pitch invasion after their stunning Carabao Cup upset of Arsenal.

The Cod Army dumped out the north Londoners thanks to a 5-3 penalty shootout victory after holding them to a 1-1 draw.

Conor Haughey sent Highbury into pandemonium by thumping his penalty into the top corner moments after Gunners summer signing Bruno Guimaraes had his spot kick saved by Jay Lynch.

Thankfully, the supporters who took to the pitch behaved themselves as they celebrated the team’s famous victory.

Sports.title: The two teenage darts superstars ready to challenge Littler
Sports.content:
Two-time World Darts Champion Luke Littler is only 19 - but there are already two other teenage superstars hot on his heels and relishing a chance to beat him.

Two-time World Youth Championship winner Mitchell Lawrie, 15, and Jayden Walker, 14, will both compete against the World No 1 in Netflix's Beat Luke Littler event on Friday, where the winner will take home an eye-watering bounty of £501,000.

The youngsters are just two of 24 finalists who could face the reigning world champion: if one of the contestants beat Littler, the event will end and they will take home the prize, with Littler having to win 24 legs in a row to deny his opponents.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking on Love The Darts, Lawrie discusses his love for Gary Anderson and his hopes of gaining a PDC Tour Card

Both Lawrie and Walker have faced Littler before and are laser-focused on the task at hand, but there is little doubt that there will be plenty more to come from the pair.

"It's life-changing money so I'm looking forward to it," Lawrie told Sky Sports.

"I just obviously hope I get to get the chance to play because I know there are also 24 other good players that have been picked. I'm just hoping to get a chance to play Luke."

Lawrie, a Target Darts ambassador, is the more experienced of the two teenagers, having already surpassed Littler's record to become the youngest player to win a match at the World Darts Federation World Championship, and has even come close to tasting victory against Littler before.

"It was three or four years ago [that I played Luke Littler]. And he beat me 3-2 - I missed a few match darts!

"But that was before he went on to be what he is. And before I went on to be what I was as well."

'I'm 100 per cent expecting to beat Littler'

Image: Lawrie won the 2025 World Youth Championship

Lawrie's lofty ambitions do not stop at beating Littler.

The Scot - who turns 16 next week - confirmed to Sky Sports he will be participating in the PDC's Qualifying School in 2027, giving him an opportunity to earn a two-year Tour card and become a regular on the professional circuit.

"No, I'm not thinking about it; I'm definitely doing [the Q-school] - that's what I want to do," he added.

"I've wanted to be a professional darts player since I started. And that's what we're going to try to do in January.

"Hopefully, I'll get my tour card there and then go on to bigger and better things.

"As I've said, I've loved the WDF system and stuff. They've been great with me and I've enjoyed that a lot. But the money's right in the PDC.

"That's where you can make a living out of darts. So, that's where you need to go."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Luke Littler failed to win a maiden European Championship as he suffered a surprise defeat at the hands of Krzysztof Ratajski

Contestants had to complete 501 in 24 darts or fewer to progress through the first stage of Netflix's auditions, powered by Target OMNI and DartCounter.

Should the Scot get the chance to face Littler once more, he will only have to win one leg, rather than the three he needed last time out - and this time, he has a clear plan of action.

He said: "100 per cent [I'm expecting to beat him].

"It's one leg. He'll be up there throwing. I don't imagine I'll be on close to the start.

"Hopefully I'll win the bull-up and then hit two trebles to start -and then we'll see where the leg takes us. But that's the plan. Win the bull-up, hit two trebles, and then we'll see where it goes from there."

Walker: I've only hit three nine-darters!

Image: Jayden Walker beat Luke Humphries in an exhibition match when he was just 12 years old

While Lawrie is vocally confident in his chances of beating Littler and his prospects as a professional, Walker - a year his junior - is more understated about his astonishing list of teenage darting achievements.

"I've hit quite a few 170s, but I've only hit three nine-darters," Walker told Sky Sports. "The last nine-darter was in February last year.

"I've been so close to hitting double 12 a few times, but hopefully it'll come. You see the professionals on the TV, they probably hit about three or four a week - compared to them, it's not much at all.

"But hopefully, as I develop my game more, I can hopefully hit more and maybe I can get one competitively in a game."

Walker beat world No 2 Luke Humphries when he was only 12 years old, averaging 102 - prompting Humphries to call him "the best 12-year-old [player] I've ever seen in my life" - but is yet to convince his parents that his aspirations of becoming a professional darts player should be his top priority.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Littler produced the second-best average in the competition's history, his 114.47 has only ever been bettered by Phil Taylor's 118.14, after defeating Nathan Aspinall at the European Championship

"My mum always tells me I have to finish my homework before I can go out to a night of darts. Because I love darts so much, I sort of make myself do the homework.

"[One of my favourite subjects is] maths - it helped me in darts, because during lockdown when I first started playing, I started focusing on it.

"The only schoolwork they set us was maths. I just did maths and all those mental arithmetics helped me with my game, with all the shots out."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking on Love The Darts, Matt Edgar discusses why Littler played in the World Youth Championships and whether he will compete in the remaining ProTour events

Like Lawrie, Walker has faced Littler before - but the Dorset native knows he stands to gain from the profile of the event even if he doesn't get the chance to face the world No 1 for the prize.

"I'm excited for Friday. Obviously, I've been putting in a few hours this morning and I'll probably be putting in a few after this interview and for the rest of the week really, so I know I've got to practise and dedicate myself to beating him.

"I've met Luke before. I've played him twice as well, actually.

"He beat me easily the first time, but then the second time it was quite a competitive game. If I do end up playing him on Friday, hopefully it'll be competitive.

"Even if I don't get to play Luke on the night, it'll be good publicity for being on Netflix. Hopefully I can get a few sponsors that can help me travel on the back of that. And a few followers, that'd be quite nice."

Both Walker and Lawrie will aim to take centre stage and beat Littler to the £501,000 on Friday - and it looks set to be the first of many times darts fans will see the teenage sensations on their screens for years to come.
