Sports.title: Arsenal dumped out of Carabao Cup by League Two Fleetwood
Sports.content:
Fleetwood Town produced one of the biggest shocks in Carabao Cup history as the League Two team dumped out Premier League champions Arsenal on penalties to reach the quarter-finals.

Mikel Arteta named a strong Arsenal side with Viktor Gyokeres and Kai Havertz up front and Martin Odegaard playing the second half.

But they were not at the races, as the team two points above the League Two relegation zone took them to a 1-1 draw after Max Dowman was sent off before the shoot-out.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Paul Merson was critical of Mikel Arteta's reaction to Max Dowman being sent off in Arsenal's loss to Fleetwood Town in the EFL Cup.

Then Bruno Guimaraes saw his penalty saved by Fleetwood goalkeeper Jay Lynch - who also made wonder saves to deny Ben White and Odegaard in stoppage time.

That left Conor Haughey to blast past Illan Meslier - picked by Arteta over penalty expert Kepa Arrizabalaga to make his Arsenal debut - to send Highbury mad.

Fleetwood deserved the shoot-out after a bonkers start to the game. An unrecognised drone hovering over Highbury forced a seven-minute delay after 90 seconds.

Then Aaron Loupalo-Bi put the fourth tier side ahead after outmuscling 17-year-old defender Marli Salmon and poking past Meslier.

Arsenal responded after half-time as Viktor Gyokoeres bundled home his first of the season at the back post after good work from Northern Ireland teenager Cedach O'Neill - making his first start for the club.

But Havertz missed chance after chance. Then came a moment of contention as Dowman was shown his marching orders for apparently kicking out at Harrison Neal. The call was described as "really harsh" by Andy Hinchcliffe on Sky Sports commentary.

But this is Fleetwood's story. A non-league club as recently as 2012, they have now knocked out the reigning Premier League champions.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player During their Carabao Cup clash at Highbury stadium, Fleetwood versus Arsenal was delayed due to a drone over the pitch.

Arteta has no complaints over Arsenal mentality after loss

Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta to Sky Sports:

"First of all, congratulations to Fleetwood for going through to the next round in the manner they've done it.

"A really sad day for us. I cannot fault at all the attitude of the players, I haven't seen anybody not doing what is required at this level but we had so much of the ball, had so many chances, so many shots and if you want the margins to be bigger than going to penalties, you have to capitalise on that. We didn't and football is about that.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta shares his thoughts following their shock Carabao Cup loss on penalties to League Two side Fleetwood Town.

"It wasn't to do with attitude otherwise I would be here fuming. I'm sad, we're all sad.

"We have a responsibility to represent this badge in the best possible way. It was nothing to do with effort, application or determination to go and win it, but we lacked other things to create much bigger margins.

"With what we produced, it should have showed in the scoreline."

Merson: The biggest shock in Carabao Cup history

Fleetwood 1-1 Arsenal (5-3 pens)

Paul Merson on Sky Sports:

"Life is about memories and they've got one for life.

"You turn up tonight [Tuesday} and you think, 'how strong are Arsenal, they could get three or four', but fair play to them [Fleetwood]. And you won't see five penalties better than that. They were off the charts.

"For those lads to take those penalties. They'll be in history now for the biggest shock in the history of the League Cup.

"Odegaard is the only one who walks off the pitch tonight and all the Fleetwood players go 'what a player'. I can't believe what I've watched tonight."

Fleetwood boss: We didn't practice penalties

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Fleetwood Town boss Matt Lawlor confirms his side didn't practice their well-taken penalties that they took against Arsenal.

Fleetwood boss Matt Lawlor to Sky Sports on the penalties:

"I'm going to be honest, we haven't practised once. I'm not going to blag that we had some meticulous penalties, we haven't.

"The lads took care of themselves. We have a 19-year-old centre-back that took the last one. I was a little bit worried when he was walking up, but Conor [Haughey] backs himself.

"I don't think it will [sink it]. I've just told the players to enjoy it and we've got a league game on Saturday. I didn't want to be the bearer of reality, but we've got a game.

"I couldn't believe it. The biggest night in the club's history in terms of opposition coming to town and we've managed to beat the champions somehow.

"We're not egotistical enough to think we're going to play the best team in the country and outplay them, so we had to ride our luck, deny space, deny options for them and we did that really well for the majority of the game."

The key moments in normal time from Highbury Stadium

1: DRONE! An unrecognised drone stops play at Highbury for seven minutes as it caused a security risk. Referee Michael Salibsury wanted to take both sets of players off but play resumed almost straight away because the drone flew off.

10: OVER! After the restart, Piero Hincapie heads over Dowman's free-kick from close range.

20: BIG MISS! Dowman skews a shot wide when played through on goal by Salmon.

21: GOAL! Fleetwood go up the other end as Loupalo-Bi outmuscles Salmon to score past Meslier.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Fleetwood Town's Aaron Loupalo-Bi gives the League Two side a shock lead over Arsenal in their Carabao Cup fourth round clash.

42: CHANCES! Jurrien Timber misses two chances to score after Havertz headed his cross over the bar.

50: GOAL! Arsenal score from their first chance of the second half as Gyokeres bundles the ball home from close range.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Viktor Gyokeres pulls Arsenal against Fleetwood level early into second-half!

59: MISSES! Havertz misses two big chances in quick succession from close range - blazing over, then hitting the side netting.

65: MORE MISSES! Lewis-Skelly misses the latest of two big second half chances as he can't finish from a few yards out.

82: ALMOST! Fleetwood nearly snatch the win as Arsenal fail to clear and Will Davies sees a shot saved by Meslier.

90: OFF! Dowman is sent off after allegedly kicking out at Neal.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Max Dowman SENT-OFF as Gunners go down to 10-men.

Sports.title: Bradford roll back the years to reach Carabao Cup quarters
Sports.content:
Bradford are through to the Carabao Cup quarter-finals for the first time since they reached Wembley in 2013 with a 2-0 win over Peterborough.

Goals from Macaulay Gillesphey and Adam Phillips settled the all-League One affair at Valley Parade.

Brandon Khela drove wide from an early Peterborough chance but it was Bradford who took the lead on 13 minutes.

Manager Michael Duff had called for his side to be more productive from corners and they obliged when Callum Connolly's set-piece was turned in by defender Gillesphey.

Reece Welch's long pass sent Jake Beesley away but Peterborough 'keeper Alex Bass denied Bobby Pointon a second goal with a sprawling save.

Bass saved again from Ibou Touray's low shot before Ethan Williams offered a threat at the other end just before the break.

Peterborough came out strongly and Jon McCracken saved from Owura Edwards and then denied Vernon Masara in a one-on-one. Williams went even closer when he hit the bar.

But Phillips scored a second for Bradford on 67 minutes and had another cleared off the line.

Sports.title: Arteta explains reaction to Dowman red card amid criticism
Sports.content:
Mikel Arteta has explained his reaction to Max Dowman as the 16-year-old went down the tunnel after being sent off in Arsenal's shock Carabao Cup exit to Fleetwood Town.

Moments before Arsenal exited the competition on penalties to the League Two side, Dowman was sent off for violent conduct for kicking out at Harrison Neal after the Fleetwood defender's strong challenge on the teenager.

As Dowman headed towards the tunnel and past the dugouts, Arteta leaned in and said something to the teenager, which Paul Merson criticised, saying the Arsenal manager should have put an arm around him.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Carabao Cup fourth round match between Fleetwood Town and Arsenal

Asked what he said to Dowman, Arteta told reporters: "It was something that we discussed before the game." Arteta refused to go into any more detail when pressed.

On Sky Sports co-commentary duty, Andy Hinchcliffe said the red card was harsh on Dowman and Arteta replied: "I haven't seen it with the camera. You can't really see what happens. The decision was made by the referee and that's it.

"And even with 10 men, we have three big chances to score the second goal."

Asked whether Dowman has something to learn from the incident, Arteta replied: "We knew when we prepared the context of the match, we were very clear on the things to expect, the things that emotionally we have to dominate."

Sports.title: Rising star Domingos hopes to mastermind England's World Cup retention
Sports.content:
England's wheelchair team head into the Rugby league World Cup as defending champions; Luis Domingos is one of the players tasked with keeping hold of the title; He had not played the sport even two years ago but has used his basketball skills to help his rapid rise

Rugby League World Cup: Meet England wheelchair's rising basketball star Luis Domingos who wants to help the side keep hold of their title

England Wheelchair Rugby League player Luis Domingos has had a rapid rise in the sport he picked up less than two years ago

Just 18 months ago, Luis Domingos had not played Wheelchair Rugby League and now he heads to Australia with the hope of defending a world title with England.

Despite picking up the sport not too long ago, it is not the first time that Domingos has made his mark on the international stage. Domingos used to represent Portugal in wheelchair basketball and was professional in the sport.

However, to finish his studies at university, he left wheelchair basketball. Then he attended a wheelchair rugby league training session and the rest, they say, is history.

After an Ashes call-up, Domingos has continued his rapid ascent in the sport and now will represent England in the World Cup, achieving a dream that did not exist just two years ago. Domingos qualifies for England due to residency.

England's wheelchair rugby league team head down under looking to defend their title as the best in the world and they start with pool games against Wales, USA, and Ireland.

Sports.title: Big foot, Bane & Bo's Broncos - Inside Denver's 5,280ft sporting empire
Sports.content:
They call it the Rocky Mountain Thunder. The stadium-shuddering racket reverberated by Denver Broncos fans stomping their feet on the metal decks of their old Mile High Stadium.

It would become a storied intimidation tactic that has since translated across to their current home Empower Field, but perhaps too an unwritten cheat code to thousands 'getting their steps in', given all I would come to learn of this fitness-enthused Mountain West metropolis.

Here was your proverbial protein shake of Colorado goodness, unbridled escapism and blood-pumping self-care flexing in the clouds some 5,280ft above sea level, as if detached from the rest of the nation. They breathe a little differently here, operate a little differently, attack sport a little differently.

The city is serene and soothing in accordance with its neighbouring nature, and yet its sporting disciples deafening. From its mountainous backdrop to its rich variety of wildlife, Denver is a laptop screensaver picture of tranquillity. From its sunrise joggers to its rock-scaling climbers, it is a breeding ground for adrenaline and activity. And between its seven major league sports teams, it is a cauldron of intense, ever-expanding fandom.

Welcome to Mile High, where an early awakening at the Limelight hotel (fuelled by some jet-lag) would kickstart my stay with a stunning sunrise view over Union Station, around which bustled coffee-grabbers, job-goers and worm-catching early birds.

Denver's major league sports teams NFL: Denver Broncos

NBA: Denver Nuggets

MLB: Colorado Rockies

NHL: Colorado Avalanche

NLL (Lacrosse): Colorado Mammoth

MLS: Colorado Rapids

NWSL: Denver Summit

I had flown in directly from London Heathrow for a dose of Denver life, another West Brom-come-Broncos fan I met that weekend had made the trip from Birmingham, and each week Sean Payton's side receive support from neighbouring states in New Mexico, Montana, Utah and Wyoming. Such is their isolated geographical position in the metaphorical 'Gods' of America, the Broncos reign supreme as a prized NFL attraction.

Saturday. My choice of cargo trousers in bronzeable heat had already come back to haunt me in a land where shorts and t-shirt tend to top the attire. Denver's 300-days of sunshine each year lend themselves to a city driven by life outside and an accompanying will to explore. This Brit stuck out, a reality only amplified by the perplexed look upon learning bars and clubs close earlier here in order to avoid squandering mornings better dedicated to fitness and training; party early, workout early. And for what it is worth, the motivation and zest to stay on the move becomes infectious.

By night, Red Rocks Amphitheatre is known as Denver's unique home of world-class music acts, where Lily Allen had been headlining on her album tour at the time of my visit. By morning, it appears to adopt the appearance of an outdoor gym, with its multiple tiers of theatre steps occupying yoga classes and workouts for families and friends of all ages.

One man is shadow boxing back-and-forth in a mask reminiscent of Batman villain Bane, a father and his four children are tackling the steep incline in unison from bottom to top and one elderly gentleman is performing kettle bell swings at the awe of younger workout partners. It is enough to guilt-trip this sluggish journalist after an evening of down-time watching the Colorado Rockies baseball team and exploring Denver's world class breweries; Ratio Beerworks, for curious travellers, and Whiskey Bar, where I witnessed the most competitive round robin of snooker games - they take sport and winning seriously here, no matter the game or level.

Image: Sky Sports were invited to watch the Colorado Rockies in their loss to the Seattle Mariners

The Rockies these days are a little less associated with success in comparison to tavern snooker and their Broncos brothers, having reached the playoffs just five times since 1993. Still, they retain a devoted fanbase that preserve baseball's unique pass-time entertainment. On this occasion families were invited to a fireworks show, dare I say to compensate for the lack of Rockies fireworks on the field. And yet their supporters keep coming back.

The Broncos, as mentioned before, top the sporting charts in Denver as three-time Super Bowl champions and one of the most successful franchises in NFL history. The team boasts the longest active sell-out streak for an NFL franchise that has remained in one city, dating back to 1970, contributing to a 20-year wait-list for season tickets.

Denver initially played their football in Mile High Stadium from 1960 to 2000, before moving into Empower Field at Mile High in 2001. The organisation is now targeting the 2031 NFL season as a completion date for their new retractable roof stadium, which would account for the Colorado elements as well as offering year-round use of the facility for events beyond football. Recent history points towards an increased chance of hosting the Super Bowl for stadiums that have a roof or can be covered.

The Broncos are the only team in the NFL to announce the number of 'no-shows' on the big screen during each home game, prompting boos from fans in attendance towards those who didn't make the journey.

Right on cue, the jeers arrived late in their Week Two victory over the Jacksonville Jaguars, where I was among 76,472 fans basking in Colorado sunshine to soak up a day that began with the Broncos' traditional pre-game skydiving Thunderstorm show and ended in a first win of the season for Bo Nix's side.

It is raucous, rattling noise from start to finish, underlining one of the most renowned fan bases in football. Oh, and boy do they hate the Kansas City Chiefs, whose travelling fans shall be alerted to that fact - if not already aware - when they head to Mile High this weekend, live on Sky Sports NFL.

Image: Red Rocks Park and Amphitheatre

They cut the figure of overlords, empowered by their respiratory nuances high in the sky, reminding teams of where they are with an unmissable sign reading: "ELEV 5280′ Altitude Sickness is Real" as opposition players walk into the stadium.

It creates an 'us versus them' unity among Broncos fans, and yet it remains a city warm and welcoming to its visitors; I met one Cowboy hat-wearing local fascinated by a British accent, so too a stadium worker who had a friend living in Clapham - because OF COURSE. It's always Clapham.

Empower Field has also served as host for events ranging from Barack Obama's Democratic presidential nomination acceptance in 2008 to Taylor Swift concerts. In March 2026 it also made history by setting a new National Women's Soccer League attendance record when 63,004 fans watched the Denver Summit expansion team play the Washington Spirit, surpassing the previous benchmark of 40,091 set by Bay FC at Oracle Park.

Denver natives do not mess around when it comes to sport. If there is a team, a game, an individual for whom to root - they are there. There are enough of them; just three years ago the Nuggets won the NBA Finals, and four years ago the Colorado Avalanche won NHL's Stanley Cup.

The Summit are something of Denver's newest, thriving hope having been accepted as an NWSL expansion team in January 2025, with legendary Broncos quarterback Peyton Manning part of their ownership group. Six Summit players were recently called up to represent the US Women's National Team during the October international break. That included midfielder Lindsey Heaps, who has won a World Cup, two Olympic medals and captained her side at the 2023 World Cup across more than 170 caps for the national team.

I attended Summit's 2-1 win over Seattle Reign, where a sold-out crowd of 12,272 watched on despite an hour-long rain delay. Chants of 'you can't do that' at the sight of a foul was a unique Americanism contrary to the more profane tirades customary to European football, but it proved yet another crowd reflective of Denver's deep-rooted sporting devotion.

Beyond its sport it is a city embodied by its gateway to the natural world.

Dedicated Broncos fans might know 'Frank the Tank' as being the childhood nickname for offensive tackle Frank Crum, while others may know it to be the legendary moose bull of Rocky Mountain National Park. Sadly (or perhaps fortunately), a day trip into the mountains did not lead me to Frank.

What it did lead me to was the otherworldly sights of Mount Blue Sky, where never-ending greenery, the whisper-inciting Echo Lake, Idaho Springs and scenic road loops along which Walter Mitty might skateboard delivered lifelong images for the mental archives. So too a buoyant tour guide who would inform us of his potential Big Foot encounter while camping in the surrounding forest area; I saw his photos, and the foot-prints are almost believable enough to sway the most stubborn of naysayer.

Anyway, it is a perfect calming complement to the city's Broncos mania, where ziplining and whitewater rafting still preserves Denver's commitment to sporting adrenaline. The views are truly something else.

It is as versatile a sporting city as you might find in the United States, my deepest regret being my inability to ski such is the access to some of the world's greatest slopes.

Denver's RiNo district plays host to trendy shops, phenomenal street murals and the multiple cuisines of Denver Central Market. It is a community that offers a reminder to Denver's diversity, with Hispanic and Latino residents making up roughly 34 per cent of the city's population - and no doubt contributing to my faultless gameday chilaquiles at The Bindery.

Shopping in Cherry Creek, the Denver Art Museum, the city's eight Michelin-starred restaurants and easy access to the Rocky Mountains occupy some days, while sport on tap awaits on every other.

Bring your shorts, and a Broncos jersey.

For more information, visit visitdenver.com.

Sports.title: Fantastic Fleetwood seal shootout success in Carabao Cup shock against Arsenal
Sports.content:
It is more than 20 years since Arsenal played at Highbury but their trip to League Two Fleetwood – and a stadium of the same name – did not bring back fond memories as they were dumped out of the Carabao Cup on penalties. It was the team with red shirts and white sleeves that triumphed, but on this occasion it caused one of the greatest upsets in English football history.

Aaron Loupalo-Bi and Viktor Gyökeres exchanged goals in normal time but Arsenal were unable to find a winner, despite being the dominant force, as Fleetwood battled to the end. The home manager, Matt Lawlor, was almost in tears, unable to cope after the tension was released when Conor Haughey smashed the ball into the top corner to settle the shootout.

That came after Jay Lynch had saved from Bruno Guimarães, a former warehouse worker stopping the Brazilian international. It is the storylines everyone wants but so rarely gets in the sanitised modern football world.

Fleetwood were aiming to earn £400,000 from the night but got something priceless in the end. Everyone in attendance will never forget they saw the fourth-tier side knock out the Premier League champions. Of course they had to ride their luck and were helped by Max Dowman’s debatable sending off but football is rarely about logic, it is one of emotion. This is once in a lifetime for the Cod Army, for anyone at their level, and they enjoyed it.

A year ago Lawlor was not even a football manager, he never played professionally and started his coaching career with the Manchester United Foundation. Lynch had spent much of his early career in non-league, only dreaming of playing a team who narrowly lost the Champions League final in the spring.

Everyone was expecting a routine victory, even with Mikel Arteta giving youngsters the chance to impress. If Arteta wanted to test his youngsters then Marli Salmon’s naivety was shown up by Loupalo-Bi, on loan from Fulham.

He has been learning his trade in the fourth tier this season and put into practice the skill of using his body against a defender, spinning and holding off the 17-year-old before slotting under Illan Meslier to bring lift-off for the second time of the night.

View image in fullscreen Aaron Loupalo-Bi fires Fleetwood into a first-half lead. Photograph: Jon Super/Reuters

By that point the game had already had a six-minute delay due to a drone being flown above the pitch. The referee Michael Salisbury had to take the players to the sidelines while the police searched for the culprit outside the ground. It was an unordinary start to what became an extraordinary night on the Fylde Coast. It had started with a plethora of pyrotechnics that created a red haze across the pitch and, frankly, it never dissipated, literally or metaphorically.

The first half was one of toil for Arsenal, unable to create anything meaningful, constantly being thwarted by the disciplined defence, well organised by Lawlor and his staff. The Gunners were pedestrian against a team happy to watch them go through the motions. Kai Havertz missed the best chance to equalise before the break but his header was wayward, summing up a difficult match for him.

View image in fullscreen Bruno Guimarães’ penalty is saved by the Fleetwood goalkeeper Jay Lynch. Photograph: Nick Potts/PA

After the break it was different as Martin Ødegaard came on to become the quarterback for Arsenal, creating the rhythm they had sorely lacked. He brought cohesion and intensity, getting them back into the game.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

It was Gyökeres who bundled home the equaliser and few would have doubted Arsenal going on to win the match but Fleetwood held firm.

The home side had been direct from the start, accepting their limitations and knowing the conditions would help them. Swirling wind helped hold the ball up in the sky and confused defenders not used to the gales by the sea.

Fleetwood’s robust play irritated Arsenal and Dowman was wound up, getting himself sent off for reacting to enforcer-in-chief Harrison Neal. He was the second Gunners teenager to learn a valuable lesson of life outside the top flight after Salmon was exposed for the goal.

It may have been harsh but it was needlessly petulant from Dowman on an already challenging night for his side. Mikel Arteta had a word with him on the way off. What did Arteta say? “Something that we discussed already before the match.”

Arsenal had two late chances through Ben White and Gyökeres to settle it before the need for spot-kicks, but Lynch produced two fantastic saves as the clock went past 90 minutes to ensure it went to a fittingly dramatic finale, where he could be the hero again on a great night for football and the town of Fleetwood.

Sports.title: An unmanageable club? Carrick the latest to suffer in Manchester United’s faded grandeur
Sports.content:
Should any football club fit the Great Man theory of history it is Manchester United. In the past 100 years, only Matt Busby and Alex Ferguson have knocked the club into shape. A pair of 20th-century Scotsmen, born 15 miles apart in Bellshill and Govan respectively, found the key. Otherwise, United has been a managerial dustbin, Michael Carrick the latest likely lobbed on the pile.

Busby and Ferguson built the club around themselves, possessing the charisma to convince others that theirs was the path to follow. Carrick, an insider, a club man, is falling victim to the same isolation as his predecessors in failure. Bruno Fernandes and Lisandro Martínez going off-piste in TV interviews to depth charge Carrick were actually following club tradition. With glamour comes decadence, the faded grandeur that has so often chased a United manager out the door.

Beyond Busby and Ferguson, each United manager who also served felt the lash of desperation of a falling giant. Each of their defenestrations has featured an infighting that would not have been out of place in ancient Rome. Favouritism, nepotism, self-interest, entitlement, complacency and sentimentality have been the betrayal of a legend, to use the title of Michael Crick’s and David Smith’s “j’accuse” book from 1989. Living with the legend and influence of those two managers leads the list of difficulties.

United fans know such history too well. “You lousy bastards, you let him down,” Brian Kidd told teammates when the bullet came for Wilf McGuinness, Busby’s immediate successor, in December 1970. Busby himself had done the deed. A December 1972 meeting at Selhurst Park with Tommy Docherty as Crystal Palace beat United 5-0 hastened the end for Frank O’Farrell.

View image in fullscreen Alex Ferguson shows off the team hat and scarf after his appointment as Manchester United manager in November 1986. Photograph: Gerry Crowther/Mirrorpix/Getty Images

Docherty’s turn came. His sacking in 1977 after an affair with the physio’s wife was announced by the club secretary, Les Olive, from behind the oak door of the chairman Louis Edwards’ Cheshire mansion. Dave Sexton was sacked in 1981 despite winning his last seven matches. Falling attendances at “Cold Trafford” did for “Whispering Dave”. Ron Atkinson turned his November 1986 sacking into a party in the office that also housed the club sunbed. Big Ron’s parting gift was the hangovers that greeted Ferguson’s first day in charge.

Ferguson’s predecessors had been intimidated by the fog of pipe smoke wafting down Old Trafford’s corridors. O’Farrell had needed to ask Busby if the former manager could vacate the manager’s office. “A fantasy world” is how O’Farrell described Busby’s coterie of gossipy former players who teed off with “the old man” at Davyhulme golf course. “There was no reality in the myth,” the Corkman dubbed “O’Failure” said in 1991.

Busby’s indulgence of George Best, careering towards oblivion, created problems O’Farrell found unsolvable. Docherty showed the political wiles to jettison Best in January 1974 but also shelling Bobby Charlton, Denis Law and Paddy Crerand created enemies. Falling in love with Mary Brown, with whom Docherty remained for the rest of his life, was enough for a boardroom moral majority to rid themselves of their turbulent manager.

Ferguson’s successors must deal with his continued presence, the face in the crowd photographers and TV directors seek. His patronage of Malcolm Glazer’s 2005 takeover is a dubious legacy dragging down those who have followed him. Ferguson mostly keeps his own counsel, a well-remunerated club ambassador until Sir Jim Ratcliffe cancelled a £2m annual stipend in 2024. There have been slips. “You should always start with your best players,” Ferguson told the mixed martial arts fighter Khabib Nurmagomedov in 2021 when Ole Gunnar Solskjær had dropped Cristiano Ronaldo, loose talk escaping to social media.

Ferguson’s part in Ronaldo’s disastrous return to Old Trafford evidenced continuing back-channel influence, echoing Busby and Best. Carrick, during his press conference last Friday, mentioned his chats with his former boss. The omission of Fernandes for the Bournemouth game, left to sulk on the bench in club tracksuit, was classic Fergie politics.

View image in fullscreen The Sir Matt Busby statue alongside the Manchester United club crest at Old Trafford. Photograph: Conor Molloy/ProSports/Shutterstock

A Ferguson facsimile is a fool’s errand. Carrick might have learned the lessons dished out to Solskjær, to whom he was assistant. After refusing to use Ferguson’s parking space and misty-eyed chat of “the boss”, nobody was buying the affable, gentle Norwegian cosplaying as a Glaswegian hard man.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Not that an injection of the alpha male has been much more use. Time has been kinder to the Louis van Gaal and José Mourinho regimes as subsequent failures pile up, but both failed to embrace the expectations of attacking football.

Not that other club traditions were avoided. The subterfuge that brought in Mourinho was as dastardly as any of the post-Busby knifings. “People know him as a larger-than-life character,” the executive vice-chairman Ed Woodward said on Van Gaal’s 2014 appointment. “My wife had to find out when she was in the lift with Woodward’s family,” Van Gaal said of finding, in the haze of celebrating the 2016 FA Cup final victory, that he was being replaced. His former Barcelona assistant had successfully lobbied Woodward. Attempts have been made by the Glazers’ operatives and, since December 2023, Ratcliffe’s Ineos, to corporatise and professionalise but United’s innate excess and anarchy keeps overtaking rationale.

View image in fullscreen José Mourinho during his tenure as Manchester United manager, in November 2018. Photograph: Nigel Roddis/EPA

Using the means of a Netflix special, Mourinho has retrofitted his part in the story, he and Ferguson revealing together the fact he turned United down in 2013. The inference is that if Mourinho had arrived then all would have been roses. It is an unconvincing attempt at airbrushing both men’s reputations. Where does that leave David Moyes, the immediate successor painted as afterthought? In July 2013, Ferguson was celebrated as kingmaker, Moyes the rightful heir.

Moyes’s reputation is another enhanced by failures that followed, including Mourinho’s grumpy, fractious tenure. When emerging reluctantly from his Lowry Hotel bolthole, the Portuguese reduced himself to mocking club history with “football heritage” rants. Such a scorched-earth policy was echoed by Ruben Amorim, while Erik ten Hag’s retention by Ineos in summer 2024 was as confusing to Ten Hag as to everyone else.

An unmanageable club? Busby and Ferguson showed it can be done, though the chance of another empire recedes the longer the vanity, plotting and self-interest that personify United continues. And for that, Busby and Ferguson deserve a share of the blame.

Sports.title: Arise, Sir Harry? Downing Street hints at Kane knighthood after Ballon d’Or win
Sports.content:
Downing Street has hinted that Harry Kane deserves a knighthood, ­praising the England captain’s “extraordinary achievement” as the first English winner of the Ballon d’Or in 25 years.

The prime minister’s spokesperson said Andy Burnham sent praise and congratulations to the England captain, who was announced as the men’s winner of football’s most prestigious individual award at a ceremony on Monday night.

No 10 said it hoped it would be the prelude to a trophy to celebrate with England “before too long” – alluding to hopes of an England win when the country co-hosts the European Championship in 2028 with Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.

11:25 Harry Kane triumphs with historic Ballon d’Or win - The Latest

The Bayern Munich player is the first Englishman to win the award since Michael Owen in 2001.

“The PM would like to congratulate Harry Kane on winning the Ballon d’Or,” the spokesperson said. “To be the first Englishman to win it in 25 years is an extraordinary achievement, and what a moment to do it here at home.

“Seventy years after Sir Stanley Matthews won the inaugural award, it caps a remarkable season and Harry continues to set a brilliant example to young players across the country, and the PM knows the whole nation will be incredibly proud of him. And, hopefully, there’s another trophy to celebrate with England before too long.”

Asked whether Burnham would like to see Kane receive a knighthood, she said: “I think everyone would agree, Harry Kane has given an enormous amount to English football, and this is a very special moment for him and the country, but, as ever, I’m not going to pre-empt the honours process.”

Kane received the award at a ceremony at the London Palladium on Monday night, beating Kylian Mbappé of Real Madrid and Barcelona’s Lamine Yamal. He is the fifth English player to win the award, the list also including Kevin Keegan and Sir Bobby Charlton.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Burnham cannot decide whether to hand Kane a knighthood, but ministers and departments can make recommendations to the honours committee, as can private individuals. The sport committee includes the presenter Sue Barker and the chief executive of the Football Foundation, Robert Sullivan.

Kane holds an MBE, awarded after England’s success in reaching the semi-finals in the 2018 World Cup. Players are often not awarded knighthoods until after retirement. The former England captain Sir David Beckham received his knighthood last year, as did the former England player and manager Sir Gareth Southgate.

Before those awards, the most recent was the former Scottish player and Liverpool manager Sir Kenny Dalglish. Owen, also a former Liverpool player, has not received a knighthood, and nor did Keegan, the former Newcastle player and manager who was also England’s captain and manager.

Sports.title: Kane’s Ballon d’Or triumph a glorious riposte to celebrity fawning of ceremony | Barney Ronay
Sports.content:
Well, there’s something new. Football: now available in new, genuinely heartwarming flavour.

There was a lovely moment at London’s Palladium theatre on Monday, with the clock creeping towards 11pm at the end of a startlingly shrill and bloated evening of never‑ending awards and never-ending award‑related excitement.

Not just for Harry Kane, who is now the 2026 men’s Ballon d’Or winner, and in the process placed indelibly in that lineage of elite footballers. But also, frankly, for anyone watching, as Kane stood on stage gazing a little shyly at his golden orb, and kicked off his speech by thanking everyone, paying tribute to everyone, everywhere, then finally cracking into tears and a strangled croak as he thanked his parents for sacrifices made, his wife for always being there, and even, in slightly jarring vibe-shift from the warm honeyed tone, José Mourinho.

11:25 Harry Kane triumphs with historic Ballon d’Or win - The Latest

Even Kane’s biggest advocates will rarely claim their man is one of a kind, sui generis, in the mode of the Ronaldo-Messi godhead. But Kane is exactly this in his own admirably humble way.

Not just an exceptional footballer, the best, most deserving men’s player in the world this year, a European golden boot, scorer of 89 goals since August 2025, Bundesliga champion, World Cup semi-final captain, model of extreme professionalism and care. He’s also quite clearly the nicest man, if not just in football, then possibly the world.

Or at least it felt like that as he walked off in that very dear and tender way, the centre of the world in that moment, but also just keen to get off the stage and let everyone get on with clearing up.

It would be wrong to say Kane’s victory in the final vote of the night redeemed the grotesqueness of the ceremonies itself. There was a roomful of hugely deserving winners here. But Kane hits particularly hard.

View image in fullscreen Alexia Putellas and Harry Kane pose with their trophies at the end of the 2026 Ballon d’Or awards ceremony in London. Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPA

And the Ballon d’Or is, let us be clear, a horrendous event, albeit a supremely popular horrendous event. There was the usual pomp around the ceremony, staged this year at a fancy theatre close to Oxford Circus.

This isn’t sport. It’s celebrity culture, red‑carpet fawning, the worship of images and people, and fame. Football isn’t supposed to be cocooned this way, to send the message that there are barriers and ropes and special people. Yeah, well, good luck with that.

The night kicked off with French Montana in spotless white tuxedo performing on an open-air double-decker bus. He definitely speaks, clearly, carried well, seemed enthusiastic. If it all goes south from here, the evidence suggests French Montana could, at the very least, get a job as a London tour bus operator.

View image in fullscreen French Montana performs during Ballon d’Or award ceremony in London. Photograph: Rasid Necati Aslim/Anadolu/Getty Images

Before long Thierry Henry and Kate Scott glided on stage, half an hour late, to add a little deft and easy charm to a furious schedule of pots and prizes.

And the awards came thick and fast. The Spain manager, Luis de la Fuente, was named coach of the year. “I hope in the future I will become in English better,” were his first words at the lectern, throwing his hat in the ring for a disastrous pension-padding six months at Manchester United two years from now.

There was a lovely moment as Burna Boy came on to present the Socrates award for charitable works to Bukayo Saka. He was asked if there were footballers who had inspired his love for the game. At which point he looked at Thierry and said, “definitely, one of them’s standing right there”, and of course he said it in his Burna Boy voice, looking Thierry deep in the eyes so smooth and deep, just almost an impossibly sexy moment.

The Ballon d’Or can be unintentionally hilarious at times such as these. There were just so, so many video tributes, so much excitingly portentous music. This is a stage where everyone happening at every moment is very clearly the most important thing ever to happen, superseded only by the next thing to happen on that stage, and then the thing after that.

View image in fullscreen The hosts of the ceremony: Kate Scott and Thierry Henry. Photograph: Matthew Childs/Action Images/Reuters

The degree of fawning is startling at first, but glazed by familiarity before long. At one point Cristiano Ronaldo appeared very briefly in a fact-cut big-screen montage and the crowd shrieked a song, clutched its hand to its fevered throat, collapsed into the aisles in sheer priapic excitement.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Although by the time the original Ronaldo emerged onstage at 10.44pm, there was a sense of the genuinely vertiginous company Kane was about to join. Ronaldo read out the name inside the envelope, and the hall collapsed into cheers and yells and roars as Kane appeared onstage.

And yes the Ballon d’Or is a fundamentally silly thing on its own terms. It jars with the basic concept of team sport, promoting instead the opposite of sport, the opposite of team culture, the modern disease of fawning parasocial engagement with star names. In many ways the world would be a better place if the Ballon d’Or was simply abolished, as an example to all who pore over reels and clips and the imagined qualities of their celebrity paramours.

But it is also fascinating, unignorable, and endlessly moreish. All the more so this time. Kane as the Ballon d’Or 2026 is a genuinely fine, uplifting, instructive moment in the spotlight.

View image in fullscreen Bukayo Saka delivers his speech after accepting the Sócrates award from Burna Boy. Photograph: Jeff Spicer/Uefa/Getty Images

It is always tempting to talk about the journey these players make. Everyone has a backstory. Most footballers come from adversity. Kane has this, in his own way, 16 years into a professional career which has names such as Leyton Orient, Millwall, Leicester and Norwich on the timelines. He was unexceptional as a junior, didn’t stand out as particularly skilful or big or outstanding in his numbers. He played as a holding midfielder for a bit while Spurs decided what to do with him.

Kane worked relentlessly. He was Millwall young player of the year in 2012, fitting bookend to the Ballon. He made it because he simply refused to go away, to stop working, honed instead the deeper skills in his quiver, the purity of his shooting, the range of his passing long and short.

And Kane is exceptional in other ways. Without ever peacocking around promoting his brand, without really trying he remains the most likable, authentic, role‑model‑ish modern-day England player. For a man who never talks big or acts big he has a happy knack of becoming the key player wherever he goes. Perhaps Kane has become cool now. He has always been likable, with that mild-mannered air of a kindly Victorian chimney sweep with a hamster in his waistcoat watch pocket. In the Bayern years, Kane has become leaner, more glossed and handsome, jawline, tan, iconic Vampire hairline.

Mainly he expresses a common confusion about what talent really is. Talent isn’t simply moments. Talent is also application, focus, craft, the ability to work, to make others better.

View image in fullscreen Harry Kane celebrates after scoring a penalty against Paris Saint-Germain in last season’s Champions League. Photograph: Christophe Ena/AP

And yet his elite career has also been oddly grudging. Somehow the idea has always been out there that Kane is undeserving of these accolades, despite his own mildness and humility, his obvious team qualities, his relentless delivery of goals, effort, leadership. It is a genuinely odd conclusion given the opposite is so manifestly true, that this is an entirely uplifting story of overachievement, of hard work and applied intelligence, as opposed to the kind of talent that just needs to be flame‑throwered in the right direction.

It is undeniably true that Kane’s levels can drop dramatically when he can’t perform at his full physical capacity. There have been moments where it has been tempting to wonder if he’s gone far enough as England’s captain in the past few years, if his body and his talent deserve a little care.

Well, that just shows how wrong you can be.

Sports.title: Pierre Sage given more time by Crystal Palace but remains under pressure
Sports.content:
Pierre Sage has been given more time to turn around Crystal Palace’s fortunes but he remains under huge pressure and could be dismissed if they lose against Tottenham on Saturday.

The Frenchman’s position was in serious doubt after another poor performance in the 2-0 defeat against Newcastle at the weekend. That followed a 5-0 thrashing against Brighton when Sage was warned that he could be dismissed if results did not improve quickly.

However the club’s chair, Steve Parish, has decided not to act given the tight turnaround in Palace’s schedule: the side face Fulham at Craven Cottage in the Carabao Cup on Wednesday, before their trip to Tottenham in the Premier League. But Sage, who attended the Ballon d’Or ceremony in London on Monday evening, is understood to have been left in no doubt that the meeting with Spurs on Saturday is crucial to his future.

Palace are 17th and have conceded 19 goals in eight Premier League matchesthis season – the highest in the division. But, it is understood, Sage retains the support of his squad, with two leading players having sent him messages saying that they still have faith he can turn things around.

Palace’s hierarchy are said to be split over whether to fire the former Lens manager after only 12 games in charge, with some in favour of bringing in Thomas Frank or Sean Dyche to steady the ship. The former Wolves manager Rob Edwards has also been mentioned as a potential contender.

There is sympathy for Sage at boardroom level given that Axel Disasi – who was signed on loan from Chelsea to replace the key defender Maxence Lacroix – has only just returned from a three-match suspension. There were also signs of improvement in the 2-2 Europa League draw at Besiktas in midweek, with Sage believed to have been delighted with Jean-Philippe Mateta’s response since returning from injury. The France striker is in the final year of his contract but failed in an attempt to have it ruled invalid by an independent Premier League tribunal and Fifa.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

There are concerns about Ismaïla Sarr, however, who missed the defeat against Newcastle after a recurrence of the groin injury that ruled him out earlier in the season. The Senegal forward has made no secret of his disappointment after Palace rejected a bid from Liverpool in the summer and Sage needs the club’s player of the year last season back on the pitch if they are to recover from a poor start to life after Oliver Glasner.

Sports.title: João Pedro out for ‘a few weeks’, reveals Alonso; Donnarumma gets Maresca’s backing
Sports.content:
1. Alonso’s Liverpool return hit by João Pedro injury layoff

Xabi Alonso will celebrate if Chelsea score at Liverpool tonight, but the manager’s attacking plan will have to change with João Pedro likely to be out until after the international break with a thigh injury.

João Pedro picked up the problem during training and faces an extended layoff after missing last Saturday’s 2-0 defeat at home by Tottenham. It is a major blow for Alonso, whose side struggled without the Brazil striker.

Chelsea will have to adjust when they visit Liverpool in the fourth round of the Carabao Cup and Alonso revealed that João Pedro would probably not be back until the end of November at the earliest.

“He has an injury on his thigh and he is going to be out for a few weeks,” Alonso said. “Let’s see how many. We don’t want to predict on that, but he’s not ready for the next games.”

Alonso clarified that João Pedro would “probably” be out until after next month’s international break, meaning he will not be available for Brazil after missing the last camp with a knee issue. For Chelsea, the question is how to play without the former Brighton forward. There was surprise at Alonso’s decision to play without a recognised striker and overlook Danny Welbeck against Spurs. Welbeck is pushing to start against Liverpool.

It will be an emotional evening for Alonso, who won the Champions League with Liverpool as a player in 2005. This will be his third game back at Anfield as an opposition manager – he lost with Bayer Leverkusen in 2024 and Real Madrid last season – and he will not hold back if Chelsea score.

“Of course I will celebrate,” the Spaniard said. “With full respect because my warmth with Liverpool was there as a player. But now, I am in a different role, I need to support my team, I need to support my club, I fight for my club and if we score, I will celebrate with whole respect.

Alonso, who travels to Anfield without the suspended Cole Palmer, was considered by Liverpool when Jürgen Klopp stepped down in 2024. “At that time I was at Leverkusen and I was aware of the situation, but I decided to stay,” he said. “That was my decision at the time.” Alonso said he never held talks with Liverpool, who instead appointed Arne Slot.

Liverpool sacked Slot last summer and replaced him with Andoni Iraola. Alonso, available after losing his job at Real Madrid last January, had already agreed to join Chelsea. He has made a promising start at Stamford Bridge, but doubts over his approach flared against Spurs, who had 68.5% possession.

Alonso was a passing midfielder who played for Pep Guardiola. He was asked whether he valued possession or saw the game in a different way. “You evolve, you adapt,” Alonso said. “You want to have possession. Knowing the context, knowing what we are building, I think that we have room for improvement in that part. I think we need to play more confidently with the ball.”

Sports.title: Police called to Florida soccer game after parents say three-year-old benched for being too good
Sports.content:
Police were called after a dispute involving the parents of a three-year-old player at a soccer game in Florida over the weekend.

The boy’s parents can be heard on police body cameras saying their son, Nevada, had been kicked out because he was too good at soccer and was embarrassing the other children. However, an organizer at the game said Nevada had pushed other children and his parents had become argumentative when their son was taken out of the game.

In police body camera footage the organizer of the event, who works for i9 Sports, a youth sports group, can be heard saying Nevada’s parents had caused a disturbance.

“The kid is good. He’s great. Really good,” the organizer says in the footage. “He’s very advanced compared to the other ones, so he’s scoring a lot of goals. But he’s pushing the kids ... So, I try to tell him, don’t push; we want to play without pushing, right?”

In audio of the 911 call, the organizer says Nevada’s mother was being “really, really disruptive, following me around and calling me names in front of this whole bunch of people.”

Nevada’s parents posted a clip of their son at the event in which he can be seen dribbling around older children with ease. The video has since gone viral. Nevada cannot be seen pushing any other children in the footage posted by his parents.

Allow Instagram content? This article includes content provided by Instagram . We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'. Allow and continue

“They’re mad at my son because he actually plays soccer. They’re literally kicking him out of this place because he’s good at soccer,” his mother says in the body camera footage. “First, they said he’s not passing, but nobody’s catching the ball when he’s passing.”

The i9 Sports worker told police they were willing to give Nevada’s parents a refund if they left.

“I just want him out. Immediately,” the organizer told police. “Just give me their names so I can give them their refund.”

The Winter Park Police Department said the family agreed to leave the event and no one was arrested.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“The family stated the game was over and they were leaving. The family was cooperative with the officers,” the department wrote in a statement on its website. “No one was arrested, trespassed, or forced to leave the park.”

i9 Sports said it was reviewing the incident and had contacted Nevada’s family.

“We are aware of concerns being shared regarding an incident at a local i9 Sports program, and we take them very seriously,” i9 Sports said in a statement. “The respectful treatment and well-being of every child and family matter deeply to us.”

One officer appeared to want to see more of Nevada though. “I kind of want to see him play. I bet he’s good,” he can be heard saying to another officer on body camera.

Sports.title: Barcelona fined £503 over their approach for Atlético Madrid star Álvarez
Sports.content:
Barcelona’s pursuit of Julián Álvarez came at a modest cost ⁠on Tuesday after the Spanish FA fined the club €602 (£503) following a complaint by Atlético Madrid over contact ⁠with ​the striker.

Atlético accused Barcelona of approaching the Argentine, whose contract runs until June 2030, ⁠without first notifying them in writing.

The sanction falls under Article 133 of the federation’s regulations. Atlético ⁠also complained to Fifa, which declared it had no ​jurisdiction over the case.

For ‌Álvarez, the repair ‌work has been rather more public.

The striker scored Atlético’s ‌winner against Deportivo La Coruna on Saturday, finding the net for a second successive match as his side moved within two points of the La Liga leaders Barcelona, before apologising for expressing his desire to join their rivals.

“It ‌was a mistake. I understand why the fans are angry. If I were a fan, ​I’d be angry too. Especially given how they’ve supported me since I arrived,” Álvarez said referring to an interview during the 2026 World Cup in which he said that ⁠he “wanted to fulfil his dream” of playing for ​Barcelona, triggering ​a transfer dispute that ​stretched through the summer transfer window.

Frequently booed by ​the home ‌fans this ​season, Álvarez ​received a standing ovation from sections of the crowd after scoring on Saturday, a sign of a thawing relationship with the Metropolitano faithful.
