World.title: Votes from Israel’s Arab citizens could help decide the election.
World.content:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of the Likud party, right, is being challenged by Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the Yashar centrist political party and a former military chief of staff.

The election in Israel on Tuesday is unlikely to yield quick answers about who might lead the next government.

Voters don’t directly pick a prime minister in Israel’s proportional parliamentary system. They choose a party or slate, the first step in determining who may be selected to try to form a government. The process is not guaranteed to succeed and can lead to another election if it does not. Here are four things to watch for.

Turnout

This is considered one of the most consequential elections in Israel’s history, and voters turned out in record numbers.

Recent polls had suggested that voter turnout could be at least as high or higher than in the last general election, in 2022. That year, slightly more than 70 percent of eligible voters — nearly 4.8 million out of nearly 6.8 million people — participated. That election followed four other votes in quick succession from 2019 to 2021 in which turnout hovered near 70 percent.

This year, there are 7.3 million eligible voters, about 540,000 more than in 2022.

The 3.25 percent threshold

Parties must clear a threshold of 3.25 percent of the total vote in order to get a seat in the Knesset, or Parliament.

But no party is expected to gain a majority of 61 parliamentary seats, according to the polls. That means there will likely be lots of post-election negotiations among those parties who pass the threshold.

Parties or lists that do not reach the threshold lose those ballots. As a result, parties and candidates lobby voters not to waste their votes on a list that seems unlikely to meet this criterion.

At least one party has also faced repeated attacks from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party and the far-right Religious Zionism party led by Bezalel Smotrich, Israel’s finance minister.

The targeted party, People of Israel, is led by Ofer Winter, a former Israeli brigadier general with hawkish views on national security. Some polls show that much of Mr. Winter’s support comes from voters who would normally choose Likud. Mr. Winter has faced claims that a vote for his party will be wasted or may end up going to the leading challengers.

While Mr. Winter initially said that he would support Mr. Netanyahu, he has refused any deals to withdraw from the race and has since signaled the pledge may have been premature.

Image Ballot boxes at the headquarters of the Israeli Central Elections Committee near the central town of Shoham this month. Credit... Jack Guez/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

Disinformation and challenges

Israeli election officials have said there is no evidence of threats to the integrity of this election in terms of widespread fraud or vote counting irregularities. But experts are concerned about disinformation campaigns undermining the vote or thwarting turnout.

Critics fear that some moves by the governing right-wing coalition may cast doubt on the outcome even before the vote happens or may thwart turnout among some voters.

Absentee voting is mostly prohibited in Israel. But by some estimates, tens of thousands of Israelis living abroad were expected to fly in to vote, a factor that could potentially swing the outcome.

Likud had filed a lawsuit challenging an initiative to fly in Israeli voters from abroad — a move widely perceived as an effort to limit opposition voters from showing up. The party had said the nonpartisan program provided benefits that could sway voters in violation of Israeli law. But it withdrew the suit this month after the initiative’s organizers agreed to limit flights and not to defray travelers’ costs.

Likud and other right-wing parties also filed motions to limit participation of several Arab candidates in the election.

The Central Elections Committee can vote to bar candidates or lists on certain grounds, such as expressing support for armed conflict against Israel. But the nation’s Supreme Court gets the final say. This month, it rejected a challenge to the Joint List, a merger of three majority-Arab parties, and to Raam, a historically Islamist party led by Mansour Abbas, who is running with Yoav Segalovitz, a former deputy minister of national security who was previously in the centrist Zionist party There Is a Future.

Voter suppression

In 2022, turnout in five of the largest Arab localities in Israel was lower, sometimes significantly, than the national figures. This year, officials in Arab communities worked to get voters to the polls in larger numbers and prepared for potential resistance.

Likud and the Religious Zionism party announced plans this month to deploy thousands of religious Jewish “observers” to “prevent fraud in voting and vote-counting in Arab communities.”

Critics contend that the presence of such observers, likely from far-right Zionist parties, was intended to intimidate Arab citizens of Israel, who make up 20 percent of the population and could be critical to the election’s outcome.

“The main issue we want to avoid is ‘fake news,’” said Abed Shahada, who leads voter turnout efforts for an organization representing mayors and other officials in Arab localities.

One major issue expected to drive voters is high crime in Arab communities. But if there are reports of or disinformation about criminal or violent episodes on Election Day that could keep people from the polls, Mr. Shahada said, teams are preparing by setting up a system to share verified information.

World.title: Norway and Finland leaders hold rare call with Putin
World.content:
The leaders of Finland and Norway have held a joint call with Vladimir Putin - rare contact between the Russian president and European leaders.

Finland's President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr StÃ¸re said the aim of the call had been to "convey messages directly regarding future negotiations" towards peace. An end to the conflict in Ukraine "will not be achieved through silence," Stubb said.

Neither side suggested the needle had been moved on ending the war, which began when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Although the Finnish leader said the conversation with Putin had been "frank and substantive," StÃ¸re added that there were "big differences in views" with Putin.

Several European leaders have recently shown willingness to engage with Russia directly, but both Stubb and StÃ¸re pointed out their initiative was taken in their capacity as neighbours of Russia, rather than on behalf of Europe as a whole.

"We've not set out to speak on behalf of anyone other than ourselves," StÃ¸re said.

Stubb added the call had been prepared in consultation with Ukraine and the US following a meeting between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, the Nordic leaders and US special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo last week.

The first trilateral US-Ukraine-Russia talks since the start of the year are tentatively planned for early November in Abu Dhabi.

Zelensky later confirmed Stubb and StÃ¸re debriefed him after the call and said he was grateful for their "active support", while his Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the call had been "the right approach".

Finland and Norway, which border Russia, initiated the 90-minute call - held from Helsinki - to "discuss Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and the diplomatic efforts to end the war and promote peace and stability in Europe", the leaders' offices said.

StÃ¸re added: "The war comes with enormous human and material costs... The suffering and destruction will impact generations."

The Kremlin said Putin told the leaders that "a just and lasting peace" would only be possible if Russia's interests were considered.

Putin also reaffirmed to the Nordic leaders what he views as the "root causes" of the conflict - his frequent shorthand for Ukraine's desire to exist as a sovereign state.

"A fair long-term peace settlement is possible only if Russia's legal interests are taken into account fully and unconditionally", Putin said.

All three parties reportedly agreed to continue their direct phone communication.

World.title: Ceasefire extended across Ukraine's Kherson region, officials say
World.content:
A ceasefire that began with the aim of getting food and medicine to the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky has been extended across the wider southern region of Kherson, according to sources.

Several thousand residents are trapped in the city with no access to food, water and electricity. On one side is the Dnipro river, while Russian forces are on the other and all the roads out are too dangerous.

However, no breaches of the truce that began early on Tuesday have so far been reported.

US First Lady Melania Trump, who helped broker the ceasefire along with Pope Leo XIV, said on Tuesday that the area involved had been expanded to provide "safe passage" for humanitarian convoys.

World.title: Mbappé sorry for 'ill-judged' Mao remark after backlash in China
World.content:
Kylian MbappÃ© has apologised for "ill-judged" comments he made about late Chinese leader Mao Zedong which led to him being dropped by several Chinese brands.

MbappÃ© had reportedly told French talk show The Bridge the meme "that makes me laugh the most, it's the one where there's a video of a guy, I think it's a Chinese dictator..." He then laughs as the clip cuts to a meme showing his face superimposed on an image resembling Mao.

The meme is part of a running joke about the Real Madrid forward being called a "dictator" because of his huge influence in football.

"My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world," MbappÃ© said in a statement.

"I apologise to everyone my words have upset."

Spain's La Liga also apologised, saying it "deeply regrets the offence that Kylian MbappÃ©'s recent comments have caused among Chinese fans".

The joke did not go down well in China, where Mao is revered by the Communist Party, despite his chaotic and often violent rule that left millions dead.

A few people came out in support of him on Chinese social media, but that is a rare response given China's tightly controlled internet, where people are expected to toe the party and government line on sensitive topics.

Few topics are as sensitive as Mao, which may explain why brands were so quick to terminate partnerships with a global sports star like MbappÃ©.

The original video is not available on the show's YouTube channel, and it's unclear when the interview hosted by Real Madrid's AurÃ©lien TchouamÃ©ni first aired. In clips that have been circulating online, MbappÃ© does not identify Mao by name. He says he "uses [the meme] with friends all the time".

The furore appeared to kick off on Monday night after Chinese football forum Dongqiudi drew attention to the comments in a statement, saying they were "inappropriate" and "hurt the feelings of Chinese people".

Screengrabs of the clip and meme have since spread quickly on Chinese social media, with people echoing this sentiment and even calling for a boycott of both the French striker and his club, Real Madrid.

But some have blurred the meme itself as well as the part of the comment they found offensive, when Mbappe refers to "a Chinese dictator".

Dongqiudi said in its statement that it was "unable to translate" his comments because they were "offensive to China and the Chinese people".

Many people are therefore also wondering what exactly Mbappe said and have responded to the angry posts and comments with questions, wanting to know more.

World.title: Lula's comeback in Brazil dents Trump's ambitions for Latin America
World.content:
If that sounds muddled, it is because the relationship between the two men is not straightforward. Trump did not explicitly endorse Lula's rival FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro, who refused to recognise the result. But Trump was a close ally of FlÃ¡vio's father, the former President Jair Bolsonaro.

When I spoke to Lula at his residence about a year ago, relations had hit rock bottom. He told me he had "no relationship" with Trump, that they had never spoken, and that he had no intention of picking up the phone. Trump had recently imposed punitive tariffs on Brazil, largely as a political response to Jair Bolsonaro's coup trial, which the US president called a "witch-hunt".

Rather than tiptoeing around Trump, as some US allies did, Lula fought back â and it paid off.

He made fiery speeches invoking Brazilian sovereignty, attacked US interference in the judicial process, and took to wearing a blue cap reading "Brazil belongs to Brazilians".

His approval ratings jumped.

He accused the Bolsonaro family, who had lobbied for the tariffs, of being unpatriotic â a blow to a political right that so often claims patriotism as its terrain.

Even some in the agricultural lobby, typically strong Bolsonaro supporters but reliant on US trade, thought Lula had a point.

The US eventually backed down and reduced the tariffs, although they have since risen again.

Relations then improved.

The two men spoke at the United Nations and later met in the Oval Office, where Trump called the talks "very good" and Lula said he left "very satisfied".

Another indication, perhaps, that Trump likes a strong leader.

World.title: Dutch zookeeper dies after being mauled by leopard
World.content:
An experienced keeper at a Dutch zoo has died days after being mauled in a leopard enclosure, the safari park has confirmed.

The woman, who had worked at Beekse Bergen park for 40 years, was caring for two Persian leopards in an indoor facility when she was attacked on Saturday.

She sustained injuries to her head and neck and had emergency surgery, but the park confirmed her death on Tuesday.

An independent investigation will be launched into the incident, it added in a statement.

Announcing her death, Beekse Bergen - in the south of the Netherlands - said the keeper began her career there when she was 17 and had worked there on-and-off for four decades.

"Her passing has deeply affected us all, and our hearts go out to her family, friends, and loved ones. At this moment, our primary focus is on supporting her family and her colleagues," the statement added.

The two leopards, which are usually kept away from staff, had been brought inside due to bad weather conditions.

It is not clear exactly what happened in the enclosure because there are no CCTV cameras inside.

Local news website NL Times reported that despite her injuries she managed to alert colleagues via her walkie-talkie. She was then taken to hospital in a helicopter in a critical condition.

A park spokesperson told Omroep Brabant, a local media outlet, that the leopards were behaving naturally and they would not be euthanised.

"They are, and remain, predators."

Beekse Bergen said it would create a memorial location for guests and staff members to share their condolences.

World.title: Ex-wife of Zimbabwe's vice-president freed after collapse of attempted murder case
World.content:
The former wife of Zimbabwe's vice-president has been freed from remand after seven years while on trial for his attempted murder.

Marry Mubaiwa was charged in 2019, after her then husband Gen Constantino Chiwenga accused her of trying to impede his medical treatment in South Africa.

Ordering her release, a magistrate said Mubaiwa had suffered mental, physical and financial prejudice during the trial, state-owned daily the Herald said.

The ruling was made after the state asked for the trial to be postponed by a month in order to engage witnesses.

Her lawyer described the ruling as a victory that had come too late, because her client's rights had been violated by the delay in the trial.

Speaking outside court in the capital Harare on Tuesday, the lawyer added that if the state moved for a new trial, they would deal with it when it happened.

Mubaiwa was accused of attempting to kill Chiwenga, while he was in hospital in Pretoria. The vice-president then went to China for four months of treatment.

Mubaiwa was remanded in custody and denied bail.

According to the New Zimbabwe news website, Mubaiwa celebrated her release outside court, and said justice had been achieved and that she was proud of her lawyer.

In 2017, Chiwenga played a key role in overthrowing then President Robert Mugabe.

World.title: Alexander brothers each sentenced to 30 years in prison in sex trafficking case
World.content:
One by one, they spoke of the psychological trauma they endured after the Alexander brothers raped them, and their desire for the shame they had felt to instead fall on the defendants.

Many asked the judge to impose the maximum sentence of life in prison for each brother.

Maya Miller told the court that after Tal Alexander raped her in 2014, she lost all sense of safety. "I carry a quiet funeral within me for the person I might've become if this never happened to me," she said.

Another victim, using the pseudoym Isa Brooks, said after being raped by Tal and Alon Alexander when she was 16, she lost the ability to trust herself.

"I had no idea the danger I was in till it was too late," she said.

Another woman said when she planned to come forward about being raped, Tal Alexander threatened her, saying he knew where her sister worked.

Prosecutor Elizabeth Espinosa said the brothers deserved the maximum punishment for their crimes, saying facts "paint a truly devastating picture".

"For years, they honed their methods of luring women with the promise of luxury," she said, adding that they were "completely unmoved by the path of suffering they left behind them."

During the women's speeches, the three Alexander brothers showed little emotion. They stared ahead or conferred with their lawyers, who said they advised their clients not to look at the victims so it couldn't be misconstrued.

Attorneys for the brothers pushed for sentences of 15 years, arguing that they had become devoted fathers whose families would suffer in their absence.

The three men all addressed the court, continuing to profess their innocence.

"We had a work-hard, play-hard mentality," Tal Alexander said, adding he saw how his behaviour "hurt people's feelings".

But their statements did not assuage Caproni, who chastised them for refusing to admit their crimes.

"How can someone who never acknowledged the wrongs they did be rehabilitated?" she asked.

At the end of the hearing, she sentenced them each to 30 years in prison for certain crimes. She also sentenced each to 20 years in prison for additional crimes, but said the men would serve the sentences concurrently.

World.title: Egypt court fines journalist Lina Attalah and orders news site's closure
World.content:
The CPJ said Mada Masr, which was founded in 2013, was a vital source of critical reporting in Egypt and that it had long faced pressure from authorities over its journalism.

The site had repeatedly sought an operating licence from the Supreme Media Regulatory Council (SMRC) since a new media law was passed in 2018, but that its applications were either rejected or left unanswered, the media watchdog added.

Amnesty International said Lina Attalah had also faced "years of harassment and intimidation", including six criminal investigations over Mada Masr's reporting.

Last week, prosecutors summoned her for questioning over allegations of publishing "false news" and operating a website without a licence.

Mada Masr's lawyer said the investigation included a recent report that the website had published about a wave of protests in prisons across the country, as well as a letter from the SMRC regarding its legal status.

Attalah was released on bail and later referred to trial before the New Cairo Misdemeanours Court on the charge of operating a website without a licence.

During Tuesday's hearing, Judge Mohammed Mubarak ordered the courtroom to be cleared of everyone except Attalah, her eight-person defence team, and Hossam Bahgat, head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), an independent human rights group.

Bahgat told AFP news agency that security personnel then filed in before the judge announced that the court was denying several procedural requests made by the defence and appointing its own lawyer for Attalah.

"In a move that astonished all those present, the judge recorded in the official court minutes that the court had appointed a lawyer from the Lawyers' Syndicate to represent the defence," he said. "Lina herself spoke up to object to this lawyer being appointed to represent her, which the judge refused to record in the court minutes.

"In an even more shocking turn, the judge proceeded to dictate motions on behalf of this lawyer - who had not uttered a single word - and entered them into the official record," he added.

The judge then announced the fine for Attalah and ordered Mada Masr's closure "amid shouts and protests from the defence", before she was detained, according to Bahgat.

On Tuesday evening, Mada Masr said it had paid the full fine to the court and that Attalah was released after several hours in custody.

"During the release procedures, Attalah learned of a one-year prison sentence issued against her in absentia in 2024, on charges of publishing false news and managing an unlicensed website," it added.

"Her lawyers took steps to challenge the ruling, with a hearing in a retrial of the case scheduled for 11 November."

Amnesty International warned that the court's verdict marked "a dark day for independent journalism" in Egypt and demanded that it be overturned.

"This draconian ruling is the culmination of years of relentless harassment and unjust proceedings designed to shut down one of the country's last remaining independent media voices," said the group's senior director for regional impact, Yasmine Ahmed.

"Lina Attalah should never have been prosecuted for exercising her right to freedom of expression and doing her journalistic job."

CPJ Regional Director Sara Qudah said: "If Egypt can put in custody one of its most respected editors and shut down her newsroom, no independent journalist in the country is safe. Attalah must be released immediately, and Mada Masr must be allowed to keep reporting."

World.title: CBD COP17: Nigeria urges developed countries to fulfil $30bn annual biodiversity funding pledge
World.content:
Nigeria has urged developed countries to fulfil their commitment to mobilise at least $20 billion annually by 2025 and $30 billion annually by 2030 to enable developing countries to effectively implement biodiversity conservation initiatives.

The Minister of Environment, Balarebe Lawal, made the call while delivering Nigeria’s national statement during the high-level segment of the ongoing 17th Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD COP17) in Yerevan, Armenia.

“Excellencies, as Founding Chair of the Ministerial Alliance for Ambition on Nature Finance, Nigeria continues to champion the mobilisation of adequate and predictable resources for biodiversity. We call for the fulfilment of the commitment to mobilise at least US$20 billion annually by 2025 and US$30 billion annually by 2030 for developing countries,” Mr Lawal said.

He said Nigeria was pleased to join the global community to reaffirm its collective commitment to protecting biodiversity and securing a sustainable future for present and future generations.

“Nigeria reaffirms its unwavering commitment to the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework and our shared ambition to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030,” he said.

Nigeria’s biodiversity targets

Nigeria completed its revised National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan (NBSAP) 2025–2030 in June 2025 and submitted it to the CBD Secretariat.

The strategy provides a national roadmap for halting and reversing biodiversity loss during its six-year implementation period.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

It aligns Nigeria’s conservation priorities with the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF) and establishes 23 national targets tailored to the country’s socioeconomic and environmental circumstances.

The targets cover critical sectors, including agriculture, forestry, infrastructure and ecosystem conservation.

The strategy also adopts a whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach, integrating biodiversity conservation into government policies and development planning while encouraging the participation of stakeholders, including Indigenous Peoples and local communities.

It further emphasises private-sector accountability and environmental risk management, including efforts to help businesses assess and disclose their dependencies on nature.

Nigeria has projected an implementation budget of approximately $474 million over six years, highlighting the need to mobilise resources to address longstanding funding gaps.

Translating commitments into action

Mr Lawal urged governments and delegates to translate their biodiversity commitments into concrete action supported by adequate financing, strong partnerships and measurable results.

He said Nigeria had continued to advance implementation since COP15, including validating its revised NBSAP in June 2025, with 23 national targets aligned with the global biodiversity framework.

He added that Nigeria had submitted its Seventh National Report to strengthen implementation, monitoring and accountability.

Mr Lawal said the country remained committed to the global 30-by-30 target of conserving at least 30 per cent of the world’s land and inland waters, as well as coastal and marine areas, by 2030.

He said Nigeria was pursuing this ambition through protected-area management, ecosystem restoration and marine conservation.

“Following the Federal Executive Council’s approval of the ratification of the BBNJ Agreement, we are advancing the necessary processes to strengthen our contribution to the conservation and sustainable use of marine biodiversity beyond national jurisdiction,” he said.

The BBNJ Agreement, also known as the High Seas Treaty, provides a framework for conserving and sustainably using marine biodiversity in areas beyond national jurisdiction.

Mr Lawal also said Nigeria was integrating biodiversity conservation, climate action and land restoration through the Global Environment Facility-supported Net Zero Nature Positive Project.

He stressed that effective biodiversity conservation must be inclusive and equitable, noting that Nigeria was promoting gender-responsive land governance, women’s access to land and natural resources, and their meaningful participation in environmental decision-making.

He added that the government remained committed to ensuring that women and vulnerable communities actively participated in and benefited from biodiversity conservation efforts.

Nigeria calls for stronger financing partnerships

Citing Decision 16/34 of the previous biodiversity conference, Mr Lawal advocated stronger collaboration between environment and finance ministers to integrate biodiversity considerations into national budgets, fiscal policies and development plans.

He said international financing commitments must be delivered through predictable, accessible and additional resources, complemented by domestic resource mobilisation, private-sector investment and reforms to harmful incentives.

He also highlighted the importance of technology transfer, capacity-building and institutional strengthening, particularly for developing countries.

Nigeria, he said, was calling for greater coordination among the three Rio Conventions on biodiversity, climate change and desertification to maximise available resources, minimise duplication and accelerate implementation.

“Mr President, COP17 must mark a decisive turning point—from commitments to delivery. Our global ambition must be matched by adequate financing, equitable access to the means of implementation, gender-responsive action and measurable progress,” he said.

Mr Lawal said Nigeria was ready to strengthen international partnerships and work with other parties to achieve the shared 2030 biodiversity goals and secure a nature-positive future for all.

World.title: Olympic Eagles begin U-23 AFCON Qualifier preparations in Ikenne
World.content:
Nigeria’s U-23 national team, the Olympic Eagles, have commenced preparations for next month’s U-23 Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers against the Democratic Republic of Congo, with 28 players participating in Tuesday’s opening training session in Ikenne, Ogun State.

The session took place at the Remo Stars Stadium under the supervision of head coach Eric Chelle, as the team began its build-up to the crucial qualifying fixtures.

However, Rangers International trio Chimobi Igwilo, Kenneth Igboke and Chibueze Oputa were excused from the session following their arrival from Algeria, where they featured for the Enugu-based club against MC Alger in the CAF Champions League.

The Olympic Eagles are currently based in Ijebu Ode, where they are staying at the AM2PM Hotel. The team will continue its training programme at the Remo Stars Stadium, which is also expected to stage the return leg of the qualifiers.

Despite the rainy weather on Tuesday evening, the players went through a light session designed to ease them into the preparations. The training began with stretching and muscle-relaxing exercises before progressing to ball work, passing drills and small-sided games.

The four goalkeepers in camp; Chinemerem Olughu, Clinton Andy, Ebenezer Harcourt and Michael Atata, initially worked separately under the supervision of goalkeeper trainer Olatunji Baruwa before the session continued.

The coaching crew has scheduled two training sessions for Wednesday at the same venue, with the first starting at 7:30am and the second at 5pm, as preparations gather momentum ahead of the qualifiers.

World.title: Benue police rescue 29 kidnap victims, arrest 34 foreigners
World.content:
The Benue State Police Command says it rescued 29 kidnap victims and arrested 34 foreign nationals during security operations across the state in October.

The Commissioner of Police, Cletus Nwadiogbu, disclosed this on Tuesday while briefing journalists on the command’s operational achievements at its headquarters in Makurdi.

He attributed the rescues to intelligence-led operations and collaboration with other security agencies and community-based security groups.

Mr Nwadiogbu said four passengers abducted after gunmen attacked a commercial vehicle along the Uzer village axis of Ayilamo-Tse-Abi Road in Logo Local Government Area on 5 October were rescued in a joint operation involving the police, Operation Whirl Stroke, Benue State Civil Protection Guards and local hunters.

He said 17 farmers abducted from Tse-Acha and Tse-Wuam communities in Bamun village, Tombo District, Logo LGA, were rescued on 7 October.

The commissioner also said eight kidnap victims, including a Catholic priest, were rescued in Ohimini LGA following their abduction along the Ugbokolo-Ajegbe-Awume Road on 13 October.

PREMIUM TIMES earlier reported that police announced the rescue of eight victims and the arrest of two suspects after the abduction along the road.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The police statement at the time did not confirm whether the rescued victims included Reverend Father John Inalegwu Otache, who was reported abducted on the same day.

Foreign nationals arrested

Mr Nwadiogbu said the command arrested 34 foreign nationals in two separate operations during the month.

He said 16 Cameroonian nationals were arrested in Otukpo LGA on 9 October after they allegedly failed to produce the required travel documents.

On 22 October, operatives intercepted 18 Nigerien nationals at Orokam while they were reportedly travelling to Ikom in Cross River State.

The commissioner said the foreign nationals were taken into custody for investigation and verification of their immigration status, with the relevant authorities, including the Nigeria Immigration Service, to be involved.

He said investigations were ongoing to establish the circumstances of their entry into Nigeria and movements within the country.

Other arrests and recoveries

The police commissioner also reported arrests in separate operations against suspected cultists and other suspected offenders in Naka, Makurdi, Aliade and Gwer East.

He said the command recovered seven locally fabricated firearms, 16 rounds of ammunition and cartridges, charms, mobile phones and ATM cards during the operations.

Mr Nwadiogbu further disclosed that a suspected bandit was killed during an encounter involving Operation Zenda personnel along Amaafu-Abaji Road in Katsina-Ala LGA on 2 October. A locally fabricated firearm was recovered during the operation.

In a separate case, the commissioner said police arrested a 60-year-old man over the alleged rape of a 10-year-old girl in Igumale, Ado LGA.

He said the incident was reported on 13 October and the victim was taken for medical examination and treatment. He added that investigations were ongoing and that the victim’s privacy and welfare would be protected.

Mr Nwadiogbu urged residents to provide credible information to security agencies, saying public cooperation was essential to preventing crime and protecting lives and property.

World.title: Kano lawmakers back establishment of state police
World.content:
The Kano State House of Assembly on Tuesday endorsed the Bill to establish a state police service.

The assembly passed the bill during its plenary session presided over by the Speaker, Jibril Ismail-Falgore.

Mr Ismail-Falgore said the house passed the bill after deliberation on clauses 1–26 at the committee of the Whole House.

“In the committee of the whole house, we deliberated on the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999 Alteration Bill 2026 from clause 1–26.

World.title: Niger governor’s convoy crash kills four students, driver
World.content:
Five people, including four students of the Federal University of Technology, Minna, have died in a road crash involving a vehicle in the convoy of Niger State Governor Mohammed Bago.

The accident occurred on Monday at Gidan Mangoro in Minna, involving a Toyota Hilux conveying the Director-General of the Government House, Dauda Chikuba, and a vehicle carrying the students, according to a report by PUNCH published on Tuesday.

The four students and the driver of the Government House vehicle died at the scene, while Mr Chikuba was taken to a hospital for treatment, the report said.

The crash reportedly occurred as the governor’s convoy was returning to Minna after a condolence visit to the Etsu Nupe and Chairman of the Niger State Council of Traditional Rulers, Yahaya Abubakar, over the death of Sagi Nupe, Aisha.

The vehicle conveying the students was travelling towards Bida when the collision occurred.

An eyewitness quoted by PUNCH described the incident as a head-on collision and alleged that the governor’s convoy was travelling at high speed.

“It was a head-on collision. We learnt that the convoy was at high speed when the accident occurred. It was a terrible accident,” the eyewitness said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The report did not independently establish the cause of the crash.

The spokesperson for the Niger State Police Command, Wasiu Abiodun, confirmed the accident and said the police had begun an investigation.

“The accident occurred this morning, and we are investigating it,” Mr Abiodun was quoted as saying.

The police spokesperson did not disclose the identities of the deceased.

Further details about the circumstances of the collision and the condition of the injured government official were not immediately available.

World.title: TRAVELOGUE: What happened in Vegas!!!
World.content:
“What happens in Vegas stays in Vegas.” I had always considered that a remarkably convenient rule. This time, however, I broke with tradition. I returned to Las Vegas for “The Assembly,” the Association of Certified Anti-Money Laundering Specialists’ conference, and the visit gave me a few stories I could not quite leave behind.

Getting to Vegas was a story of its own. After nearly 20 hours of travel, I boarded the final leg from New York’s JFK Airport to Las Vegas, thinking the hard part was over. It was a domestic flight, so I had imagined a short hop. Five hours later, I was less certain. ‘Na this one dem dey call short flight?’ That one flight was roughly as long as flying from Lagos to Cairo.

Somewhere over the United States, I found myself thinking about the debate over how Africa appears on the world map. It is right to show the continent at its true scale. But a larger Africa on paper will mean more to its people when they can move across it more easily. We need sustainable African airlines, dependable connections and routes that spare travellers the long detours that can turn a journey between African cities into an expedition.

I had been in Vegas for “The Assembly” two years earlier. The city was as dazzling as advertised, bright lights, restless crowds, and buildings seemingly designed to win an argument with the desert. I went home with plenty to say, but obeyed the unwritten Vegas rule. I must admit, it was difficult. This year’s visit felt different. Since my previous visit, I had become more aware of another side of Vegas. Beyond the spectacular hotels and casinos, I saw people sleeping outdoors; some appeared to be struggling with drug use. How could a place that displayed so much wealth also have people living this way? This time, I decided to ask.

They say the best way to learn a city’s secrets is to ask a taxi driver. In my village, we have the ‘mai shayi.’ Order one cup of tea and, before it cools, you may know who quarrelled, who settled and who is pretending they never quarrelled in the first place. Vegas was a long way from my village, but the method travelled well. I asked my driver about the people I had seen sleeping outdoors. “No be gossip o. Na the why I dey find!”

The driver was Ethiopian. His English came in short, sometimes broken phrases, and I had to listen closely. When words failed him, his hands took over. He opened one palm towards the casinos, then drew a small circle in the air as he described a path from gambling to drugs, financial distress and, for some, homelessness. I understood his point. “This is Vegas,” he said. It was one driver’s account, not an explanation for every person I had seen, but his gesture stayed with me, the circle he drew against a backdrop of dazzling buildings.

Vegas also brought back a very different memory. Tupac Shakur was killed in this city, but long before I visited it, his music had already found its way into my secondary school years. In “Changes,” he spoke of a “war on poverty” and questioned why public attention seemed to favour a war on drugs instead. Decades later, I found that question more demanding than I had as a student. It asks whether we measure progress only by the problems we confront, or also by the lives we help improve. It is a question I explored more fully in an earlier PREMIUM TIMES article, “Nigeria’s violence is not holy war; it’s sustained state of deprivation.” There, I argued that we cannot understand violence through its slogans alone; we must also examine deprivation, corruption and the public choices that allow both to persist. Tupac’s line has stayed with me since school.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

I never learned to rap, an outcome for which my loved ones should probably be grateful. But that did not stop me from taking the stage at a social night at Federal Government College Kaduna almost three decades ago. I mimed Usher’s “Can U Get Wit It” before an audience. Whether they got with it is a question I have wisely never investigated. Tupac’s words, though, were the ones I learned to listen to. Tupac was killed in Las Vegas in 1996. Thirty years later, and shortly before my return to the city, a jury convicted Duane Davis of his murder. The timing was striking. I had come for conversations about financial crime and accountability, in a city where another long pursuit of accountability had just reached a verdict.

That question of accountability followed me into “The Assembly.” At a session on Artificial Intelligence (AI) and financial crime, Tony Eastin of Google made two points that stayed with me. First, institutions spend heavily on people and processes, yet still miss warning signs that AI can help identify much faster. Second, the contest is unequal: a fraudster needs to get through the defences only once, while those protecting the system cannot afford to miss that one attempt.

AI seemed to find its way into every session I attended. At first, I wondered whether it was taking over the conference. Then my thoughts turned homeward. How prepared was Africa for this change? More particularly, what was Nigeria doing to make it useful to its people? I met a few Nigerian bankers and government officials at the conference.

Their presence brought the conversation closer to home. I found myself wondering how the ideas discussed in Vegas could translate into safer banking and better public services in Nigeria. Being part of the conversation was a useful start; putting the lessons to work would be the real test. For an ordinary Nigerian, the question need not begin with how the technology works. It can begin with something familiar: could it help protect the money in my account? Could it shorten the time I spend chasing a document in a government office? Could it help a teacher with paperwork and leave more time for teaching? These are the kinds of results that would make the excitement worthwhile.

Some of these possibilities were already being tested. In January 2025, the government announced the launch of DeepTechReady, involving 3MTT, Data Science Nigeria and support from Google.org, with a target of training 20,000 young Nigerians in AI and data skills. But training must lead somewhere. Our young people need opportunities to apply what they learn; in banks, schools, hospitals and public offices. Otherwise, we will keep applauding their potential at home and celebrating its fulfilment abroad. Consequently, we must get the basics right through affordable internet, steady power supply and accurate records. If an office cannot find your file today, an expensive AI system will not automatically perform the miracle tomorrow.

For Africa, and Nigeria in particular, the ambition should be to use AI and help build tools that understand our languages and solve our everyday problems. Progress should be measured by what improves for ordinary people, such as safer savings, quicker services and better opportunities for the talent we already have. But enthusiasm must come with judgment.

These reflections reminded me of my late Political Economy lecturer, Mohammed Wader, who introduced me to the seminal works of Samir Amin, Andre Gunder Frank and Immanuel Wallerstein. Years later, in Vegas, Mr Amin’s idea of delinking felt close at hand; our engagement with the world should serve our own development needs. For Nigeria, that means embracing AI while giving our people room to build it. Otherwise, we may enter the revolution with plenty of subscriptions and very little say in its direction.

Furthermore, Eli Wachs, CEO and co-founder of Footprint, emphasised another point that stayed with me. He posits that human oversight remains essential, as trained professionals retain ultimate responsibility for decisions made with the assistance of AI. The machine may draw attention to something unusual; a person must still examine the facts. An innocent customer should not suffer simply because a computer sounded certain. That thought took my mind back to Kaduna. In a recent Daily Trust report, the Vice Chancellor of Ahmadu Bello University, Professor Adamu Ahmed, warned that AI must not replace critical thinking. He urged postgraduate students to verify what these tools produced and remain responsible for their work. That advice belonged in the Vegas conversation too. Whether we are doing some analysis or protecting someone’s savings, “the computer said so” should never be the end of the discussion.

I left “The Assembly” convinced that Nigeria should embrace this revolution with purpose. Start with problems people recognise. Give our young people room to work. Check the results, correct the mistakes and build on what succeeds. Earlier in the journey, I had thought about Africa’s size on the map. In the conference halls, I found myself thinking about its place in the future. We should have a hand in shaping that future, and ordinary people should be able to feel the difference.

Away from the conference, there was another suggestion from my taxi driver to consider. Before we parted, he had encouraged me to try the Big Apple Coaster at (New York Hotel & Casino). One evening, I took his advice and joined the queue. The ride climbed 203 feet, dropped as far as 144 feet and reached 108 kilometres per hour. I had read those figures already. Standing beneath the track gave them a new meaning. Then India came back to me. I had once tried a ride there that was nowhere near this high, yet it frightened me enough to leave a lasting impression. In the Vegas queue, my adventurous self argued that the India experience had prepared me. My other self replied that India was precisely the reason I should go back to my hotel room with its mountain view and make a cup of coffee. Every time the coaster roared overhead, that second voice presented fresh evidence.

Still, I moved forward with the queue. I had come all the way to Vegas. Surely I could manage a roller coaster? Then I remembered that the Vice President of the United States was roughly my agemate, though, between us, “I senior the guy small.” At our age, I thought, one must learn to distinguish courage from unnecessary research into gravity. I stepped out of the queue with what I hoped looked like the composure of an elite observer. A few steps later, I was moving rather faster than an elite observer should. My taxi driver had encouraged adventure; I had listened, considered it carefully and made an honourable retreat. “No be every height person must conquer. Me, dis life no tire me o.” I love my Naija.

One of my more mischievous friends warned me to “be careful with the Vegas nightlife.” “They call it Sin City,” he reminded me, with rather more enthusiasm than concern. My dear friend, Sin City has no case against me. By the time the nightlife began, I was in my room, fast asleep. My body was still eight hours ahead, operating on Nigerian time and refusing all requests to adjust. If anyone claims otherwise, my pillow is my witness. So, there you have it, nothing happened in Vegas. Vegas happened around me while I slept.

Even leaving Vegas came with its own small drama. On the flight back to New York, three hours seemed to disappear. New York was three hours ahead of Vegas, so flying east meant moving the clock forward. The local arrival time made the journey look three hours longer than the time I had actually spent travelling. I had not lost those hours in the air, but it certainly felt as though the day was getting away from me. On the outward journey, travelling west had lent me those hours. Coming back, the clock collected its debt. No be only bank dey recover loan.

Let me leave you here and munch the last of the cheese-flavoured Doritos I imported from Vegas. During the conference, jet lag kept me sleepy, but the Doritos kept me going. Now the packet is almost empty. After everything we went through together, finishing it feels like saying goodbye to a friend. “Ha! Doritos fit stay for Vegas, but these lessons must reach Naija. We no fit travel that far come back with only crumb.”

World.title: Nigerian govt approves N70,000 monthly transport allowance for workers
World.content:
The federal government has approved a ₦70,000 monthly transport allowance for public service workers across all levels for six months, beginning in November 2026, following a conciliation meeting with the Nigeria Labour Congress (NLC).

The resolutions were contained in a statement signed by Annah Daniel, the head of press and public relations at the Ministry of Labour and Employment.

The approval was one of the resolutions reached at a meeting between government officials and the NLC leadership in Abuja on Tuesday, as both parties discussed workers’ welfare, the national minimum wage and outstanding allowances.

The government also approved the payment of peculiar allowance arrears, effective from 1 May 2026, in three equal monthly instalments beginning in November.

However, the parties failed to agree on the effective date for implementing the national minimum wage. They agreed that the Minimum Wage Negotiation Committee would be constituted and begin meetings immediately.

The resolutions were contained in a memorandum of understanding issued after the meeting, which was chaired by the Minister of Labour and Employment, Muhammad Dingyadi.

The NLC delegation was led by its president, Joe Ajaero.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The meeting followed an earlier conciliation session held on 22 October, convened by the Ministry of Labour and Employment to address disagreements between the government and organised labour.

Under the resolutions, the government also agreed to settle 19 months of outstanding allowances for health workers within three months, beginning in December 2026.

On tax relief for workers, the parties agreed that the matter would be referred to the NLC’s National Executive Council, as taxation is a statutory matter.

The meeting also considered the payment of hazard allowances to agricultural workers. The Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security has submitted the list of beneficiaries and the associated costs to the National Salaries, Incomes and Wages Commission for verification.

The commission is expected to complete the verification within two weeks and issue an implementation template afterwards.

On the Consolidated Health Salary Structure (CONHESS), the commission is expected to update the cost implications within three weeks to enable the Presidential Committee on Salaries to decide on the proposed adjustment.

The meeting urged state and local governments to adopt the intervention measures. Labour unions were also encouraged to push for their implementation at their respective levels.

Both parties agreed to reconvene after one month to assess progress on the implementation of the resolutions.

The meeting was attended by the Director-General of Budget, Tanimu Yakubu; the Permanent Secretary of the Service Welfare Office in the Office of the Head of the Civil Service of the Federation, Garba Abdul; and other government and labour representatives.

World.title: A guide to IFRS S1 and S2 sustainability implementation (4), By Innocent Okwuosa
World.content:
In a future amendment of the Sustainability Reporting Guideline (SRG Two), we will advocate for FRC to include Sustainability Practices Framework or Policy as an additional document to be submitted to it. Sustainability Practices should speak to a Sustainability Strategy to present an overall picture of how an entity is responding to or plans to respond to Sustainability Related Risks and Opportunities.

The implementation of IFRS S1 and S2 must not be approached strictly from a regulatory compliance perspective. Rather, it should lead to a change in a responsible business behaviour. For there to be this change, sustainability practices must be integrated and embedded in an entity’s operations. Today I want to provide more clarification and guidance on this.

One of the documents in the Financial Reporting Council’s (FRC) Phase Two implementation, requires an entity to identify all Sustainability Related Risks and Opportunities (SRROs) that could reasonably be expected to affect its prospect and carry out a materiality assessment of each identified SRRO. The materiality assessment enables the entity to zero in on those relevant SRROs for prioritisation. Materiality assessment is predicated on the likelihood/probability and magnitude of occurrence.

The magnitude of occurrence speaks directly to financial materiality i.e. SRRO’s effect on financial performance, position, cash flow, and access to or costs of capital. Prioritisation should be predicated on the SRROs with the highest financial effect, determined as likelihood/probability of occurrence multiplied by the magnitude. It is not my intention to go into the intricacies involved in this determination, but ultimately the entity would identify and prioritise the SRROs that could affect its prospect.

As such, the integration of sustainability begins with the entity identifying the sustainability practices that address the identified and materially assessed SRROs. Then, the entity must first update its Risk Register to include all the identified and materially assessed sustainability related risks. By doing this it would have acknowledged that they are part of the risks that it will now have to deal with and manage, going forward. If after Phase Two, an entity has not updated its Risk Register to include sustainability related risks, then there is outstanding work to be done. These form part of the risks to be integrated in the entity’s wider Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) framework. The ERM is a Phase Three document, and so it will be covered in future series.

Let us now focus on the sustainability practices to address the identified and materially assessed sustainability related risks. The implementation of IFRS S1 and S2 should embed sustainability practices within an entity’s operation, but this is not always the case, especially when implementation has been approached from a regulatory compliance perspective. The starting point in addressing the identified sustainability related risks is for the entity to come up with sustainability practices that will help manage these risks.

By instituting practices that address the SRRO, sustainability disclosures will now be about an entity’s sustainability practices. Such practices can be articulated in a document called its Sustainability Practices Framework or Policy. The implementation of IFRS S1 and S2 should result in the production of this Framework or Policy. Let us take the example of a brewery where the industry guidance shows that water is a sustainability risk facing that industry. Having identified and materially assessed this risk, then the question would be what practice the entity is putting in place to manage water. This would then form part of what is contained in the Sustainability Practices Framework or Policy.

Energy management is a material sustainability risk in the hotel business, hence the practices an entity in this industry puts in place to manage energy are part of its sustainability practices. In the financial sector, integration of ESG in credit analysis and investment management is a sustainability risk. What practices a financial institution has put in place to address this forms part of what is captured in its Sustainability Practices Framework or Policy. We can go on and on. You can now understand why identification and materiality assessment holds the key to the integration of sustainability practices in an entity’s operation.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The above explains why IFRS S2 requires the disclosure of certain industry specific metrics as a way of measuring performance on sustainability practices. That is why IFRS S2 will require an entity, for instance, in the food and beverage industry to disclose its energy management practices through metrics like (1) operational energy consumed, (2) percentage grid electricity, and (3) percentage renewable and water management practices through other metrics like (1) total water withdrawn, (2) total water consumed; percentage of each in regions with High or Extremely High Baseline Water Stress. Sustainability practices are what lead to reduction in energy and water consumption, thereby mitigating their impacts on the environment.

Evidence from the field shows that what I have stated above about a Sustainability Practices Framework or Policy is challenged, and I want to dwell a little bit on this. The first challenge stems from the fact that the FRC documentation does not require an entity to submit a Sustainability Practices Framework or Policy. Rather, what FRC requires in Phase Two is a Sustainability Disclosure Policy, and this is understandable since FRC’s focus is on reporting and disclosures, which are its mandate.

During implementation, some entities show that they have ESG or Sustainability Policy or Framework, and when one looks at these, one discovers that they are full of aspirational statements such as: “we believe the environment should be good for all,” “we will ensure we cause no damage to people and the environment and will work harmoniously with communities where we operate,” etc. In all, we see genuine intentions to evolve sustainability practices by these entities, but the missing link is evolving actual practices that address the identified and materially assessed sustainability-related risks, as opposed to just crafting aspirational statements.

Another challenge is that the existing ESG or Sustainability Framework or Policy serves different purposes and does not always mean the same thing from one entity to another. In one entity, it may contain those aspirational statements and embed the entity’s ERM and list of operational and conventional risks the entity is managing. In others, it tends towards a disclosure framework and risk governance structure. Thus, existing ESG or Sustainability Framework or Policy does not strictly address Sustainability Practices deployed to manage identified and materially assessed SRRO.

However, there are some entities in the financial sector that have done very well in articulating practices around how ESG has been integrated into their credit analysis following sustainable banking principles, but limitations still exist as these do not address financed emission, which is understandable. Similarly in other sectors, sustainability practices to manage sustainability risks are in place. In all, they do not always address all identified SRROs which IFRS S1 and S2 implementation will trigger.

Where the entity is now asked to produce the right Sustainability Practices Framework or Policy in line with the exigencies of IFRS S1 and S2 implementation, the challenge becomes the fact that it is not part of what FRC has specified, leaving it at the discretion of the entity to produce as an internal document. Yet, it is advisable for entities to still produce Sustainability Practices Frameworks or Policies, as if it is part of what should be submitted to FRC, even if they are internal documents, as these mark the beginning of embedding sustainability practices within the operation of the entities.

In a future amendment of the Sustainability Reporting Guideline (SRG Two), we will advocate for FRC to include Sustainability Practices Framework or Policy as an additional document to be submitted to it. Sustainability Practices should speak to a Sustainability Strategy to present an overall picture of how an entity is responding to or plans to respond to Sustainability Related Risks and Opportunities. In this lies the integration of sustainability practices into an entity’s operation and a change in business behaviour, since practices are bound to change behaviour. TO BE CONTINUED.

Innocent Okwuosa is the immediate past chair, NIRC; the 59th president of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Nigeria, and an adjunct associate professor at Pan Atlantic University, Lekki, Lagos.

World.title: Five epic cup shocks after Arsenal’s League Cup humiliation
World.content:
Fleetwood Town’s Irish striker #19 Ronan Coughlan (C) and Fleetwood Town’s English manager Matt Lawlor celebrate winning the English League Cup fourth round football match between Fleetwood Town and Arsenal at Highbury Stadium in Fleetwood, north west England, on October 27, 2026. Fleetwood won the match 5-3 following a penlaty shoot out. (Photo by Darren Staples / AFP) / RESTRICTED TO EDITORIAL USE. No use with unauthorized audio, video, data, fixture lists, club/league logos or ‘live’ services. Online in-match use limited to 120 images. An additional 40 images may be used in extra time. No video emulation. Social media in-match use limited to 120 images. An additional 40 images may be used in extra time. No use in betting publications, games or single club/league/player publications. /

Arsenal suffered a stunning League Cup fourth-round defeat at fourth-tier Fleetwood on Tuesday.

The Premier League champions lost 5-3 on penalties after a 1-1 draw in one of the greatest shocks in the history of English football.

AFP Sport looks at five other epic cup upsets:

Wrexham 2 Arsenal 1 (1992 FA Cup)

The previous season 90 places had separated the two clubs in the English Football League, with Arsenal having claimed their second title in three seasons under manager George Graham.

Alan Smith put the Gunners in front, but Mickey Thomas’s free-kick levelled matters with 10 minutes remaining and Steve Watkin astonishingly claimed a late winner.

Chelsea 2 Bradford 4 (2015 FA Cup)

Chelsea won the FA Cup five times between 2006 and 2018, but Jose Mourinho’s Blues were humbled by third tier Bradford at Stamford Bridge.

The Premier League leaders went 2-0 up through Gary Cahill and Ramires.

But Bradford stormed back and goals from Jon Stead, Filipe Morais, Andy Halliday and Mark Yeates left Chelsea in tatters.

Hereford 2 Newcastle 1 (1972 FA Cup)

The fourth-round tie that had everything: pitch invasions by Parka-clad fans and Ronnie Radford scoring one of the FA Cup’s greatest FA Cup goals.

Malcolm Macdonald put Newcastle ahead eight minutes from time and it seemed as if there would be no fairytale for the non-league outfit.

But Radford equalised with a screamer from 25 yards and Ricky George won it for Hereford in extra-time.

Liverpool 0 Wimbledon 1 (1988 FA Cup)

Wimbledon’s ‘Crazy Gang’ were given no chance to stop Liverpool from claiming a league and cup double in the final at Wembley.

Wimbledon had been a third-tier side four years earlier and Liverpool had won the title by a margin of nine points.

But Lawrie Sanchez headed home from Dennis Wise’s free-kick before Wimbledon keeper Dave Beasant saved John Aldridge’s penalty to seal the upset.

Grimsby 2 Manchester United 2, Grimsby won 12-11 on penalties (2025 League Cup)

United trailed 2-0 as Grimsby duo Charles Vernam and Tyrell Warren scored to expose the flaws in their supposedly superior opponents.

Bryan Mbeumo and Harry Maguire managed to take the second-round tie into extra-time.

But Grimsby won on penalties to leave then-United boss Ruben Amorim shell-shocked.

AFP

World.title: ‘A very sad day’: Arteta despair as Arsenal stunned by Fleetwood
World.content:
Mikel Arteta said Arsenal’s stunning League Cup defeat by fourth-tier Fleetwood was “a very sad day” as the Premier League champions suffered one of the most embarrassing results in their history.

Arteta’s side crashed out 5-3 on penalties in an incredible fourth round upset after the tie finished 1-1 in normal time.

Arsenal’s Bruno Guimaraes had his penalty saved by Jay Lynch in the shoot-out and Conor Haughey scored Fleetwood’s winner.

Aaron Loupalo-Bi’s first-half goal had put Fleetwood ahead before Viktor Gyokeres equalised after the interval.

Arsenal’s 16-year-old rising star Max Dowman was sent off for violent conduct in the closing stages.

Arteta paid the price for prioritising Sunday’s Premier League trip to Liverpool as his decision to make nine changes backfired spectacularly.

The Gunners boss conceded Arsenal could have no complaints, admitting it was a painful moment in his reign.

“First of all, congratulations to Fleetwood for going through the next round. The manner that they have done it, and for us a very sad day,” Arteta said.

“There is nothing to criticise the players for their attitude, their application.

“The determination, you could see that was there from the start, even with 10 men. But we conceded a really poor goal to start with that gave them some momentum.

“Obviously we have so much of the ball, so many chances, so many shots, and if you want the margins to be bigger than going to the penalties, you need to capitalise on that. And we didn’t.

“It’s football, that’s the beauty of this competition. It’s a very sad day.”

Arsenal had moved level on points with Premier League leaders Manchester City after a 2-0 victory over Everton on Saturday.

But instead of extending their run of 11 wins from their 13 previous games, Arteta’s team returned to north London red-faced after a loss that ranks among the darkest days in the club’s glittering history.

“Zero problem attitude-wise. Otherwise, I would be here absolutely fuming. I’m sad, I think we are all sad. We have a massive responsibility to carry this badge in the best possible way,” Arteta said.

“You don’t capitalise, then you cannot go through to the next round. Unfortunately, we are out.”

– ‘I just can’t believe it’ –

Although it looked a harsh decision to send off Dowman for aiming a kick towards Harrison Neal, Arteta was unimpressed with the 16-year-old, giving him a stern word as the midfielder trudged off.

“Something that we discussed already before the match,” Arteta said when asked what he told Dowman.

“It’s difficult to see on the cameras like that, so I prefer to watch it back properly and then I can assess the situation.”

Fleetwood made a mockery of the 84 places between the clubs in the English football system with a defiant display that stopped Arsenal establishing any momentum.

Their refusal to be overawed by Arsenal’s star-power was a tribute to Fleetwood boss Matt Lawlor, who won the tactical battle with Arteta by sitting deep and attacking on the counter.

“I just can’t believe it. The biggest night in the club’s history in terms of opposition coming to town and we’ve managed to beat the champions,” Lawlor said.

“We’re not stupid enough and not egotistical enough that you think we’re going to out-play the best team in the country and the most organised team in the country.

“So we had to ride our luck, we had to deny space, we had to deny options for them. And I think we did that really, really well in terms of the majority of the game.”

While Lawlor was composed during the match, his emotions poured out in his tearful celebration as jubilant Fleetwood fans invaded the pitch after the winning penalty.

“I’m just so glad that the lads have the feeling the way they are and took that performance into make that town, the club, everyone proud,” he said.

World.title: Nigerian extradited from Benin to US over alleged $100m tax fraud
World.content:
A 43-year-old Nigerian, Akinade Adedeji Raheem, has been extradited from Benin to the United States to face federal charges over an alleged scheme involving more than $100 million in fraudulent tax refund claims using stolen identities.

Raheem was arraigned in a US federal court following his extradition and ordered detained in the custody of the US Marshals Service pending further proceedings, according to the US Department of Justice.

Prosecutors alleged that Raheem and his co-conspirators filed more than 300 fraudulent tax returns between 2018 and 2023, seeking over $100 million in refunds from the Internal Revenue Service (IRS).

US Attorney Theodore S. Hertzberg said the alleged operation involved hundreds of stolen identities and significant financial losses.

“Raheem and his co-conspirators allegedly obtained hundreds of stolen identities, filed fraudulent tax returns using that information, and laundered the proceeds through prepaid debit cards and purchases of used cars that were shipped to Nigeria and other locations,” Hertzberg said.

“The scope of the alleged fraud is staggering. Thanks to the dedication of the prosecution team and our law enforcement partners around the world, Raheem has been extradited to the United States,” he added.

The indictment also named Abayomi Quadri Eletu, a resident of the United Kingdom and Nigeria, as an alleged co-conspirator. Eletu was indicted separately and arrested in the UK, where extradition proceedings are pending.

According to court documents, the suspects allegedly obtained the personal information of American taxpayers and tax professionals, including names, addresses and Social Security numbers, to facilitate fraudulent claims.

Investigators said the alleged scheme involved creating online IRS accounts to access private taxpayer information, filing false returns and directing refunds to prepaid debit cards linked to addresses controlled by the suspects.

Prosecutors further alleged that Raheem, Eletu and others laundered some of the proceeds by purchasing money orders in amounts intended to avoid reporting requirements.

The money was allegedly used to acquire used cars through auction platforms, some of which were shipped to Nigeria, as well as designer clothing and other items.

Special Agent in Charge Christopher J. Altemus Jr. of the IRS Criminal Investigation Texas Field Office said the alleged scheme affected hundreds of taxpayers.

“Raheem is an alleged co-conspirator in a nationwide identity theft scheme that victimised hundreds of taxpayers. The fraud also stole from the US Treasury, impacting programmes serving us all,” Altemus said.

He added that authorities were working internationally to bring suspects in financial crimes to justice.

“We are pursuing financial criminals to take back the stolen money and their freedom,” he said.

Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration Special Agent-in-Charge Anthony Colello said the case demonstrated the commitment of investigators and prosecutors to tackling fraud.

“The investigative efforts of the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration (TIGTA) and its partners, along with the prosecutorial work of the US Attorney’s Office, demonstrate the commitment to pursuing, capturing, and prosecuting those who try to defraud the American people,” Colello said.

According to the Justice Department, US federal agents sought to arrest Raheem at his residence in April 2026 but were unable to locate him. Investigators later discovered that he had booked a flight from Mexico City to Benin.

Raheem arrived in Benin on April 15, 2026, and was arrested by local authorities pursuant to an INTERPOL Red Notice. Beninese authorities subsequently extradited him to the United States.

The Justice Department described the extradition as only the second transfer of a suspect from Benin to the US in history.

A federal grand jury in the Northern District of Georgia indicted Raheem on February 24, 2026, on charges including conspiracy to commit wire and mail fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering, 14 counts of access device fraud and 14 counts of aggravated identity theft.

If convicted, he faces maximum prison terms of 20 years for conspiracy to commit wire and mail fraud, 20 years for conspiracy to commit money laundering and 10 years for access device fraud. The aggravated identity theft charges carry a mandatory two-year sentence, according to the Justice Department.

The case is being investigated by the IRS Criminal Investigation unit and TIGTA, with assistance from international law enforcement agencies and authorities in Benin and the United Kingdom.

Assistant US Attorney Brian Pearce, alongside Senior Litigation Counsel Michael C. Boteler and Trial Attorney Michael Jones, is prosecuting the case.

The Justice Department emphasised that the indictment contains allegations and that Raheem and other defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in court.

World.title: French Senate passes bill to make protesters pay for unrest damage
World.content:
France’s Interior Minister Laurent Nunez (centre-R) addresses the audience as the Senate, the French Parliament’s upper house examines the ‘Compensation for damage resulting from degradation committed in public spaces’ bill also referred to as the ‘rioters-pay’ (casseurs-payeurs) bill and its critized measures on the collective responsability of troublemakers and the seizure of their welfare benefits at the French Senate in Paris on October 27, 2026. Drawn up during the summer 2026, notably to respond to the damage that followed Paris Saint-Germain’s European triumph, the play of the parliamentary calendar has made it an eminently political object since the scenes of chaos of October 17, when 2,201 businesses were vandalized according to the count of the chambers of commerce and industry in France (CCI France). (Photo by Thomas SAMSON / AFP)

The French parliament’s upper house passed a bill Wednesday that would make protesters financially liable for damage caused during street demonstrations, despite warnings from critics that it could curb the right to protest.

The bill was drafted in response to riots that followed Paris Saint-Germain’s victory over Arsenal in the UEFA Champions League final in May.

But it has taken on added significance after weeks of protests over inequality and soaring prices culminated in some of the worst violence France has seen in years on October 17, when thousands of businesses across the country were damaged and looted.

The Senate passed an expanded version of the bill by 229 votes to 105, backed by a right-wing and centrist alliance which holds a majority.

The legislation has been sent to the National Assembly, which is split between France’s political factions, for debate and voting.

Far-right leader Marine Le Pen, whom opinion polls place as the frontrunner to succeed Emmanuel Macron in next spring’s presidential election, supports the legislation.

Speaking in parliament, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez stressed the “urgency” of responding to the damage and scenes of chaos seen on October 17.

“We can no longer allow the vast majority of our fellow citizens to pay for a minority of vandals,” he said.

– ‘Legal travesty’ –

Under the legislation, protesters could be ordered to pay up to 10,000 euros for damage caused during street demonstrations.

But critics argue that people who took no part in vandalism could nonetheless be held liable if they were deemed to have been associated with those responsible.

The bill introduces joint financial liability for anyone found to have “knowingly participated” in a group formed with the intent of carrying out acts of vandalism.

It would also apply to individuals who “voluntarily” continued to take part in a gathering likely to disrupt public order after two police dispersal warnings.

Welfare benefits and housing assistance could also be seized to help cover the cost of damages under the scheme, a provision that has drawn sharp criticism from left-wing parties and advocacy groups.

In the second reading, senators toughened the measure to include other social benefits such as the family supplement, back-to-school allowance and the employment bonus.

Left-wing lawmakers accused the government of an “authoritarian drift” at the expense of the freedom to demonstrate.

Communist senator Fabien Gay denounced what he called a “legal travesty that deliberately conflates protesters and rioters”.

Green senator Melanie Vogel accused the government of responding to social demands with “collective punishment.”

Supporters of the bill sought to reassure critics.

“We must not give the impression that this bill would criminalise a passer-by or a peaceful protester,” said Olivier Bitz of the centre-right Horizons party.

– ‘Disastrous consequences’ –

The government has proposed introducing protest bans targeting the most violent individuals.

Late Tuesday, the Senate approved a bill allowing authorities to demand the rapid removal of social media content calling for “insurrection or taking up arms against the state”.

“As we speak, there are calls circulating for next Saturday that are calls for insurrection. Those are the kinds of content we want to remove,” the interior minister told senators.

Platforms would be required to remove such content within 24 hours, or they could face “blocking” or “delisting.”

In an op-ed published in French daily Le Monde last week, a coalition of trade unions and student groups warned of a “serious infringement on the freedom to demonstrate.”

They argued the measures would disproportionately affect “the poorest families” and encourage “arbitrary police action.”

Amnesty International also urged the government to abandon the bill, warning the measures could push “already marginalised families further into poverty”.

“If passed, this bill would be a deeply regressive step,” Nathalie Godard of Amnesty International France said on Monday.

“Seizing family allowances, housing assistance, or the active solidarity income could have disastrous consequences for some of the most vulnerable people.”

AFP

World.title: Trump says Putin-Zelensky meeting to be set up ‘very soon’
World.content:
A man rides a bicycle past a building damaged following an air attack in Kyiv on October 27, 2026, amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine. (Photo by Serhii Okunev / AFP)

US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that a meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky would be set up “very soon.”

The announcement came as Trump’s administration ramps up diplomatic efforts aimed at ending the Russia-Ukraine war, now in its fifth year.

“There’ll be a meeting set up very soon and I think a lot of progress could be made,” Trump told reporters.

Zelensky said on Sunday that a trilateral meeting between Kyiv, Washington and Moscow would take place in November, aiming to restart stalled peace talks.

The Kremlin had previously said that a meeting between the three countries was planned to take place in the United Arab Emirates in November.

Putin, who ordered the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, has consistently rejected face-to-face talks with Zelensky and insisted Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine.

Trump came to power in January 2025 promising to end the war in 24 hours — but over a year of US-led talks have failed to produce a breakthrough, with tens of thousands killed.

In recent days Trump has once again pivoted away from Ukraine and back to Putin, trumpeting what he said was a deal for Russia to sell diesel and reduce prices sent soaring by his Iran war.

AFP

World.title: FG moves to secure farms, attract investors
World.content:
By Emma Ujah, Abuja Bureau Chief

The Federal Government has moved to address insecurity threatening agricultural investments, signing a partnership agreement to develop security arrangements for farms and attract investors to multibillion-dollar soybean and sugarcane projects in Yobe and Jigawa states.

The Ministry of Finance Incorporated (MOFI), Integranium Holdings and Defence Agricultural Assets and Projects Development Company (DAPCO), supported by Defence Holding Company Limited, signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) in Abuja.

Speaking at the signing ceremony, Dr Femi Ogunseinde, MOFI’s Executive Director, Investments, said: “We have a soybean initiative in Yobe, we have a sugarcane initiative in Jigawa—all large-scale, all multibillion-dollar projects.
