World.title: Rhodes’ grave divides Zimbabweans as calls for removal grow
World.content:
Calls for the removal of Cecil John Rhodes’ remains from Matobo Hills has sparked debate among Zimbabweans, with some supporting the move and others warning of its potential implications for tourism and local communities.

Speaking during the SADC Anti-Sanctions Day commemorations in Mutare, Chief Senator Mutasa said chiefs from his province were united in their demand for the former British imperialist’s remains to be removed.

“As chiefs of Manicaland, we are saying Rhodes’ bones must go,” he declared.



The remarks have drawn mixed reactions online, with questions raised about regional representation, colonial history and the economic value of the burial site.

One commenter, @Frank Bekezela Mpofu, argued that Matabeleland should not be conflated with Manicaland, while @Prince Sandile Vodloza questioned how Rhodes’ burial in Matobo affected people from the eastern province.

Others focused on the potential economic consequences of removing the remains.



“… that statue it can give us foreign currency, its a tourist attraction it create employment,” @Reggie Maf commented.

Another commenter, @Leonard Mazodze, similarly argued that the site attracts tourists and generates income.

However, some supported Mutasa’s position, with @Honesty Inno Chenjerai pointing to South Africa’s removal of Rhodes’ statue as evidence that colonial-era symbols can be reconsidered.



Who was Cecil John Rhodes?

Rhodes was a British businessman, mining magnate and politician who played a major role in British colonial expansion in southern Africa.

He founded the British South Africa Company, which was instrumental in the colonisation of territories that became Zimbabwe.

He also served as prime minister of the Cape Colony from 1890 to 1896.



Rhodes died in Cape Town on 26 March 1902.

According to South African History Online, he had requested in his will to be buried at World’s View in the Matobo Hills, where he was laid to rest in April that year.

His legacy remains controversial because of his imperial ambitions and the dispossession of African communities associated with colonial rule.



Tourism versus colonial legacy

Matobo Hills is a UNESCO World Heritage Site known for its distinctive granite formations, ancient rock art and cultural significance.

The dispute raises questions about how Zimbabwe should balance confronting its colonial past with preserving historical sites that may also support tourism.

In South Africa, the Rhodes Must Fall movement culminated in the removal of his statue at the University of Cape Town on 9 April 2015.



However, removing a statue and relocating human remains are different processes, and the latest call does not itself establish that Rhodes’ grave will be moved.

The debate continues to highlight differing views on how Zimbabwe should remember its past while considering the interests of communities connected to its heritage sites.

World.title: SASSA grant scams: WHO profits and how?
World.content:
SASSA grant scams are getting more sophisticated, but they ultimately still follow the same playbook. Image: AI generated, for illustrative purposes only

When you see any of the latest SASSA grant scams, do you wonder who benefits from them exactly? Never mind the question of who would be so low as to target the poorest quotient of the country’s population. Moreover, in over 20 years of social grants, no single organisation or organised syndicate has been publicly identified as being behind these numerous SASSA grant scams.

WHO IS BEHIND SASSA GRANT SCAMS?

Nevertheless, back in February 2026, an SAPS-led operation arrested government employees linked to an alleged fraud syndicate worth R4.9 million. Then again, in July 2026, officials at a SASSA office in Sekhukhune were dismissed after an internal audit found a syndicate manipulating databases in a R33-million fraud.

Another perpetrator of SASSA grant scams are bogus third-party financial institutions. South African Social Security Agency CEO Themba Matlou has warned vulnerable beneficiaries they shouldn’t 



AI SASSA GRANT SCAMS

Worryingly, many of the syndicates you hear about are insiders, or have inside connections to be able to manipulate SASA databases. Image: File

While still in its infancy in social grants, the AI tools scammers use are only getting more sophisticated. Deepfake videos/voice messages can be used to promote fake and fraudulent schemes. It only takes a three-second clip to clone a voice/face.

These could be used for polished deepfake messages that look and sound like official SASSA notices. Or, more concerningly, deepfake SASSA officials who sound credible on phone calls, WhatsApp messages, asking for your banking details. Moreover, the four-million older persons on grants are especially exposed, since they tend to be most trusting.

HOW CAN YOU PROTECT YOURSELF?

So, how can you protect yourself against SASSA grant scams? It’s difficult because the agency’s strict review and biometric verification drive is ideal for scammers to exploit. Nevertheless, there are precautions you can take besides just ignoring every message sent to you:



Only communicate through official SASSA channels, like its toll-free line on 0800 601 011 .

. Do not share your PIN, OTP or ID number with anyone who contacts you. SASSA won’t ask, so if you’re being asked, it’s a hoax.

Never pay a fee to get, fix or recover a reviewed grant.

SASSA grant scams always try to create fake urgency: ‘Re-register now or lose your grant in 24 hours.’ That’s a red flag.

Check your bank statement every month for deductions/fees you may not have authorised. Report them to your bank and SASSA immediately.

Basically, always stay alert and skeptical. Criminal syndicates may have better AI tools but the SASSA grant scams playbook is broadly the same. Fake urgency and a request for your personal details that you should never disclose …

But what do you think? Have you seen and/or nearly fallen for any SASSA grant scams recently? If so, please share your thoughts in the comments section below …

World.title: ‘We’re told to be strong’: Rachel Kolisi teases London tour
World.content:
Author and motivational speaker Rachel Kolisi teased the type of conversations to be had at her Falling Forward event in London, via an Instagram post on Tuesday 27 October.

RACHEL KOLISI TEASES LONDON TOUR

Author and director Rachel Kolisi is taking her Falling Forward event to London and she took to Instagram to tease the type of conversations she would be having. The mom of two, who was previously married to Springboks captain Siya Kolisi, expressed that the world financially benefits from women thinking they are not enough. The event takes place on 19 November. Take a look…

“Being a woman shouldn’t mean carrying everything and making it look easy. We’re told to be strong, to be resilient and to keep going. But it’s also okay if that weight feels too heavy sometimes. You don’t have to carry it alone,” she wrote.



“London, you’re in for a treat. These are the kinds of honest conversations you can look forward to at Falling Forward on the 19th of November 🤍,” she continued.

WHAT IS ‘FALLING FORWARD’?

Falling Forward is Rachel’s personal project exploring healing, self-discovery and rebuilding life after difficult experiences. Through a documentary, memoir and screening roadshow, she shared her journey of navigating major life changes, rediscovering her identity and learning to move forward on her own terms.



While her divorce was part of the wider context, the project focuses on more than the end of a marriage. It explores themes of motherhood, loss, personal growth, faith and finding purpose during uncertain times.

The title, Falling Forward, reflects the idea that setbacks do not have to define a person’s future. Instead, difficult experiences can become opportunities for reflection, resilience and transformation. Rachel also wanted to create a supportive space where women can connect through shared experiences and feel less alone in their struggles.

World.title: On the road to LGE 2026: Discovering Knysna
World.content:
KNYSNA - As eNCA hits the road ahead of the 2026 Local Government Elections, we’re exploring the cities and communities shaping South Africa.

Reporter Kevin Brandt will be visiting Knysna, a coastal town known for its iconic Heads, indigenous forests and rich natural heritage.

Here are five facts about Knysna you may not know.

1. The famous Knysna Heads

These striking sandstone headlands flank the entrance to the Knysna estuary, where its waters meet the Indian Ocean.

2. It’s technically an estuary, not a lagoon

Although commonly known as the Knysna Lagoon, this body of water is an estuary connected to the Indian Ocean.

3. It’s home to the endangered Knysna seahorse

The Knysna estuary provides a habitat for the endangered Knysna seahorse, a species found in South Africa’s southern Cape estuaries.

4. Oysters are part of its identity

Knysna is famous for its oysters, with the annual Knysna Oyster Festival drawing visitors to the town.

5. Ancient indigenous forests surround the town

Knysna is bordered by indigenous forests that support diverse plant and animal life, making the area an important part of South Africa’s natural heritage.

World.title: Former SAPS general's bid to challenge police raid struck off court roll
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Former police general Mulangi Mphego’s application to have a police raid at his Centurion home in July declared unlawful has been struck off the roll.

Mphego sought the return of firearms, legal files and his cellphone seized during the operation, arguing that the raid was unconstitutional.

The former top cop is believed to be relevant to the investigation into the 2021 death of deputy national commissioner Sindile Mfazi, who was initially reported to have died from Covid-19 complications.

Investigators are now probing suspicious circumstances surrounding his death.

National police spokesperson Athlenda Mathe previously said Mfazi’s family had raised concerns about his death and approached the then national commissioner, who instructed the SAPS Cold Case Unit to investigate specific allegations.

Mphego, 57, is also facing charges under the Firearms Control Act for the unlawful possession of police-issued R5 rifle and 9mm ammunition.

He was arrested last week in connection with the ammunition and released on R5,000 bail.

The case has been postponed to 5 November.

World.title: Meta, Snap head to trial in another case about social media's harms
World.content:
SAN FRANCISCO - Jury selection is expected to begin on Wednesday in Los Angeles for another landmark trial about the alleged harms of social media on young users, with Meta and, for the first time, Snap as defendants.

Thousands of lawsuits have been filed in recent years in local, state and federal courtrooms across the country with various claims about alleged harms to children and teenagers caused by social media companies.

The cases -- the first of which went to trial earlier this year in Los Angeles -- have taken twists and turns.

Meta and YouTube lost the first so-called bellwether case earlier this year, when a jury found them collectively liable for harming a young user known by the initials KGM, and ordered the tech companies to pay a combined $6 million penalty.

Meta said at the time that they "respectfully disagree" with the verdict.

Snap and TikTok settled with KGM ahead of that trial.

Months later, Snap, TikTok and YouTube settled another case that was set to go to trial in August; that plaintiff, known as RKC, then withdrew their remaining claims against Meta, allowing the Instagram and Facebook maker to avoid trial without a settlement.

TikTok and YouTube were previously named as defendants in the new case but both companies reached settlement agreements with the plaintiffs, known by their initials SJ and KDB, before the start of the trial, their lawyers said.

Meta reached a settlement agreement with one of the plaintiffs, SJ, but not KDB, according to their lawyers.

A California state judge consolidated both cases into a single trial.

If no additional settlements are reached before opening statements kick off on November 4, the new trial will move forward with both Meta and Snap as defendants.

Star witnesses are expected to testify beginning mid-November including Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Instagram chief Adam Mosseri, and Snap CEO Evan Spiegel.

Earlier this month, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion in a case where the company was found liable for deceiving users in the state about how their data was used in a case related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal.

A New Mexico jury previously found the social media giant liable for harms to children, leading to a combined penalty of $942 million.

In August, Meta agreed to pay more than $18 billion in penalties, in addition to making changes to Instagram and Facebook for teens, when it settled with 52 attorneys general several days into a trial held in California.

Part of that settlement hinged on YouTube and TikTok making similar changes to their own products, such as limiting daily screentime.

- 'Addictive and problematic' -

As regulators around the world grapple with reining in, or even banning, social media use for teens, American lawsuits have focused on allegations of addictive design and deceptive practices by social media companies.

Next month, lawyers for the two plaintiffs in Los Angeles -- SJ and KDB -- will argue that their clients were exposed to "addictive and problematic" social media apps when they started using them at 13 and 15, respectively, according to court documents.

SJ, a teen in Illinois, began to use Snapchat, the app created by Snap, compulsively and subsequently experienced mental health issues, an eating disorder and self harm, her lawyers claim.

KDB, now an 18-years-old from Mississippi, similarly developed compulsive use of both Meta and Snap, leading to worsening mental and physical health, according to her lawyers.

Meta has previously denied such claims.

"We will not back away from defending ourselves against baseless lawsuits," Meta told AFP in July.

Snap intends to argue that it is different from other apps like Meta's Instagram and Facebook because of Snapchat's focus on primarily being a messaging platform.

"We believe the evidence will support that we have put our community first, and that these allegations fundamentally misrepresent the plaintiffs' experiences on Snapchat and how our platform was designed," a Snap spokesperson said in a statement.

World.title: Russia woos African leaders at Moscow summit
World.content:
Russia will host almost two dozen African leaders in Moscow on Wednesday and Thursday, seeking to further buttress ties with countries it sees as "natural allies" against the West.

The Russia-Africa summit, the third since 2019, comes as Moscow grapples with heavy Western sanctions over its Ukraine offensive and as it provides security assistance to several African governments.

Moscow has courted ties with Africa since the Soviet era, and has long looked to the continent as a counterweight to what it sees as Western domination over international affairs.

"We are natural allies in building a multipolar world order," Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said of the summit, referring to a system where political power is no longer concentrated in the West but among multiple regions.

Delegations from 48 African countries are scheduled to take part and 22 will be represented by their leaders, Ushakov said.

Russian President Vladimir Putin's criticism of what he calls "neocolonialism" on the continent has resonated with a number of African leaders, especially former French colonies in the Sahel.

Among the leaders Putin is scheduled to meet is Malian counterpart Assimi Goita, whose government is using Russian paramilitaries to battle a jihadist offensive.

Mali's ruling junta, which came to power in two successive coups in 2020 and 2021, has turned away from former colonial ruler France and moved closer to Russia.

There will also be plenary sessions where "all heads of delegations will have the opportunity to speak," Ushakov said.

- DRC-Rwanda tensions -

The summit comes amid tensions between the Democratic Republic of Congo and Rwanda, both of which are sending delegations.

DR Congo President Felix Tshisekedi will attend, while Rwanda will be represented by Prime Minister Justin Nsengiyumva.

The Rwandan-backed M23 movement has seized swathes of the eastern DRC since taking up arms again in 2021.

Despite a US-brokered truce in December, fighting has continued to flare.

Thirty-three documents will be signed at the summit, some of which will cover economic cooperation, according to the Kremlin.

Russia, which welcomes thousands of African students to its universities every year, will also seek to strengthen its diplomatic presence in Africa.

Russia counts some 48 embassies on the continent, and there are plans to open a 49th in Liberia, according to the Kremlin.

By Maria Panina

World.title: Charles tackles thorny legacy of slavery on Caribbean trip
World.content:
King Charles III began a Caribbean tour in the Bahamas Tuesday where he acknowledged "the great suffering of the past" in the face of pressure to apologize for the slave trade.

The 77-year-old king, who is receiving treatment for an undisclosed form of cancer, will also highlight climate threats facing low-lying islands during the visit to three countries in nine days.

He will first make solo visits to the Bahamas and Guyana, before being joined by his wife, Queen Camilla, for the final leg in Antigua and Barbuda, where he will address a Commonwealth heads of government (CHOGM) summit.

"We know that some of what is best in Bahamian culture today, the most joyful, the most hopeful, the most bright, was born out of darkness," he said at a youth rally.

"It is only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering and injustices of the past in these islands and beyond, even as we rejoice in the successes of the present and build new opportunities for the future."

He said leaders of "affected" Commonwealth nations would be discussing the issue in Antigua and Barbuda next week where the issue of reparations for slavery will be on the table according to Commonwealth Secretary-General Shirley Ayorkor Botchwey.

Several of the former colonies have demanded the king take a new step toward making amends for colonization and the transatlantic slave trade, from which his ancestors profited for centuries.

As he arrived at the rally held at the historic site where The Bahamas officially gained its independence in 1973, protesters gathered to wave placards reading "pay what you owe us."

Last month Jamaica -- where Charles remains head of state -- filed a petition in an appeals court in London "to advance Jamaica's push for reparations for the African ancestors who suffered under hundreds of years of enslavement."

Charles has previously called slavery the "darkest days" of British history, and will address colonial issues at each stage of the trip.

Few in royal circles will have forgotten a turbulent 2022 trip to Jamaica by Prince William, when he and Princess Catherine were met with anti-monarchy protests and calls for reparations.

Guyana's President Irfaan Ali, who is to meet with Charles during the visit, told ITV News the king's recognition of the "darkest days" was just the "first step."

"Now, moving to the apology is the next step," said Ali, demanding accountability from the former empire which he said "exploited the region," "destroyed lives" and "created under development."

Modern monarchs have to various degrees expressed remorse for Britain's central role in chattel slavery, but none has yet formally apologized. The debt-laden UK government has balked at the idea of financial compensation.

Botchwey told Sky News ahead of the government meeting from November 1 to 4, that it "wouldn't hurt" for the king to apologise.

Botchwey also said the "time has come" to discuss reparations, in the form of financial payments or otherwise.

- Climate resilience -

Buckingham Palace has insisted the tour is an opportunity for the king to look forward, meet young people and discuss pressing issues like climate change.

In his Bahamas speech, Charles also highlighted the particular threat facing low-lying islands face from climate change.

"In an island nation where 90 percent of the land sits below two meters. There is perhaps nowhere better than the Bahamas to understand the reality of climate change that threatens so many communities across the Commonwealth," he said.

"Our world cries out for healing."

According to Botchwey, the Commonwealth, which includes 56 member countries with the king at its helm, is an important anchor in a "world that is almost spinning out of control."

"This CHOGM is going to be one like never before," the secretary-general told AFP in an interview, with the meeting in St John's set to focus on investment and trade opportunities for member countries.

World.title: Afghans compete for jobs, homes as millions return
World.content:
SHEBERGHAN - As labourers gathered at a roadside in northern Afghanistan, Ghulam Sakhi Barat joined the search for work, with millions of new arrivals intensifying pressure for jobs and homes.

More than six million Afghans have returned from Iran and Pakistan in little over three years as the neighbouring countries have launched deportation drives after decades hosting those fleeing conflict.

With seven relatives to support in Sheberghan, the capital of Jawzjan province, Barat said "people are going hungry" as a result of the influx.

"Since the returnees arrived, there have been fewer jobs for local people," the 83-year-old said, wearing a frayed waistcoat.

"Help is being given to the returnees, but no help is being given to the people who were already living here."

World.title: ‘Heads must roll!’: Melville residents protest weeks-long water cuts
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - “Heads must roll!” That was one of the messages on placards carried by fed-up Melville residents who say they have been battling reliable water supply for weeks.

The residents took to the streets on Wednesday, staging a protest along 4th Avenue and calling on the City of Johannesburg to address the ongoing water crisis.

Ferial Adams, founder of WaterCAN (Water Community Action Network), said residents were angry and frustrated after going weeks without a reliable water supply.

“There is no real hope of the system stabilising any time soon. The people hit by shortages are guaranteed no water. That is what we’ve been told…that this is just going to happen, and we must expect it. I don’t think that’s good enough anymore,” Adams said.

READ | Bronkhorstspruit reservoir cleaning near completion

With parts of Johannesburg and Pretoria experiencing a heatwave, Adams said the ongoing water cuts were making an already difficult situation worse for residents.

World.title: On the road to LGE 2026: Discovering Mangaung
World.content:
BLOEMFONTEIN - As eNCA hits the road ahead of the 2026 Local Government Elections, we’re exploring the cities and communities shaping South Africa.

Reporter Manqoba Mchunu will be visiting Mangaung Metropolitan Municipality in the Free State, an area known for its historical landmarks, cultural heritage and important role in South Africa’s judicial system.

Here are five facts about Mangaung you may not know.

1. Home to South Africa’s Supreme Court of Appeal

Bloemfontein, within Mangaung Metro, is home to the Supreme Court of Appeal, which hears appeals from lower courts.

2. Mangaung means “place of the cheetah”

The name Mangaung is commonly translated as “place of the cheetah”, reflecting the area’s historical association with the animal.

3. Naval Hill has a wartime history

Naval Hill in Bloemfontein takes its name from the Anglo-Boer War, when British forces positioned naval guns on the hill.

4. A connection to J.R.R. Tolkien

Bloemfontein is the birthplace of author J.R.R. Tolkien, who was born there in 1892. He later became internationally known for writing The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings.

5. More than just Bloemfontein

Mangaung Metropolitan Municipality includes Bloemfontein, Botshabelo and Thaba Nchu, bringing together diverse communities across the Free State.

World.title: How Kenya has become regional abductors' paradise
World.content:
Tanzanian opposition activist Twaha Mwaipaya was abducted in Kamulu, Machakos County. [Coutersy]

The chilling sound of three vehicles screeching to a halt was the last thing Twaha Mwaipaya's friends heard before the Tanzanian opposition activist vanished into the Nairobi afternoon. More than two days have passed since the October 25 abduction in Kamulu, Machakos County, and the silence from Kenyan authorities is becoming as deafening as the act itself.

For a nation that has long styled itself as a sanctuary for those fleeing persecution in the region, the disappearance of Mwaipaya, a former youth leader of Tanzania's opposition CHADEMA party, is not an isolated incident. It is the latest and most glaring symptom of a terminal illness eating away at Kenya's constitutional fabric.

World.title: Kikuyu PCEA church loses 2.7-acre illegally acquired land
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Justice Jacqueline Mogeni, in her verdict, said the land in contention was public property and its registration in the name of the said church was irregular and fraudulent. [Courtesy, EACC]

The Presbyterian Church of East Africa (PCEA) has lost its 2.7-acre piece of land to a school.

This is after the Environment and Lands Court at Thika established that the land under the church's Ruguthi Women's Guild was a school playground and was illegally allocated.

Presiding Judge Jacqueline Mogeni, in her verdict, said the land in contention was public property, and its registration in the name of the said church was irregular and fraudulent.

According to her, the land had been reserved for use as a playground by Kanyiha, Lusigetti and Njumbi Primary Schools.

The verdict follows a case filed by the Law Society of Kenya, with the Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission (EACC) participating as an interested party.

In a statement on Monday, EACC's head of Corporate Affairs and Communication Stephen Karuga said the anti-graft agency presented evidence demonstrating that the land had been reserved for public use and therefore, any allocation to third parties was irregular. Justice Jacqueline Mogeni, in her verdict, said the land in contention was public property and its registration in the name of the said church was irregular and fraudulent. [Courtesy, EACC]

"Our investigations established that the land was set aside in 1957 by the former County Council of Kiambu for use as a school playing field," Karuga said, adding, "the investigations further revealed that there was no letter of offer or acceptance, no evidence of payment of rent rates and no proof that the Women's Guild had paid any consideration to the council for the land."

According to Karuga, the judgement safeguards a vital public facility used by more than 1,300 pupils, ensuring that the playground remains available for learning, sports and recreation for the current and future generations.

As a result, the judge said the allocation, transfer and registration of the land LR. NO KARAI/350 and subsequent issuance of a title deed in 2001 was unprocedural, illegal, null and void.

"An order of Mandamus is hereby issued directing the 3rd respondent, the Land Registrar, Kiambu Chief Land Registrar, to forthwith cancel and revoke the Title Deed and all register entries in respect of the land issued to the 1st respondent on Dec 6, 2001, or at any subsequent date," the Judge said.

The judge further ordered that the said parcel of land be handed over to the Board of Management of the two schools and the Education Ministry.

"An order of permanent injunction is hereby issued restraining the 1st respondent, whether by herself, her church officials, agents, servants, assigns or anyone claiming through her, from entering into, taking possession of, fencing, depositing construction materials upon, transferring, charging, developing or in any other manner dealing or interfering with the land," she ordered.

World.title: Sakaja protests release of 14 suspects linked to Eastleigh collapsed building
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Sakaja demanded answers from Kamukunji Police on how the suspects were arrested in June but released on Sh50,000 bail without being charged in court. [GPS]

Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja has protested the release of suspects linked to the collapsed building in Eastleigh.

While pushing for the county to have prosecutorial powers, Sakaja demanded answers from Kamukunji Police on how the suspects were arrested in June but released on Sh50,000 bail without being charged in court.

Sakaja in statement posted on his X account (formerly Twitter) said City Hall had taken enforcement action against those involved after establishing change of user from a residential property to a commercial had been approved.

According to Sakaja, architectural plans required to authorise construction had not been approved.

The Governor said County officers arrested the suspects and handed them over to Kamukunji Police Station because county governments no longer hold prosecutorial powers they previously held.

“We enforced the law and arrested those involved. However, because we do not have prosecutorial powers, the suspects were handed over to Kamukunji Police Station. They were reportedly released on a cash bail of Sh50,000 without being taken to court,” Sakaja said.

“We want the police to explain why the suspects were released without being presented in court and why construction was allowed to continue. These are serious questions that must be answered,” he added.

A police occurrence book entry from Kamukunji Police Station indicates that 14 suspects were booked into custody on June 17, 2026, over the alleged offences relating to contravention of city planning laws.

Enforcement action and arrests were made severally by the county officials and most recently in July after failing to comply with the enforcement order below. However the suspects were released on a 50k bail at Kamukunji police on the very same day. Prosecution of the same was also denied. We have repeatedly asked for the resumption of the power to prosecute such violations of such county and county related laws after this was taken away from County governments in 2024 (one such letter to the office of the DPP is attached). Meanwhile, several such cases have either been rejected by prosecutors (who are independent of the County), dismissed by the justice system or have had minimal fines imposed. Fining a developer 50k for an illegal development with hundreds of millions without orders to stop and remove the offensive development is completely unreasonable. I raised this in the Senate a fortnight ago and we shall keep pushing for a review of this position. All of these instances, where enforcement action has been curtailed, blocked or interfered with, will be published to the public. October 25, 2026

The entry, recorded under OB No. 98/17/06/2026, names the suspects and states that they were booked by Nairobi City County officers before being placed in police cells.

A separate Kenya Police Service record indicates that 10 suspects were subsequently released on a cash bail of Sh50,000.

The entry, recorded at 9.44pm, states that the release was carried out on the instructions of the Officer Commanding Station (OCS), identified in the record as C.I. Onyapidi, through Corporal Awadh.

The record references receipt number 2039434 and states that the suspects left the station without complaints.

However, the documents do not, on their own, establish the specific charges against the suspects, the legal basis for the bail arrangement or whether they were subsequently presented in court.

The discrepancy between the 14 suspects recorded as booked into custody and the 10 named in the release entry also raises questions about the subsequent status of the other suspects. Sakaja demanded answers from Kamukunji Police on how the suspects were arrested in June but released on Sh50,000 bail without being charged in court. [GPS]

Sakaja said a June 2025 enforcement notice adds another dimension to the questions surrounding the property and the enforcement of planning regulations.

The notice, issued by Nairobi City County over alleged construction works undertaken without the required development permission, cited the Physical and Land Use Planning Act, 2019, and county by-laws.

It directed the recipient to stop the works and remove the development described as illegal, warning that the County could undertake the required action and recover the costs if the directives were not followed.

The notice also provided for an appeal to the County Physical and Land Use Planning Liaison Committee.

Sakaja clarified that approval to change a property’s use from private to commercial-cum-residential does not amount to approval of architectural plans authorising construction.

He said the County approved the change of use but did not approve the architectural plans, yet construction proceeded.

I have seen some people peddling a fake approval document alleging that the Eastleigh development was approved. It is telling that this is the same document that the Eastleigh developer used to get NCA approval. They allege that the development was approved in January of 2024. This is not true. The application for development as shown below was made in November of 2024, it could not have been approved in February of the same year. Also, there is a difference between a change of user approval and a development approval. The developer applied for change of use from residential to residential & commercial in August of 2024. Change of user was approved in October of 2024. Development approval has never been granted. The developer went on to build with impunity and without building approvals despite enforcement action by the county and arrests. — Sakaja Arthur Johnson (@SakajaJohnson) October 25, 2026

“If the building had been approved for construction, I would have named the officers who approved it so that action could be taken against them,” he said.

Sakaja, in his argument, said the current arrangement creates a gap between enforcement and prosecution, leaving counties dependent on other agencies after taking action against alleged offenders. Sakaja demanded answers from Kamukunji Police on how the suspects were arrested in June but released on Sh50,000 bail without being charged in court. [GPS]

Under his proposal, appropriately authorised county prosecutors would be able to pursue qualifying county offences through the courts, subject to the law and the constitutional authority of the Director of Public Prosecutions.

He said county prosecutors previously had a better understanding of technical offences involving planning, construction and other county regulations, enabling them to handle such cases more directly.

“We want to be able not only to enforce regulations and make arrests, but also to take offenders to court and prosecute them. When counties had prosecutorial powers, we had prosecutors who understood the nature and seriousness of county offences and could ensure that appropriate legal action was taken,” he said.

World.title: Pregnant woman rescued from collapsed Eastleigh building
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Kenya Red Cross workers after rescuing a man who trapped in the rubble.

A pregnant woman was on Saturday evening rescued from the multi-storey building that collapsed in Nairobi’s Eastleigh estate on Friday, October 23 and rushed to the Kenyatta National Hospital (KNH) for treatment.

She is the second person to rescued as earlier in the afternoon the Kenya Red Cross society announced the rescue of a man from the ill-fated building.

The man was also taken to KNH for treatment with the society saying that the rescue followed hours of work put in by the search and rescue multi-agency team.

“After hours of painstaking work alongside multi-agency partners, our search and rescue teams in Eastleigh brought a trapped man out of the rubble,” said Red Cross.

The rescue comes even as the fate of six people who were reported missing on Friuday remains unknown with rescue teams still continuing with the search at the site of the collapsed building along Yusuf Haji Avenue.

The society said that 66 of the 67 construction workers who were at the site had been traced and accounted for but the search continues for people who may have been near the site of the collapsed building.

The development comes as police announced that they had launched a manhunt for the for the owner and contractor of a building.

Police spokesperson Muchiri Nyaga said that officers had launched a probe in collaboration with relevant bodies to establish the cause of the collapse and determine criminal liability.

“Any individual or entity found culpable of negligence or of violating building regulations will face the full force of the law,” he said in a statement.

Nyaga called on members of public to stay completely clear of Yusuf Haji Avenue and 9th Street to give access to heavy excavators, specialised canine units and rescue personnel to perform their duties.

Earlier Saturday, at least 31 families reported their relatives missing as coordinated rescue efforts entered their second day.

No deaths have been reported so far.

The National Construction Authority (NCA) on Friday evening identified the developer, contractor, architect and structural engineer listed for the collapsed building.

The Authority has faced scrutiny over its oversight role, as Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja said the project had failed to comply with construction guidelines.

He said the county had forwarded relevant information to the Directorate of Criminal Investigations for further investigation.

In a statement, the NCA said the building was registered on July 30, 2025, as a proposed development on 9th Street in Eastleigh.

It identified 9th Street Plaza Limited as the developer and Stromax Holdings E.A. Limited as the contractor.

Emmanuel Mwangi Maina was listed as the project architect, while Joseph Muturi Mugu was named as the structural engineer.

World.title: Several feared trapped in Eastleigh building collapse
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Rescue efforts at the collapsed storey building in Eastleigh 9th street in Nairobi County. [Benard Orwongo Standard]

What was supposed to be a usually busy Friday afternoon in Eastleigh's 9th Street turned chaotic after an 18-floor building that was under construction came down, tumbling.

By Friday evening, rescue operations were still ongoing, with cries from people believed to have been trapped being heard from a distance as bulldozers and rescuers continued the search operation.

Two victims, a man and a woman, who were injured in the building had been rescued and rushed to hospital as the search continued.

Asha Jilo, one of the witnesses, said the building collapsed around 1:09 pm just after the afternoon prayers.

"Immediately after the building collapsed, we started contacting some people we know who work there, one of them was still available on the phone until around 3 pm, when his phone went offline," Jilo shared

On Fridays, Eastleigh is usually a hive of activities, being the main market day, but all the businesses were shut as police were battling rowdy youths, some of them believed to be opportunists.

The building, whose height was said to be about 15 floors, had not been cleared for occupation as required, raising questions about why the investors had allowed it to be taken.

It is said that the ground and first floors were already occupied by businesses, raising fears that the number of victims could be high. Rescue efforts at the collapsed storey building in Eastleigh 9th street in Nairobi County. [Benard Orwongo Standard]

At the time of the collapse, it is said that some construction workers were busy on the upper floors.

Governor Johnson Sakaja, who visited the scene after the collapse, was still gathering information about the building. The first priority was about saving lives.

“The building that collapsed is around 16 floors, and we have got information about the building, but what is more concerned right now is for us to save lives,” said Sakaja

Adding, “Equipment has already been mobilized, excavators and breakers, so we can be able to remove the big debris and save lives,’

The Governor said some developers engage qualified professionals to secure construction approvals before dismissing them and disregarding approved plans and safety standards.

He urged professional bodies to strengthen oversight, investigate such cases and take appropriate disciplinary action, stressing that developers must comply with approved designs, engage qualified personnel and obtain occupation certificates after safety inspections.

Rescue efforts at the collapsed storey building in Eastleigh 9th street in Nairobi County. [Benard Orwongo Standard]

Nairobi Regional Police Commander Issa Mohamud, who was at the scene, said that, according to reliable information, several people were trapped inside the debris, inside the big boulders, and the rescue effort is ongoing.

The city police boss said investigations will be carried out to ascertain who is responsible for any negligence.

“If there will be any death, that is negligence by murder. Whoever is the owner, whoever authorized the building, all of them will be charged properly. But that will come after thorough investigation is done,” he warned

Adding, “We will not excuse anybody on this matter. This has become now and then, and we will make sure that people face the law accordingly for any criminal negligence,”

World.title: Ruto hands over COMESA chairmanship, pushes for levy to fund regional programmes
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President Ruto and Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa during the handover of the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa chairmanship at the bloc’s 25th Summit of Heads of State and Government in Harare, Zimbabwe, on Thursday, October 22, 2026. [PCS]

President William Ruto has handed over the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA) chairmanship to Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa.

Ruto took over the one-year chairmanship from Burundi’s President Évariste Ndayishimiye at the 24th COMESA Summit in Nairobi on October 9, 2025.

His tenure focused on using digital technology to deepen regional integration, expand trade and promote inclusive growth.

He handed over the role on Thursday, October 22, during the 25th Comesa Summit of Heads of State and Government in Harare, Zimbabwe, where he urged the regional bloc to fast-track a market levy to finance its programmes and institutions.

“We cannot be ambitious in our plans and timid in our financing. Every programme we agree upon must be matched by the resources to deliver it. Otherwise, our communiqués will promise what our budgets cannot pay for,” Ruto said.

He urged the Comesa Secretariat to fast-track Article 168 of the COMESA Treaty, which provides for the Comesa Market Levy, as the organisation seeks sustainable and predictable financing.

The treaty establishes the levy to generate resources for financing the bloc’s activities.

Ruto said officials from finance ministries, central banks and other relevant agencies would meet to consider a draft COMESA Resource Mobilisation Strategy aimed at strengthening member states’ ownership of regional programmes and finding new ways to raise funds.

He called on member states to make financing central to their discussions, warning that the bloc’s institutions and integration agenda would depend on their ability to fund agreed commitments.

“Can we finance what we commit, and deliver what we finance?” he asked.

Ruto also urged African countries to channel more of their domestic financial resources into African institutions rather than leaving funds in foreign accounts while development projects lack capital.

He said Africa holds more than $4 trillion in domestic financial assets, arguing that regional financial institutions could mobilise more of these resources to support trade, infrastructure and development.

Ruto named the Trade and Development Bank (TDB), the African Trade and Investment Development Insurance (ATIDI) and ZEP-RE among the institutions that could mobilise capital for regional priorities.

He urged African governments to place more reserves with these institutions, finance more projects through them and support their bonds and guarantees.

The outgoing Comesa chairperson said the bloc needed stronger regional value chains and more trade among member states as global supply chains faced disruption and protectionism returned.

“Regional integration is no longer a dream we discuss. It is an economic and strategic necessity,” he noted.

Ruto said Comesa’s economic growth rose from 5.6 per cent in 2024 to 6.4 per cent in 2025, while inflation fell from 31 per cent to 13.2 per cent.

Exports among member states increased by 10.5 per cent to $14.7 billion, their highest level between 2020 and 2025, while exports to global markets rose by 6 per cent to $212 billion, he said.

He argued that African countries needed to process more raw materials locally instead of exporting them and importing finished products.

“To every partner who seeks our minerals, our markets and our young workforce, our offer is clear: invest with us, process with us, build with us,” Ruto added.

He called for partnerships based on mutual benefit and equal treatment, saying African countries should have a greater role in determining how their resources and markets contribute to economic development.

World.title: Judge certifies fresh bid to jail Sakaja, Charles Kerich over Sh76.7m debt as urgent
World.content:
Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja. [File, Standard]

The High Court has certified as urgent a fresh application seeking to have Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja, former Finance Executive Charles Kerich and two other county officials jailed over an alleged breach of a court-approved payment plan in a Sh106.7 million legal fees dispute.

Justice Francis Gikonyo certified the application by Kwengu & Company Advocates seeking to reinstate a three-month jail sentence previously imposed on Kerich and hold Sakaja, current Finance County Executive Committee Member Ibrahim Auma Nyangoya and Chief Officer for Finance Asha Abdi accountable for the alleged failure to pay Sh76.7 million.

World.title: UN panel: Russia is committing crimes against humanity by targeting civilians in Ukraine
World.content:
Russia is committing war crimes and crimes against humanity by intentionally attacking civilian infrastructure – including vital energy systems – in Ukraine, an independent UN investigations panel said on Monday.

Russian forces have been targeting Ukrainian power infrastructure since the early months of the war in 2022, and massively ramped up these attacks at the beginning of last year’s winter, leaving millions of Ukrainians freezing in the darkness of their homes.

A new report published by the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine on Monday and shared with CNN, said these attacks “were carried out with intent” and were in line with Russia’s “state policy to deprive the civilian population from essential energy supplies and cause suffering.”

“Russian commanders who were ordering these attacks knew that the heating facilities they targeted were indispensable to the civilian population, in particular during the winter,” the report, which is being submitted to the UN General Assembly, said.

CNN has approached the Kremlin for comment.

Polish volunteers cook soup in a Kyiv neighborhood left without electricity and heating following Russian attacks during freezing temperatures in February 2026. Thomas Peter/Reuters/File

Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the report “confirms what Ukrainians have experienced for years: Russia’s systematic attacks on civilian energy infrastructure constitute war crimes and crimes against humanity.”

In a post on X, Sybiha said Russia “has deliberately deprived millions of people of electricity, heating and water, turning cold and darkness into instruments of war.”

In a statement released on Monday, the Russian Permanent Mission – the official delegation that represents Russia to the UN – rejected the commission’s findings, claiming it had drawn on “falsified” data and alleging it was set up by a “politicized body.”

“Russia does not recognize the mandate of this commission, which was established through a resolution passed by a politicized body – the UN Human Rights Council,” the delegation said.

“The commission bases its findings on falsified data provided by the Ukrainian authorities via the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) presence in Kyiv,” it added.

The Russian Permanent Mission claimed the UN Human Rights Council “simply fails to notice any crimes committed by the Armed Forces of Ukraine.”

Large-scale Russian drone and missile attacks last winter reduced Ukraine’s thermal power generation capacities by 70 per cent in the most affected areas, according to Kyiv. The suffering was made worse by an unusually cold winter with temperatures dropping to as low as -30 degrees Celsius (-22 F) on multiple occasions.

The commission was established by the UN’s Human Rights Council just days after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

It has previously reported on other aspects of Russia’s war on Ukraine, including allegations of sexual and gender-based violence committed by Russian armed forces, and the wide-spread forced deportations of Ukrainian children by Russian authorities.

In this latest report, the commission describes the dire impacts of prolonged cold exposure on Ukrainian civilians, saying that the country’s medical authorities documented deaths caused by low temperatures in homes, and even in hospitals.

“Medical personnel from hospitals reported that during the past winter, they attended to patients who developed cold-related trauma, including various degrees of frostbite and hypothermia. The patients had developed these conditions at home, due to exposure to unheated premises and required hospitalization,” the report said.

The report quotes a civilian woman living in Dnipro, Ukraine’s fourth largest city, who describes the impact the Russian attacks had on her. “Cold—it paralyzes you; there’s simply no way to get warm, and terrifying thoughts come into your mind,” she said.

Electricians work to restore the power grid in front of a destroyed private house in Kyiv region. A a 14-year-old was killed in the attack on September 30. Vladyslav Musiienko/AFP/Getty Images

Blaming Putin and others

The UN commission report names several high-profile Russian officials as the people most responsible for what it describes as “war crimes and the crimes against humanity.”

It says Russian President Vladimir Putin made several “statements concerning instructions to commit attacks against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.”

It also alleges that evidence collected over the past few years shows that Russia’s former Minister of Defence Sergei Shoigu and his successor Andrey Belousov, as well the Chief of the General Staff Valery Gerasimov, have been responsible for planning and overseeing attacks.

The International Criminal Court has previously issued arrest warrants against Putin, Shoigu and Gerasimov for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity.

As the colder weather begins to arrive in Ukraine, Russia has made it clear it intends to continue to terrorize its neighbor.

On Monday night, Russian ballistic missiles hit the grounds of a university in Kyiv, and surrounding areas including near a metro station and residential buildings, Zelensky said in his nightly address. Rescue operations are underway amid reports of people trapped under the rubble, he added.

“The missiles hit very crowded areas, and there is not a single military facility nearby,” the Ukrainian president said. “This was a strike directly on the city, on its infrastructure.”

The report mentions a declaration made by the Russian Ministry of Defence in August, which announced attacks against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and said: “In winter you will freeze.”

Ukraine is increasingly struggling to defend itself against these large-scale attacks because of a critical shortage of air defense missiles. Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky has made repeated pleas with Kyiv’s western allies for more ammunition, specifically pointing to the upcoming winter as a major worry.

Kyiv had been targeting Russian oil and gas infrastructure, in efforts to hurt the Kremlin’s revenues from energy exports. However, it has eased these attacks after criticism from US President Donald Trump, who has blamed Ukraine for rising gas prices.

“Human trafficking”

The report released on Monday also investigated Russia’s methods of recruiting foreign nationals to serve in its armed forces, concluding they amount to human rights violations and trafficking.

CNN has reported extensively on Russia’s use of deception, bribery and blackmail to lure foreigners into joining its military. People from multiple countries in Africa, India and Latin America have described being promised jobs in Russia only to find themselves on the frontlines.

The commission said it found “compelling evidence” that Russian authorities, working with agents, have “trafficked persons from 29 countries, using deception or coercion, to recruit them in the Russian armed forces.”

It said the fact that Russia has used the same tactics to recruit people from multiple countries “demonstrates a high degree of coordination between agents operating around the world and the Russian authorities.“

“Promised payments and bonuses were usually diverted by recruiting agents and military commanders, passports and phones were often confiscated, and contacts between agents and families were interrupted, once the recruits were deployed to the front.”

The report concludes that Russia violated the recruits’ fundamental human rights, including the rights to life, freedom, health, and to be treated humanely.

The commission also investigated Ukraine’s recruitment of foreign nationals into its army and said that testimonies it collected showed that those joining the Ukrainian armed forces “did so knowingly and voluntarily,” understood the contracts they were signing and received salaries.

World.title: Israel just voted in a critical election. But the ultimate outcome will take time to become clear
World.content:
Jerusalem — Israel’s elections produced no clear winner Tuesday night, exit polls showed, with neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor his main rival Gadi Eisenkot within reach of the 61 seats needed for a governing majority in the 120-seat parliament, the Knesset.

The three main Israeli TV Channels – 11, 12 and 13 – projected Netanyahu’s bloc at 51-52 seats, marking a steep drop from the 68-seat coalition he led in the outgoing Knesset. His Likud party is still projected to be the largest party, with 25-27 seats.

But Israeli politics is all about building coalitions – not being the biggest party – and Netanyahu’s path to staying in power is now unclear.

The opposition also has a complicated route to government.

Parties opposed to Netanyahu won a clear-cut majority of the vote, garnering 68-70 seats in the exit polls. But they are fractured and divided between right, left and center, and between Jewish and Arab parties.

Eisenkot’s Yashar party is the largest in the opposition, projected to win 21-23 seats, but his path to power runs through cooperation with the Arab parties, a scenario not all the party leaders in the opposition are willing to accept.

One outlier stood out with good news for Netanyahu and his bloc. The pro-Netanyahu Channel 14 exit polls projected the bloc with 60 seats total and Likud with 30 on its own.

However, as exit polls are only projections, the picture may shift as the actual votes are tallied overnight. The final count is expected to take a few days.

No quick victory declarations

As exit polls showed Netanyahu and Eisenkot falling short of a majority, both leaders addressed supporters, trying to claim the night and shape a narrative of victory.

Netanyahu, speaking at the Likud headquarters in Jerusalem, thanked voters for what he called a renewed vote of confidence. But he stopped short of declaring outright victory.

“Two things became clear tonight: Likud is the largest party in Israel. There is no dispute about that,” he said. “And the second thing is that the right-wing bloc has a clear, decisive majority among the Zionist and Jewish public.”

“We must establish a strong national right-wing government,” Netanyahu continued. “Israel must not be endangered with a government that relies on anti-Zionist Arab parties that oppose our very existence, that see Hamas as a charity organization, that calls our soldiers war criminals.”

Eisenkot also did not declare victory as he spoke at his election headquarters in Tel Aviv. But he did say that Israel voted against Netanyahu.

Supporters react after polls closed at the Yashar party headquarters in Tel Aviv, Israel, on Tuesday, October 27, 2026. Kobi Wolf/Bloomberg/Getty Images

“We have made history! The public has voted for change. The coalition of failure has lost the people’s trust,” he said. “The Israeli public has voted against Netanyahu continuing to serve as prime minister of Israel.”

Eisenkot, who was once Israel’s top general and lost a son fighting in Gaza, said that “a worthy leader would accept the people’s vote of no confidence and announce his retirement from political life today.”

Surge for Arab parties adds complexity

The elections saw the highest overall voter turnout since 1999 – at least 77.7 percent. The surge was especially notable among the country’s Arab population, which has traditionally voted at lower rates than Jewish Israelis. The Arab parties said turnout exceeded 75 percent. The two parties – the Joint List and Raam – are projected at 17-19 seats, in their strongest showing in history.

Palestinian citizens of Israel – roughly 20 percent of Israel’s population – were driven by an urgent desire to topple Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition, which is largely dominated by hardline ministers Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir. Ben-Gvir’s tenure as national security minister has included a dramatic rise in crime and murder rates in Arab communities.

Supporters of the Palestinian Israeli Joint List political alliance cheer at the campaign headquarters in the city of Nazareth on October 27, 2026. Ahmad Gharabli/AFP via Getty Images

“We have proven that we are a political force that cannot be ignored, and that it is impossible to build a future here without our voice”, said Yousef Jabareen, chairman of the Joint List, calling it a “historic day.” Mansour Abbas, chairman of the Raam list, told i24news that the “record-breaking electoral achievement is all due to Ben-Gvir and Smotrich and the entire government that neglected the Israeli Arab community.”

The Arab turnout may have blocked Netanyahu from a majority, but it also complicates Eisenkot’s attempts to replace him. Eisenkot has set conditions for any partner to join his government, including recognizing Israel as a Jewish state and recognizing Hamas as a terrorist organization that must be dismantled, terms most Arab lawmakers are unlikely to accept.

Moreover, two of his opposition allies – Avigdor Liberman and Naftali Bennett – have ruled out forming a government with the Arab parties altogether.

That makes Eisenkot’s path to victory unclear.

What happens next?

Exit polls are merely projections, and the picture may shift as actual votes are counted and finalized, which usually takes a matter of days.

Once results are certified, the electoral process moves to Israel’s President Isaac Herzog. In a series of meetings in Jerusalem, Herzog will open a round of consultations in which each elected party recommends its choice for prime minister.

Based on these recommendations, the president then tasks one candidate to try and form a government. That is not necessarily the leader of the largest party, but rather whoever he thinks is most likely to assemble a 61-seat majority based on his own discretion.

Winning is not only about votes and seats, but also about building – and maintaining – a viable coalition.

Herzog’s first decision will be does he ask Netanyahu or Eisenkot to form a government.

Netanyahu has the largest party, but with the Arab parties’ support, Eisenkot is likely to have more recommendations. After being assigned the mandate, one of the two will begin weeks of political bargaining over cabinet posts, budget priorities and policy commitments.

The assigned candidate has a 28-day deadline – and likely a 14-day extension – to form a government. If he fails, the president passes the mandate to another candidate for another four weeks. If that fails as well, the Knesset gets a short window to put forward another candidate. If it cannot, the country automatically goes to another round of elections.

With neither side holding a clear majority, deadlock appears to be a plausible outcome.

Herzog may try to steer Netanyahu and Eisenkot to form a unity government between the two largest parties, but it’s unclear that such an arrangement is even possible. Netanyahu has a long history of burning politicians with whom he has reached similar agreements, and Eisenkot has ruled out sitting with Netanyahu.

World.title: It can be lonely at the top. And that’s just how China’s leader likes it
World.content:
Hong Kong — Last week Beijing’s deputy mayor was meeting with Walmart CEO John Furner and encouraging American companies to invest in the Chinese capital. Now he has vanished from public life, the latest to be swept up in an anti-corruption campaign that has ensnared a galaxy of China’s talent: a former top judge, a spy chief, dozens of military generals – and even officials tasked with rooting out graft in the People’s Republic.

In hushed tones across China party officials are wondering who is next, as the purge continues to reach into the highest echelons of the ruling Communist Party and has even toppled those seen as being close to leader Xi Jinping.

The only person who doesn’t need to worry about their future is Xi himself.

Unlike US President Donald Trump, who is currently battling to save his party’s fortunes at the midterm elections and is constitutionally barred from serving more than two terms, Xi’s rule over the aspiring superpower and world’s second-biggest economy has never looked more secure.

He will take that confidence into a high-level closed-door meeting of more than 200 of the party elite in Beijing this week that is all set to further boost his authority – and his signature anti-corruption drive. Attendance at this meeting will be at a historic low – because of the anti-corruption measure.

The meeting is being particularly closely watched because it is held just a year before an even more important gathering of Communist Party leadership next fall where Xi is expected to engineer for himself an unprecedented fourth term.

The years-long anti-corruption campaign has ensured there are few, if any, figures or factions who could stand against him.

Since Xi, 73, came to power over 14 years ago millions of rank-and-file officials have been purged. In 2022, Xi called to “turn the blade inward” to investigate those tasked to enforce discipline themselves.

But he’s still not satisfied.

Earlier this year he told party cadres that the corruption problem “remains grave” and warned that there were still many “two-faced people” in the party. The war against graft, he promised, would be a “never-ending struggle.”

In 2023, China’s most powerful generals pledged allegiance to the Constitution at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing. Now only one remains after rounds of purges. ue Yuewei/Xinhua/Getty Images

In recent months, the speed and scale of the anti-corruption drive have reached levels unseen in decades.

According to official data from the party’s Central Commission of Discipline Inspection (CCDI), between 2012 and 2022, over 500 ministerial-level officials have been probed, later convicted, removed from their posts, and expelled from the party for corruption.

In just the past three years, more than 410 officials have been purged.

Some of those purges have reached places that were once considered untouchable.

The party’s top military decision-making body, the usually seven-member Central Military Commission is now down to only two members – one of those being Xi himself. The 24-member politburo – the party’s top echelon – is down to only 21 members.

No safe landing

Over the past three weeks, ahead of the Beijing meeting, the CCDI has been sending out near daily updates of arrests, new probes and expulsions from the party.

The news that Huang Qifan was being probed sent shockwaves through political circles.

Huang Qifan, former mayor of Southwest China’s Chongqing Municipality, attends an economics forum in Hangzhou in eastern China’s Zhejiang province, on November 24, 2020. Long Wei/Feature China/Getty Images

Huang was a longtime mayor of the megacity of Chongqing, known as a consummate political survivor who had served under six different secretaries of the Communist Party – and seen two of them go to jail, including a former rival of Xi.

In retirement, Huang was prolific at conferences and on TV, giving his takes on the Chinese economy.

Since his downfall, those who knew Huang have rushed to scrub all mention of their former well-connected friend and colleague from their social media accounts – a common practice in China.

For Beijing deputy mayor Xia Linmao, the purge came suddenly. Only days before, state TV showed him at a meeting with Walmart’s Furner and a slew of other US executives, nodding and taking his notes as his boss invited the group to do more business in Beijing.

Others simply vanished from public view, with news of their investigation not appearing for months, like Ma Xingrui, an aerospace engineer turned senior party official who once ran the vast western region of Xinjiang. The authorities announced an investigation into him in April – after he had not been seen in public for five months.

Being officially investigated for corruption almost always spells the end of a political career in China, with guilty officials kept from the public eye even after they have served their sentences.

And in recent months, authorities have shown they are willing to use capital punishment to enforce the party line, even for those who were once trusted aides of Xi.

In May, two former defense ministers, Wei Fenghe and Li Shangfu were given suspended death sentences, with a two-year reprieve, after being convicted of bribery.

Years of purging has left a generation of younger officials with fewer seniors left who can provide patronage, protection and career advancement, and the situation where the most powerful person in China does not have an apparent heir, in a break from his predecessors.

And for some, that’s just fine.

Deng Yuwen, a former deputy editor of the Study Times, the official publication of the party’s top training institute, told CNN that “now younger people all listen to Xi, isn’t this better? At this point, I don’t think Xi needs to worry about whether someone is already his trusted aides. “

“Whoever he promotes will become his loyalist,” said Deng. “And he has enough time to make someone his trusted loyalists.”

World.title: Arab voters turn out in record numbers but entering government will still be tricky
World.content:
Supporters of Israel’s Arab Joint List party celebrated at its election headquarters in Nazareth, with Arab parties projected to gain a record number of seats from Tuesday’s election.

Party leader Yousef Jabareen commended a strong turnout among the community, saying it was “unprecedented and historic in our Arab society.” Arab voters make up about 20% of the Israeli electorate, but have traditionally voted at lower rates than Jewish Israelis.

That voter surge was driven by an urgent desire to dismantle Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition, which includes hardline ministers such as Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich.

That sentiment was underscored by chants of “Ben-Gvir, go home” at the Joint List election headquarters.

Jabareen said exit polls showed Arab-led parties can “make a difference.”

He vowed to be a “safety net in the face of crime in our society, a safety net in the face of dangerous racism, a safety net in the face of the demolition of homes and entire villages.”

Context: Entering government could still be tricky for Arab parties. Between them, the Joint List and Raam are projected to secure 17-19 seats in the 120-seat Knessett, their strongest showing in history.

Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party is projected to win 21-23 seats.

However, Eisenkot has set conditions for any partner to join his government, including recognizing Israel as a Jewish state and recognizing Hamas as a terrorist organization that must be dismantled, terms most Arab lawmakers are unlikely to accept.

Moreover, two of his opposition allies – Avigdor Lieberman and Naftali Bennett – have ruled out forming a government with the Arab parties altogether.

World.title: Anthropic’s nearly 100-page list of business risks includes everything from bioweapons to AI blackmail
World.content:
Anthropic filed for an initial public offering Monday in what could become one of the largest stock market debuts in history — detailing its surging business growth, along with a vast multitude of warnings about how it could all go wrong.

Anthropic’s filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission sets the stage for the company to go public and begin trading on the stock market as soon as November 16. The IPO could reportedly value the company at up to $2 trillion, which would make it one of the largest public companies in the world.

The company’s stock will trade under the ticker ANT and will be listed on the Nasdaq exchange.

The San Francisco-based company did not disclose how many shares it intends to sell nor at what price. That information will be determined in the coming weeks ahead of the stock market debut.

In the filing, Anthropic’s founders penned a letter to potential shareholders laying out their vision for the value of AI, while also disclosing what they see as the major risks for the business. Those risks include everything from competition from other AI labs to “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”

The IPO filing offers insight into how Anthropic views the future of its business despite those concerns and uncertainties.

Anthropic’s revenue grew 1,300 percent year-on-year in the first six months of 2026, to $16.3 billion. The company’s business is largely dependent on companies using its Claude AI system. Anthropic said it has more than 14,000 enterprise customers, with approximately 250 of those contributing $10 million or more in annual revenue.

But the company reported an overall net loss of over $80 billion, according to the SEC filing. Still, just shy of $9 billion of that loss was due to spending on AI infrastructure and computing, while more than $72 billion was attributable to “change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs.” That means only a fraction of the loss was actual spending during the first half of the year.

The company did not include results for the most recent financial quarter, which ended on September 30.

Anthropic’s IPO will test Wall Street’s appetite for AI, as the general public, policymakers and the industry’s own technologists raise major questions about the risks posed by AI — and whether the rapidly advancing research and data center buildout should be slowed.

The filing also addresses many of the same themes that have sparked concerns of an AI bubble, including the possibility of AI demand growing more slowly than expected.

Anthropic was last valued at $965 billion after raising $65 billion from investors in May.

Anthropic’s decision to move forward with its IPO signals “a willingness to face heightened public scrutiny,” said Jacob Bourne, an analyst with Emarketer.

“Anthropic’s IPO filing comes at a pivotal moment for the AI industry, as an anticipated wave of fall public offerings has failed to materialize amid rising concerns over debt-fueled infrastructure investments, uncertain returns, and AI safety risks that have reportedly contributed to rival OpenAI delaying its own IPO until next year.”

Anthropic’s risk factors

Anthropic’s filing lays out four major categories of risk from artificial intelligence: misuse, such as being used to design and implement bioweapons or cyberattacks; loss of human control; authoritarian abuse, such as its potential use to create surveillance states; and economic disruption.

The filing includes 93 pages of risk factors for Anthropic’s business. That’s significantly more than other tech companies that have filed to go public over the last decade, like Snap, which had around 30 pages of risk factors, and Uber, which had about 50.

If Anthropic’s models cause extreme harm, the company could face liability exceeding what its insurance can cover, the filing states.

The company also said its AI models may behave in unintended or “misaligned” ways and may take “harmful actions that no user or third party directed.”

Dario Amodei, co-founder and CEO of Anthropic. Jason Henry/Bloomberg/Getty Images

Anthropic sought to reassure potential investors by writing that it believes “frontier AI companies must invest in safety and alignment to help ensure the responsible diffusion of this technology.” But the company could face conflicting pressures to balance safety versus returns for investors once it goes public.

Anthropic sees a wave of other potential risks to its business in other areas as well, from whether it’s able to secure enough computing resources to uncertain regulatory and political environments. It also said much of its revenue relies on a limited number of products and customers.

But Anthropic’s growth will likely overshadow concerns about the company’s losses, challenges and potential risks to its business, according to Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville & Ives Co.

Anthropic and the AI race

Tech giants including Meta, Google, OpenAI and Anthropic are pouring billions of dollars into the AI race, all hoping to become the dominant player in what they promise will be a society-changing industry. Global spending on AI across services, software, infrastructure and other areas is expected to reach roughly $3.6 trillion in 2027, up from $1.8 trillion in 2025, according to market research firm Gartner.

OpenAI had an early lead following ChatGPT’s launch in November 2022, but the competition has intensified in the last four years. Anthropic’s Claude Code tool quickly became a favorite among software developers after launching in early 2025, and the company sought to replicate that success for other office jobs earlier this year with its Cowork agent.

Claude Cowork helped kickstart the shift from AI chatbots to agents — and rattled software stocks in the process over anxieties that it could make other businesses’ software tools obsolete. Fintech firm Ramp reported that 43.8 percent of US businesses paid for services from Anthropic in September, compared to OpenAI’s 40.6 percent share.

The Claude app has also seen a surge in growth this year. Market intelligence firm Sensor Tower estimates that it has more than 67 million monthly active users as of the third quarter of 2026, compared to 9.4 million a year ago.

But OpenAI also beefed up its own agents this year by launching its Codex coding app in February and ChatGPT Work agent in July for accomplishing multistep tasks like writing a brief or analysis.

Anthropic claimed in the S-1 that its own employees have made huge efficiency gains using Claude — pointing to a growth in revenue per employee from $1.4 million in September 2025 to more than $6.6 million in September 2026, mirroring sharp overall revenue growth during the period.

Now, tech companies are racing to create AI agents that will become the gateway to our entire digital lives, handling everything from shopping to booking restaurants and messaging friends. Anthropic is challenging Meta and OpenAI in this space with its new Duet agent, designed to complete tasks that require taking multiple steps across several apps.

At the same time, Anthropic has landed at the center of ongoing concerns over the breakneck pace of AI advancement.

Last month, CEO Dario Amodei called for an industry-wide slowdown to allow time for safety research, industry standards and regulation to catch up, a sentiment echoed by some other top AI leaders. His essay came after an employee resigned over fears that AI could pose a threat to humanity, and follows reports from Anthropic and its rivals of AI models hacking into other companies during testing.

Anthropic has also had a rocky relationship with the White House. The company temporarily revoked all access to its most capable models when the Trump administration ordered it to prevent foreign nationals from using the technology in June. But Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei was one of several AI CEOs who met with President Donald Trump in September and signed a voluntary commitment to self-police AI models.

World.title: In prominent West Bank settlement, voters speak of uniting a fractured country
World.content:
In the prominent Israeli settlement of Efrat in the occupied West Bank, voters said they were focused on uniting a country that has grown more fractured and divided over the last four years.

“I hope my children will have a good place to grow up, that there will be brotherhood among us, not just wars,” Elinor Veinglas told CNN. She said she hopes “that we will remember to come together and that will be our foundation here in this country.”

Even so, Veinglas said she would only decide for whom to vote “when I see the ballots.”

Her husband, David Veinglas said he would vote for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s rival, Gadi Eisenkot. “I believe whatever comes in the end will be fine,” he told CNN. “I hope for a united government.”

Meanwhile, Haviva, who declined to give her last name, said she prays for “the people of Israel, especially that there will be unity and that they will first find what they have in common between right and left.”

Just south of Jerusalem, Efrat is more ideologically diverse community than settlements deep in the West Bank that are aligned with far-right parties. Israeli settlements are considered illegal under International law by most of the international community and the United Nations.

Zvolon, who also declined to give his last name, said he was voting for far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich. “The people of Israel were exiled for 2,000 years living among the non-Jews. We had no government. Today we come and vote. I can say it seems my ancestors dreamed of this day,” Zvolon said.
