World.title: What exactly Democrats have pledged to do if they win in the midterms
World.content:
If Democrats can win control of either the House or the Senate, they will have seized some control of Washington back from President Donald Trump and Republicans.

They will have powerful new tools to conduct oversight and investigate Trump’s government; a seat at the table when it comes to government spending; and potentially a mandate to undo some of the changes he has imposed or push for AI regulation he has opposed.

While House Democrats may pass several partisan bills as a show of their priorities, there are limits to what the caucus would actually be able to accomplish. And maintaining unity and resolve would take work, especially since Trump, barred by the Constitution from seeking a third term, might not be willing to work with Democrats to keep the government functioning.

“What happens is I veto everything, and then the Democrats come and they want to make a deal,” Trump said last week of the prospect of working with a Democratic-majority Congress.

Any measures that the Democrats really want to become law would likely have to be part of must-pass legislation, such as the annual appropriations bills. And that would take negotiating with Republicans, at least in the Senate, since the Democrats are not expected to gain enough seats in that chamber to approve bills without GOP votes.

Here’s a look at some of the power Democrats could gain with a House or Senate majority, and what they would be able to do with it.

Cost of living

It was the affordability crisis and inflation that turned voters against President Joe Biden, and it may end up being inflation and affordability that turn voters against Trump. Democrats are promising a new focus on affordability, but there may be little they can do while Trump is president. There’s little chance they could gain the kind of majority that would allow them to overturn his veto. That means effort to pare back Trump’s tariffs or end his war on Iran would require help from Republicans.

The top Democrat in the House, Hakeem Jeffries, has said his party is creating working groups to explore how to bring down prices in five areas: housing, healthcare, caregiving, gas and utilities, and groceries and goods.

Jeffries has cited three immediate goals:

► Ending the war to bring down energy prices.

► Undoing cuts to Medicaid in the Republican tax and spending cuts bill, and renewing Obamacare’s enhanced premium subsidies to address health care costs…

► Repeal Trump’s tariffs to bring down the costs of goods…

But again, those things would require unlikely buy-in from Trump.

The power of the purse will be Democrats’ leverage

Maintenance workers are seen just after midnight at the US Capitol on October 1, 2025, when the government shut down after Congress failed to reach a funding deal. Kent Nishimura/Getty Images/FILE

Democrats’ main power point would be over the spending of taxpayer dollars, which means their leverage to force Trump to do things would be through the threat of taking away money. Trump will need legislation from Congress in order to keep the government running, although he has already overseen multiple protracted and unpopular lapses in funding during his presidencies.

Republicans sought to inoculate his immigration policy from Democrats by approving funding for the Department of Homeland Security to get through his term. Democrats could try to undo that funding, but they will likely lack votes to override Trump’s veto and they may have little control over how his DHS, flush with funding, goes about its business.

Another expected clash will be over the debt ceiling. Republicans raised the debt ceiling by $5 trillion when they passed Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act — yes, the tax cuts bill added a lot of money to the national debt. It’s expected that the debt ceiling will have to be raised again in 2027.

Look for Democrats to use their power over funding to stall or stop Trump’s DC projects, which he argues are necessary to beautify the capital, but which Democrats see as vanity projects. This is probably why Trump’s administration is trying to move quickly on things like the triumphal arch and the championship-level golf course he wants to use taxpayer money to build.

But Democrats also would have to deal with the reality that reversing or modifying some of the sweeping cuts in the “big, beautiful bill” will cost a lot of money, a daunting hurdle even for many in the caucus at a time when the national debt has topped $40 trillion.

Healthcare

Continuing the enhanced premium subsidies to Affordable Care Act enrollees has been a top priority for Democrats for the past two years. They shut down the government for a record 43 days last fall in an effort to pressure GOP leaders to extend the more generous assistance, which lapsed at the end of 2025.

The enhanced subsidies’ expiration sent premium payments soaring 58% this year, and several million people have dropped their coverage.

But the cost alone would be daunting — a permanent extension could cost $350 billion over a decade, according to the Congressional Budget Office.

As for reversing the historic Medicaid cuts in the GOP’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Democrats would have to decide which of the multiple measures to target. The first-ever federal work requirement is expected to lead to the largest loss of coverage, but it would be a big lift to remove the mandate, which is set to kick in on January 1 in most states. Democrats might seek to delay or soften some of the provisions in the law and regulations, such as those related to self-attestation, medical frailty and provider taxes.

That’s not to say that Democrats would just sit back as the Medicaid cuts take effect. They are expected to actively monitor the rollout of the provisions and publicize their impact on enrollees and other Americans, hospitals, and states, among others.

It’s also likely that they would push the Trump administration for more details on its “Most Favored Nation” deals with drugmakers. Trump would like them codified into law, but there are a lot of questions about the details of the agreements and whether they have actually driven down costs for patients.

While several progressive Democratic candidates have pushed for Medicare for All on the campaign trail, don’t expect the caucus to move forward on an expansion of Medicare to more Americans in the coming Congress.

Investigations

Left to right: Eric Trump, Jared Kushner, Ivanka Trump and Donald Trump, Jr. applaud during the inauguration of President Donald Trump in the Rotunda of the US Capitol on January 20, 2025. Kevin Lamarque/Pool/AFP via Getty Images

Oversight is likely to be one of the most immediate and visible consequences of any Democratic takeover of either the House or the Senate. With the majority comes the power to call hearings and subpoena witnesses.

Expect Democrats to launch inquiries into Elon Musk, for starters. Many questions remain about the so-called Department of Government Efficiency he launched with Trump’s blessing. Contracts awarded to Musk’s companies could also be scrutinized.

Trump’s efforts to effectively shut down agencies created by Congress like USAID, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and the Department of Education will likely get their first real scrutiny by lawmakers.

So will the actions of Trump’s children to make money during their father’s presidency. Trump has made more than $1 billion on crypto at a time when he could be overseeing its regulation.

His most controversial policies, like the Iran war, mass deportation and tariffs, will be put under the microscope.

Cabinet members like Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Attorney General Todd Blanche will also need to make more time on their calendars for public hearings and their agencies will face more scrutiny from congressional committees.

Iran war

Fires rage at the Shahran oil depot after US and Israeli strikes in Tehran, Iran, on March 8. Hassan Ghaedi/Anadolu via Getty Images

There will be bipartisan support for ending the war, but forcing Trump to abandon the project will be complicated. The War Powers Act seemingly requires congressional approval for prolonged military action, but Trump has found ways around those provisions. Plus, it would take 67 votes — which would mean help from Republicans — to override Trump’s veto. Republicans will be under immense pressure to pass a massive war funding bill in the lame duck period after the election but before new lawmakers take office in January. But the question of Pentagon funding and whether spending bills can be used to control war policy will become a major issue. If the war continues to be unpopular, pressure from Congress and the public will be hard for Trump to continue to ignore.

Food stamps

Workers for La Colaborativa hands out fresh food to Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) recipients in Chelsea, Massachusetts, on November 13. Joseph Prezioso/AFP via Getty Images

In an effort to blunt the Republicans’ historic cuts to food stamps, Democrats are expected to target a provision of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that will require states to shoulder a portion of the benefit costs if they have high rates of payment errors. Currently, the federal government covers the entire tab, but that will change next October for many states.

Democrats have already been pushing for a two-year delay to this measure as part of the Farm Bill. The Senate Agriculture Committee has passed a one-year delay but included an increase in the penalty rate for states with the highest error rate, which Democrats oppose. It’s unclear whether the Farm Bill will become law before this Congress’ term ends at the end of December.

The error rate provision has prompted some states to tighten their application and renewal processes and to add more paperwork requirements. That has contributed to more than 5.5 million people losing benefits since Trump signed the bill into law in July 2025, according to the Food Research & Action Center.

Still, the measure could take a big bite out of state budgets next year at a time when many aren’t flush with funds. That could prompt states to take even more drastic actions, which could lead to more coverage losses.

College education

Democrats will seek to draw a contrast between themselves and Republicans, who reduced the amount of federal loans graduate students and parents can take out and made student loan repayment plans less generous for many borrowers, said Jon Fansmith, senior vice president for government relations at the American Council on Education.

That might include forcing congressional Republicans to take tough votes to keep the stricter rules or requiring Trump to veto the package.

Meanwhile, they may try to address a controversial Department of Education rule that subjects nurses, physician assistants, physical therapists and certain other healthcare professionals to lower loan limits than doctors. There may be bipartisan support to change that rule, considering the shortage of healthcare professionals in the US.

Democrats could also hold oversight hearings on the Trump administration’s efforts to dismantle the Department of Education and shift its responsibilities to other agencies. They would likely look into whether these moves are helping or hurting students and their educations.

Social Security and Medicare

Don’t expect Democrats to advance any serious measures in the next year to address the looming insolvency of the Social Security and Medicare trust funds, which are projected to be drained in the early 2030s. Neither party is expected to tackle this complex and sensitive issue until closer to the deadline.

Democrats may float bills that seek to shore up the programs’ fiscal health to make it clear what their fixes would entail. They generally support lifting the income threshold on Social Security payroll taxes that would subject more of higher earners’ pay to the levy. Some would also expand benefits, such as making the annual cost-of-living adjustment more generous or increasing the minimum monthly payment.

Addressing Medicare’s financial problems will be more complicated. Democrats have supported expanding benefits, such as adding dental, vision and hearing coverage. They have also looked at ways to save the program money, such as rein in reimbursements for Medicare Advantage insurers — though not all of those would help the Medicare Part A trust fund.

Where Trump might work with Democrats

Jeffries came under some scrutiny from Democrats when he met this year with Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner about areas where the two sides could work together. The two talked about housing and criminal justice reform. Housing in particular could be an area where Democrats and Republicans negotiate.

Trump himself has also talked with Democratic New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani about housing and infrastructure projects. During his first term, Trump’s major bipartisan achievement was passing the First Step Act, an effort that brought together Democrats and Republicans in the months after voters gave control of the House back to Democrats during Trump’s first term midterm election.

World.title: Gas under Trump 2.0 is now more expensive than it was under Biden
World.content:
New York — On the campaign trail in 2024, President Donald Trump On the campaign trail in 2024, President Donald Trump promised to make gas dirt-cheap again and blamed record-high gas prices on the Biden-Harris “war on energy.”

But then an actual war got in the way: Trump’s deeply unpopular conflict with Iran.

Nearly eight months into a war that has destabilized the global energy system, the average price of gas during Trump’s second term is now more expensive than it was during the Biden era, according to a CNN analysis of AAA data.

That milestone — a nearly unthinkable outcome as recently as January — underscores the frustration over high prices that has engulfed Trump and the Republican party leading up to the midterm elections.

“It’s pretty astonishing,” Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, said of the fact that gas is now more expensive under Trump than former President Joe Biden. “I don’t think anyone would have predicted this 10 months ago.”

It’s a major reversal of the return to sub-$2 gas that Trump promised in the summer of 2024 as he successfully convinced voters to return him to the White House.

Polar opposite of Trump 1.0

During his first term, the national average for regular gas was just $2.47 a gallon. During the depths of the Covid-19 pandemic, gas prices plunged to as low as $1.77 nationally in April 2020.

The health emergency caused demand for fuel to crash to the point that the world ran out of room to store oil, a phenomenon that briefly drove crude oil futures below zero for the first time ever.

At one point in April 2020, Trump even pleaded with Saudi Arabia and Russia to stop pumping so much oil to halt a crash that threatened to bankrupt US oil companies and kill countless jobs.

The situation couldn’t be more different today.

The White House has waged a last-minute scramble to contain the damage from high fuel prices by taking a wide range of steps, including throwing farmers an $8 billion financial lifeline, buying millions of barrels of Russian diesel and examining steps to drive down extremely high shipping costs.

“President Trump is fixing these long-term problems by taking tangible steps to increase our refining capacity here in the United States, while also taking immediate actions, such as releasing oil from our (Strategic Petroleum Reserve) to add supply to the market, temporarily waiving the Jones Act, and allowing red-dyed diesel for highway use, to lower prices at the pump,” White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers told CNN.

A truck is parked at a diesel fuel pump displaying prices above $8 per gallon at a truck stop in the Wilmington neighborhood of Los Angeles on September 22, 2026. President Donald Trump expressed support for a diesel export ban, with fuel prices having surged on the back of the Middle East war. Patrick T. Fallon/AFP/Getty Images

Gas was cheap — before the war

The outlook for gasoline and diesel prices was very favorable for Americans when the year started.

Gas prices were safely below $3 a gallon, and, if anything, the energy market was worried about a supply glut that could keep fuel prices low.

“If Trump really wanted to keep his promise to keep gas prices low, what he should have done was nothing,” said Gregory Brew, senior analyst at consulting firm Eurasia Group. “The market was oversupplied. There was a lot of crude sloshing around. Inventories were quite large. But Trump reversed that with the war.”

Trump has argued that elevated gas prices are a small price to pay for keeping Iran from getting a nuclear weapon.

But the spike in gas prices has angered voters who were hoping for the opposite under Trump.

“High gas prices do not bode well for incumbents. They didn’t bode well for Biden either,” GasBuddy’s De Haan said.

Stuck above $4

Gas prices spiked even higher under Biden, zooming to an all-time high of $5.02 a gallon in June 2022 after Russia invaded Ukraine.

However, gas prices came down faster under Biden.

In fact, 2026 has already shattered the Biden-era record for the most number of days with $4 gas or higher.

The war with Iran led to the unthinkable: The unprecedented closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway the world relied on to get oil out of the Middle East.

While oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz have largely recovered, the cost to get that crude out has skyrocketed because of expensive and inefficient workarounds being used. The cost of hiring an oil tanker has skyrocketed from $65,000 a day last year to $1.6 million earlier this month.

A shortage of refining

Not only that, but the world is now grappling with a global refining shortage. Refineries that would normally churn out diesel, jet fuel and gasoline have been damaged in the Middle East and Russia. China has held back its own fuel exports.

To make up for lost refinery output, the world has drawn fuel from commercial and emergency stockpiles.

But that leaves the intricate energy system vulnerable to shocks.

Case in point: A recent, unexpected outage at ExxonMobil’s Joliet, Illinois, refinery caused gasoline prices to go through the roof in Michigan, Ohio and other Great Lakes states in recent days.

“Right now, there is no cushion. Commercial inventories are very low,” said Brew. “When there is any kind of outage, everyone starts to scramble.”

An unloaded truck, fuel tanker, and compressed natural gas fueled transit bus drive past the Marathon Petroleum Corp. Los Angeles Refinery in Carson, California, on September 22, 2026. According to the company’s website, the refinery is the largest on the West Coast with a crude oil capacity of 365,000 barrels per calendar day, producing California Air Resources Board (CARB) gasoline and CARB diesel fuel among other products. Patrick T. Fallon/AFP/Getty Images

Refiners, incentivized by the ability to make incredible profits due to the shortage, are producing as much fuel as possible even though normally this is the time of year operations slow for routine repairs.

“Refiners have been running flat-out for months. If you own a refinery, you are printing money. Some are skipping maintenance because there is money to be made right now,” said Brew. “But if you run refiners for months on end, they will break down.”

Once the Exxon refinery returns to normal, gas prices should come back down. However, that relief will likely be offset by the fact that oil prices have surged to seven-month highs as traders brace for the risk of a return to all-out war in the Middle East after the election.

De Haan said Trump is “pulling every small lever he can” to cushion the blow from high prices.

“Unfortunately, they’re not adding up to much,” he said. “Until the biggest lever — diplomacy — is pulled, he’s going to continue to fight against very elevated gas and record diesel. It’s fairly ominous.”

World.title: Liberia: After CBL Pay Shock, House Turns on Executives
World.content:
MONROVIA – Liberia’s House of Representatives has ordered a sweeping review of salaries and benefits across government, days after a rare public disclosure of a senior official’s pay reignited anger over the cost of running one of the world’s poorest countries.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

In a unanimous vote on Tuesday, the lower house of the national legislature instructed two of its committees, on Ways, Means and Finance and on Public Accounts, to examine the pay and perks of government officials and report back within two weeks. The motion was brought by Representative Alex S. Noah of Sinoe County.



Lawmakers argued that they are wrongly blamed for the country’s swollen wage bill, while ministers and the heads of state-owned enterprises earn far more.

The disclosure that lit the fuse

The vote came less than a week after Euphemia G.T. Swen-Monmia, President Joseph Boakai’s nominee for Deputy Governor for Economic Policy at the Central Bank of Liberia, appeared on October 22 before the Senate Committee on Banking and Currency for her confirmation hearing.

Asked about her pay, she did something Liberian officials rarely do: she gave the numbers. She testified that her monthly salary is US$9,000, that she receives around US$5,000 in cash benefits on top of that, and that her housing allowance should be about US$15,000. She has served in an acting capacity since August 12.

That amounts to roughly US$168,000 a year in salary and cash benefits before housing is counted. A civil servant on the government’s US$150 monthly minimum would need more than seven and a half years of uninterrupted work to earn what she receives in a single month.

Swen-Monmia is a career central banker who joined the bank in 2010 as a management trainee and rose to director of its Financial Markets Department. The controversy is not about her qualifications but about what her testimony revealed: pay at the top of Executive agencies is generous, and almost never made public.

No lawmaker cited her testimony by name during Tuesday’s debate. But the timing, and the focus of the two letters that triggered it, on officials earning more than US$5,000 a month, suggest the disclosure handed fresh ammunition to a chamber long cast as the main villain in Liberia’s debate over official pay.

‘We are suffering’

On the floor, several members described their own compensation as “peanuts” compared with Executive officials and argued the legislature deserves more because representatives serve larger numbers of constituents.

Representative Moima Briggs-Mensah of Bong County said a US$2,000 budget line meant for constituents’ school scholarships often never arrives, and that lawmakers lack the insurance enjoyed by Executive officials.

“We don’t even have Social Security benefits. We are suffering and people in the Executive are making mockery of us,” she said.

Representative Anthony Williams of Maryland County said lawmakers were being “falsely crucified” by the public while benefits such as fuel arrive months late.

“The Executive, especially SOEs are reaping the honey, while we are being falsely crucified,” he said, demanding that state enterprises disclose their gross and net pay and benefits to the House.

The numbers tell a different story

Lawmakers’ complaints sit uneasily with the figures. Senators earn US$8,000 a month each, according to the draft 2026 budget, and a bill to cut that to US$5,000, first introduced by Senator Abraham Darius Dillon in 2020, has stalled for years. In 2025, House members’ basic salary was put at roughly US$8,569 a month, with additional funding for security guards, drivers, cooks and other support staff.

The legislature as a whole has also grown more expensive. The draft 2026 budget gave lawmakers US$51.7 million, up from US$41.3 million in 2024.

That is in a West African nation of about 5.2 million people still rebuilding from 14 years of civil war that ended in 2003, whose national budget crossed US$1 billion for the first time this year. About half the population lives below the poverty line.

Meanwhile, front-line public servants struggle to get paid at all. Teachers’ U.S.-dollar pay has gone unpaid since October 2025, and nurses are demanding a monthly minimum of US$500.

A chamber in revolt

Tuesday’s vote follows weeks of turmoil inside the House over lawmakers’ own money. More than 40 members boycotted the legislature’s reopening session on October 9 in protest over unpaid benefits and allowances, including constituency visits, district projects, fuel and medical allowances. Calling themselves “Reformists,” they accused the chamber’s leadership of withholding benefits and legislative support funds.

The Senate faces its own scrutiny. A proposal from its Committee on Rules, Order and Administration, reported by FrontPageAfrica, seeks US$792,552 in the 2027 budget to raise salaries for 224 Senate staff, with some increases as high as 71 percent. The Senate has disputed the reporting and demanded a retraction; FrontPageAfrica stands by its story.

Two letters, two tones

The review was triggered by letters from two lawmakers who framed the problem very differently from their colleagues on the floor.

Representative Sumo Kollie Mulbah of Montserrado County asked the House to hold up the national budget until the Finance Ministry reports all salaries and benefits above US$5,000 a month for ministers, directors, county governors and commissioners. The central bank deputy governor’s testimony would place her nearly three times above that threshold.

Mulbah singled out housing allowances, fuel and phone-credit coupons, and overseas medical treatment on top of health insurance.

“While these elite benefits are sustained, critical national priorities like the increment of the minimum wage are continuously set aside,” he wrote.

Representative Musa Hassan Bility of Nimba County called for a special committee to review salaries, allowances, wasteful spending, duty-free privileges and tax exemptions across all branches of government, and insisted the legislature go first.

“We cannot continue to demand sacrifices from ordinary Liberians while protecting our own excessive privileges,” Bility wrote. “This must not be another selective exercise intended to embarrass particular officials for public applause.”

What to watch

The two-week deadline lands as the Executive prepares to send the 2027 budget to the legislature by October 31. The government projects total spending will fall to US$1.02 billion next year, meaning any gains for one group of officials will likely come at someone else’s expense.

The test is whether the committees follow Bility’s call to start with the legislature, or whether the review becomes, as he warned, a selective exercise aimed at the Executive. Liberians have heard promises of pay cuts before. A proposal to cut senators’ pay to US$5,000 has been on the table for six years without passing.

World.title: Liberia: Inside the Defense Bid to Overturn the Peter Bon Jallah Conviction
World.content:
A Liberian judge convicted a former national security aide of statutory rape and kidnapping but cleared him of gang rape. Four days later, his lawyers filed a motion arguing that the two halves of the ruling cannot both stand.

By Rodney D. Sieh

MONROVIA — When Judge Wesseh Alphonsus Wesseh Sr. delivered his verdict on Friday, October 23, he framed the case around three questions: whether the evidence supported a conviction for gang rape, for statutory rape, and for kidnapping. He answered no to the first and yes to the other two.



That split is now the battleground. On Tuesday, October 27, at 11:12 a.m., lawyers for Peter Bon Jallah, 63, a former special assistant to the director of Liberia’s National Security Agency (NSA), filed a motion for a new trial at Criminal Court “E” in Monrovia. The filing, received by Acting Clerk of Court Abraham Richards, asks the judge to set aside his own verdict.

The motion is the first formal test of a ruling that, by the court’s own record, states its conclusions on each charge without detailing how it weighed every witness and exhibit. That gap is what the defense is trying to exploit.

What the court decided

Jallah was arrested on January 7, 2026, after the mother of a 16-year-old boy complained to the police Women and Children Protection Section. The boy did paid chores at Jallah’s home.

A grand jury indicted Jallah and two unidentified men in February on charges of gang rape, statutory rape and kidnapping. The indictment alleged abuse at Jallah’s home on November 29 and December 24, 2025. It also alleged that on January 1, 2026, Jallah lured the boy with an offer of football boots, drove him to a building off Camp Johnson Road in central Monrovia, and held him there for three days while he and two other men abused him.

The two other men were never brought before the court. Jallah, who has denied all the allegations, chose to be tried by a judge rather than a jury.

The court acquitted him of gang rape, finding the prosecution’s evidence insufficient. It convicted him of statutory rape and kidnapping. Jallah was remanded to Monrovia Central Prison pending a pre-sentence report from the Ministry of Justice’s Bureau of Probation Services. No sentence has been imposed.

The prosecution’s case

According to the written verdict, the prosecution called 13 regular witnesses and six rebuttal witnesses. The defense called eight witnesses, including Jallah, plus three subpoenaed witnesses from the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, the mobile operator Orange Liberia and the John F. Kennedy Medical Center.

The state’s strongest scientific evidence came from Pascal Bavugirije of the Rwanda Forensic Institute, which analyzed exhibits after Liberia sent them abroad. He testified that DNA profiles from four clothing exhibits matched Jallah’s reference sample. Material collected from the alleged scene produced a mixed profile from unknown people that matched neither Jallah nor the boy.

The boy testified in August that he was assaulted three times, and the court admitted his police statement over defense objections. Investigators also told the court that phone records placed Jallah near one of the alleged scenes, contradicting his account that he had no contact with the boy.

The defense’s four arguments

The motion, signed by Counsellor G. Wiefueh Alfred Sayeh of the Law Offices of Sayeh & Sayeh, makes four main claims.

1. The kidnapping conviction contradicts the gang rape acquittal. The defense argues that the kidnapping charge rests on the alleged three-day confinement off Camp Johnson Road, the same episode at the heart of the gang rape charge. If the court found too little evidence that the gang rape happened there, the motion says, it cannot find that the boy was held there. It describes the conviction as “contrary to weight of the evidence.”

2. The court lacked jurisdiction over kidnapping. Criminal Court “E” is Liberia’s specialized court for sexual offenses. The motion argues it has no jurisdiction over kidnapping as a separate crime. This is a purely legal question, and if the judge or a higher court agrees, it could void that conviction regardless of the evidence.

3. Penetration was never proven. Under Liberia’s rape statute, penetration is an essential element. The defense points to three pieces of testimony:

* A JFK Medical Center doctor, called by the defense, testified that an examination under anesthesia shortly after the boy’s January rescue found no evidence of trauma. The hospital’s operative record lists the post-procedure diagnosis as “normal findings.” The motion says the prosecution offered no rebuttal.

* The Rwandan forensic examiner testified that DNA analysis cannot establish guilt or innocence and that his report did not show whether penetration occurred.

* A nurse examiner from the hospital’s One Stop Center for survivors of sexual violence, a prosecution witness, testified that she could not say the boy was not raped, adding that she was there only to report what she saw. The defense argues that statement does not prove rape and creates doubt that must favor the accused.

The motion goes further, accusing the judge of attributing the words “penetration” and “blunt object” to the nurse’s testimony when, it says, no witness used them.

1. The defendant did not get a fair trial. The motion alleges the judge remarked in open court that the prosecution was “asking weak questions.” It also says that after reviewing the defense’s Orange phone records, the judge on his own initiative subpoenaed Jallah’s records from a second carrier, Lonestar Cell MTN, over a defense objection that the court could not introduce evidence on the state’s behalf.

How strong are the arguments?

Each claim faces hurdles, and none has yet been tested by the prosecution’s response.

The medical findings do not settle the question on their own. Forensic medicine broadly recognizes that the absence of physical injury does not rule out sexual assault, particularly when an examination comes days after an alleged act. The prosecution can also point to the DNA findings and the boy’s testimony. A judge sitting without a jury is entitled to weigh credible testimony against an inconclusive medical record.

The kidnapping argument may be harder to dismiss. The acquittal on gang rape could reflect doubt about the two unidentified men rather than about the alleged confinement itself. Whether that distinction holds depends on reasoning the published verdict does not spell out.

The fair-trial complaint about the phone subpoena raises a recognized principle: a judge in an adversarial system is not supposed to build the prosecution’s case. How much weight the court gave those records is not clear from the verdict.

What happens next

Judge Wesseh must rule on the motion. If he denies it, the case moves to sentencing once the probation report arrives. The defense has already said it will appeal to the Supreme Court of Liberia, and the arguments in this motion offer a preview of that appeal.

The case has been closely watched in Liberia because of Jallah’s position close to the head of the country’s main intelligence agency, and because it tests how the courts handle sexual violence against children. It has already passed through two courtrooms, a failed prosecution bid to move the trial out of Monrovia, and a change of judge.

The Ministry of Justice, which prosecuted the case, had not filed a response to the motion as of Tuesday.

World.title: Liberian Activists Urge Freeze on New Mining Deals Until Decades-Old Law Is Rewritten
World.content:
A coalition of civil society groups says signing long-term contracts under Liberia’s 2000 mining law would lock in the weak oversight, lost revenue and pollution that have marked the sector for decades.

MONROVIA, Liberia — A coalition of civil society organizations in Liberia has called on the government to stop signing and ratifying new long-term mining contracts until the West African nation replaces its 26-year-old mining law.

The CSO Consortium on Minerals, Mining, and Inclusive Sustainable Development made the appeal on Monday, October 26, at a press conference in the capital. It urged President Joseph Nyuma Boakai and the national legislature to impose a moratorium on new Mineral Development Agreements (MDAs) — the contracts, typically lasting 25 years or more, that set the terms under which large mining companies operate and that carry the force of law once lawmakers ratify them.



“We strongly believe that entering into new or additional long-term mineral development agreements under an outdated legal framework risk perpetuating existing governance weaknesses,” the coalition said.

Its members include the Center for Transparency and Accountability in Liberia, Integrity Watch Liberia, the Sustainable Development Institute, Medica Liberia and ActionAid Liberia, among others.

Wealth that has not reached communities

Mining is central to Liberia’s economy. It accounts for about a fifth of gross domestic product and dominates exports, according to a March 2026 assessment by the Washington-based research group Forest Trends. Iron ore and gold are the main products.

Yet the coalition said decades of extraction have not delivered matching jobs, public services or development for the communities that host mines. It blamed weak enforcement, corruption, the export of unprocessed ore, poor transparency, environmental damage and the exclusion of local people from decisions.

The Forest Trends report reached similar conclusions. It found the government may be losing millions of dollars a year in uncollected mining revenue. Mining companies paid just over $844 million to the state between 2007 and 2023, according to figures from the Liberia Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (LEITI), the national arm of a global revenue-disclosure standard. Mining licenses now overlap more than two million hectares of forest in a country that holds about half of what remains of the Upper Guinean rainforest biodiversity hotspot.

A year of illegal mining and license violations

The call follows a year in which government inspectors repeatedly found companies mining outside the limits of their permits, or with no permit at all.

Liberia issues several tiers of mining license. Class C permits are reserved for Liberian citizens and allow only hand tools. Class B permits cover small commercial operations. Large industrial projects operate under MDAs.

In March, a committee of the House of Representatives suspended Hurine Mining Company in central Bong County after investigators found it had exceeded the limits of its Class B license.

In April, the Ministry of Mines and Energy closed JinXin Mining Company in Rivercess County for mining without a valid license on ground licensed to another firm. The ministry said JinXin had ignored an order in January to stop. Days later it shut Alex Gee Group of Companies in Grand Gedeh County, whose license had lapsed. Officers also dismantled an unlicensed site whose alleged Chinese operators fled before they arrived.

In June, officials in Gbarpolu County seized excavators working a Class C claim, where heavy machinery is banned. They also found Chinese nationals mining under another company’s license, outside its approved boundaries.

Mines and Energy Minister R. Matenokay Tingban has acknowledged that many small commercial license holders fail to account for the minerals they extract.

The problems are not new. In 2024, the then-minister sought legal advice on revoking licenses issued since 2018, citing letters from the presidency directing that license applications be routed through the Office of the President. In 2025, a ministry investigation found that two companies, Hamak Mining and its successor 79 Resources, had misrepresented their license status and owed the government more than $400,000 in fees.

Big miners under scrutiny

Concerns extend to the largest operators. An investigation by The Associated Press and The Gecko Project published this year found that Bea Mountain Mining Corporation, Liberia’s biggest gold producer, repeatedly leaked cyanide, arsenic and copper at levels the country’s Environmental Protection Agency said exceeded legal limits.

The investigation found the company failed to report a 2022 spill on time and had earlier blocked government inspectors from its laboratory. Bea Mountain exported more than $576 million worth of gold between July 2021 and December 2022.

Why the coalition wants a pause now

Liberia’s Minerals and Mining Law was enacted in 2000, before the country’s 14-year civil war had fully ended. Lawmakers opened public hearings on amendments in July. At those hearings, the Liberia Chamber of Mines, an industry body, warned that changes limited to small commercial licenses would not fix the sector’s deeper problems. It called for a full overhaul covering taxation, licensing, environmental protection and strategic minerals such as lithium, cobalt and rare earths.

In January, the legislature ratified an amendment to the contract of steelmaker ArcelorMittal, Liberia’s largest iron ore producer, extending it to 2050 with an option to renew for 25 more years. Some senators praised the deal as a model for renegotiating other contracts. Another senator abstained, citing the company’s record of unmet commitments to host communities.

For the coalition, that timeline is the core of the argument. Contracts signed under a law that government, industry and activists all describe as outdated will outlast any reform that follows.

What the activists want in a new law

The coalition drew up its proposals at a meeting with mining-affected communities on October 1 and refined them at an October 21 roundtable with government agencies, donors and companies. Its 10 recommendations include:

* Binding transparency rules for licensing, contracts and revenue, including public disclosure of who ultimately owns mining companies;

* Clear penalties for violations by companies and by officials, and legal remedies for affected communities;

* Enforceable benefit-sharing for communities, building on a 2018 land rights law;

* Requirements to process more ore locally and to prioritize Liberian workers and suppliers;

* Binding obligations for mine closure and land restoration;

* Measures to protect women, young people and people with disabilities, including against sexual exploitation and abuse in mining areas; and

* Tighter regulation of small-scale mining, including sand and quarry operations.

The coalition praised the Boakai government’s stated commitment to reform but said the new law “must go beyond updating existing provisions.”

The Ministry of Mines and Energy did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

World.title: Liberia: Grebo Leader Calls for Calm and Swift Probe Into Death of Samuel Gekor in Grand Gedeh
World.content:
MONROVIA – A prominent Liberian lawyer and leading figure in the Grebo community has called for calm and a swift investigation into the death of Samuel Gekor, a young Grebo man found dead on a cassava farm near Zwedru, the capital of southeastern Grand Gedeh County.

Gekor’s body was discovered in the Kanneh area of Electoral District Two after he had been missing for three days. The circumstances of his disappearance remain unclear.

Counsellor Kunkunyon Wleh Teh expressed deep sadness over Gekor’s death and extended condolences to his family and the wider Grebo community, one of Liberia’s major ethnic groups, concentrated largely in the country’s southeast.



Teh, a former student of Bishop Juwel High School in Zwedru, said he has spoken with Gekor’s family to offer his condolences and support.

While acknowledging the community’s grief, fear and frustration, and its legitimate demand for answers, Teh urged residents to remain calm, peaceful and law-abiding as the search for justice continues.

He called on the Liberia National Police and the Ministry of Justice to speed up the investigation, establish the facts surrounding the disappearance and death, and ensure that anyone found responsible is held accountable under the law. The family and the public, he said, deserve timely updates, transparency and credible answers.

“Every Liberian deserves the right to life, safety, and dignity, irrespective of tribe, county, or social standing. No family should be left without answers when a loved one dies under troubling circumstances,” Teh said.

He said the community’s responsibility at this moment is to stand with the family, promote peace and demand justice through lawful means, cautioning against letting grief and anger turn into actions that could endanger lives or deepen divisions.

“Justice must be pursued, truth must prevail, and peace must be preserved,” he said.

World.title: Investors, executives gather in Margibi as Liberia seeks new money for mining and energy
World.content:
MONROVIA – President Joseph Nyuma Boakai will open a two-day international mining and energy conference on Wednesday, as Liberia steps up efforts to attract foreign investment into the natural-resource sectors that underpin its economy.

The Liberia International Mining and Energy Conference and Expo (LIMEC 2026) runs October 28–29 at the Farmington Hotel in Margibi County, near Roberts International Airport outside Monrovia. Government officials, international investors, mining executives, energy developers and development partners are expected to attend.

Boakai is scheduled to deliver the keynote address, setting out his government’s plans for drawing investment and promoting responsible development of the country’s mineral resources.



Mining, chiefly iron ore and gold, is one of the West African nation’s main sources of export earnings, while chronic power shortages remain a major obstacle to industrial growth.

Held under the theme “Transforming Liberia’s Economy: Driving Development Through Sustainable Mining and Energy Investments,” the conference will feature panel discussions, presentations and exhibitions on investment opportunities in mineral exploration, production, renewable energy and related infrastructure.

Amara Kamara, president of the Liberia Chamber of Mines, said the gathering offers Liberia a chance to deepen ties with international investors, showcase its resources and build partnerships that could create jobs and drive growth.

He said the event’s value should go beyond investment promotion to opening doors for Liberian businesses, increasing local participation in the mining industry and ensuring that communities benefit from investments.

Kamara credited Mines and Energy Minister R. Matenokay Tingban and his ministry for coordinating with the Chamber of Mines and AME Trade Ltd., the international organizer, to stage the event.

Sponsors include Avesoro Resources, Mantrac Group, Huawei, CORICA Mining Services, Mansa Resources, Sarmin Metals, Westcrest Liberia, AGL Africa Global Logistics, the Liberia Electricity Corporation (LEC), the Liberia Petroleum Regulatory Authority (LPRA) and WBHO.

World.title: Liberia: IIC Survey in Grand Gedeh Reveals 87.6% of Respondents Unaware of Freedom of Information Law
World.content:
ZWEDRU, Grand Gedeh County — Sixteen years after Liberia enacted the Freedom of Information (FOI) Act of 2010, a new survey conducted by the Independent Information Commission (IIC) has revealed significant gaps in public awareness of the law in Grand Gedeh County, with 87.6% of 1,875 respondents reporting that they had never heard of the legislation.

The findings emerged from a Knowledge, Attitudes and Practices (KAP) Survey conducted by the Commission’s Outreach Department as part of a broader initiative implemented from October 14–17, 2026, aimed at strengthening public awareness, promoting transparency, and bringing access to information services closer to residents of southeastern Liberia.

The initiative combined the training of 25 locally recruited Data Collectors, a one-hour radio awareness programme on TOP FM, and a two-day community-based survey conducted on October 16–17.



According to the Commission’s final activity report, each of the 25 Data Collectors reported reaching 75 respondents, bringing the total number of survey participants to 1,875.

Beyond the limited awareness of the FOI Act, the survey revealed that 85.3% of respondents did not know how to submit a Freedom of Information request, while 85.5% did not know where such requests should be submitted.

The findings also indicated that 85.3% believed citizens were afraid to request information from public institutions, highlighting concerns about public confidence and the practical exercise of information rights.

Despite these challenges, the survey revealed strong support for transparency and accountability. Approximately 95.6% of respondents agreed or strongly agreed that citizens should have access to public information, while 94.9% believed that access to information improves government accountability.

Additionally, 90.2% of respondents supported the need for sustained public awareness campaigns on the FOI Law.

These findings present an important contrast: while many residents support the principle of government openness, a substantial proportion remain unfamiliar with the law that gives them the right to request public information.

The results underscore the need to move beyond the existence of legislation and invest in practical education that helps ordinary citizens understand how to use the law in their daily lives.

The survey also provided guidance on how the Commission could reach more residents with information about their rights.

According to the findings, 88.9% of respondents preferred radio as a channel for FOI awareness, while 80.4% identified community engagement as another important means of public education.

The results further highlighted opportunities for digital outreach, with 77.6% of respondents reporting regular internet use and 81.4% indicating willingness to use an official FOI website to learn about their rights or request public information.

These findings offer the Commission an opportunity to adopt a combination of radio discussions, community outreach, and digital platforms to strengthen awareness across Grand Gedeh and other underserved counties.

Beyond the survey findings, one of the major achievements of the initiative was the recruitment and training of 25 young people from Grand Gedeh County to serve as Data Collectors and Freedom of Information Ambassadors.

Unlike approaches that depend entirely on personnel brought from other counties, the Commission recruited local residents and equipped them with knowledge of the FOI Act, professional interviewing techniques, research ethics, data integrity, and digital data collection using KoBoCollect.

The one-day training, held on October 14, 2026, at the Administrative Building Community in Zwedru, brought together the selected Data Collectors, representatives of the county administration, and officials of the Independent Information Commission.

Welcoming the IIC delegation on behalf of the Office of the Superintendent, Hon. Tarley A. Dweh congratulated the selected participants and encouraged them to collect accurate and reliable data.

He appreciated the Commission for extending its activities to Grand Gedeh and expressed the county administration’s commitment to supporting efforts that promote public access to information.

Information Commissioner Hon. Joash T. Hodges emphasized the importance of data integrity and professionalism, reminding the participants that the information gathered would help the Commission design future programmes based on the specific needs and realities of Grand Gedeh County.

Acting Outreach Director Mr. Jutomue Doetein facilitated sessions on the constitutional and legal foundations of the right to information, citizens’ rights under the FOI Act, and the importance of professional data collection for evidence-based decision-making.

Acting Compliance Director Mr. Armah B. Johnson also educated participants on the obligations of public institutions under the law, including the appointment of Public Information Officers, proactive disclosure of information, and procedures for addressing information requests and complaints.

The training provided participants with both legal knowledge and practical skills to support the Commission’s ongoing public education efforts.

Speaking on behalf of the female participants, Ms. Purity S. Free expressed appreciation to the Commission for providing young people in Grand Gedeh with an opportunity to learn about the FOI Law and participate in a professional data collection exercise.

She particularly welcomed the decision to recruit local enumerators rather than bringing personnel from other counties.

Similarly, Mr. Fredino Wright, speaking on behalf of the male participants, thanked the Commission and encouraged his colleagues to remain committed to their responsibilities as Freedom of Information Ambassadors.

Their reflections highlighted how the initiative created opportunities for local youth empowerment while strengthening the Commission’s ability to reach communities through residents familiar with local conditions.

As part of the intervention, Acting Outreach Director Jutomue Doetein and Acting Compliance Director Armah B. Johnson appeared on TOP FM’s Morning Breakfast Programme to discuss the Commission’s mission in Grand Gedeh and educate listeners about their rights under the FOI Act.

Doetein focused on the right of citizens to request public information and the importance of access to information in promoting transparency, accountability, and public participation in governance.

Johnson explained the corresponding obligations of public institutions, emphasizing that government offices operating at county and local levels are also required to comply with the law.

During the one-hour programme, ten callers expressed dissatisfaction over difficulties they said residents faced when seeking information from public institutions in Grand Gedeh County.

Their contributions provided additional insight into the concerns of ordinary residents and reinforced the importance of ensuring that public institutions respond appropriately to information requests. While the callers’ accounts were not independently verified as violations of the law, they highlighted the need for stronger engagement between the Commission, local institutions, and community members.

The initiative also generated a proposal for the establishment of a regional Freedom of Information Hub in Grand Gedeh County.

Speaking during the Data Collectors’ training, Ministry of Justice representative Mr. Joseph Jallah commended the Commission for extending its intervention to the county and appealed for the establishment of a regional FOI Hub to serve southeastern Liberia.

He emphasized that such a facility could provide thousands of residents across the region with greater opportunities to understand and exercise their rights under the FOI Act.

The proposal reflects the broader need to decentralize access to information services and reduce the distance between citizens and institutions responsible for protecting their rights.

Following the exercise, the Commission’s report recommended sustained community-based FOI awareness campaigns, targeted engagement with county-level public institutions, continued radio education programmes, and ongoing support for the 25-trained local FOI Ambassadors.

Other recommendations include assessing the feasibility of establishing a regional FOI Hub in Grand Gedeh and expanding digital access to information services.

The findings also provide a baseline for designing future interventions and assessing improvements in public knowledge and utilization of the law.

The Grand Gedeh initiative builds on similar KAP survey activities undertaken by the Commission in Montserrado and Grand Bassa Counties in June 2026.

For the Independent Information Commission, the exercise represents more than a survey. It demonstrates the importance of bringing national laws closer to the communities they are intended to serve while empowering local residents to take an active role in promoting accountability.

The central lesson from Grand Gedeh is clear is that passing a law is only the beginning. Its real impact is felt when ordinary citizens know their rights, understand how to exercise them, and can confidently approach public institutions for information.

World.title: Liberia’s Agricultural Transformation Gains Momentum as Ministry Receives Final Consignment of Chinese-Donated Machinery
World.content:
Agriculture Ministry Advances Government’s Drive Toward Mechanized Farming, Increased Food Production, and National Food Self-Sufficiency

MONROVIA — Liberia’s ambitious journey toward agricultural modernization and national food self-sufficiency has received another significant boost as the Ministry of Agriculture, under the leadership of Hon. Dr. J. Alexander Nuetah and his team of Deputy Ministers, receives the final consignment of agricultural machinery donated by the People’s Republic of China.

The shipment, comprising 42 containers of agricultural machinery, arrived at the Freeport of Monrovia, marking another important milestone in the government’s ongoing efforts to transform Liberia’s agricultural sector through mechanization, improved productivity, and strengthened international cooperation.



According to the Ministry, the first 15 containers are being moved from the Freeport today, while the remaining 27 containers are expected to be moved in the coming days.

Strengthening Liberia’s Agricultural Transformation

The arrival of the machinery represents another step in the Ministry’s broader efforts to transition Liberia’s agricultural sector from predominantly traditional farming practices toward more modern, productive, and commercially viable agricultural systems.

Under Minister Nuetah’s leadership, supported by his team of Deputy Ministers and technical professionals, the Ministry continues to pursue initiatives aimed at improving agricultural productivity, strengthening food security, supporting farmers, and reducing the country’s dependence on imported food.

The Chinese-donated machinery is expected to contribute to these objectives by strengthening the country’s agricultural mechanization capacity and supporting efforts to improve farming efficiency.

Leadership, Partnerships, and Progress

The latest consignment also highlights the importance of international partnerships in supporting Liberia’s agricultural development agenda.

The Government of China’s contribution reflects continued cooperation between Liberia and China in advancing agricultural development, technology transfer, and food production.

For Minister Nuetah and his leadership team, the arrival of the equipment represents an opportunity to translate international development cooperation into practical support for Liberia’s farming communities.

As the Ministry continues implementing its agricultural transformation agenda, attention will increasingly focus on ensuring that modern farming equipment becomes accessible to farmers and contributes meaningfully to increased domestic food production.

Advancing the Vision of a Food-Secure Liberia

Agriculture remains central to Liberia’s economic development, rural livelihoods, employment creation, and national food security.

The Ministry’s continued emphasis on mechanization is particularly important in addressing longstanding challenges associated with low agricultural productivity, limited access to modern farming equipment, and dependence on labour-intensive cultivation methods.

With the arrival of this final consignment, the Ministry has taken another important step toward strengthening the resources available to support agricultural modernization.

The milestone reinforces the Ministry of Agriculture’s commitment, under Minister J. Alexander Nuetah and his team of Deputy Ministers, to building a more productive, competitive, resilient, and food-secure Liberia.

As the machinery moves from the Freeport of Monrovia, the next critical phase will involve its deployment and effective utilization to support farmers and agricultural production across the country.

For Liberia, the arrival of these 42 containers represents more than the delivery of agricultural equipment; it signals another opportunity to turn the country’s agricultural potential into measurable progress toward national food self-sufficiency.

World.title: Liberia: Government says Monrovia’s busiest market won’t be cleared after hundreds of traders march on Public Works Ministry
World.content:
MONROVIA – Calm has returned to Waterside Market, one of Monrovia’s busiest trading hubs, after government officials assured traders that the market will not be cleared, a day after hundreds marched on the Ministry of Public Works fearing eviction.

The standoff began when about 15 iron selling tables were removed from the main road through the market to make way for traffic diversions during construction on Vai Town Road. Traders, many of whom depend on daily sales to feed their families, feared the move was the first step toward demolishing the entire market.

Officials have since clarified that only tables blocking the main driveway from the Vai Town Bridge will be moved, so vehicles can pass during construction expected to last until July 2027. The 15 seized tables will be returned.



“Unlike yesterday when the tension was high, at least they have calmed down because the information was not properly provided before,” Waterside Market Superintendent Roland Tuazama told FrontPageAfrica on Tuesday.

Women-led march

On Monday, scores of marketers, predominantly women, staged a peaceful protest in Waterside against the removal of their selling tables along a major road corridor. The protesters accused city police officers of harassment and of introducing new restrictions without consulting their leadership, local media reported. Marching toward the Public Works Ministry, they chanted, “President Boakai, we want to sell. Give us our tables.”

The disputed tables were built during the administration of former President George Weah, under then-Monrovia Mayor Jefferson T. Koijee, as part of an effort to organize trading in Waterside.

‘It was shocking’

Tuazama said market leaders had agreed to the diversion plan about two weeks earlier after a joint inspection with the police, and the arrangement went smoothly at first.

“We agreed, we cooperated. We, along with the police, inspected the place and said okay,” he said.

Tensions flared on Sunday after reports that heavy machinery had blocked all routes into the market and that tables had been removed without consulting market leaders.

“It was shocking. We had not sat down one day to discuss the tables,” Tuazama said.

The dispute was resolved at a meeting with officials of the Ministry of Public Works, the Liberia National Police and Emmanuel Dahn, the lawmaker representing the area in the House of Representatives, who intervened to calm the protesters.

“The ministers and the police explained to us that there is construction on the road … and that they need the driveway to be clear because they will be diverting traffic,” Tuazama said. “We all agreed that the driveway should be cleared so that traffic can be free. Not all of the tables, only the road on the bridge.”

He said the Public Works Ministry has agreed to carry out the plan jointly with market leaders, and traders displaced from the roadway will be moved to available space inside the market.

“Development is coming. We all accepted it,” he said.

Tuazama called for better coordination among the ministry, the police and market leaders to avoid future clashes, stressing that traders need timely information when decisions affect their livelihoods.

“We and the police are friends; we work together. But sometimes we can have differences,” he said. “All parties concerned should work together so that there will be no hostility.”

World.title: Janza lands top job in Tanzania
World.content:
Former Zambia National Team Head Coach and FAZ Technical Director Honour Janza has been appointed as the new Technical Director for Tanzanian giants Simba SC.

Janza will work with South African Coach Steve Barker at Simba.

Simba has announced that it had reached an agreement to hire the 66-year-old Zambian to strengthen its technical bench for domestic and CAF Champions League campaigns.

“The club management has reached an agreement to appoint Honour Janza (66), a Zambian national, as the new Technical Director,” the club said in a statement.

“Janza’s arrival is aimed at strengthening the technical bench under Coach Steve Barker to improve the team’s efficiency for both domestic competitions and the CAF Champions League.”

Janza brings vast continental experience, holding a UEFA B Licence and a CAF A Licence.

He is no stranger to top-level football, having served as Assistant Coach of the Chipolopolo between 2011 and 2014, a period when Zambia dominated African football, and later as Head Coach of the senior team from 2014 to 2015.

The veteran tactician also served as Technical Director of the Football Association of Zambia – FAZ – for eight years from 2009 to 2017, while simultaneously handling the Zambia Under-20.

His club CV includes stints as Head Coach of Zesco United, Red Arrows, Eswatini’s Mbabane Swallows, and Tanzania’s Namungo FC, as well as Technical Director roles at NAPSA Stars and most recently Zesco United from 2023 to 2026.

The move marks a return to Tanzanian football for Janza, who previously coached Namungo FC in the 2021-2022 season.

Janza has previously served as Tanzania National Team interim Head Coach.

World.title: Katele Kalumba appeared for mention
World.content:
Former Cabinet Minister, Katele Kalumba, has appeared before the Lusaka Magistrates’ Court for mention in a case in which he is charged with seditious practices.

The 74-year-old former minister appeared before Magistrate Webster Milumbe, accompanied by his wife and close friends.

Dr Kalumba is charged with seditious practices, contrary to Sections 57(1)(h) and 60(1)(c) of the Penal Code, Chapter 87 of the Laws of Zambia.

Particulars of the offence allege that between August 1 and 13, 2026, Dr Kalumba published seditious statements on his Facebook page, accusing President Hakainde Hichilema of being responsible for alleged abductions, deaths and strangulations.

He is also alleged to have warned of public resistance if the August 13 general election was rigged.

During the previous court session, the court entered a plea of not guilty after determining that Dr Kalumba’s response during plea-taking did not amount to an unequivocal admission of guilt.

The court subsequently granted him bail in the sum of K100,000, with two Lusaka-based sureties.

The matter has been adjourned to November 10, 2026, for continuation of trial.

Meanwhile, Magistrate Milumbe has extended Dr Kalumba’s bail pending the continuation of the trial.

World.title: 18-year-old boy detained over death of pupil
World.content:
Eastern Province Police Commissioner Robertson Mweemba, has confirmed the apprehension of an 18-year-old boy in connection with the suspected murder of a 14-year-old pupil in Chama district.

Mr Mweemba said the deceased was a Form Two pupil at Chama Day Secondary School who went missing on Friday, October 23, 2026, after reportedly leaving home to attend Independence Eve celebrations.

“The young lady did not return home, which raised concern among her parents, as she went missing on the evening of October 23 and was not seen on October 24, before her body was found on October 25 and when investigations commenced we established that she had a boyfriend,” he added .

Mr Mweemba highlighted that police investigations later revealed that the deceased had a boyfriend, an 18-year-old Grade 10 pupil at the same school, who has since been apprehended to assist with investigations.

He disclosed that police are working to establish what transpired before the girl’s death and whether anyone else may have been involved.

The body was taken to Chama District Hospital mortuary, where it was deposited pending a postmortem examination to establish the cause of death.

Mr Mweemba said police would provide further information as investigations continue.

World.title: Vice President Mutale Nalumango defends the realignment of government ministries
World.content:
Vice-President Mutale Nalumango has defended President Hakainde Hichilema’s decision to realign government ministries, saying the move is aimed at improving public service delivery and accelerating national development.

Mrs Nalumango said Article 92 (2) (d) of the Constitution empowers the President to establish, merge and dissolve government ministries, subject to the approval of the National Assembly.

She said this when she moved a motion in Parliament today seeking approval for the proposed establishment, realignment and dissolution of government ministries.

She said the proposals are intended to create an efficient and effective public service that will connect the nation, grow the economy, enhance financing for the future and improve living standards.

She explained that the ministries proposed for dissolution and realignment include Energy, Infrastructure, Housing and Urban Development, Commerce, Trade and Industry, Lands and Natural Resources, and Youth, Sport and Arts.

The Vice-President said the proposed new ministries include Trade and Exports, Industry, Electricity, Petroleum, Infrastructure and Urban Development, Housing, Lands, Steel and Higher Education, Youth and Sports, and Culture and Arts.

She stated that the proposed changes are in line with President Hichilema’s address to Parliament on October 9, 2026, in which he emphasised that an efficient, effective and results-oriented public service is key to achieving the Grow Zambia Agenda and national development.

The Vice President said several ministries will remain unchanged, including Defence, Home Affairs and Internal Security, Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Finance and National Planning, Agriculture, Fisheries and Livestock, Small and Medium Enterprise Development, Mines and Minerals Development, Tourism, Transport and Logistics, and Water Development and Sanitation.

Others are Green Economy and Environment, Health, Information and Media, Education, Technology and Science, Justice, Labour and Social Security, Local Government and Rural Development, and Community Development and Social Services.

She, however, clarified that although the names of the ministries responsible for Tourism, Green Economy and Environment, Education, and Technology and Science will remain unchanged, some of their portfolios will be transferred to other ministries, while others will receive additional responsibilities.

The Veep said the complete list of the proposed ministries and the allocation of portfolios and statutory functions are contained in the appendices submitted to Parliament.

Mrs Nalumango thanked the legislators that participated in debating the motion

Meanwhile, the realigning, changing and dissolution of government ministries was overwhelmingly welcomed by the Members of Parliament.

Yesterday, President Hakainde Hichilema wrote to the National Assembly Speaker Nelly Mutti to request Mrs Nalumango, who is leader of Government Business in the House, to move a motion on realigning, changing and dissolving some ministries.

World.title: President Hichilema nominates Syakalima and Mutati as MPs
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has nominated former Minister of Education Douglas Syakalima and former Minister of Technology and Science , Felix Mutati as Members of Parliament (MPs).

The two took their oaths of allegiance before Speaker of the National Assembly Nelly Mutti in Parliament today.

Ms Mutti welcomed the two nominated MPs to the 14th National Assembly, in accordance with Article 260 of the Constitution, which requires persons assuming public office to take and subscribe to the prescribed oath or affirmation before commencing their official duties.

Mr Mutati returns to the National Assembly, having served during the Fifth Session of the 13th National Assembly, while Mr Syakalima is a former legislator for Chirundu Constituency.

The two former Cabinet Ministers join five other presidential nominees to Parliament, namely Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Corporation Mulambo Haimbe, Minister of Green Economy and Environment Gilbert Siame, Minister of Health, Professor Roma Chileng’I, former UPND Luena Member of Parliamen, Mubita Anakoka; and renowned economist and former National Road Fund Agency (NRFA) Board Chairperson, Noel Nkhoma.

World.title: 25 Cholera Patients from Zambia Railways passenger train evacuated to Chilanga Urban Clinic
World.content:
The Ministry of Health has evacuated 25 cholera patients from a Zambia Railways passenger train to Chilanga Urban Clinic.

The train was en route to Livingstone when it was intercepted in the Mapepe–Kachenjela area of Chilanga District, following a cholera outbreak notification.

Ministry of Health Permanent Secretary Kennedy Lishimpi has disclosed that the affected patients have been transferred to the health facility for medical attention.

According to a statement made available to the media by the Chilanga Town Council Public Relations Unit, Dr Lishimpi stated that 475 other passengers aboard the train have been vaccinated as part of the measures to contain the situation and protect public health.

He explained that one passenger who boarded the train from Kapiri Mposhi developed cholera symptoms on the train, prompting the Ministry of Health to be alerted.

Dr Lishimpi said the train was intercepted following the alert and an assessment was conducted on board.

He added that the train has been fumigated and is expected to resume its journey to Livingstone once the last passenger has received the required vaccination.

Dr Lishimpi said the Government will erect resting tents to provide temporary shelter for passengers affected by the incident as an interim measure.

“The passengers have also been provided with clean, treated drinking water and will receive food as authorities continue to attend to their immediate needs,” he said.

He added that the Ministry of Health is coordinating with its staff in Livingstone to be on the lookout for any symptoms that may develop among passengers on the train for a quick response.

World.title: Government concerned with continued boundary disputes
World.content:
Central Province Permanent Secretary Milner Mwanakampwe has expressed concern with the continued boundary disputes among chiefdoms.

Dr Mwanakampwe explained that boundary disputes have the potential to retard development in chiefdoms.

He further highlighted that boundary disputes create uncertainties, thereby discouraging investment and slowing infrastructure development in the province.

The Permanent Secretary stated that there is a need to address boundary disputes which are a major source of conflict among chiefdoms to ensure certainty and encourage investment.

He said this when a team from the Surveyor General’s office and the House of chiefs led by Clerk Julien Mulenga paid a courtesy call on him in Kabwe.

The team is in the province to discuss the boundary dispute between Chiefs Chamuka of the Lenje people of Kabwe and Chisamba and Chembe of the Lala people of Luano district.

Dr Mwanakampwe stressed the need to urgently resolve the long-standing boundary disputes stating that Chief Chemba is involved in another boundary dispute with Chief Shikabeta of Rufunsa district in Lusaka Province.

“We would like to take advantage of your presence to also deal with other disputes in Mumbwa between Chief Mumba, Chief Moono, Chief Liteta, Chief Shakumbila and the Nsanje forest. We are hopeful we can utilize this same window to manage that as quickly as possible,” said Dr Mwanakmpwe.

The Permanent Secretary emphasized that though some traditional leaders do not recognize the 1958 boundary map, it is the official reference document recognized by government for resolving the disputes.

And Clerk of the House of chiefs Julien Mulenga said the team will discuss the issue with the two traditional leaders and engage the surveyors to survey the disputed land.

Ms Mulenga said the survey will only determine the boundary and not disrupt the livelihoods of the people settled there.

World.title: Zambia, Switzerland trade investments reach $20 billion- President Hichilema
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema says trade and investment between Zambia and Switzerland has, over the years evolved, reaching over 20 Billion United States Dollars.

President Hichilema has since called for deepened relations into a comprehensive economic partnership between the two countries, to not only ease investor cooperation but also support the Grow Zambia Agenda.

The Head of State notes that the partnership model would ensure mutual benefit and protection, moving away from the traditional pattern of European firms investing in Africa without local participation.

President Hichilema said this, when Swiss State Secretary, Helene Artieda, called on him at State House, in Lusaka today.

President Hichilema highlighted opportunities not only in mining but also in commodities, agriculture, and value addition, stressing that Zambia seeks to leverage Swiss capital and technology alongside its own natural resources.

“We are now saying, seek accelerated economic growth through investment and trade and other things will fall in place”, he shared.

President Hichilema urged Swiss businesses to take advantage of Zambia’s youthful population, which needed education, skills, jobs, and opportunities.

The Head of State stressed that Zambia and Switzerland should work together as equal partners in the global arena, describing such cooperation as the best insurance policy against instability and a pathway to shared prosperity.

President Hichilema also expressed gratitude to Switzerland for its longstanding relations with Zambia, dating back to the 1060s, acknowledging its contribution to the Country’s debt management.

And Ms Artieda expressed Switzerland’s interest in investing in the country , noting that Zambia is well positioned.

She noted that Swiss investment consists of domestic value addition in sectors including extractive minerals, technology and innovation that will create jobs in Zambia.

The Swiss State Secretary further pledged her country’s support towards the Grow Zambia Agenda, noting that the private sector has a key role to play in its achievement.

“We believe that we are, hopefully, a country of choice for your excellency to continue to work with. We are fully supportive of the 10,10,5,3,3,1, 1,1. We believe that the private sector can be part of the solution”, Ms Artieda stated.
