World.title: South Africa: 14 SAMWU Members in Court Over Protests - South African News Briefs - October 28, 2026
World.content:
press review

14 SAMWU Members in Court Over Protests

Fourteen members of the South African Municipal Workers Union (SAMWU) are set to appear in the Johannesburg Magistrates' Court on charges of inciting public violence, reports EWN. They were arrested after blocking the M1 highway near Braamfontein during protests over a long-standing wage dispute with the City of Johannesburg. The union said that the municipality has failed to honour a 2016 agreement aimed at addressing historic salary disparities, with only R1.2 billion of the approximately R10.3 billion owed reportedly paid. SAMWU is opposing the city's proposed payment timeline and has vowed to continue fighting until the dispute is resolved.

Court to Deliver Judgment in Suliman Carrim Contempt Case

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The Pretoria Magistrates' Court is set to deliver judgment in the contempt case against North-West businessman Suliman Carrim, reports SABC News. He is accused of failing to appear before the Madlanga Commission despite being subpoenaed to testify. Carrim was arrested at OR Tambo International Airport while allegedly preparing to travel to Saudi Arabia via Dubai. The State is opposing bail, arguing that he poses a flight risk. His defence maintains that he intended to return to South Africa after an alleged religious pilgrimage.

Calls for Full Probe into Bronkhorstspruit Water Crisis

Deputy Minister of Water and Sanitation Jack Bloom has called for a full investigation into the Bronkhorstspruit water contamination crisis, which has left more than 800 people ill, reports EWN. The incident has been linked to the City of Tshwane's failure to chlorinate water at the Bronkhorstspruit Treatment Works for three weeks, reportedly following a dispute with its chlorine supplier over a price increase. The plant allegedly continued drawing water from a sewage-polluted river while equipment malfunctioned. The plant manager has been suspended. Bloom said that accountability must extend beyond plant officials to include those responsible at political and administrative levels.

World.title: Zimbabwe: It Was Painful! Chiwenga's Ex-Wife Marry Mubaiwa in Explosive Tell-All About Couple's Relationship - Claims They Abused Drugs
World.content:
VICE President Constantino Chiwenga's ex-wife Marry Mubaiwa has revealed startling details about their eight-year long marriage which she described as painful and revealed how both of them abused pethidine, a restricted pain drug.

Marry, who was removed from remand on Tuesday after seven years of her attempted murder trial, was speaking for the first time since her arrest in late 2019.

Married customarily in 2011, Marry and Chiwenga enjoyed a seemingly blissful period of their union before she was arrested for attempting to kill her former army general husband by pulling plugs at a South African health facility.

According to the exposè, she was forced out of her shower, ordered to dress and then taken to Avondale Police Station where her fate of a seven-year long court appearance was sealed.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"Wherever he is, Chiwenga knows I never tried to kill him," said Mubaiwa in an interviewconducted by journalist Simba Chikanza.

"I even laughed when my lawyer Beatrice Mtetwa told me I was being charged with murder before she told me that she was being serious."

She is now a stark contrast of how she looked in November 2017 when she drew attention by vigorously bouncing to Jah Prayzah's Kutonga Kwaro at the National Sports Stadium in celebration of President Emmerson Mnangagwa's inauguration after a coup her ex-husband successfully led.

Then a model of sharp lines, long limbs and glass smooth skin, Marry now has lost an arm and a leg…literally. They were amputated after she suffered symptoms similar to those Chiwenga had before he was chosen to fly to China for health care while she was ordered to stay.

Added Marry: "All Chiwenga had to do was tell me that he no longer wanted me. Chiwenga never picked me from the streets or from a poor family.

"When Chiwenga met me I had a very good life, I had very good life, I had my own cars. I was not after anything he had because I already had it.

"I no longer have any love for him, the way God intended for it to end was a bad way but it taught me many things. It was painful because I lost my hand, I lost my foot, I lost because of Chiwenga, because of the pethidine that he induced in me.

"Chiwenga destroyed my mental health, my health and this is a man I took care of.

"Chiwenga would inject himself with pethidine but order a military nurse to inject me with the same drug as he said he could not sleep without him knowing that I would also be asleep.

"For so many years I was on pethidine and the nurses who were ordered to inject me could not say no as the order was coming from their superior."

Marry said she only got reprieve from the pethidine routine only when she fell pregnant.

Close 

The couple had three children Tendai, Christian and Michael over the two Marry had from her previous marriage.

Sharing details about them, Marry said she had gone seven years without seeing or talking to them.

"I just want my children, my house and cars. If you wanted someone to just bare you kids I would have said no," she added.

"If I were to take those children and deny you access for seven years, how would you feel?"

Straying into existing factional fights within Zanu PF, Marry said she could get Chiwenga fired if she decided to share more about her ex-husband's shenanigans.

"Every dog has its own day, Chiwenga is a dog waiting for its day. My day was today, his day is coming.

"God forbids that he becomes the President of Zimbabwean, Zimbabwe will be in trouble," she said.

"He used to be a very sweet man, a very prayerful man until that day he told a lie.

"The lie he told that I wanted to kill him is a crime, but because he is a vice president can he be arrested? Chiwenga must be arrested for lying and making sure this lie carries on for seven years."

Chiwenga is eyeing Presidency at the end of Mnangagwa's term. He is in a close-cold war kind of race with businessman and Mnangagwa ally Kudakwashe Tagwirei.

"I hope God forgives you because I forgive you," said Marry.

World.title: Congo-Kinshasa: Cases Top 10,000 in DR Congo Ebola Outbreak
World.content:
DR Congo has reported more than 10,000 Ebola cases and nearly 4,900 deaths. The outbreak involves a virus for which there is no approved vaccine or specific treatment, complicating efforts to contain its spread.

Health authorities in the Democratic Republic of Congo reported that Ebola cases had risen to 10,060, with 4,887 deaths since the outbreak was identified in mid-May.

The outbreak involves the Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or specific treatment. The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention has described it as the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.

Where else have cases been reported?



Kenya has confirmed nine infections, including two deaths, after a patient traveled from DR Congo through Uganda to the capital, Nairobi.

Nigeria also confirmed an infection in a Swiss woman, the wife of a Swiss diplomat, who fell ill after visiting Uganda. Authorities are investigating where she contracted the virus. She was evacuated to Switzerland.

Why is the outbreak difficult to contain?

Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person. It can cause fever, diarrhea and, in some cases, bleeding.

Early symptoms can resemble malaria, potentially delaying isolation and treatment.

The lack of an approved vaccine or specific treatment against the Bundibugyo virus further complicates efforts to control the outbreak.

Are vaccines and treatments being tested?

Clinical trials of two antiviral treatment approaches have been underway since July.

Two further trials are investigating whether the Ervebo vaccine can protect against the Bundibugyo virus. The vaccine is currently approved and recommended only against Ebola virus, formerly known as Zaire ebolavirus.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

World.title: Nigeria: Nigeria's First Methane Disclosure Raises Questions Over Repeated Figures, Missing Data
World.content:
An analysis of Nigeria's first public company-level greenhouse gas disclosure reveals repeated emissions figures, incomplete methane reporting, and inconsistencies in the list of companies that submitted data, raising questions about the reliability of the country's emissions baseline.

Nigeria has taken an important step towards improving transparency in its oil and gas sector by publishing company-level greenhouse gas emissions data for the first time.

The disclosure, released by the Nigeria Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (NEITI) in its 2023 oil and gas audit report, is expected to help citizens, regulators and investors understand how much pollution companies emit and whether the country is making progress towards its climate commitments.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

However, an independent review of the data has identified several issues that may undermine confidence in the disclosures if left unresolved.

Using the Emissions Monitoring and Accountability Tool (EMAT), an interactive platform that organises and compares emissions data published by NEITI, this analysis found repeated emissions figures across different companies, missing methane information, and inconsistencies in the number of companies reported as having submitted emissions data.

The findings do not suggest wrongdoing by any company. Rather, they highlight areas where Nigeria's emissions reporting framework could be strengthened to improve transparency, data quality and public confidence.

Repeated emissions figures

One of the most striking observations is that Chevron Nigeria Limited and the Shell Petroleum Development Company (SPDC) reported exactly the same methane emissions figures for 2022.

Both companies reported 173,578,759.2 kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalent (COâe) and 6,943,150.368 kilograms of methane.

The values are identical across virtually all reported fields except for halons.

The figures appear in Appendix 12 of NEITI's 2022 and 2023 Oil and Gas Industry Reports, which contain Nigeria's first publicly available company-level greenhouse gas disclosures.

This became immediately visible because EMAT allows users to compare company data side by side, identical figures that may be difficult to notice in static tables.

The Chevron-SPDC entries are not isolated cases.

Another example is Aradel Holdings Plc, which reported exactly the same methane values in both 2022 and 2023: 133,522,033 kilograms COâe and 5,340,877 kilograms of methane.

Similarly, Network E&P reported 112 kilograms CO2e and 3.64 kilograms methane in both reporting years.

Repeated figures do not automatically mean the data are inaccurate. Companies with similar operations, shared production facilities, or common reporting boundaries could legitimately report similar emissions. However, exactly identical values reported to several decimal places warrant further verification against the original submissions.

Another case concerns Pillar Oil, where the same numerical value appears repeatedly across different greenhouse gases.

For example, in 2022, the value 1,610,170.7872 appears across several gases, including carbon monoxide, nitrous oxide, nitric oxide and sulphur dioxide. The same pattern appears in 2023 with 2,389,859.8050.

The published report does not explain why these different gases share identical values.

Missing methane information

The analysis also found that methane reporting is far from complete.

Of the 30 company-year records reviewed in Appendix 12, only 12 contain information across all three methane reporting fields.

The remaining 18 records contain missing information, and some of the omissions are difficult to interpret.

For instance, NAE reported 963,970 kilograms of methane in 2022 but recorded zero for the corresponding carbon dioxide equivalent.

In 2023, the company again reported methane emissions but left the carbon dioxide equivalent field blank.

Similarly, Chevron and Heirs Energies reported methane only as carbon dioxide equivalent in 2023 without providing the underlying methane mass.

Heirs Energies reported 217.4 million kilograms COâe, one of the highest methane-related figures in the dataset, yet the absence of the methane mass makes it impossible to independently verify the conversion.

In another case, Platform Petroleum appears on the reporting sheet, yet all of its methane fields are blank for both years.

The report provides no explanation of whether blank cells indicate that no emissions occurred, that no data were submitted, or that emissions were not calculated.

This distinction matters because a blank field is not the same as reporting zero emissions.

Inconsistencies in company reporting

The analysis also raises questions about how many companies actually submitted emissions data.

NEITI states that 15 out of 62 audited companies submitted greenhouse gas information, while 47 companies did not.

However, the appendix presents 15 companies on the reporting sheets, and 58 entries on the non-reporting sheet.

Taken together, the lists contain 73 entries, rather than the 62 companies referenced by NEITI.

Further review shows that Platform Petroleum appears on both the reporting and non-reporting lists.

In addition, some entries refer to joint venture interests or individual oil fields rather than clearly identifiable legal entities, making it difficult to determine exactly which companies reported emissions.

For example, the non-reporting list includes the NEPL (55 per cent) and Shoreline (45 per cent) interests in OML 30, while the reporting sheets separately list Esso's Erha and Usan fields.

A reconciled list that clearly distinguishes legal entities, operators, and production assets would significantly improve transparency.

Why this matters

Nigeria has committed to ending routine gas flaring by 2030 and reducing fugitive methane emissions from the oil and gas sector by 60 per cent by 2031.

Measuring progress towards these goals depends on reliable baseline data.

Because Appendix 12 represents Nigeria's first public company-level greenhouse gas disclosure, it effectively serves as the benchmark against which future emissions reductions will be measured. If the baseline contains gaps or inconsistencies, assessing future progress becomes more difficult.

Several practical improvements could strengthen future disclosures, including publishing the original reporting templates submitted by companies, clearly distinguishing between reported zeros and missing information, identifying the legal entity responsible for each reported asset, providing explanatory notes for unusual entries and maintaining a public log of corrections where errors are identified.

NEITI's response

NEITI was asked, through a Freedom of Information request, to respond to the issues identified in the analysis, including questions concerning the methodology used by companies, duplicate figures, missing or zero values, emissions intensity, the number of reporting companies, verification procedures, and the accessibility of the published data.

NEITI explained that under EITI Requirement 3.4, greenhouse gas reporting is encouraged rather than mandatory.

According to the agency, its reporting template requested companies to provide greenhouse gas emissions data and information on the methodology used, including emission factors, direct ground based sensors, satellite estimates, and other recognised approaches.

However, the template did not require companies to provide the Global Warming Potential values used, the specific IPCC or other scientific assessment from which those values were derived, or the time horizon used to convert emissions into COâ equivalents.

The agency said it did not convert, normalise, recalculate or adjust the data submitted by companies. The published figures, therefore, reflect the information provided by the companies.

NEITI also said there is currently no established national verification framework for these disclosures and that its role is focused on transparency, collection, and publication rather than on independent technical validation or methodological harmonisation.

Close 

Regarding repeated entries and identical figures identified in the analysis, NEITI acknowledged the observations and said it would conduct an internal review.

The agency said necessary adjustments had been reflected in the published data. It added that the original company templates and internal validation records were not intended for public disclosure.

NEITI said that any corrections or clarifications resulting from its internal review would be reflected in the published dataset. It acknowledged the observations and said it would take the feedback into account as it updates the published information.

What happens next?

NEITI's first company-level greenhouse gas disclosure represents an important starting point for public scrutiny of emissions in Nigeria's oil and gas sector.

The data provide journalists, researchers, civil society organisations and policymakers with information that was previously difficult to access at the company level.

At the same time, the analysis shows that the value of the disclosure will depend on improvements in the way emissions information is collected, standardised, verified and published.

The immediate priority should be to establish a clearer and more consistent reporting framework that enables users to distinguish between zero emissions, missing information and non-applicable data; understand the methodology behind reported figures; identify the companies and assets covered; and reproduce emissions-intensity calculations.

As Nigeria works towards its methane-reduction commitments, the quality of the underlying data will be as important as the targets themselves.

The first disclosure has opened the window of transparency. The next challenge is ensuring that the information available through that window is complete, consistent and reliable to support meaningful public accountability.

This report was supported by the Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development(CJID) as part of the Deepening Methane Emissions Transparency Initiative-Stream II

World.title: Nigeria: Niger Miners' Deaths - Govt Panel Says 37 Suspects Died From Suffocation
World.content:
A federal government panel says 37 suspected illegal miners who died in NSCDC custody in Niger State in September died from asphyxiation, following autopsies and forensic investigations.

A federal government panel investigating the deaths of 37 suspected illegal miners in the custody of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) in Niger State has attributed their deaths to asphyxiation, or deprivation of adequate oxygen.

Jonathan Kure, chairman of the 10-member independent committee, disclosed this on Tuesday while presenting the panel's report to the Minister of Interior, Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo, in Abuja, TheCable reported.

Mr Kure said the committee visited Minna, inspected the detention facility, conducted autopsies, obtained statements from NSCDC personnel, survivors, relatives of the deceased and other witnesses, and reviewed documentary and forensic evidence.



He said preliminary findings also pointed to institutional gaps and overzealousness among some officers, stressing the need for greater professionalism in handling suspects in custody.

President Bola Tinubu directed a full investigation into the deaths, prompting the federal government to constitute the committee on 19 September.

The government also suspended Niger State NSCDC Commandant Suberu Aniviye and 20 other officers in connection with the incident.

The suspects were arrested during operations on 15 and 16 September around the Mohammed Inuwa Wushishi Estate in Minna, the Niger State capital.

In an earlier statement, Mr Aniviye said scores of detained suspects were found dead in the early hours of 17 September following what he described as a suspected disease outbreak.

The deaths sparked public outrage and calls for accountability, with the federal government ordering an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the arrests, detention and deaths.

On 6 October, the committee requested a two-week extension to complete its investigation and submit its report, citing the need to review evidence and obtain forensic and pathology reports.

PREMIUM TIMES had reported that Mr Aniviye apologised to the families of the deceased during a sitting of a Niger State panel of inquiry, describing the incident as an avoidable and costly mistake.

The suspended commandant also told the state panel that he learnt about the deaths through a phone call and later found the bodies in the detention facility. His account formed part of the testimony presented during the state-level inquiry.

The federal panel's findings provide an official conclusion on the reported cause of death. Further details of the report, including any individual or institutional responsibility and recommendations for prosecution or disciplinary action, were not contained in TheCable's report.

Close 

The government has yet to disclose, in the report cited, the specific measures it will take in response to the panel's findings.

World.title: Egypt: Court Order to Shut Down and Fine Mada Masr a Devastating Blow to Media Freedom
World.content:
press release

Responding to the news that the New Cairo Misdemeanours court today convicted editor in chief Lina Attalah on charges of operating an unlicenced website, ordering the shutdown of prominent independent outlet Mada Masr and taking her into police custody pending payment of the maximum penalty of three million EGP fine (54,467 USD) Amnesty International's Senior Director for Regional Impact, Yasmine Ahmed, said:

Today's decision represents a crushing blow to press freedom in Egypt and marks a dark day for independent journalism in the country.Yasmine Ahmed, Amnesty International

"Today's decision represents a crushing blow to press freedom in Egypt and marks a dark day for independent journalism in the country. By imposing a 3 million EGP fine, ordering the closure of Mada Masr and the seizure of its property, and detaining Lina Atallah until payment is made, the Egyptian authorities are sending a clear and ruthless message: critical, independent reporting will not be tolerated.

"This draconian ruling is the culmination of years of relentless harassment and unjust proceedings designed to shut down one of the country's last remaining independent media voices. Lina Atallah should never have been prosecuted for exercising her right to freedom of expression and doing her journalistic job. The Egyptian authorities must immediately overturn this outrageous verdict, halt the forced closure of Mada Masr, and end the systematic persecution of journalists.



"Mada is one of the most fearless and staunchly independent media outlets in the country, and they have continued to report professionally and operate in full transparency. The media outlet has repeatedly attempted to apply for a licence since the new media law was passed in 2018, but the authorities have continuously denied or failed to respond to their application.

"The speed with which the investigation and trial were scheduled and the judge's refusal to adjourn today's session to give defence lawyers adequate time to prepare and his refusal of all other requests by the defence, including to submit additional documentation or to summon witnesses, raises serious due process concerns.

"Under no circumstances is shutting down a media outlet a proportionate response to operating without government authorization. International human rights standards are clear on the fact that registration systems should not be used as a mechanism of prior restraint or to pick and choose which media outlets governments like and which they wish to silence.

"Today's verdict comes at a time when independent journalism in Egypt is under assault and just weeks after the arbitrary detention of six journalists from the Matsadaash fact-checking platform amidst the continued blocking of hundreds of news websites and civil society organizations across the country.

Background

Close 

Mada has for years operated in full transparency as a non-profit company, while actively attempting since 2018 to register under the 2018 Law Regulating the Press, Media, and the Supreme Council for Media Regulation. Mada applied for a licence twice in 2018 and 2020 but received no response from the Supreme Council for Media Regulation (SCMR), the government body overseeing the media.

In 2022, Mada learned that the SCMR rejected their application without providing reasons. In the same year, Mada appealed the rejection in court but later lost the case. At a hearing in 2023, the SCMR stated its grounds for the first time. Mada reapplied this year and submitted all the documents the SCMR said were missing but never received a response.

The ruling follows years of harassment and intimidation against Lina Atallah as editor in chief of Mada Masr who has faced six criminal investigations over the past six years over their reporting. Most recently, on 4 August 2025, the authorities summoned Atallah for questioning on unfounded charges, including "spreading false news" and "operating a website without a license," over an article published on 31 July 2025 about deteriorating detention conditions in Badr 3 prison. She was released on bail pending investigation.

At least 18 journalists are currently imprisoned in Egypt according to the Committee to Protect Journalists. Hundreds of websites remain blocked in the country, including Mada Masr, other media outlets and independent NGOs.

World.title: Ethiopia: UN Reports 36,000 Ethiopian Arrivals Fleeing Moyale Conflict, Kenya Rights Commission Urges Aid
World.content:
The ongoing drought and rising insecurity forced Rukia Yaarow Ali to leave her home in Somalia, to seek refuge in Daadab refugee complex in northern Kenya.

Addis Abeba — Approximately 36,000 people have crossed from Ethiopia into Kenya to flee conflict in and around Moyale, with food, clean water, shelter, sanitation, and healthcare identified as the most urgent needs, the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) in Kenya said.

The Agency said many of those arriving were women and children, with some staying with relatives and host communities while others sought shelter in temporary locations. UNHCR, the International Organization for Migration, UNICEF, the World Food Program, and the Kenya Red Cross Society are working with Kenyan authorities and humanitarian partners to coordinate assistance.

Meanwhile, the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNCHR) said approximately 40,000 people had sought refuge in Moyale. The Commission said more than 15,000 people were being accommodated in eight temporary shelters, including St. Mary's Catholic Church, Harhosha Secondary School, Manyatta Burji, and Sessi and Lanzi Mosque Hospital, among other sites. More than 20,000 others were reportedly staying with relatives and friends, placing additional pressure on host communities and already limited resources. The commission called for an urgent, coordinated, rights-based response, warning that rainfall could worsen exposure, sanitation conditions, and the risk of disease outbreaks.

The KNCHR also highlighted urgent maternal and reproductive healthcare needs, reporting that four women had given birth at two locations in the area. It urged authorities to provide emergency medical care, food, safe water, weather-appropriate shelter, and protection services, while ensuring that asylum seekers are treated with dignity and that their rights are respected.



The Commission urged authorities on both sides of the border to work together to manage cross-border movements safely and address the underlying causes of displacement. It also called on security agencies to maintain public order while ensuring that all measures remain lawful, proportionate, and non-discriminatory. The commission stressed that the reported calm on both sides of the border presented an opportunity to coordinate humanitarian assistance, protect displaced people and host communities, and prevent further suffering.

The displacement follows the week-long conflict in Moyale, a border town straddling the Oromia-Somali regional boundary in Ethiopia, where tensions over a flag dispute intensified after 13-year-old Diqqoo Jaataan Aagaa was killed in an exchange of gunfire on October 18.

Subsequent clashes between security forces from the two regions spread to seven districts in southern Oromia, with residents reporting casualties, burned homes, and widespread displacement.

The fighting also disrupted transport and prompted residents to flee across the border into Kenya.

World.title: Somalia: Somalia Reports Deadly Fighting With Al-Shabaab As Both Sides Claim Heavy Losses
World.content:
Al-Shabaab in vehicles taken from the military

Somalia's government and Al-Shabaab militants have issued sharply conflicting accounts of deadly fighting near the southern city of Leego, with both sides claiming to have inflicted heavy losses during a battle on Monday.

The Somali defence ministry said on Tuesday that federal troops had killed 75 militants and wounded 56 others. The Al-Qaeda-linked insurgent group claimed it had killed 321 government soldiers during an attack on Turkish-trained troops and an allied militia.

Neither account could be independently verified, leaving the scale of the casualties unclear.

The fighting took place in the Lower Shabelle region, where the government is battling an insurgency that has endured for two decades despite a major international effort to defeat it.

Conflicting accounts of the battle

Al-Shabaab said it launched its attack on Monday afternoon, describing a three-hour ambush in which its fighters also captured prisoners, weapons and vehicles.

The defence ministry presented the fighting as an offensive against militant positions.

"The Somali National Army, conducting Operation Banooda, launched a major assault lasting several hours on 26 October against Al-Shabaab positions in Jameeca," it said in a statement.

The government confirmed that militants had used vehicles packed with explosives during the attack and acknowledged damage to military equipment.

"The attack damaged some military vehicles," the ministry said.

Its statement did not provide a toll for government forces or confirm Al-Shabaab's claims to have taken prisoners and seized equipment.

Local media platform Baidoa Online reported that the government had called an emergency cabinet meeting to discuss what it described as "heavy casualties and substantial military equipment losses" during the fighting near Leego.

That report added to indications of a significant confrontation, although the competing claims offered no independently verified picture of how the battle unfolded or which side suffered the greater losses.

Turkey expands military footprint in Somalia as regional rivalries intensify

Pressure on international support

The clashes come as Somalia's government faces uncertainty over international backing for its campaign against Al-Shabaab, which continues to control large areas of central Somalia.

Close 

Turkey has emerged as a key supporter of the federal government, including through the training of Somali troops. Its role has become increasingly important as the US and other major donors pull back from supporting the counter-insurgency effort.

Washington has stopped funding the United Nations logistics mission that supplies combat operations in Somalia - a vital part of the international support underpinning the campaign.

The US has cited the government's failure to make progress in uniting the country and confronting the insurgent threat as its reason for ending that funding.

The withdrawal adds pressure on Somali forces and their partners as they seek to sustain operations against a group that remains capable of mounting major attacks.

World.title: Federal judge rules Bill Essayli unlawfully serving as de facto US attorney in California
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A federal judge has disqualified Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Southern California, from overseeing two criminal cases after finding that he is unlawfully serving as a "de facto" U.S. attorney.

U.S. District Judge J. Michael Seabright ruled Tuesday that Essayli cannot participate in or supervise the prosecutions in the two criminal cases.

However, the disqualification will not take effect immediately, giving the Justice Department time to seek a stay pending appeal.

"We respectfully disagree with the court's order," Essayli said in a statement provided to Fox News.

APPEALS COURT RULES TRUMP ADMIN UNLAWFULLY APPOINTED NEVADA'S TOP FEDERAL PROSECUTOR

"The President and the Attorney General have every right to select supervisors within the Justice Department," Essayli continued, adding that "ultimately, this question will be decided by the Supreme Court, and I look forward to serving in my current role until then."

Essayli originally served as interim U.S. attorney under an appointment that expired after 120 days. Then-Attorney General Pam Bondi subsequently appointed him as a special attorney and designated him first assistant U.S. attorney. He was never formally nominated by the president or confirmed by the U.S. Senate.

Seabright previously found that the arrangement did not lawfully make Essayli acting U.S. attorney but allowed him to continue supervising prosecutions under his other titles.

BLANCHE SURVIVES REPUBLICAN DEFECTORS AS TRUMP GETS HIS NEW ATTORNEY GENERAL

However, after the Ninth Circuit ruled over the summer against a similar arrangement involving a federal prosecutor in Nevada, Seabright decided to revisit the issue, according to the Los Angeles Times.

Attorney General Todd Blanche issued a revised designation last month to narrow Essayli's authority and distinguish his situation from the Nevada case, but Seabright ruled the modified arrangement still gave Essayli enough authority to effectively occupy the vacant U.S. attorney position.

"In sum, Essayli is unlawfully serving as a 'de facto' United States Attorney," Seabright wrote.

The ruling came as Essayli has been helping lead a high-profile Justice Department effort challenging California over more than 20,000 registered voters the administration says are likely noncitizens.

NINTH CIRCUIT QUESTIONS TRUMP DOJ'S EMERGENCY REQUEST TO SET ASIDE 20,000 CALIFORNIA MAIL BALLOTS

The Justice Department has asked a federal court to require ballots associated with those individuals to be separated while their eligibility is reviewed, and U.S. District Judge David O. Carter said he would issue a ruling Wednesday on the administration's request.

"I think this case is really on the forefront of the administration's battle to fight for election integrity," Essayli said during a news conference Tuesday.

"We wanna stop illegal voting. We don't wanna chase it later," he added.

When asked about Seabright's ruling during the news conference, Essayli gave reporters a brief response.

"That case will be decided by the Supreme Court."

World.title: Rays stay alive in World Series, walk off Brewers in thrilling extra-inning Game 4
World.content:
The Tampa Bay Rays live to play another day, coming through with a two-run 13th inning to walk off the Milwaukee Brewers in Game 4 of the World Series 4-3.

The Brewers, smelling its first World Series title in franchise history after 22-year-old Cooper Pratt broke an innings-long 2-2 tie with a solo home run in the top of the 13th inning, were just three outs away from celebrating.

But after an error allowed Junior Caminero to reach base to start the frame, the Rays finally smelled some life. Liam Hicks made even more believers in Tropicana Field when his single moved Caminero to third base, and Jonny DeLuca told the Brewers, "Not so fast!"

DeLuca’s RBI single to center field scored the tying run, and the rally was on. Chandler Simpson, who had an RBI double to begin the scoring in this game, made it bases loaded with no outs.

Then, Ben Williamson, the last player on the Rays’ bench after they exhausted all options to keep the season alive, delivered a pinch-hit single to cap a thrilling Game 4 with Tampa Bay’s first win in this series, and a necessary one to force Game 5 on Wednesday night.

It truly looked as if the hero for the Brewers would be Pratt, who had a 4-for-5 night including an RBI double earlier in the game, when he finally broke a 2-2 tie with his solo blast to left field.

The last time the Brewers were in the Fall Classic was 1982, where they fell to the St. Louis Cardinals. It took 44 years to get back, and the Brewers, who owned the best record in the regular season at 103-59, were hoping to end their magical season with another sweep after doing the same in shocking fashion to the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLCS.

The only postseason game Milwaukee lost before this one was Game 3 of the ALDS against the San Diego Padres.

Heading into Game 4, it felt almost imperative the Rays score first after what transpired on Monday night in Game 3, where the Brewers scored eight runs with two outs in the fifth inning. It was a brutal loss to take at home, but weirder things have happened in sports when teams are down 3-0 in a series.

Simpson came through against Brewers starter Dustin May, doubling down the right field line to score DeLuca for the 1-0 lead.

But Pratt remained confident at the plate for Milwaukee, hitting his own double for, yes, another two-out clutch hit to tie the game.

The Rays, though, hit back with DeLuca simply putting the ball in play, and Brewers third baseman David Hamilton throwing it away in the bottom of the fourth to allow Caminero to cross the plate for the 2-1 lead in the bottom of the fourth.

However, Hamilton made up for it the next frame in a big way, leading off the top of the fifth inning with a solo home run to right center field off Griffin Jax, whose solid start ended on a bad note.

World.title: US military kills five in eastern Pacific strike on suspected drug-trafficking vessel

The U.S. military on Tuesday carried out a lethal strike on a vessel in the eastern Pacific that it said was involved in drug trafficking, killing five people it identified as "narco-terrorists," according to U.S. Southern Command (SOUTHCOM).

"On October 27, under the direction of SOUTHCOM, Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere executed a lethal, kinetic strike on a go-fast vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Eastern Pacific," SOUTHCOM said in a statement.

"Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel's active involvement in narco-trafficking," the statement continued.

SOUTHCOM said five people it described as narco-terrorists were killed during the operation.

US FORCES OBLITERATE SUSPECTED 'NARCO-TERRORIST' VESSEL IN LETHAL EASTERN PACIFIC STRIKE, KILLING 3

Tuesday's strike was the latest in the Trump administration's monthslong campaign targeting suspected cartel vessels, which has now resulted in at least 240 deaths from more than 70 strikes, according to The Associated Press.

Video of Tuesday's operation released by SOUTHCOM shows a vessel in the water before it erupts into a massive fireball.

SOUTHCOM did not specify where the strike occurred beyond identifying the eastern Pacific and saying the vessel was operating along established drug-trafficking routes.

US KILLS TWO 'NARCO-TERRORISTS' IN STRIKE 2 MONTHS SINCE LAST ANNOUNCED ANTI-'NARCO-TRAFFICKING' ATTACK

Throughout its campaign targeting suspected drug-trafficking networks, the military has released videos and statements describing those aboard the targeted vessels as "narco-terrorists" or alleging links to designated terrorist organizations. However, it has generally not identified those killed or provided evidence that the vessels were carrying narcotics.

The strikes have generated scrutiny from lawmakers, legal experts and human rights groups who have questioned the legal basis for using lethal military force against suspected traffickers outside a traditional battlefield.

SOUTHCOM's continued operations in Latin America and the Caribbean come after Secretary of State Marco Rubio said last month that the U.S. was increasingly seeking to conduct counter-narcotics operations in cooperation with regional allies and in accordance with their laws.

Rubio told reporters that while the U.S. has "the capacity to act unilaterally," it would rather work with its allies because that is "the most effective way to do it."

THE UNLIKELY SOUTH AMERICAN ALLY HELPING LEAD TRUMP'S DRUG CARTEL CRACKDOWN

Rubio also said the U.S. military would "still blow up ships if need be" and that decisions would be made on "a strike-by-strike or operation-by-operation" basis.

In recent months, SOUTHCOM has also released several videos showing military personnel intercepting and boarding vessels it said were involved in narco-trafficking before removing their crews and sinking the boats.

World.title: Halima Salman convicted of receiving ISIS military training in Syria, faces 10 years in prison
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A federal jury on Tuesday convicted Halima Salman of knowingly receiving military-style training from ISIS while living in Syria, bringing an emotional end to a closely watched terrorism trial.

The case was believed to mark the first time a woman accused of joining ISIS stood trial in a U.S. federal court.

Salman, also known as "Umm Khattab al-Muhajir," is a 27-year-old U.S. citizen and former Brooklyn resident who faces up to 10 years in prison. She is scheduled to be sentenced Feb. 2.

According to federal prosecutors, Salman's parents traveled with her and her eight siblings out of the United States in 2016, ultimately taking the family to ISIS-controlled territory in Syria.

NAVY VETERAN AMONG TRIO WHO ALLEGEDLY WANTED TO BEHEAD SOLDIER AND FUND ISIS DRONE ATTACKS ON AMERICANS

The Justice Department said she was 18 years old when she married an ISIS fighter and voluntarily sought military-style training from the terrorist organization.

Prosecutors said Salman pledged loyalty to ISIS and willingly participated in its activities.

She received authorization from ISIS to carry an assault rifle and was given a document certifying that she had completed the training. That document was later recovered from her husband's cellphone, officials said.

FIRST USE OF ALIEN TERRORIST REMOVAL COURT SENDS AFGHAN WOMAN BACK AFTER ELECTION DAY ISIS PLOT: DOJ

During the trial, jurors were shown video of Salman holding an assault rifle, a photo of her with an ISIS flag and supportive text messages she sent to her husband.

"With today’s verdict, Salman is held accountable for joining forces with a terrorist organization," U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. for the Eastern District of New York said in a statement.

"ISIS ravaged Syria and caused havoc across the globe; our Office will continue to prosecute those who supported its murderous reign," Nocella continued.

Following the reading of the verdict at the federal courthouse in Brooklyn, Salman broke down crying and was consoled by members of her defense team.

Her mother, who arrived after word came that the jury had reached a verdict, also broke down and was seen crying on her knees in the gallery. Multiple members of Salman's defense team were also visibly emotional, including her lead attorney, Mia Eisner-Grynberg.

SHE WAS MARRIED TO AN AL QAEDA MEMBER. NOW ONE WOMAN IS FIGHTING THE TERRORISM SHE SAW UP CLOSE

Tuesday's verdict came after jurors previously indicated that they were struggling to reach a unanimous verdict and were sent back twice to continue deliberations.

Salman's defense team portrayed her as a teenager who was drawn into Syria's civil war through her father and later her husband.

Salman, who was born in Brooklyn, testified that she believed the family was traveling to visit relatives in Turkey when her father instead took them across the border into Syria.

"I do blame my father for a lot of things that happened," she testified.

She also said she didn't want to be "married off" at age 18 and had tried to get a divorce.

DEPROGRAMMED: HOW A MAN RADICALIZED BY THE TALIBAN BECAME A COUNTERTERRORISM FORCE SAVING LIVES FROM EXTREMISM

"You try to leave, it is death," Salman testified.

Salman testified that she eventually fled with other refugees and separated from her husband.

She was detained in Baghouz, Syria, in 2019 by forces fighting ISIS and was arrested by U.S. authorities after returning to New York in 2024.

Salman's attorneys have asked the judge to set aside the verdict and acquit her, arguing that the evidence presented at trial was legally insufficient to sustain the conviction, according to The Associated Press.

World.title: Kylian Mbappé's embarrassing, groveling apology to China comes down to money: Dan Dakich
World.content:
It hasn't been the best few months for Kylian Mbappé.

The French superstar striker entered the 2026 World Cup with his team as clear favorites to win the tournament, only to come up well short, losing 2-0 to Spain in the semifinals. Then, on Monday night, he lost the Ballon d'Or, the award given out to the best player in international soccer, to Harry Kane.

Though Mbappé was brilliant in the "El Classico" against Barcelona, scoring a brace in the rivalry match, through the first 10 matches of the La Liga season, Real Madrid's goal differential of +15 pales in comparison to Barca's +29. He also refused to fully wear a shirt worn by the rest of his teammates, to reaffirm Cueta's status as a part of Spain after an unprecedented surge of illegal immigration from Morocco.

KYLIAN MBAPPE PREDICTABLY BENDS THE KNEE AFTER LOSING CHINESE SPONSORS FOR LAUGHING AT MEME OF DICTATOR MAO

But on Tuesday, his season somehow got even worse.

Mbappé bent the knee to China and the Chinese Communist Party, after an appearance on "The Bridge," a French talk show hosted by a teammate, Aurelien Tchouameni. His big offense? Laughing at a meme.

The one "that makes me laugh the most," he said, is "the one where there's a video of a guy, I think it's a Chinese dictator, they put my [face over it]. The show then cut to an example of the meme, his face covering an image of what looks to be Mao Zedong.

Mao was, by any reasonable definition, a dictator. And a brutal, malicious, and violent one. Most historians blame Mao's policies for tens of millions of deaths through famine and politically motivated persecution. It's not a stretch to describe him as evil, and one of history's greatest villains.

But in the modern world of professional sports, there are a few protected groups that must be protected at all costs, and the Chinese Communist Party is one of them. Why? Because there's money to be made for La Liga and Real Madrid in China, and telling the truth about the CCP's abuses is apparently forbidden.

"My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world," Mbappé wrote in a humiliating statement on Tuesday. "I apologize to everyone my words have upset. I have deep respect for the Chinese people and their history, and I am sincerely sorry."

If that wasn't enough, the entire Spanish soccer league added their own groveling, ridiculous apology.

"La Liga deeply regrets the offense caused by Kylian Mbappé’s recent comments among Chinese fans. These comments were made in a personal capacity and do not represent LALIGA. To the extent of our institutional responsibility, we apologize on behalf of LALIGA and all its clubs," the league said.

He's just the latest in a long list of athletes and personalities whose concern for human rights and social justice ends at the Chinese border. And OutKick's Dan Dakich took him to task for how he handled it.

"I don't think people fully understand soccer is, and how big soccer players like Mbappé are, all across the world. Mbappé, if you remember, one of the stars of the World Cup when he came to the USA," Dakich said.

"Mbappé has all kinds of commercials, all kinds of billboards, all kinds of business interests all over China, including anything from cheese to soft drinks ... you name it, he's got a huge, huge presence in China. Well, that's all being threatened to go away, because as you know based on what happened with Daryl Morey and others, China doesn't take kindly to any kind of slur."

Sure enough, the Chinese Minister of Foreign Affairs, of course, immediately criticized Mbappé's remarks.

"If you're going to get in bed with Communist China, if you're going to get in bed with somebody that isn't as open and free thinking as we are and Europeans are, then you better shut your damn mouth. You know, you better just sit back, take your money, and quit screwing around."

The freedoms that many athletes take for granted here are not present everywhere. And Dakich brought up that there's no awareness of how lucky they are to play where they do.



"You can be political here in the United States because we enjoy freedoms that others don't," he said. "But when you come at China, they react. This is going to cost Mbappé a ton of money. A ton. I mean, this is going to be something that he cannot recover from now. Does he care? Don't know. Should he care, don't know? I don't even a little bit.

"But I got to tell you, they always back down. Hell, you think LeBron James would practice his golf swing if he was in China listening to the Chinese anthem? Hell no. No, they're always back because it's big money."

That's the reality, that Mbappé and James and all the rest of them will do anything to avoid taking a hit to their wallet, no matter how embarrassing and humiliating it is. They're the first to speak out on social issues when it's free, and the first to back down when it matters.

World.title: GOP Sen. Lisa Murkowski endorses Democratic candidate in Alaska governor’s race
World.content:
Sen. Lisa Murkowski endorsed the Democratic candidate for governor in her home state of Alaska on Tuesday, snubbing GOP contenders who include a Trump-backed candidate a week out from Election Day.

Murkowski, one of President Donald Trump’s more vocal critics among Senate Republicans, said she is backing Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins over Bernadette Wilson, who has Trump’s endorsement.

“JKT is a young Alaskan with a view and a perspective that I think Alaska needs right now — a freshness of energy, a commonsense guy who has a known ability to be working together,” she said in an interview on NBC affiliate KTUU of Anchorage.

Murkowski said she believes the three Republican gubernatorial candidates on the ballot in Alaska, which has ranked choice voting, are too partisan.

“We need a governor who’s going to work with the Legislature,” she said. “That has got to happen for the delegation to be successful back in Washington, D.C.”

Kreiss-Tompkins, a former state lawmaker, told KTUU he was grateful for Murkowski’s support.

“I have a lot of respect for Lisa, her integrity. I think she’s worked across the aisle in Congress, which is a quality I really admire and hope to live up to if I’m elected governor,” he said. “And I’m very grateful that she wanted to step up and be a part of the coalition that we’re building.”

He added that the two of them have “had a few conversations” as his campaign has progressed, “and I think she just got to a degree where she felt she was confident in our ticket and our ability to solve problems for Alaska.”

In the race to succeed term-limited GOP Gov. Mike Dunleavy, Kreiss-Tomkins is competing with former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson, former state Attorney General Treg Taylor and Wilson, whom Trump endorsed this month.

The NBC News Decision Desk rates the governor’s race in Alaska, where Trump won in 2016, 2020 and 2024, as leaning Democratic.

In her comments to KTUU, Murkowski raised concerns that Wilson wouldn’t work at any point with Democrats.

Wilson was dismissive of her endorsement.

“Given that Senator Lisa Murkowski abandoned Alaska values a long time ago, I am not surprised that she has endorsed ‘Just Keep Taxing’ JKT,” she said in a statement, arguing that Kreiss-Tomkins’ “allegiance lies with extreme socialists hellbent on fighting President Trump to the detriment of everyday Alaskans.”

Murkowski, who isn’t up for re-election until 2028, endorsed GOP Sen. Dan S. Sullivan in his re-election bid this year. He is in a competitive race that includes a candidate named Dan J. Sullivan Jr. and Democratic candidate Mary Peltola.

The Trump administration sued election officials in Alaska last week, arguing that Sullivan Jr.’s appearance on the ballot could mislead voters who intended to support Sullivan’s re-election.

Murkowski criticized the move, writing on X, “Alaskans don’t need any help voting for their preferred candidates, and the State of Alaska has already handled this by clearly distinguishing the candidates on this year’s ballot.”

Trump tore into Murkowski the next day on social media, calling her the “Republicans’ Worst Senator, by far.”

World.title: Grand jury declines to indict former Trump aide Cassidy Hutchinson, star witness of Jan. 6 committee
World.content:
A federal grand jury Tuesday declined to indict Cassidy Hutchinson — the former White House aide-turned-star witness against President Donald Trump — on criminal charges, a senior U.S. official confirmed to NBC News.

Prosecutors were trying to indict Hutchinson for statements she made about Trump’s actions on Jan. 6, 2021.

The grand jury in Washington returned a “no bill,” meaning it rejected the Justice Department’s efforts to indict Hutchinson. Her name was not mentioned in the courtroom when the no bill was announced, but the senior U.S. official confirmed it was the Hutchinson case.

Attorneys for Hutchinson did not immediately reply to requests for comment. Neither did the Justice Department.

The Justice Department’s investigation had centered on Hutchinson’s testimony in 2022 before the now-defunct Democratic-led congressional Jan. 6 committee, which Trump railed against for years.

The failure to secure an indictment is the latest in a string of such denials in cases the Justice Department has brought against people Trump has portrayed as his political enemies.

The Hutchinson case was brought by officials in the Civil Rights Division, which is headed by Trump appointee Harmeet Dhillon. The division has traditionally sought to protect constitutional freedoms by enforcing federal civil rights and antidiscrimination laws.

The grand jury’s refusal to indict Hutchinson does not bar the Justice Department from trying to charge her again.

Trump has called Hutchinson a “scam artist” who lied under oath, and he has suggested she be prosecuted.

“What is the Justice Department going to do about this?” he wrote on Truth Social in 2022. In March, he posted a link to a Breitbart article about House Republicans’ referring her to the Justice Department for prosecution.

Hutchinson, who had been a senior aide to then-White House chief of staff Mark Meadows, made several damaging claims to the committee about Trump’s behavior in the days leading up to the Jan. 6, 2021, storming of the U.S. Capitol and during the riot itself.

Among the incidents she testified about was Trump’s urging that metal detectors be removed from the area near the White House where he was speaking on Jan. 6. She quoted him as saying the rally attendees are “not here to hurt me” and “I don’t f---ing care that they have weapons.”

Hutchinson also testified that Trump was determined to go to the Capitol on Jan. 6 and that a Secret Service official told her that Trump grabbed for the steering wheel of the presidential limo — and the throat of one of his bodyguards — when the bodyguard refused to take him to the Capitol.

Secret Service officials denied that account. Hutchinson has maintained that she provided truthful testimony.

A grand jury heard evidence against Hutchinson in early October, a person familiar with the effort told NBC News this month.

The Justice Department has been investigating and in some cases secured indictments of Trump’s perceived political enemies. Those who have been investigated or charged include Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif.; former CIA Director John Brennan; New York Attorney General Letitia James; and former FBI Director James Comey. Trump has accused all four of criminal wrongdoing, which they have denied.

After an initial case against James was dismissed on technical grounds, the Justice Department tried to secure an indictment three separate times, all of which were denied.

The Trump administration also tried and failed to indict six Democratic members of Congress over a social media video Trump disliked that told members of the military and intelligence communities not to obey unlawful orders.

Attorney General Todd Blanche told NBC News in April that the failed prosecutions showed “that we’re working hard.”

“It could be that the grand jury just made the wrong decision,” he said then, referring broadly to failed indictments. “The grand jurors don’t get everything right, just like nobody gets everything right all the time. So some of those, it’s a tough case, and some of those we’re continuing to investigate.”

The spike in denials led the chief federal judge in Washington to issue a policy this year requiring the Justice Department to notify the magistrate judge on duty when a federal grand jury rejects the department’s attempt to indict someone.

Trump has continued to try to rewrite the narrative about the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol during the presidential vote certification.

He pardoned the rioters — including people convicted of attacking law enforcement officers — on the first day of his second term, and he reached an agreement with the Justice Department this year to launch a $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization fund” that could provide government payouts to those involved in the attack.

The proposed fund, which was part of a settlement of an unrelated lawsuit Trump had filed against the IRS, was later scuttled.

World.title: Alexander brothers, ex-luxury real estate brokers, sentenced to 30 years in prison for sex trafficking
World.content:
Two former luxury real estate brokers and their brother were each sentenced to 30 years in federal prison, seven months after they were convicted of drugging and raping women in a sex trafficking ring.

Federal prosecutors sought life sentences for Oren and Alon Alexander, a pair of former powerful real estate brokers, and their brother, Tal, in a New York City courtroom Tuesday afternoon. Attorneys for the brothers, who have asserted their innocence, asked the judge to give the men the mandatory minimum, instead.

U.S. District Judge Valerie Caproni characterized the brothers as “Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde.” On one side, they were described as gentlemen who loved their children, she said, and on the other, they were described as “sadistic, misogynistic, sexual predators.”

“Your conduct was monstrous,” Caproni said in her sentencing.

But Caproni added that she did not believe the Alexander brothers were beyond redemption, declining the request to give them life sentences.

In addition to 30 years of incarceration, she ordered 10 years of supervised release and sex offender treatment approved by the probation office. They are not to have contact with any child under age 18 unless it is approved by the probation office.

Twins Alon and Oren Alexander, 39, were ordered to pay $300,000 each in fines. Tal Alexander, 40, was ordered to pay $350,000.

Caproni said she will ask the Bureau of Prisons to consult with experts about whether they should be allowed to be held together, as she believes they are bad influences on one another.

The men were found guilty in March of 10 counts, including conspiracy to commit sex trafficking and sex trafficking by force, after a trial that included testimony from 11 women who described being lured, drugged and sexually assaulted over a period of years.

Six of the women were part of the indictment.

Tal Alexander and Oren Alexander in New York in 2016. Sean Zanni / Patrick McMullan via Getty file

In a sentencing memo, prosecutors in New York’s Southern District said more than 70 women came forward with allegations of abuse and accused the brothers of exploiting their wealth, influence and connections to target victims.

Victim statements from 11 women, some using court-assigned pseudonyms, were read at the hearing before the judge’s decision. The women asked Caproni to impose a sentence that was appropriate for the profound impact the men had on their lives.

One victim, Maya Miller, described the trauma of her rape by Tal Alexander as having settled into her nervous system.

“I carry a quiet funeral inside me,” Miller said.

Another victim, Olivia Lane, told the judge that she was “profoundly incapacitated” after having had a fraction of one drink while meeting Oren Alexander. She described being raped at least a dozen times while she was terrified and in pain.

She then directly addressed the men.

“You are weak. You are inhumane,” Lane said. “You never had power, and look at you now.”

Two women described the men as having almost inhuman eyes during their assaults. Isa Brooks said, “Their eyes went black during the attack, like I was being mauled by animals.” Lane said, “I remember looking at him and seeing a monster, black eyes.”

The women also emphasized the Alexander brothers’ lack of remorse or acknowledgment of their victims throughout the trial. Victim Katie Moore noted in her statement that after five weeks of trial and having been found guilty, the men “cannot even look us in the eye as we speak today.”

“These men spent years treating women and girls like their humanity meant nothing,” Moore said.

The brothers honed their methods together, attacking women in a way that was designed to humiliate and degrade them, prosecutor Elizabeth Espinosa said at the sentencing.

“When they were done, they bragged to each other and their friends. ... The defendants knew exactly what they were doing, and they did it anyway, and they did it over and over and over again,” she said.

Oren Alexander, 37, center, and his twin brother, Alon, center-right, speak to their attorney Joel Denaro during their bond hearing at the Richard E. Gerstein Justice Building on Dec. 13, 2024, in Miami. Matias J. Ocner / Miami Herald via Getty file

At trial, prosecutors said the brothers raped the women after having promised them parties and trips. One woman testified that she lost control of her body after she had a drink with Alon Alexander at a New York City club.

When she awoke, she testified, they were naked on a bed. She kept trying to get up, and he kept pushing her back down, she said.

When she told him that she didn’t want to have sex with him, she testified, he responded, “‘You already did.’”

In a sentencing submission, attorneys for the brothers acknowledged that they sometimes behaved insensitively toward women but categorically denied that any of them had raped or sexually assaulted anyone.

At trial, the attorneys described the sex as consensual and said the women were motivated in part by financial gain.

“All the stories were rehearsed,” Tal Alexander’s attorney, Deanna Paul, said in her closing argument. “They’re looking for money.”

Paul urged the judge to consider giving her client the mandatory minimum of 15 years in prison, saying the verdict has not changed her view of the evidence. She said 15 years is already an extraordinary punishment, so “what would another 20 or 30 years accomplish?”

Attorneys for the two other brothers similarly asked Caproni to give the men 15 years. Marc Agnifilo, who represents Oren Alexander, told her the men all stopped their “sexually aggressive” behavior after they met their wives.

“All three defendants stopped, and that matters,” Agnifilo said.

Each of the brothers was given an opportunity to address the court directly before he was issued his sentence.

Oren Alexander was the first to ask Caproni for a lighter sentence. He once again denied the assaults in his comments before he assaulted her that he has built a new life and family.

“My son needs me, and I need to be there for him, and I ask your honor to impose the minimum sentence,” he said.

Tal Alexander, who was next to speak, expressed regret over his past actions. “The person who stands in court is not the same man as before,” he said, asking Caproni to consider the entirety of his life in the decision.

“I wish I showed more maturity,” he said. “I cannot undo moments when I was immature and careless with other people’s feelings. I understand the jury found me guilty, and I know words cannot change that.”

The last brother to speak, Alon, insisted that he was innocent and that he had never raped any women. He invoked his two young daughters in asking for the mercy of the court.

“I am afraid of being Daddy in the photograph,” he said.

Caproni appeared unmoved by their statements, emphasizing that the rapes were not a result of “party culture or hookup culture” as they described. She said it was not enough to rape the women — the brothers sought to humiliate them, she asserted.

“That marriage would transform them from sexual predators to normal gentlemen, I disagree,” Caproni said. “Rape is about power. ... Having a girlfriend or a wife doesn’t mean you are not going to rape or humiliate women.”

World.title: Fed expected to hold interest rates steady as inflation tops midterm voters’ concerns
World.content:
The Federal Reserve is meeting in Washington this week, when it will consider whether to raise interest rates in an effort to tamp down on inflation.

The meetings come at a moment when rising prices are shaping large parts of the U.S. economy and inflation is set to play a key role in next Tuesday’s midterm elections.

Yet members of the bank’s interest rate-setting committee are widely expected to keep benchmark rates steady this month.

There are several reasons the Fed is unlikely to move on rates Wednesday. Most of them come down to a sense among top officials that the central bank shouldn’t rush into interest rate decisions — and that it definitely shouldn’t do so less than a week out from Election Day.

“Inflation remains above our goal,” Michelle Bowman, the Fed’s vice chair for supervision, said Oct. 14. “We have some time to wait and see how financial conditions evolve before we take more action.”

The Fed last raised rates by a quarter of a percentage point in September after a string of monthly inflation readings well above its target of 2% and no signs that prices were coming down anytime soon.

“The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh said at the time.

Inflation figures for September, released this month, underscored Warsh’s point, with the annual inflation rate rising to 3.7% from 3.4% the previous month.

Some analysts believe Warsh and the Fed will be taking a risk if they vote to hold rates steady, given the trajectory of inflation.

“The case for skipping [a rate hike in] October is not terribly compelling,” analysts at Deutsche Bank wrote.

Fed officials, however, point to a core tenet of the dual mandate that Congress has assigned to the Fed, of promoting maximum employment while maintaining stable prices.

Specifically the “stable” part, which underpins the Fed’s famously slow and deliberative approach.

“I don’t feel urgent that ​we have to decide with a limited set of information,” San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said in a recent interview. “I think we have the ⁠time that we need.”

Another guiding principle at the Fed that is most likely tipping expectations about Wednesday is its tradition of staying far away from politics.

If the Fed were to raise rates just days before the midterms, it could, at best, risk looking like a politically motivated decision. At worst, it could influence people’s votes.

“We could imagine that all else equal the Fed might prefer to stay out of the headlines for raising rates just ahead of a midterm election where affordability is the principal concern,” the Deutsche Bank analysts wrote.

Voters have repeatedly told pollsters that rising prices, especially in the housing and energy sectors, are their primary concerns as they cast their ballots.

With control of both the House and the Senate on the line in Tuesday’s election, voters are clear about whom they blame for the higher prices: President Donald Trump’s war in Iran and his global tariff regime.

The most recent NBC News poll found Trump’s approval rating at 27% for his handling of the cost of living and just 29% for his handling of the war with Iran.

Two-thirds of Americans said the soaring gas prices triggered by Trump’s Iran war were either a “very serious” or a “somewhat serious” problem.

Likewise, more than half of respondents said current economic conditions had caused them to change what kinds of groceries they buy.

All that adds up to a very difficult political environment for Trump’s fellow Republicans, who are struggling to balance their general support for him with how unpopular his policies have become with voters.

Even the Trump administration, which normally maintains an upbeat view about the economy and inflation, sounded concerned after the most recent inflation reading earlier in the month.

“This was a disappointing number,” said Kevin Hassett, director of the White House National Economic Council.

Asked by Fox Business hosts why voters had such negative views of the current economy despite higher spending, Hassett was unsure. “It’s a puzzle that we’re noodling about every day,” he said.

World.title: White House tempers its tough talk on Canada trade as inflation tops voter concerns
World.content:
The Trump administration’s combative approach to Canada appears to be softening slightly, just days before the midterm elections in the U.S., where tariff-fueled inflation is a primary concern for voters.

Trade talks with Washington have seen a “slight intensification” in recent days, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Monday.

President Donald Trump, likewise, seemed to back off some of his angrier rhetoric over the weekend, when he told reporters a potential trade deal with Canada would be “settled pretty soon.”

“They’re willing to give us anything at this moment,” Trump added.

Carney, however, said the opposite. “To the extent any progress has been made, it’s because the U.S. is coming closer to our position,” he told reporters in Ottawa.

Ever since advanced trade talks collapsed in August, the Trump administration has slapped 50% tariffs on hundreds of categories of Canadian imports. Ottawa has responded in kind.

But the two leaders’ most recent statements came after the United States unilaterally announced that it would lift some tariffs on Canada late last week and replace them with others.

The move to alter tariffs came at the urging of Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who is facing a tight re-election battle in Maine.

Control of the U.S. Senate will be decided Tuesday by a handful of very close races, several of them in Canadian border states where polls show Trump’s tariffs are broadly unpopular.

In Alaska, candidates across the political spectrum have called out Trump’s trade war with Canada as a drag on consumers.

The same is true in Michigan, where the Republican nominee, former Rep. Mike Rogers, has called for an end to the trade war with Canada.

The economies in all three of these states are deeply intertwined with their Canadian neighbors.

In Washington, a White House official who is not typically involved in trade talks suggested over the weekend that a trade agreement was imminent.

The U.S. and Canada are “very close to finally having a deal,” said Kevin Hassett, director of the National Economic Council, on Fox News.

But neither the American nor the Canadian statements since then appeared to support such a sunny reading of the situation.

The Commerce Department, which oversees trade, did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday from NBC News.

“Canada remains in constructive dialogue with our U.S. counterparts on a range of priorities,” said a spokesperson for the minister responsible for trade with the United States.

Meanwhile, Carney said he didn’t know whether the motivations of American officials hoping to revive talks were different this time.

“We have very clear bottom lines, red lines, which meant that we were not willing to sign what was offered in August,” he said Monday.

World.title: They bought cabins to live on a luxury cruise ship. High fuel costs got them kicked off in Cambodia.
World.content:
A residential cruise ship halted operations in Cambodia on Tuesday amid soaring fuel costs, leaving passengers in limbo after the U.S. company that operates it ordered them to disembark.

Florida-based Villa Vie Residences said in a news release that it was working to identify “temporary living arrangements” for people aboard The Odyssey, a 642-foot cruise ship that launched from Belfast, Northern Ireland, three years ago and promised passengers “an unparalleled lifestyle of luxury and exploration” as it toured the planet.

Cabins on The Odyssey were for sale or rent.

According to the company, the ship can accommodate 650 residents; it isn’t clear how many were on board Tuesday or where in Cambodia they disembarked.

An executive with the company, Mikael Petterson, declined to provide additional details in an email to NBC News. In a release this year announcing the company’s second residential cruise ship, Petterson said The Odyssey was 85% sold.

The company said in Tuesday’s release that it had taken significant measures to reduce fuel consumption but that those steps had failed to offset the spike in costs.

Global oil prices have surged since the war with Iran began this year, disrupting the world’s flow of fuel. In recent days, oil prices have climbed to their highest levels in months.

The Odyssey in Belfast Harbour in 2024. Peter Morrison / AP

“Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution,” the company said. “Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees while we work toward restructuring and recapitalization over the next 60 days. That work is ongoing, and no outcome is assured.”

Randy Cassingham, a resident on the boat, wrote in a blog post that he learned his journey was over after a company official posted a note on a message board for the ship shortly after 7 a.m. Monday.

The Odyssey was entering a “temporary lay up” period — indicating it would no longer be used — and everyone had to disembark by 2 p.m., the message said, according to Cassingham, who runs ResidentialCruising.com and didn’t immediately reply to an interview request.

Cassingham attributed the development to a “cascade of problems” that he would detail later.

Pamela Reckamp, who rented a cabin with her husband and disembarked this month, said in an interview that she wasn’t surprised that the ship’s journey was over.

Reckamp, 59, recalled having attended a meeting in early September at which a company official asked cabin owners to help them raise $1 million so they could leave Ha Long Bay, Vietnam.

“She said, ‘If we don’t get this money, we have about four days of the ship running,’” Reckamp recalled. “‘Then the lights will go off and the AC will go off.’”

When the ship’s financial issues were raised during another meeting a few weeks later, Reckamp recalled, a woman stood up and said she’d bought a cabin in August and hadn’t been made aware of the issues.

“I sold my house,” Reckamp recalled the woman saying. “I sold my car. I bought my home on this ship.”

Reckamp said she felt terrible for the residents and the staff, who she said were lovely.

“We dodged a bullet,” she added.

Villa Vie Residences didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday night.

In a lawsuit filed last year, a company that bought a cabin on The Odyssey for $469,000 accused Villa Vie Residences of fraud, alleging it misrepresented its financial stability.

The company’s business model was not financially sound, the suit alleges, “but rather precarious.”

The plaintiffs are asking for a jury trial and unspecified damages of more than $100,000. Villa Vie Residences denied the allegations in the suit, which is ongoing.

Other cabins on the ship were available for significantly less money. Even though 85% of the ship was sold, the company said in 2024, prospective residents could still “secure their dream home starting at just $119,000.”

“When we launched Odyssey, we set out to prove that residential cruising wasn’t just possible — it was sustainable,” Petterson said in July.
