World.title: Brazil's Flávio Bolsonaro heading for Ecuador, Argentina says
World.content:
Brazilian Senator Flávio Bolsonaro and his family were en route to Ecuador after leaving Brazil and stopping off in Argentina, the Argentine National Directorate of Migration said on social media. Bolsonaro lost Brazil's hotly contested presidential election over the weekend.

Bolsonaro, his wife and two daughters arrived in Argentina Tuesday night through the Tancredo Neves International Bridge border crossing, the directorate said, then boarded a private plane for a flight to Guayaquil, Ecuador.

There was no word on whether they would remain in Ecuador.

Earlier, a senior State Department official told CBS News Bolsonaro and his family would receive U.S. visas.

Bolsonaro, an ally of President Trump, and his family will be allowed entry into the U.S., the official said.

Bolsonaro departed Brazil for the U.S. after being defeated by incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Sunday's election, according to multiple Brazilian media reports.

A spokesperson for Bolsonaro did not respond to a request for comment. His campaign manager Rogério Marinho also refused to comment.

Silva said Tuesday it was "shameful" that Bolsonaro had fled Brazil.

"A person who sneaks out of their country must have something to hide," Silva said, per Agence France-Presse. "The act of leaving Brazil is shameful."

Bolsonaro's brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, who lives in Texas, had publicly encouraged him to leave Brazil if he lost the election.

Bolsonaro has touted his relationship with Mr. Trump and visited the White House in May. The family connections go deeper: Brother Eduardo Bolsonaro was convicted in absentia in June of illegally lobbying the Trump administration and sentenced to four years in prison. A warrant was recently issued for his arrest.

Mr. Trump did not offer a full-throated endorsement of Bolsonaro in the runoff against Lula, as he has with some other right-of-center candidates in Latin America. But he suggested on Monday, without providing evidence, that Brazil's election was "rigged."

But he told reporters Wednesday that said he approves of Bolsonaro coming to the U.S.

"It would be OK with me," Mr. Trump said.

Flávio Bolsonaro speaks during a press conference following the runoff election in Brasilia, Brazil, on Oct. 25, 2026. Arthur Menescal / Bloomberg via Getty Images

Bolsonaro's decision to leave Brazil came as a deadline for him to surrender his regular and diplomatic passports expired at noon Tuesday. It remained unclear whether he had complied.

"This is what the Bolsonaro family is like: Brazil is their second nation, the U.S. is the first," Lula said Tuesday, according to Reuters.

Bolsonaro was served with the order to surrender his passports Monday, a day after his stunning loss. Bolsonaro said he received it outside the home where his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for attempting a coup following his 2022 election loss to Lula. After his 2022 defeat, Jair Bolsonaro fled Brazil for Florida. He returned three months later.

The sealed Supreme Court order, viewed by The Associated Press, was issued Sunday. Bolsonaro has refused to concede defeat and has made unsubstantiated allegations of election fraud.

Lula, who turned 81 on Tuesday, received more than 64 million votes, compared with fewer than 60 million for Bolsonaro, a margin of nearly 4%.

World.title: Iran war has cost $47 billion, U.S. military says
World.content:
The war with Iran has cost the U.S. military at least $47.1 billion as of mid-October, according to a new estimate from U.S. Central Command obtained by CBS News.

The bulk of the war's price tag is the cost of replacing expended munitions, which CENTCOM pegged at around $29 billion, according to the latest estimate, which was provided to lawmakers. The military also tallied $6.1 billion to replace lost equipment and around $11.9 billion in incremental costs like support for American service members.

The estimate does not include the cost of damage to U.S. military bases in the Middle East, many of which were targeted by Iranian drones and missiles.

By comparison, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told lawmakers three months ago the war had cost around $37.5 billion, not including damaged U.S. bases.

The Congressional Budget Office said last month the war could cost $2 billion to $3 billion per month for as long as it continues, in part due to the need to replace interceptor missiles to defend against Iranian attacks. That cost could rise during tit-for-tat exchanges between the U.S. and Iran, which were common over the summer but have been quiet in recent weeks.

CBS News has reached out to the Pentagon for comment.

The Iran war will enter its ninth month this week, and the conflict's future is unclear. President Trump has suggested he might restart hostilities with Iran after next month's midterm elections unless Iran agrees to a deal. "We may do another little Epic Fury, or they'll agree," he told supporters during a rally in Florida last week.

The Pentagon's inspector general said last month the U.S. is facing "strategic inventory shortfalls" due to the number of munitions expended during the war, leading the Defense Department to work to speed up production. The Trump administration has argued the military isn't facing shortages, with Mr. Trump saying in early September, "we have virtually unlimited amounts of Mid to High Grade Ammunition, far more than we could ever use."

The administration asked Congress to approve tens of billions of dollars in supplemental military funding earlier this year, in part due to the Iran war. That request has not yet passed, and Democrats have pressed Hegseth for a more detailed accounting of the war's cost.

World.title: Alexander brothers sentenced to 30 years in prison for sex trafficking
World.content:
The Alexander brothers were each sentenced Tuesday to 30 years in federal prison for sex trafficking, after the trio was convicted of drugging and raping dozens of women over more than a decade.

Federal prosecutors had accused Alon and Oren Alexander, 39, and their brother, Tal Alexander, 40, of exploiting their wealth, power and social status to lure and sexually assault women, including, they alleged, two teenagers.

Their sentences also include 10 years of supervised release.

"Today's sentence makes clear that this craven, sinister conduct is extraordinarily serious and will be met with serious punishment," U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said in a statement Tuesday. "Our Office is proud to seek justice on behalf of victims, and we are deeply grateful to the brave victims in this case who came forward to ensure that the defendants can no longer harm others."

Some women provided victim impact statements in the New York City courtroom where the sentences came down. New York was one of several locations where victims said they were assaulted by the Alexander brothers, who lived in Miami. The sentencing hearing lasted about six hours.

As they spoke of the "life sentence" of trauma and pain they say they're facing, some of the women cried and addressed the brothers as they gave their statements.

"I never imagined my first time to the Hamptons would become a nightmare," said Bela Koval. "What looked like a beautiful place became a mansion of horror, a place full of dark secrets."

Lindsey Acree said she decided not to read her written statement.

She addressed Oren, saying: "Why? For you? Because you did some really messed up stuff. I don't think, a life sentence doesn't even begin to cover it."

Acree spoke emotionally about her 8-year-old daughter and said she will do whatever it takes so her child doesn't live in a world where people are as "demented as you guys are."

"I'm going to walk out of this room and I hope something I did makes a difference," Acree said. The victims in the courtroom clapped as she walked out.

A woman using the pseudonym Isa Brooks — who said she was raped by Tal, Alon and their friends at 16 years old — recalled how "their eyes went black as though I was being mauled by animals."

"The reverberations of this have lasted half my life," Brooks said. "It radically altered the trajectory of my life."

Katie Moore described the brothers as "hardened criminals with no remorse." She said Alon and Tal had carried on a casual conversation as Alon raped her.

"They can't even show respect for myself and these women by looking us in the eye as we speak today," Moore said while looking at the brothers. "We are not disposable. And they are not untouchable."

The women and prosecutors asked U.S. District Judge Valerie Caproni to impose maximum sentences on each of the brothers, while defense lawyers asked for the minimum of 15 years.

Caproni described the conduct of the brothers as "monstrous."

"The witnesses credibly described sadistic, misogynistic sexual predators," Caproni said.

She also noted that the evidence was "overwhelming that they administered drugs surreptitiously."

Caproni also indicated it was unclear if the brothers should be imprisoned together, saying she did "not have the adequate expertise to conclude they should not be incarcerated together."

Before their arrests in December 2024, Alon and Oren had risen to prominence by way of their real estate business, earning the nickname "The A Team" while brokering luxury properties in New York, Los Angeles and Miami. Tal held an executive role at their family's private security firm after graduating from law school.

Jurors convicted the brothers in March of all 10 criminal counts that had been brought against them, including conspiracy to commit sex trafficking and multiple charges of sex trafficking by force, fraud or coercion. The brothers had pleaded not guilty to the charges.

Prosecutors said in a court filing that the trio raped or sexually assaulted at least 70 women, calling them "serial rapists" who used their influence as real estate scions and proximity to celebrities to take advantage of their victims, in a pattern that began as early as 2001 or 2002, when they were still in high school. According to an indictment, the brothers drugged the women whom they targeted and abused them once they were incapacitated, sometimes taking photos during the assaults.

During their trial, the brothers' attorneys argued that the encounters were consensual, saying the three men's "obnoxious" or inappropriate banter "doesn't constitute a crime."

But U.S. Attorney Jay Clayton said in a statement at the time that the Alexander brothers' crimes "are all too prevalent in our society and all too often go unreported and unpunished," adding: "The truth is sex trafficking and other federal sex offenses are present in many walks of life and we have not done enough to root it out."

In their statements Tuesday, each of the brothers denied the allegations against them.

"My brothers and I have never drugged and raped anyone or conspired to harm," Oren told the court, adding that he had reflected on his own "stupidity" in prison and that he was "ashamed of how I behaved."

Said Alon: "I'm not a perfect man, but I'm innocent of these charges. I've never raped or trafficked anyone."

World.title: Judge continues to block Trump from cutting down trees at D.C. golf course
World.content:
A federal judge on Monday barred the Trump administration from removing trees from East Potomac Golf Links in Washington, D.C., in a colorful ruling that follows a weekslong controversy over President Trump's plans to overhaul the publicly owned course.

"The Court earlier stated, 'I am not the Lorax. I do not speak for the trees,'" U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes wrote. "The Court still does not speak for the trees. It speaks only for the rule of law."

In a 70-page preliminary injunction ruling, Reyes prohibited the government from "removing or damaging" any trees on the golf course while a lawsuit challenging the renovation plan works its way through the court system. The judge also required 10 days' notice before the government makes "any irreparable modification" to the course.

The judge had previously blocked tree removal through Monday.

The government notified the court Tuesday that it intends to appeal. In a Truth Social post, Mr. Trump called the ruling "unconstitutional" and added that the government would move forward with closing the course on Nov. 15.

"To have to give advanced notices to a judge who has no expertise in Golf, Architecture, Landscaping, Construction, or anything else having to do with building such a World Class Project, is not fair, appropriate, or Constitutional," the president wrote, arguing the project is "totally 'as of right.'"

Mr. Trump has sought to overhaul the golf course — which sits beside the Potomac River — for months, pitching a "World Class Championship Golf Course" fit to host high-profile professional tournaments instead of the current "dysfunctional" course. The D.C. Preservation League sued over the planned changes to the course, arguing the government violated the National Environmental Policy Act by failing to analyze the project's impacts.

Reyes has sparred with the government since it cut down hundreds of trees earlier this month with little notice to the court or plaintiffs. In a hearing two weeks ago, after more than 430 trees were felled, the judge told lawyers for the government that they had "lost credibility," and she was "furious" and "thoroughly unamused."

Mr. Trump said last week the course would close for construction beginning in November, and it would reopen in 15 months. He later said work would begin "IMMEDIATELY."

In her ruling Monday, Reyes argued Mr. Trump's statements about the renovation plans were tough to square with government lawyers' position that it's legally too early to challenge the plans in court because there was no final decision.

"Rarely, if ever, has the United States Department of Justice urged a federal court not to believe the sitting President," she wrote. "This started as a case about golf. That good walk spoiled. But it has become much more. It now forces the Court to reconcile assertions by President Donald J. Trump with the sworn testimony of multiple government employees and the argument of senior Department of Justice attorneys."

A golfer walks past the stump of a large tree at the East Potomac Golf Links, Monday, Oct. 12, 2026, in Washington. AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein

Reyes said she was initially reluctant to intervene in the case, writing that she "would much prefer not to have to resolve Lorax v. Once‑ler redux" — a reference to an earlier court hearing in which Reyes invoked the Dr. Seuss character to explain why she wasn't interested in micromanaging the federal government's tree management efforts.

She said she only intervened "because the Government did what it assured all it would not do," by chopping down hundreds of trees on the golf course.

Reyes found that the D.C. Preservation League is likely to succeed in showing the Trump administration's plans for the golf course violate the legal requirement for an environmental review.

She also found that the tree removals were part of Mr. Trump's renovation plan, rejecting the government's argument that they were part of an unrelated maintenance effort.

The judge said she did not find statements by the Department of Interior's deputy chief of staff to be credible, including his description of the agency's tree management plan as "cleaning up" the course.

CBS News has reached out to the Justice Department and the Department of Interior for comment.

Mr. Trump has feuded with Reyes, calling her a "crazed lunatic."

Earlier this month, the Trump administration asked Reyes to recuse herself from the case, arguing that she had shown "open hostility" to the government and that her "histrionics in prior hearings have clearly demonstrated she is no longer impartial."

"To name just a few examples of bias, Judge Reyes has unfairly questioned Trump Administration attorneys' intelligence, allowed her disdain for the Trump Administration to influence how hearings unfold, and systematically disregarded basic separation of powers principles and Article III constraints on judicial authority," government attorneys wrote.

Reyes rejected that request and denied that she is biased, listing out compliments that she has paid government lawyers.

"So what happened? Not sudden onset bias," Reyes wrote in her denial. "Instead, the Government decided to remove over 500 healthy, non-invasive trees from East Potomac Golf Course. It waited until 4:55 p.m. on the Friday of a holiday weekend to give notice that it would begin removing trees within 15 hours. It removed nearly 430 trees in one day and would have destroyed hundreds more but for a rain delay."

World.title: Israeli election exit polls show race headed toward stalemate
World.content:
Exit polls from Israel's major television networks project that a majority of Israelis voted against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition in Tuesday's election, but his Likud party still emerged as the largest party among all the contenders. Neither bloc, Netanyahu or the opposition, has a clear majority.

While Netanyahu appears to have won fewer votes than his main challenger, according to the early exit polls, both candidates will likely struggle to cobble together a coalition.

One or the other would need to obtain majority support in Israel's 120-seat parliament, known as the Knesset, in order to form a government.

Israel's two Arab parties won more seats in parliament than in any previous election. That electoral success comes after what some Arab voters told CBS News was a difficult time for them in the country under the hard-right government of Netanyahu, prompting a historic turnout for the minority community.

Both Netanyahu and those opposing him have vowed not to form a government reliant on Arab parties, arguing it would endanger the country if they gain enough seats to influence Israel's engagement in its myriad conflicts. Arab citizens of Israel are around 20% of the population.

If the opposition breaks their preelection vow — a common occurrence in Israeli politics — they could take power and remove Netanyahu. A central tenet of Netanyahu's election campaign was keeping the Arab parties out of power.

This is the first election since the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks by Hamas, which authorities have acknowledged as Israel's most catastrophic security failure since the country's founding in 1948. Israelis headed to the polls with their country still fighting in the subsequent multifront war in Gaza, Lebanon and Syria, and after two direct rounds of conflict with Iran and Netanyahu advocating for renewed strikes.

For many Israelis, after three years of war on multiple fronts, the election is seen as existential, and voter turnout appeared to be high.

Netanyahu vs. the "change bloc"

Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister and leader of the Likud party, is seeking to form another coalition similar to his current government, which relies on partnerships with ultranationalist and Jewish religious parties.

Netanyahu is telling voters that Israel's campaigns in Gaza, Lebanon and especially Iran, are ongoing, and he needs more time to finish what his government started.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaks to supporters during a campaign event last week in Tel Aviv. Amir Levy / Getty Images

President Trump offered a full-throated endorsement of Netanyahu last week. He reiterated his administration's firm support for the war the two men launched jointly against Iran almost eight months ago, and warned that he could be disinclined to continue with it if Netanyahu doesn't hold onto power.

"If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Running against Netanyahu is a diverse group of parties with different ideologies but one clear common denominator: They all want Netanyahu out of power.

The front-runner to lead the "change bloc," should its various parties collectively win enough seats to build a coalition, is former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot, who leads the centrist Yashar party.

"The Israeli public has voted against Netanyahu's service as Israel's prime minister," Eisenkot said in a rally late Tuesday, according to Reuters. "…A worthy leader would have accepted the people's non-confidence and announced today his retirement from politics."

Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot waves to supporters at a rally on Sunday in Tel Aviv. Erik Marmor/picture alliance/Getty

Eisenkot lost his son and two nephews while they were serving in the military in Gaza. He was part of the Israeli war cabinet for much of the first year of the Gaza war, working alongside Netanyahu. About half of his party's candidates in Tuesday's election are women, in stark contrast to the male-dominated Netanyahu coalition.

Eisenkot is framing himself as a humble veteran who wants to reunite Israel after years of division that he blames on Netanyahu.

What happens next?

In the event that neither bloc wins a clear majority in the Knesset, there are several paths forward to a new Israeli government.

One option is that parties or individual lawmakers could break election promises and switch sides, for which there is plenty of precedent in Israeli politics. There could be weeks of negotiating before a coalition is agreed on.

Another possibility is the change bloc, if it wins a significant share of the votes but not quite a majority, could seek to form a minority government. To do that, the parties just need to win more seats collectively than the other side, even if it's not more than the 50% of the 120 available.

Arab parties could give the change bloc that plurality by either voting in favor of a minority government, or just abstaining and not voting against its formation.

If there's a stalemate and neither side can build a coalition government, the country will have to hold new elections. There is plenty of precedent for that scenario, too.

Between 2019 and 2022, Israel held five elections due to electoral deadlock.
