World.title: Trump says he's ending restrictions on climate-warming methane from oil drilling
World.content:
Trump says he's ending restrictions on climate-warming methane from oil drilling

toggle caption i Annie Rice/AP

BILLINGS, Mont. — President Donald Trump said Tuesday that his administration is "terminating" a Biden-era rule that aimed to cut planet-warming emissions of methane from oil and gas drilling.

Trump said during a campaign rally in Texas that the change would save companies and consumers billions of dollars and unlock 210 million barrels of oil. That's equivalent to about 10 days of U.S. petroleum consumption.

The move aims to encourage more domestic drilling as Trump faces criticism over high fuel prices amid the war in Iran.

Methane is responsible for about a third of planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions, scientists estimate.

toggle caption i David Goldman/AP

Cuts in methane emissions have emerged in recent years as a global priority to slow the rate of climate change. Oil and gas operations are the largest industrial source of methane, which is the main component in natural gas and far more potent to the atmosphere than carbon dioxide in the short term.

Sponsor Message

The invisible gas leaks from equipment and is released into the atmosphere or burned off as a waste product by oil drillers.

Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin previewed the changes last month, saying they would eliminate the agency's "Super Emitter Program" that requires companies to investigate and repair major methane releases from oil and natural gas facilities. The agency would also set less restrictive standards for small oil and gas wells.

Trump said during Tuesday's rally in Lubbock for Texas Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton that Biden's plan "crushed the small operators" with crippling regulations.

"I'm officially terminating Biden's expensive and unnecessary methane regulations to save consumers and energy producers $45 billion in costs," Trump said.

The loosening of the emissions rule comes as Trump and Republicans in Congress have been methodically dismantling climate policies enacted under former President Joe Biden. That's included the revocation of a scientific finding that was central to U.S. action on greenhouse gas emissions, lower fuel economy standards for vehicles and a move to repeal emission restrictions for coal and natural gas power plants.

Environmental groups said the latest rollback will let companies continue polluting the atmosphere with gas that could be captured and provide energy to millions of households.

Sponsor Message

Environmental Defense Fund President Fred Krupp said it gives a "free pass" to companies at the expense of American consumers.

"EPA should be fighting this waste, not making it easier," he said.

Zeldin has said the methane rule would have cost $18 billion and was holding back the U.S. energy industry.

The Biden methane rule was announced by officials including former Vice President Kamala Harris during a 2023 U.N. climate conference in the United Arab Emirates.

Federal officials under Biden said it would prevent an estimated 58 million tons (52.6 million metric tonnes) of methane emissions by 2038 and reduce other pollutants that cause health problems.

By 2034, the rule was projected to yield $98 billion in benefits. That figure was derived by calculating the future "social costs" of greenhouse gas emissions on public health and the environment, an approach rejected by Trump's EPA.

While previous regulations focused only on new oil and gas wells in the U.S., the Biden rule regulated existing wells. Operators also would have needed to plug leaking methane from smaller wells that produce just 6% of the nation's oil and gas while accounting for up to half of all methane emissions from oil and gas fields.

The final rule was published in 2024. The EPA last year imposed an 18-month delay to give companies time to meet new inspection requirements and other provisions.

The rule was crafted to be coordinated with a methane fee, approved in the 2022 climate law. The fee program would have levied a "waste emissions charge" of as much as $1,500 per metric ton of methane on energy producers that exceed a certain level of methane emissions.

The fee marked the first time the U.S. government directly imposed a fee, or tax, on greenhouse gas emissions. Congress repealed it weeks after Trump took office.

Officials also tried to rein in methane from oil and gas under former President Barack Obama, but that effort was scaled back during Trump's first term.

World.title: Rays stun Brewers with 2-run rally in 12th inning and force World Series Game 5
World.content:
Rays stun Brewers with 2-run rally in 12th inning and force World Series Game 5

toggle caption i Morry Gash/AP

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Jonny DeLuca and pinch-hitter Ben Williamson singled home runs in a stunning 12th-inning rally, and the Tampa Bay Rays staved off World Series elimination with a 4-3 win over the Milwaukee Brewers on Tuesday night that forced Game 5.

Cooper Pratt hit a tiebreaking home run off Ian Seymour in the top of the 12th for his fourth hit of the game as Milwaukee neared a sweep and its first World Series title.

But the Rays, also seeking their first championship, rallied in the bottom half after a throwing error by third baseman Joey Ortiz on Junior Caminero's leadoff grounder against reliever Antonio Senzatela.

Sponsor Message

Liam Hicks singled off rookie left-hander Shane Drohan, who relieved in his first appearance since Oct. 15, and DeLuca's single to center drove in pinch-runner Cedric Mullins to tie the score at 3.

Chandler Simpson's single loaded the bases and Milwaukee employed a five-man infield with the infield in.

Williamson, who had been 1 for 15 in the postseason, batted for Victor Mesa Jr. and hit a chopper over first baseman Jake Bauers into right field.

"That was totally what I told him to do," Rays manager Kevin Cash said, drawing laughs.

"Pretty big swing. I've got to go back and recall everything that took place."

toggle caption i Chris O'Meara/AP

Tampa Bay became the fourth team in World Series history to avoid elimination with an extra-inning comeback, according to OptaSTATS. The first three all went on to win the championship (1912 Red Sox, 1986 Mets, 2011 Cardinals).

"We've got a lot of fight in us. We're never going to shy away," Simpson said. "We were going to keep fighting until the end — the last inning, the last out, the last play, the last pitch. We were going to keep fighting. That's what we did tonight."

Game 5 in the best-of-seven matchup is Wednesday night at Tropicana Field, with NL Cy Young Award favorite Jacob Misiorowski scheduled to start for the Brewers. Cash said he hadn't decided on a starter yet.

Sponsor Message

Tampa Bay became just the fifth of 26 teams that fell behind 3-0 in the World Series to win Game 4. The previous four lost Game 5.

Of 43 teams to trail 3-0 in any best-of-seven postseason matchup, the only one that rebounded to win was the Boston Red Sox against the New York Yankees in the 2004 American League Championship Series.

"It just shows the resiliency of this group," Williamson said. "We continue to fight, and that's been the motto this series and this full season, is just fight."

Caminero was replaced by Mullins at third base and hobbled off the field with an ailing left foot. But the All-Star slugger said he'll definitely play Wednesday night.

"He'll play tomorrow on one leg. I'll make sure of it," Cash said.

Tampa Bay ended an eight-game winning streak by the Brewers, who were bidding to become only the second team to sweep a League Championship Series and the World Series.

"If you want to win a championship, you've got to survive some hard things," Milwaukee captain Christian Yelich said. "Like I said earlier, it's supposed to be hard. It's supposed to test you. We understand that."

toggle caption i Ashley Landis/AP

David Hamilton also homered for the Brewers. Jackson Chourio had a single and double, improving to 10 for 20 in the Series.

Pratt, a 22-year-old rookie whose go-ahead hit sparked the Brewers to a 5-4 win in Game 2, drove a slider into the left-field seats against Seymour. Pratt had tied the score at 1 with an RBI double in the second.

Milwaukee players bounded out of the dugout to greet Pratt, who debuted in June and became the first rookie to hit an extra-inning homer in the World Series.

"This kid responds to everything," Brewers manager Pat Murphy said.

Seymour also allowed Frelick's tying homer in Game 2.

Milwaukee fans in the crowd of 40,514, many waving yellow towels and some wearing cheeseheads, brought a Badger State feel to Tropicana Field.

Sponsor Message

Tampa Bay returned to its white home jerseys, a day after playing in Devil Rays throwbacks.

Simpson hit an RBI double off starter Dustin May in the second, but Milwaukee tied the score in the fourth against Griffin Jax when Frelick hit a two-out single and came around on Pratt's double.

Caminero singled leading off the bottom half to chase May and advanced on a groundout. DeLuca hit a hard grounder to Hamilton and Caminero twisted toward the grass to avoid the third baseman's tag, then came home when Hamilton bounced his throw past Bauers for an error.

Hamilton, Milwaukee's No. 9 hitter, drove an 0-2 fastball at the letters from Jax into the right-field seats for his second home run of the postseason — half his regular-season total and just his second since June 6.

World.title: U.S. to issue visas to Flávio Bolsonaro as his whereabouts remain unclear
World.content:
U.S. to issue visas to Flávio Bolsonaro as his whereabouts remain unclear

toggle caption i Ton Molina/Getty Images South America

RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil — The United States says it will issue visas to Flávio Bolsonaro and his family, amid multiple reports that the defeated Brazilian presidential candidate has left the country following Sunday's election. His whereabouts have not been independently confirmed.

Bolsonaro, a conservative politician and ally of President Donald Trump, lost Sunday's presidential election to incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva by more than four million votes, just three weeks after winning the first round. While Bolsonaro's Liberal Party has since recognized Lula's victory, Bolsonaro has refused to concede defeat.

On Tuesday a senior U.S. administration official said that the State Department would issue visas to Bolsonaro and his family, allowing them to enter the country.

Sponsor Message

The visa announcement comes as Bolsonaro faces multiple investigations in Brazil, including allegations of money laundering and tax evasion, which he denies. On Monday Brazil's Supreme Court ordered him to surrender his passports within 24 hours and barred him from leaving the country.

The order followed comments by Bolsonaro's brother Eduardo, who lives in self-imposed exile in Florida, suggesting Flávio should leave Brazil if he lost the election.

In a video released that day, Bolsonaro said federal police officers had stopped him outside the home of his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, and ordered him to surrender his passports. The former far-right leader is under house arrest after being sentenced to 27 years in prison for plotting a coup following his own defeat by Lula in the 2022 presidential election.

"I never thought about leaving the country," Flávio Bolsonaro said in the video. "I will hand over my passports and defend myself against this aberration." He described the order as an attempt to intimidate him.

On Tuesday, Brazilian media reported that Bolsonaro had left for the United States. His campaign manager, his lawyer and other political allies had earlier said they did not know his whereabouts.

Lula won the election with just over 51% of the valid votes, or approximately 64.2 million, compared with more than 48%, or nearly 59.8 million, for Bolsonaro.

Sponsor Message

President Trump has repeatedly cast doubt on Lula's victory, suggesting on Monday that the election was "rigged", without offering any evidence. He returned to the subject at a campaign rally in Texas on Tuesday night, as he accused Democrats of election fraud.

"Brazil is also doing a good job of it, aren't they? Did you see that? I didn't take sides, but it didn't look very good," he said.

Lula criticised Bolsonaro's reported departure during celebrations for his 81st birthday in Brasília on Tuesday.

"Those who have nothing to hide have nothing to fear," Lula told supporters.

"He could have stayed and proven that the accusations [against him] are not true," Lula said, adding that he regretted Bolsonaro's departure.

He also took aim at the Bolsonaro family's close ties to the Trump administration. "Brazil is their second home; their first home is the United States," he said.

World.title: Southwest flood damage estimates are hundreds of millions for New Mexico alone
World.content:
Southwest flood damage estimates are hundreds of millions for New Mexico alone

toggle caption i Navajo Nation Police Department

Intense rainstorms linked to a very active El Niño-driven Pacific hurricane season have left thousands of people in the Four Corners states displaced or facing massive cleanups from flooding.

The adjoining states of Colorado, New Mexico, Utah and Arizona all saw substantial flooding last week, and damage assessments are just starting to trickle in from cities, towns and some of the most remote territory in the continental U.S.

The northern New Mexico city of Farmington was hit particularly hard after torrential rains fell on the San Juan mountains in Colorado, sending floodwaters down the San Juan River that passes through Farmington on its way to Lake Powell on the Utah-Arizona border.

San Juan River saw some of biggest surges

Small towns all along the river, from Pagosa Springs, Colorado, to Bloomfield, New Mexico and Bluff, Utah all saw historic flooding and are now assessing recovery challenges.

About 46,000 people live in Farmington, long a center for coal, oil and natural gas production. It's also an important hub for the northeast side of the Navajo reservation, which sprawls across three states.

Sponsor Message

Farmington residents started getting evacuation notices on their phones as early as Wednesday night.

"My sister was notified on Thursday that she had to get out," said Connie Gooch, who has lived in Farmington for more than 65 years.

Gooch's sister owns a house in a suburban neighborhood near the San Juan River.

"Every year she goes through this," Gooch said. "The river starts rising, and she starts making sandbags to put around. But this year it was so fast she didn't have time to do that."

toggle caption i San Juan County Office of Emergency Management

According to National Weather Service data from a river gauge in Farmington, the San Juan grew 13 times larger in just 36 hours, late last week.

In the wee hours of Thursday morning, the river was about 3.5 feet high. By Friday, it was 14 feet high, flooding neighborhoods across the city, and possibly setting a record for the highest water ever recorded in the city.

This even after the Navajo Reservoir upstream from Farmington was able to mostly contain water rushing down from the mountains. But downstream of the reservoir, flood surges into the city came from two normally dry tributaries, Gobernador Canyon and Cañon Largo.

"This is a catastrophic flood of historic proportions," said Devon Neeley, San Juan County's public information officer.

Sponsor Message

"This river got wider than we have ever seen it in our lifetimes."

toggle caption i Navajo Nation Police Department

From Colorado peaks to Arizona deserts

Similar reports are coming in from the other side of the San Juan mountains in Colorado.

"It's nothing like most of us have seen before," said Tyler Schmidt, captain of the fire and rescue team in the small town of South Fork, Colo. on the banks of the Rio Grande. "We had several neighborhoods that were under two to three feet of water."

Colorado Public Radio's Dan Boyce reports that responders' immediate priorities are lifting final evacuation orders as waters recede. Damaged bridges need to be assessed. Well water all down the Rio Grande's path in the San Luis valley needs to be tested.

Other drinking water impacts from the storm include sewage spills from flooded treatment plants in Sedona, Arizona and other locations. KNAU reports extensive damage on the Hopi reservation.

The Hopi reservation is surrounded by the Navajo reservation, where there have also been reports of rescues, washed out roads and flooding of historic proportions.

San Juan County, New Mexico's Neeley said fire crews, police officers, National Guard troops, and even out-of-state swift water teams rescued between 200 and 300 county residents.

"We have pulled people out of vehicles stuck in running washes. We have pulled people by helicopter off of rooftops," Neeley said. "We have used not only high-clearance vehicles from the National Guard, but amphibious vehicles because the water is so high. It's been a lot."

toggle caption i Navajo Nation Police Deparment

Some relief in the works

By Sunday, the rain had eased, river levels were falling, and some residents started returning home to assess flood damage.

Connie Gooch delivered tarps and other materials to her sister's house.

"The river was up four feet in her house," she said.

She found a neighborhood full of people moving furniture out of their homes and piling demolition debris in their front yards.

Sponsor Message

"There were trucks and cars all over the place," Gooch said. "There was a guy in front of me carrying a loaded trailer full of sheet rock that they'd chipped out of somebody's house."

But officials want the thousands of evacuated residents to stay out for now.

"The public is anxious to get back in; we recognize that, we're sympathetic to that," said San Juan County Fire Chief David Vega at a public briefing Sunday. "Now that the swift water component is out of the way, that exposes a whole new set of hazards for us," Vega added.

Public officials are concerned about hazards like raw sewage and damaged gas lines, live power lines, and the floodwater itself.

"The water is not healthy," Vega said. "Stay out of the water. Gas, diesel, pesticides, fertilizer, these are not things that you want on your clothes."

toggle caption i Navajo Nation Police Deparment

New Mexico Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham visited San Juan County on Monday.

Grisham said that the damage to infrastructure alone could cost hundreds of millions of dollars.

"I hope we're only spending 30 to 40 million (dollars)," Lujan Grisham said, responding to recovery cost estimates from San Juan County manager Mike Stark.

"We think this could be closer to between 200 and 300 million (dollars)," Lujan Grisham said. "The environmental issues and the road issues and infrastructure issues alone, really are expensive."

Monday night, Governor Lujan Grisham released an announcement, stating that the federal government has "partially granted" New Mexico's request for an emergency declaration in response to the regional flooding. Yesterday, Lujan-Grisham signed executive orders making $8.25 million more in state funding available for flood response.

World.title: Israel's voter turnout soars as Netanyahu faces a tight election
World.content:
Israel's voter turnout soars as Netanyahu faces a tight election

toggle caption i David Goldman/AP

Israeli voters turned out in their highest numbers in more than two decades in a tense national election on Tuesday to decide whether to stick with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his far-right coalition or change course.

Netanyahu was in a tight race with his top rival, Gadi Eisenkot, a center-right former military chief of staff, as exit polls appeared to swing slightly in one and then the other candidate's favor.

Still, the final vote tallies may take some time. And even when they're complete, if no bloc wins a majority, it could take days or weeks to decide who will be Israel's next prime minister, as party leaders try to assemble a governing coalition.

Israelis consider this one of their most consequential votes in history — the first parliamentary election since the October 2023 Hamas-led attack and the start of the wars in Gaza and elsewhere in the Middle East.

Highest turnout in 27 years

The Central Elections Committee said 77.7% of voters cast ballots as of 10 p.m. — calling it the highest turnout since 1999.

Sponsor Message

Enthusiasm was high among voters seeking to replace Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, with almost two decades in office across multiple tenures.

" Important is an underestimation, because it's much more than important. It's crucial," voter Naama Aaronsohn said of the election. "I'm worried. ... What's going to become of our country if there's not a major change?"

Another voter, Itamar Ariel, cast his ballot for Netanyahu. He said there are problems in Israel but no one can replace him. It's a matter of security for Israel.

But many Israelis question Netanyahu's ability to keep them safe after the deadly Oct. 7, 2023, attack. They have been reeling from reports that the government had repeated warnings from countries in the region that Hamas was planning a major assault on Israel.

Israel's subsequent wars in Gaza and the region, and its policies in the occupied West Bank, have badly strained its relations with many international governments, and public support for Israel in the United States has plummeted, worrying many Israeli voters.

Citizens in majority-Arab areas also took the opportunity to make their voices heard.

"This government it's not good for us and ... not good for anyone," said Nur Abu Na, a 30-year-old nurse. There are two predominantly Arab blocs in the elections.

Sponsor Message

Netanyahu voiced alarm throughout the day, in multiple social media posts, alerting followers to the high number of Arab citizens of Israel who were voting. He urged his right-wing supporters to get out and vote too.

"Good outcome for Eisenkot" but too soon to tell

toggle caption i Nir Keidar/Anadolu via Getty Images

The early exit polls suggested Netanyahu's Likud Party won the most seats, with Eisenkot's Yashar party coming second. No party won a majority in the 120-seat parliament, known as the Knesset.

The final results will depend on the math and negotiations among broader alliances.

Opposition leaders quickly reacted to the preliminary results, saying they suggested voters dealt a blow to Netanyahu's coalition.

Shira Efron, an Israeli policy analyst at the Rand Corp. think tank, told NPR it was a "very good outcome for Eisenkot" and his recently formed party.

At an election party in Tel Aviv, Eisenkot's supporters cheered as the first exit polls were announced after voting closed at 10 p.m. local time.

""We made history! The public has voted for change," Eisenkot said in a speech.

But votes will continue to be counted on Wednesday, and the electoral map could shift. Eisenkot's bloc could lose, or have difficult political negotiations ahead if he is chosen to form a government.

"I'm anxious. Listen, the results are good, but they're complex. It takes time before we have a full picture," said opposition supporter Ophelie Namiech.

Netanyahu supporters hold out hope

toggle caption i Jalaa Marey/AFP via Getty Images

At the Likud election night party in Jerusalem, giant screens played Hollywood-style videos of soldiers marching, airstrikes blowing up buildings and other destruction. Some clips appeared to show massive explosions of villages in Lebanon, where Israeli destruction of civilian infrastructure has drawn condemnation from human rights groups as potential war crimes, which Netanyahu's government denies.

The videos also repeatedly showed President Trump shaking hands with and endorsing Netanyahu. The two leaders plan to potentially launch major attacks against Iran after the Israeli and U.S. midterm elections. Trump urged Israeli voters to reelect Netanyahu to "finish the job that we started."

Sponsor Message

Netanyahu's supporters were confident that their candidate, a master political survivor, would pull through.

" I've been here many times at different campaigns where at the first hour, that's what the exit polls show, and then you wait a little bit. And Prime Minister Netanyahu has had a knack of getting over the top when he needed it," said Netanyahu supporter Elie Pieprz.

He said in the end, he believes that Israelis will stand by their current leadership at a time of war.

"Right now we're in a war ... as unattractive as that may be to sound internationally, that's the reality," he said. "I think it is much more likely that they [Israeli voters] will understand that Prime Minister Netanyahu needs to lead this war against Iran, particularly with President Trump, and will come together because they, we need to have a certain amount of unity."

In the early hours of Wednesday, Netanyahu addressed supporters at the event. "Israel faces a singular historical opportunity, together with our partner President Trump, to remove the existential threat of Iran once and for all," he said.

Netanyahu celebrated that Likud was voted to be the largest party in the Knesset, and said the party awaited final results, but vowed to form "a strong right-wing, national government."

Daniel Estrin reported from Tel Aviv, Israel. Ruth Sherlock reported from Jerusalem. Samantha Balaban, Itay Stern, Shir David and Alon Avital contributed reporting in Israel.

World.title: The Ebola outbreak is breaking records -- and just marked a grim milestone
World.content:
The Ebola outbreak is breaking records — and just marked a grim milestone

toggle caption i Marie Ruwet/AFP/via Getty Images

The fastest spreading Ebola outbreak in history has surpassed another grim milestone. More than 10,000 people have been infected since the outbreak was first declared in May, according to the latest government figures from the Democratic Republic of Congo.

"It's a milestone that we're all surprised to be passing this quickly," says Katie Thomas-Canfield, interim Ebola response director for the International Rescue Committee. "10,000 people affected by Ebola in such a short period is really staggering," she says, noting that at this point in the West Africa outbreak of 2014-2016, only about 4,000 people had been infected. But that earlier outbreak still has the highest case count — more than 28,000 cases.

Sponsor Message

The current outbreak is also the largest ever in geographic scope, spanning Nigeria to Kenya. It is second in the death toll, with nearly 5,000 deaths compared to the previous toll of over 11,000.

About a third of those who've died in this outbreak have been kids. Children under 5, with their developing immune systems, are hit especially hard — roughly three out of four infected have died.

"Behind every figure is a life interrupted, a family mourning, a health worker under pressure and a community seeking reassurance," said Mohamed Janabi, regional director for the World Health Organization Africa, at a press conference last week. "We must reach people earlier, bring safe care closer, and strengthen trust before fear becomes a barrier to survival."

toggle caption i Jospin Mwisha/AFP/via Getty Images

Here's a look at some of the key questions about the 2026 outbreak.

Why has the outbreak become so bad so fast?

Part of the answer lies in uncertainty over when the virus started circulating

While the outbreak was officially declared in May, more recent evidence suggests the virus likely started spreading in February or March.

"That's a really long time for things to be undetected in communities, and that means we started at a disadvantage," says Thomas-Canfield. A confluence of factors contributed to the delay.

Sponsor Message

First, there's the fact that a rarer species of Ebola is behind the outbreak — Bundibugyo. Existing tests weren't calibrated for this species , leading to delays. What's more, this region of northeastern DRC is remote and beset by conflict. And U.S. cuts to foreign aid may have slowed disease surveillance efforts, says Nahid Bhadelia, an infectious disease physician at Boston University.

toggle caption i Xinhua News Agency/via Getty Images

In those early days, "the writing was on the wall that this would be a hard road and it would need international cooperation," says Bhadelia. International cooperation and support have been slower in coming than in previous Ebola outbreaks.

In 2014, for example, healthcare workers from around the globe traveled to West Africa to bolster the response. Bhadelia was one of them.

"I think you are seeing a lot less American or other healthcare workers coming into DRC because of U.S. policy that Americans may not be allowed back even if they're sick," says Bhadelia. That's different from the policy in the prior major outbreak. "That means that a lot of the burden is being carried by DRC and regional healthcare workers."

Despite pledges of funding from around the world, including more than $880 million from the U.S., some health workers on the ground say that money is slow to materialize. "The scale of financing that's available for this response is really a fraction of what it was in our previous response," says Thomas-Canfield. "I think the degree of international solidarity has been a lot less."

toggle caption i Bright Emoja/AFP/via Getty Images

Are we making progress?

The response on the ground has improved over the past several months. There are now two dozen or so diagnostic labs and more than 50 treatment centers.

"We're up toward almost 2,000 treatment beds for Ebola, so there's been a lot of progress," says Douglas Noble, global incident manager for Ebola at UNICEF. Nonetheless, roughly two-thirds of deaths are occurring in the community, not in treatment centers — a sign that people are not coming forward with symptoms. That figure has been stubbornly constant for months and needs to improve for the outbreak to get under control, says Noble.

Sponsor Message

Part of why people aren't seeking care may be that Bundibugyo infections can seem mild at first. "Things like fever, headache, body ache, they're all symptoms of the most common and largely treatable endemic diseases in the region," says Thomas-Canfield. Those who are infected with Ebola may not decide to seek treatment until it's too late, he says.

A bigger hurdle, say many healthcare workers on the ground, is community distrust.

An October survey from the International Rescue Committee found that 85% of respondents in North Kivu — a current hotspot — say that distrust of community responders is keeping them from seeking care.

"We're constantly fighting different kinds of rumors, different kinds of misinformation," says Thomas-Canfield of the International Rescue Committee. Many community members question whether Ebola is real or believe responders are just trying to make money. Others wonder why teams come for Ebola and not other diseases that afflict the region, like malaria or typhoid.

Community health workers are working hard to rebuild that trust. "I do think that in areas where we've been able to establish a longer-term presence, we're better able to respond," says Thomas-Canfield. But the virus is rapidly spreading to new health zones. Building trust from scratch is hard, she says. That's especially true in conflict zones, where fighting makes it hard to work, and armed groups actively sow disinformation.

When trust is low, people don't seek care or engage with health officials trying to find new cases and isolate their contacts. Roughly 80% of new cases are still coming in from people who weren't on health officials' radar. Until that rate goes down, the outbreak will remain out of control, says infectious disease doctor Bhadelia.

She points to the cases in Nigeria and Kenya this month as proof of that point. "The sporadic cases that we're seeing in neighboring countries is a sign of the growth in DRC," she says. While daily case counts seem to be plateauing, she says there's likely many regions where the virus is spreading undetected. "It's so far out of control."

Sponsor Message

Is there any hope that an Ebola vaccine or better treatments could tamp down numbers?

No vaccine or treatment is licensed for the Bundibugyo species of Ebola. Several are in the works , but all far from being used in this response.

There is an existing vaccine for Ebola. It's called Ervebo, but it targets a different species of the disease. It hasn't been widely deployed, but healthcare workers began receiving the vaccine in late August and researchers just started a clinical trial, dubbed Tumaini after the Swahili word for hope, aimed at testing how well Ervebo works against Bundibugyo. If it proves effective, "that would be amazing, that could make a difference," says Bhadelia. But she cautions that vaccines and new treatments are not a silver bullet.

toggle caption i Michel Lunanga/Getty Images

"Targeted medical countermeasures are necessary, but they are not sufficient," she says. These interventions need to be coupled with basic public health measures, like tracing all the contacts for a newly infected person and isolating and treating those who are stricken. Improving these strategies takes more work and resources, she says, and she worries that the needed support may not come fast enough.

"In this moment, the question that scares me more than anything is will the international community turn its eyes and forget about DRC?" she says. "I am worried the funding will dry out, that we will not keep paying attention to a public health disaster that is much deeper and bigger in this moment than people realize."

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

World.title: A judge halted D.C. golf course renovations. Trump says they'll still start next month
World.content:
A judge halted D.C. golf course renovations. Trump says they'll still start next month

toggle caption i Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images

After weeks of tense hearings and late-night court filings, a federal judge has temporarily blocked the Trump administration from making any further alterations to East Potomac Park, the municipal D.C. golf course that the president wants to redevelop into a championship-level venue.

The long-simmering legal battle kicked into high gear in recent weeks, after the government cut down 430 trees on the golf course with less than a day's notice. That prompted a pair of lengthy court hearings that at times turned heated, with government officials repeatedly insisting that the tree-clearing was unrelated to the renovations President Trump had touted on social media. They contradicted the president's own social media posts from that very morning by saying there was no final plan for those renovations at all.

Sponsor Message

"Rarely, if ever, has the United States Department of Justice urged a federal court not to believe the sitting president," U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes wrote in her 70-page opinion. "And yet, here we are."

Reyes extended what was initially a two-week halt to tree removal, ordering the government not to cut down "or substantially prune or otherwise damage or impair" any trees at East Potomac Park without a court order. She also ordered it to provide "no less than ten business days' written advance notice" before closing or making any "irreversible modification" to any parts of the park while the legal battle plays out.

"By issuing this preliminary injunction, the Court does not end the round: it simply marks the ball until the parties can fully and fairly litigate this case," Reyes wrote.

Monday's ruling is a win for the D.C. Preservation League and a pair of local golfers who sued to prevent renovations earlier this year — and for the growing grassroots movement to protect the municipal course and the surrounding recreational area, which is beloved by runners, cyclists, birders and others.

"We are grateful the court intervened to stop the Trump-Vance administration's greed and lawlessness while the case continues, and we are eager to argue the case in court," said Skye Perryman, the president of the nonprofit Democracy Forward, which is representing the plaintiffs.

Sponsor Message

In a Truth Social post late Monday, Trump said the Department of the Interior will appeal the ruling. NPR has reached out to the Department of Interior but did not hear back in time for publication.

Trump also doubled down on his earlier announcement that construction will begin on Nov. 15 and keep the park closed for 15 months, adding that the "judge has absolutely no right to hold up this very important and beautiful Project."

"To have to give advanced notices to a judge who has no expertise in Golf, Architecture, Landscaping, Construction, or anything else having to do with building such a World Class Project, is not fair, appropriate, or Constitutional," Trump wrote.

Reyes herself has said she is not interested in policing the federal government's landscaping efforts.

That's why, as she explained in Monday's opinion, she repeatedly declined to intervene in the case — instead issuing repeated warnings against any unannounced major alterations — until "the Government did what it assured all it would not do."

"The Court earlier stated, 'I am not the Lorax. I do not speak for the trees,'" Reyes concluded. "The Court still does not speak for the trees. It speaks only for the rule of law."

On Tuesday afternoon, Reyes made a record of Trump's post and gave the government about 24 hours to clarify whether a plan exists to close East Potomac in mid-November and, if so, "how that can be reconciled" with what its lawyers previously told the court. She said she will schedule a status hearing for either Friday or Monday.

toggle caption i Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images

The judge took aim at the government's contradictions

Reyes' strongly-worded 70-page opinion came exactly a week after a seven-hour hearing in which she clashed repeatedly with the government's lawyers. She had already rejected the administration's request to recuse herself from the case because of alleged bias.

Sponsor Message

Last week's hearing featured sworn testimony from several officials from the Department of the Interior and National Park Service, to provide a fuller account of the origins and purpose of the controversial tree-clearing. But it teed up bigger questions about whether the administration had misled the court and the public over its intentions for the golf course.

"This started as a case about golf. That good walk spoiled. But it has become much more," Reyes wrote on Monday. "It now forces the Court to reconcile assertions by President Donald J. Trump with the sworn testimony of multiple government employees and the argument of senior Department of Justice attorneys."

Much of Reyes' opinion examines the gap between what Trump has said publicly and what his administration has told the court.

The most notable: Trump posted online the morning of last week's hearing that work would begin on the golf course "immediately." But hours later, in the courtroom, administration officials said in sworn testimony that they were not aware of any final plan.

Weaving together timelines and testimonies, Reyes ultimately agreed with plaintiffs that there does seem to be a golf course renovation plan (they refer to it as the "Washington National Plan") despite the administration's repeated denials.

"To be sure, the Court cannot pinpoint the exact date at which the Plan became final," Reyes wrote. "But it determines without hesitation that it occurred at some point well before October 15, 2026."

She doesn't accept the government's explanation that it cleared hundreds of healthy, non-invasive trees on such short notice to enact vegetation recommendations from a 2019 National Park Service Report (whose other recommendations, including for the city's other two municipal golf courses, went largely unaddressed in the last seven years). She called that justification "pretextual."

She took particular aim at the credibility of one witness, Gregory Wischer — a deputy chief of staff at the Interior Department — who was photographed carrying rolled-up concept plans while accompanying Trump and golf course architect Tom Fazio on a tour of East Potomac in June.

Sponsor Message

"Yet Wischer maintains that he — as Deputy Chief of Staff to the Secretary of the Interior — just spontaneously became interested in tree and vegetation management. In mid September. At the East Potomac Golf Course," Reyes wrote.

Reyes said the government "has made no compelling factual rebuttal." At one point, the administration accused the plaintiffs of conjecture "based on a handful of tweets." Reyes shut that down in Monday's opinion.

"The 'handful of tweets' are not complaints about the Red Sox's latest blown lead in the ninth. They are statements from the President of the United States, and from the Secretary of the Interior, about actions within their purview," she wrote. "And the posts say, in no uncertain terms, that a plan exists and that construction will start imminently — one even contains a final schematic of the Course's redesign."

toggle caption i Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images

What's next for East Potomac?

Trump said as recently as Monday night that he believes the renovations do not require approval. But, as Reyes pointed out in her opinion, administration officials acknowledged in a July hearing that major renovations would require federal environmental and historic preservation reviews.

Last week, however, administration lawyers presented an "alternative argument" that the renovations actually cannot be reviewed under the Administrative Procedure Act.

"It says, Emily Litella-style: 'Never mind,'" Reyes wrote, referring to the perpetually about-facing Saturday Night Live character. "But parties cannot change course whenever and however the evidence suits them … And so the Court does not credit this new argument."

Plaintiffs in the lawsuit argue that the government is purposefully approaching the golf course renovations as smaller projects — like dumping debris from the White House East Wing demolition last year or cutting down hundreds of trees this month — to avoid federally required environmental reviews.

That argument seems to hold water with Reyes, who said, the Interior Department likely violated the National Environmental Protection Act "by impermissibly segmenting its review of the Plan's environmental effects."

Sponsor Message

Monday's ruling — and the administration's promised appeal — could slow that process even more. Trump said on social media that work "must begin, immediately, if it is to be completed in a timely and seasonal manner."

But there are still many questions about the final product.

The rendering Trump shared earlier this month shows the park's three courses of varying ability levels combined into one that overtakes the entire peninsula, seemingly removing the perimeter road that runners and bikers use every day and raising questions about whether the historically affordable golf course could soon be less accessible.

Trump said Monday the redeveloped course will be able to host events like the PGA Championship and Ryder Cup, but will also be "open to the Public, at a reduced rate for those living in Washington, D.C."

The project is one of many ways he's looking to make his mark on the nation's capital, from building the White House ballroom to adding his name to the Kennedy Center to pushing through plans for a triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery.

World.title: Bolsonaro's party accepts Brazil election defeat, but he refuses to concede
World.content:
Bolsonaro's party accepts Brazil election defeat, but he refuses to concede

toggle caption i Eraldo Peres/AP

BRASILIA, Brazil — Brazil's Liberal Party, the party of defeated presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, has acknowledged the results of Sunday's presidential election, recognizing incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's victory. But Bolsonaro himself has yet to formally concede defeat.

The party's president, Valdemar Costa Neto, said in a statement Monday that the party recognizes the election results but believes "questions raised about the vote" still need to be clarified.

The concession came as President Trump questioned the election's legitimacy, telling reporters Monday, "I didn't take sides, but it looked like another rigged election." Trump offered no evidence of fraud.

Bolsonaro initially said he would seek to annul the election results, citing alleged irregularities, including a last-minute extension of voting hours.

On Sunday, the Supreme Court ordered polling stations to remain open for two additional hours, until 7 p.m., following an appeal by Lula's campaign, which cited public transportation disruptions. Bolsonaro's campaign also requested an extension, citing heavy rain in southern Brazil.

Sponsor Message

In a video posted Monday, Bolsonaro shifted his approach, saying he would seek to have Lula's election victory disqualified over alleged abuses of political and economic power. "The law must apply to everyone," he said. "The competition must be fair and equal, which did not happen." Bolsonaro did not provide any evidence for this claim.

Bolsonaro also said Brazil's Federal Police had ordered him to surrender his passports after he visited his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, in Brasília.

The former far-right president is under house arrest after being sentenced to 27 years in prison for his role in the 2022 coup attempt against Lula.

"I was ordered right on the street to hand over my passports, and I'm also prohibited from leaving the country," he said in the video. Bolsonaro said the order was based on remarks by his brother Eduardo, who lives in the U.S., suggesting he should leave Brazil if he lost the election. The passport order was issued by Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes in connection with a separate investigation.

Lula won just over 51% of the valid votes, or approximately 64.2 million, compared with more than 48%, or nearly 59.8 million, for Bolsonaro.

The result marked a major comeback for Lula, who trailed his challenger in the first round, and put the breaks on a run of right-wing electoral victories in Latin America.

toggle caption i Alexandre Schneider/Getty Images

Lula's victory celebrations rang out across Brazil on Sunday night. Near downtown Rio de Janeiro, supporters hugged, shouted and sang the national anthem. Gains in major cities, including Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo, helped Lula overcome his first-round defeat, along with support from younger, older and working-class voters.

Sponsor Message

In his victory speech in São Paulo, Lula singled out young people who had helped mobilize support for his campaign.

"I wanted to thank the Brazilian people for the generosity they have shown me for a long time," he said. "And in this second round, I want to thank the Brazilian youth for their generosity in taking to the streets. They took to the streets to defend democracy in the country."

17-year-old Brisa Pereira cast her first vote at a busy polling place in one of Brasília's sprawling suburbs. She said Lula's journey from poor factory worker to president had inspired her. She also wanted to send a message to Trump and what she described as his push to dominate Latin America.

"It's not the '90s anymore. We have rights, and Donald Trump can't speak for all of America," Pereira said.

Lula had to win over voters across different demographic and geographic groups to defeat Bolsonaro. He gained more than 10 million additional votes compared with the first round, helped by increased turnout and support from voters who had backed other candidates or had previously stayed away from the polls.

"No wonder pollsters said a Lula victory was almost impossible," said Thiago Vidal, a political analyst with Prospectiva consultants.

"This was a nationwide victory, a systemic victory — from top to bottom, and from left to right," Vidal said.

The decisive margin gives Lula a mandate to govern, Vidal said, but the next four years will be challenging. Bolsonaro's Liberal Party made significant gains in Congress, leaving Lula facing a conservative opposition and a deeply divided electorate.

Vidal said Lula also learned important lessons about communicating with voters, particularly through social media. The president, who had relied more heavily on traditional media, embraced a more digital campaign in the final weeks.

toggle caption i Andre Penner/AP

"Part of that has to do with communication, and part of that therefore has to do with Lula, setting aside the traditional media and becoming more digital," Vidal said.

Sponsor Message

Much of that shift was credited to André Janones, a congressman from the bellwether state of Minas Gerais who helped direct Lula's online campaign. Janones used Instagram and WhatsApp to reach younger voters and mobilize supporters. His WhatsApp channel, dubbed "Lula's Army," attracted over 10 million followers.

In an election-night Instagram post, Janones captured the spirit of the celebrations with a message summing up the campaign: "Nothing is more powerful than when the people unite."

World.title: Hamilton steel plant owner says he could sell next year after becoming 'persona non grata in Canada'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The head of Stelco's American parent company says he's willing to sell the Hamilton-based steel plant as a dispute with the federal government looks like it's headed to the courts.

In a Tuesday interview with CBC's Power & Politics, Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves bristled at recent suggestions from Industry Minister Mélanie Joly that there are buyers interested in Stelco's assets.

"I take a lot of exception on having the minister of industry talking openly to buyers. The company is not for sale," Goncalves told host David Cochrane.

"I will sell the company after we operate the company for a while — and now that I know that I'm persona non grata in Canada, I will do that."

Goncalves later floated the idea that such a sale would take place within "another year."

WATCH | Stelco in 'full compliance,' says CEO: Stelco in 'full compliance' with commitments to Ottawa, says CEO | Duration closed caption 14:18 With the federal government locked in a showdown with Stelco over its layoffs in Hamilton, Power & Politics speaks to the American owner of the steel plant about whether this standoff could wind up in the courtroom.

The CEO's comments come after Cleveland-Cliffs responded to Joly's recent demands that it reverse layoffs announced last month or face potential legal action. The company said on Tuesday that it's in "full compliance" with the obligations it made under the Investment Canada Act when it bought the steelmaker in 2024.

The government argues that the company agreed to keep the number of unionized Stelco employees at 2024 levels through to 2029 when the purchase was made.

Joly indicated in a letter to the company last week that if the government proceeds with legal action, it would be asking the courts to issue monetary penalties against Cleveland-Cliffs and potentially direct the company to divest from Stelco.

Goncalves said that his original aim when purchasing Stelco was to keep the plant from undercutting in the U.S.

"I bought Stelco because I could not afford anymore having Stelco flooding the market here in the United States to the detriment of my own company," he said.

WATCH | Ottawa willing to use 'full force of the law,' Joly says: Ottawa willing to use 'full force of the law' in showdown with Stelco, Joly says | Duration closed caption 12:25 In a dispute over job cuts at a Hamilton steel plant, the federal government is prepared to take Stelco's U.S. owner to court over alleged violation of the company's obligations under the Investment Canada Act. Industry Minister Mélanie Joly speaks with Power & Politics.

In a separate interview on Power & Politics, Joly said she wants further explanation of Goncalves's original intentions for Stelco.

"I think he needs to explain more what he means by that, because if he says that basically he bought it to ultimately keep the plant idle, he's proving our case," the minister said.

Goncalves said that the company is prepared to "defend ourselves" if the federal government turns to the courts.

When announcing the layoffs last month, the Stelco said it was in order to "ensure the survival" of the company, as U.S. tariffs on steel squeeze its sales.

Goncalves has voiced support for U.S. tariffs on Canada in the past. When pressed on Tuesday about those comments, the CEO said his motivation is to protect the U.S. steel industry from cheaper products flooding the market from overseas. He said he wants Canada to take stronger action on foreign steel as well.

"Block the border, allow me to bring the workers back. If you don't block the border there's no way to bring the workers back," he said.

WATCH | Potential buyers interested, minister says: Potential buyers already interested in Stelco, minister says | Duration closed caption 1:07 Industry Minister Mélanie Joly told reporters there are 'potential buyers interested' in Stelco's Canadian assets after she sent a demand letter to the American parent company Cleveland-Cliffs on Thursday. 'They need to abide by their undertakings,' said Joly of the U.S. steel firm.

Joly argued that the government has taken measures to tighten the steel market, but that the country needs to maintain a certain level of access to overseas steel for now.

"We need to make sure that across the country for our business and Canadians, they need to have access to some steel that is not made in Canada," she said.

"That is something that is key for many of our manufacturers."

The minister added that Goncalves knew the market conditions when he purchased Stelco in 2024.

Despite the company insisting the layoffs are required to ensure its survival, Cleveland-Cliffs said last week that Stelco's third quarter this year was its "strongest" since it acquired the Hamilton plant.

World.title: This year will be a super-duper El Niño. Here's what Canadians can expect this winter
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

No doubt, most Canadians have heard of this year's El Niño, a warming in an area of the central Pacific Ocean that has an influence on weather patterns around the world and which drives up the global temperature. Early forecasts had called for one of the most powerful on record, and it has certainly lived up to its expectations.

This "super" El Niño hasn't even peaked yet — that's expected to happen some time in December — but it has broken records with daily ocean temperatures reaching nearly 3.5 C above the 1991-2020 average. The highest temperature before that was in 2015 at 3.08 C.

It may be hard to imagine, but what happens in the Pacific Ocean doesn't stay in the Pacific Ocean. Instead, this natural phenomenon can bring more rain, droughts or warmer-than-average temperatures across different parts of the world.

So what does this mean for Canada this winter? It depends where you are.

Don't blame El Niño just yet

First, don't blame El Niño just yet for any weather you may or may not like.

Well, not unless you're in Atlantic Canada. That region has already felt the effects of an El Niño, specifically, no hurricanes or subtropical storms.

Early forecasts for this year's Atlantic hurricane season had called for reduced activity in the region, typical of most El Niño years. And those predictions were bang on: there has been only one named storm in the Atlantic basin so far, and the hurricane season ends on Nov. 30.

WATCH | I've tracked El Niño for years — I've never seen this before: I’ve tracked El Niño for years — I’ve never seen this before | Duration 3:17 It’s set to be a record-breaking few months of weather, driven by a 'super' El Niño. As Johanna Wagstaffe explores, a natural surge of warm ocean water is colliding with a planet hotter than ever before, bringing more extreme heat, floods, and droughts. But this 'super' El Niño could also help us prepare for what's coming.

But otherwise, the weather we're experiencing now is just, well … weather.

In terms of El Niño's larger impacts across Canada, Bill Merryfield, a research scientist with Environment and Climate Change Canada, says those generally don't set in until late December.

"They tend to sort of intensify as the winter sets in," he said.

Warm and dry

If you're not a fan of the cold, good news: You can expect a warmer winter.

"We tend to see unusually mild winters really from coast to coast across the provinces. And as an example, winter temperatures during the last two events of this type in 1997 into 1998 [and] 2015 to 2016 in the Prairies were as much as five degrees or more above historical norms."

People practise their golf swings at the Shooters Family Golf Centre in Winnipeg at the end of January 2024. It was the earliest the centre had opened amid unusually warm temperatures in Manitoba. (Jaison Empson/CBC)

The bad news, particularly for the West, is that it tends to be drier, with reduced precipitation. That's not great for the fire risk in some regions experiencing drought conditions, especially heading into 2027, which is expected to be the warmest year on record.

At the moment, according to Berkeley Earth, a non-profit climate analysis organization, 2026 has a 96 per cent chance of being the warmest on record beating out 2024.

"For the high latitude, starting in December, we're going to see much rainier conditions in the western U.S. and southeastern U.S., and we're going to start seeing drier conditions in the northwest U.S. and British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Alberta, the western provinces of Canada," said Zeke Hausfather, a climate scientist with Berkeley Earth.

Yes, it will still be cold

Now, there's no guarantee for anything when it comes to weather, but Hausfather looked at eight of the past strong El Niños, and said that currently 12 of the 13 modelling groups around the world expect those regions to experience 19 per cent less rainfall.

Hausfather also looked at the models for warmth.

"All of Canada is warmer. And again, some of this is climate change, right? Because this is the 1991 to 2020 average," he said. "And it's particularly pronounced in central and northern Canada, and to an extent in Eastern Canada."

This map illustrates the El Niño 2026-2027 forecast for North America from October 2026 to February 2027. Canada is expected to experience a warmer-than-normal winter, particularly in the north. (Zeke Hausfather)

And while it will be warmer than average, that doesn't mean that we won't experience cold days, even days that are colder than normal or days with snowstorms.

Hausfather says most of north central Canada is going to be two degrees warmer than normal. "So you're still going to have a lot of variation day to day and week to week," he said. "Weather isn't going away."

World.title: Transport minister questioned over Air Canada's use of safety exemption to deny compensation
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Go Public investigation revealed Air Canada shuffled planes around, cancelled flights — claiming safety-related maintenance — then denied compensation. Minister of Transport Steven MacKinnon says he is 'reluctant to give them instructions' as the airline is an independent agency.

Minister questioned after Go Public investigation into airline's use of 'safety-related maintenance' exemption

Canadians across the country want federal Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon to come down hard on Air Canada and WestJet, the country's major air carriers.

The calls come after two CBC Go Public investigations revealed both Air Canada and WestJet cancelled flights — citing safety-related maintenance — then used those working planes on other routes and denied passengers compensation.

On Parliament Hill Monday, MacKinnon said the Canadian Transportation Agency (CTA) is an "independent agency."

"I'm reluctant to give them instructions directly," he told CBC News.

In dozens of emails to Go Public, passengers on various air carriers outline how they had their flights cancelled due to maintenance and were denied compensation — and now wonder if they too were wrongly denied.

"This is probably just a small tip of the iceberg," said Montreal lawyer Sylvie De Bellefeuille, a consumer advocate with Option consommateurs.

Concerns raised about maintenance loophole

De Bellefeuille and other advocates have urged Ottawa for several years to change the Air Passenger Protection Regulations, so airlines can't use "safety-related maintenance" as a reason to deny compensation.

"We cannot rely on the information that is provided [to passengers]," said De Bellefeuille. "And if they [airlines] lie to the authorities, that's even worse."

The European Union only allows airlines to cite maintenance in rare circumstances.

Got a story you want investigated? Contact Erica and the Go Public team gopublic@cbc.ca

The emails to Go Public follow a story we reported earlier this week about Juan Rojas, a Gatineau, Que., man whose flight from Montreal to Bogota was cancelled due to "unforeseen aircraft maintenance."

Under the protection regulations, passengers can be entitled to up to $1,000 for delayed flights, but only if the delay is within the airline's control and not required for safety.

Air Canada denied Rojas compensation. He escalated his claim to the CTA, where Air Canada submitted documents showing a plane had to be taken out of service after getting struck by a catering truck.

But Rojas did some digging and learned the broken plane was a different aircraft — not the one originally assigned to his flight.

"They are clearly misrepresenting information," said Rojas. "To cheat the system to avoid paying $1,000."

WATCH | Passengers speak-up about compensation denial: Growing number of WestJet passengers question compensation denials over maintenance | Go Public | Duration closed caption 2:18 Go Public uncovers more cases of WestJet passengers denied compensation after plane swaps. Passenger advocate calls it 'fraud.'

The regulator sided with Rojas and ordered Air Canada to pay him the compensation. Though Rojas asked for one, the CTA declined to issue an administrative penalty.

Michael Odobas of Vancouver said he was incredulous that Air Canada submitted records about a different plane and faced no consequences.

"If an airline can incorrectly deny compensation, lose a regulatory dispute and face no financial penalty … what incentive does it have to comply (with the rules)?" wrote Odobas in an email to Go Public.

"That's a question Canadians deserve an answer to."

Should airlines face 'profit-altering fines?'

Conservative MP Dan Albas (Okanagan Lake West—South Kelowna) also raised the issue when MacKinnon appeared Monday before the standing committee on finance.

"Does swapping aircraft to another route qualify as a safety exemption?" he asked.

"The CTA is the regulator," the minister replied.

Conservative transport critic Dan Albas questioned the transport minister on Monday about the safety-related maintenance exemption. (CBC)

The regulator also didn't fine WestJet in cases where that airline denied people compensation while incorrectly claiming safety-related maintenance — cases Go Public reported on earlier this year.

At the time, WestJet's vice president of airline operations said, "when an unexpected issue occurs, WestJet carefully considers the approach that minimizes disruption for the greatest number of guests overall."

WATCH | Understanding how it works: How a 'maintenance loophole' is costing air passengers compensation | Go Public | Duration closed caption 2:11 Air Canada has been accused of using a safety maintenance 'loophole' to deny compensation for cancelled flights. Advocates are urging the government to adopt regulations from other countries that prevent airlines from citing safety maintenance to avoid payouts.

"I'm profoundly troubled that this type of dishonest behaviour is going unpunished," said Gabor Lukacs, founder of Air Passenger Rights.

"That behaviour should be stopped. … And the only way would be to issue profit-altering fines."

In a statement to Go Public, Air Canada said it's allowed to move planes around, cancel flights and deny compensation — calling it a "commercial decision."

That position conflicts with previous CTA decisions saying airlines can do what they want with their flight schedules, but must provide compensation to affected passengers unless a mechanical issue is the direct cause of a cancelled flight.

World.title: 'Puppy angel on earth': B.C. man killed while on volunteer animal rescue mission in Ukraine
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

B.C.'s animal rescue community is grieving the death of a Sooke man who was killed in Ukraine Sunday.

Jesse Adams, co-founder of RainCoast Dog Rescue Society, was evacuating animals from Kramatorsk, a city in eastern Ukraine, when he was killed, according to Animal Rescue Kharkiv (ARK).

"An enemy FPV [first-person view] drone attacked our vehicle, which had just been loaded with rescued animals," ARK said in a post on Facebook.

Adams, who volunteered with ARK as an animal rescue mission worker, was severely injured and taken to a local hospital.

"Tragically, despite their best efforts, they were unable to save his life," ARK said.

Jesse Adams is seen at RainCoast Dog Rescue Society in 2021. (Submitted by Lori Kalef)

The organization said Adams had rescued hundreds of animals with them, calling him kind and compassionate.

"When someone travels halfway around the world and chooses to work beside you in some of the most difficult conditions, it means more than words can say."

Langford resident Chadalee Howie got her dog Winston from Adams in 2024, and said he was an amazing, kind-hearted person.

"He's like a puppy angel on earth."

She said Adams paid for the first bag of puppy food and gave her a gift certificate for groceries.

"To just run away to one of the world's most dangerous places and start rescuing animals, that's who he is."

Adams is seen in 2018 with one of the cats at the rescue. He was in Ukraine rescuing animals. (Submitted by Lori Kalef)

Penny Stone, executive director of the Victoria Humane Society, said Adams was a "go-to guy" if they needed help.

"There was no animal too small, too big, too scary, too aggressive," Stone said.

Even while in Ukraine, Adams was still doing adoptions and taking calls for RainCoast, Stone said.

"He loved animals, but he also loved people," she said.

"He'll be remembered as an animal rescuer, but he certainly had a lot more good qualities than just that."

Adams was remembered for rescuing a large number of animals on Vancouver Island and in Ukraine. (Submitted by Lori Kalef)

Emma Hamill, regional manager of animal care services for the B.C. SPCA who worked with Adams in Victoria, described him as collaborative and open-minded.

She said he had a gift for reaching vulnerable people, particularly in remote areas where larger organizations can be limited.

"His power to build relationships and help people and animals together was such a big piece of his legacy," Hamill said.

Adams was described as the heart of the charity that he co-founded. (Submitted by Lori Kalef)

Savannah Eanes, a friend of Adams who adopted a dog from RainCoast, said that he would provide spaying and neutering services in rural and remote communities as part of his work.

"They do so much good and so much advocacy and fundraising and to lose the beating heart of that ... it's hard to think about, you know, what's next for RainCoast," she said.

Rescues with international reach

Lori Kalef, director of programs for SPCA International and Adams' longtime friend, said she first met him in 2013 when rescuing a dog from Iraq.

"The dog was very, very difficult and had behavioural issues, so I was given Jesse's name right away," Kalef said.

Two hours later, Kalef said, he showed up and said, "no problem."

He adopted the dog and called him Teddy, Kalef said.

She said Adams worked in rescues all over the world and at home.

Jesse Adams is seen with Lori Kalef of the SPCA in this image. (Submitted by Lori Kalef)

Kalef added that he was instrumental in helping evacuate almost 300 dogs and cats from Afghanistan in 2021 when the government collapsed and the Taliban took over.

Kalef said Adams connected various groups and planned a temporary makeshift shelter for the animals at Vancouver International Airport.

Once Adams started working, Kalef said, there was no turning back.

"Every single animal was 'muffin' or 'sweetheart.' Every single dog that was blind or deaf, he handled with the utmost love, like they were his animals."

RainCoast helped find homes for most of the dogs rescued from Afghanistan, Kalef said.

"He had a footprint — and a pawprint — in so many areas in the world."

'My privilege': Adams on his work

On Oct. 20, Adams shared a message on his Instagram account describing his travels to the "frontline city of Kramatorsk in Eastern Ukraine."

He said the group helped evacuate 80 dogs and cats.

"These poor animals do not understand war and are simply innocent victims of another country invading Ukraine," wrote Adams last Tuesday. "Each day more and more innocent civilians and animals are injured or killed by drones, bombs, and missile attacks."

"It breaks my heart that we even have to do this type of work, but it is my privilege and honor to be a small part of helping these animals reach a better life for themselves and their families, or to be adopted into new families."

Stone said Adams died a hero and "doing what he loved to do."

World.title: Big wins, shocking losses, and goodbye to a 46-year mayor: what to know about Ontario's 400+ elections
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

There were more than 400 municipal elections in Ontario Monday, so naturally the results were all over the map.

From an anti-incumbent wave that hit many politicians, including one of Canada's longest-serving mayors, to several big cities that brought back almost every incumbent, here are some of the key headlines and takeaways from last night.

Chow wins easily in Toronto

After polling had suggested a "statistical dead heat," Toronto's incumbent Mayor Olivia Chow defeated challenger Brad Bradford with relative ease.

Political strategist Blue Knox, who served as former mayor John Tory's director of communications, said the Chow campaign struck a nerve with Torontonians by going after Bradford's pledge to create a public utility company to handle the city's water and wastewater. Chow said it would mean the city losing control of an asset and opening the door to privatization.

"Canadians like for their public institutions to stay public," Knox said.

Chow will oversee a progressive, new-look council with several of her key allies elected, putting her in a strong position to pursue her agenda.

Mississauga's first male mayor since 1978

Polling at only 12 per cent as recently as August, Alvin Tedjo climbed from those depths to the Mississauga mayor's chair, defeating incumbent Carolyn Parrish and former mayor Bonnie Crombie.



Tedjo is just the fourth person to hold the job in nearly half a century, marking a significant generational shift in a city long led by political veterans. He's also the first man to hold the job since 1978.

WATCH | Tedjo wins: Alvin Tedjo wins Mississauga mayoral race | Duration 1:01 Breaking news: Alvin Tedjo has won the 2026 Mississauga mayoral election. Tedjo was elected as Ward 2 councillor in 2022, and gained attention after being the only mayoral candidate endorsed by the Peel police union. He secured the election following concessions from his rivals.

Horwath out in Hamilton

Since amalgamation in 2000, Hamilton's incumbent mayors have lost their seats more often than they keep them, and that held true on Monday. Andrea Horwath, the former Ontario New Democratic Party leader and former Hamilton Centre MPP, was unable to secure a second term.

The new mayor is Keanin Loomis, former president and CEO of the Canadian Institute of Steel Construction and former head of Hamilton's Chamber of Commerce, who will be joined by eight new councillors in a strong vote for change in the city.

Milton's 46-year mayor ousted

At least two dozen incumbent mayors lost their seats Monday, including nine who had served their cities for more than a decade.

Gordon Krantz, Canada's longest-serving mayor of a major municipality, had been in charge of Milton council since 1980. He lost handily to councillor George Minakakis.

And in Sarnia, the area's Chamber of Commerce CEO Carrie McEachran defeated mayor Mike Bradley, who had held the chair since 1988.

Other long-time mayors who lost include Oakville's Rob Burton (20 years) and Niagara Falls' Jim Diodati (16 years).

Some larger cities stay the course

The winds of change did not sweep away everyone in Ontario.

Ottawa, Brampton, London and Kitchener were among the communities that kept their mayors and most of their councils.

Zack Taylor, an associate professor of political science at Western University in London, said limited information about candidates can make it harder for challengers to gain traction. Taylor described the London campaign as relatively quiet compared with some previous election cycles.

“It could just be that [London Mayor] Josh Morgan benefited from incumbency and also not really having any kind of scandals occur,” Taylor said.

Mark Sutcliffe gives a victory speech after being re-elected as mayor of Ottawa on Monday. (Keito Newman/The Canadian Press)

A good night for women

Niagara Falls, Port Colborne and North Bay each elected their first female mayors, Ottawa's council has more women than men for the first time since the 2001 amalgamation, and the community of Merrickville-Wolford elected an all-female council.

At her victory party, Niagara Falls mayor-elect Lori Lococo downplayed the accomplishment.

"I always hope that people vote for people based on their experience and skills, not because of their gender," she said.

Women made up 32 per cent of the candidates province-wide.

WATCH | North Bay's new mayor: North Bay mayor-elect Maggie Horsfield speaks with reporters | Duration closed caption 2:14 Maggie Horsfield has won the election in North Bay, Ont., making her the first woman mayor in the city's history. She spoke with reporters at her election night event.

Taxes, homelessness were key issues

Taxes were a running theme across many municipalities.

Tedjo in Mississauga promised a two-year tax freeze; Loomis in Hamilton promised to get taxes "under control"; and Windsor's new mayor Fred Francis promised to hold the line on taxes.

Other popular discussion points during the campaign were homelessness, encampments and community safety. These were key issues in places like Windsor, Thunder Bay and Oshawa.

Thunder Bay councillor-elect Julie-Ann Colquhoun said she wants to "help build a community where people feel safe … and people experiencing homelessness are supported with an understanding of the complexities they face."
