World.title: 25-year-old Lucelle Lucia Usher from Punta Gorda graduates as physician and surgeon from University Of San Carlos of Guatemala
World.content:
25-year-old Lucelle Lucia Usher from Punta Gorda graduates as physician and surgeon from University Of San Carlos of Guatemala

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 25-year-old woman from Punta Gorda Town is celebrating a major academic achievement after graduating as a physician and surgeon from the University of San Carlos of Guatemala, marking the culmination of years of dedication to her medical studies.

Lucelle Lucia Usher officially graduated on October 22, 2026, during a ceremony held at 10 a.m. at the university’s Centro Universitario de Oriente (CUNORI) in Chiquimula, Guatemala.

Usher began her academic journey at Toledo Community College, where she completed high school in 2017. She subsequently attended St. John’s College Junior College, earning an associate degree in 2019 before moving to Guatemala that same year to pursue her medical education.

Her qualification, Médica y Cirujana, is awarded through the university’s medical programme, which prepares graduates for careers as physicians. Her graduation research examined the correlation between neonatal polycythemia, hyperbilirubinemia and hypoglycemia, conditions affecting newborn babies.

According to information shared with Breaking Belize News, Usher plans to remain in Guatemala for some time as she hopes to pursue further specialization in pediatrics, a field dedicated to the medical care of infants, children and adolescents.

Described by those close to her as hardworking, dedicated and determined, Usher’s achievement represents a proud moment for her family and community in southern Belize.

Her graduation also marks the beginning of another chapter in her medical career as she works toward her ambition of specializing in children’s health.

World.title: Appeal delayed again for police officer and BDF soldier convicted in Jessie Escobar case
World.content:
Appeal delayed again for police officer and BDF soldier convicted in Jessie Escobar case

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A police officer and a Belize Defence Force (BDF) soldier serving prison sentences for perverting the course of justice in connection with the 2021 shooting death of BDF soldier Jessie Escobar will have to wait until January 2027 for their appeals to be heard.

Police Corporal Juan Carlos Morales and BDF Private Ramon Alberto Alcoser appeared before High Court Justice Derick Sylvester on Tuesday, October 27, where their appeal hearing was adjourned to January 13, 2027.

The adjournment came after Director of Public Prosecutions Cheryl-Lynn Vidal informed the court that written submissions from the men’s attorney, Orson “OJ” Elrington, had only been filed on Friday, October 23. Vidal requested additional time to prepare the Crown’s response.

The court was informed that the appeal involves approximately six to seven grounds that must be addressed, with both sides agreeing that at least two hours would be required for oral submissions.

Morales and Alcoser were convicted on November 12, 2025, after a Senior Magistrate found that they deliberately provided false and misleading statements and omitted critical details during the investigation into Escobar’s death.

Escobar was fatally shot during a confrontation involving a joint police-BDF patrol in Santa Familia Village, Cayo District, on September 5, 2021. Surveillance footage subsequently contradicted accounts provided by the two law enforcement officers.

On December 12, 2025, Morales was sentenced to one year and 11 months in prison, while Alcoser received one year and two months.

Both men are challenging their convictions and sentences. Their appeals have faced multiple adjournments since first coming before the High Court earlier this year.

Morales and Alcoser remain incarcerated at the Belize Central Prison pending the January 13 hearing.

World.title: Emerson Elijio pleads guilty to manslaughter in 2023 killing of vegetable vendor Jose Lopez
World.content:
Emerson Elijio pleads guilty to manslaughter in 2023 killing of vegetable vendor Jose Lopez

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 24-year-old Belize City man has pleaded guilty to manslaughter in the 2023 shooting death of a vegetable vendor who was robbed outside a bar on Barbara Harris Street.

Emerson Elijio changed his plea from not guilty to guilty on Tuesday, October 27, before High Court Justice Nigel Pilgrim, following proceedings concerning the admissibility of a caution statement he gave police in which he admitted participating in the robbery.

The victim, 35-year-old Jose Antonio Lopez, was a father of four from Valley of Peace Village who was fatally shot on April 12, 2023, while leaving a bar in the Gungulung area of Belize City.

According to court reports, Elijio admitted in his caution statement that he and two other men had planned to rob Lopez after noticing him displaying a large sum of money at the establishment. The men reportedly returned several hours later and confronted Lopez as he left the bar.

Elijio maintained that he was not the gunman and never intended for Lopez to be harmed. However, he acknowledged knowing that one of his accomplices was armed when they carried out the robbery.

During proceedings on Monday and Tuesday, the prosecution sought to establish that Elijio’s caution statement had been given voluntarily. Elijio had challenged the statement, claiming police obtained it under duress.

Justice Pilgrim also explained the principle of joint enterprise, under which persons participating in a criminal act may be held liable for offences committed by their accomplices, depending on the circumstances.

Elijio was originally charged with murder alongside Milton Nunez in April 2023. However, the charge against Elijio was subsequently reduced to manslaughter after prosecutors reviewed the evidence.

The killing had attracted attention after Lopez was shot during the robbery. He was transported to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, where he later succumbed to his injuries.

Following his guilty plea, Elijio was placed in custody. Justice Pilgrim adjourned sentencing until December 1, 2026, when Elijio is expected to learn how much time he will serve for the killing.

World.title: International News: US to issue visas to Flávio Bolsonaro and family after election defeat
World.content:
International News: US to issue visas to Flávio Bolsonaro and family after election defeat

By Zoila Palma: The United States will issue visas to Brazilian Senator Flávio Bolsonaro and his family following his defeat in Brazil’s presidential election, a senior U.S. State Department official said.

The announcement comes as questions remain about Bolsonaro’s whereabouts after reports that he left Brazil following his loss to incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, AP reports.

The official, who spoke anonymously due to visa privacy laws, confirmed that the State Department would allow Bolsonaro and his family to enter the United States but did not clarify whether they had already departed Brazil or were on their way.

Bolsonaro’s campaign manager, Rogério Marinho, said he had received a message from the defeated candidate indicating that he wanted to take a break before speaking with his team.

Bolsonaro’s reported departure comes after a Brazilian Supreme Court order requiring him to surrender his regular and diplomatic passports by Tuesday.

He is under investigation in Brazil for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion, all of which he denies. Before the deadline, Bolsonaro said he had no intention of leaving the country and vowed to challenge what he described as an attempt to intimidate him.

The development could further strain relations between Brazil and the United States, as Bolsonaro has maintained ties with U.S. President Donald Trump, who suggested that Brazil’s election was “rigged.”

World.title: Minister of Culture and UNESCO discuss cooperation opportunities
World.content:
Minister of Culture and UNESCO discuss cooperation opportunities

By Zoila Palma: On Friday, October 23, 2026, Minister of Culture, Francis Fonseca, met with Yuri Peshkov, Head of the Culture Programme at the UNESCO Office for the Caribbean.

Discussions included funding, technical support, and opportunities for cooperation with the National Institute of Culture and History (NICH).

The meeting was attended by NICH President Albert Vaughan, Advisor Yasser Musa, and UNESCO Belize Secretary General Arreini Palacio Morgan

World.title: Second fisherman recently charged for carrying work-knife after forgetting he had it on him
World.content:
Second fisherman recently charged for carrying work-knife after forgetting he had it on him

By Breaking Belize News Staff: For the second time in less than two weeks, a Belize City man who uses a knife for fishing-related work has found himself before the Magistrate’s Court on a charge of possessing an article with a blade.

The latest case involves 31-year-old Alexander Turcious, a fisherman from the Belama area, whose guilty plea was rejected on Monday, October 26, after he explained that he had been working with his uncle and forgot he was still carrying his knife.

According to police, officers conducting a mobile patrol on Coney Drive stopped and searched Turcious, discovering a silver knife that was subsequently measured at nine inches.

During his arraignment, Turcious initially pleaded guilty but told the magistrate that he had been working as a fisherman with his uncle and had forgotten to leave the knife at home.

The magistrate rejected his plea after determining that his explanation raised a possible defence to the charge. The matter will now proceed to trial, where the prosecution must establish its case.

The incident comes just 12 days after Breaking Belize News reported that 52-year-old Denroy Ingram, a homeless man who uses a kitchen knife to scrape fish, was fined $155 after police found him carrying a three-inch blade near the intersection of George and Orange Streets around 1:15 a.m.

Unlike Turcious, Ingram pleaded guilty and his plea was accepted, despite explaining that he used the knife to clean fish.

Under Belize’s Crime Control and Criminal Justice Act, possession of certain bladed articles in public between 8:00 p.m. and 5:00 a.m. is prohibited unless a lawful excuse applies, raising questions about how the law affects people whose occupations require them to carry knives.

Turcious was granted bail of $2,000, which he met, but was first required to settle an outstanding $55 fine stemming from a previous loitering conviction.

He is scheduled to return to court on November 30, 2026.

World.title: Bayto Banner charged over allegedly forged vehicle title from Benque Viejo Traffic Department
World.content:
Bayto Banner charged over allegedly forged vehicle title from Benque Viejo Traffic Department

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 25-year-old construction worker from Belize City is out on bail after being charged with possession of a forged document involving a Belize Vehicle Certificate of Title purportedly issued by the Benque Viejo Traffic Department.

Bayto Banner appeared unrepresented before a magistrate in Belize City on Monday, October 26, where he was read a single charge of possession of a forged document.

Police allege that Banner was found in possession of the certificate in Ladyville on October 21, 2026, knowing that the document was false or not genuine.

No plea was taken during the arraignment after the prosecutor informed the court that directions were being sought from the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions on whether the matter would proceed summarily in the Magistrate’s Court or on indictment before the High Court.

With no objection from the prosecution, Banner was granted bail of $3,000, which he met. His bail conditions required one surety of $3,000 or two sureties of $1,500 each.

Banner is scheduled to return to court on December 28, 2026.

World.title: Antwone Rivero remanded after crashing SUV and being found with illegal ammunition and Stanley cutter
World.content:
Antwone Rivero remanded after crashing SUV and being found with illegal ammunition and Stanley cutter

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 28-year-old Belize City construction worker has been remanded to prison after police allegedly discovered two live 9mm rounds of ammunition and a Stanley cutter inside an SUV that crashed during a police pursuit early Friday morning.

Antwone Alburn Rivero appeared unrepresented before a magistrate in Belize City on Monday, October 26, where he was charged with keeping ammunition without a gun licence and going equipped to commit burglary or theft.

According to court reports, the incident unfolded around 1:45 a.m. on October 23, when police received information to intercept a black Nissan Rogue SUV bearing licence plate BZ-85381.

Officers subsequently encountered the vehicle after it reportedly crashed into a fence near the intersection of Kelly and Wilson Streets. Two men allegedly fled into a nearby yard but were apprehended following a police chase that ended on Cran Street.

The suspects were identified as Rivero and 25-year-old Patrick Kerr.

A search of the SUV reportedly uncovered a yellow Stanley cutter, several pairs of slippers, clothing and a schoolbag containing documents linked to Kerr. Officers also discovered two live 9mm S&B rounds of ammunition beneath the front passenger seat.

During his arraignment, Rivero initially requested a sentencing indication, explaining that he had a young child and that the child’s mother was recovering from a Caesarean section.

However, after learning that the offences could carry imprisonment, Rivero entered a plea of not guilty.

He was denied bail and remanded to the Belize Central Prison until December 28, 2026.

Meanwhile, Kerr’s arraignment was postponed because he remains hospitalized at the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, where he is receiving treatment for an injury to his hand.

World.title: Holness points to sabotage
World.content:
A woman walks past these Hurricane Melissa-wrecked buildings in Black River, St Elizabeth, last Friday. Today marks the first anniversary of the Category 5 storm that inflicted heavy damage on sections of the island. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness has signalled that changes are coming to the public sector as there are individuals deliberately delaying or derailing government programmes. As such, he said the country should prepare for a shake-up in how the public service operates.

Holness said he was increasingly concerned that some public officers were obstructing the Government’s plans, warning that it could no longer be “business as usual” as Jamaica continues to recover from Hurricane Melissa.

“I don’t usually speak in extreme terms, and there are some subjects that it is better not to speak about them. But more and more I’m coming to the conclusion that there are persons in the public sector who are determined to, again, to use the very harsh word, sabotage. And I don’t say it lightly, they delay, derail policies, programmes, and initiatives of the Government. I see you, [and] I’m preparing the country to expect these changes, as it cannot be business as usual,” he said.

The prime minister was speaking at a special press briefing at Jamaica House on Tuesday during which he outlined plans to reduce government spending and improve the delivery of public services as the country faces the continuing cost of hurricane recovery.

While announcing further spending restrictions, Holness said the Government would also examine how ministries, departments, agencies, and public bodies operate, with the aim of removing duplication, improving coordination, and speeding up decisions.

He indicated that personnel changes would form part of that process, particularly where leadership, capacity, or performance needed to be strengthened.

Holness said the changes were necessary to ensure that the public service could respond more effectively to the country’s needs, especially as the Government tries to move recovery projects forward while controlling expenditure.

“Government must be reset and reorganised to meet the needs of our country. Government must be frugal and disciplined in its use of public resources, agile in its decisions, and responsive to the people it serves,” he said.

The warning comes as the Government intensifies its efforts to redirect funds towards hurricane recovery, including an additional $9.65 billion for the Restoration of Owner and Occupant Family Shelter (ROOFS) programme.

Holness said the Government could not meet every demand without making difficult choices, and that savings would have to be found in some areas to finance higher-priority needs.

“If I have to find $9.65 billion for the ROOFS programme, some things will have to be cut elsewhere,” he said.

Among the measures announced on Tuesday was an immediate pause on the purchase of motor vehicles for public officials until March 31, 2027, alongside a review of Government property leases and restrictions on hotel retreats and end-of-year celebrations.

The measures build on a moratorium on non-essential official overseas travel announced last week, scheduled to remain in effect until March 31, 2027.

Holness said greater financial restraint must be matched by improvements in how public institutions work, arguing that Government leaders and senior officials must make priorities rather than attempt to satisfy every demand at once.

He said the Government would be expected to make changes to its systems and procedures, while warning that officials who delay or derail its programmes could not expect the existing arrangements to continue unchanged.

World.title: Sagicor delivers double boost to Melissa-hit schools
World.content:
Little London High School grade 11 student Alyssa Hinds (second right) presents a plaque of appreciation to Christopher Zacca (second left) — president and CEO of Sagicor Group Jamaica Limited, and chairman, Sagicor Foundation Jamaica — in recognition of the organisation’s support. Sharing in the moment are Latoya Harris Ghartey, executive director, National Education Trust; and Garfield James, principal, Little London High School.

SAGICOR Foundation Jamaica on Monday handed over restored facilities at two schools damaged by Hurricane Melissa last October and announced the allocation of an additional $30 million to support further school restoration.

The $30 million, the foundation explained, will build on the record $152 million raised through the 2026 Sagicor Sigma Corporate Run, which surpassed its $150-million fund-raising target.

“Last year, following the hurricane, Sagicor allocated $200 million to national recovery efforts, separate from and in addition to the funds raised through the Sagicor Sigma Corporate Run. I am pleased to share that $30 million of that allocation will support additional school projects, helping to fast-track restoration and return more children to safe, welcoming spaces,” Sagicor Group Jamaica President and CEO Christopher Zacca said during the handover at Little London High School in Westmoreland.

The foundation said that restoration works, at a combined value of approximately $50.4 million, have been completed at Little London High and Mayfield Primary and Infant School in St Elizabeth.

Approximately $22.2 million was invested at Mayfield Primary and Infant School while approximately $28.2 million funded restoration and infrastructure works at Little London High School. The projects addressed priority sections damaged by the hurricane rather than complete school-wide refurbishments.

The two schools are among five selected to benefit from the 2026 run. Work at the remaining beneficiaries — Hopewell High, Green Pond High, and Salt Marsh Primary and Infant — is nearing completion, the foundation said in a news release.

The foundation also said it will work with the Ministry of Education and the National Education Trust (NET) to identify additional schools with the greatest need for restoration support.

On Monday, Zacca credited the public’s support for helping turn the fund-raising effort into completed improvements.

“The real value is a student focusing on a lesson instead of a leaking roof, a teacher working in a safe space, and parents sending their children to school with greater peace of mind. After the year these communities have endured, that stability means everything,” the release quoted Zacca.

“When we asked Jamaica to ‘Run for the West’, people answered the call. They registered, donated, volunteered and supported because they understood that getting our children back into safe and functional schools had to be part of the recovery of western Jamaica. Today, we can actually see what that generosity has accomplished. These improved spaces mean students and teachers can focus again on what matters most — teaching, learning and building a better future,” Zacca added.

Sagicor Foundation board member Brigette Azan said restoring schools is ultimately about protecting opportunity for Jamaica’s children.

“Education remains one of the greatest tools we have for creating opportunity. Not every child starts life with the same advantages or resources, but every child deserves the opportunity to learn, discover their talents, and fulfil their potential. That is why getting our students back into safe, welcoming schools matters so much,” Azan said.

Latoya Harris Ghartey, executive director of NET, said the completion of the projects demonstrates what can be achieved through purposeful partnerships centred on students and their education.

“When we first began this process, the priority was clear: identify the schools where the need was greatest and help get our children back into safe spaces where they could learn and thrive. NET was pleased to work with the Sagicor Foundation from those early stages, supporting the process of identifying the beneficiary schools and the areas requiring attention. Seeing the work completed at Mayfield Primary and Infant School and Little London High School is especially meaningful because, ultimately, this is about ensuring that the disruption caused by Hurricane Melissa does not become a lasting barrier to our children’s education,” Harris Ghartey said.

World.title: Kranium: A ‘glitch in the dancehall matrix’
World.content:
Kranium recently returned to New York for a performance at Sony Hall after a four-year absence.

“I am a glitch in the matrix.”

For Kranium, the statement is more than a catchphrase. It is his unapologetic assessment of a career that has challenged conventional thoughts about what it takes to establish oneself in dancehall, particularly the long-held assumption that an artiste must be physically based in Jamaica to remain connected to the culture and build a successful career.

Born in Jamaica, but based in New York, USA, for much of his professional journey, the Nobody Has to Know hitmaker has established an international presence while operating outside the island’s borders.

And while he is not seeking recognition for changing the game, he believes the evidence of his impact is already there.

“I don’t just feel that way; I know it for a fact,” Kranium told the Jamaica Observer when asked whether he considers himself among the artistes who helped change perceptions about where a dancehall career can be built.

“The facts and the history are there: I took dancehall music and cemented myself as a household name while living outside Jamaica. Unfortunately for those who withhold that information it is already written: Kranium is a glitch in the matrix,” he added.

It is a confident position, but one Kranium believes his body of work supports. Attributing his success to more than just overcoming geographical barriers, the entertainer shared that he has had to tap into his creativity while ensuring he remained authentically himself.

“I didn’t feel like I had to work twice as hard. What I had to do was create authentic, quality music and be real with myself,” he said.

That commitment to authenticity has helped Kranium to cultivate a catalogue that includes songs that have received gold and platinum certifications across three major markets.

For him, those milestones are both a measure of achievement and an incentive to keep pushing.

“Seeing them gives me more motivation to take things to the highest level at my own pace,” he said. “Most importantly, seeing them on my wall reminds me that I am a very talented artiste. It gives me all the validation I need.”

He also sees room for Jamaican music to compete more forcefully on the international stage, provided the ambition extends beyond simply being successful within the genre.

“Yes, I think we can compete at the highest level once we understand that we need to be the best in the school, not just the class,” he said, indicating that geography is not the defining factor in whether a song travels. He explained that the quality of the music and the way it is introduced to audiences matter more than an artiste’s physical location.

“I know how to make authentic music. Even if I were under a rock, if the song is a hit, it will take off with the right juggling,” he said. “I think you can still stay connected as long as you remain true to the culture and understand the importance of paying attention to the current state of dancehall.”

His comments take on added significance against the backdrop of his recent return to New York for a performance after a four-year absence.

The city has played a significant role in his development as an artiste, making the occasion more than another date on an international schedule. The timing also coincided with the anniversary of his first album, We Can, achieving gold certification, creating what he described as the right moment to reconnect with the market.

“Now was the right time to return because everything aligned — the anniversary of my first album, We Can, going gold and, most importantly, the fact that I hadn’t done a show there in four years,” he said.

For Kranium, the performance felt like a homecoming, and he approached it with the intention of making the night memorable for the audience. From the energy of the show to his choices of fellow performers, he was deliberate about how the experience unfolded.

“It felt like a homecoming. That’s why I worked so hard to make sure the show stayed active all night, right down to who I wanted to share the stage with,” he said.

The return also signals that he intends to maintain that connection without over-saturating the market. While he recognises the value of appearing regularly before an audience, he is mindful of the balance between being present and overdoing it.

“There’s a fine line between being in the market frequently and overdoing it. But, for sure, it won’t take that long for me to hold another event there,” he said.

World.title: ON THE BRINK
World.content:
Jamaican football superstar Khadija Shaw (Photo: AFP)

KHADIJA “Bunny” Shaw has long been one of Jamaica’s brightest stars. However, her historic achievement at the women’s Ballon d’Or has strengthened the belief that she deserves greater global recognition, with the dream of becoming the world’s best player closer than ever before.

Reggae Girlz superstar Shaw finished third in the Ballon d’Or Féminin rankings on Monday at the awards ceremony in London. She finished behind winner Alexia Putellas of Spain, who claimed her third hold on the award, while compatriot and former Barcelona teammate Ewa Pajor finished second.

Shaw, the only Jamaican and fourth non-European player to finish in the top three in the award’s history, had an incredible 2025/2026 season with Women’s Super League (WSL) and FA Cup champions Manchester City, where she finished with 35 goal contributions including 21 goals in 22 games to win her third-straight WSL golden boot.

The reigning WSL Player of the Season, Professional Footballers Association (PFA) Player of the Year and Football Writers Association (FWA) Footballer of the Year joined male superstars Erling Haaland and Kevin De Bruyne as the only Man City players to finish in the top three.

Women’s football writer with The Guardian in the UK, Tom Garry, told the Jamaica Observer that Shaw’s third-place finish shouldn’t be underestimated.

“The mere fact that she made the top three despite not playing Champions League football last season, said a lot about how revered she is and how immensely well-regarded she is across the world,” Garry said. “Almost every colleague I interact with in the media considers Shaw to be the best out-and-out central number nine in the world.”

Since joining City in 2021, Shaw has established herself among England’s elite, scoring 127 goals in 146 appearances in all competitions.

However, some in the sport believe she hasn’t received the level of recognition she deserves in the UK and wider Europe for her performances, particularly when compared with other top players.

Sports reporter and presenter with UK football outlets Hayters TV and FourFourTwo, Ayisha Gulati, who covered Monday’s Ballon d’Or ceremony, believes the lack of recognition is no fault of Shaw’s and expects that to change in the near future.

“I think there have been times when Bunny Shaw has been overlooked, although some of that comes down to the wider landscape of women’s football,” Gulati told the Observer. “Barcelona have been the dominant force in the women’s game in recent years, with global superstars like Alexia Putellas and Aitana Bonmatí attracting a lot of attention and dominating conversations about who the best players in the world are.”

“By comparison, Manchester City haven’t been competing in the Champions League in the same way, while Jamaica are not a leading nation in international football. Those factors can influence how much global exposure a player receives, regardless of their individual quality. But Shaw’s performances and the individual awards she has collected make it increasingly difficult to overlook her.”

Garry also believes Shaw warrants far greater appreciation on the international stage.

“I do think she is sometimes overlooked, and that is probably because so much emphasis is placed on performances at senior international level and especially at major international tournaments such as a World Cup and — through no fault of Bunny’s — that means the players who are part of more successful international teams are naturally getting more credit. That’s a shame, because Bunny and — for example, Ewa Pajor of Poland or Melchie Dumornay of Haiti — deserve more awards than they get.”

Shaw described being named the third-best player in the world as a “huge honour”. She finished 24th in the 2023 rankings before climbing to 15th in 2024.

Gulati and Garry believe her performances in Man City’s European campaign, along with her exploits at FIFA World Cup could be key to her bid to lift the prestigious golden ball.

“The Ballon d’Or is an individual award, but team success and performances in high-profile matches has a big influence on how players are perceived,” Gulati said “Manchester City must compete deep into the Champions League and delivering in those decisive knockout games would give Shaw an even bigger platform to showcase her ability. Internationally, Jamaica qualifying for and performing well at the next World Cup would also help, however, that is not entirely within her control and she can only do so much.”

Garry said, “Realistically, in 2027 she would either need to be part of a Champions League-winning side with Manchester City or a Jamaica side that goes into the latter stages of the Women’s World Cup, or perhaps if she was able to win the Golden Boot for the most goals at the World Cup, regardless of how far Jamaica progressed overall. The former will be very difficult because Barcelona are the heavy favourites for the Champions League.”

Next month, Shaw could cap off an already remarkable year by helping the Reggae Girlz secure a third-straight World Cup appearance when they battle Costa Rica in the quarter-finals of the Concacaf W Championship in Texas.

It will be the 50th senior cap for Shaw, who has 67 international goals to her name, including seven so far in 2026.

World.title: Get ready to ‘Shop the Sales’ as TSO returns this weekend
World.content:
Jamaica Observer Senior Lifestyle Editor and Takes Style Out (TSO) conceptualiser Novia McDonald Whyte is flanked by Jamaica Observer Managing Director Dominic Beaubrun (right) and designer Robert Young at the launch of TSO 2026 at the newspaper's headquarters in St Andrew on Tuesday, October 27, 2026. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

It promises to be a shopping bonanza this weekend as the Jamaica Observer Takes Style Out (TSO) returns for its 17th iteration, encouraging consumers to ‘Shop the Sales’.

The three-day shopping event from October 29 to October 31 will feature steep discounts and a special guest appearance by Trinidadian designer Robert Young of ‘The Cloth’.

Young was present at the launch event at the Jamaica Observer’s Beechwood Avenue headquarters on Tuesday, alongside the newspaper’s Senior Lifestyle Editor and TSO conceptualiser Novia McDonald Whyte, and a specially invited group of TSO sponsors and participating realtors.

TSO began as a direct offshoot out of the first Fashion’s Night Out in New York in 2009, created to get people shopping again after the economic downturn in 2008.

Even though Fashion’s Night Out in New York ended, the local event, committed to providing a night of genuine discounts to Jamaicans, has endured.

“When we talk about a sale, we’re talking about 50 per cent, 60 per cent, 70 per cent off, not 10 per cent and 20 per cent,” McDonald-Whyte explained.

“Fashion’s Night Out ended, but we continued, because it proved to be an economic booster in Jamaica,” she shared.

The scope of the event was emphasised by chief operations officer at Jamaica Electronic Transfer Services Limited (JETS Limited), Natalie Samuels Buckle.

“What I can say is that Takes Style Out is well embraced by the Jamaican shopping public. From where I sit, we see that Takes Style Out is a Richter-scale shopping event,” she explained.

JETS, the company behind the multilink debit card network which connects financial institutions across the country, is a key sponsor of the event alongside the National Commercial Bank (NCB) and Island Car Rentals.

Edmundo Jenez, Chief Executive Officer of JETS, maintained that retail has been recovering post Hurricane Melissa, driven by customers.

“We found that customers have been quite resilient. They’ve been able to bounce back, and we’re seeing it, just as we’ve mentioned before, the numbers are there,” he shared.

NCB Vice President of Payment Services and Digital Channels, Danielle Cameron Duncan emphasised the country-wide effect that the event has on the Jamaican public.

“Each sale is an opportunity to build a relationship, and each positive experience is a reason for a customer to return. That is what makes Takes Style Out valuable. It brings attention to businesses across Jamaica and gives them a platform to show customers what they can do,” she explained.

Cameron Duncan acknowledged the bank’s position in the consumer framework locally, including at Takes Style Out, noting that NCB processed over a trillion transactions for its merchants in the last financial year.

Emphasising the individuality and creativity of Jamaican style, Marketing Manager of Island Car Rentals Kerry Ann Harrison lauded the event.

“Takes Style Out is more than an event; it is an opportunity to celebrate individuality, to spotlight Jamaican talent, encourage creativity and to remind us that style belongs to everyone who has the confidence to own it,” she said.

Special Guest Robert Young also spoke to the Observer about fashion and individuality.

The mind behind fashion brand ‘The Cloth’, Young describes himself as an artist working with clothing. His pieces have been displayed at the Smithsonian National Museum of African Art, Washington, DC, the Museum at FIT, New York and Savvy Contemporary, Berlin.

In commenting on fashion microtrends defined by the rapid-fire TikTok algorithm, from ‘clean girl’ to ‘old money’, Young commented on style and individuality, as well as its wider reflection of a people.

“I don’t have a style,” he said with a laugh, adding that “Style exists. Style is definable by the person. But also as a perception… We have to find our own style and slowly find it as Caribbean people. And that has to be decolonised…We have to find our own language to describe it. We have to find something else other than the word ‘style.’”

He urged Caribbean people to question the reasons behind why certain things become relevant and assess the catalysts of certain laws surrounding what is acceptable fashion in the region, from the way hair is groomed to what we wear.

“We have to ask, what do these styles represent, and why are we attracted to it?” Young shared,

Retailers in the room included Fontana Pharmacy, Onya’s Kloset, Dunns Electrical, Moda Home Goods, Haven Beauty House, Loud Fashion, Ammars, Sakred, SOHO, Signature Styles, and Clarks Original. The general consensus from the specially invited retailers was that the event serves as a good lead-in to the Christmas shopping season.

“Our customers really, really appreciate it, We have up to 50 per cent [discounts], and we’ll honour all three dates… overseas, they look for Black Friday. In Jamaica, we look forward to Takes Style Out,” Karen Smith D’Aguilar, of Signature Styles Clarks Originals, said. “We really, really appreciate Observer.”

Anne Chang of Fontana Pharmacy shared that the company even extends the sale by one day due to popular demand.

This year’s event will be supported by dozens of stores and businesses. The full list of merchants offering discounts will be published in the Jamaica Observer newspaper on Thursday.

World.title: WATCH: Jamaicans divided over proposed 20-year minimum sentence for gun crimes
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — Jamaicans have expressed mixed reactions to a proposal by the National Security Council (NSC) to increase the mandatory minimum sentence for gun crimes from 15 to 20 years, with some welcoming the move as a crime-fighting measure while others believe the penalty is too harsh.

Observer Online took to the streets to gauge public opinion on the proposal, which was announced Sunday by the NSC, chaired by Prime Minister Andrew Holness.

The proposal has already drawn criticism from the Opposition People’s National Party (PNP), with Opposition Spokesperson on Justice, Zuleika Jess, arguing that it was put forward “without adequately addressing the legislation’s flaws”.

The existing 15-year mandatory minimum sentence under the Firearms (Prohibition, Restriction and Regulation) Act, 2022, has also faced scrutiny from members of the legal fraternity, who have raised concerns about its broad application and staged demonstrations calling for legislative reform.

Speaking with Observer Online, some individuals supported the proposed increase, arguing that tougher penalties could deter individuals from possessing illegal firearms and help curb gun violence.

“Twenty year minimum, 20 years. It’s a bit harsh, but I feel like the Government is working a way to try to reduce crime because there’s a lot of fatality with gunman and all of them things…” one respondent said.

Another agreed, suggesting that the prospect of spending two decades behind bars could discourage illegal firearm possession.

“I think it’s appropriate because if you know you’re going to get sentenced to 20 years for having illegal firearms, [would] you put yourself in that position? No, I agree with it,” she said.

Another Jamaican encouraged those interested in owning firearms to pursue legal avenues rather than risk facing criminal penalties.

“Gun is a thing weh protect you and thing. Some man use it fi do wrong thing, some use it fi do the right but sometimes you can get right out of wrong same way. You have to just get your thing license, go to the proper place and look bout your thing. If you love gun so much, prefer you have a gun license or if you wah really be a gunholder, go inna the force or go join the JDF or police,” he said.

However, not everyone was convinced that a longer mandatory sentence was justified.

One respondent described the proposal as excessive, raising concerns about the consequences for young people who may become involved in firearm-related offences without having committed a violent act.

“I believe that it is excessive. I’m thinking that 20 years of someone’s life is like a half of their lifetime. What time would you get for one mistake? Especially if it’s a situation where you did not commit a crime, as in murder anyone or shoot up anyone or even use a firearm. Suppose it’s a situation where your teenager or young adult was caught up in bad company. It’s a harsh penalty. Your entire future is lost in 20 years,” she said.

(Video by: Llewellyn Wynter)

World.title: Mother, son killed in St Mary crash on her birthday
World.content:
An undated photo of 38-year-old Abigayle Whitehorn of Hamilton Mountain, St Mary,

ST MARY, Jamaica — What should have been a week of birthday celebrations ended in tragedy on Monday after a St Mary woman and her teenage son were killed in a motor vehicle crash along the Wilderness main road in Galina.

The deceased have been identified as 38-year-old Abigayle Whitehorn of Hamilton Mountain, St Mary, and her 18-year-old son, Tyreke Cameron.

Whitehorn was reportedly celebrating her birthday on the day of the fatal collision, having enjoyed an early celebration with friends at the Port Maria Bus Park on Sunday night.

According to police reports, the crash occurred about 2:00 pm when a white Toyota Hiace bus travelling towards Port Maria reportedly went out of control, veered into the opposite lane and collided head-on with a grey Toyota Fielder motor car.

Whitehorn, her son and another passenger were travelling in the Fielder towards Oracabessa when the collision occurred.

Several occupants of both vehicles sustained injuries and were rushed to the Port Maria Hospital, where Whitehorn and Cameron were pronounced dead.

The other injured individuals remain under medical care for serious injuries.

In the wake of the fatal crash, the St Mary police are appealing to motorists to exercise extreme caution while travelling on the nation’s roadways.

Investigations into the circumstances surrounding the crash are ongoing.

World.title: Criminalise gun couriers
World.content:
CHAMPAGNIE... it was also my expectation and hope that the National Security Council would have looked at specific criminalisation of couriers or shippers who are used to import illegal firearms into this country

Senior attorney Peter Champagnie, KC — who has been strident about the shortcomings of the 2022 Firearms Act since inception — on Monday welcomed amendments proposed by the National Security Council but is urging criminalisation of couriers or shippers who import illegal firearms into the country by virtue of lax inspection protocols.

His call comes in the wake of Sunday’s announcement by the Office of the Cabinet that the National Security Council (NSC) has recommended that individuals convicted of illegal possession of a firearm should now face a new minimum mandatory sentence of 20 years imprisonment instead of the current 15-year minimum.

The NSC also proposed that adults who groom children to use, store, transport, or acquire illegal guns will face a new criminal offence under the pending amendments to the Act “to address the gap whereby gangs seek to recruit and enlist minors in the commission of gun crimes”.

Additionally, the NSC agreed that further consideration should be given to how cases involving children found with illegal firearms are handled and assured that concerns raised regarding imitation firearms will be “clearly addressed to distinguish between toy guns and guns designed to realistically imitate a weapon”.

The council also said the review would include concerns surrounding firearms with expired licences. In the meantime, however, it said before the new provisions take effect, the Government will provide a gun amnesty and cash buy-back programme, giving anyone holding an illegal gun the opportunity to surrender it. The Ministry of National Security and Peace has been directed to have the draft legislation ready by the end of November 2026 for wider consultations.

On Monday, Champagnie, in an interview with the Jamaica Observer, applauded the pending changes but said, “It was also my expectation and hope that the National Security Council would have looked at specific criminalisation of couriers or shippers who, because of the lack of diligence that is applied to scrutinise and inspect shipments, are used to import illegal firearms into this country.”

“As I understand it presently, as it relates to Customs and what obtains, the worst that can be expected if a shipment is contaminated by illegal weapons or anything illegal is that there is perhaps a penalty or a hearing, or there is a suspension of that person’s licence or revocation. But I do believe that it needs to go further in the way of criminalisation, because what the National Security Council needs to also focus on is not just the tail end of the problem; that is to say, persons who are in possession of illegal firearms, but also the source of these firearms, because we do not manufacture firearms here; they have to come from somewhere other than Jamaica. And I think there needs to be stiffer penalties, or indeed penalties, in relation to that. Not just mere trafficking; it has to also reach the shippers and couriers, that is my view,” the prominent defence attorney said.

“They could easily create a mandate where shippers or couriers are required to containerise their shipment in a sterile era where it is video-recorded and presented, and where they would have to show that they took all reasonable steps to ensure that their cargo or the shipment is not contaminated,” Champagnie suggested.

Making it clear that he was speaking in a personal capacity and not on behalf of other legal bodies, Champagnie said he had no quarrel with the proposal to increase the statutory mandatory minimum from 15 to 20 years.

“That is the supremacy of Parliament. I can’t say that they have no authority for so doing and indeed, I have been on record over the years to say that this idea of giving someone who is caught with an illegal weapon three years or 18 months or even a fine is unacceptable. So I support the statutory mandatory minimum, and if they want to increase it, then that’s their right. However, I do believe that there needs to be a holistic approach with the Firearms Act to facilitate guilty pleas,” Champagnie maintained.

“There must be some incentive for persons wanting to plead guilty, and there must be some exceptional circumstances where a person found in possession of a firearm must be allowed to have a kind of discretion for that person to receive a sentence below the statutory mandatory minimum, and in those circumstances, there is authority for it in other jurisdictions where exceptions are specifically laid out. But certainly, in relation to the hardcore criminals and those that use imitation firearms to commit offences, they must expect severe penalties,” he argued.

Champagnie, in the meantime, said legislation which addresses the appeal process in circumstances where a sentence is excessive should also be revisited.

“We must also bear in mind that the prosecution now has the right to appeal if a sentence is given that is considered to be woefully inadequate for the circumstances, and there have been cases that have settled that. So, I would want that to be also considered, and I look forward to the actual details of the report and the recommendations beyond what has been issued by way of a press release, because one is not able to fully appreciate all of the nuances and the extent of the recommendations until we actually are able or in a position to examine the actual paper that is in the way of recommendations,” he told the Observer.

He said the planned silent protest on September 23 and a sit out by some attorneys as part of the push for a review of the Act had not been in vain.

“When the attorneys sought to bring some kind of pressure for the Government to re-examine the Firearms Act, the first comment that was made was that the legislation was up for review next year, and therefore we should await that period. I note, however, that there is a shift now, where there seems to be an intention to have recommended changes effected within this year. That is good, but what it demonstrates is that we are able to pivot and we are able to move with alacrity if the need arises,” he said in urging the authorities to ensure that practitioners from both the private and public bar are at the discussion table.

“I don’t think ever before in our legal history, we have had a situation where a legislation, in the way of the administration of the criminal justice system, has received universal comments in the way of shortcomings by not just the private bar but also the public bar, the prosecution, and in some instances the judges, as it relates to it facilitating guilty plea, and that is a major, major point to be made,” he argued.

“Anyone who is involved in the practice of law day to day will tell you that there are real issues. There are real issues also with licensed firearm holders who run the risk of getting 20 years just by being in possession of a licensed firearm and being caught for instance in a physical confrontation with another person even when they are not using it, so these are fundamental issues that I think need to be examined,” he said.

Section 14(3) of the Act dictates that a person commits a felony if they are in possession of a firearm or an imitation firearm at the time of committing, or when being apprehended for, any specific serious offence listed in the First Schedule of the provision.

World.title: The Putin call dividing EU leaders
World.content:
Europe’s united front on Ukraine is showing cracks. Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre have opened a direct line to Vladimir Putin, drawing criticism from some fellow European leaders — even as Ukraine backs their efforts. Nicholas Vinocur and Paul Dallison examine the fallout and the growing scramble over who gets to speak for Europe in peace talks.

Also on the pod: Brussels unveils a sweeping overhaul of Frontex, giving the EU border agency a much bigger role in deportations, new powers to monitor social media and plans for a major expansion.

World.title: EU prosecutors still have questions for von der Leyen over Pfizergate
World.content:
Asked to respond to the assertion that von der Leyen has failed to provide a statement on the so-called Pfizergate affair, Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said: "The Commission has demonstrably cooperated extensively with EPPO to clarify facts and assess events."

"This was always done on behalf of and with the full support of the President. The President has always been, and continues to be, very cooperative in answering to any open questions — within the limits of her duties and her availability as President of the Commission.”

In an interview with POLITICO, EPPO chief prosecutor Laura Codruța Kövesi, who wraps up her seven-year tenure on Friday, said she has on multiple occasions dealt with EU officials who refused to answer summons from her office. “Some politicians think that they are above the law,” she said. “If you are called in for a statement, you have to come.”

She added: "I will not be shy to tell you that especially when important people are involved in the investigation — be it high-profile politicians or rich people who are connected to the political class, we have difficulties in exercising our competence."

When asked whether von der Leyen was one of the officials in question, Kövesi said she wouldn't comment on specific investigations.

Killing EPPO softly

EPPO, set up in 2017 and operational since 2021, is tasked with rooting out crimes involving EU funds. As head of the organization, Kövesi said she has faced repeated attacks and attempts to undermine the institution and its work.

World.title: EU Public Prosecutor’s Office will be ‘killed softly for doing its job’ says outgoing chief
World.content:
We had support of different stakeholders in some cases, but when I say that I’m concerned that EPPO is going to be killed softly for doing its job, I have three main reasons. It’s easy, it’s a pattern. If you want to destroy an institution, you can do three things, that are happening now. First, you are underfunded. On paper we should have 230 European delegated prosecutors, and we have money only for 180. We have money for only one third of what security service costs, and I would have endless examples.

Second, a lot of delays. Since 2021, we said that the revision of the EPPO regulation has to start earlier. It’s delayed. Thirdly, I have learned that here everything is complicated — and I thought that Romania is complicated. To give you an example, there are these endless discussions about anti-fraud architecture. We discovered a new continent of crime, and we see the criminal organizations are growing, defrauding the EU budget and national budgets. In the middle of this, should be the fight against organized criminality. Instead, we have endless discussion about how to complicate the life of the prosecutors, and we discuss a lot about this joint intake registry. If there is money to have this new registry electronically, how is it possible that money doesn’t exist for what we really need?

Do you feel that you have managed to shake things up? Have people or institutions started behaving differently?

A lot of changes happened due to the EPPO. The level of detection increased in most of the member states, the level of successful cases increased, and obviously the protection of the EU budget is higher with the EPPO. But still, there are things that are not working the way they should be.

If you had the chance to do it all over again, what is the main thing that you would do differently?

Nothing. I would do the same things, but maybe the others should change their behavior. I thought that there is a big difference between Brussels and what I saw in Romania. But in Romania, or other member states, people are used to work with prosecutors, they know what the prosecutors are doing.

World.title: Serbian opposition landslide exposes cost of EU’s bet on ousted Vučić
World.content:
When POLITICO reached him, Gašić was in the middle of grading student papers — a fitting snapshot of a new parliamentary majority made up largely of professors, doctors and other political novices.

The Student List won an outright parliamentary majority at the weekend: a stunning result for a leaderless movement born out of protests.

The party’s first order of business will be undoing much the legacy of Vučić and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), starting with reversing years of rule-of-law rollbacks. But it will also reset Serbia’s relationship with Brussels, which the Student List argues the former leader managed more as a transactional tool than a genuine path to EU membership.

“Ultimately, [Vučić] always represented his own interests and not the interests of Serbia,” said Gašić.

Representatives for the SNS didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Even among Serbia’s most committed pro-Europeans, Brussels’ willingness to route all progress through Vučić personally has left a bitter aftertaste.

World.title: The US and Canada are talking trade. That doesn’t mean they’re near a deal.
World.content:
A senior Canadian government official told POLITICO that talks remain informal as of Tuesday.

The uptick in engagement — what Carney called “un petit intensification” speaking in French to reporters in Ottawa Monday — has triggered a flurry of headlines on both sides of the border as well as White House boasts that a deal is near. The North American trade spat will be “settled pretty soon,” Trump predicted at a rally Sunday in Michigan.

But unlike Trump, Carney has little political incentive to make concessions at the moment — or bail out Trump right before congressional elections heavily focused on affordability, including tariffs’ impact on prices. The Canadian prime minister is riding high in domestic polls after standing up to the American president and walking away from trade negotiations in August. And he is days away from welcoming European Union leaders to Montreal for a landmark summit aimed at deepening their alliance — and building an implicit counterweight to the U.S.

Neither side, moreover, has dropped its original demands, according to half a dozen current and former government officials, industry representatives and others with knowledge of the talks. Those outstanding sticking points include Carney’s ask for lower auto tariffs and Trump’s push for increased access to the Canadian alcohol and dairy markets.

The lack of new concessions or tangible breakthroughs is a sign that the recent flurry of outreach may be more of a White House effort to soothe Republicans’ midterm worries — particularly in border states whose economies are tightly connected to Canada’s — than to secure an immediate deal. The people say any denouement between the two countries is likely weeks if not months off, even as they expect the two North American neighbors to ultimately hammer out an agreement to lower tariffs and stabilize one of the world’s largest trading relationships.

“I think that we’re going to make a deal with Canada. I mean, first of all, we made a deal with Canada. They reneged on the deal,” Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) said in an interview. Asked if the deal will come before the election, Moreno said, “I don’t know.”

World.title: Quebec’s separatist leader threatens to play spoiler at Carney’s EU summit
World.content:
Ottawa also turned down a September request from the previous Quebec government to host a reception on the sidelines of the summit, Sarrazin noted.

Prime Minister Mark Carney hit back, saying St-Pierre Plamondon had himself turned down an invitation to the Thursday night summit dinner. “It’s his decision to leave an empty chair again,” Carney told reporters in French.

The tiff threatens to overshadow an international gathering that Carney, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa have billed as a step change in mutual relations, driven by U.S. President Donald Trump’s aggressive tariffs and scorn for the postwar Western consensus.

Early drafts of the joint declaration include a digital trade deal and a pact that lets the European Investment Bank finance Canadian critical minerals projects. Many of those deliverables fall under provincial jurisdiction, such as natural resources.

“'When you’re not at the table, you’re on the menu,' Prime Minister Carney told us,” Sarrazin said in her statement. “The federal government has chosen to prevent Quebec from having a say on its own territory.”

Whatever agreements are signed at the summit, “Quebec is sovereign in its fields of jurisdiction internationally, so it will have the last word,” Sarrazin warned.

World.title: UK budget 2026: What to watch for as Healey vows ‘breathing space’ for Brits
World.content:
Financial Services Reporter Eleanor Myers

A hike in bank taxes is all but inevitable in today’s budget – but the City of London will be nervously watching how high the increase goes. Along with the lenders, I’ll be looking out for how much taxes are raised, whether any changes are temporary, and whether the City — Britain's financial powerhouse — gets anything in return.

The easiest move for Healey is to increase the surcharge banks pay on top of corporation tax. That currently stands at 3%, after Conservative Chancellor Jeremy Hunt reduced it from 8% in 2023 to account for higher corporation taxes. Healey could simply reverse the surcharge to 8%, which would be unpopular with the banks and might not even go far enough for campaigners: the Trades Union Congress has called for an increase to 16%.

I’ll also be closely watching for how the bond markets react to the first budget under Burnham. Despite the prime minister describing Britain as “in hock” to the bond markets before he took office, odds are on for a “boring” budget, without any huge spending commitments that might spike borrowing costs.

People view the City of London from Parliament Hill on Jan. 3, 2025. | Benjamin Cremel/AFP via Getty Images

But any cautious policy changes designed to placate the bond market will have to be tempered alongside demands from the Labour Party. It’s a tricky balance, and Labour MPs showed under Keir Starmer that they were willing to rebel when it mattered.

Senior U.K. Energy Correspondent Charlie Cooper

A sharp, painful spike in energy bills is coming for Britain; at this budget we’ll find out how much power Healey and Burnham have to help.

The latest energy price cap forecasts are brutal. Energy firms expect average, annual household bills to rise by more than £450 in January. They could go even higher in April. Why? Mainly because of gas. The fallout from the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has sent wholesale prices soaring to levels not seen since December 2022.

World.title: Israel votes in a pivotal election but no clear winner emerges
World.content:
Elections in Israel: Key legislative elections in Israel show incumbent Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu standing ahead of the opposition Wednesday morning after 50% of votes have been counted. This is according to figures from the Central Elections Committee. Netanyahu's bloc is projected to win 56 of the 120 seats in the parliament, compared with 49 for the opposition bloc and 15 for the Arab parties.

 

Eylon Levy, former Israeli government spokesperson, just said on Europe Today that there are three options facing the political elite: form a unity government, form a minority government, or fresh elections. “All of those are going to require someone to surrender on some very serious coalition promises.” Watch.

What is likely to come next is weeks of wrangling among parties to form a governing coalition and declare a new prime minister. In the meantime, Netanyahu remains as interim caretaker head of the government.

What is clear is that the country remains deeply divided over Netanyahu's leadership and remains damaged by the Hamas-led 7 October attacks and the wars that have since shaken the Middle East.

Phone a friend: The leaders of Finland and Norway spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the phone for 90-minutes on Tuesday to restart the peace process. According to statements, the two leaders urged Putin to end the full-scale invasion and engage in meaningful negotiations to reach a stable, peaceful settlement.

As my colleague Jorge Liboreiro reports, that chat was followed by a phone call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who thanked the duo for their “active” support and called for de-escalatory steps. (More analysis of the play-by-play below).

What is important to highlight now is that the Stubb-Støre move comes as the European Commission and the European Council prepare a joint team of senior officials to be sent to the next round of talks.

As Sasha Vakulina writes, Russia, Ukraine and the US could meet in Abu Dhabi on 4 November for talks. That’s according to an announcement by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk on Tuesday.

According to Tusk, the provisional date emerged as European leaders coordinated diplomatic efforts with Kyiv and Washington ahead of possible negotiations. What’s interesting is that this is occurring one day after the US midterm elections scheduled for Tuesday 3 November.

The timing raises questions about what comes next for Washington's efforts to end Moscow’s war.

For those uninitiated: The midterms matter because they occur in the middle of a president’s four-year term and determine the composition of the two chambers of Congress: the Senate and the House of Representatives.

The vote not only offers an opportunity for citizens to elect lawmakers — Republican or Democrat, for example — but also serves as a temperature check on a president’s term in office. For US President Donald Trump, this is a mandate pockmarked by trade wars, hostility towards Ukraine, and a retreat from the transatlantic security architecture. Can the damage from the last 24-months be undone at the ballot box?

Keith Brannum, Truman National Security Project fellow and strategist, just told Europe Today that this Congress has been “subservient” to Trump. Democrats, however, have been “very vocal” about holding the president to account. “We are in uncertain times,” he said, with no clear projection of the future. Watch.

Brussels news: Polish ambassador Agnieszka Bartol will depart Brussels to take a cabinet position at Tusk’s government in Warsaw. She will remain his sherpa, having built on years of experience where she cut a reputation of smooth operator and became a fan-favourite of journalists in the Belgian capital. Polish Andrzej Domański is poised to become the country’s next deputy prime minister.

More Brussels news: EU energy and defence commissioners Dan Jørgensen and Andrius Kubilius will today hold talks on energy security at the Berlaymont, bringing together stakeholders including NATO officials and industry heavyweights.

According to a leaked agenda obtained by my colleague Marta Pacheco, discussions will focus on EU fuel production for defence, particularly jet fuel output and logistics to meet a “potential demand surge”.

Caspar Hobhouse, a research analyst at the EU Institute for Security Studies, said Europe’s militaries primarily rely on two fuel sources: jet fuel for aviation and diesel to serve as backup power for military bases. “In the case of a military conflict, the demand is enormous,” he told me.

‘Very, very short business’: Securing these fuel supplies is becoming more difficult due to the war in Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Without major replenishments, Europe’s current fuel reserves would leave it “very, very short business” in the event of armed aggression, Caspar said.

MEP Riho Terras, and former commander of the Estonian Defence Forces, welcomed the talks, warning that aggression is imminent and stressing the need for proper planning. “We have to be prepared,” he said, including for plan Bs. “In 2007 I served in Iraq, then the whole country experienced a very big shortage of energy, and we dealt a lot with diesel generators there. In times of war, you need to have backups,” Riho enthused.

Cash investment: A NATO spokesperson said it is “vital” that Europe’s fuel production capacity can support both civil and military demands, particularly during crises and conflicts. In July, allies approved a €27 billion NATO Fuel Supply Chain Capability Programme Plan, which includes pipelines along the alliance’s eastern and south-eastern corridors to ensure supplies for “warfighting readiness”.

So what will come out of the talks? Monitor Euronews for updates.

Life after Vučić: After 14-years of Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) rule, the status quo was shattered on Monday when election results rolled in and foretold a new era for the Western Balkan country. This is one predominantly without former president Aleksandar Vučić, a free press and a reset of EU relations.

In the days since the seismic election, onlookers have witnessed scenes unfold on social media, of the lead anchor from national broadcaster Radio Television of Vojvodina (RTV) apologising to viewers for the last decade of alleged one-sided reporting.

On Tuesday, European Council President António Costa even called Ilija Srdanović, the leader of the Student List political movement, to say that parliament and government is expected to be formed swiftly. On top of this, most importantly, he communicated that “Serbia’s place is in the European Union.”

Marko Prelec, Balkans expert at the International Crisis Group, just told Europe Today that the new political elite “clearly seek” better relations with Europe and the EU itself. But how this will actually materialise is yet to be seen. Watch.

As the EU attempts to find the right tenor when speaking with China to eradicate an eye-watering trade deficit, it seems that a French football star has irritated officials in Beijing.

Mao migraine: Top French footballer Kylian Mbappé has lost several of his biggest sponsorship deals in China after a video circulated online in which he appears to joke about Mao Zedong, the founder of the People’s Republic of China, that led to a backlash that he has now apologised for.

"My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world," Mbappé said in a statement he published in French, Chinese and English on Tuesday. "I apologise to everyone that my words have upset."

Ken Early, Irish football commentator, just told Europe Today that this is not the first time a political controversy has disrupted the activities on the pitch. “The German player Mesut Özil who played for Arsenal at the time, in 2019, posted on social media about the plight of the Uyghur people in China,” he said.

“In that instance, they said, ‘Okay, Arsenal won't be on Chinese television anymore.” Watch.

After months dithering, Europe shows it's ready for talks with Russia

After months of bickering, Europe is sending its strongest signals yet that it is ready to speak directly with Russia to end the full-scale invasion of Ukraine and decide the future of the continent's security architecture.

Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre marched ahead and held a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin to discuss the imminent restart of the peace process.

Though Stubb and Støre lacked a mandate to speak on behalf of Europe — they did so as “leaders of their respective countries” — their overture on Tuesday immediately positioned the Nordic duo as preeminent interlocutors. In its read-out, the Kremlin said that the three had "agreed to maintain direct telephone contact in the future".

The Stubb-Støre surprise move comes as the European Commission and the European Council prepare a joint team of senior officials to be sent to the next round of talks, scheduled to be held in Abu Dhabi in early November.

Is it notable that Brussels is openly stating its intention to hold the negotiations in a multilateral format, which would mean having Europeans, Ukrainians, Americans and Russians at the same table and at the same time. It is even more notable that Russia, rather than rejecting European presence, is now actively seeking it.

In his latest analysis, Jorge explains why Europe is more ready than ever to expand its diplomatic role and make its voice heard vis-a-vis Russia.

More from our newsrooms

Von der Leyen’s Canada ‘associate membership’ spurs battle of words with EU capitals. Last month, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen made a bombshell offer to Canada: to become the first EU “associate member”. Now the term is proving hard to swallow for several member states, including her own Germany. Luca Bertuzzi has the must-read information.

Norway says 'successful' cyberattacks against the country have tripled in last six months. The country's National Security Authority said the rapid growth of artificial intelligence technology also posed a "serious risk" to Norwegian businesses and organisations. Read more of this story by Nathan Rennolds.

European disease control centre sends experts to Nigeria while Ebola cases surpass 10,000 in Congo. With the Ebola outbreak continuing to spread beyond the epicentre in the Democratic Republic of Congo — where it surpassed 10,000 cases — ECDC sent a team led by its senior expert in epidemic intelligence to Nigeria, the fourth African country to report an Ebola case. Giedre Peseckyte has the details.

We’re also keeping an eye on

Members of the European Parliament’s committee centred on civil liberties and justice will deliver a press conference in Hungary following a fact-finding mission.

European Commissioner for the Environment Jessika Roswall will be in Yerevan, Armenia for the UN Biodiversity Conference (COP17). She will deliver a press conference at 2:30 pm CET.

European Parliament President Roberta Metsola continues her visit to Malta.

European Commissioner for Justice Michael McGrath speaks at the meeting of the Freeze and Seize Taskforce.

That’s it for today. Jorge Liboreiro and Sasha Vakulina contributed to this newsletter.

World.title: EU Inc: Is the EU’s flagship start-up plan really dying over workers’ rights?
World.content:
Proposed by the Commission on 18 March, EU Inc. would be an optional company form alongside the 27 national systems, with digital registration within 48 hours, a cost of up to €100, and no minimum share capital.

 

Two Legal Affairs Committee votes were cancelled in October because political groups could not agree on workers’ rights. Companies would follow the employee-participation rules of their chosen country of registration. Unions and centre-left MEPs fear firms could choose weaker board-level protections. Business-friendly lawmakers say applying multiple national systems would complicate the plan.

The EU-INC campaign, backed by more than 26,000 supporters and figures linked to Stripe, Mistral AI, Klarna and Wise, says the opposite problem is real. It points to the deletion of the central EU register from the Council text and limits on harmonised stock options. Commissioner Stéphane Séjourné has said the regime cannot work without stock-option harmonisation.

A new committee vote is pencilled in for 5 November, and a first plenary vote for 12 November. Both dates are provisional. The project is not dead, but the fight is now over how much of it survives.

World.title: Serbian police kill attacker outside Israeli Embassy in suspected ‘terrorist attack’
World.content:
Serbian police said an attacker was shot dead after assaulting a guard with knives outside the Israeli Embassy in Belgrade early Wednesday.

 

Interior Minister Ivica Dacic described the incident as a suspected “terrorist attack”, saying authorities had raised the country's terror alert to its highest level and increased security at key sites.

Dacic said that “a minor, so far unidentified … shouting Allahu Akbar, attacked the member of Gendarmerie and attacked him with two knives.”

The officer was lightly wounded and shot the attacker dead in what Dacic described as “self-defense.”

People celebrate in Belgrade, Serbia, on 26 October 2026, a day after the student-led opposition defeated Aleksandar Vucic's ruling party in parliamentary elections. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

The Minister said Serbian security services had been monitoring the suspect, whom he described as a supporter of the Islamic State group.

According to Dacic “he kept the black flag in support of the Islamic State on his Instagram” account.

The attack comes days after Serbia's early parliamentary election on Sunday, which saw a youth-led movement defeat former President Aleksandar Vucic's long-dominant political camp following nearly two years of anti-government protests. However, Vucic and his allies remain in control of the police while a new government has yet to be formed.

The incident also follows Tuesday's parliamentary election in Israel.

World.title: Travellers are making more sustainable choices to ‘enhance’ journeys, new study finds
World.content:
Amid the rising impact of climate change, more holidaymakers are considering sustainable options for deciding when, where and how to travel, according to findings from Trip.com’s Sustainable Travel Consumer Report.

 

The survey of 8,777 respondents, from 29 countries across four global regions, found that 37.2% of travellers would consider destinations with a lower risk of weather disruptions. This comes after Europe experienced a summer that was the “worst on record”, according to a separate report.

Trip.com also found that 75.4% of respondents highlighted sustainability as “important when making travel decisions”, while 56.8% intentionally choose more sustainable travel options.

“Every journey depends on the world around it: the places we discover, the nature we enjoy and the communities that make each destination unique,” said Jane Sun, CEO of Trip.com Group. “For travel to thrive for generations to come, that world must thrive too.

“Sustainability is becoming an important part of what travellers value. It is not just a responsibility, but a way to experience more – from exploring nature and taking scenic rail journeys to discovering less-visited destinations.”

Among younger travellers, there is a particular interest in experience-led options, like rail journeys, outdoor activities and hotels with strong sustainability practices. Their older counterparts, however, are more interested in travelling to places with less crowds and going outside of peak seasons.

According to the report, younger travellers show “stronger engagement with more sustainable travel across intention, action and platform choice”. For Gen Z respondents, 44.3% agreed sustainability is "very important" when making travel decisions, compared to just 23% among Boomers.

Sustainable travel choices

Price remains a large consideration and perceived barrier, with 32.9% of travellers willing to pay just an additional 1%-5% for sustainable travel. However, nearly six in 10 Gen Z and Millennials are willing to pay a premium for a more sustainable travel experience.

“This suggests that price sensitivity does not necessarily translate into an unwillingness to spend more on more sustainable travel experience,” the report said.

The survey also found that exploring nature and outdoor destinations was the top sustainable travel choice thought to enhance experiences, cited by 41.6% of respondents.

This was followed by scenic rail journeys (34.1%), visiting lesser-known destinations with fewer crowds (32.7%), staying in hotels with strong sustainability practices (31.9%), and travelling during off-season (29.6%).

Extreme weather and destination appeal

Extreme weather has prompted changes to travel plans, as 29.9% of respondents have delayed or rescheduled a trip, while 23.6% changed the season or timing of travel. Further, 21.9% felt the need to change the destination.

When it comes to a destination’s appeal, 56% are attracted to good public transport or lower-carbon mobility options and 50.6% are attracted to destinations that protect natural and cultural heritage. In contrast, 37.2% of travellers would opt to travel to a place with a lower risk of weather disruptions.
