World.title: Ithaca's natural horseshoe harbour is picturesque – but it hides a dirty secret
World.content:
On the Greek island of Ithaca, Vathy is known for its natural horseshoe harbour. But the beautiful port hides a dirty secret.

 

A volunteer diving team recently removed around 1,300 kilograms of solid waste from the wider harbour area. The two-day operation marked the start of this year's 'We Dive We Clean' campaign.

This was the group's 186th mission, across 13 years of underwater environmental work in different parts of Greece. According to figures released by the team, its total haul now stands at almost 73 tonnes of solid waste recovered from Greek seabeds.

Bottles, nets, tyres and an almost entire plastic boat

The scene that greeted the volunteer divers on the harbour floor highlights the scale of marine pollution and the variety of objects that end up in Greek waters.

Among the waste brought up were plastic and glass bottles, aluminium cans, fishing lines, nets and fish traps, as well as batteries, tyres of various sizes, rugs and assorted plastic items.

Equally striking was the number of objects linked to human activity and navigation in the harbour. Divers recovered parts of boats and dinghies, personal belongings and accessories that appear to have fallen overboard, chairs, traffic cones, bicycles, metal objects and anchors.

One of the most notable finds was an almost complete plastic fishing boat.

Removing such items is an important step towards improving the condition of the seabed, as discarded materials can burden the marine ecosystem, trap sea creatures and undermine the quality of the coastal environment.

13 years of voluntary work in Greek waters

The operation in Vathy forms part of We Dive We Clean's long-term effort to remove solid waste from the Greek seabed and to draw attention to the problem of marine pollution.

Founded in 2013, the group has carried out underwater clean-ups in harbours and coastal areas across the country, building up significant experience in lifting objects of different sizes and weights. Its work combines the practical removal of waste with efforts to raise public awareness about the need to protect the marine environment.

Underwater clean-ups require proper training, specialised equipment and careful planning, particularly when large or heavy items are involved. The process begins with the removal of the largest objects and is followed by the collection of smaller pieces of debris, using the necessary lifting gear.

The volunteers' regular presence in different parts of Greece has helped document a problem that often remains invisible from the surface: the build-up of waste in harbours, fishing shelters and other coastal locations.

Encouraging signs, but no room for complacency

The team says that much of the waste now being recovered from the seabed appears to date back many years.

This creates a sense of cautious optimism among the volunteers, who believe there may be growing public awareness of environmental protection and waste management.

However, this finding does not mean the problem has been solved. Keeping the seas clean calls for continuous effort, responsible behaviour from residents and visitors alike, proper waste management and an end to dumping rubbish in the water or along the shoreline.

The operation in Vathy offers a stark reminder that even today large quantities of objects remain on the seabed of Greek harbours, out of sight in everyday life. At the same time, it highlights the importance of voluntary work and coordinated environmental action.

With almost 73 tonnes of waste already removed from Greek waters, We Dive We Clean is continuing its mission with a clear message: protecting the seas does not stop at cleaning them; it begins with preventing pollution and changing our daily habits.

World.title: Zoom in, zoom out: Deeply personal and political pictures dominate Hungarian press photo exhibition
World.content:
If the themes of political change, ballerinas and parental care took pride of place at last year's Hungarian Press Photo exhibition, the show this is dedicated to imminent social revolution sparked by technology.

 

At the opening of the 44th edition at the Robert Capa Contemporary Photography Center in Budapest, managing director Orsolya Kőrösi stressed that the work of photojournalists is becoming increasingly important: "The photojournalist does not just take pictures, but is present, bears witness, selects and interprets, while putting their own name to the claim that what they show is close to reality,"

Kőrösi pointed out that in the age of artificial intelligence, when it is increasingly difficult to distinguish the genuine from content created artificially, the role of a place where authentic photojournalistic work, assumed with a name and responsibility, is presented, protected and celebrated becomes particularly valuable.

More than 6,200 works were submitted by 258 photographers. The exhibition showcases the top three entries and the special prize-winners in each of the sixteen categories.

It also presents works considered by the jury to be exceptionally important or exciting, according to photographer András Bánkuti, who's also chair of the Hungarian Press Association (MÚOSZ) Photojournalists Section.

"With us you cannot retouch a picture even if, say, a politician has a spot. The moment you do that, it counts as interference and the picture is immediately out of the competition," Bánkuti explained. "It can still be printed on any paper; that is not our responsibility. Our responsibility today, when the greatest value and credibility are attached to a picture being real, we have to be very careful about that."

Prize-winning pictures

This year the MÚOSZ Grand Prize went to freelance photographer Diana Nemeh for her series titled "Nimród", while the André Kertész Grand Prize was awarded to Telex photographer Noémi Napsugár Melegh.

Napsugár Melegh has been constant recorder of almost all major protests but her greatest recognition has come from documenting her own personal tragedy. After the death of her 18-year-old younger brother, she spent years photographing her grieving family and his classmates.

"It was very difficult to make these pictures, especially in situations where my brother should have been there. I actually went to the same secondary school as he did, and it was quite surreal that 15 years later I was in the same places, at the same freshers' camp where he should have been," said Napsugár Melegh.

"On the one hand I had to force myself to be there so I could take these pictures; on the other, for a long time I was making them for the drawer, I did not show them to anyone. After a year and a half I began to show them to my closest professional friends, and that broke through something in my own process of mourning as well," she added.

The 44th Hungarian Press Photo Exhibition is at the Robert Capa Center in Budapest until 8 November.

World.title: Israel election: Netanyahu-led bloc in slight lead with half of votes counted
World.content:
Skip next section Netanyahu bloc holds slight lead after more than half of votes counted: elections committee

Partial results issued by Israel's Central Elections Committee and reported by the Times of Israel after 57.3% of votes were counted have shown the pro-Netanyahu bloc with a projected 55 seats, seven seats ahead of the anti-Netanyahu bloc with 49.

Neither side so far has the 61 seats needed to form a secure majority and are not expected to do so.

Arab parties so far are projected to win 15 seats.

These are partial results that will change as counting progresses.

In particular, the special votes cast by people outside their assigned polling stations, such as those of soldiers, are counted later.

A record 650,000 such absentee votes are expected this year, equivalent to around 14 seats in the Knesset.

This means the absentee votes could markedly affect the final election result, the Israel Hayom newspaper reported.

World.title: India news: Cyclone Arnab brings heavy rain, disruption
World.content:
10/28/2026 October 28, 2026 India faces high economic cost of heatwaves, new Lancet study shows

Half of the heatwave days that people in India were exposed to on average were directly attributable to climate change between 2016 and 2025 Image: Debarchan Chatterjee/NurPhoto/IMAGO

India ranked among the top countries where the elderly and infants are most exposed to heatwaves, the latest Lancet Countdown on Health and Climate Change report said, putting the nation in the same basket as China, US and Russia. But that's not all.

As per the report, the economic cost is steep for the nation.

Extreme heat cost Indian workers an estimated $174 billion (€156.5 billion) in potential earnings in 2025. That's 4.2% of the nation's GDP. Moreover, 54% of the losses were from the agriculture sector.

"Increasing heat exposure is affecting health, physical activity, sleep and labor capacity in India, with substantial consequences for livelihoods, particularly in agriculture," the report said.

Published by the presitigious British medical journal ahead of the COP 31 climate summit in November, the 10th edition of the report brought together 146 researchers from 30 countries to assess the impact of climate change on the health of the world's population.

It said there were a record 710,000 heat-related deaths in 2023 with more than 70% of that toll linked to human-caused climate change.

The report called for climate change to be formally recognized and addressed as a global health emergency.

World.title: Experts urge 'global health emergency' as climate harms accelerate
World.content:
Heat, drought and storms linked to climate change are already killing millions worldwide. Researchers want global warming to be declared a global health emergency as the health harms from it escalate faster than ever.

As heat deaths, drought and food insecurity accelerate worldwide, nearly 150 researchers from more than 30 countries are calling for climate change to be declared a "global health emergency."

The health and economic toll of planetary heating has risen sharply in the decade since countries signed the Paris climate accord — a landmark deal to stop climate change that was hailed by the World Health Organization (WHO) at the time as "the most important public health agreement of the century."

Yet, climate change was responsible for more than half a million heat deaths in 2023 alone and nearly 3 million since 2016. The area affected by extreme drought, which threatens food and water supplies and raises the risk of disease, grew more than 700% faster than in the decade before. And heat cost the world an estimated $1.07 trillion (around €962 billion) in lost potential income last year, all according to the annual Lancet Countdown on Health and Climate Change .

"This cannot continue," said Alan Dangour, director of climate and health at Wellcome Trust, one of the world's largest charities, which funded the Lancet report. "We must change course and put the health and well-being of people at the heart of our response to climate change — measuring success not through emissions targets or degrees Celsius but by lives saved and health outcomes improved."

Climate extremes are the new health threats — here is why To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Climate-linked health harms growing faster than before

The latest findings from the Lancet study show how rapidly the health risks are growing by comparing this decade to the one before the Paris Agreement was signed.

Heat is the starkest example. Climate change was responsible for 68% of heat-related deaths between 2016 and 2023, up from 55% in the previous decade. The yearly increase in climate-driven heat deaths more than doubled over the same period.

But deaths are only "the tip of the iceberg," said Ollie Jay of the University of Sydney's Heat and Health Research Center. "Except that iceberg is not melting, it's growing every year." Beneath the surface are also heatstroke, lost sleep and worsening chronic health conditions.

Older people are particularly vulnerable to extreme heat Image: Rolf Vennenbernd/dpa/picture alliance

The economic harms are mounting too. Working in extreme heat puts people at risk of heat exhaustion, illness or injury and, ultimately, losing income and livelihoods.

Heat wiped out 573 billion potential working hours in 2025, with farmworkers bearing the brunt. Vulnerable economies in Africa and South-East Asia were hit hardest with losses reaching 5% of GDP, compared with 0.5% in the more developed economies.

"The economic toll is battering vulnerable sectors and communities the hardest," Marina Romanello, executive director of the Lancet Countdown, who is based at University College London, told journalists at a press briefing.

Water extremes are intensifying too. Satellite data show that since 2003, 43% of the world's land has been steadily drying out, while 37% has been getting wetter. Together, that is more than 80% of land shifting to extremes that threaten crops, food supplies and sanitation.

Why Europe's extreme summers are getting worse To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Drought can leave people without safe drinking water and raises the risk of infectious disease, while floods bring drowning, injury and contaminated water.

Heat waves and droughts pushed nearly 128 million more people into food insecurity in 2024, compared with the 1981–2010 average.

"This isn't a gradual worsening; it's a step change," Romanello said.

What would declaring a global health emergency change?

To save lives and protect human health, experts are calling for a new WHO instrument to help countries share information, coordinate responses, monitor threats and disburse funds. The United Nations and its member states would create the mechanism.

The closest existing version of this is the WHO's Public Health Emergency of International Concern mechanism (PHEIC) used during the COVID-19 pandemic and mpox outbreaks. But built with short-term emergencies in mind, it falls short of addressing a complex threat that requires sustained global action across multiple sectors, like climate change.

The world needs a broader approach, "so that we're not responding to emergency after emergency," said Romanello. "We're doing a cohesive long-term response that builds resilience, builds capacities and builds the possibilities of countries to avoid further emergencies."

Progress happening but not nearly fast enough

Romanello told journalists that "we have more than enough proof" that such action does improve health outcomes. "Early warning systems informed by climate, have already seen a reduction in the adverse impacts of these extreme weather events," she said.

The growth in renewable energy has also partly aided a reduction in deaths from fossil fuel air pollution in half of 140 countries assessed since 2016, preventing an estimated 323,000 deaths a year.

And 56 countries now have national plans to adapt their health services for climate impacts, such as heat waves and disease outbreaks, up from just 14 in 2015.

An increase in renewable energy and other climate actions have helped reduce air pollution in some countries. But not everywhere Image: Muda Sagala/AFP

But progress remains too slow, according to the report.

Fossil fuels, the burning of which releases emissions fueling planetary heating as well as other pollutants, still supply more than 80% of the world's energy.

Energy-related emissions hit a record high in 2024. The world's 100 largest oil and gas companies are on track to produce 150% more oil and gas by 2040 than is compatible with limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit). A year ago, that figure was 138%.

Investing in an old technology

Governments continue to fund fossil fuels, with net subsidies doubling since 2016 to $6.2 trillion. In 2024, 10 countries spent more on such subsidies than on their entire health systems.

Yet as fossil fuel prices rise and renewables become cheaper, these polluting technologies are becoming increasingly uneconomical, said Romanello.

Romanello likened new fossil fuel investment to "investing in Blockbuster when you have Netflix," — a bet on an old technology, referring to the once ubiquitous video rental store that failed to adapt to streaming.

Meanwhile, money to help health systems adapt to climate change is scarce. Developing countries estimate they need around $3.3 billion a year for such adaptations, which the Lancet authors say is likely an underestimate. Only about a third of that was committed in 2024. Foreign aid reductions, led by the US and followed by Germany, which made the second-largest cut, are widening the gap.

"This report is a stark warning that climate change is a health emergency," said Helen Clark, former prime minister of New Zealand and chair of the Lancet Countdown's board. "What's missing is not evidence, but the political will to act on it."

World.title: Egypt orders closure of independent news site Mada Masr
World.content:
Editor-in-chief Lina Attalah was briefly detained and fined over licensing violations. Rights groups condemned the ruling as a major blow to press freedom in Egypt, where independent media face growing pressure.

An Egyptian court on Tuesday ordered the closure of independent news website Mada Masr after convicting its editor-in-chief, Lina Attalah, of operating without a license.

Attalah, one of Egypt's most prominent journalists, was detained for several hours following the verdict before being released after paying a fine.

The court imposed a fine of 3 million Egyptian pounds (around $53,400; €48,112), the maximum penalty for the offense. It also ordered the website to shut down and its equipment to be confiscated.

Mada Masr, founded in 2013, is one of Egypt's few remaining independent news outlets. It is known for investigating corruption, human rights violations and the military's powerful role in the country.

What happened during Lina Attalah's trial?

Attalah's lawyers said the court rejected their requests to review the case file and submit additional evidence during Tuesday's hearing in Cairo.

According to Hossam Bahgat, head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), who attended the hearing, the judge then appointed a new lawyer to represent Attalah despite objections from her eight-person defense team.

"In an even more shocking turn, the judge proceeded to dictate motions on behalf of this lawyer, who had not uttered a single word, and entered them into the official record," Bahgat told news agency AFP.

The judge announced the verdict amid protests from the defense before security officers detained Attalah.

She was released after Mada Masr paid the fine, her lawyer Hassan al-Azhari confirmed. The outlet plans to appeal the closure order.

During her release procedures, Attalah also learned that she had been sentenced in absentia in a separate case in 2024 to one year in prison and a fine of 20,000 Egyptian pounds.

That conviction concerned charges of spreading false news and operating an unlicensed website. Her lawyers have challenged the ruling, with a new hearing scheduled for November 11.

Why has Egypt targeted Mada Masr?

Mada Masr has faced years of legal battles with Egyptian authorities, who have blocked access to its website inside the country since 2017.

The outlet says it first applied for a license in 2018 but received no response. It only learned that its application had been rejected when prosecutors raised the issue during another case in 2022.

Mada Masr challenged that decision and says its latest application has been awaiting a response since 2023.

Six cases have been brought against the outlet and its journalists over the past six years, but Tuesday's trial was the first of its kind.

Egyptian authorities maintain that the country respects freedom of expression but insist that media organizations must comply with the law, protect national security and counter misinformation.

How have press freedom groups reacted?

The ruling drew widespread international condemnation.

A coalition of 119 rights organizations and media outlets, including Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), described the prosecution as an "unprecedented attack on press freedom."

"Today's decision represents a crushing blow to press freedom in Egypt and marks a dark day for independent journalism in the country," Amnesty International said.

Reporters Without Borders (RSF) called the ruling "outrageous" and "shameful."

"If Egypt can put in custody one of its most respected editors and shut down her newsroom, no independent journalist in the country is safe," said CPJ regional director Sara Qudah.

US Senator Chris Van Hollen also criticized the prosecution, describing the charges as baseless and saying that "journalism is not a crime."

What is the state of press freedom in Egypt?

The case comes amid a broader crackdown on independent journalism.

Six journalists from the fact-checking platform Matsadaash were arrested in September and subsequently charged with terrorism-related offenses.

Authorities accuse them of links to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood and spreading false information to undermine confidence in state institutions and encourage protests.

The journalists have reported being tortured following their arrests, according to EIPR. Egypt's Interior Ministry has denied the allegations.

On Tuesday, prosecutors extended their pretrial detention by another 15 days. Rights groups warn that such detention can continue for months or even years.

According to EIPR, Egypt currently holds 26 journalists in connection with their work.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

World.title: Flavio Bolsonaro flees Brazil for US amid investigation  — reports
World.content:
Flavio Bolsonaro is on the way to the US, according to reports citing people close to the senator. The US State Department said it will issue visas to the senator and his family.

Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has left the country for the United States after he was defeated in Sunday's presidential election, Folha de S.Paulo and Reuters reported, citing sources close to the senator.

The US State Department will issue visas to Flavio Bolsonaro and his family to allow them to enter the US, a senior State Department official told Reuters and other news agencies.

Leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who secured the runoff victory in elections , told supporters outside the presidential residence in Brasilia on Tuesday that Bolsonaro had left the country, but he didn't have information about Bolsonaro's exact whereabouts.

Brazil is "the second country" of the Bolsonaro family, Lula added.

"The first is licking American boots," the reelected president said. "Those who are not liable do not fear. A fellow that secretly leaves his country, that's because he is liable for something."

Bolsonaro wasn't allowed to leave Brazil

The Supreme Court had asked Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, to surrender his passports to stop him from leaving the country amid investigations into the senator.

It was reported that Bolsonaro had refused to comply with the order, although other reports contradicted this.

The AFP news agency cited a police official as saying that Bolsonaro's passports had been cancelled and there was no official record of him leaving the country.

Brazilian newspaper Folha de S.Paulo reported that Bolsonaro's plane was scheduled to land in either Miami or Dallas.

How did Bolsonaro exit Brazil?

Argentine news outlet Infobae reported earlier today that Bolsonaro had crossed into Argentina to board a plane to the US.

A spokesperson for Argentina's Ministry of Security denied the reports that the conservative Brazilian senator had entered the country.

Brazilian media reports earlier said that the federal police were still searching for him.

Bolsonaro leaves Brazil after losing presidential election: What to know

Bolsonaro lost Brazil's presidential election runoff on Sunday after an incredibly tight voting count through the evening until his challenger, Lula, surged ahead.

Bolsonaro had initially said he would seek to annul the election results, citing alleged irregularities. But Bolsonaro's Liberal Party on Tuesday acknowledged the results.

In a video on Instagram on Monday, Bolsonaro said he had been served with a Supreme Court order to hand over his passports so he couldn't leave the country.

He had said he was planning to hand over his passports, but reports on Tuesday said the deadline had passed leading to their cancellation.

What are the investigations against Flavio Bolsonaro about?

The senator has been accused of laundering money through a sports betting company, money that was deducted from government pensions to senior citizens.

A second investigation is looking into Bolsonaro's connections to a disgraced banker from whom he allegedly accepted millions of dollars to finance the biopic about his father, titled "Dark Horse."

Bolsonaro loses his immunity from prosecution once his Senate term comes to end in February 2027. He has denied wrongdoing in both cases.

Bolsonaro asked to surrender passports: What to know

Bolsonaro said that he had received the Supreme Court order outside the home where his father, Jair Bolsonaro, is under house arrest.

He said the order was issued by Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, the same judge who sentenced his father to prison.

He also pointed to comments made by his brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, who said on a podcast last week that his sibling should leave the country if he lost the election.

Eduardo, who lives in the US, was convicted in absentia in June of illegally lobbying the Trump administration. He was sentenced to four years in prison and a warrant was issued for his arrest.

Brazil's Lula celebrates election victory as Bolsonaro rejects results To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: EU proposes giving Frontex border agency new major powers
World.content:
The European Commission has unveiled a new plan to give Frontex more resources to ensure the return of irregular migrants, including by supporting non-EU countries. The move comes after the tragedy in Ceuta.

The European Commission on Tuesdayunveiled a new proposal to beef up the powers of the EU border agency in order to empower it to support the return of irregular migrants.

The proposed legislation gives the agency, called Frontex, more resources to act beyond EU territory.

The plan would give the agency the power to support non-EU countries to return migrants to their countries of origin.

The proposal comes as EU member states increasingly focus on returns, saying too many people who are asked to leave the bloc remain.

EU border agency to be beefed up after Ceuta humanitarian crisis of summer

The new role for Frontex comes after the humanitarian crisis in Ceuta this summer.

The tragedy in the Spanish exclave was seized upon by some EU member states as an example of where the EU could do more to block people from reaching the EU.

Italy, for example, placed some temporary border controls on travel from Spain.

Spain's prime minister at the time criticized several EU member states for their "selfish" response to the influx of migrants to Ceuta.

"Today we propose that Frontex becomes the central EU actor on returns," Magnus Brunner, commissioner for internal affairs ​and migration, told reporters.

"It will be able to act faster, with a quick reaction force that can ⁠deploy within ⁠24 hours and spot risks ⁠early, before an ​event becomes a crisis," Brunner added.

How the far right hardened Europe's migration stance To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Frontex to be given wide powers to support deportation of irregular migrants

The ability to deport migrants from non-EU countries means that Frontex could, for instance, deport a Bangladeshi national from Libya, where many migrants start the final leg of their journey into the bloc.

The plan envisages gradually expanding Frontex's standing corps to 30,000 officers by creating a new "European border and return reserve" of 17,000 officers within the next 15 years.

Those officers would remain at the disposal of member states and could be deployed when needed, the commission said in a statement.

The proposal would also create a new EU Return Coordination Center within Frontex and expand the agency's role across the entire deportation process.

It would also include a new online monitoring center to track border-related developments on social media and support action against content linked to border security risks.

Frontex reform criticized by rights groups

Frontex has been responsible for guarding the external borders of the EU as well as ensuring the rights of new arrivals.

It has been criticized for its lack of accountability in the past.

The planned reform shrinks the scope of the agency's internal rights watchdog, with complaints to be referred to national authorities.

"The Commission is pandering to populism and the far right on migration," said Tineke Strik, a Dutch MEP from the Greens/EFA group.

"We need a human rights-based approach to border management and Frontex plays a key role. But instead the Commission ​risks turning Frontex into a European version of ICE," she said.

Edited: Alex Berry

World.title: Mbappe apologizes as Chinese sponsors drop him and TV broadcasts are halted over Mao dictator remark
World.content:
French soccer star Kylian Mbappe has apologized after apparently referring to Mao Zedong as a dictator. Chinese sponsors have dropped him, while state television has suspended Spanish league broadcasts.

France striker Kylian Mbappe apologized after apparently referring to China's founding leader Mao Zedong as a dictator in a video that circulated online.

The controversy prompted three major Chinese companies to sever sponsorship ties with the Real Madrid forward, while Chinese state television suspended broadcasts of Spain's La Liga.

What did Mbappe say about Mao?

The controversy began when a video circulated showing Mbappe discussing his favorite internet meme featuring himself.

In the clip, apparently filmed ahead of an appearance on the French online talk show The Bridge, Mbappe referred to an image depicting his face superimposed on the body of "some guy ... I think he's a Chinese dictator."

The image appeared to depict Mao Zedong, who founded the People's Republic of China in 1949 and ruled until his death in 1976. Jokes about country's former leader and descriptions of him as a dictator remain taboo.

Mbappe has previously been depicted as authoritarian leaders in online memes mocking his perceived influence over teammates and suggestions that he has the power to influence club decisions.

Mbappe has been nicknamed "the dictator" in the European press.

How did Mbappe apologize?

"My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world," Mbappe said in a statement.

"I apologize to everyone my words have upset. This was absolutely not my intention. I have deep respect for the Chinese people and their history, and I am sincerely sorry."

Mao remains revered by many in China despite his policies causing tens of millions of deaths (FILE: October 1, 1949) Image: AP

Chinese sponsors cut ties with Mbappe

Chinese beverage company Dongpeng, dairy producer Mengniu and cheesemaker Milkground announced they were ending their partnerships with the French international.

In similarly worded statements, each said that they oppose "any words and actions that hurt national sentiment."

China Media Group, which oversees state broadcaster CCTV, also suspended broadcasts of La Liga matches and removed s featuring Mbappe.

La Liga apologized for the controversy, saying Mbappe's comments were made in a personal capacity and did not represent the Spanish league.

Chinese state broadcaster CCTV subsequently said it would consider Mbappe's apology but would also judge his future actions.

In response to a question about the controversy, China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun said that "words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with joint opposition from all sectors of Chinese society."

Why is Mao such a sensitive subject in China?

Mao remains a revered figure in China, where public criticism of the former Communist leader is politically sensitive.

His rule was also marked by disastrous political campaigns, including the Great Leap Forward, which contributed to a famine that killed tens of millions of people.

The ruling Communist Party acknowledges some of his mistakes but maintains that his achievements outweighed them, making criticism of his legacy politically sensitive.

Edited by: Alex Berry

World.title: Myanmar: Is the US undermining the EU's diplomatic blockade?
World.content:
With the US reopening talks with Myanmar's military-backed government, and several Southeast Asian countries restarting diplomatic contacts, the EU is facing uncomfortable questions about its own boycott of the junta.

The US government has begun a quiet reproachment with Myanmar's military-backed government, holding two rounds of talks since September with State Department representative Michael Vance. American diplomats reportedly meet Myanmar officials in Naypyitaw and then in Tokyo earlier this month.

Washington wants to tackle online scam centers, secure the release of imprisoned American businessman Adam Castillo, and potentially gain access to Myanmar's rare-earth resources. The market for the valuable minerals is currently controlled by the US rival China.

Meanwhile, Southeast Asian governments are also increasingly questioning their policy of isolating Myanmar's military leadership. Multiple countries have already renewed direct diplomatic contacts.

The EU, however, continues to reject the legitimacy of the military junta in the war-torn country. The European bloc has also remained unmoved by the 2025/2026 election, which ended with military chief Min Aung Hlaing becoming the president. The military retains control over the political system.

Human Rights Watch's Elaine Pearson on Myanmar election To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

EU's sanctions still in force

The EU responded to Myanmar's February 2021 military coup by suspending direct financial assistance to the government, imposing targeted sanctions and sharply reducing diplomatic engagement with the military authorities.

Despite the Western boycott, junta leader Min Aung Hlaing has made official trips to India, China and Russia [FILE: June 1, 2026] Image: Manish Swarup/AP Photo/picture alliance

Its sanctions currently cover 105 individuals and 22 entities connected to the military. In April, the EU extended these measures for another 12 months.

At the same time, Brussels is providing humanitarian assistance to displaced communities and Rohingya refugees and is supporting civil society organizations.

Thailand-Myanmar border clinic helps people fleeing war To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The EU also stopped short of withdrawing Myanmar's preferential trade access because of concerns about the consequences for workers, particularly the mostly young women employed in the country's garment industry. Last year, bilateral goods trade was worth about €4 billion ($4.46 billion), up from €3.4 billion in 2019.

Brussels supports ASEAN's peace deal

The civil war triggered by the 2021 coup has killed an estimated 100,000 people. Rebel groups still control or contest large swathes of Myanmar, and over 4 million people have been internally displaced, according to UN data.

The EU "continues to uphold its policy of non-recognition of the current military regime," in view of "the ongoing violence and the attack against its own population," an EU spokesman told DW.

At the same time, the bloc "is closely monitoring developments in the discussions and positions of the United States, Japan, ASEAN countries and other major actors with representatives of Myanmar's military regime."

"It also supports ASEAN efforts, in particular the Five-Point Consensus, which has yet to be fully implemented," the spokesperson added, referring to the peace deal proposed by the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in 2021.

Myanmar diplomats reach out to European partners

In the aftermath of the coup, ASEAN took the unprecedented decision to exclude Myanmar's military leaders from its highest-level meetings after the junta failed to implement the regional peace plan.

However, ASEAN's position is showing signs of change. Some member states, most notably Myanmar's neighbor Thailand, signal growing frustration with the lack of progress towards ending Myanmar's civil war.

New Thai labor scheme offers hope for Myanmar refugees To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Last week, Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow welcomed Washington's renewed engagement and suggested that ASEAN members would hold substantive discussions about Myanmar's future at their summit in Manila next month.

Myanmar's authorities are also seeking to break their diplomatic isolation. In September, Myanmar's leader Hlaing gave an interview to Time magazine, his first with a major Western publication since the coup, as part of an apparent effort to rebuild relations with Western governments.

On October 22, Burma Campaign UK, a London-based human rights organization, accused the British government of making a "significant shift in approach" after the British Foreign Office hosted Win Zeyar Tun, the charge d'affaires of Myanmar's military-controlled embassy in London, at an ASEAN diplomatic gathering days earlier.

According to an article published by Intelligence Online this month, the regime's charge d'affaires in Brussels, Khin Thidar Ay, has also sought contacts with European politicians, including Czech MEP Ondrej Dostal, a member of the European Parliament's delegation for Southeast Asia.

EU's isolation 'has achieved relatively little'

Kristina Kironska, of Palacky University Olomouc in the Czech Republic and an expert on the EU's policy on Myanmar, told DW that the EU has little reason to follow Washington's apparent shift towards engagement with the Myanmar junta.

The US strategy "appears to be pursuing specific interests" such as rare earth mining and cybercrime, she said.

Thailand: Rare earth mining pollutes rivers To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

However, the most important rare earth mining operations are no longer controlled by the military, but by rebels such as the Kachin Independence Organization in Kachin State. "It remains to be seen what the US can achieve through negotiations with the junta," she said.

The EU has long positioned itself as a defender of democracy and human rights in Myanmar, "so abandoning this now because the US is exploring a new, perhaps more transactional approach would undermine the EU's credibility," Kironska added.

"At the same time, isolation has achieved relatively little. The question is therefore not whether the EU should engage, but rather with whom and under what conditions."

Balancing act between Myanmar's rebels and junta

The EU is forced to consider risks to its own influence. If Washington, ASEAN governments and other regional powers increase their engagement with Myanmar's authorities, the EU risks becoming increasingly marginal in discussions about the country's political future.

Yet greater engagement with the military could undermine Brussels' relations with Myanmar's democratic opposition and ethnic resistance organizations, many of which control substantial territory.

"The key question for Brussels is whether it can remain a credible defender of democratic change while ensuring that it still has a meaningful voice in the negotiations that will determine Myanmar's future," Sabe Soe, director of the NGO Burma Centre Prague, told DW.

One possibility is for Brussels to maintain its sanctions against military leaders and their businesses while expanding diplomacy through ASEAN, the UN and other regional partners. The EU could also tie any easing of restrictions to humanitarian access, improvements in political freedoms and progress towards peace.

Soe also suggested that the EU could pursue economic engagement in areas administered by revolutionary and ethnic resistance forces, offering an alternative to engagement centered on the military authorities in Naypyidaw.

This approach would allow the EU to remain involved in Myanmar's future without necessarily recognizing its military-backed government, she said.

For now, Brussels seems to have little appetite for a fundamental policy rethink. But this could change as more governments reopen their doors to Myanmar's generals.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

World.title: Netanyahu gana las elecciones en Israel, pero su coalición no logra la mayoría
World.content:
El bloque favorable al primer ministro lograría 56 escaños sobre 120, y la oposición judía, 48, una vez contabilizados más del 66% de los votos. Los partidos árabes serán claves en las negociaciones

El partido de Benjamín Netanyahu ha ganado las elecciones legislativas celebradas el martes en Israel, pero el primer ministro no lograría, ni siquiera con los apoyos de sus aliados ultranacionalistas y religiosos, la mayoría de escaños del Parlamento necesaria para seguir gobernando.

A las 9.00 am del miércoles (08.00 en España) y una vez escrutado más del 66% de los votos, el partido del primer ministro, el Likud (derecha), aumentaba poco a poco su ventaja y habría obtenido 28 diputados sobre un total de 120. Yashar (centroderecha), de su adversario, Gadi Eisenkot, sumaría 21, menos de lo que vaticinaban las encuestas previas a estos comicios, que lo situaban como primera fuerza.

Netanyahu gana las legislativas, pero también pierde. Su formación es la más votada, pero no llega a los 32 escaños logrados hace cuatro años. Además, sus socios ultranacionalistas y religiosos tampoco han ampliado su base electoral. Esto hace imposible que el bloque llegue a 61 diputados, es decir, la mayoría suficiente para formar un Gobierno. El actual Ejecutivo de coalición sumaría unos 56 escaños, frente a los 63 que tiene hoy en el Parlamento. El bloque anti-Netanyahu, formado por Eisenkot y sus aliados (una mezcla heterogénea de partidos judíos, principalmente de centroderecha y derecha) se sitúa en 48, según estos resultados parciales. Las dos listas electorales árabes sumarían 16 escaños y serían indispensables para la formación de un futuro Gobierno y evitar así nuevas elecciones.

Estos comicios, los primeros desde el ataque de Hamás en Israel en 2023 y una sucesión de guerras en Oriente Próximo, registraron un 77% de participación, una cifra muy alta e inédita desde hace más de 25 años.

“Debemos formar un Gobierno nacional de derechas y fuerte”, ha celebrado Netanyahu durante la madrugada ante las decenas de seguidores que le aguardaban en Jerusalén. “Ha quedado claro algo incontestable: el Likud es la primera fuerza de Israel”, ha asegurado el primer ministro, que ha vuelto a demostrar que nunca hay que subestimarlo ya que es capaz de dar la vuelta a meses de encuestas desfavorables.

Pero parece claro que, tras 19 años en el poder en tres etapas distintas desde los años noventa del siglo pasado, Netanyahu comienza a pagar en las urnas la factura de una legislatura marcada por el radicalismo de sus socios en el Gobierno, el cruento ataque de Hamás y el incremento de los problemas domésticos, comenzando por el aumento del coste de la vida y la negativa a obligar a los ultraortodoxos a realizar el servicio militar obligatorio, en un momento en que faltan soldados y sobran terrenos de conflicto para Israel, como Gaza y Líbano.

También ha pesado en la decisión de los votantes israelíes la negativa del primer ministro a crear una comisión independiente de investigación sobre los graves fallos de seguridad que se cometieron el 7 de octubre de 2023. Además, los electores tampoco olvidan su claro interés en evadir la justicia, que quiere sentarlo en el banquillo por corrupción, es otro de los temas que más indigna a sus críticos.

No obstante, el mensaje que han enviado las urnas es que rechazan más a los socios de Netanyahu que al primer ministro. Por ejemplo, dentro de su coalición, el partido ultraortodoxo sefardí Shas pasa de 11 escaños a ocho. A esto se suma el aparente castigo a sus dos socios de extrema derecha religiosa. Poder Judío, liderado por el ministro de Seguridad Nacional, Itamar Ben Gvir, tiene pobres perspectivas, con siete diputados, pese a que en campaña, el líder ultra se jactaba de poder llegar a 15 escaños. Y Sionismo Religioso, del titular de Finanzas, Bezalel Smotrich, se conformaría con otros siete parlamentarios.

El líder opositor israelí Gadi Eisenkot, ondea una bandera israelí tras el cierre de los colegios electorales, el 27 de octubre. Shir Torem (REUTERS)

Un nuevo Gobierno sionista y estable

Eisenkot, que fue jefe del Estado Mayor con Netanyahu en el poder, entre 2015 y 2019, aseguró el martes de madrugada que dedicará “todas sus fuerzas” a construir un “Gobierno sionista, estable y bueno para todos los ciudadanos de Israel”. Además, ante las informaciones sobre un posible ataque a Irán durante las negociaciones para formar Gobierno, provocado por la coalición de Netanyahu, Eisenkot ha lanzado un mensaje al primer ministro: “No te atrevas a usar la seguridad de Israel para tu propio beneficio político”.

Seguidores de Benjamin Netanyahu celebraron los resultados electorales el martes en Jerusalén. David Goldman (AP Photo/David Goldman)

Dentro del bloque contra Netanyahu, Los Demócratas, una lista de izquierda que conjuga el laborismo histórico con el pacifista Meretz, logra siete escaños, según estos resultados parciales. “Se nos ha brindado una oportunidad histórica para formar un auténtico Gobierno de cambio en Israel, y no tenemos intención alguna de dejarla pasar”, ha celebrado Yair Golán, su líder. “El mandato que hemos recibido hoy de la ciudadanía es una orden operativa para reconstruir el país ante la que no cabe vacilación, luchas de egos, ni espacio para maniobras políticas”, ha agregado.

Además, en la coalición contra Netanyahu también está Israel Beitenu, la formación de derecha laica del exministro Avigdor Lieberman, que podría subir de seis a ocho, y la coalición de centroderecha Beyahad, que conseguiría 11 escaños, según los resultados parciales, y se convertiría en la tercera fuerza política en la Kneset. La encabezan Naftali Bennett y Yair Lapid que se alternaron en la jefatura de Gobierno en 2021-2022, la única legislatura sin Netanyahu desde 2009.

Los partidos árabes, imprescindibles

Si la tendencia de estos resultados parciales se confirma, Israel tiene por delante semanas de negociaciones políticas en las que los partidos árabes tendrán un papel fundamental. Una vez se contabilicen todos los votos, el presidente, Isaac Herzog, encargará a un diputado (normalmente el líder del partido más votado) que intente formar Gobierno. El aspirante tendrá 28 días para negociar y 14 de prórroga. Si logra la mayoría necesaria y presenta una propuesta que el Parlamento aprueba por mayoría simple, se constituye el Gobierno. Si fracasa, el presidente puede elegir a otro candidato y en última instancia, a un tercero. Si todos estos intentos quedan en nada, habrá nuevas elecciones.

Las dos listas árabes son las grandes triunfadores de los comicios. La Lista Conjunta, una coalición de tres partidos, habría obtenido 12 diputados, y la islamista moderada Ra’am, cuatro. Todo ello gracias a una movilización sin precedentes de sus votantes, que se sienten discriminados y tratados como ciudadanos de segunda categoría en Israel, sobre todo desde los ataques de Hamás de 2023.

Estas formaciones representan sobre todo a los palestinos con nacionalidad israelí, es decir, a un quinto de la población, pero también reciben votos de votantes judíos, que los consideran la verdadera oposición en este momento en Israel.

Está descartado que el bloque de Netanyahu pacte con los partidos árabes. El miércoles de madrugada, el primer ministro ha considerado una “vergüenza” que los partidos judíos de oposición sean capaces de “poner en peligro a Israel y establecer un gobierno que dependa de partidos árabes antisionistas” que llaman “criminales de guerra” a los soldados israelíes.

Si quiere el puesto de primer ministro, Eisenkot tendrá que aceptar un pacto con una de las listas árabes o tal vez con los dos, pese a que durante la campaña ha asegurado que no estaba dispuesto a negociar con ellos, salvo si aceptan a Israel como Estado judío y democrático y califican a Hamás de grupo terrorista. En una sociedad traumatizada por los ataques de Hamás del 7 de octubre del 2023, lo contrario le habría restado apoyos. Solo Los Demócratas se dijeron dispuestos a aceptar en un futuro Gobierno a Ra’am, formación liderada por Mansur Abbas.

Palestinos con nacionalidad israelí celebran los resultados del partido árabe Ra'am, en la localidad de Sakhnin, el martes por la noche. Mahmoud Illean (AP Photo/Mahmoud Illean)

Este líder ya tendió la mano el martes a la oposición a Netanyahu para construir una mayoría. “Espero que salgan las cuentas y podamos garantizar que haya 61 escaños en la Kneset”, ha dicho Abbas. Ra’am se convirtió en 2021 en el primer partido árabe en formar parte de un Gobierno israelí, en este caso presidido por Naftalí Bennett y Yair Lapid. El Ejecutivo solo se mantuvo algunos meses debido a las profundas diferencias ideológicas internas. La Lista Conjunta, liderada por Yousef Jabareen, siempre se ha mostrado más recelosa a apoyar un gobierno sionista, debido a sus políticas contra los palestinos.

Durante la jornada electoral, el primer ministro publicó varios mensajes en sus redes sociales sugiriendo que los partidos árabes estaban “robando las elecciones”, sin explicar en qué se basaba. El martes por la noche, uno de los ministros más ultra del Gobierno, Bezalel Smotrich, dijo que no iba a dejar que las formaciones árabes celebren su avance histórico en las urnas. “Creen que podrán dar marcha atrás a la revolución de los asentamientos en Judea y Samaria (nombre bíblico de Cisjordania), y yo les digo que no lo conseguirán”, ha zanjado.

World.title: Información genética para una medicación más segura y eficiente
World.content:
Con una simple muestra de saliva, la farmacogenética permite el análisis de decenas de genes y cientos de fármacos de uso habitual y revela por qué un simple analgésico quita el dolor a una persona y a otra le produce una reacción adversa

Según estima la Agencia Española de Medicamentos y Productos Sanitarios, entre el 3% y el 6,5% de la población tiene una variante genética que provoca que su hígado transforme la codeína (un compuesto presente en medicamentos o soluciones tan frecuentes como las pastillas para la tos) en morfina. Este proceso, que se produce a gran velocidad incluso si la dosis administrada es normal, puede desembocar en una sobredosis accidental, que en algunos casos termina en el fallecimiento del paciente.

El ejemplo lo pone Javier Suela, director técnico del laboratorio de genética de Sanitas (Madrid). Él mismo pertenece a este pequeño grupo poblacional de riesgo: “Hay mucha evidencia acumulada de la toxicidad de ciertos medicamentos en ciertos pacientes. Estas reacciones adversas van desde un brote cutáneo hasta la muerte en casos extremos, como este mismo de la codeína”, explica.

Suela trabaja para reducir esa peligrosidad al mínimo. En el laboratorio que dirige, desde el pasado mayo, se extrae el perfil genético de quien lo solicite para “determinar si tiene un componente genético, una proteína, que produce que determinados fármacos se procesen de una forma que no es habitual”, sintetiza.

El perfil genético, en tres pasos 1 Recepción de las muestras e identificación de cada paciente El paciente lleva una muestra genética (basta la saliva, por ejemplo) en un tubo. Este tubo va a una primera máquina que realiza una preanalítica y transforma las muestras en placas que identifican a cada persona: en la posición A1 está la muestra de un paciente concreto y en la B1, otro, y así sucesivamente. 2 Procesado del material genético El material genético de la placa, que contiene muestras de hasta 96 pacientes, se prepara y depura (se corta, se colorea...) en otra máquina para el análisis final. Lo que se obtiene, tras cuatro horas de refinado, es la placa definitiva (en la imagen) que se usará para extraer el perfil genético. 3 Obtención del perfil genético La placa, con el material genético ya refinado, se introduce en un escáner que analiza cada celda, que contiene más de un millón de variables (cada una asociada a un genotipo) que procesar. Cuando este escáner finaliza se obtiene el perfil genético del paciente, el resultado final del proceso.

Esta disciplina se conoce como farmacogenética y en Sanitas está disponible para todos sus asegurados bajo el nombre de Mi Farmagen. “Un ser humano puede metabolizar todos los fármacos, pero en función de ciertas variables genéticas los metaboliza a distintas velocidades; entonces el medicamento puede funcionar demasiado bien o demasiado mal. Esto es lo que da lugar a reacciones adversas o reacciones inexistentes, es decir, cuando el fármaco no funciona”, detalla.

29 genes y 125 fármacos analizados

Mi Farmagen analiza hasta 29 genes y más de 125 fármacos de uso habitual, y ofrece un informe con las reacciones a cada uno de estos medicamentos. Y siempre es útil, tanto si se obtiene antes o después de la prescripción, ya que “permite ajustar la medicación sin perder efectividad, pero evitando posibles efectos adversos y aumentando la seguridad”, incide Suela.

Hay casos en los que un cambio anticipado de medicación puede salvar la vida del paciente, pero también situaciones más cotidianas en las que esta información es de mucha utilidad. Así lo explica Andrea Azcárate, jefe de servicio de Endocrinología del hospital Sanitas de La Moraleja (Madrid): “Es el ejemplo de un paciente con colesterol alto al que le sienta mal un tipo de estatina, que es el tratamiento habitual para esta patología. Para corroborarlo, se le hace la prueba farmacogenética. A partir de ahí, probablemente escojamos otro tipo de estatina que vaya a tolerar mejor”. Sin embargo, cada caso, en opinión de Azcárate, no es blanco o negro: “Lo que el análisis nos da es una predisposición de respuesta, una información probabilística que nos permite individualizar el tratamiento”, puntualiza.

0:00 ANDREA AZCÁRATE, jefe de servicio de Endocrinología del hospital Sanitas de La Moraleja (Madrid)

Azcárate y Suela inciden, precisamente, en la importancia de la interpretación facultativa de esta información, que por sí sola vale poco. “Es fundamental la interpretación y el ajuste, algo que siempre se ha hecho: la medicación, en función de las características clínicas del paciente, las casuísticas y las edades, se individualiza”. Y eso mismo se hará a partir de ahora, subraya: “Ajustaremos caso a caso, pero con más información. Es una herramienta más, muy buena y útil, pero hay que tener prudencia a la hora de incorporarla”.

En esa misma línea se expresa Suela: “El informe son páginas de metabolización, nada más. No vale de nada sin facultativo detrás que las interprete. Y, sobre todo, hay que combinar toda la información: igual tienes un paciente del que el análisis dice que el fármaco le va a sentar muy bien, pero esa misma persona tiene unas condiciones físicas complicadas o es un paciente polimedicado, en el que es fundamental medir las interacciones entre fármacos”. Es una cuestión de personalización, como dicta la tendencia actual en la medicina, pero con un conocimiento más preciso.

Así funciona Mi Farmagen Mi Farmagen analiza cómo las variantes genéticas influyen en la respuesta a determinados medicamentos.

influyen en la respuesta a determinados medicamentos. Permite conocer cómo metabolizamos determinados fármacos para aumentar su eficacia y reducir posibles efectos adversos.

para aumentar su eficacia y reducir posibles efectos adversos. Analiza hasta 29 genes y más de 125 fármacos de uso habitual, y ofrece un informe con las reacciones a cada uno de estos medicamentos.

y más de de uso habitual, y ofrece un informe con las a cada uno de estos medicamentos. En Europa ya se han hecho más de 1.000 perfiles farmacogenéticos con este sistema.

Hacia un pasaporte genético

En el futuro, coinciden los especialistas, se abre paso la idea de que todo ciudadano cuente con un carnet genético. Esta posibilidad existe gracias a la tecnología, explica Suela, que ha multiplicado el poder de las técnicas de genotipado: “Antes hacíamos un solo caso, un solo paciente, con cientos de marcadores. Ahora procesamos hasta 96 casos y en cada uno analizamos millones de marcadores. El salto es impresionante”.

0:00 JAVIER SUELA, director técnico del laboratorio de genética de Sanitas (Madrid)

El objetivo es que la farmacogenética sea útil, no un mero postulado teórico. Y ya lo es, pero todavía a pequeña escala. Mi Farmagen acumula ya mil análisis farmacogenéticos a pacientes con aplicación real. “Necesitamos que poco a poco todos tengamos un carnet farmacogenómico. En la actualidad esa información que tenemos ya nos salta a la historia clínica de forma automática como alerta a la hora de prescribir medicamentos con un programa propio, Farmacheck, y esta información también está a disposición del paciente en su app para poder ajustar e individualizar el tratamiento. En pocos años será un estándar”, señala Azcárate. Suela añade: “Nuestro sueño sería que en más del 90% de las prescripciones se tuviese en cuenta esa información genética de manera previa”.

Todo con un fin: obtener la mayor seguridad para el paciente, ya que, hasta hoy, “a la hora de prescribir algunos fármacos, operábamos con un método prueba-error: si no funcionaba uno, o si funcionaba mal, se probaba otro. Pero con la farmacogenética se abre otro camino, de máxima seguridad, basado en evidencias clínicas rigurosas”, afirma Suela.

World.title: La inmobiliaria me mintió sobre las humedades del piso antes de comprarlo. ¿Puedo actuar contra ella y la comunidad?
World.content:
Pregunta. Cuando compré el piso se veía una humedad en el techo de una habitación. La agente de la inmobiliaria me dijo que era de la fachada y que ya estaban esperando a los técnicos para arreglarla. Era mentira, la comunidad no sabía nada. Ahora, el perito ha dicho que efectivamente es de la fachada y que hay que arreglarla. La comunidad está poniendo problemas porque solo me afecta a mí y el coste es alto. ¿Puedo hacer algo contra la inmobiliaria?, ¿puedo obligar a la comunidad a que asuma una derrama? D. Queiro

Respuesta. Un defecto oculto es un problema relevante que no era visible en el momento de la compraventa, que ya existía con anterioridad a la transmisión y que afecta al uso normal, la habitabilidad o el valor del inmueble. No basta con que el comprador descubra una circunstancia que no le satisfaga; el defecto debe tener la suficiente entidad y, además, no haber podido detectarse mediante una revisión ordinaria.

Los vicios ocultos se regulan en los artículos 1484 a 1490 del Código Civil y resultan de aplicación en compraventas entre particulares o de viviendas de segunda mano. El plazo para reclamar es de seis meses desde la entrega del inmueble y la reclamación debe dirigirse contra el vendedor. Se trata de un plazo de caducidad, por lo que una reclamación extrajudicial, como el envío de un burofax, no interrumpe ni suspende dicho plazo.

Las manchas que aparecen tras las primeras lluvias, las filtraciones en terrazas, cubiertas o patios, o las humedades ocultas tras muebles, pintura o revestimientos pueden tener la consideración de vicios ocultos y, por tanto, ser reclamables al vendedor dentro del plazo indicado. Para ello, resulta aconsejable contar con un informe pericial elaborado por un arquitecto o ingeniero especializado que determine el origen, la antigüedad y el alcance del defecto, así como una valoración económica que permita cuantificar los daños reclamados.

También podría plantearse una reclamación frente a la inmobiliaria por una eventual mala praxis, siempre que sea posible acreditar que facilitó información o publicidad engañosa. Sin embargo, esta vía no suele ser la más habitual debido a las dificultades probatorias que normalmente presenta, especialmente cuando la información se proporcionó de forma verbal. En estos casos, suele resultar más adecuado dirigir la reclamación por vicios ocultos contra el anterior propietario o vendedor.

Por otro lado, la comunidad de propietarios está obligada a realizar las obras necesarias conforme a lo dispuesto en la Ley de Propiedad Horizontal.

El artículo 10.1.a) establece que tendrán carácter obligatorio y no requerirán de acuerdo previo de la junta de propietarios, impliquen o no modificación del título constitutivo o de los estatutos, y vengan impuestas por las Administraciones Públicas o solicitadas a instancia de los propietarios, las siguientes actuaciones: los trabajos y las obras que resulten necesarias para el adecuado mantenimiento y cumplimiento del deber de conservación del inmueble y de sus servicios e instalaciones comunes, incluyendo, en todo caso, las necesarias para satisfacer los requisitos básicos de seguridad, habitabilidad y accesibilidad universal, así como las condiciones de ornato y cualesquiera otras derivadas de la imposición, por parte de la Administración, del deber legal de conservación.

Por lo tanto, la comunidad estaría obligada a reparar el elemento común (la fachada) que origina las filtraciones en la vivienda, en cumplimiento de su deber de conservación y para garantizar las adecuadas condiciones de habitabilidad del inmueble. Al tratarse de obras necesarias, su coste deberá ser asumido por los propietarios integrantes de la comunidad o agrupación de comunidades. La junta únicamente deberá pronunciarse sobre la distribución de la derrama correspondiente y sobre las condiciones de su abono, de conformidad con lo previsto en el artículo 10.2 de la Ley de Propiedad Horizontal.

Si tiene dudas, sugerencias o simplemente quiere contarnos su caso, puede enviarnos un email a vivienda@elpais.es .

World.title: Sports club members becoming less tolerant of homosexuality
World.content:
Acceptance of homosexuality in Dutch sports clubs has declined significantly in the last generation, according to a survey of attitudes by the Mulier Institute.

The organisation found that 66% of people had no objection to a fellow member of a sports club being gay, while in 2008 the figure was 85%.

Just over half (55%) of respondents said they had no problem sharing a shower with a gay team-mate of the same sex, which also represented a drop from 73% in 2008.

The Mulier Institute said the findings reflected a social trend that has also been seen in schools, where the proportion of boys aged between 12 and 16 with a positive view of homosexuality has dropped from 40% to 22% since 2021.

The Dutch Olympic Committee NOC*NSF said the findings were “highly regrettable” and pledged to step up its efforts to make sport more inclusive.

But the John Blankenstein Foundation, which campaigns for LGBT emancipation in sport, said it had noticed declining enthusiasm for its workshops and growing numbers of parents who voiced objections.

Karin Blankenstein, who set up the organisation in 2008, told NOS: “I get the sensitivity around transgender people in sport at the top level, but this is about amateur sport.”

World.title: Beekse Bergen zookeeper dies after leopard attack
World.content:
A zookeeper at Beekse Bergen safari park has succumbed to her injuries after being attacked by a leopard in one of the park’s enclosures on Saturday.

The woman, who had spent nearly 40 years working with the animals, was said to be a highly committed and experienced member of the park.

Two male Persian panthers, a type of leopard, had taken shelter in an enclosure in the park amid stormy weather over the weekend. It is unclear how or why they attacked the keeper as there is no CCTV footage and entering an indoor enclosure with the animals is highly unusual.

She managed to call for help via a walkie-talkie during the attack but was mauled badly on her head and neck.

Emergency workers, including an air ambulance, rushed to the scene. Her injuries were so serious that officials at the park said it was unlikely she would survive.

An investigation into the accident has been launched by the labour inspectorate.

World.title: Rare “angel of death” mushroom found growing in Soest
World.content:
An extremely rare poisonous mushroom known as the “angel of death”, or formally Amanita virosa, has been discovered growing in Soest, a town in the Utrecht countryside.

It is considered a “notorious” species of fungus among mycologists, according to RTV Utrecht, for its toxicity and rarity. It was presumed extinct in the region and is designated as endangered.

Mycologist Rob Chrispijn told RTV he “jumped for joy” when he found one growing while leading a tour of the De Paltz estate in Soest. The species’ decline has come amid increased acidity in the soil, something related to the nitrogen crisis.

The fungus can be easily mistaken for an edible button mushroom, but failing to distinguish it before picking and eating could be life-threatening.

Chrispijn said that symptoms wouldn’t be immediate, but later you could suffer severe gastrointestinal problems and nausea after digesting, and “after two days, the liver and kidneys are affected, and the consequences can be permanent.”

Only two of the mushrooms were found on the estate, one of which is being examined for research. The other is remaining in the ground where it was, but Chrispijn said he isn’t worried anyone will be careless enough to eat it.

World.title: Education minister threatens to pull funding from Islamic school
World.content:

Junior education minister Judith Tielen has threatened to withdraw funding from an Islamic secondary school in Amsterdam unless it drastically improves exam performance.

The Cornelius Haga Lyceum has been told to appoint two extra board members, draw up a plan for improvements and send a progress report to the ministry every four weeks.

Tielen said it was “unacceptable that these pupils receive a substandard education every day” after inspectors found that their results were lagging behind children in other schools.

“School should be a place where children can develop and make progress,” Tielen said. “School administrators have a responsibility to make sure of that.”

Inspectors concluded in July that the Islamic Education Foundation (SIO), which runs the school, was guilty of mismanagement and the quality of education on offer was below acceptable standards.

In the last three years only 35% of students at the mavo level, a vocational stream, passed their exams, against a national average of 91%.

Wouter Pors, the lawyer for the school, told NOS that the board accepted the need for improvements, but the government was partly responsible for the problems.

“It is difficult for all schools to find qualified teachers, but for the Haga Lyceum it is even harder in practice. Applicants for secondary roles regularly withdraw, which leads to high numbers of lessons being cancelled.”

World.title: Fatal Rotterdam explosion suspect acquitted for lack of evidence
World.content:
A man suspected of causing an explosion in Rotterdam two years ago, in which three people died, has been acquitted.

Jalal O., a 37-year-old man who rented a garage in the Schammenkamp area of the city, was accused of using the premises as a drugs lab for processing cocaine.

In the aftermath of the explosion he climbed through the rubble looking for victims, and was initially perceived by local residents as a “hero”, according to media reports.

The explosion tore through the apartment complex above it, spreading a fire and partially collapsing the building. Besides the three who died, several were seriously injured and some lost their homes permanently.

After investigators analysed the scene, they found evidence including more than 40 acetone containers, traces of cocaine and procaine, and other paraphernalia. Prosecutors also found app messages between O. and his nephew they said were related to drug dealing.

In a procedural hearing after O.’s arrest in 2024, it was also disclosed that he had a previous conviction for drugs offences in Spain. He has always maintained his innocence and said at the time he had never been involved in the drug trade.

Prosecutors sought a seven-year sentence. If he had been convicted, the surviving victims would also have been eligible for compensation. They could instead take out a civil case against O. now that he has been acquitted.

The court found there was not enough evidence to convict him, and found no proof that the premises had been used as a drugs lab. It noted that the exact reason for the explosion remains unknown.

O. was a tenant of the garage but had sublet the space, and the court said the prosecution could not prove beyond a reasonable doubt that he was responsible.

World.title: How to balance a career and a master’s in the Netherlands
World.content:
Working full time while studying for a master’s can be a tough balancing act. Melina Gkiolma, a sustainability consultant and currently a student on the Online Master Sustainability Management at Rotterdam School of Management, Erasmus University (RSM) in Amsterdam, talks about how she handles the burden.

For many internationals in the Netherlands, going back to university means fitting lectures and assignments around a full-time job, family commitments and trips back home. Finding the time and the energy is often the biggest hurdle.

Melina, who is originally from Athens, has worked in the sustainability sector for five years, having spent the past 2.5 years as a sustainability consultant at Kōan, a boutique consultancy in Amsterdam. She started her career at Deloitte Luxembourg. She helps organisations deal with sustainability reporting requirements and changing regulations across Europe and beyond.

She wanted a part-time course she could follow online, so she could keep working while building her academic background in a field where she sees her long-term career. “This programme seemed like the perfect fit because it met all the criteria I was looking for,” she said.

Finding a routine

Returning to study took some adjustment. “I admit that returning to academic study after several years in the workplace was a little challenging at first,” she said, “but I’ve found a balance that works for me.”

She tries to join the live class every week and usually studies in the evening after work, when she is “already in a productive mindset”. She also puts in some time at weekends, but makes a point of keeping time free to relax.

Weekly updates from the programme managers on upcoming activities and assignment deadlines help her stay on top of the workload, she said.

Studying on the move

Because the course is entirely online, Melina can keep studying wherever she is – at home, on work trips or visiting her family in Greece.

She also found it more sociable than she expected. “People often assume online learning can feel impersonal, but my experience has been the opposite,” she said. Live classes, discussion forums and informal virtual coffee chats have helped her build strong ties with classmates around the world.

The international mix is one of her favourite parts of the course, with students from almost every continent. “It’s eye-opening to hear about people’s different experiences depending on where they live and their different professional backgrounds,” she said.

Theory into practice

Melina has been able to use what she learns at work straight away. Earlier in the programme, students were asked to develop key performance indicators (KPIs) for a logistics company. When a new client later asked her for help setting KPIs for its carbon emissions, she drew on the research she had done for that assignment.

“The master’s has also helped me broaden my horizons in sustainability. Because I work in sustainability reporting, there are many topics I hadn’t explored in depth before. One module I found particularly interesting focused on ethics and leadership. It made me reflect on what I want to stand for in my work, my moral compass, and the purpose behind the things I do. It really got me thinking.”

“Be kind to yourself”

Her advice to anyone thinking of combining a job with a part-time master’s is to go easy on themselves. “Working full time while studying for a part-time master is a significant challenge, but you can find the balance that works for you,” she said.

“And remember, pursuing further education while advancing your career is a major achievement in itself.”
