World.title: Putin warns of ‘serious consequences’ if Russia is excluded from global gas markets
World.content:
Any attempt to exclude Russia from the global gas market will have serious consequences, Vladimir Putin said at Tuesday’s summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) in Moscow.

Putin recalled the proverb that whoever digs a pit for someone else may fall into it themselves. “In my view, this is precisely what is happening to the countries of the European Union today,” he said.

He also described the explosions that damaged the Nord Stream gas pipelines as an act of terrorism.

Russia seeks to strengthen its position in the gas market

Putin pointed out that Russia ranks first in the world in terms of natural gas reserves and second in production. He described his country as a responsible exporter and a reliable partner.

He identified supply disruptions and the disappearance of large volumes of gas from the market as the main challenges facing the sector. With demand increasing, he argued that gas transport routes around the world needed to be optimised and supply expanded.

The Russian president called on gas-exporting countries to establish closer technological partnerships based on their own technical expertise. He also announced that Russia was considering the possibility of co-operation with the United States on natural gas extraction in the Arctic.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Putin calls for a non-political approach to energy

Putin acknowledged that every country decides for itself which forms of energy production it wishes to develop. However, he stressed that natural gas accounts for around a quarter of the world’s energy balance.

He also noted that liquefied natural gas (LNG) shipments now account for almost half of global gas trade.

According to Putin, gas-producing countries support the development of green energy, but he emphasised that environmental issues should not be used for political purposes.

The Gas Exporting Countries Forum includes Algeria, Bolivia, Equatorial Guinea, the United Arab Emirates, Egypt, Iran, Qatar, Libya, Nigeria, Russia, Trinidad and Tobago, and Venezuela. Together, these countries hold approximately 70% of the world’s natural gas reserves.

If you missed it: Russia says Viktor Orbán remains eligible for UN top job but rules out nominating him

Fourth Russian diesel tanker set to sail for the US

Meanwhile, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Aleksandr Novak announced at the same event that a fourth tanker carrying Russian diesel was due to depart for the United States on Wednesday. Novak announced the departure of the first three tankers on Friday.

World.title: Rosatom presses ahead with Paks II despite delays as Hungary reviews nuclear project
World.content:
Russia’s state-owned nuclear energy giant Rosatom says it will continue working on Hungary’s Paks II nuclear power plant project, despite significant delays and uncertainty over the Hungarian government’s position on the investment.

Rosatom expects next handover in November

Rosatom chief executive Alexey Likhachev said on Tuesday that the company was continuing its work on Paks II in line with its annual production plan, even though it did not yet fully understand the Hungarian government’s position on the project, Portfolio reported.

“We continue to work actively and are proceeding according to the annual production plan. The next stage of handing over the work to the Hungarian customer is expected in November,” Likhachev said in response to a question from Russian state news agency TASS.

“We are proceeding according to plan. We do not yet know exactly what the Hungarian government’s position is, but we are working, working,” he added.

The comments suggest that Rosatom intends to maintain its activities on the project while Budapest reassesses the future of the long-delayed investment.

If you missed it: Reuters: Hungary could drop Russia’s Rosatom from Paks nuclear project

Hungary’s review could conclude in early 2027

No final government decision has yet been made on the future of Paks II. In an October interview with Hungarian business outlet Portfolio, Economy and Energy Minister István Kapitány said the review of the project was expected to be completed either by the end of 2026 or in early 2027.

The minister also highlighted the scale of the delays. According to his assessment, the two planned new reactor units could be completed no earlier than around 2034–2035.

The timeline represents a substantial setback for a project that is intended to expand Hungary’s nuclear power generation capacity. The investment has faced years of delays, leaving its eventual completion date uncertain.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Paks II assessed alongside Hungary’s wider energy strategy

The government is examining Paks II as part of a broader review of Hungary’s future energy mix.

The assessment also includes the possible extension of the operating lifetimes of the existing Paks nuclear power plant units, as well as other options for securing the country’s energy supply.

This means that the final decision on Paks II will be considered alongside alternatives for maintaining Hungary’s electricity generation capacity in the coming years.

World.title: Budapest traffic restrictions announced for All Saints’ Day weekend – What drivers need to know
World.content:
Temporary traffic restrictions will be in place around Budapest’s cemeteries from Friday until Sunday evening ahead of All Saints’ Day and All Souls’ Day, the Budapest Police Headquarters (BRFK) has announced on its official website.

The measures will include road closures, one-way traffic systems, parking bans and restrictions on turning, so motorists should plan their journeys carefully over the weekend.

Road closures around Budapest cemeteries

From Saturday morning until Sunday evening, the following roads will be closed:

Tátraszirt sor, between Lóca utca and the cemetery. District XVIII: Reményik Sándor utca.

Temető köz. District X: Újhegyi út, between Maglódi út and the roundabout in front of the New Public Cemetery (Új Köztemető).

In District XVI, access to the section of Simongát utca in front of the cemetery will also be prohibited, except for vehicles used by people with reduced mobility.

Several streets will become one-way

Temporary one-way traffic systems will be introduced on the following roads:

Sírkert út and Kozma utca. District XXII: Debrő utca and Víg utca.

Debrő utca and Víg utca. District XII: Bürök utca.

Parking bans and turning restrictions

From Friday, parking will be prohibited on designated sections of roads leading to several cemeteries.

At the New Public Cemetery in Rákoskeresztúr, the restrictions will affect Sírkert út and Kozma utca. Other affected locations include Zala György utca in Rákospalota, Nefelejcs utca in Pestszentlőrinc, and sections of Darányi Ignác utca, Kassa utca, Kolozsvár utca and Temető köz in Kispest.

Around the Pesterzsébet Cemetery, parking will be prohibited on designated sections of Tartsay utca, Külső Vörösmarty utca, Vasfű utca and Temetősor.

Restrictions will also apply near Farkasréti Cemetery, affecting sections of Hegyalja út, Németvölgyi út and Érdi út, as well as Márton Áron tér.

Police urge motorists to take extra care

All Saints’ Day falls on 1 November, while All Souls’ Day is observed on 2 November in the Christian tradition. Both occasions traditionally bring increased visitor numbers to cemeteries as people pay their respects to deceased relatives and friends.

World.title: BREAKING: Hungarian authorities ambush criminal network behind overpriced Covid ventilator deals linked to former government – Video
World.content:
Hungary’s National Tax and Customs Administration (NAV) has launched a major operation against an alleged criminal network involved in supplying ventilators and medical masks to the state during the Covid-19 pandemic.

Arrests and assets seized across two countries

The investigation concerns companies that sold medical equipment to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade, then led by Péter Szijjártó, and other state bodies in deals worth HUF 15.6 billion (EUR 40 million at the time).

According to NAV, the suspects allegedly generated more than HUF 3 billion in profits from the transactions, then used a network of companies and fictitious invoices to evade over HUF 660 million in tax. The operation took place in several locations across Hungary and, with international assistance, in Austria in the early hours of 27 October.

Overpriced contracts and shady companies

The contracts, signed in 2020, resulted in the delivery of 800 ventilators and three million medical masks from China. Investigators allege that the network created a structure of companies with no genuine business activity to conceal profits and reduce the VAT payable on the equipment sales.

According to the tax authority, companies within the network issued false invoices for purported IT services, allowing the businesses involved to claim unjustified reductions in their tax liabilities. Some of the profits were allegedly transferred to a company registered in the United Arab Emirates, while the remainder was withdrawn in cash in Hungary.

NAV shared the video of the operation

During the operation, authorities seized or froze assets worth HUF 1.5 billion. One man was arrested in Austria under a European Arrest Warrant and taken into custody. Eleven other people were questioned as suspects in Hungary, two of whom were also detained.

An international arrest warrant has been issued for another alleged leader of the network, who investigators believe may currently be in Indonesia. NAV is investigating suspected large-scale budgetary fraud committed as part of a criminal organisation, money laundering and other offences. The allegations have not been established by a court.

Stay up-to-date: Hungary issues international arrest warrant for former central bank governor’s son

Separate investigation into overpriced ventilators

The case also raises questions about the controversial procurement of medical equipment during the pandemic, when Hungary spent heavily to secure supplies amid global shortages. The National Bureau of Investigation is conducting a separate criminal investigation into the procurement itself, examining suspected breach of trust, possible overpricing and whether the equipment was suitable for its intended purpose.

The distinction is significant: the tax investigation focuses on the alleged concealment of profits and evasion of tax by companies involved in the transactions, while the separate inquiry examines potential wrongdoing connected with the purchase of the equipment.

The latest operation marks a significant development in scrutiny of the pandemic-era deals. However, the authorities have not announced that Péter Szijjártó or the ministry’s officials are suspects in the tax case, and the available statement does not establish that the minister personally directed or knew about the alleged tax scheme.

The investigations are continuing, with the authorities seeking to trace the money and establish the responsibilities of those involved.

World.title: Hungary’s new expressway opens – Drivers can use it for free for now!
World.content:
The first 28-kilometre section of Hungary’s M49 expressway, connecting the M3 motorway with Ököritófülpös, has been completed and opened to traffic. The four-lane road became available to motorists at 2 PM on Tuesday, the Minister for Transport and Investment announced at a press conference at the site.

Dávid Vitézy said the HUF 138 billion (EUR 376 million) project, financed from the Hungarian state budget, would take traffic away from Main Road 49, which leads towards the Hungarian-Romanian border. The new expressway is expected to reduce through traffic in Mátészalka and surrounding settlements by 70%.

Photo: MTI

When will the M49 become a toll road?

Construction is already under way on the next section of the M49, which will extend to Csenger, near the Hungarian-Romanian border. Under the contract, the HUF 141 billion project is scheduled for completion in 2029. It is then expected to connect with the Romanian expressway section running from the border to Satu Mare, which is also due to be completed that year.

Motorists can use the newly opened Hungarian section of the M49 free of charge for the rest of 2026. The road will be added to the country’s toll road network in 2027, Vitézy announced in a Facebook video.

Photo: MTI

A long-awaited transport project

The minister recalled that the development had been planned for many years. The first plans for the road connection appeared in 2007, while the former National Infrastructure Development Company (NIF) commissioned route assessments and environmental impact studies in 2010.

Detailed planning for the construction permit and the selection of the final route took place in 2018 and 2019. NIF signed the construction contract with Duna Aszfalt in 2022.

The completed section features 22 new structures, including bridges. Four junctions have been built, including the connection to the M3 motorway, alongside new roundabouts and connecting roads. A separate 3.3-kilometre bypass has also been constructed near Győrtelek, Vitézy said.

Photo: MTI

If you missed it: New motorway connecting Hungary to southern neighbour is only one approval away

Next section faces funding changes

Vitézy noted that the previous government had redirected funding allocated to the continuation of the M49 to other projects before the election. Although the construction contract remains valid and work is continuing, the necessary funding had not been secured in the central budget.

In recent weeks, the ministry reviewed the project and revised its funding plans. Under the new financing arrangements, implementation will be rescheduled through to 2029, the minister explained.

The ministry has also asked the contractor to cut costs. As a result, a planned ten-lane border crossing facility on the Hungarian-Romanian border will not be built. Vitézy said the aim was to reduce the construction contract’s value by at least HUF 3 billion, a proposal already put to Duna Aszfalt.

On the Romanian side, the construction contract for the expressway was signed in October 2025. Work on the section connecting Satu Mare with the Hungarian border could begin in spring 2027, with the Romanian continuation of the M49 expected to be completed in the second quarter of 2029.

Photo: MTI

More funding for road maintenance and railways

The minister also outlined wider transport plans. The government intends to increase funding for the maintenance of the national road network fivefold and strengthen the capabilities of state-owned road operator Magyar Közút by increasing its budget.

The government is also working to end motorway concession arrangements. From 1 April 2027, Magyar Közút is scheduled to take over the operation of Hungary’s motorway network.

Turning to regional public transport, Vitézy said a detailed feasibility study was being prepared for a comprehensive reconstruction of the Debrecen–Mátészalka railway line. Meanwhile, the construction tender for the modernisation of the Debrecen–Nyíregyháza railway line is expected to be published at the end of this year or early next year.

World.title: Hungary’s energy giant MOL emerges as leading contender for one of Saudi Aramco’s European assets
World.content:
Hungarian energy group MOL could be the leading candidate to acquire some of Saudi oil giant Saudi Aramco’s assets in Poland, including its 30 per cent stake in the Gdańsk oil refinery, according to Polish media reports. A deal would strengthen MOL’s position in one of Central Europe’s key fuel markets, although no sale has been confirmed.

MOL could link Polish retail and refining operations

Polish newspaper Rzeczpospolita reports that Saudi Aramco has appointed investment bank JPMorgan Chase to assess potential options for its Polish interests. Three prospective buyers have reportedly been identified, with MOL considered a strong contender alongside international energy companies BP and Shell.

A potential acquisition would build on MOL’s existing presence in Poland. In 2022, the Hungarian company bought 417 filling stations in the country for more than USD 600 million (approximately EUR 538.4 million) as part of the asset disposals associated with the merger of Polish energy groups Orlen and Lotos.

Buying a stake in the Gdańsk refinery could allow MOL to source fuel more directly for its Polish service stations, potentially strengthening its supply chain and expanding its role beyond retail distribution into refining.

Analysts cited by Rzeczpospolita see the refinery interest as commercially attractive, although fluctuating refining margins could make its value difficult to assess. The newspaper reports that a complete Saudi Aramco withdrawal from Poland is considered less likely than a sale of selected assets, which could include the fuel wholesaler Aramco Fuels Poland and the refinery stake.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Orlen faces restrictions on buying back its stake

Poland’s state-controlled Orlen owns the remaining 70 per cent of the Gdańsk refinery. However, it may not be able simply to buy back the Saudi stake.

The European Commission required the disposal of certain Lotos assets as a condition of approving the Orlen-Lotos merger, with the aim of preserving competition and preventing excessive market concentration. That history complicates the ownership question, although Polish authorities could have a significant say in assessing a potential new investor, given the refinery’s importance to national energy security.

Any transaction would therefore involve more than a straightforward commercial decision, with competition rules and the interests of the Polish state likely to be important considerations.

If you have missed it: MOL signs deal to buy Russian stake in Serbia’s NIS oil company – UPDATE: MOL reaction

Regional expansion brings opportunities and risks

The reported sale discussions come as MOL is also pursuing a possible acquisition of the Russian-owned stake in Serbia’s NIS oil company. If both transactions were completed, they could significantly strengthen the Hungarian group’s refining and fuel-market position across Central Europe.

However, expanding on two fronts would also bring substantial financing requirements and potential regulatory hurdles. Competition authorities would need to assess the implications of any deal, while the commercial case would depend on the price of the assets and future refining profitability.

For now, Saudi Aramco is reportedly examining its options rather than committing to a sale. MOL’s status as a potential frontrunner remains based on Polish media reporting and analyst assessments, and the eventual buyer, scope and timing of any transaction are still uncertain.

World.title: Breaking: Hungary issues international arrest warrant for former central bank governor’s son
World.content:
Hungarian authorities have issued European and international arrest warrants for Ádám Matolcsy, the son of former National Bank of Hungary governor György Matolcsy, and businessman György Stofa in connection with an investigation into suspected economic fraud and other alleged offences.

Suspects believed to have left Hungary

The Budapest-Capital Regional Court confirmed on Tuesday that the warrants had been issued by the Buda Central District Court. The proceedings concern suspected fraud causing particularly substantial financial damage and the alleged use of forged private documents. According to the court, investigators considered it necessary to question both men as suspects.

However, authorities have been unable to establish their whereabouts or carry out the interviews, and measures to locate them have so far proved unsuccessful. Neither man is at his registered address in Hungary. Investigators have received information suggesting that both may have left the country and could be outside Europe. Nevertheless, the court considered it justified to seek them within the European Union as well as internationally.

The warrants will become visible in the relevant databases once the necessary administrative procedures have been completed. Hungarian authorities are seeking the men’s extradition or surrender so that criminal proceedings can be conducted. The court said it had considered whether issuing the warrants was proportionate, concluding that the nature of the alleged offences and the potential penalties justified the measure.

Screenshot from police.hu

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Alleged roles in suspected financial fraud

Based on the evidence currently available, prosecutors believe that Ádám Matolcsy may have instigated alleged economic fraud causing particularly substantial financial damage, as well as the use of forged private documents. Stofa is suspected of having participated in the alleged fraud as a co-perpetrator and of directly committing the document-related offence.

These are allegations at the current stage of the investigation and have not been established by a court verdict. Stofa was previously associated with Optima Zrt., the company involved in managing funds linked to foundations established by the National Bank of Hungary, according to Hungarian watchdog K-Monitor.

Stay up-to-date: The UN was no friend of Orbán – So why is he now linked to its top job?

Wider investigation into central bank-linked funds

The warrants form part of a broader investigation into suspected financial misconduct connected with the central bank’s affairs. On 21 October, prosecutors detained former central bank governor György Matolcsy, who was questioned by the Central Investigative Prosecutor’s Office and named as a suspect in alleged economic fraud and the use of forged private documents.

Two other individuals were also detained: a representative involved in a loan agreement with the Central European III Private Equity Fund and a lawyer who participated in a securities transaction. Hungarian news outlet Válasz Online reported that those detained included Mihály Valkó, chief executive of Quartz Investment Fund Management, and Tamás Sándor, a lawyer who regularly represented the Matolcsy family.

The investigation continues, with the international warrants marking a further step in efforts to locate and question two people whom authorities say they have so far been unable to reach.

World.title: Hungary launches Wekerle housing scheme with cheaper mortgages and EUR 1.7 billion for renovations
World.content:
Hungary has unveiled an extensive new housing programme offering discounted mortgages for younger buyers, state subsidies for energy-efficient home renovations and the return of government-backed housing savings. The Wekerle programme, announced by Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s government, is designed to make homes more affordable while encouraging construction and modernisation across the country.

The measures will be introduced in stages from October 2026, with the wider programme expected to run until 2030. The government also plans to expand affordable rental housing and student accommodation, using both domestic and European Union funding.

Cheaper mortgages for buyers aged 18–45

The new Wekerle+ Purchase and Construction Loan becomes available from 28 October, although individual banks may need a few extra days to prepare their systems.

Applicants aged 18–45 can apply for a fixed-rate mortgage to purchase or build a home. The annual interest rate will be 3% for new properties and 5% for existing homes, with interest-rate support available for up to 25 years.

The scheme is not conditional on marriage or having children. However, the property must serve as the buyer’s home rather than an investment, and borrowers will be required to live there for five years.

The government has introduced price limits to prevent public money from supporting luxury property purchases. The maximum eligible price is HUF 100 million for an apartment and HUF 150 million for a family house, while the price per square metre cannot exceed HUF 1.5 million.

Parents or siblings may also join an application as co-borrowers if the applicant’s income is insufficient, although they will not acquire ownership of the property through this arrangement.

Existing Otthon Start (Home Start) mortgage contracts will remain valid. Some buyers who have already signed purchase agreements may also have a 15-day transition period to switch to the new scheme, subject to the applicable conditions.

Finance Minister András Kármán, Prime Minister Péter Magyar and Economy and Energy Minister István Kapitány. Photo: MTI

If you missed it: Government measures could give Hungary’s housing market the boost it needs

HUF 633 billion for home renovations

One of the programme’s largest elements is a HUF 633 billion (EUR 1.7 billion) funding package for energy-efficiency improvements, covering everything from panel blocks and brick-built apartment buildings to detached houses.

The renovation support will help households pay for insulation, window and door replacement, shading systems, more efficient split air conditioners and, in some cases, solar panels. The government also plans to support heating-system upgrades.

The Wekerle+ Renovation Support and Loan scheme will offer fixed-rate loans at 3% interest, with the maximum loan amount rising from HUF 6 million to HUF 15 million. Depending on the property’s energy performance, applicants may also qualify for a non-repayable grant covering 30–50% of eligible costs, up to HUF 7.5 million.

To qualify, renovations must deliver energy savings of at least 30%. Unlike the purchase mortgage, the renovation scheme is not restricted by age, marital status or parenthood, and will be available across Hungary.

The programme is expected to launch in stages in 2027, with support for family houses scheduled to begin in February and applications for apartment-building renovations opening in March.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

State-backed housing savings return in 2027

Hungary will also reintroduce state-supported housing savings from January 2027, reviving a system whose previous government subsidy was abolished in 2018.

Under the Wekerle+ Housing Savings scheme, the state will supplement eligible deposits for up to ten years. During the first five years, the subsidy will cover 10% of contributions, up to HUF 120,000 annually. From the sixth to the tenth year, the rate will rise to 20%, with an annual cap of HUF 240,000.

The maximum subsidy will therefore be available to savers who deposit HUF 100,000 per month. Over ten years, the government contribution could reach HUF 1.8 million, excluding interest and subject to the scheme’s conditions.

Participating banks must offer at least 3% interest on savings. The money can be used to purchase a property, finance renovations or cover a mortgage deposit. The scheme will be open regardless of age, location or family status.

Affordable rentals and student accommodation planned

The Wekerle Sándor Housing and Dormitory Construction Programme will address another persistent problem: the shortage of affordable rental homes and student accommodation.

The government plans to allocate HUF 30 billion in EU funding in the first year, followed by a further EUR 550 million over the next three years. New housing is expected to be concentrated in areas with good public transport connections.

Together, these measures are intended to increase the supply of homes while improving access to both home ownership and affordable renting.

Government expects no major construction price surge

Prime Minister Péter Magyar said the government does not expect the programme to drive up construction and renovation prices significantly. Rather than introducing price caps, the government intends to spread support across different groups and types of housing.

The administration also expects smaller businesses to benefit indirectly, as local construction companies and contractors carry out much of the building and renovation work.

The funding for energy-efficiency improvements will partly come from EU Cohesion Fund money previously frozen and subsequently brought back to Hungary, according to the government’s announcement.

The Wekerle programme is intended to create a more sustainable housing market, combining support for buyers with investment in existing homes, new construction and affordable rentals.

Where to find the details: The government has published information about the schemes on the official Wekerle programme website. As the measures launch in stages, applicants should check the relevant eligibility rules and bank requirements before applying.

World.title: After the Election Party, What Lies Ahead for Serbia?
World.content:
After more than 14 years, Vucic has fallen. He fell not only because he was vulnerable, but because a solution to Serbia’s authoritarian catch-all system was finally found. That solution proved lethal to the old system, but it doesn’t tell us much about the new reality, the one that comes after the days of pride, glory and partying.

The most important pillars on which the Vucic regime rested were: absolute, top-down party control over all state resources; relentless pressure to win by large margins; serving the interests of financial power centres, criminal structures, drug cartels and hooligan groups; and the control and absorption of political organisations across the entire political spectrum. Let’s start with the last one.

The closure of the political arena was achieved in much the same way Milo Djukanovic and his Democratic Party of Socialists achieved it in Montenegro. Every partner that offered a share of power became an appendage of the ruling party, entirely dependent and eventually so weakened that remaining with Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) became the only rational option.

World.title: Plebiscites Signal Fight for Slovenia’s Soul under ‘Authoritarian’ Jansa
World.content:
Janez Jansa might have lost two of four referenda held this month, but analysts say the Slovenian prime minister is unlikely to give ground on his autocratic, national conservative agenda.

Amid relatively high turnout of almost 55 per cent, Jansa’s right-wing coalition government lost a consultatory referendum on scrapping the licence fee for public Radio Television Slovenija, RTVSlo, as well as a binding plebiscite on expanding parliament’s powers of inquiry. The margins were wafer-thin.

Winning consultatory referenda on scrapping voting rights for citizens of third countries and making welfare benefits for able-bodied individuals conditional on participation in socially beneficial work was of little consolation.

World.title: Murder in Ecuador: The Polish Activist, the Missing Files and the Albanian Mafia
World.content:
A hard drive and missing files

During this time, a man reached out to BIRN through an intermediary, claiming to be in possession of a hard drive belonging to Silva-Koniuszek. As proof, he sent us some of the files; a few weeks later, he handed over the entire drive, which contained documentation compiled by Silva-Koniuszek regarding land scandals and ties between politicians and the drug trade.

There are nearly 500 files, some of which provide a detailed account of the activities of the Panamanian company Sunshine Management Limited. In these documents, Silva-Koniuszek indicates that an extensive network of shell companies linked to the firm was used for a cross-border money-laundering scheme between Ecuador and Panama. Six US citizens, listed as shareholders, were involved in the operation. Among them was an individual who held stakes in over 900 companies – many of which were established on the same day – as well as two other people who had previously been convicted for their roles in drug smuggling.

Silva-Koniuszek indicates in the files that on July 14, 2025, she sent all the information she had gathered in separate letters to Lawrence Petroni, the US ambassador in Quito; the office of Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa; and Interior Minister John Reimberg.

In her letters, she points to a key issue: the purchase of land by the municipality of Santa Elena, during Otto Vera’s time in office as mayor, from a private consortium linked to this Sunshine Management. The transaction, valued at over 10 million dollars, was settled using “credit notes”. In exchange, land was handed over for a housing project that was never built. Instead, a network of companies connected to Sunshine Management acquired, among other assets, prime coastal property in Manglaralto, including protected mangrove areas.

Silva-Koniuszek presents evidence that municipal officials falsified cadastral codes and land registry records, facilitating the seizure of private plots in Punta Blanca – not far from where the body of Ruben David Cherres Fagglioni had been discovered in March 2023 bearing signs of torture. Cherres Faggioni ran an illicit influence-peddling network that offered corporate positions in exchange for bribes; according to the Ecuadorian prosecutor’s office, he was also linked to the Albanian mafia. The scandal involving him was one of the factors that led to the initiation of impeachment proceedings in 2023 against the then-president, Guillermo Lasso.

A prosecution investigation into Sunshine Management and the misappropriation of public funds was blocked and shelved in 2018. This allowed the then-mayor of Santa Elena, Otto Vera, to take office as a member of parliament and serve as vice president of the National Assembly.

In November 2025, Deputy Interior Minister Jorge Andres Rivadeneira Brown responded to a notification submitted by Silva-Koniuszek to his ministry about an investigation into Sunshine Management. He stated that the matter had been referred to Mauricio Torres, the Comptroller General of the State, who was conducting a “special audit”. In response, Silva-Koniuszek filed a request for a parliamentary inquiry into the Comptroller General, alleging that he had obstructed corruption cases involving prominent politicians. She also accused him of nepotism. In turn, he filed a defamation lawsuit against her.

Silva-Koniuszek’s defence is being led by Dr Jorge Washington Andrade Escobar, a well-known attorney from Quito and one of the initiators of the current impeachment proceedings against Ecuadorian President Noboa over alleged corruption in the energy sector, among other things. Their strategy – the case is ongoing, emphasises Andrade Escobar – is to demonstrate that Silva-Koniuszek’s public statements were true and fact-based, which would negate any criminal intent to defame.

The judge granted the defence’s motions, officially ordering entities including the Attorney General’s Office and the Council of the Judiciary to provide information regarding nepotism within the Comptroller’s office.

Another person familiar with the matter, who wished to remain anonymous, tells BIRN: “The Comptroller’s wife worked for the Council of the Judiciary, while the ex-wife of the president of the Council of the Judiciary worked in the Comptroller’s office. They could have exerted influence over the judges, thereby silencing the Polish woman.”

“Even after news of Monika’s death had become a widely known public fact, the judge continued with the case and scheduled further hearings. Consequently, I filed a formal disciplinary complaint with the Provincial Directorate of the Council of the Judiciary, as, in my view, the judge committed serious errors,” says Andrade Escobar.

By the spring of 2026, when the date for the first defamation hearing was set, Silva-Koniuszek was genuinely fearing for her life. Consequently, the judge agreed to hold the hearing online. At that time, she was attempting to leave Ecuador with her two daughters; in her desperation, she sought assistance from the US embassy in Quito, offering, as she herself wrote on social media, to provide the Americans with confidential documents.

On the aforementioned hard drive, BIRN discovered traces of correspondence between Silva-Koniuszek and a representative of the US mission.

On March 12 of this year, Silva-Koniuszek messaged the embassy representative (whose personal details are known to us) via an online chat platform. They arranged to meet at the Nuts and Coffee café in Quito at 14:00 the same day. The American mentioned that he would be accompanied by two women – an analyst and an agent – specifying that they were “gringas” (slang for American women).

Early the following morning, the Silva-Koniuszek messaged the same man again. Later that night, she sent another message: “I’m worried that you aren’t responding.” Once again, she received no reply. Six days after the scheduled meeting, Silva-Koniuszek informed the American that she had been waiting at the embassy for a considerable time, and that the security guards had suggested she call the person with whom she had been in contact.

As far as BIRN has been able to establish, Silva-Koniuszek had travelled to Quito to seek protection from the US Drug Enforcement Administration, or DEA. She hoped for American assistance, given that the US is actively combating cartels in the region; for instance, it recently designated the Ecuadorian gang “Los Chone Killers” as a “terrorist” organisation. She was also reportedly set to hand over confidential documents to the Americans – documents that implicate not only influential figures involved in land scandals but also concern Noboa Trading, an export giant owned by the family of Ecuador’s current president.

It is an open secret that the province of Santa Elena, where Silva-Koniuszek lived, is controlled by the president’s associates. Noboa himself began his political career as an MP representing this region.

A year ago, Ecuadorian journalist Andres Duran alleged that Noboa Trading was involved in drug smuggling to Europe. He confirmed that a 600-kilogram shipment of cocaine, seized in Turkey in 2023, had been hidden inside banana cartons belonging to the firm. He also presented evidence of cocaine shipments to countries such as Italy and Croatia between 2020 and 2024 – a period that includes the time during which Noboa was already serving as president.

Following the publication of reports on the official “Ecuador en Directo” YouTube channel – in which the president and his relatives were accused of having ties to cartels – Duran was summoned to testify before the National Assembly of Ecuador. Faced with death threats, he left the country and currently resides in Spain.

“When I got involved in the case, Monika reached out to me,” the journalist tells BIRN. “At first, I didn’t take it seriously, but at one point she provided me with a series of documents and several leads regarding individuals linked to the corporation Noboa Trading – information she seemingly obtained from former employees of the firm. I immediately urged her to flee Ecuador. She had crossed a powerful mafia that has entrenched itself within our country.”

Even before her meeting with the US embassy representative on March 12, Silva-Koniuszek had sent the official a document containing text and a name: “Jose Luis Rivera Baquerizo”. He is the son of a customs broker at the port of Guayaquil and was the subject of four drug-smuggling investigations between 2017 and 2024. He was employed by Roberto Ponce Noboa – a cousin of the president – and in one of the cases, he was represented by a close advisor to the president. He was never formally charged.

Despite the evidence provided – which, according to the Polish activist, points to drug smuggling by the Ecuadorian president’s family business – the documents show the American official stopped answering her calls. We, too, were unable to reach him despite numerous attempts, and the US embassy in Quito did not respond to our inquiries.

“To put it bluntly: the Americans blew her off. And it’s not as if she just walked in off the street and said, ‘Hey America, Putin killed a woman in a bathroom’,” says a lawyer whom Silva-Koniuszek consulted. “She possessed confidential documentation detailing the operational side of the company’s exports – a firm that, after all, handles the export of bananas worldwide, controls ports in Ecuador, and wields significant influence in both politics and business.”

Following journalistic investigations into drug smuggling, President Noboa and the company’s management categorically denied any direct involvement by the firm in these crimes. They argued that drug cartels often infiltrate the supply chains of global logistics companies, hiding narcotics within legitimate cargo.

World.title: EU Commission Unveils Reforms to Beef Up Border Agency
World.content:
The European Commission unveiled on Tuesday a series of measures designed to give the EU’s border control agency, the Warsaw-based Frontex, more powers to combat the entry and enhance the return of illegal immigrants.

“The new reality requires a new mandate for Frontex,” European Executive Vice-President for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy Henna Virkkunen told a press conference. “With these important proposals we are significantly strengthening our external borders and the support we can offer our member states.”

Key measures the European Commission are proposing, which will still need to be agreed by the member state governments in the Council of the EU, include more resources and operational capacity, a Quick Reaction Force to intervene in crisis situations, and a new Online Monitoring Centre to scan social media and identify bad actors in order to early detect potential threats at the borders. It will also develop a dedicated Return Coordination Centre so Frontex will be able to help carry out returns of migrants from third countries by facilitating deportations from return hubs.

While the irregular entry of migrants to the bloc are well down from their peak during the migration crisis of 2015-2016, when almost 1.5 million first-time asylum applications were made by new arrivals, the latest EU-wide Eurobarometer survey still found 65 per cent of EU citizens were concerned about uncontrolled immigration. This has led to big electoral gains by far-right parties in the member states and the European Parliament, prompting the European Commission to take a more robust approach to irregular migration.

More recently, July’s Ceuta migrant crisis, when an estimated 70,000 to 80,000 Moroccan migrants mass-crossed the border into the Spanish North African enclave, partly fuelled by disinformation online, has added to the sense that more must be done to strengthen border security.

“Our borders face new challenges: orchestrated crossings by smuggling networks, changing routes, hybrid threats, instrumentalization of migration – no member state can meet these challenges alone,” said European Commissioner for Internal Affairs and Migration Magnus Brunner. “Our response has to be faster, stronger and better coordinated.”

Brunner noted that the return rate of migrants who have no right of stay in the EU was still too low at 32-33 per cent, and the proposed new powers for Frontex will make the agency “the central EU actor on returns”.

Following the entry into force of the new Return Regulation on October 16, the European Commission is proposing a new regulation to digitalise the return, readmission and reintegration procedures across the EU, with the aim of modernising the handling of return cases by simplifying and speeding up administrative procedures through digitalisation, reduced administrative burdens, and improving data collection and sharing.

This will require more manpower and the European Commission is proposing to gradually increase Frontex’s standing corps to 30,000 officers by doubling the amount of Frontex’s own standing corps officers and creating a new “European border and return reserve” of 17 000 officers ready to be deployed when needed. According to Politico, the agency had around 7,800 personnel in its standing corps in early 2026 and is working towards a target of 10,000 by 2027.

World.title: Bulgarian Govt Criticised for Using State Resources to Promote Presidential Candidate
World.content:
Allegations that the Bulgarian government used official channels to promote presidential candidate Iliana Iotova have sparked a slew of accusations between opposition leaders and media associations on one side and Prime Minister Rumen Radev and his government on the other.

On Tuesday, the Association of European Journalists – Bulgaria accused Prime Minister Radev, who backed Iotova for the presidency at the first round of elections last weekend, of trying to force the media to be his mouthpiece.

The row erupted on Monday, after Radev said that voters in the upcoming second-round runoff will have to choose between “peace and war”. The suggestion was that Iotova can maintain balance in relations with Russia while opposition candidate Andrey Gyurov’s pro-EU and pro-Ukraine positions equate to warmongering.

The same message was published in a post on the government’s official Facebook page and in a press release sent out on Monday by the government’s press office, which included the message, “Let’s vote for Iliana Iotova so Bulgaria can be in safe hands.”

Gyurov and other opposition politicians claimed that Radev’s government was breaching the electoral code, which prohibits government information services from being used for partisan promotional purposes. The Central Election Committee has been notified of the allegations.

Later on Monday, the government’s official Facebook page published a statement saying there was no violation since the campaigning for the November 1 runoff has not yet started and the prime minister’s statements should “be covered in their entirety” by the media.

The statement also criticised “the negative example” of “some media outlets” who “silence, twist, manipulate, cut down and insinuate political narratives in the words of the prime minister”.

The Association of European Journalists – Bulgaria retorted with a statement saying that the government’s “attempt to lecture the media on professional journalistic standards” was “dangerous”.

“The expectation that all media outlets should republish the prime minister’s statements ‘in their entirety’ demonstrates a profound lack of understanding of journalistic work,” the statement said.

“Under the Bulgarian Media Code of Ethics, journalists are committed to ensuring the accuracy of information. This provision is important, but it is a distortion to interpret it as prohibiting journalists and media outlets from critically analysing the Prime Minister’s positions,” it added.

The first round of the presidential election was held on Sunday with no candidate receiving an outright majority. A runoff between acting President Iotova and opposition candidate and former interim prime minister Gyurov is scheduled for November 1.

Sunday’s results were unexpected as Gyurov had been far behind in opinion polls before the vote. The elections were also notable for their low voter turnout, with one polling agency estimating that only 22.5 per cent of eligible voters cast ballots.

World.title: What Does Aleksandar Vucic’s Defeat Mean for Balkan Autocrats?
World.content:
When the student protests in Serbia gathered momentum in 2025, Aleksandar Vucic, the president at the time, promised that he would defeat them and write a book on how to prevail against “colour revolutions” – an unmistakable allusion to Ukraine’s Maidan uprising, which unseated a corrupt administration.

Instead, he may now have to write another book on how power is lost through arrogance, institutional capture and the mistaken belief that fear can substitute for legitimacy. His defeat in the snap parliamentary elections of October 25 is not merely a change of government; it represents a profound rejection of the model of autocratic governance he built over more than a decade.

Yet this defeat did not occur in a vacuum. It followed nearly two years of student-led mobilisation that gradually expanded beyond universities and became one of the broadest civic movements in Serbia’s post-communist history.

World.title: Bosnian Court Verdicts for Wartime Sexual Violence Show Leniency and Disparities
World.content:
At the entity level, cases involving wartime sexual violence are notable for the inconsistency of judgments.

In the Federation, sentences ranged from one year to 13 years and six months, for offences including the rape of women, girls and men, multiple rapes, sexual abuse in camps and a combination of sexual and physical violence.

The average sentence was just over six years, while in some cases the perpetrators, including those whose victims were minors, were sentenced to just a year in prison having struck plea agreements. Such agreements can allow the convicted perpetrator to avoid prison altogether in exchange for paying an 18,000-euro fine.

Sentences in Republika Srpska ranged from two to 15 years in prison. In the case of the shortest sentences, the courts cited mitigating circumstances. In one, for example, the District Court in Banja Luka cited the fact the accused was an older juvenile at the time the offence was committed. In some cases, the courts cited no aggravating circumstances at all, despite the crimes involving sexual violence.

In the Federation, some cantonal courts cited as mitigating circumstances the accused’s marital status, the fact he had children and no prior convictions, and his conduct during the trial. In one case, the court cited the fact that the accused had not committed any other criminal offences since the crime in question. The passage of time was also taken as a mitigating circumstance, as was the accused’s advanced age.

In the autonomous Brcko District, sentences ranged from four to 15 years, and most commonly between four and six years even in cases of multiple rapes.

The cases in Brcko include that of Monika Karan, one of the few women convicted of war crimes in Bosnia. Karan was found guilty in 2013 of the psychological and sexual humiliation of detainees in the ‘Luka’ camp. The court found Karan had forced a detainee to strip naked, touched his genitals and forced him to touch her under threat of death.

Though finding that Karan’s acts caused her victim great psychological suffering, the court sentenced her to just four years in prison – below the statutory minimum.

As mitigating circumstances, the court cited her age at the time the offence was committed – 26 – as well as her family circumstances and the absence of prior convictions.

“Unfortunately, sexual violence leaves lasting consequences on victims, and such lenient sentences do not reflect the seriousness of that crime,” said Midheta Kaloper, head of the Association of Victims of War – Foca 92-95.

Experts say that overly lenient sentences undermine public trust in the judicial system and discourage victims from reporting violence.

“That is why it is high time that the sentencing policy was seriously reviewed,” Kaloper told BIRN.

“Institutions and society need to send a clear message that such acts must not be tolerated. Victims’ associations have advocated and appealed for these cases to be tried exclusively before the Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina.”

‘Long-standing disproportion’

World.title: Journalist-Turned-PM Faces Daunting Challenges in Romania
World.content:
What do journalism and diplomacy have in common? For Luca Niculescu, both offer the opportunity of direct engagement with people, demand effective communication, and require an ability to build relationships and ask the right questions.

Diplomacy, however, operates by different rules, particularly when it comes to freedom of public expression. This limitation is offset, according to Romania’s new prime minister, by the satisfaction that comes from serving the public interest and making a tangible difference to people’s lives.

Niculescu, 55, began his career as a radio journalist in 1992 and went on to become editor-in-chief of Radio France Internationale, RFI, while also contributing regularly to several French media outlets.

In 2016, he made the transition to diplomacy as Romania’s ambassador to France. He returned to Bucharest in 2022 to coordinate the country’s bid to join the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, OECD, and last week became prime minister.

World.title: Calls for Protest Are Spreading Across Zagreb
World.content:
October the 28th, 2026 – Calls for a protest are currently spreading across Zagreb, with the organisers insisting that there are no political parties involved.

Posters have begun appearing across Zagreb calling on the public to a protest named “Voice of Change/Glas Promjene”, announced for Saturday the 21st of November, at 10:00 on Ban Josip Jelačić Square. Behind the call stands the civic initiative “Time for Change/Vrijeme za Promjenu”, which, via social media, is inviting people to gather against corruption, abuse of power and institutional irresponsibility.

Index reports that the posters highlight the message “All of Croatia, one voice”, and the organisers say they want to bring together people who are dissatisfied with the standard of living, the political situation and the work of institutions. “Want change? Then don’t be the person who doesn’t come to Ban Josip Jelačić Square at 10:00 on the 21st of November,” one of the posts calling for the protest states.

“no more empty promises”

The organisers point to the rising cost of living, the increasingly difficult independence of young people and the feeling that wages are not keeping up with prices. “Basic life needs are becoming a luxury, young people cannot afford to leave their parents’ home for something of their own, wages are getting lower, while the quality of life and prices demand more and more,” they state in a post.

The organisers answered several questions about the goals of the protest. “The protest is directed against corruption, abuse of power and the lack of institutional accountability. We demand transparent management of public money, equal laws for everyone, accountability of those who hold public office and concrete systemic changes, not just empty promises,” they said. They emphasised that the initiative is not connected to any political party and that its goal is not to replace one set of politicians with another. “The initiative is not tied to any political party, nor is the goal to replace one politicians with others, but to demand a system in which institutions work in the interest of citizens,” they stated.

They added that they want to shape the concrete demands together with citizens so that they are clear, achievable and measurable.

is the protest against hdz or just corruption asa vague term?

One of the questions put to the organisers was whether the protest is directed against HDZ. “The protest is directed against corruption, abuse of power and the lack of institutional accountability, regardless of who is in power. That includes the actions of the HDZ when they are the subject of such criticism,” they replied. In a separate post they further emphasised that the protest is not organised in the name of any political party and that they do not belong to any political option. “This is a civic initiative for all people who have had enough of corruption, lack of transparency, institutional irresponsibility and an uncertain future for us and our children,” they said.

serbian protests were mentioned

The organisers also commented on the protests in Serbia, answering the question of whether the situation there prompted them to organise a gathering in Croatia. “The situation in Serbia has certainly shown how important civic unity and persistence are, but the motivation is much broader than that,” they stated. They added that their goal is to encourage citizens of different political views to act together. “The goal is for all of us, regardless of political views, to become active and together build a better future. Change begins when we stop just watching and decide to participate,” they said.

they want to see protests across croatia

Although a protest in Zagreb has so far been announced, the organisers are also thinking about gatherings in other Croatian cities. When asked whether the protest would have a greater impact if all citizens gathered in one city, they replied that for the start it is more important to enable people to participate in their own communities. “I think that for the start it is important to enable people to gather in their own cities because not everyone has the possibility to travel to another location,” they stated. They added that, depending on the turnout and organisation, one large joint gathering could later be held. “And when we see the turnout and the strength of the organisation in each city, we can make one large joint gathering that will send an even stronger message. Step by step, city by city,” they said.

who is actually behind this initiative?

Calls for the protest are spreading via social media, among other things through the Instagram profile @vrijemezapromjene and the TikTok profile @glas.promjene. One of the posters also lists the TikTok profile @ala_secera as a contact for joining the Zagreb group. The organisers emphasise that all citizens can participate in the protest, regardless of age or occupation, including students, high-school graduates, employed people and pensioners. It is not yet known who the people behind the initiative are, how many of them are involved in the organisation, or whether the protest has been reported to the police. Details of the gathering programme have also not been published. The protest is, once again, announced for the 21st of November at 10:00 on Ban Josip Jelačić Square in central Zagreb.

World.title: Why Did Over 100,000 Croatian Landlords Turn Their Backs on Protesters?
World.content:
October the 28th, 2026 – Over 100,000 Croatian landlords who rent out their properties to tourists turned their backs on protesters fighting for their rights in Zagreb, but why?

The recent protest by private landlords held at Zrinjevac in Zagreb once again opened key questions about representation, expertise and the future of private accommodation in Croatia. Morski reports that although the organisers’ communication channels were burning with announcements of a mass turnout and a blockade of the capital, digital engagement analytics and sociological parameters indicated in advance the modest reach of the gathering. Despite the protest platform on social media gathering around 15,000 followers, the rate of active interaction at the peak of the campaign barely reached 10 percent. When these figures are run through the usual conversion rates to physical turnout, the final outcome on Zrinjevac brought only a few hundred people, a number comparable to a larger group of mushroom pickers rather than a serious national protest.

This modest turnout confronted the organisers with the relentless mathematical reality. Application of the sociological model of the Law of Dispersion of the Passive Majority clearly shows that in moments of major legislative upheavals the vast majority of affected actors consciously choose passivity and distance themselves from reactive groups. In this case, support from as many as 105,000 Croatian private landlords was absent from the public uproar. The silent majority, which avoids street activism, thereby sent a clear message that it rejects street pressure and demands institutional strength, expertise and well-founded arguments.

a hidden internal division…

The relatively weak turnout is also a direct consequence of a completely failed communication model. The use of populist rhetoric permeated with expressions about “serfs”, “cash machines” and accusations of a “witch hunt”, along with bizarre political constructions about secret coalitions and open threats of electoral votes from the podium, disqualified the organisers from serious professional dialogue. Serious professional associations do not negotiate with the authorities through street blackmail, but with exact indicators, legal analyses and constructive proposals.

Additionally, the protest revealed a deep, though publicly unspoken, socio-economic stratification within the sector itself. Namely, around 43,000 high-category facilities with 4 and 5 stars, in which significant funds have been invested, attract guests of higher purchasing power and naturally no longer share the same interests with the rest of the base that persists with the basic 3-star model. Nevertheless, owners of higher-quality accommodation, for pragmatic reasons and the desire to preserve good-neighbourly relations in local communities, choose complete passivity, leaving the protest margins to the loudest groups.

are amendments making landlords kick the can down the road?

On the other hand, uncertainty on the ground has been further heightened by the fact that the Government and the Ministry of Tourism and Sport (MINTS) have, through months of administrative silence, delayed precise clarifications of the new legislative amendments and the announced re-categorisation. This created information vacuum has served as fuel for the spread of panic, although it is clear that the state does not want to wipe out private accommodation, but to introduce necessary regulatory order and balance the interests of landlords with the remaining 90 percent of people. It is also expected that expert teams will take a sharper approach towards non-commercial accommodation which, under the guise of hosting, often represents a source of unfair competition.

Despite the tensions, the financial contribution of private landlords to Croatian tourism remains extremely significant. On the basis of around 600,000 registered beds, landlords through the fixed lump-sum tourist membership fee of €5.97 per bed generate around €3.58 million annually, while through the lump-sum tourist tax, with a conservative average of €50 per bed, they pay an additional €30 million. As such, more than €33.5 million of original money flows into the budgets and the system of tourist boards every year.

a constructive proposal…

Instead of directing these funds into ineffective general promotion or spending from the general state budget, a real and sustainable alternative offers the redirection of part of this earmarked pool into a National Programme of Targeted Vouchers for Apartment Transition. Modelled on successful European practices, such as Italian regional micro-grants in Tuscany and Apulia or the French Gîtes de France network, this model would directly help raise the quality of accommodation on the ground. The proposed vouchers would not be distributed in cash nor would they be intended for high-category 4- and 5-star facilities that already operate well. They would be used exclusively for co-financing the costs of interior modernisation and the purchase of equipment in 3-star facilities that demonstrably move into a higher category. Functioning as closed instruments intended for payment of works to registered domestic craftsmen and companies and for the purchase of equipment in Croatian shops, these millions would return directly into the entire Croatian economy, turning fiscal contributions into a driving force of sustainable market evolution.

World.title: Hungary Bins Orbán and Serbia Bins Vučić, Is Croatia Next?
World.content:
October the 28th, 2026 – Hungary toppled Viktor Orbán after 18 years in power, and now Serbia has binned Aleksandar Vučić, many are now asking the question of whether or not a big change for Croatia is next.

After almost 14 years of political dominance, Aleksandar Vučić just suffered a staggering electoral defeat in Serbia. Only a few months earlier, Viktor Orbán was toppled from power in Hungary after 16 years. Can Croatia, where the HDZ has been in power continuously since 2016, be next? Vedran Salvia reports for Index that although it is abundantly clear that Plenković’s government has not built an authoritarian system of the kind established by Orbán and Vučić, all three countries share long-term dominance by a single political option that has over time developed a strong network of influence in state institutions and the public sector.

Croatia is thus marked by strong clientelism, party-based appointments, corruption and seriously eroded institutions. During the ten years of Plenković’s rule, the HDZ has not attempted to confront this way of running the state, but has further strengthened it. A party membership card and connections still all too often count for more than knowledge and ability, and the consequences of such a system are felt in almost all parts of society.

both hungary and serbia seek to forge new paths

Interestingly, neither Orbán nor Vučić was defeated by the traditional opposition parties. In Hungary this was achieved by Péter Magyar, a former man of Orbán’s system, who with his party Tisza gathered a broad circle of voters dissatisfied with long-term rule. Among them were also people who had previously supported Orbán’s Fidesz. In Serbia, the situation was somewhat different. Vučić was defeated by the Student List, which emerged from the protests after the tragedy in Novi Sad, where on the 1st of November 2024, a railway station canopy collapsed and killed 16 people. The accident opened questions of corruption and institutional responsibility, and the protests grew into a mass movement against Vučić’s government.

75% of people think croatia is heading in the wrong direction

In Croatia, there is no shortage of dissatisfaction with the government. According to the latest CRO Demoskop, conducted from 6 to 8 October, more than 75 percent of respondents believe that the country is going in the wrong direction. Only a little over 17 percent think that Croatia is going in the right direction. At the same time, HDZ, although recording a drop in popularity, remains the strongest individual party with 25 percent support. The SDP is at a little under 20 percent, Možemo at almost 14 percent, and Most has approached 10 percent.

Interestingly, both HDZ and SDP are declining at the same time, while Možemo is growing. In other words, dissatisfaction with those in power is not automatically translating into growth for the largest opposition party, and this is one of the biggest differences between Croatia and the two neighbouring countries. In Hungary, Tisza managed to become the main political alternative to Orbán. In Serbia, the students almost completely pushed aside the traditional opposition and turned into a movement that can win power on its own.

Croatia does not have such a political force. It has several opposition parties, some of which govern important cities and have significant voter support, but none has so far managed to gather such a broad circle of dissatisfied citizens. At the same time, the Croatian opposition doesn’t have an individual who, like Magyar, could attract a significant part of the ruling party’s voters. Magyar’s success was not based solely on criticism of Orbán. As a man who came from within the Fidesz system, he was able to convince even some conservative voters that a change of government does not necessarily mean abandoning their political beliefs.

electoral maths still favours hdz…

Croatian electoral mathematics are also highly important. Croatia is divided into ten territorial electoral units, in each of which 14 seats are distributed separately. Therefore it is not only the total number of votes that matters, but also their distribution. HDZ greatly benefits from a strong party organisation and stable support in numerous parts of the country.

The boundaries of the electoral units were redrawn in 2023 after the Constitutional Court repealed the previous law. The new model was adopted by an HDZ majority and drew criticism for the illogical linking of certain areas. Political scientist Goran Čular then warned for Gong: “The prime minister said that the arrangement of electoral units is a technical issue, but HDZ is doing everything to ensure that it is not just a technical issue.” Nevertheless, HDZ’s victory back in 2024 cannot be attributed solely to the electoral system. Its coalition won 61 seats, fully 19 more than the SDP coalition, and it formed the government again with the help of the Homeland Movement. The electoral system can be an additional advantage for it, but for a change of government the opposition must first and foremost win significantly broader voter support.

the clear differences between hungary, serbia and croatia

Political scientist Tihomir Cipek, a professor at the Faculty of Political Science in Zagreb, spoke about why long-term governments fell in Hungary and Serbia, while in Croatia the HDZ still does not have an equally strong opponent. Cipek emphasises that the situations in Croatia, Hungary and Serbia are different. “In Hungary, a strong movement against Orbán was formed, which Péter Magyar gathered around his new party. Something similar happened in Serbia with the Student List. There we have a broad movement that brought together very different people, from liberals open to the world and cooperation with the European Union to Serbian nationalists who accused Vučić of betraying Kosovo and Metohija. Among them are both those who support sanctions against Russia and those who oppose them. Despite major political differences, what connected them all was opposition to Vučić,” Cipek said.

why has no similar movement emerged in croatia?

He explained that a similar movement against Plenković’s government has not emerged in Croatia because the political scene is already clearly divided among the existing parties. “In Croatia, the political system is structured along party lines. The type of people who found themselves together on the Student List in Serbia are already organised in different parties here. Here you have Možemo, which is for a more open society and, for example, cooperation with the EU, and on the other side Most, which has different views on migration and the openness of society.

It’s very difficult to imagine them all uniting into one front against the government. In addition, the electoral system in Croatia must also be taken into account. Serbia is one electoral unit, while Croatia has ten, so it is important how the opposition will perform in each of them,” Cipek explained. He believes that the successes of the students and Magyar show that even long-term power is no guarantee of political survival. “That victory in Serbia shows that nothing is certain. You can be in power for a long time, build strong influence in state structures, but citizens can still remove you with their activity and energy. In Croatia it is much harder to create such a broad movement, but that does not mean that it is impossible to change the government,” Cipek concludes.

is there even any potential for governmental change in croatia?

“There is potential for a change of government because dissatisfaction is high. The key is how it will be politically articulated. If the SDP and Možemo organise well, change is possible,” Cipek says. He believes that the opposition parties have drawn lessons from earlier electoral defeats, when they ran separately or tried to form alliances that did not bring the expected result. “There is dissatisfaction, but it needs to be turned into a political programme. With clear messages, good organisation and voter mobilisation it is also possible for the Croatian opposition to win. Nothing is eternal,” Cipek concluded.

World.title: Dubrovnik Airport: The Biggest Corruption Scandal Involving EU Cash?
World.content:
October the 28th, 2026 – The mayor of Dubrovnik has referred to the situation with Dubrovnik Airport being “the biggest corruption scandal involving EU cash in Croatia”.

Dubrovnik’s Ruđer Bošković Airport had to return a total of €22 million in European Union funds due to irregularities in public procurement procedures during a major airport modernisation project. Index reports that in addition to all kinds of financial problems, it was also revealed that part of the expensive infrastructure was never put into operation. Among such projects is the aircraft fuel supply system, in which pipes of the type used for sewage systems were allegedly installed.

These are irregularities in the modernisation project for Dubrovnik Airport that was carried out from 2013 to 2017. Around €200 million was secured from EU funds for the renovation, but due to disputed public procurement procedures, part of that money had to be returned. The latest obligation of three million euros recently became due. Dubrovnik Airport director Viktor Šober explained how the irregularities financially burdened the airport’s operations. “In one part we returned it, in one case it was automatically deducted from us, so we had to take out loans ourselves or use our own funds to make up for that shortfall which occurred primarily because of problematic public procurement procedures,” Šober said.

dubrovnik’s mayor calls out the airport’s director

Dubrovnik’s HDZ mayor Mato Franković recently spoke about the problems at Dubrovnik Airport and, at a session of the parliamentary Transport Committee, called out the former airport director Roko Tolić.

“When you take the overall damage that occurred at Dubrovnik Airport, we can say that this is the biggest corruption affair involving European money in the Republic of Croatia that no one is talking about,” Franković said. Tolić ran Dubrovnik Airport for a long period, more specifically from 2009 to 2018, when he was dismissed due to irregularities in public procurement. Since 2024 he has held the position of executive director of Aerodromi Crne Gore, the company that manages the airports in Podgorica and Tivat.

Tolić was previously politically active in the HSS. From 2000 to 2001 he was deputy mayor of Dubrovnik under Vito Bogdanović as a representative of that party. In the 2021 local elections he ran for Dubrovnik-Neretva County prefect as an independent candidate with the support of the SDP and HNS, but did not make it to the second round.

the alleged installation of sewage-type piping

In addition to returning an enormous sum of EU money, Dubrovnik Airport is also facing problems due to the unfinished aircraft fuel supply system. Although the system was paid for, it has not been used for years because serious mistakes were made during design and construction.

“The problem here is incorrect design and incorrect execution of the works. Plastic and glass pipes were installed that are essentially not used for the flow of fuel. Later, when studying the technical specifications, we realised that pipes used for sewage systems were installed there,” said Marina Bukvić from Ruđer Bošković Airport. The airport management hired a German company to check whether the system could be repaired and put into operation. However, the experts concluded that additional investments of several million euros would be needed to make it functional. This means that the airport has already paid for infrastructure it cannot use, and repairing it would require new large expenditures.

“we bought something we can’t use”

Šober warns that a way to solve the problem will have to be found, and he does not rule out legal steps either. “If this is not resolved, of course that part will be problematic for us as an airport. We paid for something we cannot use. In that case we will have to look for some solutions. Whether of a legal nature or some kind of agreements, but difficult talks certainly await us on this,” Šober said. Former director Roko Tolić did not wish to comment on the accusations against him. Dnevnik.hr also contacted the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) to check whether an investigation has been launched against those responsible for the irregularities in public procurement. They have not yet received a response.

World.title: Ryanair Directly Connects Zagreb and Warsaw Over Winter
World.content:
October the 27th, 2026 – Ryanair has directly connected Zagreb with the Polish capital of Warsaw during the winter schedule, with flights for as little as 17 euros.

The wildly popular Irish low-cost carrier Ryanair has introduced yet another brand new air route connecting Zagreb and Warsaw, specifically Warsaw-Modlin Airport. Poslovni reports that the first flight was operated as part of the winter timetable for the 2026/2027 season on October the 26th, giving passengers from Croatia another option for travelling to Poland. The new route will operate on Mondays and Saturdays, with two flights a week from Zagreb and two from Warsaw.

There are some ultra-cheap tickets being offered on this new route, with the differences in prices show that having a certain degree of flexibility when choosing your desired travel dates can really pay off. Since prices change depending on demand and seat availability, it is always recommended to check the current offers on Ryanair’s website or on the company’s mobile app before booking.

On the occasion of launching this new route from Zagreb Airport, Ryanair’s Director of Communications Jade Kirwan highlighted the importance of expanding the offer for passengers from Croatia. “We’re very pleased that we saw off the first flight operating on the new Zagreb–Warsaw (Modlin) route, on which the first set of very many passengers who will travel with us this winter departed,” Kirwan said.

She added that the new route will give passengers a greater choice of destinations at affordable prices. “The route will operate four times a week, offering passengers from Croatia even more travel options at the most affordable prices in Europe. The entire winter timetable for 2026 is available for booking via our app and website,” she stated.
