World.title: FACT CHECK: Castro spoke about Rodrigo Duterte, not Marcos, in spliced drug-use clip
World.content:
The original clip is from a September 11 briefing in which Castro cited former president Duterte's admissions of drug use. The viral clip was edited to replace Duterte's name with Marcos'.

Claim: Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. admitted to using marijuana and abusing fentanyl because it felt like “cloud nine.”

Rating: ALTERED

Why we fact-checked this: A Facebook post by “Wilfredo Villacastel Orencejr,” published on October 24, carries the claim. Its caption reads, “Ay naku, Ante Claire binubuking mo na yung boss mo, Ante.”

(Oh, Auntie Claire, you’re exposing your boss, auntie.)

The video shows Castro speaking in a supposed interview, with a breaking news label overlaid on top. In the clip, Castro says, “Inamin mismo ni Pangulong Marcos Jr. na siya’y gumagamit ng marijuana, at inamin niya rin na ang paggamit niya ng fentanyl ay inabuso niya dahil masarap daw ang pakiramdam, cloud nine.”

(President Marcos Jr. himself admitted that he uses marijuana, and he also admitted that he abused fentanyl because it supposedly felt good, cloud nine.)

As of writing, the video has garnered over 709,000 views, 11,000 reactions, 1,300 comments, and 5,600 shares.

The facts: Castro did not say Marcos used marijuana or abused fentanyl. The viral clip altered what she said during September 11 press briefing in New Delhi, where she was referring to former president Rodrigo Duterte.

In the genuine clip, Castro was asked to respond to Vice President Sara Duterte’s accusation that Marcos was an “addict.” She said: “Inamin mismo ni dating Pangulong Duterte, pangulo na siya, na siya’y gumagamit ng marijuana. At inamin niya rin na ang paggamit niya ng fentanyl ay inabuso niya dahil masarap daw ‘yung pakiramdam, ‘cloud nine’ ang feeling.”

(Former president Duterte himself admitted, while already in office, that he used marijuana. He also admitted to abusing fentanyl because he enjoyed the feeling, describing it as being on “cloud nine.”)

The viral clip replaces Duterte’s name with “Pangulong Marcos Jr.” (President Marcos Jr.) and omits the phrase “pangulo na siya” (when he was already president).

GMA News reported Castro’s original remarks, which match the Presidential Communications Office transcript and RTVM livestream on September 11.

No credible report shows Marcos admitting to using marijuana or abusing fentanyl.

Duterte’s original remarks: Duterte acknowledged using fentanyl in December 2016, saying he took it for a spinal injury from motorcycle accidents but had exceeded the prescribed dose. He denied being addicted, saying he used it only when prescribed.

In a 2017 Davao City speech, he recalled using an entire fentanyl patch instead of cutting it into four pieces, saying it made him feel “on cloud nine,” the phrase Castro later repeated. He later told critics he had made up the fentanyl story.

In 2018, Duterte said he used marijuana to stay awake during official functions, later calling the remark a joke. Both statements were made while he was president, as Castro said.

Drug-use feud: Castro’s press briefing was a response to the Vice President’s accusation that Marcos was an “addict.” Duterte made the statement at her September 11 arraignment in Quezon City.

The accusation against Marcos is not new. Senator Imee Marcos made a similar claim at a rally in November 2025, which Malacañang rejected, citing a negative drug test.

Rappler also published a fact-check of a similar manipulated clip falsely attributing the remarks to Marcos, along with several other fact-checks debunking his alleged drug use:

– Cyril Bocar/Rappler.com

Efren Cyril Bocar is a journalist from Llorente, Eastern Samar who graduated with a degree in English Language Studies at the Visayas State University. Cyril is also a graduate of the Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: Goodbye, SPNEC: MVP rebrands Leviste’s solar firm, lines up P5-B deal
World.content:
A new name, five more solar businesses, and a possible "re-IPO," but Meralco's makeover can't quite banish Leviste's past or the P10.34-billion headache that comes with it

Manuel V. Pangilinan is giving Leandro Leviste’s old solar crown jewel quite the makeover. First, shed the SPNEC name. Next, bring in nearly P5 billion worth of other renewable energy businesses.

And perhaps, pitch the shiny new thing to stock market investors all over again.

SP New Energy Corporation (SPNEC) is now officially MGEN Renewables Inc., (MGENR) after securing Securities and Exchange Commission approval on Monday, October 26; its stock ticker is also set to change to MGENR.

Officially, the renaming is part of the Meralco group’s broader rebranding strategy. Conveniently, it also removes a reminder of Solar Philippines, the controversial empire Leviste built before Pangilinan’s group took control.

And there’s quite a history behind SPNEC.

FROM SPNEC to MGENR. This Rappler diagram shows the ownership of the rebranded solar company as of September 1, 2026 and before the proposed share swap. Diagram by Raphael Reyes/Rappler.

Leviste made his fortune assembling landholdings and securing solar development rights that attracted deep-pocketed investors, including Pangilinan himself. Industry sources that Rappler spoke with describe the young billionaire as a talented “flipper.”

But getting the rights to build solar farms and actually getting them built are two different businesses.

The Department of Energy (DOE) terminated 33 contracts tied to Leviste’s wider Solar Philippines group, covering around 11,400 megawatts of proposed capacity, and sought around P24 billion in financial obligations. His camp disputes the claims.

While much of the P24-billion mess relates to Leviste’s other companies, SPNEC is dragged into this too.

In a December 23, 2025 letter seen by Rappler, Energy Secretary Sharon Garin terminated the service contract for SPNEC’s 280-megawatt Santa Rosa Nueva Ecija 2 project and demanded P10.34 billion.

The DOE cited missed work-program commitments, an unrenewed performance bond, and missing documents, including a feasibility study and proof of land rights. Most of the demand came from P12.38 billion in work-program commitments, less P2.04 billion credited for reported accomplishments.

MGEN insists SPNEC is legally separate from Solar Philippines and not liable for the wider group’s P24 billion obligation. But it acknowledges that Santa Rosa belongs to SPNEC and says that it invoked force majeure over transmission delays and sought reconsideration.

Separately, Leviste and his mother, Senator Loren Legarda, face graft and plunder complaints involving solar contracts awarded to Leviste-linked companies. Both deny wrongdoing.

Leviste himself has kept his distance from his now Meralco-controlled company, resigning from the board in January and cashing out P3-billion worth of shares, leaving his holding company with an 11.51% stake.

New name, new MGENR

So, what’s next for MGENR?

On Tuesday, October 27, MGEN Renewables’ board approved a proposed P4.98-billion deal to take in stakes in five solar businesses from its controlling shareholder, MGEN Renewable Energy Inc., another Meralco subsidiary.

The companies have interests in operating solar plants across Luzon:

Greenergy for Global Inc. – 52.7-megawatt solar plant in Isabela

Greentech Solar Energy Inc. – 19.8-megawatt solar plant in Nueva Ecija

CACI Power Corporation – Linked to an 80.1-megawatt solar plant in Rizal

Nuevo Solar Energy Corporation – 68.7-megawatt solar plant in Ilocos Norte

PowerSource First Bulacan Solar Inc. – 55-megawatt solar plant in Bulacan

Instead of paying cash, MGEN Renewables will issue around 3.1 billion new shares to its controlling shareholder. If completed, the share swap deal would strengthen Meralco’s control while further diluting Leviste and other investors.

Then comes the more intriguing possibility, a “re-IPO” targeted for March 2027.

Since Leviste already took SPNEC public in 2021, this would be another share offering in the now bigger company under Meralco’s control, rather than a second listing. Nothing has been finalized.

This time, there’s more to show investors. Its P200-billion MTerra Solar project began commercial operations in August, while MGEN Renewables forecasts P774 million in profit for 2026, reversing a P4.1-billion loss in 2025.

The group also plans to invest up to another P7.815 billion in Terra Solar, subject to lender and investor approvals. – Rappler.com

World.title: #CourageON: Highlights from #MoveCebu 2026
World.content:
Rappler’s civic engagement arm MovePH brings #MoveCebu to the University of San Carlos, gathering over 200 people during the public forum to define what a liveable city should be

Last week, Rappler’s civic engagement arm MovePH brought #MoveCebu to the University of San Carlos, gathering over 200 people during a public forum to define what a liveable city should be.

To solidify our long-term commitment to campus journalism and civic engagement, we proudly signed memoranda of understanding with the University of San Carlos, and the University of the Philippines Cebu.

Rappler multimedia reporter John Sitchon, who reports on Cebu and the Visayas region, joined us as we worked directly with participants. You can check out these stories to read more about what happened during the roadshow:

Taking advantage of the momentum generated by the forum, we dove into focused workshops with 35 newly-trained Movers, and leaders from Cebu’s civil society groups to bridge reporting with civic organizing.

Our Movers who chose the civic mobilization track pitched bold, ground-level initiatives tackling community realities across Cebu province.

For example, participants designed action plans to address food safety at the Colon Night Market. Some Movers want to address the lack of housing for displaced families in Minglanilla. One Mover hoped to champion the rights of people with dwarfism.

Meanwhile, Movers who wanted to specialize in community journalism pitched stories tackling gut issues in Cebu, like substandard flood control projects, child labor, and how neighborhood carinderias navigate inflation to keep meals affordable.

Our civil society and academe partners matched this energy during our Partners’ Huddle, where they decided to prioritize four crisis clusters: Ecological, Governance, Services, and Displacement. Together, partners committed to lobbying local councils to prioritize environmental policy over profit, conducting citizen audits, raising awareness of and tackling the energy crisis plaguing Cebu, and fighting for humane relocation sites and protected municipal waters for fishing communities.

Movers and partners are already coordinating on next steps in the Padayon Cebu chat room on the Muni app. To be part of the action, you can join the chat room by downloading the Rappler app for free. If you would like to support Rappler’s Cebu coverage, we hope you consider becoming a Rappler+ member. Rappler+ is our premium membership program that allows you to experience the best of our journalism, while supporting our work. You can join Rappler+ here. – Rappler.com

World.title: PH spotlights South China Sea, ‘fragmenting world’ in ASEAN defense chiefs’ meeting
World.content:
Philippines Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro delivers opening remarks during the 20th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Defence Ministers' Meeting (ADMM) at the Mactan Expo in Cebu, Philippines 28 October 2026.

Chinese Defense Minister Dong Jun skips the ADMM-Plus meeting, as bilateral ties between Manila and Beijing hit their tensest note yet

CEBU, Philippines — Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. told Southeast Asian defense chiefs, whose countries have widely varying ties with superpower China, that the bloc should “not allow differences to divide us from within.”

“ASEAN [Association of Southeast Asian Nations] was founded on the belief that our strength lies in our diversity. We must therefore not allow our differences to divide us from within, and where such differences exist, including in the South China Sea, we shall settle them through peaceful and legal means,” said Teodoro, chairman of the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting, to open the event on Wednesday, October 28.

Regional security, as well as bloc cooperation over issues like disaster risk reduction, will be among the key issues defense officials are expected to tackle in meetings and sideline events from October 28 to 29 at the Mactan Expo in Lapu-Lapu City.

Ministers, as well as working groups, are also expected to tackle protection of underwater critical infrastructure, cooperation for food and energy security, and preparedness for the super El Niño and its possible effects on security.

Play Video

ADMM and the ADMM-Plus is an annual gathering of defense ministers from Southeast Asia and “plus countries” or ADMM dialogue partners Australia, China, India, Japan, New Zealand, South Korea, Russia, and the United States. It is the largest defense diplomacy gathering in ASEAN for the calendar year.

Aside from all 11 defense chiefs from Southeast Asia, their counterparts for almost all plus countries, including US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Japan Defense Minister Koizumi Shinjiro, are participating in the meetings.

As chair of ADMM, Teodoro will preside over all meetings, including two separate “informal meetings” with the US and Japan.

China’s Dong Jun will not be attending ADMM+. Beijing will instead be represented by its defense attache assigned to the Chinese embassy in Manila.

Cebu province has hosted several meetings under the Philippines’ chairmanship, including the first Foreign Ministers’ meeting, and the Summit in May.

Tense PH-China ties

“In a fragmenting world, our internal stability and intra-ASEAN unity are vital, perhaps even, in the future, existential. For it is only when we are united that we can effectively uphold ASEAN centrality and the principles that bind us, such as mutual respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, peaceful settlement of disputes, and the renunciation of the threat or use of force,” said Teodoro, in remarks that preceded a direct mention of the South China Sea.

While disputes over and tensions in the critical waterway won’t be the center of discussions in Cebu, they certainly backdrop the Philippines’ chairmanship both of ASEAN and ADMM.

Teodoro, among the loudest critics of Beijing in the Philippine government, is barred from entering and transacting in China over his statements against the Asian superpower. Just weeks before ADMM, China’s ambassador to Manila was criticized for saying the Philippines should be thankful that they do not use force in its disputes — a statement made in reaction to Teodoro’s assertion that it was Beijing who was causing trouble in the region.

China claims almost all of the South China Sea, based on a supposed historical claim that a landmark 2016 Arbitral Award deemed invalid. Their claim overlaps with maritime claims and entitlements of several ASEAN members, including the Philippines.

In the West Philippine Sea, an area that includes the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone, those overlapping claims have meant recurring confrontations between Chinese and Philippine maritime forces in some areas and features.

Tensions in the South China Sea is a concern for ASEAN not only because several members are claimants. The waterway is where up to a third of global trade passes through.

“ASEAN was founded on the belief that our strength lies in our diversity. We must therefore not allow our differences to divide us from within, and where such differences exist, including in the South China Sea, we shall settle them through peaceful and legal means,” said Teodoro.

ADMM CHAIR. Philippines’ Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. waits for his counterparts’ arrival during the 20th ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting (ADMM), Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026, in Cebu, central Philippines.

US, Japan ties

As chair of ADMM, it’s the Philippines who steers the agenda. It’s almost no surprise that in Cebu, the Philippines is hosting two “informal meetings” with treaty-ally United States and close partner Japan.

Manila’s defense and security ties are deepest and most developed with Washington DC and Tokyo. The two countries are its staunchest partners in South China Sea issues and in its push to modernize the Philippine military. Manila is the first recipient of Japan’s Official Security Assistance (OSA). The US has allocated over $2.5 billion over five years in foreign military financing for the Philippines.

Teodoro is also expected to host a quadrilateral meeting between Hegseth, Koizumi, and Australian Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Minister Richard Marles, a grouping known colloquially as the SQUAD.

The Philippines’ defense engagements — both with traditional and new partners — is spurred, in no small way, by maritime tensions with China.

In ASEAN, member states have varying degrees of closeness and cooperation with Beijing. It’s a difference that’s made cohesion a challenge, especially in a bloc that puts centrality and unanimity at the center of its decision-making and policy-making process. – Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: No report of Trump courtesy call on Sara; Marcos remains president
World.content:
Trump is coming for the ASEAN Summit hosted by Marcos, and Duterte remains Vice President on trial in the Senate

Claim: US President Donald Trump will make a courtesy call on Vice President Sara Duterte when he visits the Philippines next month, and Duterte will be the president by then.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: On October 22, Facebook user Rey Cano Salarda published a post that carries the claim.

It is a text card on a green background that reads, “U.S PRES TRUMP WILL VISIT PHIL. NEXT MONTH COURTESY CALL TO VP SARA, SI VP SARA NA PALA ANG PRESIDENTE NEXT MONTH” (So VP Sara will already be President next month).

As of writing, the post has 29,000 reactions, 2,200 comments, and 1,200 shares.

The facts: There is no report, Palace statement, or White House announcement about a planned Trump courtesy call on Duterte. Trump’s planned visit will be for the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit, which is hosted by the Philippines.

Also, Duterte will most likely not be replacing Marcos as the president next month. Marcos remains in office, and he has not resigned or been removed. Under Article VII, Section 8 of the Constitution, the Vice President takes over only if the President dies, becomes permanently disabled, is removed, or resigns.

The Palace has dismissed as “delusional” claims from Duterte’s camp that the Vice President is ready to replace Marcos.

Duterte is currently on trial before the Senate impeachment court. The trial resumes on November 9, when her defense team begins presenting its evidence on the remaining unexplained wealth article. The trial may or may not lead to her conviction and removal from office, not elevate her. (READ: Dropping 3 impeachment articles vs Sara, who benefits?)

Trump’s visit: Malacañang confirmed on October 14 that Trump will attend the ASEAN Summit and Related Summits in Manila. Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said that while it is confirmed, the rest of the details will not come from her.

The summits run from November 16 to 18 at the Philippine International Convention Center in Pasay City. The Philippines chairs ASEAN this year. Marcos declared those days as special non-working days in Metro Manila.

The White House said Trump will take part in the summit on November 16 before heading to Shenzhen, China for the APEC summit. A US official said Marcos has been inviting Trump for some time. This will be his first visit to the Philippines since 2017.

At the summits, Trump will meet ASEAN leaders and other dialogue partners. The Department of Foreign Affairs expects leaders of China, Japan and South Korea to attend, along with UN Secretary-General António Guterres for the ASEAN-UN Summit. – Cyril Bocar/Rappler.com

Efren Cyril Bocar is a journalist from Llorente, Eastern Samar who graduated with a degree in English Language Studies at the Visayas State University. Cyril is also a graduate of the Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: Hackers target US FEC system, disrupting campaign finance disclosures days before midterms
World.content:
CYBERSECURITY. Silhouettes of laptop users are seen next to a screen projection of binary code are seen in this picture illustration created on March 28, 2018.

The outage prevents organizations from filing the Federal Election Commission's 24-hour and 48-hour spending reports, which show how much political groups and others are spending on specific races

NEW YORK, USA – The US Federal Election Commission’s website was targeted by a hacker or hackers, according to an email seen by Reuters, disrupting the agency’s electronic filings system a week before the November 3 elections.

The hack comes as so-called super PACs and dark money groups spend record sums in the final days of the races. The elections will determine whether President Donald Trump’s Republicans maintain their majorities in Congress for the next two years.

In a statement, the FEC said, “At this time, the FEC’s electronic filing system is currently offline and our IT staff are actively working to restore service.” The FEC, which tracks the spending of candidates and political committees, said users could still search the website for past reports. A status message posted by the FEC said its filing system had been down since around 10 pm ET on Monday (0200 GMT; 10:00 am Tuesday Philippine time).

Around 8 pm ET on Tuesday (0000 GMT; 8:00 am Wednesday Philippine time), a new status message said the issue “has been identified and a fix is being implemented.” The FEC did not immediately return a message seeking comment and a notice on its website said its filing system remained offline.

The FEC does not play a role in administering US elections and the outage should have no effect on voters’ ability to cast ballots.

The outage does prevent organizations from filing the FEC’s 24-hour and 48-hour spending reports, which show how much political groups and others are spending on specific races.

“I’ve never seen this in 26 years,” said Steven Mele, president and CEO at political finance compliance firm MBA Consulting Group.

The FEC posted the notice to its website after campaign finance officers could not file mandatory reports late on Monday.

“We have a bad actor attempting to breach FEC systems. As a result, we’ve had to temporarily shut down our web facing services,” an FEC electronic filings officer said in the email to several campaign compliance firms that night.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and the FBI both referred questions to the FEC.

The midterms are now the most expensive US election in history with roughly $11.21 billion spent on advertising and future reservations so far, according to political ad tracker AdImpact. They have surpassed the previous record set in the 2024 elections when $11.2 billion was spent on all races, including $3.2 billion on the presidential race between Trump and former Vice President Kamala Harris, AdImpact said.

Much of the spending is being driven by super PACs, which can accept unlimited amounts of money from wealthy individuals and corporations and spend as much as they want on campaigns with few restrictions.

The sums being spent in recent weeks are staggering as Democrats gain ground in several Republican strongholds.

Super PACs and dark money groups have spent an average of over $50 million per day over the last week, said Brendan Glavin, research director at nonpartisan campaign watchdog group OpenSecrets. More than $250 million in spending was reported on October 20 alone, he added.

“It’s a big deal,” he said of the outage, which leaves voters in the dark until the filing system is back online.

“These are the key reports that tell us what is happening,” Glavin said. “In the last days of the election this is the only way for us to keep track of where the money’s being spent” and who’s spending it. – Rappler.com

World.title: Marquez’s plan as chief justice bet: No more overburdened courts by 2032
World.content:
FOR CJ. Associate Justice Jose Midas Marquez during the Judicial and Bar Council's public interview for chief justice on October 26, 2026.

'While a courtroom or a courthouse is a physical representation of justice, the true measure of a court is not its buildings or facilities, but the quality of justice it provides,' Marquez says

MANILA, Philippines – Associate Justice Jose Midas Marquez made a big promise when he faced the Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) for his interview as a chief justice candidate.

Marquez, who once served as head of the Supreme Court’s (SC) Office of the Court Administrator, said there will be no more overburdened courts six years from now if he is selected as Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo’s successor.

“By 2032, we should no longer have [an] overburdened court,” said the aspiring chief justice during his public interview on Monday, October 26.

“While a courtroom or a courthouse is a physical representation of justice, the true measure of a court is not its buildings or facilities, but the quality of justice it provides. Citizens do not come to court because of the structure that houses it; they come because they seek protection of their rights, resolution of disputes, and assurance that the rule of law will prevail,” Marquez added.

Marquez is one of the five SC associate justices in the running to become Gesmundo’s successor. The JBC concluded the interviews on Monday and will proceed to deliberations.

Afterwards, the council will submit to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. a short list of nominees. Marcos will then appoint the country’s 28th chief justice.

Marquez is currently the most junior among the candidates and is holding seat no. 12 at the High Court. If chosen, he will serve as chief justice for 10 years, or until 2036.

Plans for the judiciary

During the interview, Marquez said the judiciary faces three perennial problems: congestion of court dockets, delay in resolution of cases, and the perception of alleged corruption.

“So to enhance our court processes, court management, pagandahin pa natin ‘yong internet connectivity not only here in NCR (National Capital Region), but especially in far-flung areas para mas papabilis ang takbo ng resolution ng mga desisyon,” the magistrate said.

“Dapat po meron tayong continuous monitoring of the dockets of all courts nationwide, ‘di lang ang congested courts,” he added.

(So to enhance our court processes, court management, let’s improve our internet connectivity not only here in NCR, but especially in far-flung areas to improve the resolution of cases. We should have a continuous monitoring of dockets of all courts nationwide, not only those which are congested.)

Marquez said that if selected, he will launch his Strategic Plan for Judicial Innovations 2.0 (SPJI) that will run from 2028 to 2032.

SPJI is the brainchild of outgoing Chief Justice Gesmundo which contains the innovations for the judiciary, including digitalization. It has been running since 2022 and will conclude in 2027.

The aspiring chief justice said his SPJI 2.0 will focus on the following:

Sustain and institutionalize SPJI reforms

Invest in people development and people encounter

Reinforce the Court as both a place and a service

Strengthen the Judiciary’s independence and fiscal autonomy

Harness technology and digital transformation to address judicial inefficiencies

Continuous monitoring of the Rules of Court

Initiatives for the Philippine Judicial Academy, which is the “training school for justices, judges, court personnel, lawyers, and aspirants to judicial posts.”

Initiatives for the JBC

More power to the Judicial Integrity Office (JIO). This is the SC office that handles administrative disciplinary cases and ensures accountability within the judiciary.

More power to Office of the Judiciary Marshals. This office was established under Gesmundo to deal with threats and violence against members of the bench and court personnel that affect not only their lives and safety, but also undermine judicial independence.

Play Video

When asked to give at least three laws that the Congress may pass to help the judiciary, Marquez said he wants legislation that will will focus on the creation of more courts – both regular and Shari’ah (Islam) courts.

He said that he also wants a law that clearly defines the role of the Department of Budget and Management in the preparation of the budget of government branches and agencies. Marquez added he also wants a law that will strengthen the mandate, powers, and authority of the SC’s JIO.

As to additional courthouses, Marquez said the construction of halls of justice is not only a concern of the judiciary, but also of local government units (LGU).

“Para sa akin po, ‘yong construction ng hall of justice po, kasi kasama po sa trabaho ng LGU, pasensya na po (For me, the construction of hall of justice is part of the LGU’s job, I’m sorry). Because if you want your LGU to be the best LGU, you have to provide all these services,” he explained.

Marquez also said he wants to standardized the allowances of judges. He explained that it’s an independence issue that some of the judges are receiving allowances from LGUs where their courts are located.

“For me, para po talaga mawala na ‘yong usapin ng independence [of our judges] being encroached upon by the LGUs, may siguro dapat pong pag-usapan or pag-isipang mabuti how we can increase the allowances of our judges and give that allowance,” he said.

(For me, to eradicate the issue on our judges’ independence being encroached upon by the LGUs, maybe we can talk or think carefully how we can increase the allowances of our judges and give that allowance.)

From intern to chief justice?

During the interview, Marquez was also asked about the SC’s power of judicial review – or the mandate to revisit whether another branch of government erred in following rules and in case it violated the Constitution.

He explained that his years as associate justice were honed by his past experiences inside the High Court. He explained that when resolving cases involving other branches, he always looks at the mandate of that specific branch.

“That’s the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court, the judiciary. Maingat na maingat po ako doon (I am really careful about that). I don’t want to overstep the mandate or overreach the mandates of either the executive or the legislative,” the magistrate said.

If he becomes chief justice, Marquez said he will lead, like Gesmundo, with collegiality.

“Kung paano ang naging pamalakad ni Chief Justice Gesmundo, palagay ko po kaya ko rin pong gawin, tularan, o kung kaya pong higitan pa, gagawin po natin (I can emulate the leadership style of Chief Justice Gesmundo, and if I can go beyond it, we will),” he added.

Marquez also revealed during the interview that his age and experience in the bench – being the most junior candidate – were part of the things he considered when he accepted the nomination. The justice said he rose from the ranks – he started out as an intern, court lawyer, spokesperson, and court administrator.

Marquez said he will lead by example if chosen as the next head of the judiciary.

“Para sa akin, I’ve always led by example. So pinapakita ko lang po na inire-respeto natin silang lahat, nagtatrabaho po tayo nang maayos, at nakikinig po tayo sa lahat ng dapat pong pakinggan (For me, I’ve always led by example. So I just show that I respect everyone, I work professionally, and we listen to those who need to be listened to),” Marquez said.

“You just have to do your work…. Do not look for promotion. Just do your work and do it well. There’s no substitute for hard work,” he added. – Rappler.com

World.title: US costs of Iran war rise to over $47B – Pentagon data
World.content:
PENTAGON. The Pentagon building is seen in Arlington, Virginia, US, October 9, 2020.

The Pentagon's latest estimate is tied to the operational costs of carrying out the war, with a projected cost of more than $29 billion to replace expended munitions used in the conflict

WASHINGTON, USA – The US military has spent over $47 billion so far to prosecute the war in Iran, more than 25% higher than the Defense Department’s estimate in July, according to Pentagon data obtained by Reuters.

The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment on its estimate, which has not been shared publicly.

The disclosure about the rising cost of the Iran war comes as Republicans wrestle with the political fallout of the unpopular conflict ahead of the November 3 election that will determine control of Congress for the next two years.

The war’s impact on global energy costs has weighed on support for Republican candidates and hurt President Donald Trump’s approval ratings. Trump’s Republican Party holds a narrow majority in both chambers of Congress.

The Pentagon’s latest estimate was tied to the operational costs of carrying out the war, with a projected cost of more than $29 billion to replace expended munitions used in the conflict.

More than $6 billion would be needed to replace military equipment and so-called “platform losses,” which include the loss of aircraft including many drones lost during the war.

Trump launched the Iran war jointly with Israel in February, predicting ​that the conflict would last a short time.

Trump’s initial strategy in the Iran war focused on first using expensive, high-end precision missiles to bomb Iran’s defenses so it could later use less expensive munitions, including gravity bombs like the air-launched JDAMs, which are plentiful.

But an April ceasefire gave time for Iran to dig out underground storage facilities, bringing back online some Iranian defenses, as well as missiles and drones that had been inaccessible.

Trump has since imposed a naval blockade on Iran to starve it of oil export revenue and held out the possibility of restarting combat operations after the midterm elections. US officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, say the Pentagon has been planning to restart heavy fighting if ordered to do so.

The latest Pentagon estimate compares to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth‘s July estimate of $37.5 billion for the cost of the war.

While the figures include a host of operational costs, from flight operations to cyber support, the US military’s Iran war cost estimates did not clearly account for the massive expense expected to repair damage to US bases sustained by Iranian missile and drone attacks. Rappler.com

World.title: Myanmar Migrant Applications Plunge at Thai CI Centers Amid Boycott
World.content:
The number of Myanmar migrant workers applying for Certificates of Identity (CI) in Thailand has dropped sharply in the past few days following the launch of a social media campaign against the CI process, according to migrant groups and agents.

The Myanmar regime opened five Thai hubs on October 14, offering migrant workers CI required for residency and work. In exchange, workers must comply with a new Labor Ministry mandate to remit 25 percent of their wages through official channels and pay 2 percent annual tax.

The number of registered Myanmar workers in Thailand rose to nearly 3 million as of November 2025, but a significant population remains undocumented.

Many migrants say that as low-wage workers they can barely afford CI application fees, while the regime’s mandatory 6,000-baht remittance rule adds an extra layer of cost.

Labor activists say the boycott is also being driven by reluctance to legitimize the regime or help fund its ongoing military attacks on civilians.

Migrants launched the online campaign on Oct. 18, calling on the Thai government to grant them residency-work permits without CI documents.

Regime Labour Minister Maung Myint slammed the campaign on Oct. 20, insisting the new process was meant to ease CI registration for workers in Thailand. He claimed that around 1,500 workers had used the new centres in the first few days. However, migrant workers groups and agents said applications have plunged as the campaign gains momentum.

“Very few workers are applying for the CI,” Khaing Gyi of the Aid Alliance Committee, which assists migrants, told The Irrawaddy on Tuesday.

“Normally, the CI centre in Samut Sakhon alone receives over 1,000 CI applications daily,” he said, adding that the hub has gone quiet in the past few days.

He estimated that at least 500,000 workers are due to apply for their CI, but few are showing up at centers.

Labor activists said workers were also delaying CI renewal because of the cost.

“Migrants’ income levels vary,” Naing Aung Aung of the Arkan Worker Organization in Thailand told The Irrawaddy. “Some took loans to pay for passport and visa issuance. They don’t have extra savings.”

He said the regime’s remittance scheme is unviable given it can easily be bypassed by bribing corrupt officials. Applicants can secure a CI without evidence of remittance for a fee of 1,500 baht, according to labor activists and agents.

Experts note the new policy benefits the cash-strapped regime while piling financial burdens on low-paid workers and cutting remittance lifelines for their families at home. They argue that instead of restrictions and punishment, workers should be offered incentives to remit money through official channels.

Under the current scheme, Myanmar workers lose at least 5,000 kyats for every 100 baht they remit via regime-endorsed channels. While official channels offer 125 kyat per baht, informal markets offer upwards of 130.

The Labour Ministry continues to push the new scheme, projecting that 2026 inflows will match last year’s total of US$ 5.6 billion. Annual remittances have more than doubled since 2019, driven by the mass emigration of workers escaping the turmoil and economic collapse that followed the 2021 coup.

World.title: Hostage Diplomacy: How the Myanmar Junta Is Weaponizing Jailed Aung San Suu Kyi
World.content:
As the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)’s November summit approaches, the Myanmar junta—desperate for international recognition—has made a series of minor concessions regarding access to jailed civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi.

Highlighting the regime’s ongoing atrocities against civilians, observers and anti-regime groups have warned that the regime’s moves are merely a ploy to win resumption of full participation in ASEAN and ease international pressure.

Since the 2021 coup, the Myanmar regime has been barred from attending high-level ASEAN summits for failing to comply with the bloc’s peace plan, which calls for the immediate cessation of violence against civilians and the opening of a dialogue among all concerned groups, among other things.

Aung San Suu Kyi was allowed to meet with ICRC representatives in Naypyitaw on August 3, and to receive books and a diplomatic letter from King Charles on October 19. The jailed Nobel Peace Prize laureate was also permitted to talk with her youngest son, Kim Aris, on October 22, for the first time in the five years since her arrest.

Domestic and regional observers warn that the regime has started using Aung San Suu Kyi as a political bargaining chip to gain access to the bloc’s upcoming summit.

“The regime led by the sham president Min Aung Hlaing has been trying to scam the world by using hostage diplomacy,” said Debbie Stothard, founder and coordinator of the Alternative Asean Network on Burma.

She cited another recent instance of hostage diplomacy, in which the junta jailed 78 Filipino trafficking victims who had escaped from scam centers. Instead of repatriating them, the regime used the victims as a bargaining chip in negotiations with Maria Teresa Lazaro, the Philippine foreign secretary, who was forced to request the release of her compatriots during a visit to Naypyitaw in January, then thank the internationally-isolated regime for freeing the jailed Philippine nationals.

An ASEAN humanitarian delegation led by the bloc’s special envoy Maria Teresa Lazaro is scheduled to visit Myanmar for two days starting Wednesday.

The tactic was used again with the detention of U.S. citizen Adam Castillo, which allowed the regime to secure engagement with the U.S, Stothard said. A delegation of U.S. officials visited Naypyitaw to secure Castillo’s release.

“The regime continues to use its hostage diplomacy by … dangling Aung San Suu Kyi to secure normalization of relations with ASEAN,” she said. “ASEAN and the international community shouldn’t be easily scammed this way. They shouldn’t be normalizing relations with a gangster who is the architect of genocide and war crimes.”

Thailand welcomed the U.S. engagement with the regime and expected discussions to be held at the upcoming ASEAN summit in Manila on how to proceed with the Myanmar issue, Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow told media on Friday.

The minister, who is working to improve relations between ASEAN and the military regime, commented that the regime’s granting of permission for Aung San Suu Kyi and her son to speak represented a positive development.

Further evidence of the regime’s concerted effort to secure ASEAN’s recognition and support can be seen in Naypyitaw’s recent decision to form an ASEAN Affairs Committee to communicate and cooperate with the bloc.

Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe, who chairs the committee, said it was formed to foster additional channels of engagement with ASEAN. The regime is currently engaging regional neighbors on a country-by-country basis according to priority levels, he added.

Coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing has been engaging with the U.S., and in recent months has visited ASEAN members Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam and Malaysia.

David Gum Awng, deputy foreign affairs minister of the civilian National Unity Government (NUG), told The Irrawaddy he shares the view that the regime is using Aung San Suu Kyi as a political bargaining chip to secure Min Aung Hlaing’s attendance at the upcoming ASEAN summit.

“Civilian leader Daw Aung San Suu Kyi is entirely innocent and is merely a political hostage unjustly detained by the regime for political reasons. Allowing her to receive books and gifts sent by King Charles and permitting a 20-minute phone call with her son is purely a political transaction by the regime,” he said.

He said the regime’s recent moves are a political ploy, despite some ASEAN member countries’ characterization of them as a positive development, and warned that “ASEAN needs to see this reality.”

Mon Mon Myat, lecturer at the Department of Peace Studies at Thailand’s Payap University, remarked that the junta’s apparent relaxation regarding access to the jailed civilian leader “might include hopes of being allowed to attend the ASEAN summit. It appears they urgently need both international recognition and assistance. On the other hand, they might be pushing for this out of fear of becoming more isolated on the international stage if the ICJ ruling comes out later this year.” The International Court of Justice is considering a genocide case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar over the military’s persecution of the Rohingya minority in Rakhine State.

The regime’s charm offensive may be having some effect. Former Japanese Prime Minister Fumio Kishida said in an exclusive interview with Nikkei Asia on October 12 that Japan should assist in Myanmar’s reintegration into ASEAN. For the time being, however, ASEAN as a bloc is upholding its summit ban, citing the failure to honor its peace plan. Known as the Five-Point Consensus, the plan established over five years ago in Jakarta includes calls for an immediate end to violence and the holding of dialogues. Both coup president Min Aung Hlaing and his rubber-stamp parliament have formally rejected the plan. Meanwhile, the regime continues its five-year campaign of airstrikes, shelling and village burnings.

The NUG’s David Gum Awng said ASEAN must clearly and decisively call out the regime’s total failure to implement the peace plan. He warned that bilateral engagement with the junta by individual member states is emboldening the regime’s war crimes against civilians, rather than applying necessary pressure.

“While ASEAN member states may have different views on the country’s crisis, there must be definite consequences if the junta fails to comply with the agreements. Without clear repercussions for their defiance, the regime has absolutely no incentive to cooperate,” he added.

Citing the junta’s ongoing attacks on civilian targets, Stothard noted that hostage diplomacy is a smokescreen for the regime’s continued brutality against its own people.

“ASEAN and the international community should not be engaging or dancing with a regime that has turned Burma into a transnational crime hub, created the worst humanitarian crisis in the region, and will negatively impact ASEAN for years to come,” Stothard said.

World.title: The Fatal Flaw in China’s Myanmar Policy is Economic Collapse
World.content:
While Beijing’s military‑centric approach — backed by its “three bottom lines” — defines China’s Myanmar policy, the ground reality shows that civil war is not the only source of instability. Alongside the widening conflict, Myanmar’s foundations are being shaken by a deepening economic crisis with historical echoes. The collapse of General Ne Win’s Burma Socialist Programme Party regime four decades ago was not triggered by battlefield defeat, but by economic breakdown — a reminder that today’s regime faces the same danger.

Deepening economic crisis

When Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi visited in August 2024, the junta was facing not only military setbacks but also severe inflation marked by surging commodity prices. Thanks to Chinese financial assistance, inflation eased after his trip and the kyat stabilized at around 4,000 per US dollar. But it plunged again after military-staged elections early this year and now hovers near 4,600 per dollar.

Starved of hard currency, the junta restricted imports and choked off border trade. The cost of fuel and cooking oil surged, followed by staples such as rice, eggs, and onions, as well as household electronics and medicines. Vehicle prices soared, and black markets reemerged. Domestic manufacturing, agriculture, and livestock industries — reliant on imported technology, seeds, feed, fertilizers, and medicines — were hit hard, while foreign investment also dwindled.

As the kyat weakens, commodity prices are surging again and shortages are widespread. This is not merely a policy miscalculation: the junta channels all foreign currency into military spending, compounding the economic crisis. Without an end to war, the economic crisis cannot be fixed.

Corrupt state apparatus

Another major issue is systemic corruption in the bureaucracy. Graft grew steadily under military rule from 1988 to 2010 but was restrained somewhat by public oversight during the 2010–2020 reform period. But since the 2021 coup, the entire machinery of government — from Min Aung Hlaing and the top brass down to the lowest ranks — have exploited power for personal gain.

Legal restrictions and licensing requirements have become tollbooths for bribery. Payment is required for import permits, ID cards, passports and the right to travel at home or abroad. Importers routinely pay bribes, while ordinary people face extortion by soldiers and police on the streets. This endemic corruption has also facilitated the boom in narcotics production and online fraud gangs.

Narcotics and online scams

Myanmar is among the world’s largest producers of heroin, methamphetamine, and synthetic drugs, with output now rising annually as officials, soldiers and police turn a blind eye in exchange for bribes.

Online scam syndicates previously confined to borderlands are now spreading inland. Evidence from Karen State and northern Shan’s Kokang shows that gangs are relocating under the protection of military‑linked MPs, administrators, border guards, police, and senior officials. Even as criminal syndicates elsewhere in northern Shan are dismantled, Muse—the only border town Naypyitaw still controls thanks to China—remains an online scam hub, highlighting the regime’s complicity in cyber-fraud.

In other words, the economic crisis is not a standalone problem, but deeply intertwined with systemic corruption, narcotics production, and scams.

Poverty and social collapse

Illicit revenues from narcotics and scam syndicates have flooded Myanmar, fueling inflation and driving property values to unsustainable heights. Ordinary citizens are bearing the brunt as the country’s economic crisis deepens. Chinese loans cannot solve this problem.

The persistent civil war, combined with entrenched corruption and criminality, rampant inflation, and worsening shortages, has created a dire situation. While a handful of elites hoard wealth, most of the population struggles to afford basic food, leaving Myanmar society fractured and unstable.

A UNDP report released on October 8 revealed that one in three Myanmar citizens — over 17 million people — are already experiencing multidimensional poverty, with another 19 million at risk. In total, about 37 million people, or 68 percent of the population, are either poor or vulnerable to poverty.

Years of conflict, displacement, economic collapse, and climate shocks have devastated housing, healthcare, education, and livelihoods, worsening deprivation.

China’s other Myanmar headaches

Beyond these crises, China must also reckon with four other problems.

First is anti‑China sentiment — which is rising not only among resistance forces but also within the regime itself. Resistance anger is fueled by Beijing’s support for a failing military regime, not hostility toward Chinese people.

For the regime, however, anti‑China sentiment remains a core worldview. In times of political, economic, or military crisis, the Myanmar military often resorts to Burman nationalism, routinely stoking anti‑China and anti‑Muslim prejudice. In this way, it diverted public anger over rice shortages in 1967 by orchestrating anti‑Chinese riots. Today, the regime sponsors ultranationalist groups such as Ma Ba Tha to sustain this narrative.

Propping up the regime offers China no protection from Naypyitaw’s deep-seated disdain. This hostility is not incidental but fundamental; Beijing will be forced to confront it again and again no matter how much support it provides.

Second, the regime’s corrupt apparatus continues to protect online scam syndicates, undermining China’s efforts to suppress them.

Third, the regime has closed key border trade gates including Muse and Chinshwehaw once worth billions annually to China. At a time when Chinese goods are cheaper than Japanese or Western equivalents, the border-trade shutdown is a major loss. Meanwhile, talk of opening trade routes with India has alarm bells ringing in Beijing.

Fourth, the regime is seeking to reestablish relations with the United States. While China might accept restoration of normal diplomatic ties, anything deeper would be difficult for Beijing to tolerate given its red line over Western engagement with ethnic armed groups.

‘Three bottom lines’ collapse

China’s policy goal is stability in Myanmar. But by betting on the Myanmar military to deliver it, Beijing has tethered itself to failure. The regime’s reliance on force over negotiations, corruption over the rule of law, entanglement with narcotics and scams—coupled with economic breakdown—guarantee perpetual instability.

Despite Beijing’s support, Myanmar remains mired in conflict and crisis. The “three bottom lines” have not been upheld: civil strife is intensifying, ASEAN engagement is faltering, and international powers are finding new entry points.

China’s core objective — stability in Myanmar — remains unfulfilled.
