World.title: Malaysia to Seek Clarification Over Reports of Detained Myanmar Returnees
World.content:
KUALA LUMPUR—Malaysia will seek clarification from Myanmar over reports that hundreds of migrants recently returned to the country are being held in military detention, Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan said on Monday.

Malaysia in late September sent back around 1,500 Myanmar nationals as it launched a scheme that rights groups say may endanger migrants by returning them to the war-torn country.

Kuala Lumpur said the group agreed to “voluntary” repatriation from detention centers amid an uptick in anti-migrant sentiment in Malaysia.

Myanmar pledged “safe and dignified” returns for its citizens displaced abroad, after criticism from the United Nations and rights groups.

Mohamad told parliament on Monday that Malaysia’s charge d’affaires in Myanmar would investigate the allegations and learn the condition of those reportedly detained.

“If there is news that the 300 people are still being detained, we will ask the Myanmar government to explain to us,” he told parliament in response to a lawmaker’s question.

“We will ask the Myanmar government to ensure that the assurances it gave us are honored,” he added.

Myanmar news outlet the Democratic Voice of Burma reported on Thursday that more than 400 ethnic Rakhine residents who returned from Malaysia earlier this month “remain in military custody” after arriving in Yangon.

They were among a group of 1,476 returnees who arrived by ship outside Yangon, the first of 5,000 that Kuala Lumpur says Myanmar agreed to take back amid the anti-migrant sentiment in Malaysia.

An additional 3,524 people are expected to be repatriated in a second phase.

The UN has warned conditions in Myanmar, which has been consumed by civil war since a 2021 military coup, mean safe homecomings cannot be guaranteed as required under international law.

Myanmar’s coup leader turned president Min Aung Hlaing has been a pariah in many capitals abroad since the putsch, but Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim invited him for talks about returning Myanmar migrants earlier this month.

During the visit, Min Aung Hlaing said migrants from his country held in Malaysian detention centers will be returned home “as soon as possible”.

“We will take those verified nationals back as soon as possible,” he told a joint news conference with Anwar.

The opaque repatriation scheme has been criticized by rights monitors, some fearing ethnic Rohingya may be sent back to a country where they have experienced persecution that rights experts say amounted to genocide.

World.title: Regime Disguises Military Jet Fuel as Diesel to Evade Sanctions: JFM
World.content:
The Myanmar regime and companies linked to it have engaged in international trade fraud, using proxy firms and misclassifying aviation fuel as diesel to conceal imports of fuel used in airstrikes targeting civilians, according to an investigation released Monday by rights group Justice For Myanmar (JFM).

The findings are based on leaked documents from the regime’s Ministry of Commerce, confidential records from its Foreign Exchange Supervisory Committee (FESC), and an analysis of supply networks and market prices.

JFM said the FESC plays a critical role in approving imports of jet fuel that are intentionally and falsely declared as diesel, and in concealing the true buyers.

The FESC was established in 2022 to centralize and strictly regulate foreign currency conversions, imports and overseas transfers. It consists of six high-level regime officers, including Vice-President Nyo Saw, who has served as its chairperson since 2024.

Known to be an important figure in the management of the personal business empire of regime leader Min Aung Hlaing’s family, Nyo Saw is himself sanctioned by the EU and Canada.

The evidence indicates that six aviation fuel shipments arrived using these “evasive measures” between December 2024 and November 2025, JFM said.

During the same period, the regime stepped up airstrikes nationwide as it prepared for its sham election held in December 2025 and January 2026. The imports covered 843,000 barrels worth US$109.6 million and originated in or transited through Singapore and South Africa, the group said.

According to its findings, two Myanmar companies, Dynamic Wave and PP Petroleum Co. Ltd, were listed as importers in the contracts in order to hide the identity of the real buyer, National Energy Prime Aviation Services Co. Ltd (NEPAS).

Contracts naming Thai company Tawan-Oil Trading as the seller showed that Dynamic Wave served as a proxy importer for NEPAS in three shipments valued at $68.49 million and comprising 527,624 barrels.

Separately, Reuters reported on Monday that jet fuel imported under contracts identifying South Africa as the source was actually shipped from Iran. It said Tehran was the Myanmar military’s primary supplier of jet fuel between October 2024 and December 2025.

PP Petroleum imported another three shipments of aviation fuel misclassified as diesel, worth $41.06 million, according to contracts listing Singapore as the loading port. These were also for NEPAS, according to JFM.

NEPAS is a joint venture between regime-controlled Myanmar Petrochemical Enterprise and partner Asia Sun Group.

Asia Sun Group, a network of companies monopolizing the jet fuel supply chain, has established many shell companies in response to sanctions and public scrutiny. PP Petroleum is part of Asia Sun Group.

Some Asia Sun Group companies are sanctioned by the U.S., UK, EU, Canada and Australia—with sanctions dating back to 2022 and 2025—but NEPAS and MPE remain unsanctioned, JFM noted.

Based on its examination of regime documents and an analysis of market prices, JFM found that the regime deliberately mislabeled jet fuel as high-speed diesel to avoid scrutiny, bypass international regulations and minimize sanctions exposure risk.

Highlighting Thai supplier Tawan-Oil Trading and Singapore’s role as a loading hub, JFM called on both countries to investigate the Myanmar regime’s customs fraud and bar their territory, ports and banks from enabling jet fuel shipments.

The rights group demanded that South Africa block all fuel exports to Myanmar and investigate regime documents falsely listing the country as the fuel’s origin. It called on governments to stop granting “false legitimacy” to the regime.

JFM spokesperson Yadanar Maung said the regime’s use of trade fraud to facilitate jet fuel imports suggested that sanctions and public pressure “are biting,” but “clearly not enough.”

She urged governments to coordinate sanctions against the aviation fuel supply networks feeding the regime, and to investigate trade fraud by the regime and its partners to halt the “slaughter of civilians.”

The UNHCR, the UN’s refugee agency, said Myanmar military airstrikes remained the main cause of civilian deaths in the country, and called for an end to the transfer of arms, ammunition, jet fuel and dual-use equipment to the regime.

More than 6,200 civilians have been killed in over 14,000 regime airstrikes since the 2021 coup, according to the now-dissolved Human Rights Ministry of the National Unity Government.

World.title: Myanmar Regime’s Minimum Rice Price ‘a License to Squeeze Farmers’
World.content:
Rice farmers across Myanmar have voiced concern that the minimum price set by the regime is far below market rates and would not even cover their skyrocketing production costs.

The regime’s Committee for the Protection and Promotion of the Rights and Interests of Farmers last week set the minimum floor price for 100 baskets or about 2.09 tons of rice at 1.35 million kyats (around US$300) for monsoon paddy or unmilled rice harvested this year and summer paddy to be harvested next year.

Farmers report that the current market price for 100 baskets ranges from 1.9 to over 2 million kyats, with some areas seeing around 3 million kyats. Premium Paw San rice is selling for 5 to 6 million kyats.

“Here in Naypyitaw, the market price is 1.9 to 2 million kyats,” one farmer told The Irrawaddy. “And even at that rate, after deducting labor and other expenses, almost nothing is left. Costs are too high. Setting the base price at 13.5 million kyats is unacceptable.”

In principle, the base rate is set only in case the market rate is for some reason lower and aims to ensure that farmers are paid fairly—in other words, farmers cannot be paid less than the base rate but can be paid more.

But farmers fear the yawning gap between the two rates is apt to push down market prices to the point where they no longer make any profit at all. That means the regime is tacitly encouraging brokers to weaponize the base price to negotiate lower rates, and farmers burdened with debt will be forced to sell anyway.

Instead, farmers say the calculation should take into account fertilizer, pesticide and labor costs plus loan interest. Farmers say they cannot buy supplies at the regime’s official prices either but must pay market rates for fertilizer, pesticides and harvest labor.

“Fertilizer is sold for 80,000 to 150,000 kyats a bag, and if we buy on credit, monthly interest is 3,000 to 5,000 kyats for each 100,000 kyats borrowed,” said a farmer from Ayeyarwady Region. “So a base price of 1.35 million kyats doesn’t even cover expenses.”

Farmers estimate production costs per acre are around 1.2 million kyats excluding interest, but this year’s monsoon harvest has fallen to only 68 to 75 baskets per acre. If paid the base price of 1.35 million kyats for 100 baskets, they would lose around 200,000 to 300,000 kyats per acre.

According to the Myanmar Rice Federation, Myanmar earned $338 million from rice exports in the first half of fiscal 2026, which began in April.

World.title: Myanmar War Crimes Survivors Look to Denmark for Justice
World.content:
Forty homes. That is how many a woman, now living in Denmark, watched burn in her village in Chin State, western Myanmar. Family members and friends were killed or left permanently disabled by landmines planted by the junta. Like tens of thousands of others from Chin State, she was driven across the border into India.

On Monday, she is asking the Danish authorities to investigate the men responsible.

She has filed a criminal complaint in Copenhagen against members of the Myanmar junta. For her safety she cannot be named. The crimes in the complaint include deliberate killing, mass arson and the forced displacement of tens of thousands of people.

This is possible because of a change in Danish law. Legislation that came into force last year specifically criminalizes war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide. It gives Danish prosecutors a route that did not exist before.

Her lawyer, Copenhagen-based Eddie Omar Rosenberg Khawaja, puts it plainly. “Under the new Danish legislation it no longer matters where the crimes took place, or the nationality of the perpetrators or the victims,” he says. “Victims living in Denmark can request that Danish authorities hold commanders under whose watch atrocities against them occurred responsible.”

That matters because there is nowhere else to go. Myanmar’s courts are controlled by the generals. The Security Council has failed to act. International courts in The Hague—the International Criminal Court and the International Court of Justice—have also been slow. For the people of Chin State, a Danish police station may be one of the few doors that open.

It also fits Denmark’s own history. Tracy Bawi Hlei, chairperson of Myanmar Action Group Denmark (MAGD), which supports the case, says: “Denmark has a history of aligning itself with the pro-democracy movement in Myanmar since before the 1990s, through development aid, support of activists, bypassing the military government and standing in solidarity with human rights movements.”

She sees this case as the next step. “Now, Myanmar people and Danish activists who are part of communities and movements in Denmark are taking a stand for accountability and the international rule of law.” Survivors and crucial evidence, she explains, were identified within Denmark through a collaboration of civil society groups, including MAGD and the Chin Community Denmark (CCDK), which also supports the case.

I run the Myanmar Accountability Project, which supports cases against the junta in Southeast Asia and Europe. I believe the basis for a Danish case is strong.

The Danish government has said so itself. In a statement to the UN on September 30, 2025, Denmark said, as a matter of public record, that Myanmar suffers from a lack of accountability and continued impunity. This complaint invites Denmark to act on that.

The timing is pointed. The Danish Foreign Ministry is closing its embassy in Myanmar. This case allows the Danish government to send a signal that it remains engaged with issues of justice and accountability, and that the rightful aspirations of the people of Myanmar to a just, peaceful and dignified life must be respected.

Meanwhile, the junta is seeking legitimacy. Min Aung Hlaing, the general who led the coup, is now president after sham elections that offered the people of Myanmar no real choice. Those who lived through his campaigns of burning and killing are expected to accept this as normal. They do not.

The country’s condition leaves no room for complacency. According to the latest UN report, more than 16 million people need aid, and the junta is blocking humanitarian access to vast areas where the need is greatest. Nearly 3.8 million people are estimated to have been displaced, many of them several times. A UN Development Programme report published last month found that two-thirds of the population are living in poverty or at immediate risk of falling into it.

The violence is on a scale that few outside the region grasp. More than 100,000 people have died in conflict-related violence since the coup. That makes Myanmar’s conflict the fourth deadliest in the world. This is not a frozen conflict. It is a war on civilians, and state-wide repression compounds the inhuman levels of killing, making justice and accountability even more important.

What the complainant seeks is limited. She is not asking Denmark to end a war. She is asking its police to open an investigation and its prosecutors to take her evidence seriously. She is asking that the commanders responsible be held accountable.

Denmark has said impunity in Myanmar must end. Its new law now gives it a way to act on that. She has come forward, at a risk to herself that most of us will never face. It is now for Danish authorities to decide whether the law means what it says.

Chris Gunness is founder and director of the Myanmar Accountability Project.

World.title: Tokayev Pledges $14 Billion for Infrastructure, Sets 2029 Energy Surplus Target
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan will allocate 6.5 trillion tenge (US$14.3 billion) from the National Fund by the end of 2029 to modernize infrastructure nationwide, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said in his annual state-of-the-nation address on Oct. 28.

Tokayev outlined a People’s Construction program to develop social, transport and engineering infrastructure, create jobs and stimulate economic growth. He described it as potentially the largest infrastructure project in the country’s history.

“I am deeply convinced that this initiative will provide jobs for hundreds of thousands of people, and our entire nation, especially the younger generation, will benefit from it,” Tokayev said.

He characterized the program as a nationwide effort to renew and rebuild civilian infrastructure, but warned that relying solely on state resources would be inappropriate for a project of this scale.

“The logic behind the decisions being made is simple: state funds must become a guarantee for attracting private investment,” President Tokayev said.

He also highlighted that Kazakhstan’s gold and foreign exchange reserves, along with the National Fund’s assets, have exceeded $130 billion.

“The main goal and mission of the National Fund is to carefully preserve and increase the country’s wealth, as well as use it for the benefit of present and future generations,” Tokayev said, noting that the fund had contributed to the country’s financial stability over the years.

Roads and air corridors: Kazakhstan’s logistics ambitions

Tokayev said global logistics was undergoing a major transformation, with vulnerabilities in maritime routes increasing the strategic importance of land-based transport corridors. According to him, around 85% of freight transported from China to the European continent already passes through Kazakhstan. However, he warned that the country could not afford to remain a passive transit territory.

“Being satisfied with the current favorable situation would condemn us to the role of a follower in the future,” Tokayev said. “We must already move toward becoming a full-fledged organizer of international freight flows.”

He called for the development of domestic logistics operators, cargo consolidation and distribution centers, and new manufacturing facilities and commercial sites around transport hubs.

Tokayev also instructed the government to complete the high-quality reconstruction of all road border crossing points next year. He described the condition of Kazakhstan’s roads as an urgent problem, criticizing central and local executive bodies for shifting responsibility and allowing the issue to remain unresolved.

“I repeat: we need very high-quality roads,” he said.

“Without quality roads and modern roadside service infrastructure, Kazakhstan cannot claim the status of a global transit corridor or a Eurasian transport and logistics hub,” Tokayev added.

Tokayev also highlighted Kazakhstan’s strategic position along major air corridors connecting Europe and Asia, describing it as a significant competitive advantage that the country had yet to fully capitalize on.

“For now, enormous revenues are literally flying past our country,” he said, criticizing the lack of tangible progress.

He added that Kazakhstan needs to complete several key tasks to establish itself as a major Eurasian transport hub, with full digitalization of the transport sector among its priorities.

“In the age of artificial intelligence, managing global transit flows with paper waybills is absurd,” Tokayev said. “And it is the shortest path to nowhere.”

Sustainable electricity surplus

Tokayev identified electricity supply as a decisive factor in national competitiveness and economic sovereignty, describing the current period as an “era of electricity.”

Tokayev said the annual volume of 123 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity was critically insufficient for a country expanding its industrial, construction and agricultural sectors while pursuing economy-wide digitalization and the adoption of artificial intelligence, which would require the construction of data centers.

He pointed to the country’s recurring electricity shortages, particularly during winter peak-demand periods, when Kazakhstan buys electricity from neighboring countries at high prices and sells it back in summer at much lower prices.

“This simple ‘business’ has been going on for decades,” he said, questioning claims that the arrangement was normal practice in the energy sector.

Tokayev also criticized delays in developing new generating capacity, citing the previously halted construction of the Balkhash thermal power plant and delays in bringing generating facilities online in Turkistan, Kyzylorda, Almaty and Ekibastuz.

He set a strategic target of achieving a sustainable electricity surplus by 2029. Tokayev instructed the government to update Kazakhstan’s unified long-term energy balance through 2035.

New nuclear power projects

Tokayev also emphasized the strategic importance of nuclear energy, saying Kazakhstan had made the right decision by supporting the construction of a nuclear power plant in a nationwide referendum.

Tokayev described a proposal to establish a state strategic uranium reserve as worthy of serious consideration, saying it could cover the needs of Kazakhstan’s nuclear power plants for the next century.

“I believe it is possible and perhaps necessary to begin construction of the Balkhash nuclear power plant as early as next year and sign a comprehensive cooperation agreement to accelerate the start of construction of the Moyinkum nuclear power plant,” he said.

He stressed that negotiations must be carefully prepared and aligned with Kazakhstan’s national interests.

World.title: Kazakhstan, UN Discuss Steps to Strengthen Cooperation Among Nuclear-Weapon-Free Zones
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and the United Nations have discussed practical measures to strengthen cooperation among nuclear-weapon-free zones and advance the implementation of recommendations from a new UN comprehensive study on the subject.

The forum was hosted by Kazakhstan’s Permanent Mission to the UN in cooperation with the UN Office for Disarmament Affairs (UNODA) on Oct. 27. The event marked the 20th anniversary of the signing of the Semipalatinsk Treaty and the publication of the new UN study, the first comprehensive assessment of nuclear-weapon-free zones in 50 years.

Discussions focused on implementing the study’s recommendations, strengthening cooperation among existing nuclear-weapon-free zones and engaging with nuclear-weapon states.

Participants included UN Under-Secretary-General and High Representative for Disarmament Affairs Izumi Nakamitsu, Mexico’s Deputy Permanent Representative to the UN Porfirio Thierry Muñoz Ledo, Nuclear Threat Initiative Vice President Paul Dean, diplomats from UN Member States, representatives of international organizations and experts in nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation. Ryan Musto of William & Mary in the United States moderated the discussion.

In his opening remarks, Kazakhstan’s Permanent Representative to the UN Kairat Umarov said rising nuclear risks underscored the need to strengthen effective cooperation mechanisms. He called for the study’s recommendations to serve as a basis for concrete joint initiatives and highlighted Central Asia’s contribution to regional security and the nuclear non-proliferation regime.

Nakamitsu commended the longstanding partnership between the UN and Kazakhstan, highlighting their joint efforts to promote cooperation among nuclear-weapon-free zones. Earlier, Kazakhstan and UNODA organized international workshops in Astana in 2019 and 2024 to strengthen cooperation between the zones and improve consultation mechanisms.

Describing the Semipalatinsk Treaty as an example of successful regional diplomacy, Nakamitsu said the study’s lasting value would depend on the practical implementation of its recommendations. She reaffirmed UNODA’s readiness to support further efforts.

Muñoz Ledo emphasized the need to strengthen the institutional capacity of nuclear-weapon-free zones while accounting for their regional differences. He also called for continued dialogue with nuclear-weapon states on legally binding security assurances.

Dean highlighted the potential of nuclear-weapon-free zones to reduce nuclear risks, drawing on the experiences of Kazakhstan, South Africa, Brazil and Argentina. He also outlined plans for an interzonal meeting in Vienna and the development of a dedicated online learning resource for diplomats.

During the open discussion, the ambassadors of Brazil and the United Kingdom stressed the importance of regular consultations among nuclear-weapon-free zones and constructive dialogue with nuclear-weapon States. Experts and civil society representatives proposed stronger coordination, information-sharing and educational cooperation, including initiatives to engage young people.

A representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross highlighted the complementary nature of nuclear-weapon-free zone treaties and the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons.

Concluding the forum, Umarov proposed closer coordination among the five regional nuclear-weapon-free zones and Mongolia to advance shared priorities in dialogue with nuclear-weapon States.

As a follow-up, Kazakhstan, with UNODA’s support, will prepare a concise summary of the discussions outlining participants’ key proposals and potential areas for further cooperation.

World.title: Prince William Praises Kazakhstan’s Success in Restoring Saiga Population
World.content:
ASTANA – Prince William has praised Kazakhstan’s efforts to restore its saiga population, highlighting the country’s conservation achievements during an appearance on the BBC’s The Graham Norton Show on Oct. 23.

The Prince of Wales noted that saigas, which were once on the brink of extinction, have made a significant recovery, emphasizing the role of the Kazakh government in supporting conservation efforts.

According to the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources, Kazakhstan’s saiga population has grown from just 21,000 in 2003 to 4.689 million, according to the results of the spring 2026 census. The recovery has received international recognition. In 2024, Kazakhstan’s Altyn Dala Conservation Initiative won the Earthshot Prize, founded by Prince William, in the Protect and Restore Nature category.

Established in 2005, the initiative is a long-term partnership involving Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources, the Association for the Conservation of Biodiversity of Kazakhstan and international conservation organizations. Its work focuses on restoring saiga populations, protecting their habitats and preserving the country’s steppe ecosystems.

The initiative also participated in London Climate Action Week from June 23 to 27, joining international leaders and organizations to advance climate and nature solutions. Its representatives met with influential figures, including Prince William, during events such as Leading with Impact and Investing for Impact.

Kazakhstan’s saiga recovery has become a prominent example of wildlife conservation, demonstrating the potential of sustained government support and partnerships between national and international conservation organizations.

World.title: Air Astana Expands Winter Flights as Vietjet Offers Promotional Fares to Hanoi and Prague
World.content:
ASTANA – Air Astana has introduced its winter flight schedule, adding new international destinations and increasing frequencies on popular holiday routes, while Vietnamese carrier Vietjet is expanding its network and offering promotional fares from $135 on flights from Almaty to Hanoi and Prague.

Air Astana’s winter schedule, effective from Oct. 25 through March 27, 2027, includes new routes to Japan, Oman and Malaysia, alongside additional flights to popular destinations in Asia and the Middle East.

The airline will launch regular flights between Almaty and Tokyo’s Narita Airport on Nov. 30, operating twice a week. Direct flights between Astana and Bangkok will begin on Dec. 11, with departures on Tuesdays and Fridays, complementing daily services from Almaty.

Flights to Salalah, Oman, from Almaty and Astana began on Oct. 23. From Dec. 25 through March 27, 2027, Air Astana will also operate three weekly flights from Almaty to Langkawi, Malaysia.

The airline is increasing frequencies on several established holiday routes. From late October, flights from Almaty to Malé in the Maldives will operate six times a week, with daily departures during peak periods around New Year and Nauryz. Services to Phu Quoc, Vietnam, will run five times a week from Almaty, increasing to daily flights in December, while Astana will have three weekly flights to the island.

Flights from Almaty to Dubai will increase to 12 per week, while services from Astana will rise to 10 per week. Flights from Almaty to Phuket, Thailand, will increase to seven per week, rising to nine per week from early December. The airline will also continue services between Almaty and Shanghai and between Astana and Guangzhou.

In 2026, the Air Astana Group added eight regular and charter destinations from Astana: Guangzhou, Bangkok, Larnaca, Dalaman, Batumi, Issyk-Kul, Salalah and Yining. Together with the seven routes launched in 2025, the group’s network from the capital has expanded to 32 destinations. Weekly international flights from Astana have increased from 99 to 116.

“During the 2026–2027 winter season, Air Astana is expanding its international route network by launching flights to Tokyo, Oman and Langkawi. Increased frequencies to the Maldives, Phuket and Dubai will allow passengers to plan their winter holidays and festive travel more conveniently,” said Yerbolat Baisalykov, senior vice president for commercial planning and revenue management at Air Astana.

Meanwhile, Vietjet is offering one-way Eco fares starting at $135, including taxes and fees, on flights between Almaty and Hanoi and between Almaty and Prague.

The promotional fares are available for booking until 9 p.m. on Nov. 1 through the airline’s official website and mobile app. The offer applies to flights departing between Nov. 1 and March 31, 2027, according to the company’s press service.

After launching flights between Almaty and Hanoi and between Almaty and Prague earlier in October, Vietjet is further expanding its Asian network. The airline will introduce flights between Hanoi and Tainan and resume services between Ho Chi Minh City and Chiang Mai. Both routes will operate four round-trip flights per week.

Vietjet’s international network also includes services connecting Ho Chi Minh City with the Maldives, Cebu and Clark, as well as routes linking Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City with other destinations in Asia.

The new services are expected to provide travelers from Kazakhstan with more options for exploring Northeast and Southeast Asia via Vietnam, while supporting tourism, trade and cultural exchange across the region.

World.title: Kabul’s Qosh Tepa Canal and Water Security Challenges for C5
World.content:
Domestic political, economic and security dynamics in Afghanistan directly impact countries in close proximity to Kabul. This includes Central Asian states, which find themselves impacted by the ongoing Qosh Tepa Canal project. It originates from the Amu Darya River in Afghanistan’s Balkh province and extends to Jawzjan, Faryab while finishing at the Andkhoy district. Conceived in the 1970s under President Daoud Khan, feasibility studies were conducted in 2020, a year before the U.S. withdrawal from Kabul in 2021. Since then, the interim Taliban government prioritized its development as an integral, water driven project to address food security shortages amid dwindling reserves and massive poverty.

Spanning 285 kilometers, a width of 100 meters and depths of 8.5 meters, the Qosh Tepa’s intake is located adjacent to Uzbekistan’s Surkhandayra region near Termez. It is financed entirely through Afghan revenues generated from customs and taxes with Phase II of the project dealing with excavation witnessing significant progress. As per Kabul’s National Development Corporation, excavation reached 98% completion while structural construction of canal embankments and slope readiness stood at a readiness of 90.5%. Institutional shifts have also been underway in Phase 1.

However, despite assurances from the Taliban that regional cooperation for Qosh Tepa needs to take place, the project has resulted in lingering mistrust between Afghanistan and downstream riparian states. The Taliban has opted for unilateral measures on water management resulting in large amounts of water being potentially lost to sandy soils in the absence of concrete walls and reinforced banks. The unilateral completion of the Qosh Tepa clearly constitutes an existential water security threat as it alters the balance of influence of countries along the Amu Darya River basin. While Central Asian states have a vested stake in witnessing Afghanistan’s domestic prosperity and water security, the unilateral pursuit of Qosh Tepa intensifies water stress levels for the Central Asian states along the northern border.

Alarm bells rang as early as March 2026 when Uzbekistan’s water resources minister cautioned that Afghanistan’s annual withdrawals of approximately four billion cubic meters could translate into significant agricultural risks for Tashkent. Uzbekistan remains particularly vulnerable as large swathes of its agricultural land remain dependent on Amu Darya water in regions of Karakalpakstan and Khozerm.

Lack of unfettered access to critical water supplies during peak periods would hence, entail significant losses to Uzbekistan’s crop yields which, in turn, increases operational costs for water management and negatively impacts rural areas acting as agrarian ecosystems. This is significant in the year 2026 as the Amu Darya River remains integral for localized irrigation systems otherwise damaged due to the decades long dryness of the Aral Sea which initially lied between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. The Tuyamuyun Reservoir for example fell by more than 600 mcm with volumetric depletion resulting in larger salination risks. Additionally, unilateral pursuits from Kabul come amid Central Asian states having to contend with rising temperatures, glacial melts, possibilities of Glacial Lake Outburst Flooding (GLOF) and seasonal variations as existential threats. Amid this backdrop, Kabul continues to invest in capacities beyond water historically allocated to it in the absence of being a party to post Soviet regional water sharing mechanisms.

Turkmenistan’s case is another pertinent one in this regard. As another increasingly dependent country, on the Amu Darya River for agricultural sustenance, reduced access to water increases competition for Ashgabat between three key nodes of its local economy including production of crops, agricultural settlement needs and environmental requirements. These issues can potentially be addressed through pursuing bilateral technical cooperation with Afghanistan towards more durable and predictable water mechanisms for irrigation efficiency in downstream networks. This however, remains dependent on the Kabul regime being open to pursuing bilateral cooperation with states directly affected which has so far remained elusive amid the unilateral pursuit of the Qosh Tepa Canal. Fluctuations due to seasonal flows, jolts to reservoir operations and hydropower development challenges also remain integral for countries such as Tajikistan that are heavily reliant on agricultural sectors and remittances to support local economies. The Qosh Tepa Canal, however, makes existing frictions with Afghanistan over water allocations more pronounced given that Dushanbe has to balance its energy requirements with declining water levels.

With almost half of the project complete and maximum completion slated for 2028, downstream countries are clearly facing multidimensional challenges from Kabul’s unilateral pursuits. The threat remains palpable despite calls for regional cooperation. Central Asian governments can hence propose the establishment of an Amu Darya Dialogue with Afghanistan for permanent contact groups with relevant ministries and technical experts. There is also a need to negotiate a practical water management mechanism for dispute resolution with proper monitoring of the Qosh Tepa to avoid discrepancies. These measures however, remain dependent on Afghanistan being open to pursuing this project through multilateral frameworks (which it has politically), but is concomitant with its unilateral pursuits.

For all five Central Asian states however, the water security threat is real and the key is to act now.

The author is Hamzah Rifaat, the president of Initiate Futures, a policy think tank. He is also an author for the Trends Group in Abu Dhabi and is cooperating with Nightingale Int.

World.title: South Korean Burger Chain Mom’s Touch to Open 50 Outlets in Kazakhstan
World.content:
ASTANA – South Korean burger chain Mom’s Touch plans to open at least 50 outlets in Kazakhstan over the next decade as it expands into Central Asia through a franchise agreement with local food group Shin-Line, The Korea Herald reported Oct. 26.

The first outlet is expected to open in the first half of 2027. The agreement also covers the Kyrgyz Republic, while the company plans to expand into major Kazakh cities, including Astana.

“We are preparing to open our first store in the first half of next year and develop Kazakhstan into a key base for our Central Asian operations,” a Mom’s Touch official said in a comment to The Korean Herald.

Mom’s Touch plans to introduce its signature chicken burgers made with whole chicken-thigh fillets, along with fried chicken and pizza.

Its local partner, Shin-Line Group, has a cold-chain logistics network serving about 10 countries and operates more than 70 outlets of a South Korean convenience store chain, mainly in Almaty.

The expansion follows Mom’s Touch’s entry into Uzbekistan in 2025.

Founded in South Korea in 2004, Mom’s Touch built its brand around chicken burgers made with whole chicken-thigh fillets rather than ground meat. Its signature Thigh Burger has helped establish the chain as a major domestic competitor to international fast-food brands.

World.title: Kazakhstan Targets Domestic Drone Industry Development by 2029
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan aims to develop its domestic drone industry by 2029, focusing on local manufacturing, digital flight management, workforce training and the use of unmanned systems across key economic sectors, the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development reported on Oct. 27.

Eighteen government bodies, including the ministries of transport, defense and internal affairs, will coordinate efforts to establish common regulations, develop infrastructure and expand the use of drones while addressing public safety concerns.

Domestic production and digital infrastructure

Kazakhstan plans to introduce a unified digital platform for unmanned aircraft systems and automated traffic management (UTM). The service will bring aircraft registration, applications and flight route approvals into one electronic system. To support local manufacturing, the government proposes incentives, public procurement preferences and long-term offtake contracts for companies registered with Astana Hub. Support will target production of critical hardware, communications systems and secure software, rather than basic assembly alone.

The country also aims to establish at least two research and development centers in partnership with universities and international technology companies and train at least 1,000 specialists, including engineers, drone operators, software developers and cybersecurity experts.

From classrooms to industry

Drone education is expected to expand from schools to technical colleges and universities. Planned measures include aeromodelling classrooms, specialized equipment for science and technology education, updated university curricula and annual student competitions in unmanned technologies.

The government also wants to expand drone use in agriculture, energy, mining, logistics, municipal services, emergency monitoring and environmental protection. Relevant agencies will identify practical applications and develop guidelines and incentives for businesses and public institutions.

Supporting infrastructure will include vertiports, drone ports, automated charging stations, radio frequencies and satellite communication channels. A pilot project to test autonomous freight transportation is scheduled for 2027-2028.

Safety and regulation

The government is considering transferring some oversight of drone operations to the Ministry of Internal Affairs, introducing mandatory liability insurance for drone owners, and setting cybersecurity requirements for communications. Operator certificates would be issued through specialized public service centers. The ministry has invited domestic entrepreneurs, developers and engineers to submit projects with export potential and proposals for implementing the initiative.

The broader objective is to build a domestic industry that can supply Kazakhstan’s economy and compete in international markets.

World.title: Kazakhstan Maps Water Risks Through 2040 as Regional Cooperation Takes Center Stage
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan is seeking to make water-sharing across Central Asia more transparent through real-time monitoring and shared data as it prepares for possible declines in water availability through 2040. The country does not currently face a nationwide water deficit, but its dependence on rivers flowing across national borders makes water security a regional issue, Water Resources and Irrigation Minister Nurzhan Nurzhigitov said in an interview with Tengrinews published on Oct. 27.

Kazakhstan’s average annual river runoff is about 100 billion cubic meters, with approximately 45% of its river water coming from abroad. The economy, agriculture, industry and housing and utilities sectors collectively use about 25 billion cubic meters annually, according to the minister.

Seven of Kazakhstan’s eight river basins are connected to transboundary waters. The country receives water from the Kyrgyz Republic, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, China and Russia.

The dependence is particularly pronounced in the south, where much of the country’s irrigated agriculture is concentrated. About 90% of the water supplied by the Syr Darya River to the Turkistan and Kyzylorda regions is transboundary. Approximately 75% of the water available to the Zhambyl Region from the Chu River comes from Kyrgyzstan.

“Water availability has become a strategic issue and a matter of national security,” Nurzhigitov said.

Building trust through shared data

One of Kazakhstan’s priorities is to improve the transparency and accuracy of information exchanged by countries that share river basins. Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan have agreed to automate water accounting at 10 sites along the Syr Darya, with five in each country. The German Society for International Cooperation, or GIZ, helped prepare the project documentation. Kazakhstan has already built two hydrological monitoring stations using funds from the Turkistan regional administration. The minister said the two countries had jointly checked the stations and could now see the same data in real time.

In January 2026, Kazakhstan proposed developing a plan to digitize the entire Syr Darya basin. Tajikistan agreed to participate, and a working group was established involving Kazakhstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. Its first meeting was planned for early November, with Kyrgyzstan potentially joining the initiative later.

“If we digitize the entire basin, we will see how much water flows through it and how each country fulfills its obligations. This will increase trust. There will be no situation where one country says, ‘I sent this much water,’ while another claims it received nothing,” Nurzhigitov said.

The plan for automated water accounting across the Syr Darya basin has already been developed and sent to the countries concerned, according to a note accompanying the Tengrinews interview. However, the minister did not specify a timeline or cost for a fully integrated system. The current initiative is narrower than a shared digital platform covering all five Central Asian countries. Its initial working group involves three countries, with Kyrgyzstan expected to be invited later.

Kazakhstan is also developing its own water information infrastructure. The ministry is creating a national information system and plans to open public access to selected data in 2027. The ministry is also developing the TALSIM hydrological modeling system for flood forecasting, developed in cooperation with the United Nations Development Program (UNDP), and wants to add drought-prediction capabilities.

Cooperation or competition over water?

Nurzhigitov emphasized the importance of regional cooperation, saying that water brings Central Asian countries together rather than inevitably pushing them toward conflict.

“Water unites us,” he said.

In 1992, the five countries’ water ministers signed an agreement in Almaty to use water jointly and rationally. The International Fund for Saving the Aral Sea and its associated commissions provide additional mechanisms for regional dialogue.

According to Nurzhigitov, the commissions meet at least four times a year to discuss water forecasts, available volumes and allocation limits. He said there had been no violations of agreed limits over the past three years.

Kazakhstan has also proposed a framework convention on the rational use of Central Asia’s water resources. The ministry has approved the draft domestically and sent it to neighboring countries. Discussions are underway to combine the countries’ proposals into common rules that could help limit climate change’s impact.

Asked whether one country might decide to take more water than agreed, Nurzhigitov pointed to water diplomacy and the obligations shared by countries along transboundary rivers.

“That will not happen, because water diplomacy and accountability exist. These are transboundary rivers, and each country has obligations that must be fulfilled. That is why this will never happen,” he said.

Drought exposes the limits of regional agreements

Kazakhstan’s experience in 2021 demonstrated the economic and social consequences of severe drought. According to official figures published by the Prime Minister’s press service on Aug. 12, 2021, 1,161 head of livestock had died in the Mangystau Region by Aug. 10. Another 553 livestock deaths were reported in the Aral district of the Kyzylorda Region amid a lack of water at watering points and dry pastures.

Water shortages again threatened agricultural production in the Zhambyl Region in 2023, when low inflows affected the Chu and Talas river basins. Reporting by Kazinform on Aug. 11, 2023 detailed the scale of the shortfall. From April 1 to Aug. 11, inflow into the Kirovsk Reservoir in Kyrgyzstan, which supplies the Talas River, reached just 60 million cubic meters, compared with 300 million cubic meters during the same period a year earlier. Inflow into the Orto-Tokoy Reservoir, which releases water into the Chu River, reached 55 million cubic meters, against 256 million cubic meters in 2022.

The shortage put about 4,000 hectares of onions and sugar beets at risk, Kazinform said, citing a regional official from the agency responsible for maintaining hydraulic structures.

Tengrinews’ background information accompanying its interview noted that the 2023 shortage was not simply a matter of Kyrgyzstan failing to meet its obligations. Low snowfall and rainfall had also reduced water availability on the Kyrgyz side, leaving both countries affected by the dry conditions.

Such episodes highlight a central challenge for the region: agreements can establish rules for sharing water, but they cannot guarantee sufficient supply when river flows decline.

Planning for 2040

Nurzhigitov also shared Kazakhstan’s plans for all eight water basins over five-, 10-, and 15-year horizons, extending through 2040. The plans will assess three water-availability scenarios and estimate how much water different sectors could receive under each. The minister said drinking water supplies would take priority if water were scarce.

Separately, the ministry’s press service told Tengrinews that the basin plans would account for scenarios involving reductions in water availability of 50% and 75%.

The longer-term outlook is a key reason for moving from annual allocation decisions toward more detailed planning. Nurzhigitov said forecasts suggest that water availability across Central Asia could decline by 15 billion cubic meters by 2040. This is a forecast, not a certainty, but it underscores the need to prepare for several possible outcomes.

The plans aim to help the government determine where water infrastructure is needed, how to allocate available resources, and which economic activities can be sustained under different conditions.

The ministry is also working to reduce losses and improve water efficiency at home. Agriculture accounts for about 60% of Kazakhstan’s water use, according to Nurzhigitov. Water-saving technologies were being applied to more than 700,000 hectares in 2026, with estimated savings of about 1 billion cubic meters.

By 2030, Kazakhstan aims to expand the area using such technologies to 1.3 million hectares, potentially saving an additional 2 billion cubic meters. Industrial enterprises are also expected to increase water reuse and recirculation.

As part of a broader package of measures, Kazakhstan aims to save and accumulate about 10 billion cubic meters of water by 2030 through infrastructure upgrades, new reservoirs, digitalization and more efficient water use.

World.title: Aliyev discusses peace, external threats and ‘double standards’ at Baku forum
World.content:
Aliyev’s speech at Baku Dialogue Forum

Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev spoke at the opening of the 7th World Forum on Intercultural Dialogue in Baku on 27 October. In his speech, he addressed peace efforts with Armenia, the role of international organisations, Azerbaijan’s foreign policy and security.

Aliyev said the country faced no internal threats, criticised “double standards” in international politics and proposed using Azerbaijan’s experience of transitioning from war to peace to help resolve other conflicts.

The World Forum on Intercultural Dialogue brings together representatives of governments, international organisations and experts from different countries to discuss intercultural and interfaith dialogue. The forum was first held in Baku in 2011 as part of the Baku Process initiative launched by Azerbaijan in 2008. It was originally intended to take place every two years. After a break caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, the forum resumed in 2024. This year’s seventh edition takes place from 27 to 29 October under the theme “Dialogue for a Shared Future”.

Intercultural dialogue and national unity

Aliyev described Azerbaijan’s geographical position between Europe and Asia as an important factor in fostering intercultural ties. He said religious and ethnic tolerance, as well as traditions of multiculturalism, were among the foundations of the country’s stable development.

The president said members of different ethnic and religious groups in Azerbaijan enjoyed equal constitutional rights and lived in an atmosphere of mutual understanding. According to him, the idea of Azerbaijani identity united different ethnic groups, and this unity had been evident even during the most difficult periods in the history of independent Azerbaijan. As an example, he cited the participation of members of different ethnic and religious groups in the Second Karabakh War.

Aliyev recalled that October marked the 35th anniversary of the restoration of Azerbaijan’s independence. He stressed that, despite changes in political systems, the Azerbaijani people had managed to preserve their language, traditions and national identity. The president said the country’s achievements since independence were the result of the Azerbaijani people’s efforts and that its development had taken place without international assistance.

“All potential threats come from beyond our borders”

In the part of his speech devoted to security, Aliyev said Azerbaijani society demonstrated unity on all issues. In his assessment, the country faced no internal threats, while all potential risks came from abroad.

“All potential threats come from beyond our borders,” the president said.

He compared ideological risks to physical threats and stressed the need to remain vigilant to protect national identity, statehood, independence and the country’s way of life. However, Aliyev did not specify which countries or organisations might pose such threats.

Karabakh negotiations and military operations

Aliyev said that restoring Azerbaijan’s territorial integrity had been the country’s main goal for most of its independence. The president criticised the years of negotiations over the Karabakh conflict, saying they had been aimed not at resolving the conflict but at freezing it.

He justified Azerbaijan’s military actions by citing the right to self-defence under the UN Charter.

According to the president, Azerbaijan restored its territorial integrity and sovereignty as a result of the 2020 war and the 2023 military operation, independently securing the implementation of UN Security Council resolutions adopted in 1993.

Peace with Armenia and experience of ending war

Speaking about relations with Armenia, Aliyev said that Azerbaijan had initiated peace efforts after the end of hostilities. According to him, the draft peace agreement initialled in the summer of 2025 had also been prepared by Baku.

The president stressed that Azerbaijan had not sought a protracted war and had decided not to continue the confrontation after achieving its military objectives. He noted that the desire for revenge could make war endless. In Aliyev’s view, it was important not only to achieve victory but also to know when to stop and offer peace.

The president suggested that parties involved in armed conflicts study Azerbaijan’s experience. He acknowledged that every conflict had its own characteristics but noted that ambition, aggression, the pursuit of superiority and a sense of impunity all played a role in their emergence.

UN resolutions, sanctions and “double standards”

Aliyev called for special attention to be paid to establishing a mechanism to ensure the implementation of UN Security Council decisions as part of discussions on UN reform. He criticised the failure to implement four resolutions on the Karabakh conflict for many years and the absence of sanctions against Armenia.

The president recalled that numerous sanctions had been imposed on countries to Azerbaijan’s north and south, describing the different approach towards Armenia as an example of “double standards”. He accused Armenia of occupying around 20% of Azerbaijan’s territory, carrying out ethnic cleansing and destroying religious and historical monuments. According to him, one million Azerbaijanis had been forced to flee their homes, while 65 mosques had been destroyed in Karabakh.

In criticising “double standards”, Aliyev addressed not only the international community’s response to wars. He also described attempts by other countries to dictate how Azerbaijan should live and what decisions it should make as unacceptable.

The president said Azerbaijan did not interfere in the internal affairs of other countries and expected the same treatment in return. According to him, displays of disrespect towards Azerbaijan and attempts to impose outside demands on the country had always met with firm resistance and would continue to do so. Aliyev also noted that relations based on mutual respect could help reduce the number of international conflicts.

Partnerships with US, China and Europe

Speaking about foreign policy, the president described Azerbaijan as a pillar of stability in an unstable region. He attributed the country’s stronger international standing to its independent policies, economic potential and role in the energy and transport sectors.

Aliyev highlighted strategic partnerships with China and the US, as well as strategic partnership agreements with ten EU member states. The president said Azerbaijan would host a summit of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation in 2027 and a summit of the European Political Community in 2028.

He also recalled the summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia, held in Baku in October. According to him, Azerbaijan’s chairmanship of the organisation had been extended for another two years, and the country had been invited to become a full member of the Central Asian Consultative Format. Aliyev described these decisions as recognition of Azerbaijan’s growing role on the international stage.

External debt, energy and transport routes

Turning to economic issues, Aliyev said Azerbaijan’s external debt stood at just over 5% of GDP. He highlighted energy exports and international transport links as factors strengthening the country’s position.

In his view, Azerbaijan’s infrastructure and political ties, as well as its geographical location, played an important role in the development of international transport routes.

The president stressed that developing international transport links required maintaining good relations not only with neighbouring countries but also with their neighbours.

Peace agreement initialled in Washington and region’s future

Concluding his speech, Aliyev noted that both positive and negative developments had taken place around the world since the previous forum. He cited the outbreak of new wars in neighbouring regions as negative developments and the peace process with Armenia as a positive one.

The president recalled that the text of a peace agreement had been initialled in Washington in August 2025, with the participation of Donald Trump. Aliyev stressed that, at that stage, the agreement had only been initialled, not signed. The US president had, however, signed a trilateral declaration as a witness. According to Aliyev, this process marked a new chapter for the South Caucasus.

World.title: ‘We want to help Armenia find markets beyond Russia’, says Dutch foreign minister
World.content:
The Netherlands to support Armenian entrepreneurs

“The Netherlands wants to help Armenian businesses, including flower growers, find alternative markets for their products outside Russia,” Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen said in Yerevan.

At a joint news conference with his Armenian counterpart, Ararat Mirzoyan, he stressed that Russia’s economic restrictions were creating difficulties for Armenian businesses, particularly in the flower-growing sector.

“We welcome the opportunities that the EU’s autonomous trade measures offer Armenia. We hope Armenia will make full use of this opportunity. The Netherlands will continue to support efforts to diversify Armenia’s economy,” he said.

On 24 September, the Council of the EU gave final approval to a regulation introducing autonomous trade measures for Armenian goods. The regulation removes import duties on around 80% of Armenia’s exports to the EU. The preferential trade regime will remain in force for two years.

Dutch foreign minister offers help in finding missing persons

The Dutch foreign minister welcomed the steps Armenia and Azerbaijan have taken over the past year as part of the peace process.

“For peace to take hold in this region, it is crucial that the process culminates in the signing of a peace agreement. We fully support you,” he stressed.

Berendsen announces initiative for both Armenia and Azerbaijan

The initiative will provide funding to help establish the fate of people missing on both sides.

“It is vital to build bridges of trust and make this an integral part of the peace process. The Netherlands stands ready to provide financial support and, where possible, assistance in other forms.”

Armenian Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan thanked his Dutch counterpart for the initiative.

“The issue of missing persons is extremely sensitive and important for both Armenia and Azerbaijan. In my view, the involvement and contribution of third parties such as the Netherlands in this area will be welcomed by everyone.”

Asked by journalists about Armenian prisoners held in Baku, the Dutch foreign minister did not give a direct answer. He reiterated that his country supports the establishment of lasting peace between Armenia and Azerbaijan. He noted that the process would require the resolution of both “simple and difficult issues”.

‘There may be a political motive’: Armenian foreign minister on plans to expel Armenia from the EAEU

Journalists asked Armenia’s foreign minister for his views on a document recently prepared by the Eurasian Intergovernmental Council concerning the possible expulsion of Armenia from the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU).

The document itself states that the charter of the Russian-led economic bloc contains no mechanism for terminating a country’s membership at the decision of the other members. This means that Armenia itself would have to decide to change its membership status.

However, the council’s experts, who prepared the document, cite the Vienna Convention to support their argument that Armenia’s membership could be suspended. The convention allows other states to terminate a country’s participation in a multilateral treaty if it commits a material breach.

“For such a scenario to become possible, a partner — the one whose actions the others are unhappy with and whom they want to expel or suspend — would have to breach its obligations within the organisation. The other four partners could then say: ‘You are breaking our rules, dear fifth friend. Thank you and goodbye.’ But Armenia has breached nothing and has no intention of doing so,” Ararat Mirzoyan explained, commenting on the convention’s provisions.

He stressed that Armenia had fulfilled its commitments in good faith and expected its EAEU partners to do the same.

The minister believes Armenia’s EAEU partners have tried to find legal grounds for expelling the country, but he rejects their arguments.

“We all understand that there is a political motive here, possibly even a political instruction to lawyers to find a legal justification for a political decision.”

Experts in Armenia have linked the actions of its EAEU partners to the country’s efforts to diversify its international ties and move closer to the European Union.

Mirzoyan said Yerevan would make its decisions based on its own national interests and sovereign rights, which were not up for negotiation. At the same time, Armenia would continue constructive co-operation with its partners in the bloc. Alongside Russia, the EAEU includes Belarus, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan.

Armenia–Netherlands bilateral co-operation

Ararat Mirzoyan praised the Netherlands for supporting democratic reforms in Armenia and efforts to deepen relations between Armenia and the EU.

He said the two sides discussed the situation in the South Caucasus and the wider region during a one-to-one meeting and subsequent expanded talks. They also reviewed their bilateral agenda, with a particular focus on economic co-operation. The talks paid special attention to implementing the priorities set out in the Joint Declaration on Strategic Partnership, which the two countries signed in March 2025.

“Political dialogue is at a very high level. It is active and effective. We can also see economic co-operation gradually developing, with the figures growing. However, we recognise that significant potential remains untapped,” the minister said.

He added that the two countries planned to deepen co-operation in several areas, including healthcare, infrastructure, agriculture and floriculture. On the latter, he said that “our flower-producing companies have already established ties with world-renowned Dutch firms”.

Meanwhile, the Centre for the Promotion of Imports from developing countries (CBI) has launched a year-long programme in Armenia. The initiative aims to help 21 Armenian producers of dried fruit and nuts develop their export potential and enter markets in the Netherlands and other EU countries.

World.title: “Gossip, myths and manipulation” – fifth day of hearings on banning opposition parties held in Georgia
World.content:
Georgia opposition ban trial

On 27 October, Georgia’s Constitutional Court held the fifth day of hearings on the merits of a lawsuit filed by the ruling Georgian Dream party seeking to ban five opposition parties. At this stage, the court is hearing arguments from the parties involved in the case.

The lawsuit names the United National Movement, Coalition for Change, Lelo – Strong Georgia, Gakharia for Georgia and the Federalists. Georgian Dream argues that these parties have violated Article 23 of the Constitution, which prohibits political parties whose aims include overthrowing or forcibly changing the country’s constitutional order. One of the arguments is that the parties refuse to recognise the legitimacy of the current authorities. The lawsuit also accuses them of organising attempts to overthrow the government. The United National Movement faces additional accusations of undermining Georgia’s independence and violating its territorial integrity. The lawsuit holds the party responsible for the August 2008 war with Russia over South Ossetia, when it was in power. All five opposition parties reject the accusations. Hearings are scheduled to continue through 30 October. The court must deliver its final ruling by 24 June 2027.

At the 27 October hearing, three representatives of the United National Movement appeared before the court: Ana Tsitlidze, Levan Bezhashvili and Alika Kuprava.

Ana Tsitlidze spoke for the longest time. She criticised the legal grounds for the lawsuit and the evidence presented, and questioned the judges’ impartiality. She argued that the case was politically motivated and that banning the parties would restrict political pluralism.

Tsitlidze spoke at length about high-profile criminal cases from the period when the United National Movement was in power in Georgia. She also addressed corruption allegations, relations with international partners and the events of the August 2008 war.

Whenever she mentioned a particular official by name, the presiding judge urged her to be more restrained and interrupted her speech.

With these statements, one of the parties defending itself in the case, the United National Movement, concluded its presentation to the court.

At the end of their speeches, none of the party’s representatives used the standard legal phrase: “I ask the court to dismiss the claim.” Instead, each speaker ended by appealing to the judges’ conscience.

The judges seemed to find it extremely difficult to hide their irritation at this unusual conclusion.

On 28 October, the Constitutional Court will begin hearing arguments from representatives of the Coalition for Change. They have announced in advance that they have prepared an extensive set of documents and will need a full day to present their case.

Below are the main points from the 27 October hearing.

Ana Tsitlidze: “Political gossip, myths and manipulation”

Ana Tsitlidze said the court must draw a clear line between the state’s legitimate powers and the use of constitutional procedures to target political opponents. In her view, the lawsuit filed by the ruling Georgian Dream party lacks legal grounds and amounts to nothing more than “political gossip, myths and manipulation”.

Tsitlidze said she was not trying to shield the United National Movement from responsibility for its political or legal record. On the contrary, she was ready to discuss every decision the party had made in the past, including those that were difficult to defend.

However, she argued that Georgian Dream’s lawsuit had no legal basis and relied on a selective interpretation of historical events.

“If maintaining a critical attitude towards the government and questioning the legitimacy of elections can become grounds for banning a party, then political pluralism in Georgia is over and the country has become a one-party dictatorship.”

Judge interrupts Tsitlidze: “How can you say that a man was killed?”

When the discussion turned to the circumstances surrounding the death of Nugzar Putkaradze, a Batumi City Council member who died in November 2021, presiding judge Revaz Nadaraia interrupted Ana Tsitlidze.

Putkaradze represented the United National Movement in Batumi City Council, in the Ajara region. He died of a heart attack. A few days before his death, his party said that representatives of the ruling party had been putting him under “unbearable pressure”.

“There is concrete evidence that Georgian Dream put pressure on him. This evidence has been made public. Nugzar Putkaradze was offered $100,000 to betray the National Movement and switch sides to Georgian Dream. In the end, he suffered a heart attack and died,” Tsitlidze said.

“How can you say such a thing? Think about your words! This is a very serious allegation. How can you make such statements from the podium in a courtroom? On what grounds are you claiming that a man was killed?” Judge Nadaraia asked.

“But the entire argument put forward by the parliamentary investigative commission, which prepared a report for this court, was based precisely on the claim that the National Movement had allegedly killed people as part of systematic crimes,” Tsitlidze replied.

Tsitlidze on controversial actions by the United National Movement in power and double standards

Ana Tsitlidze recalled several high-profile cases from the previous government’s time in office, including the Aprasidze family case, the case of Roin Shavadze, the murder of Sandro Girgvliani and the death of Yuri Vazagashvili.

She argued that the possible crimes of individuals should not automatically be grounds for banning an entire political party.

Speaking about the case of Roin Shavadze, Tsitlidze said she also had questions about it.

Shavadze was a former military officer who fought in the August 2008 war with Russia. He was arrested in Batumi on 24 August 2008, shortly after the war, and later killed. The case involved allegations of torture and extrajudicial killing. The circumstances remain the subject of political and legal disputes.

“The Roin Shavadze case was a problem for the United National Movement. I myself support reopening the investigation.

“But how can this case be used as grounds for banning the National Movement when the lead investigator was Resan Kontselidze, who later became a Georgian Dream MP? Moreover, the deputy prosecutor at the time was Vasil Roinishvili, who is now a Constitutional Court judge,” Tsitlidze said.

Turning to the Sandro Girgvliani case, Tsitlidze pointed out that the presiding judge was Levan Murusidze, who was later appointed as a judge for life by Georgian Dream.

In January 2006, when the United National Movement was in power, Sandro Girgvliani, a young man, and his friend were abducted and brutally beaten by people linked to senior Interior Ministry officials following a dispute at a cafe in Tbilisi. Girgvliani later died from his injuries. Four former senior officials were convicted in the case. However, their subsequent pardons and early releases sparked public outrage.

“Georgian Dream divides the careers of judges Murusidze and Chinchaladze into two periods. Their work before 2012, when Georgian Dream came to power, is portrayed as criminal because it helps build the case for banning the opposition. Yet the same judges’ work after 2012 is presented as a model of integrity and independence. This is a double standard, and such double standards undermine the very concept of justice,” Tsitlidze said.

In her view, Georgian Dream’s use of past misconduct within the judicial system as grounds for banning a political party is contradictory, especially since people who continue to work within that same system are not being held to the same standard.

Tsitlidze on Zurab Adeishvili and former officials from his circle now sitting in judgment on the opposition

Ana Tsitlidze noted that Zurab Adeishvili, a senior official under the United National Movement government, is mentioned 25 times in Georgian Dream’s constitutional lawsuit.

Adeishvili was an influential figure in President Mikheil Saakashvili’s administration. He served as Georgia’s chief prosecutor from 2004 to 2008 and as justice minister from 2008 to 2012.

The plaintiffs argue that his actions were so systematic and unconstitutional that the entire party should be banned.

Tsitlidze said she had never met Adeishvili in person. However, Constitutional Court judge Vasil Roinishvili knew him well: when Adeishvili was justice minister, Roinishvili served as deputy chief prosecutor.

Tsitlidze challenged the judges with the following question:

“How can someone be banned from political activity on the basis of the actions of a person they have never even met, while a former senior official from that very same system is now allowed to sit on the court and take part in constitutional justice?”

Tsitlidze on fake prison videos, planted drugs and weapons, and violations of privacy

Ana Tsitlidze cited criminal cases from the period when Georgian Dream was already in power. These included staged prison videos and cases involving drugs and weapons allegedly planted on people.

She noted that well-known figures Tamaz Elizbarashvili and Lado Bedukadze had spoken about prison footage being staged.

On the issue of drugs and weapons being planted, she recalled the December 2024 arrest of Giorgi Akhobadze, an active participant in pro-European protests. Akhobadze was charged with acquiring and possessing drugs. He was later acquitted, and the court ordered his immediate release in the courtroom.

Tsitlidze also raised the issue of violations of privacy.

One of the arguments in the lawsuit is that the United National Movement committed systematic crimes by distributing recordings of people’s private lives while in power. Tsitlidze argued that those responsible for publishing private recordings of journalists and politicians during Georgian Dream’s time in office should also be held accountable.

Tsitlidze: UNM accused of corruption as Georgian Dream officials jailed for corruption

Ana Tsitlidze noted that the plaintiffs accuse the United National Movement of corruption, despite serious questions surrounding senior officials from the ruling Georgian Dream party itself.

She cited the cases of former Prime Minister Irakli Garibashvili, former State Security Service chief Grigol Liluashvili and former Defence Minister Juansher Burchuladze, all of whom have been convicted of corruption.

Given these cases involving members of their own party, Tsitlidze said, it was unclear why the plaintiffs believed the United National Movement should be banned over individual cases of corruption within its ranks.

Georgia’s international partners and sanctions

Tsitlidze criticised the argument that the opposition had worked with international partners to persuade them to impose sanctions on Georgia’s current authorities.

She said that engaging with international partners was a normal part of political activity, while decisions on sanctions were made by the partners themselves.

Tsitlidze’s closing words to the judges “The choice of which path to take is yours”

“I am not asking you to dismiss this lawsuit. Georgia’s history has never been one-dimensional. We have had people like Antsukhelidze and Sergo Ordzhonikidze, Ilia and Berbichashvili. The choice of which path to take is yours,” Ana Tsitlidze concluded.

“Would it not have been better to simply state, instead of making rhetorical remarks…” the presiding judge began, cutting himself off mid-sentence as he tried to hide his irritation. “You are asking the court to dismiss the lawsuit, are you not?”

“We are not asking for anything” Tsitlidze replied.

Levan Bezhashvili “The rule of law must not fall with those in power”

The speeches by the two other United National Movement representatives, Levan Bezhashvili and Alika Kuprava, were relatively brief.

“Today, you are deciding not only the fate of political parties, but also whether the Constitution will remain a check on government power in Georgia or become entirely dependent on the will of those who hold that power,” Levan Bezhashvili told the Constitutional Court judges.

“History does not remember who held more power at any given moment. It remembers what people did with that power. Your decision will be judged by whether you defended the rule of law at the moment when it was most difficult to do so. A party may be defeated, a politician may leave office, but the rule of law must not fall with those in power,” Bezhashvili stressed.

Reactions to the hearing

Badri Japaridze, one of the leaders of Lelo – Strong Georgia, told journalists that when it was his party’s turn to speak, its representatives would use every legal means available to expose what he called Georgian Dream’s real aim: to eliminate the opposition in the country.

Maia Kopaleishvili, a member of the Coalition for Change, told journalists that Georgian Dream had presented nothing but hearsay in its lawsuit.

“The hearings of the parliamentary temporary investigative commission, which form the basis of the lawsuit, are built on gossip and cannot provide sufficient grounds to accuse a political party of unconstitutional activity,” Kopaleishvili said.



Representatives of the United National Movement who addressed the court. Photo: Batumelebi, 27 October, Batumi.
