World.title: Victorian caravan maker Essential Caravans enters voluntary administration
World.content:
Victorian caravan manufacturer Essential Caravans has entered voluntary administration, with about 80 jobs lost in a restructure before administrators were called in.

The Melbourne-based business appointed administrators on October 21, joining a string of Australian caravan manufacturers to have collapsed within recent years.

It followed a restructure that saw the company close its factory in Somerton, in Melbourne's outer north, and consolidate operations with its sister company, Design RV, in Pakenham.

Jamie Johnson, the director of both companies, said economic conditions could not sustain two Melbourne-based factories.

Essential Caravans director Jamie Johnson said it was a sad day for the company. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

"I had to make some very hard decisions to make sure that we stabilised the other parts of the business by going into importing ... and lowering the cost by moving to one facility," he told the ABC on Wednesday.

"It is a sad day, but to think that it's not going to continue on the trend that it's continuing on now is naive.

" We just don't have the support for Australian manufacturing. "

Company intends to fulfil current orders

A spokesperson for Essential Caravans said 92 employees were directly affected by the closure of the Somerton factory, of which 12 workers chose to transition to roles at the Pakenham facility.

They said the company intended to fulfil all current orders, and that administrators were reviewing current builds and delivery schedules to minimise disruption to buyers and dealership partners.

Mr Johnson said he was "fully committed" to ensuring customers were not affected by the administration process.

"There's no customer that won't get their van that's on order," Mr Johnson said.

"There's no customer that's got a van in for warranty with us currently that won't get their van back."

The company has manufactured more than 5,000 caravans since 2015. (ABC News)

He said it was too early to determine how much money creditors were owed, an issue he said was "in the hands of administrators".

Mr Johnson said the two Victorian factories were producing a third of the caravans they were once capable of making, and the volume was insufficient to maintain both sites.

Essential Caravans has built more than 5,000 caravans since 2015, according to its website, and moved into its Somerton factory in 2021.

Industry under pressure as imports rise

More than 90 per cent of Australia's caravans and RVs are produced in Victoria, according to Caravan Industry Victoria (CIV).

CIV's latest State of the Industry Statement said the Australian caravanning industry was navigating one of the most significant periods of economic and structural change in recent years.

Deal to salvage Zone RV leaves caravan customers short-changed A Melbourne-based company has purchased Zone RV, but customers who collectively paid millions before its collapse will be left out of pocket.

More Australian businesses were entering administration or ceasing to trade, while international imports were up 16 per cent from the previous year.

Essential Caravans's membership with CIV is on hold as a result of the administration process.

"While it is not appropriate to comment on individual circumstances, Caravan Industry Victoria continues to support a strong, sustainable and resilient industry and will work with members as they navigate evolving market conditions," CIV CEO Daniel Sahlberg said.

"Our focus remains on supporting consumers, exhibitors, manufacturers, dealers and industry stakeholders, while respecting the administration process."

Do you know more about this story? Contact Jesse Thompson at jpjt@protonmail.com. If you're sharing sensitive information, read our tips on how to contact us confidentially.

Mr Johnson previously brokered a deal to purchase Zone RV, a Queensland-based luxury caravan manufacturer, after it collapsed owing millions in December.

On its website, Zone RV emphasised that its new parent company, Adventure Zone RV, was a separate company to Essential Caravans and that the company’s administration did not change its plans.

Essential Caravans bought collapsed caravan company Zone RV earlier this year. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Josh Dye)

Mr Johnson is not a director of Zone RV, but said his family was involved in the company.

“It operates in a different market segment which seems to be largely unaffected by the current economic climate, unlike that sub-$120,000 sector, which has been heavily affected,” he said.

Design RV last week posted a statement saying it was also unaffected by the Essential Caravans administration.

World.title: Puppy farmer jailed after more than 100 dogs found in 'horrendous' conditions
World.content:
A Perth puppy farmer who kept more than 100 dogs in appalling conditions during the height of summer has been sent to prison, as a magistrate called for the practice to end.

WARNING: Readers are advised that this story contains details of animal cruelty, which some people may find distressing.

Many of the dogs, discovered at a Canning Vale property in December 2024, were found to have major health issues and the RSPCA had to put some down.

However, as many as 80 per cent have now been re-homed by the animal protection organisation.

The canines had been abandoned by Jia Xu Dong at a time when temperatures were exceeding 40 degrees Celsius.

Puppies Rosemary, Anise, Ginger and their littermates shortly after being seized from the property. (Supplied: RSPCA WA)

Magistrate Sandra De Maio sentenced Dong to nine months in prison and fined him $5,000 for breaching orders.

"The practice of puppy farming should be abolished," she said.

Dong had pleaded guilty to 36 charges of animal cruelty, and two charges of breaching a court order.

'Horrendous' conditions

Magistrate De Maio said Dong had claimed he was a "hapless lover of dogs who sold puppies accidentally born".

She said he was most definitely involved in selling puppies.

A sickly golden retriever was among the dogs found at Jia Xu Dong’s Canning Vale property. (Supplied: RSPCA WA)

"I simply do not believe a word he says," she told the court.

" His story changes like the tides. "

She noted that Dong, who had lived in Australia since he was 13, had an interpreter in court but hardly used him.

The magistrate says she does not believe a word Jia Xu Dong says. (ABC)

Dong had kept the animals at a Canning Vale property in conditions the magistrate described as "deplorable" and "horrendous".

Puppies were sold at a Como house which the magistrate described as a "showroom".

Dogs put down

A City of Canning ranger told the RSPCA of the situation in December 2024 after dogs had escaped.

RSPCA inspectors found puppies and adult dogs, including cocker spaniels, corgis, French bulldogs, golden retrievers, groodles, and other mixed breeds.

There was a build-up of faeces, while some dogs had recent wounds from fights, and about 15 had dental issues.

A scared puppy is helped by RSPCA WA staff at the Canning Vale property. (Supplied: RSPCA WA)

Others had matted coats, embedded grass seeds, conjunctivitis, ear infections, or were malnourished.

There were dogs with psychological issues.

About 20 per cent had to be put down.

Puppy farming laws restrict dog sales New animal welfare laws come into effect in WA from Monday which require pet stores to source dogs only from rescue centres, but none have applied to do so.

The court heard Dong had abandoned them "in the heat" and gone to Albany.

During an earlier two-month trip Dong made to China, 65 puppies were born, the court heard.

Magistrate De Maio said Dong was "uncaring of their welfare and indifferent to their pain," and "he'd failed them entirely in all aspects of their care".

She said Dong, who had been treating wounds with honey, would only allow the RSPCA to take the dogs if they paid for them.

The magistrate said Dong had concocted psychiatric symptoms to explain his behaviour and had even "professed a desire" to start a dog refuge in China.

A terrified golden retriever in an RSPCA WA vehicle after being rescued from the kennels. (Supplied: RSPCA WA)

The court heard Dong bred 366 live puppies between 2021 and 2025, although the RSPCA's estimate was 390.

The RSPCA had estimated Dong could have made $1.17 million from puppy sales.

Puppies saved

Speaking outside court, RSPCA senior inspector Jayde Palin welcomed the prison sentence.

RSPCA Senior Inspector Jayde Palin says most of the dogs have been saved. (ABC News: David Weber)

"Where you walk into a house and there's just a mass number of dogs that are all suffering, desirable breeds, that people pay a lot of money for these dogs, you would expect them to be well cared for," she said.

She said it was "heartwarming" that most of the dogs could be saved, and it was important to see accountability for their treatment.

Peanut, the French bulldog, was among the canines taken into care. (Supplied: RSPCA WA)

"Knowing that there are 70 to 80 per cent of dogs that I have helped that are now in the homes they've deserved ever since they were born, living their best lives or trying to live as normally as possible, I think that makes the job worthwhile," she said.

World.title: Peptide users seeking free syringes overwhelm harm-minimisation charities
World.content:
Needle and syringe programs (NSPs) established to stem the spread of blood-borne viruses, including HIV, are struggling with an "enormous surge" in peptide use, with social media influencers suggesting people access free syringes at the harm minimisation charities.

Directions Health Services in Canberra is funded by the ACT government to offer safe injecting equipment to drug users but says it has had to limit the stock it can give clients due to an increased demand from peptide users.

Directions Health Services acting chief executive Stephanie Stephens said for the past decade, NSPs had predominantly helped those seeking to inject heroin or amphetamine.

"But in the past year … we've seen an enormous surge in people accessing sharps and needles to administer peptides," Ms Stephens said.

"Month-by-month we see an increase."

Directions Health Services says its resources are being stretched. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Peptides are short chains of amino acids that make up proteins in our bodies.

There are a number of peptide-based medicines that are approved by the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA), but many other products are unregulated.

"I think a core thing with the peptide interest is this wish [for people] to have a quick solution, a bit of a silver bullet whether it's to weight loss, to beauty, to recovery," Ms Stephens said.

"And while we love responding to new community groups and people who we can work with to reduce harms — and there are unique harms associated with peptide use — we're also concerned about the pressure that puts on our supply.

"We know that people are often buying these unregulated peptides through social media, so if they're in a position to also be buying the sharps, the syringes they need … we'd suggest they take that course of action."

She said NSPs needed to preserve their stock for "marginalised communities, such as [intravenous] drug users."

Suppliers can't meet stock orders

The service is able to gauge the rise in peptide use because staff ask clients what the last drug they injected was.

NSP team leader Tammy Waters said most people were "really honest".

"They tell us if they're using steroids, peptides, heroin, ice, or anything … [but] they don't have to answer," she said.

Directions Health Services needle and syringe program team leader Tammy Waters says the objective is harm minimisation. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Ms Waters said staff at the service build a strong rapport with clients, who were able to present anonymously.

"Sometimes they don't even come in for equipment; they come in because they feel it's a safe place to come, they feel they can talk to us … to not be judged, stigmatised," she said.

" A hello and a goodbye is a big difference in some of our clients' days. "

She said NSPs also have food, clothing, and can link people with other health services.

Directions Health Services says social media promotion is driving up demand for free injectable equipment. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Ms Waters said the uptick in peptide use had put pressure on NSPs nationwide, with suppliers unable to fulfil orders.

"[Our supplier] can't give us as much of the stock as I actually order," she said.

Directions Health Services has also seen an increase in the cost to safely remove and dispose of the clinical waste.

The service said a typical syringe could cost between 15 cents and $1, and it was able to help people who do have the means to buy the equipment by sharing a list of places to purchase.

World.title: Beale called up for Wallabies Spring Tour ahead of Rugby World Cup
World.content:
Veteran playmaker Kurtley Beale has been summoned for the Wallabies' spring tour of the UK in a big development ahead of next year's Rugby World Cup in Australia.

Beale on Wednesday answered an SOS call from coach Les Kiss to join the squad for next month's three Tests against England, Scotland and Wales before the inaugural Nations Championship finals in the UK from November 21-23.

The 95-Test-capped Beale will replace midfielder Hunter Paisami, who is unavailable due to personal reasons, while James Ramm and Kalani Thomas were also named to join the touring group.

No Wallabies call yet for Nawaqanitawase The Wallabies are confident star code-crosser Mark Nawaqanitawase wants to play for Australia at next year's Rugby World Cup, but he still has a choice of three nations.

But the 37-year-old's inclusion will be the major talking point as Kiss seemingly considers biting the bullet and ending Australia's revolving door of flawed five-eighths by backing a proven number 10 to steer the wobbly ship ahead of next year's global showpiece.

Kiss's predecessors Joe Schmidt, Eddie Jones, Dave Rennie and Michael Cheika have used almost a dozen different playmakers since Bernard Foley guided the Wallabies — under Cheika — to the 2015 World Cup final in England.

But none of the likes of Noah Lolesio, Ben Donaldson, Carter Gordon, Tane Edmed or Harry McLaughlin-Phillips has been able to hold down the spot.

Fellow stalwarts James O'Connor, Quade Cooper and Matt Toomua have also had cracks without commanding the role.

Cheika has turned to Foley to rejoin the NSW Waratahs from Japan, more than a decade after the duo masterminded the club's one and only 2014 Super Rugby premiership.

Now it appears Kiss is seriously considering Beale to revive the Wallabies' fortunes after Australia slipped to number seven in the world rankings after losing the Bledisloe Cup for a 23rd straight year this month.

Kurtley Beale last played for the Wallabies against Wales in 2021. (Getty Images: Stu Forster)

Beale last appeared in a Wallabies squad in 2024 before an Achilles injury prematurely ended his season. His most recent appearance in the gold jersey was against Wales in Cardiff in 2021.

But the silky-skilled talent and former World Player of the Year nominee boasts three World Cup experiences from 2011, 2015 and 2019 since first being called up by Wallabies coach John Connolly as a schoolboy prodigy.

"With Hunter's unavailability, we're excited by what Kurtley can bring to the group," Kiss said of the super versatile talent.

"He's got 95 caps worth of Test experience, and whilst he will primarily cover inside centre, he has the versatility to play a number of positions across the back line.

"Kurtley's also been in great form for the Western Force in Super Rugby Pacific and Super Rugby AUS and is excited to contribute to the environment."

AAP

World.title: Alexander brothers sentenced over 'monstrous' sex trafficking
World.content:
Three brothers convicted of leveraging their wealthy lifestyle to drug and rape dozens of women have learned their fate after being found guilty of sex trafficking earlier this year.

US District Court Judge Valeri E Caproni slammed their behaviour as monstrous as she sentenced each brother to 30 years in prison.

Tal, Oren and Alon Alexander, known collectively as the Alexander Brothers, stared blankly as Judge Caproni announced their punishment, which was less than the life sentences that federal prosecutors sought.

Oren, Tal and Alon Alexander depicted in a courtroom sketch. (Reuters: Jane Rosenberg)

"Your conduct was monstrous," Judge Caproni told the men, equating them to Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde during her sentencing remarks.

The brothers claimed being fathers and husbands had changed them from the partying, womanising ways of their youth, which Judge Caproni rejected.

"It's hard for me to believe the defendants changed their spots just like that," she said.

The brothers, jailed without bail since their 2024 arrests, must also each pay at least $US300,000 ($420,000) in fines.

Oren Alexander was ordered to pay another $US50,000 for producing child sexual abuse material by recording a video of him raping a 17-year-old girl.

Oren and Tal Alexander (pictured), dubbed "the A-team" of real estate, were sentenced for sex trafficking alongside their brother, Alon. (AP: Amy Sussman via Details Magazine)

While the brothers — twins Oren and Alon, 39, and Tal Alexander, 40 — expressed regret for how they treated and regarded women, they all denied drugging and raping anyone.

"That's entirely a lie, and you all know it," Judge Caproni told them, adding that she hoped they some day feel "deeply ashamed of themselves".

The brothers speak ahead of sentencing

None of the brothers testified at their trial, but each spoke before sentencing.

Oren Alexander said he and his brothers came of age at the height of hook-up culture and Howard Stern's hypersexualised radio show.

Looking back as a father, he said he regrets many of the things he said about women at that time. However, he insisted that they never broke the law.

Choking up, Tal Alexander asked Judge Caproni to "understand how difficult it is to stand here" and express "genuine regret about something I did not do".

"I feel like an atomic bomb has been dropped on my life and destroyed everything in its wake," he said.

Alon Alexander said he had evolved and acknowledged that having a wife and daughter does not excuse messages he wrote that degraded women or times when he bragged to others about sex.

"The party life you heard about and saw in the courtroom ended long before the FBI came knocking," Alon Alexander said.

"Six years before my arrest, I was building a different life."

The brothers asked to be assigned to the same prisons, which Judge Caproni said she would leave up to the bureau responsible for such arrangements.

She agreed to recommend they be locked up near Miami, where they grew up and have relatives, but added she would have them sent to different lock-ups.

"I believe that they are and will continue to be bad influences on each other," she said.

Victims describe a lasting dread

The accusers who spoke in court, and another whose statement was read by a prosecutor, were among at least 70 women who prosecutors say were assaulted by one or more of the brothers over the last two decades in posh locales including the Hamptons and Aspen, Colorado.

Lindsey Acree, an artist and gallery owner, testified that she was raped by Tal Alexander and another man at a Hamptons home in 2011 after taking a drink that she said left her feeling paralysed.

Scrapping her prepared remarks, she told Judge Caproni that a life sentence would not begin to do justice for the women whose lives were irreparably harmed.

"This has wasted my damn time. It's wasted your time. It's wasted everyone in this room's time," Ms Acree told the judge.

Turning to the brothers, she asked them why they did what they did.

"I don't understand the cruelty. I don't understand the hatred toward women," she told them.

Stars of New York real estate scene

Oren and Tal Alexander were once nicknamed real estate's "A Team" for their ultra-high-end sales and celebrity clientele.

After smashing sales records at industry powerhouse Douglas Elliman, they started their own firm.

Alon Alexander ran their family's private security company.

The brothers projected an exclusive lifestyle of yachts, private jets and waterfront mansions in Miami, but prosecutors said they began sexually assaulting women as early as 2001 or 2002, when they were in high school.

Over time, they developed a pattern of drugging and raping women, who they enticed to join them on luxury getaways, the court heard.

AP

World.title: Ex-60 Minutes reporter frontrunner for Hobart mayor
World.content:
Former 60 Minutes reporter Charles Wooley is a frontrunner to become Hobart's new lord mayor, with votes from council elections across Tasmania being tallied.

Across Tasmania's 29 councils, 441 candidates are contesting 213 councillor positions, with 258 also standing for mayor or deputy mayor.

Most mayoral results are expected to be finalised by Wednesday evening, with larger councils continuing into Thursday morning.

To be elected mayor, candidates must be elected as a councillor first.

The TEC said the voter participation rate was 85.6 per cent, an increase on the 2022 council elections. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

As of Wednesday evening, Mr Wooley, a veteran journalist and author whose campaign included a "moratorium on new bike lanes" and an end to council infighting with "reason, not ideology", is leading the count for Hobart councillors.

Former cinema owner and businessman John Kelly and the Greens' Bill Harvey are also polling strongly.

The three are also vying for the lord mayor position, which was vacated by Anna Reynolds, who did not seek re-election.

Tasmanian election analyst Kevin Bonham told 936 ABC Hobart it was "too early to say" who would be Hobart's next lord mayor.

"Charles Wooley has a substantial lead over John Kelly. It's likely that one of those two will make it to the final two and then probably defeat Bill Harvey," Dr Bonham said.

"Kelly is likely to make some gains off some candidate in the preference flow, but he is a fair way behind, and it's going to be tricky for him to close that gap."

Mr Kelly and Mr Harvey are both incumbent councillors, and are expected to be re-elected.

Mr Wooley is currently leading the count for councillor positions.

"If you were a candidate with a profile as high as Charles Wooley's and you make a reasonable effort that people do notice you so … you're not really an outsider in the sense of a candidate running for the first time," Dr Bonham said.

Sue Hickey is set to be re-elected as Glenorchy mayor. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

In the Glenorchy City Council, Sue Hickey will be re-elected mayor "very easily", Dr Bonham said.

Ms Hickey, a former Hobart lord mayor, Liberal politician and speaker of the House of Assembly, is also leading the count on the councillor ticket.

In Launceston, incumbent mayor Matthew Garwood is well ahead of his rivals for a council position.

Dr Bonham wrote on his blog that he had "heard that Matthew Garwood is very easily retaining as mayor".

Matthew Garwood is the incumbent mayor for Launceston. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Alison Jarman has been re-elected as mayor of the Devonport City Council, securing almost 65 per cent of the vote.

Council elections enter final week With fewer seats on offer and several mayors stepping aside, Tasmania's council elections may radically shake up local government across the island.

Gerard Blizzard has also been re-elected as Circular Head Council mayor, after being first elected to the council in 2018.

In the Meander Valley, where Mayor Wayne Johnston did not seek re-election, Stephanie Cameron, who was first elected in 2018 and has been deputy mayor since 2022, secured almost 64 per cent of the vote to become the next mayor.

Rachel Summers has also been re-elected as Flinders Island Council mayor. Vanessa Grace will be her deputy, elected unopposed.

Council spot guaranteed without election Fancy being on a local council, but can't stomach doing campaigning? In some Tasmanian areas, candidates are so hard to attract that anyone who puts their hand up can have a crack.

Giovanna Simpson is leading in first preference votes for Burnie City Council.

Greg Dawson has been elected as George Town's mayor, while Cheryl Fuller has been re-elected as mayor for Central Coast Council.

Leigh Gray will remain mayor in Brighton.

Rhys Beattie has been re-elected as mayor of Dorset.

John Hall has been elected unopposed as deputy mayor of the Central Highlands.

The Tasmanian Electoral Commission said the final statewide participation rate was 85.6 per cent, an increase on the 84.8 per cent participation rate in the 2022 council elections.

World.title: I suspect a neighbour of befouling my recycling bin. The only option is to get petty
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsRecycling Opinion I suspect a neighbour of befouling my recycling bin. The only option is to get petty Claire Heaney Writer October 28, 2026 — 7:00pm

October 28, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

I used to fancy myself as a binfluencer, the first mover on bin night, leading the way and signalling to the neighbourhood what colour bin they should be wheeling out this week. But all that changed one morning a few years back as I left for work and went to pop an empty cereal box into my yellow-lidded recycle bin. I was shocked to see a half-drunk bottle of chardonnay (who wastes good wine?) and a shopping bag containing a shoebox with worn stilettos. Sneaked into my bin in the dead of night. So many bins: but do you get them in the right place? Jason South I soon landed on a list of suspects. Eliminating elderly neighbours who had graduated to sensible shoes, and the tradies renting across the road – unless they were cross dressers – I was fairly sure I knew the culprit. In my head, I dumped the items on their verandah but in truth I placed them in the right bins and just added it to my mental list of grievances about their selfish parking and generally up-themselves demeanour. My husband rolled his eyes.



While I’m an occasional bin fairy, reciprocating with neighbours to wheel bins back in after they are emptied, my bins now go out at the latest possible time. I know. It’s petty. Each household pays rates and what does it matter? But for some of us it does matter. We care about our consumption, weighing up packaging and ability to recycle or reuse said packaging in our buying choices. It’s one thing sorting your items, but contamination is a huge problem. If someone drops their doggy do-do bag in my yellow recycling everything turns to poo, literally. (Yes. It has happened and in my Food Organics and Garden Organics, FOGO, bin too). Illustration: Jim Pavlidis We sort our waste across the bins and take advantage of programs to recycle tablet blister packs, E-waste, globes, pet food pouches, plastic plant pots, old towels to the vet and much more. I know it sounds like a lot of work, but it isn’t really. Many European countries, according to the World Population Review, have very high rates of recycling due to strong policy, public engagement, product stewardship and infrastructure to avoid having to burn or bury waste.



I’ve landed on a system and organise drop-offs of recyclables to coincide with other activities. I do realise when I place an item in a recycling bin it is a leap of faith. RedCycle soft plastics, anyone? Related Article Opinion

Friendship Who suffers FOMO any more? I’m more likely to have ROMO Claire Heaney Writer With nearly 540 municipal councils across Australia and 79 in Victoria, post the Jeff Kennett 1992 amalgamations, and 128 in NSW, there’s a range of different waste collection programs. While my inner Melbourne council still has weekly rubbish or red-lidded bin collections, many of the councils next to me have fortnightly waste collection. This has turned into a state election issue with the Liberal opposition pledging weekly waste collection. I think I could easily manage fortnightly because I look for alternative places to get rid of waste, but I realise it is different for everyone, depending on their age and stage. Festering nappies, incontinence and medical waste products are often cited by those opposed to fortnightly collections. For others, full bins are just laziness. I visited a FOGO recycler and was shocked to see nappies, plastic and other rubbish being fished out on a conveyor belt. Real people have to do this job.



My council, as I am sure others do, slaps stickers on bins with wrong items to shame residents. I see recidivist offenders. I’m embarrassed for them. I wonder if it’s an innocent mistake, they don’t care or a neighbour has put the incorrect rubbish in their bin. To be fair, it takes some time for my husband and I to fix things when one of our kids dumps everything from their floordrobe in the rubbish bin. Related Article Opinion

Real life Dear fellow pedestrians, keep to the left, you drongos Claire Heaney Writer My council was an early adopter of the now controversial purple glass bin, rolling them out in late 2020. I reckon they jumped the gun and should have waited until the Container Deposit Scheme started. Inner suburban dwellers like me don’t have the room to store four bins. For some people storing these bins would be an access risk for emergency services in a fire not to mention accessibility on tight streets. I’m lucky to put mine out once every two months while the share house up the street puts their purple bin out every month. I know people will say I have too much time on my hands. But we’re in a rubbish crisis. Our population is booming; landfill sites are filling fast and the cost to ratepayers of disposing of our rubbish is skyrocketing. If I can put some things in the right places, improving their chances of being recycled or upcycled it’s a small help.



I’ve got to admit, though, it’s been tough relinquishing my self-appointed role as a binfluencer. On Tuesday after bin day, as I walk to the tram, I see still full yellow and purple bins put out on the wrong week. If only they had a binfluencer in the street to guide them. Claire Heaney is a Melbourne writer. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Frail in your 40s? What to know about ‘pre-frailty’ and how to reverse it
World.content:
LifestyleHealth & wellnessAgeing Frail in your 40s? What to know about ‘pre-frailty’ and how to reverse it Paula Goodyer October 28, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

When some women first walk into the gym at The Bone Clinic, their bones are thinning, their bodies are stooped, and they’re often leaning on a walking stick. “They see people lifting heavy weights and say, ‘I could never do that’. But they do, and it’s not long before they’re standing straighter and carrying their own groceries,” says Professor Belinda Beck from the School of Allied Health, Sport Sciences and Social Work at Griffith University, and director of the Brisbane-based clinic which runs an exercise program to strengthen muscle and bone. Avoiding frailty is more than just lifting weights. Getty Images “Frailty isn’t inevitable with age, and it can be reversed. Our bread and butter is seeing people become functional again.” Frailty might seem a long way off in your 40s, but research from Flinders University has found that almost half of 40- to 49-year-olds have what’s known as “pre-frailty”, meaning they already have signs of poor muscle strength and poor balance. But why?



You could blame convenience technology, like the computers, remote controls and robot lawn mowers that have stolen so much movement over the last few decades, but it’s more complex than that. “In our study, pre-frailty was associated with more loneliness, more negative attitudes towards ageing, and having a sense of feeling older than your chronological age,” says researcher Dr Tom Brennan of Flinders University, one of the authors of a 2024 review of interventions to prevent or reverse pre-frailty and frailty. Related Article Illness In her 70s, Elettra had an aching back and sore legs – then she started dancing “If we want to prevent frailty, we should ask more about what’s happening in someone’s life. How confident are they about being active? Do they see changes in their health as something they can work on improving, or something they have to accept as they get older?” he says. “But part of the challenge is that people in middle age may think ‘frailty’ has nothing to do with them – talking about maintaining strength, confidence and the ability to keep doing things they enjoy may make prevention feel more relevant.”



Another reason to head off frailty sooner rather than later is new research linking frailty in older adults to a 74 per cent higher dementia risk. “Muscle is important for so many reasons as you get older. If you’re frail, you’re less able to engage in things that help prevent dementia, like physical activity and social interaction. If it’s becoming harder to go out, you might not be seeing friends, and we know that social connection is linked to dementia risk,” says Dr Katya Numbers from the UNSW Sydney’s Centre for Healthy Brain Ageing (CHeBA) who did the research into frailty and dementia. The effect of muscle loss on the brain may also be playing a part. When muscles exercise, they produce myokines (substances that help protect the brain), which may be part of why a University of Sydney study found that lifting weights slowed or stopped degeneration in parts of the brain vulnerable to Alzheimer’s. Maintaining independence, including being allowed to do household tasks, is more important than many people realise. Getty Images But preventing frailty – now affecting more than 20 per cent of over 65s – isn’t always as simple as urging older people to pick up weights, Numbers says, adding that the CHeBA study also found living alone seemed to compound dementia risk in people who were frail.



“Frail older adults living alone had almost double the risk of dementia compared with robust adults living alone. We need to look at the whole person. You’re not going to 



Her research at Griffith University into building bone strength is the basis of The Bone Clinic’s program. Called ONERO, it combines high-intensity resistance training and impact exercises with balance training. It’s supervised by exercise physiologists and available around Australia. “I want to get the program available on the Medicare Benefits Schedule, so that cost isn’t a barrier. If more people could access strength training programs, the effect would be huge – we would have fewer hip fractures, and keep more people out of aged care. Ultimately, it’s about quality of life,” she says. “The message that frailty isn’t a normal part of ageing and can be prevented needs to target people at all life stages – not just once you’ve crossed the threshold into frailty,” says Dr Coralie Wales who heads Strong Australia, a charity that promotes the importance of maintaining strength. “If you lose physical strength, you lose the foundation of a healthy old age and your enjoyment of life.” Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. Get it in your inbox every Monday.

World.title: Albanese trips over the truth when it suits. If he’s not careful, it could be contagious
World.content:
NationalNSWNSW State Parliament Opinion Albanese trips over the truth when it suits. If he’s not careful, it could be contagious Michael McGowan State political editor October 28, 2026 — 7:00pm

October 28, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

When Premier Chris Minns stood up over the weekend and announced the government would reverse ferret on a planned overhaul of train timetables, he sounded like someone who had listened. The planned changes to the T4, T8 and South Coast lines timetables, he conceded, had been unpopular. Rather than digging in, he was ditching them. NSW Premier Chris Minns has every incentive to look and sound as little like his federal counterpart as possible. “I’d rather apologise and backflip on a policy like this than implement a change that people don’t want,” he said. He sounded, in other words, not at all like the prime minister.



Amid all the fear within the NSW Labor government over the potential for One Nation to derail their re-election, the person who looms largest is not Pauline Hanson, or her NSW leader Mike Newman. It’s Anthony Albanese. Over and over, in their internal polling, and when MPs go door-knocking or are out in their electorates, the overwhelming feedback is that voters have it out for federal Labor. Related Article Government grants Albanese admits ‘sewage’ claim for $6 million grant was wrong If bad and worsening economic conditions weren’t enough, the prime minister in his second term is living long enough to see himself become the villain, metamorphosing into a man tripping over the truth when it suits. Of all things to repeatedly entangle yourself in, the saga of a $6 million grant to the Marrickville Golf Club must be the most ridiculous. Since the ABC first reported the grant, Albanese has seemed to reach for new and more absurd ways to continue giving the story oxygen, lurching Sideshow Bob-like from one rake to the next. Most recently, the prime minister was forced to correct the record after claiming the grant was for sewage upgrades despite issuing a press release at the time stating the money would go to a series of improvements including a renovation of the clubhouse and other amenities.



Rather than own the grant — or, God forbid, concede that the kind of pork-barrelling Labor railed against while in opposition was not up to scratch — Albanese first went after the ABC for not reporting his (false) sewage claims before claiming he hadn’t been to the club “for many, many years”. The saga is particularly funny for anyone who lives in Sydney’s inner west and frequents the club. In the general manager reports they sometimes send out to members, the $6 million grant has been referred to as the “Albanese upgrades” or “Albanese building works”, such was its connection – in their minds, at least – to the prime minister. (I should disclose that, like Albanese, I am also an honouree member, in so far as I last paid my $5 membership fees about five years ago but can still flash my expired card and get a discount on beers). Related Article Government grants ‘The system is a farce’: Constitutional expert Anne Twomey slams Albanese golf grant as ‘grey corruption’ The club is also a significant source of pride for the local Labor fraternity because, in 2020, it was they who led the charge to successfully defeat a Greens-backed plan to cut the course down to nine holes. Labor figures, including Albanese, fiercely resisted the proposal. Together with the then-MP for neighbouring Barton, Linda Burney, he said it risked undermining “the spirit of the inner west”. To now see Albanese acting as though he’s barely heard of it is a mammoth credulity-stretching exercise.



The point is not that Labor gave the club the grant — it really could use a reno — but Albanese’s strange, reflexive instinct to insist black is white (“I didn’t fall off the stage”), and continue bleeding on issues for no reason. From the Helen Haines “integrity sheet” to the ban on credit card surcharges, the government seems unable to either anticipate controversies or react normally to them when they arise. Minns, then, has every incentive to look and sound as little like his federal counterpart as possible. On Thursday, the government changed tack again, stifling a growing backlash against changes to rules requiring cafes to have recyclable cups by agreeing to water down the most controversial aspects of the changes. There is obviously nuance to this. Albanese is hunted by elements of the conservative press in ways Minns is not, and the premier has often been criticised by his own side for being too willing to abandon Labor principles in his eagerness to court the middle and centre-right of the electorate. Loading That same dynamic though means that while Minns is not loved by the base in the way the prime minister is, he is more appealing to socially conservative voters, or those who might be considering voting for One Nation.



MPs in seats believed to be at risk from One Nation consistently report that, when they are door-knocking, voters react far more positively once they make the distinction between the federal and state governments. Much has been written about the testy relationship between the pair, and Minns has come under fire at times for being too quick to point criticism at Albanese and the federal government. But more than picking fights with the feds, Labor strategists believe Minns’ most vital task over the next five months is creating enough differentiation between the two governments that when voters go to the polls, they aren’t treating it as a referendum on Labor. World.title: ‘Not invited, not welcome’: Russian ambassador attends Greens leader’s speech denying Ukraine military aid
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalRussia-Ukraine war ‘Not invited, not welcome’: Russian ambassador attends Greens leader’s speech denying Ukraine military aid Andrew Probyn October 28, 2026 — 6:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Greens Leader David Shoebridge has been embarrassed by the attendance of the Russian Ambassador at his inaugural National Press Club address in which he doubled down on calls to deny Ukraine military aid – a policy critics say is pro-Kremlin. Shoebridge, who says he did not invite Mikhail Petrakov to the event, said the Greens partyroom stood for “peace and non-violence” but was “rock solid” in its support for the people in Ukraine. Greens leader David Shoebridge addresses the National Press Club. Alex Ellinghausen “We 100 per cent rock solid support the people of Ukraine to resist the illegal and immoral war,” the Greens leader told the Press Club. “Rock solid support for their struggle against an illegal invasion by Russia, rock solid support for humanitarian and direct financial support to the people of Ukraine and the government of Ukraine.



“And we also support the firmest, clearest, most unambiguous sanctions against the state of Russia. Russia’s invasion is illegal, it’s immoral and it is wrong.” But when challenged by Nine News as to why the Greens’ support doesn’t extend to giving Ukraine military aid, he said the party “hold true to our pillar of peace and non-violence”. Shoebridge said he did not know Petrakov was listening to his speech. “One hundred per cent not welcome, 100 per cent not invited, I don’t want him here,” he told Nine News. Russia’s ambassador to Australia Mikhail Petrakov seen at the National Press Club on Wednesday.



Ukraine’s Ambassador Vasyl Myroshnychenko, who has been lobbying Shoebridge to change his foreign policy on military aid, was outraged by Petrakov’s attendance. “I just find it really appalling that he actually shows up there. But I mean, in this particular case, I believe he feels quite comfortable coming to Senator Shoebridge’s presentation,” he said. “No military aid to Ukraine aligns with the priorities of Russia.” He said the Greens in Germany supported giving Ukraine military aid and the Australian Greens should follow suit. Labor and the Coalition have both criticised the Greens for their Ukraine aid policy.



“The first policy pronouncement of the leader of the Greens political party was to say that he does not and will not support our military aid to the brave people of Ukraine over $1.8 billion – the only person that helps is Vladimir Putin,” Assistant Minister for Defence Peter Khalil said. Related Article Greens Shoebridge says Steele-John’s social media posts ‘obviously not the way to resolve’ issue “I would hope that he would reconsider and support the military aid that we’ve provided to Ukraine because the international community support is the only thing that’s keeping Ukraine alive in this war.” Shadow Defence Minister James Paterson said he was not surprised the Russian ambassador was in attendance for Shoebridge’s speech. “He would have liked what he was going to hear. The Greens foreign policy under David Shoebridge is Putin-friendly,” he said. “He wants to hand a veto over Australia’s defence assistance for Ukraine to Vladimir Putin through the United Nations Security Council.”



Shoebridge’s Senate colleague Sarah Hanson-Young has already disagreed with his Ukraine stance, saying military aid should be provided if needed. “I think we need to be doing everything we can to support the people in Ukraine,” she told ABC’s 7.30. “If (military aid) is the support that people need in order to defend themselves from the invasion of Russia, I think Australians need to support that. “You can’t allow people to be left fending for themselves.” Paterson commended Hanson-Young’s stance.



“It’s to Sarah Hanson Young’s great credit that she’s gone public with her discomfort with David Shoebridge’s Vladimir Putin-endorsed foreign policy,” he said. Shoebridge was pictured at a dinner with the then-Russian ambassador and Liberal figures in 2022, but he and the Liberals said they were blindsided by the envoy’s presence. World.title: ‘Can’t have a life’: Kanga joins welfare push for later starting times in racing
World.content:
SportRacingVictorian racing ‘Can’t have a life’: Kanga joins welfare push for later starting times in racing Danny Russell Updated October 28, 2026 — 6:35pm ,first published 4:57pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Colourful racing identity John Kanga has joined a push for later training hours on the eve of Melbourne Cup week, saying it was time to improve working conditions for stable staff. The former Melbourne Racing Club chairman, who obtained a Racing Victoria stable hand licence earlier this year, said the long-held tradition of 4am starts and split shifts needed an industry-wide review. John Kanga is calling for a better work-life balance for strappers, track riders and horse trainers. Eddie Jim Kanga has joined Australian Trainers’ Association president Troy Corstens in calling for a better work-life balance for strappers, track riders and trainers now that stables were juggling the extra demands of twilight and night meetings. “I’ve never been a great believer in doing something simply because we’ve always done it that way,” Kanga told The Age.



Related Article Blinkers On

Victorian racing The Melbourne Cup is not the only vital race being staged at Flemington “We quite rightly spend an enormous amount of time talking about the welfare of our horses. Surely, the welfare of the people looking after those horses deserves just as much attention.” Kanga, who controversially resigned from the MRC board on the eve of last year’s Caulfield Cup carnival, no longer holds an official position in the racing industry. But he said he obtained a stable-hand licence through Racing Victoria’s Stable Start program to gain a broader understanding of the growing demands on trainers and their staff. He regularly spends time visiting Flemington stables.



“Some of the best ideas in racing don’t come from the boardroom. They come from the people doing the work,” he said. When asked if he intended to return to the sport in an official capacity, such as nominating for the upcoming Victoria Racing Club board elections, Kanga said, “I’ve never needed a title to contribute to racing, and I’m not about to start now.” Training starts at Flemington before the crack of dawn. Getty Images The VRC agreed to a later starting time at Flemington in July, delaying the course opening from 4am to 4.30am. A 5am start will be trialled after the spring carnival. But Corstens, a second-generation trainer based at Flemington, has been pushing for a 6am start – a prospect that would clash with working hours for track-management staff.



“Ideally, if we started at six, we’d need a closing time of 10am, and the VRC would have to work with their track staff and renegotiate their EBA [enterprise bargaining agreement],” Corstens said. Related Article Spring racing carnival Record-breaking trainer’s warning for punters on Melbourne Cup favourite “I’ve been pushing for a long time, and the main reason that I’m doing that is because I think it will attract a hell of a lot more people to the game [for work].” Training centres have opened before dawn for more than a century. The reasons were varied – trainers had second jobs, they wanted first access to grass tracks, they liked to work their horses in secret under the cover of darkness, they had to work their gallopers before going to the races, and curators needed access to the racecourse.



There are still trainers who don’t want to break with the tradition. “Everyone’s entitled to the way they want to do it, but I just think that it’d open things right up if we had a look at it and did have a change,” Corstens said. “I think sleep is the most important factor in anybody’s life. And if you’re starting at 3 o’clock in the morning, these kids can’t have a life. “They are having to go to bed at seven and 8 o’clock at night, they can’t do anything. “My family’s used to me going to bed at 8 o’clock every night. Would I like to spend more time with them? Of course, I would, but you know, a lot of the time I’m buggered, and I need to hit the hay.”



Editor's pick Melbourne Cup First look at the Melbourne Cup form – we rate the top 24 horses Corstens also called for government assistance to streamline the visa process for international track riders to help service the Victorian industry. He said regional training centres and the thoroughbred breeding industry found it difficult to attract suitable staff at different times of the year. “I think the process could be simpler, a lot simpler than it is,” he said. “Andrew Hore-Lacy [Thoroughbred Breeders Association CEO] has been working very hard in the background, trying to improve the situation for us all.” Kanga, who races horses with Danny O’Brien and Dom Sutton, said stable staff were the backbone of the racing industry.



“Without them, there are no horses prepared, no races and no industry,” he said. “This isn’t about making racing easier. It’s about making racing sustainable, both for the people who work in it and the generations who will follow us.” Kanga was MRC chairman for 12 months, from October 2024 until October 2025, before resigning after questions from The Age. In that time, his committee was credited with stoping the sale of Sandown Racecourse for housing development, opening up the inside track at Caulfield for jump outs and offering cheaper food and drink. Fit for a King: Star on the brink of a Cup start after Bendigo win



Rachel King is known for her timing, and the Sydney-based jockey delivered the perfect ride at the perfect moment on Wednesday to all but book a last-minute slot in next week’s Melbourne Cup. King’s winning steer on So You Are was enough to win the group 3 Bendigo Cup over 2400 metres and is expected to attract a sizeable enough weight penalty that would push the Bjorn Baker-trained gelding into the starting field for the race that stops the nation. Rachel King and So You Are win the Bendigo Cup. Racing Photos In doing so, she dashed the hopes of several other contenders. Soulcombe, owned by several premiership-winning Richmond Tigers including Tom Lynch, needed to finish in the top three but blew his chances at the start. He flopped out of the gates and finished ninth.



Danny O’Brien’s Litzdeel fell agonisingly short again, running home strongly for third, while Gai Waterhouse’s The Euphrates and Ciaron Maher’s Kings Valley could not sustain a solid tempo in front. If Racing Victoria handicapper David Hegan lumps So You Are with an extra 1.5-kilogram penalty on Thursday, it will be enough to push it up the Melbourne Cup order. That is not unreasonable. It would then shuffle import Hopewell Rock back into 25th place and one spot outside the field. Only Racing Victoria’s strict safety protocols, which include scans of all Melbourne Cup runners this week, could then change the make-up of Tuesday’s Cup field. “He’s done everything he can, the horse – he deserved to be there and hopefully that’s enough to get him in,” Baker’s racing manager Luke Hilton said.



So You Are has won his past three races on the trot – the Tatts Cup (2400m) at Randwick in September, followed by victories in the group 3 Colin Stephen Quality (2400m) at Rosehill and the group 3 St Leger (2600m) at Randwick. “We thought he may get in after winning the St Leger, but he needed a few more points,” Hilton said. “We had a look at the Moonee Valley Cup and Bjorn and [owner] Mr Ramsey put their heads together and came up with this plan today, and it’s come off. Let’s hope it’s enough. “Rach and Bjorn have done a lot of work with him. His form was a little bit questionable Melbourne way, that was probably the only glitch that we thought he might have, but he really handled it well today.” It has been a fruitful spring for King, who became the first female jockey to win the Caulfield Guineas on Warwoven earlier this month.



“He had a couple of runs in Melbourne and probably not run up to standard before, so it was good to see him get it done the other way around,” King said. “He’s just a horse in really good form. He’s tough, he puts himself on speed, he makes life easy, and he doesn’t want to let one get past him.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

Anthropic will offer shares as part of its blockbuster initial public offering directly to Australian investors, bringing a fresh artificial-intelligence bet to a market still reeling from the high-profile collapse of a data centre start-up’s float. The IPO will be accessible to local retail investors after Anthropic submits a prospectus to the Australian Securities and Investments Commission, according to a filing on Monday with the US sharemarket regulator. The number of shares on offer will be disclosed in a later filing. Investors are expecting a fair valuation of between $US1.4 trillion and $US1.75 trillion ($2 trillion and $2.5 trillion), people familiar with the matter have said. Anthropic’s IPO will give local investors a chance to directly invest in one of the biggest AI players. Bloomberg The Australian offering will give the Claude chatbot maker exposure to Australia’s $4.8 trillion superannuation industry as well as a retail investor base starved for an opportunity to buy into a major company at the heart of the AI trade.



The collapse of Firmus’s IPO, which would have ranked among this market’s largest ever listings, dealt a blow to sentiment after it fell apart as demand from international investors failed to materialise. “Many Australian investors will be keen to participate in Anthropic’s IPO,” according to Cameron Gleeson, head of investment strategy at Betashares. “Anthropic is a very different proposition to Firmus. Anthropic is selling a product that customers are already paying for and only increasing their spending on.” Australia is one of a few countries around the world where retail investors are able to directly buy into the Anthropic IPO. Compared with the technology-heavy markets across North Asia and the US, Australia lacks the same semiconductor or hyperscaler companies that have been the focus of sharemarkets in recent months. The shortage of exposure helped support SpaceX’s local offering this year, with retail investors driving demand. Australia is one of a few countries around the world, along with Japan, Canada and parts of Europe, where retail investors are able to directly buy into the Anthropic IPO.



Professional and sophisticated investors will be able to participate in Anthropic’s US offering directly without having to wait for an Australian regulatory filing, according to Anthropic’s prospectus. Super funds and other large institutional investors fall into the professional category. Sophisticated investors include individuals with net assets of at least $2.5 million or gross income of at least $250,000 per year. Related Article Opinion

AI ‘Bold, but sane’? The future of AI is riding on Anthropic’s float Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Among Anthropic’s 22 underwriters, Macquarie’s capital-raising arm is expected to lead the local offering. CommSec will lead retail marketing, the Australian Financial Review reported, citing people briefed on the matter. CommSec also handled SpaceX’s Australian retail marketing this year. The brokerage at the time said it received more than 28,000 applications – a record. It didn’t say how many shares were eventually allotted to its clients.



Anthropic’s offering “should draw strong local interest after years of the biggest names in AI growing behind closed doors,” said Josh Gilbert, lead analyst for Asia Pacific at eToro in Sydney. While Firmus asked investors to back an expansion story leaning heavily on debt, “Anthropic’s numbers put it on a much firmer footing, and it offers something public markets have barely had: direct exposure to a frontier model maker.” Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. World.title: I suspect a neighbour of befouling my recycling bin. The only option is to get petty
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsRecycling Opinion I suspect a neighbour of befouling my recycling bin. The only option is to get petty Claire Heaney Writer October 28, 2026 — 7:00pm

October 28, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

I used to fancy myself as a binfluencer, the first mover on bin night, leading the way and signalling to the neighbourhood what colour bin they should be wheeling out this week. But all that changed one morning a few years back as I left for work and went to pop an empty cereal box into my yellow-lidded recycle bin. I was shocked to see a half-drunk bottle of chardonnay (who wastes good wine?) and a shopping bag containing a shoebox with worn stilettos. Sneaked into my bin in the dead of night. So many bins: but do you get them in the right place? Jason South I soon landed on a list of suspects. Eliminating elderly neighbours who had graduated to sensible shoes, and the tradies renting across the road – unless they were cross dressers – I was fairly sure I knew the culprit. In my head, I dumped the items on their verandah but in truth I placed them in the right bins and just added it to my mental list of grievances about their selfish parking and generally up-themselves demeanour. My husband rolled his eyes.



While I’m an occasional bin fairy, reciprocating with neighbours to wheel bins back in after they are emptied, my bins now go out at the latest possible time. I know. It’s petty. Each household pays rates and what does it matter? But for some of us it does matter. We care about our consumption, weighing up packaging and ability to recycle or reuse said packaging in our buying choices. It’s one thing sorting your items, but contamination is a huge problem. If someone drops their doggy do-do bag in my yellow recycling everything turns to poo, literally. (Yes. It has happened and in my Food Organics and Garden Organics, FOGO, bin too). Illustration: Jim Pavlidis We sort our waste across the bins and take advantage of programs to recycle tablet blister packs, E-waste, globes, pet food pouches, plastic plant pots, old towels to the vet and much more. I know it sounds like a lot of work, but it isn’t really. Many European countries, according to the World Population Review, have very high rates of recycling due to strong policy, public engagement, product stewardship and infrastructure to avoid having to burn or bury waste.



I’ve landed on a system and organise drop-offs of recyclables to coincide with other activities. I do realise when I place an item in a recycling bin it is a leap of faith. RedCycle soft plastics, anyone? Related Article Opinion

Friendship Who suffers FOMO any more? I’m more likely to have ROMO Claire Heaney Writer With nearly 540 municipal councils across Australia and 79 in Victoria, post the Jeff Kennett 1992 amalgamations, and 128 in NSW, there’s a range of different waste collection programs. While my inner Melbourne council still has weekly rubbish or red-lidded bin collections, many of the councils next to me have fortnightly waste collection. This has turned into a state election issue with the Liberal opposition pledging weekly waste collection. I think I could easily manage fortnightly because I look for alternative places to get rid of waste, but I realise it is different for everyone, depending on their age and stage. Festering nappies, incontinence and medical waste products are often cited by those opposed to fortnightly collections. For others, full bins are just laziness. I visited a FOGO recycler and was shocked to see nappies, plastic and other rubbish being fished out on a conveyor belt. Real people have to do this job.



My council, as I am sure others do, slaps stickers on bins with wrong items to shame residents. I see recidivist offenders. I’m embarrassed for them. I wonder if it’s an innocent mistake, they don’t care or a neighbour has put the incorrect rubbish in their bin. To be fair, it takes some time for my husband and I to fix things when one of our kids dumps everything from their floordrobe in the rubbish bin. Related Article Opinion

Real life Dear fellow pedestrians, keep to the left, you drongos Claire Heaney Writer My council was an early adopter of the now controversial purple glass bin, rolling them out in late 2020. I reckon they jumped the gun and should have waited until the Container Deposit Scheme started. Inner suburban dwellers like me don’t have the room to store four bins. For some people storing these bins would be an access risk for emergency services in a fire not to mention accessibility on tight streets. I’m lucky to put mine out once every two months while the share house up the street puts their purple bin out every month. I know people will say I have too much time on my hands. But we’re in a rubbish crisis. Our population is booming; landfill sites are filling fast and the cost to ratepayers of disposing of our rubbish is skyrocketing. If I can put some things in the right places, improving their chances of being recycled or upcycled it’s a small help.



I’ve got to admit, though, it’s been tough relinquishing my self-appointed role as a binfluencer. On Tuesday after bin day, as I walk to the tram, I see still full yellow and purple bins put out on the wrong week. If only they had a binfluencer in the street to guide them. Claire Heaney is a Melbourne writer. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Frail in your 40s? What to know about ‘pre-frailty’ and how to reverse it
World.content:
LifestyleHealth & wellnessAgeing Frail in your 40s? What to know about ‘pre-frailty’ and how to reverse it Paula Goodyer October 28, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

When some women first walk into the gym at The Bone Clinic, their bones are thinning, their bodies are stooped, and they’re often leaning on a walking stick. “They see people lifting heavy weights and say, ‘I could never do that’. But they do, and it’s not long before they’re standing straighter and carrying their own groceries,” says Professor Belinda Beck from the School of Allied Health, Sport Sciences and Social Work at Griffith University, and director of the Brisbane-based clinic which runs an exercise program to strengthen muscle and bone. Avoiding frailty is more than just lifting weights. Getty Images “Frailty isn’t inevitable with age, and it can be reversed. Our bread and butter is seeing people become functional again.” Frailty might seem a long way off in your 40s, but research from Flinders University has found that almost half of 40- to 49-year-olds have what’s known as “pre-frailty”, meaning they already have signs of poor muscle strength and poor balance. But why?



You could blame convenience technology, like the computers, remote controls and robot lawn mowers that have stolen so much movement over the last few decades, but it’s more complex than that. “In our study, pre-frailty was associated with more loneliness, more negative attitudes towards ageing, and having a sense of feeling older than your chronological age,” says researcher Dr Tom Brennan of Flinders University, one of the authors of a 2024 review of interventions to prevent or reverse pre-frailty and frailty. Related Article Illness In her 70s, Elettra had an aching back and sore legs – then she started dancing “If we want to prevent frailty, we should ask more about what’s happening in someone’s life. How confident are they about being active? Do they see changes in their health as something they can work on improving, or something they have to accept as they get older?” he says. “But part of the challenge is that people in middle age may think ‘frailty’ has nothing to do with them – talking about maintaining strength, confidence and the ability to keep doing things they enjoy may make prevention feel more relevant.”



Another reason to head off frailty sooner rather than later is new research linking frailty in older adults to a 74 per cent higher dementia risk. “Muscle is important for so many reasons as you get older. If you’re frail, you’re less able to engage in things that help prevent dementia, like physical activity and social interaction. If it’s becoming harder to go out, you might not be seeing friends, and we know that social connection is linked to dementia risk,” says Dr Katya Numbers from the UNSW Sydney’s Centre for Healthy Brain Ageing (CHeBA) who did the research into frailty and dementia. The effect of muscle loss on the brain may also be playing a part. When muscles exercise, they produce myokines (substances that help protect the brain), which may be part of why a University of Sydney study found that lifting weights slowed or stopped degeneration in parts of the brain vulnerable to Alzheimer’s. Maintaining independence, including being allowed to do household tasks, is more important than many people realise. Getty Images But preventing frailty – now affecting more than 20 per cent of over 65s – isn’t always as simple as urging older people to pick up weights, Numbers says, adding that the CHeBA study also found living alone seemed to compound dementia risk in people who were frail.



“Frail older adults living alone had almost double the risk of dementia compared with robust adults living alone. We need to look at the whole person. You’re not going to 



Her research at Griffith University into building bone strength is the basis of The Bone Clinic’s program. Called ONERO, it combines high-intensity resistance training and impact exercises with balance training. It’s supervised by exercise physiologists and available around Australia. “I want to get the program available on the Medicare Benefits Schedule, so that cost isn’t a barrier. If more people could access strength training programs, the effect would be huge – we would have fewer hip fractures, and keep more people out of aged care. Ultimately, it’s about quality of life,” she says. “The message that frailty isn’t a normal part of ageing and can be prevented needs to target people at all life stages – not just once you’ve crossed the threshold into frailty,” says Dr Coralie Wales who heads Strong Australia, a charity that promotes the importance of maintaining strength. “If you lose physical strength, you lose the foundation of a healthy old age and your enjoyment of life.” Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. Get it in your inbox every Monday.

World.title: Albanese trips over the truth when it suits. If he’s not careful, it could be contagious
World.content:
NationalNSWNSW State Parliament Opinion Albanese trips over the truth when it suits. If he’s not careful, it could be contagious Michael McGowan State political editor October 28, 2026 — 7:00pm

October 28, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

When Premier Chris Minns stood up over the weekend and announced the government would reverse ferret on a planned overhaul of train timetables, he sounded like someone who had listened. The planned changes to the T4, T8 and South Coast lines timetables, he conceded, had been unpopular. Rather than digging in, he was ditching them. NSW Premier Chris Minns has every incentive to look and sound as little like his federal counterpart as possible. “I’d rather apologise and backflip on a policy like this than implement a change that people don’t want,” he said. He sounded, in other words, not at all like the prime minister.



Amid all the fear within the NSW Labor government over the potential for One Nation to derail their re-election, the person who looms largest is not Pauline Hanson, or her NSW leader Mike Newman. It’s Anthony Albanese. Over and over, in their internal polling, and when MPs go door-knocking or are out in their electorates, the overwhelming feedback is that voters have it out for federal Labor. Related Article Government grants Albanese admits ‘sewage’ claim for $6 million grant was wrong If bad and worsening economic conditions weren’t enough, the prime minister in his second term is living long enough to see himself become the villain, metamorphosing into a man tripping over the truth when it suits. Of all things to repeatedly entangle yourself in, the saga of a $6 million grant to the Marrickville Golf Club must be the most ridiculous. Since the ABC first reported the grant, Albanese has seemed to reach for new and more absurd ways to continue giving the story oxygen, lurching Sideshow Bob-like from one rake to the next. Most recently, the prime minister was forced to correct the record after claiming the grant was for sewage upgrades despite issuing a press release at the time stating the money would go to a series of improvements including a renovation of the clubhouse and other amenities.



Rather than own the grant — or, God forbid, concede that the kind of pork-barrelling Labor railed against while in opposition was not up to scratch — Albanese first went after the ABC for not reporting his (false) sewage claims before claiming he hadn’t been to the club “for many, many years”. The saga is particularly funny for anyone who lives in Sydney’s inner west and frequents the club. In the general manager reports they sometimes send out to members, the $6 million grant has been referred to as the “Albanese upgrades” or “Albanese building works”, such was its connection – in their minds, at least – to the prime minister. (I should disclose that, like Albanese, I am also an honouree member, in so far as I last paid my $5 membership fees about five years ago but can still flash my expired card and get a discount on beers). Related Article Government grants ‘The system is a farce’: Constitutional expert Anne Twomey slams Albanese golf grant as ‘grey corruption’ The club is also a significant source of pride for the local Labor fraternity because, in 2020, it was they who led the charge to successfully defeat a Greens-backed plan to cut the course down to nine holes. Labor figures, including Albanese, fiercely resisted the proposal. Together with the then-MP for neighbouring Barton, Linda Burney, he said it risked undermining “the spirit of the inner west”. To now see Albanese acting as though he’s barely heard of it is a mammoth credulity-stretching exercise.



The point is not that Labor gave the club the grant — it really could use a reno — but Albanese’s strange, reflexive instinct to insist black is white (“I didn’t fall off the stage”), and continue bleeding on issues for no reason. From the Helen Haines “integrity sheet” to the ban on credit card surcharges, the government seems unable to either anticipate controversies or react normally to them when they arise. Minns, then, has every incentive to look and sound as little like his federal counterpart as possible. On Thursday, the government changed tack again, stifling a growing backlash against changes to rules requiring cafes to have recyclable cups by agreeing to water down the most controversial aspects of the changes. There is obviously nuance to this. Albanese is hunted by elements of the conservative press in ways Minns is not, and the premier has often been criticised by his own side for being too willing to abandon Labor principles in his eagerness to court the middle and centre-right of the electorate. Loading That same dynamic though means that while Minns is not loved by the base in the way the prime minister is, he is more appealing to socially conservative voters, or those who might be considering voting for One Nation.



MPs in seats believed to be at risk from One Nation consistently report that, when they are door-knocking, voters react far more positively once they make the distinction between the federal and state governments. Much has been written about the testy relationship between the pair, and Minns has come under fire at times for being too quick to point criticism at Albanese and the federal government. But more than picking fights with the feds, Labor strategists believe Minns’ most vital task over the next five months is creating enough differentiation between the two governments that when voters go to the polls, they aren’t treating it as a referendum on Labor. Michael McGowan is state political editor for The Sydney Morning Herald. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis.
