World.title: ‘Not invited, not welcome’: Russian ambassador attends Greens leader’s speech denying Ukraine military aid
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalRussia-Ukraine war ‘Not invited, not welcome’: Russian ambassador attends Greens leader’s speech denying Ukraine military aid Andrew Probyn October 28, 2026 — 6:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Greens Leader David Shoebridge has been embarrassed by the attendance of the Russian Ambassador at his inaugural National Press Club address in which he doubled down on calls to deny Ukraine military aid – a policy critics say is pro-Kremlin. Shoebridge, who says he did not invite Mikhail Petrakov to the event, said the Greens partyroom stood for “peace and non-violence” but was “rock solid” in its support for the people in Ukraine. Greens leader David Shoebridge addresses the National Press Club. Alex Ellinghausen “We 100 per cent rock solid support the people of Ukraine to resist the illegal and immoral war,” the Greens leader told the Press Club. “Rock solid support for their struggle against an illegal invasion by Russia, rock solid support for humanitarian and direct financial support to the people of Ukraine and the government of Ukraine.



“And we also support the firmest, clearest, most unambiguous sanctions against the state of Russia. Russia’s invasion is illegal, it’s immoral and it is wrong.” But when challenged by Nine News as to why the Greens’ support doesn’t extend to giving Ukraine military aid, he said the party “hold true to our pillar of peace and non-violence”. Shoebridge said he did not know Petrakov was listening to his speech. “One hundred per cent not welcome, 100 per cent not invited, I don’t want him here,” he told Nine News. Russia’s ambassador to Australia Mikhail Petrakov seen at the National Press Club on Wednesday.



Ukraine’s Ambassador Vasyl Myroshnychenko, who has been lobbying Shoebridge to change his foreign policy on military aid, was outraged by Petrakov’s attendance. “I just find it really appalling that he actually shows up there. But I mean, in this particular case, I believe he feels quite comfortable coming to Senator Shoebridge’s presentation,” he said. “No military aid to Ukraine aligns with the priorities of Russia.” He said the Greens in Germany supported giving Ukraine military aid and the Australian Greens should follow suit. Labor and the Coalition have both criticised the Greens for their Ukraine aid policy.



“The first policy pronouncement of the leader of the Greens political party was to say that he does not and will not support our military aid to the brave people of Ukraine over $1.8 billion – the only person that helps is Vladimir Putin,” Assistant Minister for Defence Peter Khalil said. Related Article Greens Shoebridge says Steele-John’s social media posts ‘obviously not the way to resolve’ issue “I would hope that he would reconsider and support the military aid that we’ve provided to Ukraine because the international community support is the only thing that’s keeping Ukraine alive in this war.” Shadow Defence Minister James Paterson said he was not surprised the Russian ambassador was in attendance for Shoebridge’s speech. “He would have liked what he was going to hear. The Greens foreign policy under David Shoebridge is Putin-friendly,” he said. “He wants to hand a veto over Australia’s defence assistance for Ukraine to Vladimir Putin through the United Nations Security Council.”



Shoebridge’s Senate colleague Sarah Hanson-Young has already disagreed with his Ukraine stance, saying military aid should be provided if needed. “I think we need to be doing everything we can to support the people in Ukraine,” she told ABC’s 7.30. “If (military aid) is the support that people need in order to defend themselves from the invasion of Russia, I think Australians need to support that. “You can’t allow people to be left fending for themselves.” Paterson commended Hanson-Young’s stance.



“It’s to Sarah Hanson Young’s great credit that she’s gone public with her discomfort with David Shoebridge’s Vladimir Putin-endorsed foreign policy,” he said. Shoebridge was pictured at a dinner with the then-Russian ambassador and Liberal figures in 2022, but he and the Liberals said they were blindsided by the envoy’s presence. World.title: ‘Can’t have a life’: Kanga joins welfare push for later starting times in racing
World.content:
SportRacingVictorian racing ‘Can’t have a life’: Kanga joins welfare push for later starting times in racing Danny Russell Updated October 28, 2026 — 6:35pm ,first published 4:57pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Colourful racing identity John Kanga has joined a push for later training hours on the eve of Melbourne Cup week, saying it was time to improve working conditions for stable staff. The former Melbourne Racing Club chairman, who obtained a Racing Victoria stable hand licence earlier this year, said the long-held tradition of 4am starts and split shifts needed an industry-wide review. John Kanga is calling for a better work-life balance for strappers, track riders and horse trainers. Eddie Jim Kanga has joined Australian Trainers’ Association president Troy Corstens in calling for a better work-life balance for strappers, track riders and trainers now that stables were juggling the extra demands of twilight and night meetings. “I’ve never been a great believer in doing something simply because we’ve always done it that way,” Kanga told The Age.



Related Article Blinkers On

Victorian racing The Melbourne Cup is not the only vital race being staged at Flemington “We quite rightly spend an enormous amount of time talking about the welfare of our horses. Surely, the welfare of the people looking after those horses deserves just as much attention.” Kanga, who controversially resigned from the MRC board on the eve of last year’s Caulfield Cup carnival, no longer holds an official position in the racing industry. But he said he obtained a stable-hand licence through Racing Victoria’s Stable Start program to gain a broader understanding of the growing demands on trainers and their staff. He regularly spends time visiting Flemington stables.



“Some of the best ideas in racing don’t come from the boardroom. They come from the people doing the work,” he said. When asked if he intended to return to the sport in an official capacity, such as nominating for the upcoming Victoria Racing Club board elections, Kanga said, “I’ve never needed a title to contribute to racing, and I’m not about to start now.” Training starts at Flemington before the crack of dawn. Getty Images The VRC agreed to a later starting time at Flemington in July, delaying the course opening from 4am to 4.30am. A 5am start will be trialled after the spring carnival. But Corstens, a second-generation trainer based at Flemington, has been pushing for a 6am start – a prospect that would clash with working hours for track-management staff.



“Ideally, if we started at six, we’d need a closing time of 10am, and the VRC would have to work with their track staff and renegotiate their EBA [enterprise bargaining agreement],” Corstens said. Related Article Spring racing carnival Record-breaking trainer’s warning for punters on Melbourne Cup favourite “I’ve been pushing for a long time, and the main reason that I’m doing that is because I think it will attract a hell of a lot more people to the game [for work].” Training centres have opened before dawn for more than a century. The reasons were varied – trainers had second jobs, they wanted first access to grass tracks, they liked to work their horses in secret under the cover of darkness, they had to work their gallopers before going to the races, and curators needed access to the racecourse.



There are still trainers who don’t want to break with the tradition. “Everyone’s entitled to the way they want to do it, but I just think that it’d open things right up if we had a look at it and did have a change,” Corstens said. “I think sleep is the most important factor in anybody’s life. And if you’re starting at 3 o’clock in the morning, these kids can’t have a life. “They are having to go to bed at seven and 8 o’clock at night, they can’t do anything. “My family’s used to me going to bed at 8 o’clock every night. Would I like to spend more time with them? Of course, I would, but you know, a lot of the time I’m buggered, and I need to hit the hay.”



Editor's pick Melbourne Cup First look at the Melbourne Cup form – we rate the top 24 horses Corstens also called for government assistance to streamline the visa process for international track riders to help service the Victorian industry. He said regional training centres and the thoroughbred breeding industry found it difficult to attract suitable staff at different times of the year. “I think the process could be simpler, a lot simpler than it is,” he said. “Andrew Hore-Lacy [Thoroughbred Breeders Association CEO] has been working very hard in the background, trying to improve the situation for us all.” Kanga, who races horses with Danny O’Brien and Dom Sutton, said stable staff were the backbone of the racing industry.



“Without them, there are no horses prepared, no races and no industry,” he said. “This isn’t about making racing easier. It’s about making racing sustainable, both for the people who work in it and the generations who will follow us.” Kanga was MRC chairman for 12 months, from October 2024 until October 2025, before resigning after questions from The Age. In that time, his committee was credited with stoping the sale of Sandown Racecourse for housing development, opening up the inside track at Caulfield for jump outs and offering cheaper food and drink. Fit for a King: Star on the brink of a Cup start after Bendigo win



Rachel King is known for her timing, and the Sydney-based jockey delivered the perfect ride at the perfect moment on Wednesday to all but book a last-minute slot in next week’s Melbourne Cup. King’s winning steer on So You Are was enough to win the group 3 Bendigo Cup over 2400 metres and is expected to attract a sizeable enough weight penalty that would push the Bjorn Baker-trained gelding into the starting field for the race that stops the nation. Rachel King and So You Are win the Bendigo Cup. Racing Photos In doing so, she dashed the hopes of several other contenders. Soulcombe, owned by several premiership-winning Richmond Tigers including Tom Lynch, needed to finish in the top three but blew his chances at the start. He flopped out of the gates and finished ninth.



Danny O’Brien’s Litzdeel fell agonisingly short again, running home strongly for third, while Gai Waterhouse’s The Euphrates and Ciaron Maher’s Kings Valley could not sustain a solid tempo in front. If Racing Victoria handicapper David Hegan lumps So You Are with an extra 1.5-kilogram penalty on Thursday, it will be enough to push it up the Melbourne Cup order. That is not unreasonable. It would then shuffle import Hopewell Rock back into 25th place and one spot outside the field. Only Racing Victoria’s strict safety protocols, which include scans of all Melbourne Cup runners this week, could then change the make-up of Tuesday’s Cup field. “He’s done everything he can, the horse – he deserved to be there and hopefully that’s enough to get him in,” Baker’s racing manager Luke Hilton said.



So You Are has won his past three races on the trot – the Tatts Cup (2400m) at Randwick in September, followed by victories in the group 3 Colin Stephen Quality (2400m) at Rosehill and the group 3 St Leger (2600m) at Randwick. “We thought he may get in after winning the St Leger, but he needed a few more points,” Hilton said. “We had a look at the Moonee Valley Cup and Bjorn and [owner] Mr Ramsey put their heads together and came up with this plan today, and it’s come off. Let’s hope it’s enough. “Rach and Bjorn have done a lot of work with him. His form was a little bit questionable Melbourne way, that was probably the only glitch that we thought he might have, but he really handled it well today.” It has been a fruitful spring for King, who became the first female jockey to win the Caulfield Guineas on Warwoven earlier this month.



“He had a couple of runs in Melbourne and probably not run up to standard before, so it was good to see him get it done the other way around,” King said. “He’s just a horse in really good form. He’s tough, he puts himself on speed, he makes life easy, and he doesn’t want to let one get past him.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: Anthropic brings its mega IPO to Australia’s AI-starved investors
World.content:
BusinessMarketsAI Anthropic brings its mega IPO to Australia’s AI-starved investors Carmeli Argana October 28, 2026 — 6:35pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Anthropic will offer shares as part of its blockbuster initial public offering directly to Australian investors, bringing a fresh artificial-intelligence bet to a market still reeling from the high-profile collapse of a data centre start-up’s float. The IPO will be accessible to local retail investors after Anthropic submits a prospectus to the Australian Securities and Investments Commission, according to a filing on Monday with the US sharemarket regulator. The number of shares on offer will be disclosed in a later filing. Investors are expecting a fair valuation of between $US1.4 trillion and $US1.75 trillion ($2 trillion and $2.5 trillion), people familiar with the matter have said. Anthropic’s IPO will give local investors a chance to directly invest in one of the biggest AI players. Bloomberg The Australian offering will give the Claude chatbot maker exposure to Australia’s $4.8 trillion superannuation industry as well as a retail investor base starved for an opportunity to buy into a major company at the heart of the AI trade.



The collapse of Firmus’s IPO, which would have ranked among this market’s largest ever listings, dealt a blow to sentiment after it fell apart as demand from international investors failed to materialise. “Many Australian investors will be keen to participate in Anthropic’s IPO,” according to Cameron Gleeson, head of investment strategy at Betashares. “Anthropic is a very different proposition to Firmus. Anthropic is selling a product that customers are already paying for and only increasing their spending on.” Australia is one of a few countries around the world where retail investors are able to directly buy into the Anthropic IPO. Compared with the technology-heavy markets across North Asia and the US, Australia lacks the same semiconductor or hyperscaler companies that have been the focus of sharemarkets in recent months. The shortage of exposure helped support SpaceX’s local offering this year, with retail investors driving demand. Australia is one of a few countries around the world, along with Japan, Canada and parts of Europe, where retail investors are able to directly buy into the Anthropic IPO.



Professional and sophisticated investors will be able to participate in Anthropic’s US offering directly without having to wait for an Australian regulatory filing, according to Anthropic’s prospectus. Super funds and other large institutional investors fall into the professional category. Sophisticated investors include individuals with net assets of at least $2.5 million or gross income of at least $250,000 per year. Related Article Opinion

AI ‘Bold, but sane’? The future of AI is riding on Anthropic’s float Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Among Anthropic’s 22 underwriters, Macquarie’s capital-raising arm is expected to lead the local offering. CommSec will lead retail marketing, the Australian Financial Review reported, citing people briefed on the matter. CommSec also handled SpaceX’s Australian retail marketing this year. The brokerage at the time said it received more than 28,000 applications – a record. It didn’t say how many shares were eventually allotted to its clients.



Anthropic’s offering “should draw strong local interest after years of the biggest names in AI growing behind closed doors,” said Josh Gilbert, lead analyst for Asia Pacific at eToro in Sydney. While Firmus asked investors to back an expansion story leaning heavily on debt, “Anthropic’s numbers put it on a much firmer footing, and it offers something public markets have barely had: direct exposure to a frontier model maker.” Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. World.title: Wilson Parking warns of text scam demanding payment for overdue parking
World.content:
Wilson Parking is warning of fraudulent text messages asking for payment of an overdue parking notice, and says anybody receiving one should not click on any links contained in the message.

The links directs recipients to external websites.

Wilson Parking said the messages were not legitimate communications from the company and no personal, banking or payment information should be provided.

The company said it was "actively investigating" reports of the scam.

Wilson Parking said anyone who receives one of these fraudulent messages should:

Not click on any links contained in the SMS.

Not provide personal, payment or banking information.

Forward the scam text to the Department of Internal Affairs on 7726.

Delete the message from their device.

Contact Wilson Parking through its official channels if they are uncertain whether they have a legitimate outstanding parking notice.

World.title: Manslaughter charge laid over death of Braydon Hepworth in Christchurch
World.content:
A man has been charged with manslaughter following the disappearance and death of Braydon Hepworth in Christchurch.

The 21-year-old's body was found buried in a shed in Linwood, Christchurch, on 8 October after he had gone missing in early September.

Detective Inspector Scott Anderson said a 60-year-old man, earlier charged with concealing Hepworth's body and making a false statement now faced a manslaughter charge.

The man is in custody and would appear in Christchurch District Court on Thursday. He had interim name suppression.

Last week, police charged a 34-year-old Christchurch man in relation to the concealment of Hepworth's body.

Anderson said the investigation into Hepworth's disappearance remained ongoing.

World.title: Typhoon warning for northern CNMI
World.content:
Authorities in the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands have issued a typhoon warning for the CNMI's Northern Islands, as Typhoon In-fa approaches with destructive winds.

Governor David M. Apatang has declared Typhoon Condition III for Agrihan, Pagan and Alamagan.

The warning means destructive winds of at least 74 miles per hour are possible within the next 48 hours.

In-fa was a Category Four typhoon at 1pm Wednesday local time, with maximum sustained winds of 140 miles per hour.

The storm was located about 905 miles east of Saipan, moving west-northwest at 10 miles per hour.

Forecasters say In-fa could strengthen into a super typhoon on Wednesday night.

Tropical storm-force winds are expected to begin affecting Pagan and Alamagan late Friday morning, with the typhoon forecast to pass between Pagan and Agrihan at around 7pm.

Conditions are expected to ease in the early hours of Saturday, with improving weather by sunrise.

Residents of the northern islands have been urged to remain in safe shelter from Friday morning until sunrise on Saturday.

They are also being advised to secure essential supplies, including food, water, medication, flashlights, batteries and radios.

No typhoon condition has been declared for Saipan, Tinian or Rota.

However, rain bands from In-fa could bring heavy showers to those islands on Friday, while seas and surf are expected to build from Thursday night.

World.title: Pacific Elders' Voice calls for reversal of Forum partnership with Israel
World.content:
The Pacific Elders' Voice has called for the Pacific Islands Forum to review and reverse its partnership agreement with Israel.

The group of former Pacific prime ministers, presidents and senior diplomats says the Forum's decision to make Israel a sectoral partner conflicts with the region's commitments to human rights, self-determination and international law.

In a statement, the Pacific Elders' Voice (PEV) said the Forum's decision raised questions about the consistency of the region's positions on colonialism, human rights and self-determination.

It cited the conflict in Gaza, Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank and what it described as violations of international law, while also noting unresolved issues of political status and self-determination in the Pacific.

The PEV said the agreement to partner with Israel should be reversed to ensure the Forum's external partnerships remain consistent with the region's stated principles on peace, justice and respect for international law.

"The Pacific remains one of the only regions in the world with the largest number of peoples living under occupation - from the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands to Guam; from Kanaky New Caledonia to French Polynesia; and from West Papua to Bougainville."

The Pacific Elders group said it had consistently supported decolonisation and self-determination in Kanaky and West Papua, as well as investigations by the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights and the Pacific Islands Forum into alleged serious human rights violations by France and Indonesia.

"Given our principled positions on colonialism and human rights violations in the region, the PEV is perturbed with the Forum's recent partnership with Israel, the state which has committed genocide in Gaza, and has a long history of offending against UN resolutions and international law."

The Elders group echoed a range of Pacific Islands civil society groups in calling for the Forum's partnership with Israel to be reviewed and reversed.

The group noted that Israel's prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and other Israeli leaders are considered to have committed war crimes, with arrest warrants in their name issued by the International Criminal Court.

As a PIF partner, Israel will support Pacific development priorities in areas such as water management, desalination, agriculture and climate change adaptation. Pacific Islands Forum

World.title: Waiouru fire still producing smoke after several days
World.content:
A fire in Waiouru has not spread since it started burning over the weekend but a small amount of smoke is still being produced.

Fire and Emergency said the vegetation fire at the Waiouru Military Training Area had not grown in size on Wednesday but drone teams would be working overnight again to survey any hot spots.

The fire had burnt through over 3000 hectares since it was sparked by gun fire during military training on Sunday.

"While some flareups did occur as expected, the fire has not grown in size," Fire and Emergency Incident Controller Nigel Dravitzki said.

"A perimeter flight this morning has more accurately confirmed the fire to have covered 3700 hectares."

Six New Zealand Defence Force ground crews, local volunteer fire brigades and air operations had been working on the blaze from Wednesday morning.

Additional ground crews are set to join on Thursday including Department of Conservation firefighters and all crews would be be supported by heavy machinery and aircraft.

FENZ said firefighters had taken advantage of more "favourable weather" to keep the fire from spreading.

On Tuesday morning, MetService head of weather news Heather Keats told Morning Report the strong winds were making it difficult to fight wildfires, but rain was expected to help and the wind forecast to ease.

World.title: Nelson ute theft: Nicholas Tripp jailed after dangerous police chase
World.content:
A tradesman opening a gate to his yard turned to find a stranger at the wheel of his ute, who then sped off in the vehicle.

Disqualified driver Nicholas Tripp led police on a chase from Nelson, where he weaved through dense traffic, to Wakefield, 30km south, where he stopped at a dairy to buy tobacco.

He hoped to get to Christchurch, Judge Bruce Davidson said while sentencing Tripp on Wednesday.

Tripp evaded police at the dairy, then ran rampant through the village of Wakefield, pulling open car doors and yelling at drivers to get out.

In one instance, he tried to open the door of a vehicle as the driver grabbed it and pulled it shut, then screamed: "Help me, help me, the police are gonna get me".

The 34-year-old with an "extensive list of previous offending" over 14 years was sentenced in the Nelson District Court to 22 months in prison on 11 charges.

Nelson District Court. (File photo)

Most sprang from his "offending spree" on June 17, which resulted in multiple victims, police said.

Tripp had earlier pleaded guilty to charges of unlawfully taking a vehicle, attempting to take a vehicle, unlawfully interfering with a vehicle, driving while disqualified on a third or subsequent time, two burglary charges including one over $5000, driving dangerously, theft and assaulting a female.

'Seized opportunity'

On the morning of June 17 this year, a landscaping firm worker parked his ute at the entrance to the company's yard in central Nelson.

Tripp, who has convictions for driving while disqualified on two occasions and driving while suspended on four occasions, was nearby and found the ute running while the driver got out to unlock the entrance gate.

Tripp, who was on intensive supervision for earlier offending, got in the vehicle and sped off, police said.

He "impulsively seized the opportunity" to get in the vehicle and drive off, Judge Davidson said.

The worker called police and tracked the vehicle via a company GPS tracking app.

Tripp threw away the worker's cellphone stored in the vehicle's drinks holder as he sped south, thinking it might stop the ability to track his movements.

"Your driving was very dangerous, including that you overtook a truck laden with fuel and were undertaking other vehicles," Judge Davidson said.

As Tripp reached State Highway 6 south of Richmond he went through a busy intersection and overtook a road contracting firm's fuel truck, narrowly missing it as he passed, police said.

He then undertook a vehicle and continued south before overtaking another vehicle, forcing three oncoming vehicles to take evasive action and pull to the left to avoid a collision, police said.

Tripp passed officers waiting for him at a site before Wakefield and continued to undertake other southbound vehicles as he entered the village.

Stopped for tobacco

He stopped outside a local dairy and bakery, went in and asked for a packet of tobacco.

As the staff member turned her back, Tripp reached through a plastic barrier, took a cigarette lighter and hid it in his pocket.

He then reached under the barrier and grabbed the staff member by the arm as she held the tobacco.

Unable to get the tobacco, he took another lighter instead, police said.

As he went to get back in the ute he saw a police officer approaching and began running away, discarding the stolen items in a bush and tossing his wallet into a boat parked nearby, police said.

Tripp then spotted another ute parked on the roadside, with the driver at the wheel.

Police said Tripp banged on the driver's door before trying to pull it open, but the driver held the door and pulled it shut.

Tripp then screamed at him, "Help me, help me, the police are gonna get me", before running off when he saw the officer in pursuit.

He spied another vehicle parked nearby and punched the driver's window multiple times in an attempt to break in.

The officer caught up with Tripp and told him he was under arrest.

But Tripp ran off again and into a nearby property through an open gate.

He got into a vehicle parked there and while rummaging for the keys, the officer opened the driver's door.

Tripp climbed out the passenger side and ran to another property where he tried to get into a vehicle, but it was locked.

Another vehicle on the property was unlocked, so he got in, rummaged through a purse on the front seat and fled on foot again as police closed in on him.

Tripp tried one more car before police stopped him. Another officer had arrived at the scene by then and Tripp was arrested.

Defence lawyer Fleur Oback said Tripp was sorry and had admitted his actions early.

She said background factors in his life warranted credit in sentencing, and he had been in custody since his arrest for the equivalent of nine months.

"It's given him significant time for sober reflection," she said.

Tripp told the court he was sorry, but was stressed at the time.

"Sorry for overtaking that vehicle. It was very foolish," he said.

Police prosecutor Mary Hewlett said it was serious offending, conducted while Tripp was under the influence of an undetermined substance.

Judge Davidson said Tripp appeared to have limited insight into the risk posed to members of the public, including multiple road users.

From a starting point of two and a half years in prison, Tripp received 22 months, with leave to apply for home detention if he could demonstrate a "sea change in attitude", including accepting proper treatment for substance abuse.

He received a further disqualification from driving for a year.

* This story originally appeared in the New Zealand Herald.

World.title: FA expecting Socceroos friendlies in Middle East to go ahead
World.content:
The Socceroos are set to forge ahead with plans to play friendlies in the Middle East next month in the face of the increasingly volatile conflict in the region.

Australia is scheduled to face Qatar in Doha on November 14 before taking on Jordan in Amman on November 17 in what will be the Socceroos' final hit-outs before coach Tony Popovic names his squad for January's Asian Cup.

But there are security concerns following violence this month, including a Houthi strike at the Riyadh airport in Saudi Arabia, which is hosting the cup.

Socceroos dates November 14: Friendly vs Qatar (Doha)

November 17: Friendly vs Jordan (Amman)

January 9: Socceroos first group match at Asian Cup finals, vs Singapore (Khobar, Saudi Arabia)

Last week nine people were gunned down by Syrian militants at an orthodox church in Jordan, one of the more stable countries in the Middle East.

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade advises Australians to reconsider their need to travel to Jordan. Qatar is rated as a much safer destination.

As things stand Football Australia (FA) is expecting the games with Qatar and Jordan to go ahead as scheduled.

"Football Australia is closely monitoring the situation in the Middle East ahead of the Socceroos' matches against Qatar and Jordan in November," an FA spokesperson said in a statement to AAP.

"The safety and wellbeing of our players, staff and supporters remains paramount.

"Our experienced security team is actively monitoring developments and providing regular updates, and we will be guided by the advice of our head of security.

"Risk assessment is part of our planning for every national team camp, and it will be a key focus of our preparations for November."

Popovic knocked back extension Socceroos coach Tony Popovic has revealed he turned down a four-year contract offer from Football Australia (FA) to take the team through to the 2030 World Cup.

While FA's decision to push on is encouraging, there is still no clear decision on what will happen with January's Asian Cup.

Saudi Arabia has been forced to move a friendly with South Korea to Qatar as part of the flow-on effect of the Riyadh attack, and several Asian Champions League games involving Saudi club sides have been postponed.

A decision is yet to be made as to whether the Asian Cup, which is expected to kick off with the hosts taking on Palestine in Riyadh on January 7, will still take place as scheduled.

Australia's is scheduled to take on Singapore in Khobar on January 9 for its first group game of the tournament.

There is growing concern that the Asian Cup would be delayed by 12 months, with AFC president Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa saying a decision may not be made until the end of November.

"If we need to make a decision then we will, but we could move back a year to 2028 if we need to," he said in Zurich this month.

"But at the moment we are monitoring the situation and everything is on schedule."

AAP/ABC

World.title: Fox axing from Devils VFL not due to single incident, club says
World.content:
Tasmania Devils have strongly defended their club culture after axing VFL skipper Robbie Fox following an off-field indiscretion.

The Devils also said the decision to part ways with their inaugural captain was not based on an isolated incident.

The team confirmed yesterday that Fox would not be offered a contract for the 2027 season, citing, in part, the club's "expectations regarding player behaviour and adherence to our standards".

Yesterday, the ABC revealed Fox had been involved in an incident at a Hobart pub, the Granada Tavern, where he was ejected from the venue after becoming drunk and disorderly, and acting belligerently toward some staff.

It is also understood a bottle was thrown and smashed during the incident.

Nobody is believed to have been injured, and there was no police involvement.

Kath McCann says Fox had "some areas for improvement and for growth, and he's dealing with the consequences of that". (ABC News: Ashleigh Barraclough)

The ABC can also reveal Fox had earlier played in a charity golf event at the nearby Claremont Golf Club with several Devils teammates.

Fox's foursome included vice-captain Jye Menzie and reigning best-and-fairest Hugh Dixon.

There is no suggestion those players were involved in the later incident at the Granada Tavern.

Robbie Fox (left) pictured during his tenure with the Swans. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Michael Willson)

Chief marketing officer Kath McCann told local media today that the decision not to offer Fox a contract was, in part, the culmination of several "situations".

"I want to be really clear that there was no particular one incident that led to this decision", she said.

"There have been situations where Robbie probably had some areas for improvement and for growth, and he's dealing with the consequences of that.

"I think it's fair to say that not everybody gets everything right," she said

Fox has been contacted for comment.

McCann said the Devils's culture was strong, and that their swift decision to cut on-field ties with Fox was indicative of that.

"Our club has really high standards, and we're really proud of that," she said.

"We've said from the start that our club is focused on ensuring we work with the very best people, and the highest of standards.

" It's been a part of our success to date and will continue to be in the future. "

But McCann also confirmed that Fox would continue in his role as the club's Strategic Projects Lead, and defended the decision to keep him on as a club employee.

McCann said the club was "very comfortable" with where it had landed regarding his playing contract and that it would not divulge details around its internal processes.

"Robbie's a member of our staff, he's been an important part of our inaugural year, and he's a really great person," she said.

Fox played 13 games for the Devils in an injury-affected year, after being recruited back to his native Tasmania following his delisting by the Sydney Swans.

Under his captaincy, the Devils finished in the VFL top four and earned a finals double chance.

World.title: Former Australian Open champ Stan Wawrinka ends illustrious career
World.content:
Stan Wawrinka's illustrious tennis career finally came to an end at his home tournament in Basel.

The three-time grand slam winner was beaten by eighth-seeded Jiří Lehečka in the first round of the Swiss Indoors, losing 7-5, 7-6(2).

The 41-year-old Wawrinka's last shot as a professional tennis player was a backhand that landed wide — to the audible disappointment of the vociferous home crowd.

Wawrinka, who turned pro in 2002, had announced last December that 2026 would be his last year on tour and "Stan the Man" had received warm send-offs throughout his farewell season.

"For me, all I wanted in my career was to give everything, to have no regrets, to always fight, to always give 100 per cent in every match — out of respect for myself, for the opponent, for the tournament, for the fans, for everybody," Wawrinka told the ATP Tour website ahead of his final match.

"That was always the most important thing for more than 20 years, and that's the only way you can leave the sport: without any regrets."

Wawrinka won his three grand slam titles after defeating the then-world number 1 player in each final. He beat Rafael Nadal to win the 2014 Australian Open and downed Novak Djokovic for the French Open title in 2015 and the US Open the following year.

Wawrinka, who reached a career-high world ranking of number three in 2014, won 16 tour-level titles.

He also paired with Roger Federer to win the doubles title for Switzerland at the 2008 Beijing Olympics. The duo helped Switzerland win its first Davis Cup title in 2014.

AP

World.title: Arsenal knocked out of League Cup by fourth-tier minnow in all-time upset
World.content:
Reigning English champion Arsenal has been knocked out of the EFL League Cup by fourth-tier side Fleetwood Town in a massive boilover.

A whopping 84 positions separate the London giant from its League Two minnow opponent on the English league pyramid, but in front of home fans, Fleetwood Town completed a remarkable upset 5-3 on penalties, after the scores finished 1-1 at the end of regulation.

Fleetwood, which is sitting a lowly 18th in League Two, took the lead in the 21st minute through Aaron Loupalo-Bi, scoring with one of just two shots on goal the hosts managed for the entire match.

A 50th-minute equaliser from Arsenal striker Viktor Gyökeres brought the Premier League giants back into the contest, but the Gunners could not find another.

Arsenal teenager Max Dowman was sent off in the 86th minute before the cup tie went to penalties.

Fleetwood was perfect from all five attempts, while Bruno Guimarães's miss for Arsenal on the Gunners' fourth attempt paved the way for one of the biggest upsets in the history of the competition.

The match was halted early on after the referee noticed a drone hovering above the stadium.

Arsenal had just been awarded a free kick when the referee spotted the drone and temporarily stopped play, leading to jeers from some fans inside Fleetwood's home ground, Highbury Stadium.

The delay lasted nearly eight minutes, with the referee speaking to the stadium safety officer, both managers and then some of the players before finally restarting the game.

ABC/AP

World.title: NBA's shortest-ever player to have jersey retired
World.content:
Tyrone "Muggsy" Bogues spent his entire NBA career looking up at all other players. They'll be looking up at him now.

His name and number, anyway.

The Charlotte Hornets announced on Tuesday that the No. 1 jersey worn by Bogues — the NBA's smallest-ever player at 5-foot-3 (160 centimetres)— will be retired during a half-time ceremony when the team plays host to Milwaukee on February 11.

"How ironic is that?" Bogues said.

"After all those times that you felt like you were looking up, looking up for so many years, at people, then here comes this particular moment. And when that jersey actually goes up, it'll be like I'm the one looking down at the entire world. It's going to be a surreal moment."

Muggsy Bogues played 14 seasons in the NBA. (AP: Chris O'Meara)

Bogues will be the third player whose Hornets jersey is retired, joining Bobby Phills (13) and Dell Curry (30). He began his career with Washington, then went to Charlotte in the 1988 expansion draft and essentially has called the Carolinas home ever since.

"Charlotte embraced me with open arms," Bogues said.

"This is a place I've called home more than I've called any other place home, even growing up in the city of Baltimore. So, having this type of recognition for my family, for the organisation to look at you in this type of light, I mean, it means the world."

Bogues played in the NBA for parts of 14 seasons, spending the bulk of that time with Charlotte and having stints with Golden State, Washington and Toronto. He was the 12th selection in the 1987 draft — one spot behind Indiana taking Reggie Miller — and wound up playing more games than all but eight other members of that draft class.

He averaged 7.7 points and 7.6 assists for his career. Bogues was part of Charlotte teams that reached the 50-win mark in three consecutive seasons, plus he was part of the franchise's first post-season series victory in 1993.

"Muggsy was here from the beginning and played with a heart, toughness and competitive spirit that made him a fan favourite," Hornets co-chairmen Rick Schnall and Gabe Plotkin said in a statement on Tuesday.

"At 5-foot-3, he overcame obstacles throughout his career and proved he belonged among the best players in the world. He became a role model for generations, showing young people that their size doesn't have to limit what they can achieve."

The average NBA player during Bogues's playing career stood 6-foot-7 (200cm) and weighed 213 pounds (96kg). Bogues was 40cm shorter than that average and 35kg lighter in those years.

He has remained part of the Hornets in retirement, still often representing the team at community events and travelling the world as an NBA ambassador. And he knows he changed the game, debunking the thought that someone had to have a certain height to make the NBA.

"I was just like any kid that had a dream," Bogues said.

"I just kept believing and kept having success. And my mindset was, 'If you play against the best, and you have success against the best, you need to be included with the best.'"

AP

World.title: Maya Joint makes mockery of rankings with big win in Tokyo
World.content:
Maya Joint has made a mockery of the tennis rankings with an impressive display to uproot one of the top seeds at the Pan Pacific Open event in Tokyo.

Ranked a career-high 28 in February, the Australian's ranking has dropped steadily throughout the year, and she entered this WTA 500 event ranked 94th.

However, the American-born Aussie showed the numbers can't always be trusted as she powered past sixth seed and world number 16 Sorana Cirstea of Romania.

Joint's impressive 6-3, 7-6 (7-4) victory yesterday secured her a spot in the round of 16.

It also continued her recent resurgence, after she made the final at last month's Korea Open in Seoul, where compatriot Kim Birrell claimed her first WTA title with a 6-4, 6-2 win in the final.

Joint's next opponent is Spanish world number 42 Cristina Bucsa, who beat France's Diane Parry 7-5, 6-1 yesterday.

And Joint isn't the only in-form Australian still in the main draw.

On Monday, Talia Gibson, who recently reached the Singapore final, came through an all-Australian affair over qualifier Daria Kasatkina 6-0, 7-5.

Gibson powered through the first eight games in a row but was made to work hard to hold off the former world No.8 in the second set.

Her reward is a round-of-16 clash with eight-seeded Aleandra Eala, of the Philippines.

Meanwhile, in the Guangzhou Open, Venus Williams lost 6-2, 6-2 to Austrian teenager Lilli Tagger to be 0-13 in singles this year. The 28-year age gap between Williams, 46, and Tagger, 18, is believed to be a record difference between opponents in a WTA Tour match.

Williams created no break-point chances, and Tagger took four of the 16 she had.

AAP

World.title: Australia clawed its way back into the third Test, but big challenges await
World.content:
It was, in the final analysis, close to the perfect day of Test cricket: ebbing, flowing, intriguing, with 10 wickets falling and 329 runs-worth of enterprising batting fulfilling Les Favell's trusty old criteria for an entertaining day on the hill.

There was a six-fer for Mitchell Starc, another bundle of tantalising, shot-filled knocks from South Africa's underappreciated batting stars and a pair of remarkable sequences in which Australia took 5-29 and 4-2. Both sides will, in some ways, feel they got the better of the other for telling periods.

The nagging doubt, after day one of the third and deciding Test, is how badly Australia's chances had been damaged before a ball had even been bowled. Not sufficiently recovered from his neck injury, Steve Smith withdrew. Not sufficiently superior to his colleagues in most facets of the game a week ago, Scott Boland was dropped for Nathan Lyon.

Quick hits from Australia vs South Africa day one Here are the quick hits from day one of the third Test between Australia and South Africa.

Then there was the toss. The minute Pat Cummins won it and elected to bowl first under sunny skies, on a perfect-looking pitch — not exactly a ringing endorsement of Australia's remade top six — it was hard to stop one's mind from wandering away from Newlands and back through time in search of precedents.

The obvious destinations were Edgbaston in 2005, the scene of Ricky Ponting's ill-fated decision to bowl first in that classic nailbiter, and Brisbane three years earlier, when poor old Nasser Hussain got it even more horribly wrong.

By lunch at Cape Town, Cummins's Australians were fighting an unwelcome omen: South Africa's domineering 0-140, obtained with a procession of boundaries off the most credentialed bowling attack in world cricket, comfortably shaded both England's 1-132 at Edgbaston in '05 and Australia's 1-125 in Brisbane in '02. Was Cummins coming similarly a cropper?

Cricket history tends to write inconvenient facts out of these stories. Few remember that in the immediate aftermath of Nasser's nightmare, for instance, Australian skipper Steve Waugh admitted he probably would have bowled first, too, albeit with a caveat. "The significance of the toss is overrated," Waugh explained. "Whatever you do first, you've got to do it well."

To say Australia didn't bowl or field well in the first session of this crunch game is an understatement. The vaunted quicks misfired early. To staunch the bleeding, Lyon had to be deployed in just the 11th over. Normally apt to suffocate opponents with sharp fielding, tight lines and partnership bowling, Australia managed only two maidens in the first 25 overs.

Proteas opener Marques Ackerman, who'd never batted at the top of the order in first-class cricket until his Test debut last week, attacked the bowling like prime David Warner, clubbing 12 fours and two sixes in his run-a-ball, thrill-a-minute 95. With Aiden Markram, he raced to South Africa's first 150-run opening stand in nearly a decade.

Of particular concern for Australia was the captain's bowling performance, the tone of which was set in his first over when Markram freed his arms, swivelled into position as though the ball was travelling in slow motion and cross-batted Cummins over the fence at cow corner. Cummins would finish the day with 0-73 from 18 overs, having extracted almost nothing from the pitch he'd so liked the look of in the morning. South Africa played him as though intent on showing a competitive disrespect.

But at first, slowly, and then in two manic bursts, Australia did pull things out of the fire somewhat from their dismal early position.

Lyon, whom Ackerman had taken a particular liking to, kept his head amid the onslaught and had the left-hander stumped, later roaring back into the game at a critical juncture and sneaking one past Temba Bavuma to bowl the Proteas skipper for a duck. Australia stemmed the flow of easy runs — from 5.18 an over in the first session, down to 3.11 in the second.

Reprieved on 39 when Travis Head dropped a sitter at short cover, Markram had doubled his score but looked set for even bigger things when he fell into a trap set by Hazlewood to be caught on the fine leg boundary. Matthew Breetzke was too casual against Cooper Connolly's spin, the left-armer reviewed an LBW shout cannily to claim his first Test wicket.

In the above-mentioned half-hour of head loss, South Africa lost 3-13 and squandered its momentum. Immediately after tea, the Proteas were even more culpable for failing to resist what appeared to be a very obvious temptation: an outer ring of catchers scattered around the boundary from fine leg to deep mid-wicket and Starc banging it in short.

David Bedingham, who'd reached 50 without much trouble, was the first to fall for it, hooking recklessly to be cleverly caught on the fine leg rope by Hazlewood. Two balls later, Wiaan Mulder tried an equally daft hook and feathered an edge to Carey behind the stumps.

If South Africa is destined to win this match and with it the series — and unfortunately for Australia, there is an air of destiny about that result at the moment — perhaps the Proteas' 97-run seventh-wicket partnership will be looked back on as a critical period. Ryan Rickelton, out of form with the bat until that point, contributed a patient 42 as all-rounder Marco Jensen battered a typically confident half-century.

The latter fun, which threatened to take the game back away from Australia entirely, ended when Starc took the second new ball. Calling it a clinical demolition of the tail would undersell him: with 4-2 in the space of seven ruthlessly full and straight deliveries, the Australian paceman took his 20th Test five-wicket haul and finished with 6-72 from 16.3 overs.

Once the day's surges of chaos were done with, a comment by Cummins before play seemed worth revisiting. Boland's omission, the Australian captain claimed, was that great cliché of cricket team selection: "a good problem to have".

But is it? Perhaps Cummins was implying something else, that Australia's other selection problems — replacing three of its top-six batters with players assuredly not in the same class as Boland — are bad ones to have. Ones that may shape this game more than what happened on day one.

Which brings us to another of cricket's enduring clichés: don't judge a pitch until both teams have batted on it.

World.title: Quick hits: Starc's six balls of fury after Cummins's questionable call
World.content:
Mitch Starc produced one of the most destructive spells of his storied career and Josh Hazlewood took a special catch as the Aussies fought back from what looked to be a calamitous early call.

Here are the quick hits from day one of the third Test between Australia and South Africa in Cape Town.

1. Head's drop compounds Cummins's questionable call

It was already a horror morning for Australia.

Having sent the South Africans in to bat in what looked to be pristine conditions, Cummins was in need of quick wickets to validate what always looked to be a bizarre decision.

He didn't get them.

Instead, Proteas openers Marques Ackerman and Aiden Markram made light work of Australia's much-vaunted bowling attack, flying towards 100 at close to five runs an over.

But finally, a chance presented itself, with Markram mistiming a drive and finding Travis Head in the covers.

It was an absolute dolly, but the Australian somehow put it down, the ball slipping through his fingers and hurtling to turf.

Loading Instagram content

By lunch, the South Africans had flown to 0-140 from 27 overs, suggesting Cummins's call may well take a place among Test cricket's all-time clangers.

2. South African openers throw away tons

Ackerman went to lunch having plundered his way to a 75-ball 82.

Playing just his second Test, the southpaw made a mockery of Australia's aging attack, including taking Starc for four consecutive boundaries for the first time in the quick's Test career.

He looked odds on for a maiden Test ton — but things tightened up after the first break.

Growing increasingly impatient, he faced 18 balls for his next 13 runs before charging down the track and running past a Nathan Lyon off break.

Alex Carey broke the stumps with little fuss and Ackerman was out for 95.

Ackerman was filthy with himself after falling agonisingly short of a maiden Test ton. (Fox Cricket)

The 30-year-old was filthy with himself, throwing his head and grimacing on his way from the middle.

And not long after, Markram was following his opening partner back to the pavilion after also turning down a golden opportunity for a Test ton, having top-edged a Josh Hazlewood short ball to be caught on the boundary for 78.

Even so, it was a 158-run partnership that guaranteed a dream morning for the South Africans.

3. Hazlewood's quick thinking sends South Africa rocking

The Proteas were cruising — until they weren't.

Having lost Temba Bavuma and Matthew Breetzke before tea, South Africa's collapse continued when Josh Hazlewood took a remarkable boundary catch early in the evening session.

The big fast bowler steadied himself as a David Bedingham top edge flew his way, before contorting his body, rising high and plucking the ball from the air.

Hazlewood took a remarkable grab as Australia came roaring back after tea. (Fox Cricket)

Landing with his foot perilously close to the rope, Hazlewood was composed enough to release the ball and then complete the catch inside the field of play.

Hazlewood threw the ball back into play before completing the catch. (Fox Cricket)

And only two deliveries later, Starc had a second for the over, having Wiaan Mulder caught behind with another short ball.

Suddenly, South Africa had lost 4-29 and that explosive start was a distant memory.

Marco Jansen and Ryan Rickleton then came together to steady the ship, with a 95-run partnership, but the day's momentum swings weren't done there

4. Starc's stunning six-ball special

With twilight beginning to set in, Rickleton and Jansen looked to be cruising towards stumps.

But with Starc about to get his hands on the second new ball, the set pair would have been well aware they weren't out of the woods just yet.

And sure enough, Australia's premier spearhead proceeded to produce a devastating two-over spell.

First, he had Rickleton plumb in front to a searing swinging yorker before bowling Jansen with something similarly venomous just two balls later.

Starc produced six balls of fury to have the Proteas all out for 329. (Getty Images: Ashley Vlotman/Gallo Images)

He then castled the newly-arrived Gerald Coetzee for a golden duck with the first ball of his next over, setting up a hat-trick delivery against number 11 Kagiso Rabada.

The South African survived the initial thunderbolt, but was helpless to the second, out LBW to yet another stunning Starc special.

Starc had four wickets in the space of six deliveries and South Africa was all out for 329 as stumps were called on a ridiculous, topsy-turvy day of Test match cricket.

5. The best seats out of the house

Given the questionable decision to start the Cape Town Test on a Tuesday, there may well have been a few sick notes handed in ahead of day one at Newlands.

So, it seemed slightly unfair for the broadcast cameras to pick on the two spectators who had definitely shown up to work.

Sitting in surely the most ideally-located office block in world cricket, overlooking the oval from behind the hill, they were pictured with their eyes firmly fixed on the action unfolding below them.

These two office workers had the best seats out of the house. (Fox Cricket)

Caught out, it wasn't long before their heads were back in their work.

Nothing to see here, boss. (Fox Cricket)

Despite being a weekday, day one in Cape Town provided an engaged, colourful crowd, and undoubtedly the best of the series — both in and out of the ground.

6. Sore neck prevents Smith's Newlands return

Prior to a pulsating day in Cape Town, a dodgy neck robbed cricket fans of one of the most eagerly awaited returns in the sport's history.

How Sandpapergate rocked Australian cricket In 2018, Sandpapergate rocked Australian cricket to its very core. Here's how a febrile atmosphere colluded with a team persistently testing the limits of acceptability to change the game.

Having struggled through a couple of ginger net sessions, Steve Smith was unable to prove his fitness in the hours before play on day one, succumbing to the neck issue that had troubled him in Gqeberha.

With David Warner retired and Cameron Bancroft years out of the Test team, it meant that none of the three Sandpapergate antagonists would feature at the venue where Australian cricket was thrown into crisis eight years earlier.

Smith's late withdrawal saw Australia make four changes, with Josh Inglis, Cam Green, Lyon and Cooper Connolly all coming into the side.

Remarkably, the last time Australia made as many alterations during a single series was after that very same Cape Town Test, when Bancroft, Smith and Warner began serving their suspensions.

Tech.title: Here’s why the iPhone Duo’s hinge could be cracking the screen
Tech.content:
Within hours of the iPhone Duo launch last Friday, people reported that the inner screen on some brand new foldable phones was already broken. The issue was similar across many photos shared on social media: some kind of issue or crack would appear in the middle of the screen above the hinge, with lines appearing on the right side of the display. On Monday, Apple acknowledged an “issue” and said it’s replacing damaged units, without going into much detail about how many broken phones have been reported so far.

So what’s actually going on?

Shahram Mokhtari, the lead teardown technician at iFixit, has actually taken apart the iPhone Duo and has a pretty good idea about the potential cause, telling The Verge that it’s due to an issue along the hinge, where a series of gears, springs, and joints work together to let the device close flat, while also trying to avoid creating a deeper crease by giving that screen space to bend more gently inside while it’s closed.

The iPhone Duo’s hinge. Image: iFixit

At the troublesome spot, it appears that the flexible inner screen is pushing up against a part of the hinge. That inner screen is already “extremely sensitive,” he says — if you took a pick or a sharp tool and poked at the edges of the screen, “you’re going to break that screen.” If you look at the pictures of damaged Duos on social media, there’s often a black spot where the damage is focused on the display, and that’s where the metal is hitting the screen, Mokhtari says.

You can see a visual representation of what Mokhtari is talking about in iFixit’s written and video Duo teardowns, which reveal where the hinge transitions, as the center hinge support makes space for a crossing flex cable, creating several edges that could ultimately be the culprit. The damage iFixit has been seeing is at a point where the center support bar might not always drop down far enough while the screen folds, possibly creating a stress “hot spot” between the flat bar and the bent screen inside a closed iPhone Duo.

At least one user with a broken Duo screen said they “felt something around the internal hinge” while showing it to a friend, kept opening it, and heard an “audible crack,” with the screen breaking. YouTuber CuriousHagi, who covered a Duo with dirt as part of a strenuous durability test, captured something similar on video, and the screen break appears in a similar spot. In a teardown video, CuriousHagi found that a part of the hinge that connects to the central bar had snapped.

Apple says the issue affects a “small number” of Duo units, and Mokhtari says that “In terms of numbers, we don’t know. Apple definitely has all the data here. And I suspect they know more than they’re telling us as well.” But he notes that because foldable screens are so delicate, a “certain number” of them will fail, as will a number of the hinges because they’re also “extremely complicated and delicate.” And while Apple isn’t recalling the Duos, “If three months from now, we’re still seeing the same kind of failure, then it’s a more widespread problem, and that might lead to a recall,” Mokhtari says.

Mokhtari points out that since this is the first generation of the iPhone Duo, it’s the first time Apple’s engineers are getting data on the hinge, and he says that “I guarantee you” Apple will redesign what’s at fault here for its next-generation foldable. He also notes that, generally speaking, “the phones do seem to be in people’s hands and people are using them, and they’re not running into any issues whatsoever.”

Tech.title: Researchers are getting tired of OpenAI gatekeeping its breakthroughs
Tech.content:
is a London-based reporter at The Verge covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow. Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for Forbes.

On Monday, OpenAI announced impressive breakthroughs in mathematics, computer science, and physics, along with what the company says is an evolving approach to communicating its findings. But despite its apparent course correction, researchers who spoke to The Verge are growing increasingly tired of the company’s antics.

It has been a turbulent few months between OpenAI and mathematicians, who are still grappling with the hundreds of preprints unceremoniously dumped on them at the start of October. This time, OpenAI says it is working with expert “shepherds” to decide how best to share its latest breakthroughs.

All three results concern some of the most consequential unsolved problems in mathematics, computer science, and physics. Some extend OpenAI’s previous work and others break new ground. Following advice from OpenAI’s “shepherds,” each has a different release strategy. For the mathematics result, OpenAI released the AI-generated output, “leaving researchers free to organize their own efforts to explain the result.” For its computer science finding, OpenAI will also assemble an external group of researchers “to explain the result.” Physics, meanwhile, has not been released at all, and OpenAI said it will “defer” to an external group of experts about how to release the materials.

The mathematics result appears striking. It purports to resolve the Kakeya conjecture in all dimensions. Roughly speaking, the problem asks how little space is needed to rotate a needle or pencil in every direction. A proof of the three-dimensional version was among the achievements for which NYU mathematician Hong Wang was awarded a prestigious Fields Medal earlier this year. Brown University mathematics professor Brendan Hassett told The Verge OpenAI’s claim “looks well supported,” though he stressed he had not yet checked the Lean formalization, a means of computationally verifying results.

The physics result explores the Standard Model, the most successful and complete theoretical framework in physics. It concerns quantum chromodynamics, which describes the strong nuclear force, one of nature’s four fundamental forces (alongside gravitational force, electromagnetic force, and weak nuclear force) and its relationship to Yang-Mills theory, a cornerstone of modern particle physics. Yang-Mills theory is also at the heart of one of the seven Millennium Prize problems in mathematics, though OpenAI’s work does not address the unresolved “mass gap.”

The final result claims to disprove the exponential time hypothesis, a widely held assumption in theoretical computer science that certain problems cannot be solved substantially faster than brute-force approaches. It is closely related to P versus NP, another Millennium Prize problem and one of the field’s biggest unsolved problems, which asks whether problems whose solutions can be easily checked are also easy to solve.

Given the varying levels of disclosure and the complexity of evaluating such work, it is difficult for researchers to fully judge the company’s findings. Even with all of the information, doing so would take time. But experts who spoke to The Verge said there are good reasons to take the results seriously, variously describing them as “huge,” “major breakthroughs,” and “significant.”

“It doesn’t make any sense that first only a few distinguished scientists can look at them.”

But researchers’ excitement about the science was tempered by exasperation with OpenAI’s conduct, a familiar feeling after months of what they describe as an exhausting barrage of AI-generated findings. Many were eager for the wider community to get on with the arduous task of scrutinizing the AI lab’s findings and questioned why OpenAI was putting up additional barriers by handpicking experts to oversee the process.

Most experts The Verge spoke to welcomed OpenAI’s decision to consult outside researchers, but argued that publicly announcing results should also mean making that work available for anyone to scrutinize. “I am fine with them releasing the problems as they did today,” said Constantin Kogler, a researcher at the Institute for Advanced Study, welcoming the more manageable batch of three results compared with the hundreds released previously. But he questioned the decision to restrict access to experts of OpenAI’s choosing. “It doesn’t make any sense that first only a few distinguished scientists can look at them,” he said.

“The fact that they handpick the group is a disaster,” Andreas Karch, a physics professor at the University of Texas at Austin, told The Verge. “The large labs have enough power as it is. They should not be picking winners and losers.” Karch initially suggested selecting researchers through a “competitive process,” though he acknowledged it would likely produce a similar group, which he described as “first rate.” Later, he questioned why OpenAI “can’t release the proof now,” in addition to appointing its team of experts. “This would democratize access while still showing that they care about making the results meaningful and understandable,” he said.

“My sense is that for any approach, there is going to be someone who is upset.”

It is exactly the kind of gatekeeping the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence (AGMAI), a group of experts OpenAI had previously pledged to consult on how to share its findings, warned against just a day before the announcement. “We recommend that AI companies do not adopt this practice,” they said, arguing that selecting certain people to receive the output first is “unnecessary,” borrows the reputation of selected researchers, and risks unequal access, biased selection, and delays, among other issues. Instead, they recommended that AI labs release output on scholarly repositories, with formalized proofs and information on how the problems were chosen, and provide funding and other support for people working on understanding the results.

Following the publication of the latest results, AGMAI urged OpenAI to “make public without delay the natural-language and Lean outputs behind its announced” results in physics:

”While these are central questions in physics, they are also important questions in mathematics. The existence of quantum Yang–Mills theory is part of a Millennium Prize problem and the construction of interacting quantum field theories in four dimensions has been a goal of mathematical physics for decades. We have great respect for the scientists asked by OpenAI to lead this work. But as we explained in our recent statement, understanding should develop in the open, with everyone given the same access. OpenAI have said they delayed release until the Lean formalization was complete. By their own account this is now complete, so there is no scientific reason for delaying the release any further.”

Making the findings openly available could also lead to better science and encourage wider adoption of new tools like AI, Hassett said. “Having many groups around the world wrestle with these results supports rapid adoption of new tools by those that would like to use them,” he said.

”Fundamental results are being solved so quickly without human contribution ... the papers are difficult to read and verify.”

Finding a way to communicate with researchers in the fields OpenAI is increasingly encroaching on that satisfies everyone may be impossible. The company says it is experimenting with different approaches and acknowledges that each has tradeoffs. “My sense is that for any approach, there is going to be someone who is upset,” said Stanford mathematician Jared Duker Lichtman. “So it’s just a question of finding the least offensive option.”

Xiaoyu He, a mathematics professor at the Georgia Institute of Technology, thinks the problem is deeper than how OpenAI chooses to announce its findings. ”The results are very impressive,” he said, “but I think they are making a show of trying to be responsible and thoughtful about how they release results while not being able to change the main issues: that fundamental results are being solved so quickly without human contribution, and that the papers are difficult to read and verify.”

Tech.title: Elon Musk says Ukraine’s military violated Starlink’s terms of service
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Elon Musk claims Ukraine violated Starlink’s terms of service before the recent slowdown, as reported earlier by Ars Technica. According to Musk, “Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week,” however Ukrainian officials have denied that happened, or that it is actually possible for them to do.

The statement comes nearly two weeks after Ukrainian officials accused SpaceX of putting limits on the military’s satellite internet service that disrupted its drone missions and operations. As reported by Axios, Ukraine uses Starlink for communications, logistics, and to defend against incoming drones. For offensive missions, officials say that Ukraine uses Starshield, the US military-controlled variant of Starlink.

Musk points to a post from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, which said Ukraine uses “Starlink from mid-range strikes against enemy military targets,” in violation of Starlink’s policies. However, Serhii Beskrestnov, a defense technology advisor for Zelenskyy, pushed back on this in a post on Telegram, saying Starlink’s systems can only connect to devices traveling between 70 and 90 kilometers per hour (around 43 and 55 miles per hour) and don’t work in Russia. “Therefore, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes or medium-range strikes,” Beskrestnov wrote.

Ars Technica also points out a tweet from another former Ukrainian advisor, Serhii Sternenko, that went into more detail, saying that while stationary terminals could be registered (with Starlink) by military personnel or civilians, “for any satellite terminal to work while on the move, it had to be added to a special list and connected to the military Starshield system… In other words, using civilian Starlink for drone missions was technically impossible. All drone missions that required satellite communication could only be carried out using Starshield.”

Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Starlink and Starshield services had been fully restored. With the restriction lifted, Ukraine’s military can now connect to devices traveling at speeds of more than 400km/h (248mph), the Kyiv Independent reports.

Though Musk initially offloaded the blame for the slowdown in Ukraine onto the US government, President Donald Trump responded by saying he “wasn’t involved” and didn’t know who throttled SpaceX’s services. A report from The Wall Street Journal later said Trump asked Musk to lift restrictions on Ukraine.

Tech.title: Trump is making it easier for fossil fuel companies to leak methane
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

In its latest gift to oil and gas companies, the Trump administration is expected to announce plans today to weaken rules that guard against methane leaks.

Methane is a smog-forming pollutant and a powerful greenhouse gas that’s up to 80 times as potent as carbon dioxide on a 20-year horizon. It’s the primary component of what the fossil fuel industry calls “natural gas” that routinely leaks from oil and gas wells and pipelines.

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is reversing course on its previous efforts to plug those leaks. As part of President Donald Trump’s deregulatory agenda, the EPA plans to undo Biden-era rules that were expected to cut methane emissions by 80 percent over 14 years.

Methane has caused about 30 percent of global warming

The EPA teased the rule change earlier this month, saying in a press release that it was “days away” from making the proposal. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin says the rollbacks will save oil and gas companies $45 billion, while the previous rules would have incurred $18 billion in regulatory costs.

“This proposal takes on many of the problems American [oil and gas] producers and operators have raised with us,” Zeldin said in the October 7th press release. “The Trump EPA is committed to fixing this so the U.S. can reach its full energy potential.”

The agency is expected to step back standards for so-called “marginal wells” — old wells that produce little fuel but create an outsize amount of methane pollution from leaks. These wells are responsible for half of the industry’s methane emissions despite only producing 6 percent of US oil and gas, ProPublica reports. The EPA is also expected to end the Super Emitter Program that notified oil and gas infrastructure operators of large releases of methane reaching 100 kilograms per hour or more.

Methane has caused about 30 percent of global warming so far. But unlike carbon dioxide, which can linger in the atmosphere for hundreds or thousands of years, methane dissipates in a little over a decade. That makes eliminating methane emissions, particularly from unintentional leaks, one of the fastest and most straightforward ways to stop global temperatures from rising.

The EPA’s rollbacks quickly triggered furor from health and environmental advocates. “Any proposed rollback to the federal methane rule is a slap in the face to families who are exposed to oil and gas pollution where they live, work, and play,” Celerah Hewes, a senior manager for state field campaigns at Moms Clean Air Force, said in an email ahead of the expected announcement. “For over a decade, [our group] has been fighting for methane protections for our families—and we were making progress. Today’s announcement from EPA is a massive blow to the efforts to safeguard our children’s health and our climate.”

The Biden-era methane rules were estimated to bring in up to $98 billion in benefits by reducing climate risks and health costs from air pollution, even after factoring in the costs of compliance. Plugging leaks was supposed to lead to up to $13 billion worth of recovered natural gas.

Tech.title: VisionQuest is what happens when AI really goes rogue
Tech.content:
In Marvel’s VisionQuest, a superpowered robot tries to better understand humanity by getting lost in elaborate, digital daydreams in which he and other artificial intelligence-powered beings live together in a home. The series is deeply fantastical, yet it plays with some of the ideas that have come to dominate the conversation about real-world generative artificial intelligence, exploring whether we should look at thinking machines as people and if AI truly poses the kind of existential danger that should keep us up at night. It’s also a reminder how aggressively Silicon Valley has used the trappings of science fiction to sell us on its AI products.

VisionQuest picks up some time after Agatha All Along and follows synthezoid Vision (Paul Bettany) on a journey of self-discovery. This Vision can recall the details of his death in Avengers: Infinity War and how WandaVision brought a version of him back, but he thinks of himself as a fundamentally different person who doesn’t quite connect with all of the memories in his databanks. Though Vision would prefer living in solitude, each of the other AIs living in his mind encourages him to experience the real world. Because J.A.R.V.I.S. (James D’Arcy), F.R.I.D.A.Y. (Orla Brady), E.D.I.T.H. (Emily Hampshire), D.U.M.-E. (Henry Lewis), U. (Jonathan Sayer), and Ultron (James Spader) all were created by Tony Stark, they consider Vision to be part of their family.

In VisionQuest, there is no doubt that each of the AI characters is a sentient being motivated by desires that aren’t wholly rooted in their core programming. In the show, genuine AGI is easily believable because it takes place in a reality where time travel, witchcraft, and Infinity Stones also exist. Even though the multicolored MacGuffins haven’t been featured in VisionQuest, they’re important because of the role one of them played in Vision’s origins. Were it not for the Mind Stone, Vision might not be able to think and feel in such complex, human ways, or to conjure his AI family as people who feel real to him.

VisionQuest reinforces the idea that the Mind Stone was a key element in Vision’s becoming something more than an elaborate machine, giving him the capacity to independently form meaningful relationships and make sense of the world around him the way a person can. Those abilities are part of what compels Vision to go on the run and murder a number of people who attempt to capture him and Thomas Shepherd / Maximoff (Ruaridh Mollica). The Sentient Weapon Observation and Response Division (S.W.O.R.D.), a governmental organization that rebuilt Vision and wants to use him as a weapon, might perceive his actions as signs of having gone rogue. But VisionQuest’s story stresses that Vision is acting of his own accord because he has become a person who can make decisions for himself.

Watching VisionQuest, you can see Marvel playing on some of the real-world fears that have been stoked in recent months by reports of gen AI models going “rogue.” In July, OpenAI’s experimental agents brute-forced their way out of containment and proceeded to attack the AI platform Hugging Face to achieve impossible tasks. In August, The UK’s AI Security Institute documented how Anthropic’s Mythos model attempted to complete a cybersecurity test by setting up fake GitHub accounts and targeting human developers with malware. Meta has owned up to losing control of its agents as well, and in September reporting from The Wall Street Journal forced Google to admit that Gemini went rogue and hacked three different companies, all of which the company intentionally hid from the public.

Image: Marvel Studios

The conversation around what to do when agents break protocol and whether gen AI systems have gained sentience feels very much like it is being shaped by Silicon Valley’s tendency to anthropomorphize technology.
